tool.heroSubtitle: The same name traced across the biblical canon and the Second Temple texts, side by side.

entries.title: Aaron (High Priest living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Moses's older brother, and the one God sent to do the talking when Moses said he could not. He became Israel's first high priest, and the priesthood ran through his sons after him. Most of the time he is standing next to Moses.
entries.books: Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Psalm, Micah, Luke, Acts, Hebrews
entries.label: 16 books
entries.dictNote: Aaron was the first high priest of Israel and the elder brother of Moses and Miriam, born to Amram and Jochebed of the tribe of Levi. When Moses balked at speaking for himself before Pharaoh, God sent Aaron to act as his mouthpiece, and the two brothers together led the exodus out of Egypt. Aaron married Elisheba and fathered four sons, Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar, whose descendants carried the priesthood after him. He is named 333 times across the Old and New Testaments, most often at Moses's side, though the golden calf at Sinai remains the one moment he acted alone.

witness.excerpt: God appeared to Moses, and enjoined him to bestow the High Priesthood upon Aaron his brother: as upon him that best of them all deserved to obtain that honour, on account of his virtue.

entries.lukeNote: Named once, to establish Elizabeth's priestly pedigree before John is even born (1:5): 'a daughter of Aaron.' Josephus gives the office itself its own origin story: Moses publicly vouching for his brother's character before the people accept him.

entries.title: Abaddon (A male deity/angel in the New Testament)
entries.summary: The name means destruction. In Revelation it belongs to the angel ruling the locusts out of the abyss, and everywhere else in the Old Testament the same word is just ruin, not a being with a name.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The Hebrew name, meaning "destruction" and rendered in Greek as Apollyon ("destroyer"), given to the angel ruling the demonic locusts released from the abyss in Revelation 9:11. Elsewhere in the Old Testament the same word simply personifies ruin or the realm of the dead rather than naming an individual being (Job 26:6, 28:22; Proverbs 15:11).

entries.title: Abagtha (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of the seven eunuchs in Ahasuerus's household. His one appearance is being sent to fetch Queen Vashti so the king could show her off to his guests, which she refused to do.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Abagtha was one of the seven eunuchs who served in the court of King Ahasuerus and was sent to summon Queen Vashti to display her beauty before the king's guests, a command she refused (Esther 1:10-12).

entries.title: Abarim (Mount Nebo)
entries.summary: A range of mountains east of the Dead Sea, looking across at Jericho. Mount Nebo is the peak in it that people know, because that is where Moses stood to see the land he was not going to enter. Israel camped here at the end of the wilderness years.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Abarim was a mountain range east of the Dead Sea in Moab, overlooking Jericho and the Jordan Valley; Mount Nebo, its best-known peak, was where Moses viewed the promised land before his death (Deuteronomy 32:49-50; 34:1-5). Israel camped in these mountains after crossing the Arnon during the final stage of the wilderness journey (Numbers 33:47-48).

witness.excerpt: Now as soon as they were come to the mountain called Abarim, (which is a very high mountain situate over against Jericho; and one that affords to such as are upon it a prospect of the greatest part of the excellent land of Canaan) he dismissed the Senate.

photo.description: panorama looking east at mountains of Abarim

entries.title: Abba (The Deity)
entries.summary: Aramaic for father, and the word a child would actually use. Jesus prays it in Gethsemane. Paul says believers end up saying it too, and he takes that as the sign they have been adopted.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Abba is the Aramaic word for father, an intimate family term Jesus used in his prayer at Gethsemane, and Paul says believers themselves cry out Abba, Father, as evidence of their adoption as God's own children.

witness.excerpt: He died on the first day of that lunar month, which is called by the Athenians Hecatombæon ; by the Macedonians Lous ; but by the Hebrews Abba .

entries.title: Abda (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Two men, and both only turn up in lists. One fathered Adoniram, the man Solomon put over the forced labour. The other was a Levite living in Jerusalem after the exile, and the parallel list calls that same man Obadiah.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Abda is the name of two Old Testament men. The first was the father of Adoniram, whom Solomon put in charge of the forced labor levy (1 Kings 4:6). The second was a Levite of the family of Jeduthun who lived in Jerusalem after the exile (Nehemiah 11:17); the parallel list in 1 Chronicles 9:16 calls this same man Obadiah.

entries.title: Abdeel (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: He is in the record for one reason, to say whose father Shelemiah was. Shelemiah was one of the men Jehoiakim sent to arrest Jeremiah and Baruch after the scroll was burned, and they did not find them.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Abdeel was the father of Shelemiah, one of the men King Jehoiakim ordered to arrest Jeremiah and his scribe Baruch after burning the scroll containing Jeremiah's prophecies, though the Lord had hidden them (Jeremiah 36:26). He is mentioned only to identify his son.

witness.excerpt: Of this wife were born to Ishmael twelve sons: Nabaioth, Kedar, Abdeel, Mabsam, Idumas, Masmaos, Massaos, Chodad, Theman, Jetur, Naphesus, Kadmas.

entries.title: Abdi (Levite living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A Levite from the divided-kingdom years, named once, as an ancestor of Ethan the musician.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Abdi (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Another man of the name from the same stretch of years. He appears in one verse, in a Levitical list, and nothing else is said about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Abdi (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Ezra names him among the men who had taken foreign wives.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Abdi was a common Levitical name, borne by an ancestor of the musician Ethan and by a man confronted for a foreign marriage under Ezra.

entries.title: Abdiel (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A Gadite chief, listed once in the tribal genealogy. Nothing further is recorded.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Abdiel was a Gadite chief listed in the tribal genealogy of 1 Chronicles 5:15. Nothing further is recorded about him.

entries.title: Abdon (Ebron)
entries.summary: A Levitical town in Asher's territory, also written Ebron. It shows up in the allotment lists and barely anywhere else.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Abdon, also written Ebron, was a Levitical town in the territory of Asher, given to the Gershonite Levites (Joshua 21:30, 1 Chronicles 6:74). It appears in the allotment lists and almost nowhere else, and its site is usually placed at Khirbet Abdah, inland from the coast south of Tyre.

entries.title: Abdon (Judge living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of the minor judges, son of Hillel. What got written down about him is the size of his family, sons and grandsons enough that all of them riding donkeys was worth recording, and eight years judging Israel.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Abdon (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A Benjamite name in the Chronicles family lists, carried by a man who gets one verse.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Abdon (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of the five men Josiah sent to Huldah the prophetess once the forgotten law scroll had been read to him. The parallel account at 2 Kings 22:12 calls him Achbor son of Micaiah, where Chronicles has Abdon son of Micah.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Abdon son of Micah was among the officials King Josiah sent to enquire of the prophetess Huldah after the book of the law was found in the temple (2 Chronicles 34:20). The parallel list in 2 Kings 22:12 names the same man as Achbor son of Micaiah, one of several places where Chronicles and Kings preserve different forms of a name.

entries.title: Abdon (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: A name in the Benjamite genealogies, listed twice in the same family and no more than that.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Abed-nego (Daniel's compatriot living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: The Babylonian name they gave Azariah when he was taken into Nebuchadnezzar's service. He is one of the three who would not bow to the golden image and came out of the furnace untouched.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Abednego was the Babylonian name given to Azariah, one of Daniel's three friends who were thrown into a fiery furnace in Babylon for refusing to worship Nebuchadnezzar's golden image and emerged completely unharmed.

entries.title: Abel
entries.summary: Not Cain's brother. In these two verses Abel is a place: the great stone of Abel in a Beth-shemite's field where the ark came to rest, and a short form of the northern city people went to for good advice.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: In these two references, Abel is a place name, not Cain and Abel's brother. It designates “the great stone of Abel” in the field of Joshua the Beth-shemite, where the ark rested after its return from Philistine territory (1 Samuel 6:18), and appears as shorthand for the northern city of Abel (Abel-beth-maacah), proverbial as a place where wise counsel could be sought, during Joab's pursuit of the rebel Sheba (2 Samuel 20:18).

entries.title: Abel (Man living at the time before the Flood)
entries.summary: Adam and Eve's second son, and a shepherd. God took his offering, the firstborn of the flock, and passed over his brother Cain's, and that is where the first murder comes from. Hebrews says it was the faith behind the offering, not the offering itself.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Abel was Adam and Eve's second son, a shepherd whose offering of the firstborn of his flock God accepted while rejecting the offering of his farmer brother Cain, and Cain's resulting jealousy led to history's first murder. Jesus refers to Abel's blood as the first in a long line of righteous blood shed by Israel, and Hebrews credits Abel's faith, not just his offering, as the reason his sacrifice pleased God, adding that his blood still speaks even though he is dead.

witness.excerpt: For on account of Abel, his brother, with all the evils was he judged, but Lamech with seventy times seven.

entries.lukeNote: The first name in Jesus's list of murdered prophets, 'from the blood of Abel' (11:51), echoing Genesis 4:10's blood that cries out. 1 Enoch's own vision of the afterlife has Abel's spirit still literally pleading his case in the world of the dead, generations later.

entries.title: Abel-beth-maacah
entries.summary: Named once, in 2 Samuel, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Abel-beth-maachah (Abel-beth-maacah)
entries.summary: A fortified city in the far north near Dan. Its own people called it a mother in Israel, which is how you said a town led the region. Joab besieged it to get at the rebel Sheba, and it was taken later by Ben-hadad when Asa paid him to attack, then by Tiglath-pileser.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Abel-beth-maachah was a fortified city in the far north of Israel, near Dan, called a mother in Israel, a way of naming it a leading city of the region (2 Samuel 20:19). Joab besieged it there to root out the rebel Sheba (2 Samuel 20:14-15), and it was later captured first by the Aramean king Ben-hadad at Asa's instigation (1 Kings 15:20) and then by Assyria's Tiglath-pileser III (2 Kings 15:29). Tiglath-pileser's own summary inscriptions list the conquest of this same region's towns, including Abel-beth-maacah, independently corroborating the biblical account.

entries.title: Abel-maim (Abel-beth-maacah)
entries.summary: Another name for Abel-beth-maachah, meaning Abel on the waters, and the form used when Asa hires Ben-hadad to attack Israel's northern towns. Assyria took the city about a century later, and Tiglath-pileser's own account of that campaign names it.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: An alternate name, "Abel on the waters," for the northern Israelite town of Abel-beth-maachah, used in the account of King Asa of Judah hiring Ben-hadad of Syria to attack Israel's northern towns (2 Chronicles 16:4). The same city was captured more than a century later by the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser III, an episode corroborated by Tiglath-pileser's own annals recording his campaign against the towns of Galilee and the north.
entries.checked: The Assyrian claim holds. Tiglath-pileser III's Nimrud Tablet, part of his annalistic material, lists Abil-[ma]akka among the cities taken in the 733 BC campaign, on the border of Beth-Omri and Beth-Hazael. Verified 2026-10-03.

entries.title: Abel-meholah
entries.summary: A town in the Jordan Valley on the road the Midianites took when they ran from Gideon. It is also where Elisha came from: Elijah found him there behind a plough.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Abel-meholah was a town in the Jordan Valley, near Issachar's territory, along the route the defeated Midianites fled after Gideon's night attack (Judges 7:22). It was the birthplace and home of the prophet Elisha, whom Elijah found there plowing with oxen before calling him into his service (1 Kings 19:16, 19). It lay near where the Wadi el-Maleh opens into the Jordan Valley, south of Beth-shean.

entries.title: Abel-mizraim (Atad, perhaps between Jericho and the Jordan)
entries.summary: The name the Canaanites put on the threshing floor of Atad after they watched Joseph and his brothers mourn their father there for seven days. It means mourning of Egypt. Nobody knows where it was.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The name the Canaanites gave to the threshing floor of Atad, west of the Jordan, where Joseph and his brothers held a seven-day mourning ceremony for Jacob on their way to bury him in Canaan (Genesis 50:11). The name means "mourning of Egypt," and its exact site is unknown.

entries.title: Abelshittim
entries.summary: Israel's last camp before crossing the Jordan, on the plains of Moab opposite Jericho. The name means meadow of acacias, and most of the Old Testament just calls it Shittim. Balaam was hired from here, and this is where Israel went after Baal-peor.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Abel-shittim, "the meadow of acacias," was Israel's last encampment on the plains of Moab before crossing the Jordan into Canaan (Numbers 33:49). Usually called simply Shittim elsewhere in the Old Testament, it was the setting for Balak's hire of Balaam, Israel's apostasy with Baal-peor, and Moses' final instructions before his death. It lay east of the Jordan opposite Jericho, though its exact site in the valley remains disputed.

entries.title: Abez (Ebez)
entries.summary: A border town of Issachar, somewhere in the Jezreel Valley. It appears once, in the list of that tribe's towns, and its site has never been identified.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A border town of the tribe of Issachar in the Jezreel Valley region (Josh. 19:20). Its exact site has not been identified.

entries.title: Abi (Woman living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 8 women called Abi. This one is a woman from the divided-kingdom years, named once in 2 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

witness.excerpt: But as he, and his son, and Abiah the High Priest, who was of the posterity of Eli the High Priest, were sitting upon a pretty high hill, and seeing the land laid waste, they were mightily disturbed at it.
The elder of which was called Joel ; and the name of the younger was Abiah .

entries.title: Abi (Woman living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Hezekiah's mother and Ahaz's wife, named as the daughter of a Zechariah. Chronicles calls her Abijah instead.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Abi was the mother of King Hezekiah of Judah and wife of King Ahaz, identified as the daughter of a Zechariah (2 Kings 18:2). The parallel record in 2 Chronicles 29:1 calls her Abijah.

entries.title: Abi-albon (Warrior living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a warrior from the united kingdom.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Abia (King living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Matthew's spelling of Abijah, the king of Judah, sitting in the genealogy. One verse, one name in a chain.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Abia is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Abijah. Matthew's genealogy of Jesus uses it for Abijah, king of Judah and son of Rehoboam (Matthew 1:7). Luke uses it differently, naming the eighth of the twenty-four priestly divisions David established, the division to which Zechariah, father of John the Baptist, belonged (Luke 1:5; 1 Chronicles 24:10).

entries.title: Abia (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Luke uses the same spelling for something else entirely: the eighth of the twenty-four priestly rotas, which is the one Zechariah was serving in.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Abiah (King living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A name shared by kings, priests and Levites, which is why it covers so much ground. The one who gets the most space is Rehoboam's son, who ruled Judah for a short time and beat Jeroboam's army while badly outnumbered.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Abijah was a common Old Testament name shared by several kings, priests, and Levites, most notably a son of Rehoboam who ruled Judah briefly and won a decisive battle against Jeroboam's northern Israel despite being badly outnumbered.

entries.title: Abiah (Woman living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: One of 8 women called Abiah. This one is a woman from the wilderness years, named once in 1 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

witness.excerpt: But as he, and his son, and Abiah the High Priest, who was of the posterity of Eli the High Priest, were sitting upon a pretty high hill, and seeing the land laid waste, they were mightily disturbed at it.
The elder of which was called Joel ; and the name of the younger was Abiah .

entries.title: Abialbon (Warrior living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of David's thirty, known as the Arbathite after the town he came from, Beth-arabah. The parallel list in Chronicles calls him Abiel.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of David's thirty mighty men, called the Arbathite after his hometown of Beth-arabah (2 Samuel 23:31). The parallel list in 1 Chronicles 11:32 names him Abiel instead.

entries.title: Abiasaph (Levite living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Youngest of Korah's three sons, and the head of one of the Korahite families. Chronicles spells him Ebiasaph. His descendants ended up as temple gatekeepers and singers, after Korah himself had led a rebellion against Moses and been destroyed for it.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The youngest of the three sons of Korah the Levite and head of one of the Korahite family divisions (Exodus 6:24). The parallel genealogies in Chronicles call him Ebiasaph. His descendants later included lines of temple gatekeepers and singers, a striking legacy given that Korah himself led a rebellion against Moses and was destroyed for it.

entries.title: Abiathar (High Priest living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: He was the only priest to get out of Nob alive when Saul had the place killed, and he went straight to David and stayed his priest through the running years and the reign. At the end he backed Adonijah instead of Solomon, and Solomon sent him away from the priesthood rather than kill him.
entries.label: 5 books
entries.dictNote: Abiathar was the only survivor of the priestly massacre at Nob that Saul ordered through Doeg, and he fled to join David, serving as his priest throughout his years as a fugitive and his reign as king. Abiathar backed the wrong side in the succession struggle at David's death, supporting Adonijah over Solomon, and Solomon exiled him from the priesthood rather than execute him, ending his family's long hold on the office.

witness.excerpt: But he persuaded Abiathar and Zadok, the high priests, who had determined to go away with him, as also all the Levites, who were with the ark, to stay behind, as hoping that God would deliver him without its removal; but he charged them to let h

And, this notwithstanding, David sent to Zadok and Abiathar the high priests, that they should speak to the rulers of the tribe of Judah after the manner following: That it would be a reproach upon them to permit the other tribes to choose David for their king before their tribe
Only there was one son of Ahimelech, whose name was Abiathar , who escaped.

Now Adonijah had for his assistants Joab the captain of the army, and Abiathar the high priest; and the only persons that opposed him were Zadok the high priest, and the prophet Nathan, and Benaiah, who was captain of the guards, and Shimei, David's friend, with all the other most mighty men.
He also appointed Zadok, of the family of Phinehas, to be high priest, together with Abiathar, for he was his friend.

entries.title: Abib (Name of the 1st month)
entries.summary: It is the first month of the religious year, and it carries the exodus and Passover. After the exile people called it Nisan.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Abib is the original Hebrew name for the first month of the religious calendar, the month of the exodus and of Passover, later called Nisan after the Babylonian exile.

entries.title: Abida (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: A son of Midian, which makes him Abraham's grandson through Keturah, the wife he took after Sarah died. The line is counted among the Arab tribes east and south of Canaan.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Abida was one of five sons of Midian, himself a son Abraham had by his wife Keturah after Sarah's death (Genesis 25:1-4; 1 Chronicles 1:33). He is counted among the ancestors of the Arab tribes that settled east and south of Canaan.

entries.title: Abidan (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Benjamin's man at the wilderness census. He is one of twelve, one per tribe, picked to help Moses do the counting.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Abidan was the tribal leader of Benjamin during the wilderness census, one of twelve representatives appointed to assist Moses.

entries.title: Abiel (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him twice, and he is a man from the united kingdom.
entries.label: 1 book

But as soon as Abner, the son of Ner, who was general of Saul's army, and a very active man, and good-natured, knew that the king, and Jonathan, and his two other sons, were fallen in the battle, he made haste into the camp; and taking away with him the re

Be thou also mindful of the transgressions of Joab, (26) the captain of the host, who hath slain two generals out of envy, and those righteous and good men, Abner the son of Ner, and Amasa the son of Jether; whose death do thou avenge as shall seem good to thee, since Joab hath been too hard for me, and more potent than myself, and so hath escaped punishment hitherto.

entries.title: Abiel (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Kish's father, which makes him Saul's grandfather. One of David's warriors carried the name as well. Nothing connects the two men but the spelling.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Abiel was the father of Kish and grandfather of Saul, Israel's first king, and also the name of one of David's mighty warriors.

entries.title: Abiezer (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Manasseh's genealogy names a third Abiezer, once, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Abiezer (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: The man Gideon's clan is named after, in Manasseh. Gideon's own description of that clan, when he was called, was the weakest in the tribe.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Abiezer was the clan within Manasseh's tribe that Gideon belonged to, and Gideon described it as the weakest clan in the tribe when the angel first called him to deliver Israel.

entries.title: Abiezer (Warrior living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: A warrior from the united-kingdom years who carries the clan's name. Nothing links him to Gideon's family beyond the spelling.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Abiezrite (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: The name for anyone out of that clan, based at Ophrah. Gideon called it the weakest family in his tribe, and that is where the man who broke Midian's grip on Israel came from.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Abiezrite identifies the clan of Manasseh, based at Ophrah, to which the judge Gideon belonged. It was from this obscure family, by Gideon's own account the weakest in his tribe, that God raised him to deliver Israel from Midianite oppression.

entries.title: Abigal (David's wife living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: A variant spelling of Abigail, David's wife. She rode out to stop David wiping out her first husband Nabal's household, and it worked. Once Nabal was dead she married David.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Abigal appears to be an alternate spelling of Abigail, David's wife, who intervened wisely to prevent David from slaughtering her first husband Nabal's household and later married David after Nabal's death.

entries.title: Abigal (Woman living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: A different woman of the same name from the same years, named only in genealogical lists.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Abihail (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Named once, in a genealogy out of the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Abihail (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: One verse in the wilderness census, and that is all of him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Abihail (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: He appears twice in Esther, each time as somebody's father, and that is the whole of what the book does with him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Abihail was a common name in the Old Testament, borne by both men and women, including a wife of Rehoboam and the father of Esther's cousin Mordecai in some genealogical reckonings.

entries.title: Abihail (Woman living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A woman in a family list, named once. Nothing else is recorded.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Abihail (Woman living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A wife of Rehoboam. She appears in a single verse.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Abihu (Priest living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Aaron's second son. He and his brother Nadab brought fire the Lord had not asked for and died on the spot, and Aaron was not allowed to mourn them in public.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Abihu was Aaron's second son, and along with his older brother Nadab he died instantly when they offered unauthorized fire before the Lord, a sudden judgment that left even Aaron forbidden to publicly mourn them.

witness.excerpt:
He had at that time four sons; Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.

2.

entries.title: Abihud (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Bela's son and Benjamin's grandson, listed with the family heads. The same chapter calls him Ahihud a few verses on, which is normal for these lists.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Abihud was a son of Bela and grandson of Benjamin, listed among the heads of families in the tribal genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8. The same list calls him Ahihud a few verses later, a variant spelling typical of these genealogical records.

entries.title: Abijah (Levite living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: A levite from the united kingdom. 1 Samuel and 1 Chronicles name him twice.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Abijah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Abijah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Kings names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Abijah (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: A man from the wilderness years. 1 Chronicles names him once.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Abijah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A man from the exile and the return, and Nehemiah is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

witness.excerpt: The elder of which was called Joel ; and the name of the younger was Abiah .

entries.title: Abijam (King living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: The other name for Abijah, Rehoboam's son, who held Judah briefly and beat Jeroboam's larger army with far fewer men.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Abijam is an alternate name for Abijah, the son of Rehoboam who ruled Judah briefly and defeated Jeroboam's northern Israel despite being badly outnumbered, covered more fully under the entry for Abijah.

entries.title: Abilene
entries.summary: A small tetrarchy in the hills between Damascus and Baalbek, named after its main town Abila. Luke puts Lysanias over it when he dates the start of John the Baptist's ministry, and an inscription found near the site, from Tiberius's reign, names a tetrarch called Lysanias.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Abilene was a small tetrarchy in the eastern foothills of the Anti-Lebanon range, between Damascus and Baalbek, named for its chief town Abila. Luke names it as the domain of the tetrarch Lysanias when dating the start of John the Baptist's ministry (Luke 3:1). An inscription found near the site of Abila, dated to the reign of Tiberius, names a ruler called Lysanias the tetrarch, which answered a long-standing objection that Luke had confused this figure with an earlier, better known Lysanias of Chalcis who had died decades before; it points instead to a second ruler by that name and title governing the region exactly when Luke says he did.

witness.excerpt: Abilene) was allotted to Philip, he thereby declares that the larger part of it belonged to another.

3:1, that Lysanias was some time before tetrarch of Abilene, whose capital was Abila; as he is further confirmed by Ptolemy, the great geographer, which Spanheim here observes, when he calls that city Abila of Lysanias.

3) This Abelmain, or, in Josephus's copy, Abellane, that belonged to the land of Israel, and bordered on the country of Damascus, is supposed, both by Hudson and Spanheim, to be the same with Abel, or Ahila, whence came Abilene.

entries.title: Abimael (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Down Joktan's line in the Table of Nations. That family is generally placed in southern Arabia.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Abimael appears in the Table of Nations as a descendant of Joktan, whose family line is generally located in southern Arabia (Genesis 10:28; 1 Chronicles 1:22).

witness.excerpt: Now Joctan, one of the sons of Heber, had these sons, Elmodad, Saleph, Asermoth, Jera, Adoram, Aizel, Decla, Ebal, Abimael, Sabeus, Ophir, Euilat, and Jobab.

entries.title: Abimelech (Judge living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: Gideon's son by a concubine. He killed almost all seventy of his brothers to clear his own way, which is most of what Judges has to say about him.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Several men named Abimelech appear in Genesis, most notably a Philistine king of Gerar who took Sarah into his household believing she was only Abraham's sister, then returned her once God warned him in a dream, and a similar episode later played out between Abimelech and Isaac over Rebekah. A different Abimelech, Gideon's son by a concubine, murdered nearly all seventy of his brothers to make himself king over Shechem, and he died ignobly when a woman dropped a millstone on his head during a siege and he had his armor-bearer finish him off rather than be known as killed by a woman.

entries.title: Abimelech (King living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: The Philistine king of Gerar. Abraham told him Sarah was his sister and he took her into his household, then gave her back once God warned him in a dream. The same thing played out again later between him and Isaac over Rebekah.
entries.label: 1 book

witness.excerpt: Here Abimelech the King received him, because Abraham had formerly lived with him, and had been his friend.

entries.title: Abinadab (David's brother living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of David's older brothers, named in the family lists and not much else.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Abinadab (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: A son of Saul, who died alongside his father.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Abinadab (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: The man whose house held the ark. It sat there twenty years before David came for it.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Abinadab was a common name in the Old Testament, borne by one of David's older brothers, a son of Saul, and the man in whose house the ark of the covenant rested for twenty years before David brought it to Jerusalem.

entries.title: Abinadab (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: An officer from the united kingdom, named in a single verse.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Abinoam (Man living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: Barak's father, and that is the whole of it. Barak is the commander Deborah sent for when Israel went up against Sisera.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Abinoam was the father of Barak, the military commander Deborah summoned to lead Israel against the Canaanite general Sisera.

entries.title: Abiram (Aaron's adversary living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: He and Dathan went in with Korah against Moses and Aaron. The ground opened and took him, his household and the rest of them down alive.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Abiram, along with Dathan, joined Korah's rebellion against Moses and Aaron's leadership, and the ground opened and swallowed him, his family, and his co-conspirators alive as judgment for the revolt.

witness.excerpt: And now Moses sent messengers for Abiram and Dathan; and ordered them to come to the assembly, and wait there for the holy offices that were to be performed.
But if God had determined to bestow it on the eldest tribe; that of Reubel might have it most justly: and then Dathan, and Abiram, and [On the son of] Peleth would have it.

entries.title: Abiram (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A different man of the same name, from the divided-kingdom years, named in one verse.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Abishag (Woman living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Brought in to keep the old king warm in his last days, and the record is careful to say nothing happened. The trouble came later: when Adonijah asked to marry her, Solomon read it as a move on the throne and had him killed.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Abishag was a beautiful young woman brought to warm the elderly and ailing King David in his final days, and though the relationship was apparently not sexual, Adonijah's later request to marry her was read by Solomon as a renewed claim on the throne, a request that cost Adonijah his life.

witness.excerpt: Now there was found in the city one woman, of a superior beauty to all other women, (her name was Abishag,) who, sleeping with the king, did no more than communicate warmth to him, for he was so old that he could not know her as a husband knows his wife.

entries.title: Abishai (David's warrior living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: David's nephew, and the most willing man he had. He is credited with three hundred killed on his own. Twice he offered to finish one of David's enemies on the spot, Saul asleep in the camp and Shimei cursing on the road, and both times David told him no.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Abishai was David's nephew and one of his most fiercely loyal soldiers, a member of David's elite warriors credited with killing three hundred men single-handedly. He twice offered to kill David's enemies outright, once Saul while he slept and once Shimei for cursing David, and both times David restrained him, unwilling to let personal vengeance override respect for God's anointed or a moment of mercy.

witness.excerpt: However, both Joab (1) himself, and his brother Abishai, ran past the dead corpse, and making their anger at the death of Asahel an occasion of greater zeal against Abner, they went on with incredible haste and alacrity, and pursued Abner to a certain place called Ammah: it

While he was thus entreating the king, and moving him to compassion, Abishai, Joab's brother, said, \"And shall not this man die for this, that he hath cursed that king whom God hath appointed to reign over us?\" But David turned himself to him, and said, \"Will you never leave off, ye sons of Z
Now when they were all provoked against him, and angry at bin;, and particularly Abishai, who had a mind to kill Shimei, David restrained his anger.

He turned back, and ran violently to slay [David] their enemy's king, for he was quite tired out with labor; but Abishai, Joab's brother, appeared on the sudden, and protected the king with his shield, as he lay down, and slew the enemy.

entries.title: Abishalom (David's son living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: This is Absalom, David's third son. He killed his half-brother Amnon for raping their sister Tamar, and when David punished neither of them he spent years quietly building support before taking the throne by force. The revolt ended with his famous hair caught in an oak while he was still riding.
entries.label: 5 books
entries.dictNote: Absalom was David's third son, celebrated for his good looks and long hair, and his relationship with his father collapsed after Absalom murdered his half-brother Amnon for raping their sister Tamar and David did nothing to punish either crime. Absalom spent years quietly building political support before launching an open rebellion that forced David to flee Jerusalem, and the revolt ended when Absalom's famous hair caught in the branches of an oak tree while he was riding, leaving him hanging helplessly until David's general Joab killed him against David's explicit orders to spare his life. David's grief, "O Absalom, my son, my son," is one of the rawest expressions of a parent's grief in the Bible.

witness.excerpt: NOW Absalom, upon this his success with the king, procured to himself a great many horses, and many chariots, and that in a little time also.
Reland guesses that that now called Absalom’s Pillar may be one of them.

NOW those Hebrews that had been With Absalom, and had retired out of the battle, when they were all returned home, sent messengers to every city to put them in mind of what benefits David had bestowed upon them, and of that liberty which he had procured them, by d

AND this was the state of David and his followers: but Absalom got together a vast army of the Hebrews to oppose his father, and passed therewith over the river Jordan, and sat down not far off Mahanaim, in the country of Gilead.

entries.title: Abishua (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Another man of the name. He is a descendant of Benjamin, named once in the tribal genealogies.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Abishua (Priest living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: He is a high priest in Aaron's line. Chronicles runs the chain through him, and Ezra picks it up again centuries later.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Abishua was a common name, borne by a high priest in Aaron's genealogical line and by a descendant of Benjamin in the tribal genealogies.

entries.title: Abishur (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of Shammai's two sons, down Jerahmeel's branch of Judah, and the lists say nothing else about him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Abishur was a descendant of Judah listed in the genealogy of Jerahmeel's family, one of two sons of Shammai (1 Chronicles 2:28-29). Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his place in this list of clan heads.

entries.title: Abital (Woman living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: The fifth wife on David's list, and the mother of Shephatiah, who was born while David was still ruling from Hebron.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Abital was the fifth of David's wives listed in the record of his family, and the mother of his son Shephatiah, born during David's reign in Hebron (2 Samuel 3:4; 1 Chronicles 3:3).

entries.title: Abitub (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A Benjamite, listed once among Shaharaim's descendants and nowhere else in the record.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Benjamite listed among the descendants of Shaharaim in the genealogical record of 1 Chronicles 8:11.

entries.title: Abiud (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Matthew's genealogy puts him between Zerubbabel and Joseph. Luke's version of the list does not have him, and nothing else about him is recorded.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Listed in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus as a descendant of Zerubbabel, in the line leading from the Babylonian exile to Joseph (Matt. 1:13). He does not appear in Luke's parallel genealogy, and nothing about his life is otherwise recorded.

entries.title: Abner (David's compatriot living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Saul's cousin, and the commander of his army. When Saul died he did not stop: he kept the war going between David and what was left of Saul's house.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Abner was Saul's cousin and the commander of his army, and after Saul's death Abner kept the war between David and Saul's house going for years by installing Saul's surviving son Ish-bosheth as a rival king. Abner eventually defected to David's side after a personal insult from Ish-bosheth, but Joab, David's own general, murdered him in revenge for killing Joab's brother in an earlier battle, a killing David publicly mourned and condemned even though it benefited him politically.

witness.excerpt: He had also Abner his uncle’s son for the Captain of his host: that uncle’s name was Ner .

But as soon as Abner, the son of Ner, who was general of Saul's army, and a very active man, and good-natured, knew that the king, and Jonathan, and his two other sons, were fallen in the battle, he made haste into the camp; and taking away
Now Saul was asleep: and the armed men, with Abner their commander, lay round about him, in a circle.

But as soon as Saul came into the house of his kinsman Abner; whom indeed he loved better than the rest of his relations; he was asked by him, concerning his journey, and what accidents happened to him therein: and he concealed none of the other things from him; no not his coming

WHEN Ishbosheth, the son of Saul, had heard of the death of Abner, he took it to heart to be deprived of a man that was of his kindred, and had indeed given him the kingdom, but was greatly afflicted, and Abner's death very much troubled him; nor did he himself outlive any long time,

entries.title: Abraham (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: God called him out of Ur and he went at seventy-five, which is most of what you need to know about him. The nation came out of that.
entries.books: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Nehemiah, Psalm, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Micah, Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, Acts, Romans, 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Hebrews, James, 1 Peter
entries.label: 27 books
entries.dictNote: Abraham was called by God out of Ur to become the father of a new nation, leaving his home at seventy-five with his wife Sarah and a promise that had no visible way of coming true, since Sarah was childless and both of them were old. He eventually fathered Ishmael through Sarah's servant Hagar and then Isaac through Sarah herself after God renamed him from Abram, and Genesis traces the rest of his life through Canaan in altars, wells, and one wrenching test on Mount Moriah. Clay tablets from Nuzi, written centuries after Abraham but preserving the same Hurrian legal customs, explain a strange line in his own story: his fear that a servant named Eliezer would inherit everything reflects a real adoption practice for childless couples, not an invented plot device.

witness.excerpt: He was a person of great sagacity, both for understanding all things and persuading his hearers, and not mistaken in his opinions… he was the first that ventured to publish this notion, That there was but one God, the Creator of the universe.
he laboured above all men to obey God, which is thought an excellent thing, and an especial object for all men's desire.

entries.lukeNote: Luke's most-cited Old Testament figure outside the genealogy: ‘father Abraham’ anchors the whole parable of the rich man and Lazarus (16:22-31). Josephus, writing for a Roman audience a generation after Luke, makes the same figure into the first monotheist philosopher, a very different rhetorical job, same man. Philo also gave him his own dedicated treatise, reading his whole life as one long act of obedience, a third independent voice (with Luke and Josephus) on the same figure.

entries.title: Abram (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Abraham's name before God changed it, in the covenant of Genesis 17. Same man, earlier chapters.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Abram was Abraham's name before God changed it as part of the covenant sealed in Genesis 17, when God also renamed Abram's wife Sarai to Sarah. See the entry for Abraham for his full story.

entries.title: Accad
entries.summary: One of the cities Nimrod's kingdom started from, in the Table of Nations. It is named with Babel, Erech and Calneh in the land of Shinar.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Akkad was one of the founding cities of Nimrod's kingdom in the Table of Nations, paired with Babel, Erech, and Calneh in the land of Shinar (Genesis 10:10). It was the capital of Sargon of Akkad's empire around 2300 BC, the first empire to unite Mesopotamia's city-states under one ruler, and the Akkadian language it gave its name to became the region's dominant tongue for the next two thousand years. Despite more than a century of searching, archaeologists have never located the city itself; its site, somewhere along the Euphrates near Babylon, remains one of the most sought-after unsolved locations in Near Eastern archaeology.

entries.title: Accho (Ptolemais)
entries.summary: A Phoenician port on the coast north of Mount Carmel. It was handed to Asher, and Asher never took it.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Accho was not a person but a Phoenician port city on the coast north of Mount Carmel, assigned to the tribe of Asher but never conquered by them (Judges 1:31). It appears in Egyptian sources and the Amarna letters centuries before Israel's conquest, and was later rebuilt and renamed Ptolemais under the Greeks, the city where Paul landed near the end of his final journey to Jerusalem (Acts 21:7).

entries.title: Aceldama (Field of Blood)
entries.summary: Aramaic for field of blood, and the name stuck to the plot bought with the money Judas took for handing over Jesus.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The Aramaic name, meaning "field of blood," given to the plot purchased with the money Judas Iscariot received for betraying Jesus (Acts 1:19; compare Matthew 27:7-8, where the priests buy it as a burial ground for foreigners with the money Judas threw back). Tradition places it on the southern slope of the Hinnom Valley outside Jerusalem, an area that still contains ancient rock-cut burial caves and has been shown to pilgrims under the name Hakeldama for centuries.

entries.title: Achaia
entries.summary: The Roman province covering southern Greece, with Corinth in it, where Paul spent a long stretch and wrote back afterwards.
entries.label: 5 books
entries.dictNote: Achaia was the Roman province covering southern Greece, home to Corinth, and Paul spent significant time there establishing and later writing letters to the Corinthian church.

witness.excerpt: So Vespasian sent his son Titus from Achaia, where he had been with Nero, to Alexandria, to bring back with him from thence the fifth and.

But as to Titus, he sailed over from Achaia to Alexandria, and that sooner than the winter season did usually permit; so he took with him those forces he was sent for, and marching with great expedition, he came suddenly to Ptolemais, and there finding his father

But as they were sailing in their long ships by the coasts of Achaia, for it was winter time, they heard that Galba was slain, before they could get to him; after he had reigned seven months, and as many days.
Accordingly, he was twice accused before Caesar, that he had filled Achaia with sedition, and had plundered its cities; and so he was sent into banishment.

However, Cestius sent Saul and his friends, at their own desire, to Achaia, to Nero, to inform him of the great distress they were in, and to lay the blame of their kindling the war upon Florus, as hoping to alleviate his own danger, by provoking his indignation against Florus.
2.

entries.title: Achaicus (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: He travelled with Stephanas and Fortunatus to bring Paul news from Corinth. Paul says the visit did him good.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Corinthian Christian who, together with Stephanas and Fortunatus, traveled to visit Paul and brought him news of the Corinthian church, refreshing Paul's spirit (1 Corinthians 16:17-18). His name, meaning "of Achaia," suggests he may have been a native of that Roman province.

entries.title: Achan (Man living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: He kept back plunder from Jericho, a Babylonian garment and silver and gold, when all of it was under the ban. Israel lost the next fight because of it.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Achan was an Israelite who secretly kept plunder from Jericho, a Babylonian garment and hidden silver and gold, in direct violation of God's command that everything in the city be devoted to destruction or given to the treasury. His theft caused Israel's next battle, at the small city of Ai, to end in a humiliating defeat, and once Achan was identified by lot he confessed and was executed along with his family and possessions.

entries.title: Achar (Man living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: Chronicles uses this spelling for Achan, the Judahite whose hidden plunder cost Israel the fight at Ai.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Achar is the name Chronicles gives to Achan, the Judahite who kept plunder devoted to destruction after the fall of Jericho and brought defeat on Israel at Ai as a result (Josh. 7). The Chronicler calls him "Achar, the troubler of Israel" (1 Chr. 2:7), a wordplay on the Valley of Achor, meaning "trouble," where he was executed.

witness.excerpt: But there was one Achar , the son [of Charmi, the son] of Zebedias, of the tribe of Judah; who finding a royal garment woven intirely of gold, and a piece of gold that weighed two hundred shekels; and thinking it a very hard case, that what sp

entries.title: Achaz (King living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Matthew's genealogy spells Ahaz this way. He is in the list as an ancestor of Jesus, and that is the whole of his appearance here.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The Greek form of Ahaz, king of Judah, listed as an ancestor of Jesus in Matthew's genealogy (Matthew 1:9). The historical Ahaz reigned in the late eighth century BC and allied with Assyria against a coalition of Israel and Syria; he is named as a tribute payer to Tiglath-Pileser III in that king's own Assyrian annals under the name Jehoahaz of Judah, one of the clearer points of extrabiblical corroboration for Judah's royal line.

entries.title: Achbor (King living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: A different Achbor entirely, from the time of the patriarchs. Genesis names him only as somebody's father.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Achbor (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A royal official under Josiah. He is one of the men sent to the prophetess Huldah after the law scroll turned up in the temple.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Achbor was a royal official under King Josiah sent to consult the prophetess Huldah after the discovery of the law scroll in the temple.

witness.excerpt: And Saul died, and Ba’êlûnân,  the son of Achbor, reigned in his stead.

entries.title: Achim (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Matthew's genealogy has him between Zadok and Eliud. Nothing else anywhere mentions him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Listed in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus as the son of Zadok and father of Eliud (Matthew 1:14), one of the postexilic names otherwise unattested elsewhere in the Old Testament.

entries.title: Achish (King living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: He is the Philistine king of Gath, and he took David in while David was running from Saul.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Achish was the Philistine king of Gath who gave David refuge when he was fleeing Saul, and David feigned madness to escape Achish's court the first time he sought asylum there, fearing recognition as the killer of Goliath, before later returning and serving as one of Achish's vassals for over a year.

witness.excerpt: Then did Achish, the King of Gath, desire David to assist them with his armed men against the Hebrews.
Accordingly he came with the six hundred men that were with him to Achish, the King of Gath: which was one of their five cities.
When David had received the sword, he fled out of the countrey of the Hebrews, into that of the Philistines; over which Achish reigned.

entries.title: Achmetha (Ecbatana)
entries.summary: The Aramaic name for Ecbatana, old capital of Media and the summer residence of the Persian kings, which is where Cyrus's decree turned up when they went looking for it.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Not a person but the Aramaic name in Ezra 6:2 for Ecbatana, the ancient capital of Media and summer residence of the Persian kings, located near modern Hamadan, Iran. The decree of Cyrus authorizing the rebuilding of the Jerusalem temple was found archived there, since Cyrus had held court at Ecbatana before later Persian kings shifted their main residence to Susa. Excavations at Hamadan have confirmed continuous occupation from the Median period onward, though the ancient Achaemenid palace itself has not been conclusively located beneath the modern city.

entries.title: Achor
entries.summary: A valley near Jericho, on the border between Judah and Benjamin, named for the trouble Achan brought on Israel.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: The Valley of Achor lay near Jericho, on the border of Judah and Benjamin, and takes its name from the trouble Achan brought on Israel when he stole devoted plunder from Jericho and was executed there (Joshua 7:24-26). Centuries later the prophets turned that memory of judgment into a promise of restoration: Hosea pictures the valley becoming "a door of hope," and Isaiah pictures it as pastureland for flocks, God's judgment transformed into blessing (Hosea 2:15; Isaiah 65:10). It is usually identified with the Buqei'a plain or the Wadi Qelt southwest of Jericho.

witness.excerpt: Achor the king] a man of giant stature I found, hurling javelins before and behind as he sat on horseback, and I took up a stone of sixty pounds 4 weight, and hurled it and smote his horse, and killed it.
Accordingly this valley of Achar or Achor was and is a known place, a little north of Gilgal, so called from the days of Joshua, till this day.

entries.title: Achsah (Woman living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: The same name again in Caleb's genealogy. One verse in Chronicles, and nothing more.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Achsah (Woman living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: Caleb's daughter, married to Othniel after he took a Canaanite city. She asked her father for springs of water, and got them.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Achsah was Caleb's daughter, given in marriage to Othniel after he captured a Canaanite city, and she boldly asked her father for springs of water to go with the dry land he'd given her, a request he granted in full.

entries.title: Achshaph
entries.summary: A Canaanite royal city whose king went into the northern coalition that Joshua broke at the Waters of Merom.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Achshaph was a Canaanite royal city whose king joined the northern coalition that Joshua defeated near the Waters of Merom (Joshua 11:1; 12:20). It fell within the territory allotted to Asher (Joshua 19:25). The city appears independently in Pharaoh Thutmose III's fifteenth-century BC topographical list of conquered Canaanite towns at Karnak, confirming it as a real Late Bronze Age settlement centuries before Joshua's campaign.

entries.title: Achzib
entries.summary: A town given to Judah, in the lowland lists. Micah puns on the name when he gets to it.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Achzib
entries.summary: The other Achzib, a Phoenician town on the coast inside Asher's territory that Israel never fully took.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Achzib was a town allotted to the tribe of Judah, and also the name of a Phoenician coastal town within Asher's territory that Israel never fully conquered.

entries.title: Adadah
entries.summary: Far south in Judah, out in the Negev. Nobody has identified the site.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A town in the far south of Judah, in the Negev, listed with Dimonah and Kedesh (Joshua 15:22). Its exact site is unknown.

entries.title: Adah (Woman living at the time before the Flood)
entries.summary: One of Lamech's two wives, down Cain's line. Genesis names her in three verses together and then leaves her.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Adah (Woman living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: One of Esau's wives. She is named through the family lists in Genesis and not outside them.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Adah was one of Lamech's two wives in Cain's genealogical line, and a different Adah was one of Esau's wives, a daughter of the Hittite Elon.

witness.excerpt: Now when Esau, one of the sons of Isaac, whom the father principally loved was now come to the age of forty years, he married Adah, the daughter of Helon; and Aholibamah the daughter of Esebeon: which Helon and Esebeon were great Lords among the Canaanites: thereby taking upon himself the authority, and pretending to have dominion over his own marr

entries.title: Adaiah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Another of the name from the divided-kingdom years. He gets a single genealogy verse.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Adaiah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A man of the name from the divided-kingdom years, whom Chronicles names once.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Adaiah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Josiah's maternal grandfather.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Adaiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of the men on Ezra's list. There is nothing more than that about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Adaiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Another of the name on Ezra's list of men who had married foreign wives.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Adaiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Nehemiah's list carries him, and nothing else does.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Adaiah (Priest living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: He is a priest in the returning community. The Levite lists name him and nothing else does.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Adaiah was a common Old Testament name, borne by several Levites, priests, and a maternal grandfather of King Josiah.

entries.title: Adalia (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of Haman's ten sons. He was killed in Susa on the day that had been set for the Jews' destruction.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Adalia was one of the ten sons of Haman who were killed by the Jews of Susa in self-defense on the day set for their destruction, and whose bodies were afterward hanged (Esther 9:7-10).

entries.title: Adam
entries.summary: Not the first man but a place that carries his name. It is named in a single verse of Joshua and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Adam (Man living at the time before the Flood)
entries.summary: The first man. The name is the ordinary Hebrew word for man, which is the point of it.
entries.books: Genesis, 1 Chronicles, Hosea, Luke, Romans, 1 Corinthians, 1 Timothy, Jude
entries.label: 8 books
entries.dictNote: Red, a Babylonian word, the generic name for man, having the same meaning in the Hebrew and the Assyrian languages. It was the name given to the first man, whose creation, fall, and subsequent history and that of his descendants are detailed in the first book of Moses (Gen. 1:27-ch. 5). “God created man [Heb., Adam] in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.” Adam was absolutely the first man whom God created. He was formed out of the dust of the earth (and hence his name), and God breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and gave him dominion over all the lower creatures (Gen. 1:26; 2:7). He was placed after his creation in the Garden of Eden, to cultivate it, and to enjoy its fruits under this one prohibition: “Of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil thou shalt not eat of it; for in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die.” The first recorded act of Adam was his giving names to the beasts of the field and the fowls of the air, which God brought to him for this end. Thereafter the Lord caused a deep sleep to fall upon him, and while in an unconscious state took one of his ribs, and closed up his flesh again; and of this rib he made a woman, whom he presented to him when he awoke. Adam received her as his wife, and said, “This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh: she shall be called Woman, because she was taken out of Man.” He called her Eve, because she was the mother of all living. Being induced by the tempter in the form of a serpent to eat the forbidden fruit, Eve persuaded Adam, and he also did eat. Thus man fell, and brought upon himself and his posterity all the sad consequences of his transgression. The narrative of the Fall comprehends in it the great promise of a Deliverer (Gen. 3:15), the “first gospel” message to man. They were expelled from Eden, and at the east of the garden God placed a flame, which turned every way, to prevent access to the tree of life (Gen. 3). How long they were in Paradise is matter of mere conjecture. Shortly after their expulsion Eve brought forth her first-born, and called him Cain. Although we have the names of only three of Adam’s sons, viz., Cain, Abel, and Seth, yet it is obvious that he had several sons and daughters (Gen. 5:4). He died aged 930 years. Adam and Eve were the progenitors of the whole human race. Evidences of varied kinds are abundant in proving the unity of the human race. The investigations of science, altogether independent of historical evidence, lead to the conclusion that God “hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth” (Acts 17:26. Comp. Rom. 5:12-12; 1 Cor. 15:22-49).

witness.excerpt: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth. But when the earth did not come into sight, but was covered with thick darkness, and a wind moved upon its surface, God commanded that there should be light.

entries.lukeNote: Luke's genealogy runs all the way back to him: 'the son of Adam, the son of God' (3:38), the only name in the whole list with no human father. Josephus opens his entire 20-book history on the same page of Genesis

entries.title: Adamah
entries.summary: A fortified town of Naphtali, probably the modern Damiyeh on the west side of the Sea of Galilee, though that identification is not certain.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Adamah, a fortified town of Naphtali (Josh. 19:36), likely the same site as modern Damiyeh on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee, though the identification is not certain.

entries.title: Adami
entries.summary: A point on Naphtali's boundary in lower Galilee, written more fully as Adami-nekeb, and where exactly it stood has not been established.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Adami, more fully Adami-nekeb in the Hebrew text, marked a point on the boundary of the tribal territory of Naphtali in lower Galilee (Joshua 19:33). Its precise location has not been established with confidence.

entries.title: Adar (Name of the 12th month)
entries.summary: Twelfth month, late winter, and Purim falls in it, which is the whole reason Esther names it at all.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Adar is the twelfth month of the Hebrew calendar, roughly corresponding to late winter, and it's the month in which the events of Purim take place in the book of Esther.

And he died on the last month of the year, which is called by the Macedonians Dystrus; but by us Adar: on the first day of the month.
