entries.title: Ahitub (Priest living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Generations further down the same priestly line, a later Ahitub appears in 1 Chronicles 6 and again at Ezra 7:2.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Ahitub (Priest living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Zadok's father, named in the list of officials at 2 Samuel 8:17 and in the priestly genealogy of Chronicles.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Ahlab
entries.summary: Asher was given this Phoenician town and never took it, so its Canaanite inhabitants went on living there beside the Israelites. It is generally identified with Khirbet el-Mahalib on the Lebanese coast, a few miles north of Tyre.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Ahlab was a Phoenician town within Asher's allotted territory that the tribe failed to conquer, so its Canaanite inhabitants continued living there alongside the Israelites (Judges 1:31). It is generally identified with Khirbet el-Mahalib, a site on the Lebanese coast a few miles north of Tyre, matching "Mahalliba," a town among the Phoenician cities that submitted to the Assyrian king Sennacherib during his 701 BC campaign, recorded in his own annals. The identification rests on both geographic fit and the close sound of the two names.

entries.title: Ahlai (Warrior living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a warrior from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ahlai (Woman living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Sheshan had no sons, so this Ahlai is usually taken to be his daughter, the one through whom the family line went on by way of an Egyptian servant, Jarha.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Ahlai is named in 1 Chronicles 2:31 as a child of Sheshan, who according to the surrounding genealogy had no sons, so Ahlai is usually taken to be a daughter through whom the family line continued by way of an Egyptian servant, Jarha. Zabad, one of David's mighty warriors, is called "son of Ahlai" in 1 Chronicles 11:41, likely as a descendant of this same line rather than a direct son.

entries.title: Ahoah (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: A son of Bela and grandson of Benjamin. The same chapter also calls him Ahiah, and elsewhere he is Iri. His descendants, the Ahohites, include Eleazar, one of David's three chief mighty men.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A son of Bela and grandson of Benjamin, also called Ahiah in the same chapter and Iri elsewhere (1 Chronicles 8:4, 7; 7:7). His descendants, the Ahohites, included Dodo and his son Eleazar, one of David's three chief mighty men (2 Samuel 23:9).

entries.title: Ahohite (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Three of David's fighting men carry this label, marking them as descendants of Ahoah: Dodo, his son Eleazar, who was among the three mightiest, and Zalmon of the thirty.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Ahohite marks descent from Ahoah, a Benjamite, and is applied to three men connected with David's military: Dodo, one of his officers; Dodo's son Eleazar, counted among the three mightiest of David's warriors; and Zalmon, one of the thirty.

entries.title: Aholah (Woman living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: The name Ezekiel gives Samaria in his allegory of two sisters. She and Oholibah, who stands for Jerusalem, are charged with adultery for their alliances with foreign powers.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Oholah is a symbolic name Ezekiel uses for Samaria in an extended allegory alongside her sister Oholibah, representing Jerusalem, portraying both cities' political alliances with foreign powers as spiritual adultery.

entries.title: Aholiab (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Oholiab of Dan, the skilled craftsman God appointed alongside Bezalel to make the tabernacle and its furnishings.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Oholiab was a skilled craftsman from the tribe of Dan whom God appointed alongside Bezalel to help design and construct the tabernacle and its furnishings.

witness.excerpt: Besaleel and Aholiab appeared to be the most skilful of the workmen: for they invented finer works than what others had done before them: and were of great abilities to gain notions of what they were formerly ignorant of.

Now their names are set down in writing in the sacred Books; and they were these: Besaleel , the son of Uri , of the tribe of Judah, the grandson of Miriam, the sister of their conductor; and Aholiab the son of Ahisamach , of the tribe of Dan.

entries.title: Aholibah (Woman living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Ezekiel's name for Jerusalem in the allegory of the two sisters. Her sister Oholah is Samaria, and both cities' political alliances with foreign powers are painted as adultery.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Oholibah is a symbolic name Ezekiel uses for Jerusalem in an extended allegory alongside her sister Oholah, representing Samaria, portraying both cities' political alliances with foreign powers as spiritual adultery.

entries.title: Aholibamah (Woman living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: She was one of Esau's wives, the daughter of a Hivite chief, and her sons became tribal leaders among the Edomites.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Oholibamah was one of Esau's wives, a daughter of a Hivite chief, and her sons became tribal leaders among the Edomites.

witness.excerpt: Now when Esau, one of the sons of Isaac, whom the father principally loved was now come to the age of forty years, he married Adah, the daughter of Helon; and Aholibamah the daughter of Esebeon: which Helon and Esebeon were great Lords among the Canaanites: thereby taking upon himself the authority, and pretending to have dominion over his own marriages, without so much as asking the ad

entries.title: Ahumai (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: He headed one of the Zorathite families, from Judah through Shobal. Nothing further is known about him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Ahumai was a descendant of Judah through Shobal, listed as the head of one of the families of the Zorathites in 1 Chronicles 4:2. Nothing further is known about him.

entries.title: Ahuzam (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Ashur, who founded Tekoa, had him by his wife Naarah. He shows up only in this one listing, beside his brothers Hepher, Temeni and Haahashtari.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Ahuzam was one of the sons of Ashur, the founder of Tekoa, born to his wife Naarah (1 Chronicles 4:6). He appears only in this genealogical listing alongside his brothers Hepher, Temeni, and Haahashtari.

entries.title: Ahuzzath (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: He came with Abimelech, the Philistine king of Gerar, when the king made a treaty with Isaac after the disputes over wells.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A friend or advisor of Abimelech, the Philistine king of Gerar, who accompanied him when he came to make a treaty with Isaac after their earlier disputes over wells (Genesis 26:26).

witness.excerpt: And he called the name of that place the "Well of the Oath"; for there he had sworn to Abimelech and Ahuzzath his friend and Phicol the prefect of his host.  27.

entries.title: Ai
entries.summary: A fortified Canaanite city near Bethel. Israel's first attack was thrown back because of Achan's hidden sin, and once that was dealt with Joshua took the city by ambush. The site is usually identified with et-Tell, though digging there has turned up little from the right period.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Ai was a fortified Canaanite city near Bethel that first repelled an overconfident Israelite attack because of Achan's hidden sin, then fell to Joshua's ambush once the sin was dealt with, becoming the second Canaanite city Israel captured. It was later resettled by Benjaminites returning from exile. The site is usually identified with et-Tell, though excavations there have found little significant Late Bronze Age occupation matching the traditional conquest period, a discrepancy that continues to divide scholars over the city's exact location or the dating of the conquest. A separate, minor Ai in Ammonite territory is mentioned once by Jeremiah.

entries.title: Ai
entries.summary: Named once, in Jeremiah, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Aiah (Edomite living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Genesis and 1 Chronicles name him twice, and he is a man from the patriarchs.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Aiah (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: A father named to place his daughter. Rizpah was one of Saul's concubines, and Aiah's only part is to say whose daughter she was.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Aiah was the father of Rizpah, one of Saul's concubines, and also the name of a Horite chief listed among Edom's earlier inhabitants.

entries.title: Aijalon
entries.summary: In the valley of Aijalon Joshua told the moon to stand still alongside the sun during the battle against the Amorite coalition. Later it marked the boundary of Danite and Benjamite territory.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Aijalon was a valley and town where Joshua commanded the moon to stand still alongside the sun during the battle against the Amorite coalition, and it later marked the boundary of Danite and Benjamite territory.

entries.title: Ain
entries.summary: Given to Simeon inside Judah's territory, and later made one of the cities handed to the Levites.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Ain was a town allotted to the tribe of Simeon within Judah's territory, later designated as one of the cities given to the Levites.

entries.title: Ain
entries.summary: Named once, in Numbers, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Akan (Edomite living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: He was Ezer's son and one of the Horite clan chiefs descended from Seir, in the land of Edom before Israel had a king. 1 Chronicles 1:42 spells him Jakan.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Akan, called Jakan in the parallel list of 1 Chronicles 1:42, was a son of Ezer and one of the Horite clan chiefs descended from Seir in the land of Edom before Israel had a king (Genesis 36:27).

entries.title: Akkub (Levite living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: The name keeps turning up among the Levites, gatekeepers and temple servants who came back from exile, in Ezra and Nehemiah alike.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Akkub was a common name among Levites, gatekeepers, and temple servants listed among the returning exiles in Ezra and Nehemiah.

entries.title: Akkub (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Akkub (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of 4 men called Akkub. This one is a man from the exile and the return, named once in Ezra.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Akkub (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A man from the exile and the return, and Nehemiah is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Alameth (Alemeth)
entries.summary: Named once, in 1 Chronicles, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Alameth (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: This Alemeth belongs to the family lists at 1 Chronicles 8:36 and 9:42. The town of the same name and Becher's son are different entries altogether.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Alameth, elsewhere spelled Alemeth, names both a town and two different men in the Old Testament. The town was a Levitical city in Benjamin's territory, given to the priestly line of Aaron along with Geba and Anathoth (1 Chronicles 6:45); the parallel list in Joshua 21:18 calls the same town Almon. Among the men who share this name, one Alemeth was a son of Becher, a grandson of Benjamin (1 Chronicles 7:8), while a different Alemeth was one of the sons of Jehoadah, a descendant of Jonathan several generations removed who kept Saul's royal line alive after the northern kingdom had already fallen (1 Chronicles 8:36; 9:42).

entries.title: Alameth (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: One of 3 men called Alameth. This one is a man from the wilderness years, named once in 1 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Alammelech (Allammelech)
entries.summary: The name means king's oak. It sat inside Asher's border, between Achshaph and Amad, and its site is unidentified.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Alammelech, "king's oak," was a place within Asher's territory, named between Achshaph and Amad in Joshua's boundary description (Joshua 19:26). Nothing else is known of it, and its site is unidentified.

entries.title: Alamoth (A musical term)
entries.summary: It literally means maidens, and it turns up in the temple records and in a psalm heading, probably marking a high part.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Alamoth is a musical term found in the record of temple worship and in the headings of the Psalms, most likely indicating a high pitch or treble voice, literally "maidens" or "young women" (1 Chronicles 15:20). It appears as the heading of Psalm 46, and probably describes how the psalm was meant to be sung or played rather than naming any person.

entries.title: Alexander (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: A coppersmith who did Paul great harm, and Paul warns Timothy about him.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Alexander was a common name among several minor New Testament figures, including a coppersmith Paul warns did him great harm and a Jewish man put forward during a riot in Ephesus, distinct from Alexander the Great, who is not named directly in the Bible though his empire is described symbolically in Daniel's visions.

witness.excerpt: Alexander and Aristobulus were much grieved that the privilege of the first-born was confirmed to Antipater; as was Antipater very angry at his brethren that they were to succeed him.
So Alexander, out of fear of his coming, dug a deep ditch, beginning at Chabarzaba, which is now called Antipatris, to the sea of Joppa, on which part only his army could be brought against him.

NOW Alexander left the kingdom to Alexandra his wife, and depended upon it that the Jews would now very readily submit to her, because she had been very averse to such cruelty as he had treated them with, and had opposed his violatio
WHEN Alexander had reigned twelve years, and after him Ptolemy Soter forty years, Philadelphus then took the kingdom of Egypt, and held it forty years within one.
His son Alexander also was beheaded by Sci-pio at Antioch, and that by the command of Pompey, and upon an accusation laid against him before his tribunal, for the mischiefs he had done to the Romans.

entries.title: Alexander (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: A man from the New Testament, and Acts is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Alexander (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Mark names him once, and he is a man from the New Testament.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Alexander (Priest living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: One of 4 men called Alexander. This one is a priest from the New Testament, named once in Acts.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Aliah (Edomite living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Another spelling of Alvah, one of the chiefs of Edom descended from Esau. The two Edomite lists in Genesis and Chronicles differ in small ways like this throughout, and nothing further is recorded of him.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Aliah is an alternate spelling of Alvah, one of the tribal chiefs (“dukes”) of Edom descended from Esau (Genesis 36:40; 1 Chronicles 1:51). The two Edomite king-lists in Genesis and Chronicles show minor spelling variation of this kind throughout. Nothing further is recorded of him.

entries.title: Alian (Edomite living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Also called Alvan. He was a son of Shobal and a Horite clan chief in Seir, and nothing further is known.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Alian, also called Alvan, was a son of Shobal and a Horite clan chief in the region of Seir, listed in the genealogy of Edom's earlier inhabitants (Genesis 36:23). Nothing further is known of him.

entries.title: Allon
entries.summary: A Simeonite in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 4:37. His line was the clan that drove the descendants of Ham out of the valley of Gedor in Hezekiah's day.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Easton's dictionary treats "Allon" as two unrelated items: an oak tree used as a boundary landmark on the border of Naphtali in Joshua 19:33, and a Simeonite named in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 4:37, an ancestor of the clan that drove out the descendants of Ham from the valley of Gedor in the days of Hezekiah. The reference here, 1 Chronicles 4:37, belongs to the second, genealogical sense, so despite the place tag, the text actually names a person in a family line rather than a location.

entries.title: Allon-bachuth (Allon-bacuth)
entries.summary: Oak of weeping. It is the place near Bethel where Rebekah's nurse Deborah was buried, and it was likely the same landmark later called the palm tree of Deborah, where the judge Deborah held court.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Allon-bachuth, meaning "oak of weeping," is not a person but the site near Bethel where Rebekah's nurse Deborah was buried (Genesis 35:8). It was likely the same landmark later called the palm tree of Deborah, near Bethel, where the judge and prophetess Deborah held court (Judges 4:5).

entries.title: Almighty (The Deity)
entries.summary: It translates El Shaddai, a Hebrew title for God used most in the stories of the patriarchs and in Job. It describes who God is and what he can do, and it is not anyone's name.
entries.books: Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Ruth, Job, Psalm, Isaiah, Ezekiel, Joel, 2 Corinthians, Revelation
entries.label: 11 books
entries.dictNote: Almighty translates a Hebrew title for God, El Shaddai, used especially in the patriarchal narratives and the book of Job, and it is a description of God's character and power rather than the name of any person.

witness.excerpt: And God Almighty bless thee and increase and multiply thee that thou mayest become a company of nations, and give thee the blessings of my father Abraham, to thee and to thy seed after thee, that thou mayest inherit the land of thy sojo
And the Lord appeared to Abram, and said unto him: "I am God Almighty; approve thyself before Me and be thou perfect.

There was now a prophet of God Almighty, of Thesbon, a country in Gilead, that came to Ahab, and said to him, that God foretold he would not send rain nor dew in those years upon the country but when he should appear.

entries.title: Almodad (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: First of Joktan's sons in the Table of Nations. His descendants are usually put somewhere in the Arabian peninsula, though which tribe has not been settled.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Almodad was the first named of the sons of Joktan in the Table of Nations, understood as the ancestor of an Arabian tribe (Genesis 10:26; 1 Chronicles 1:20). His descendants are usually placed somewhere in the Arabian peninsula, though the exact tribe has not been identified with certainty.

entries.title: Almon (Alemeth)
entries.summary: One of the towns given to the priestly Levites inside Benjamin. 1 Chronicles 6:60 calls it Alemeth, and it is generally placed near the village of Almit, northeast of Jerusalem.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Almon was one of the towns assigned to the priestly Levites within the territory of Benjamin (Joshua 21:18). It is called Alemeth in the parallel list of Levitical cities in 1 Chronicles 6:60, and is generally located near the modern village of Almit, northeast of Jerusalem.

entries.title: Almondilathaim (Dibon)
entries.summary: Better known as Almon-diblathaim. Israel camped here in Moabite territory, between Dibon-gad and the mountains of Abarim, one of the last stops before the plains of Moab opposite Jericho.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Wilderness campsite in Moabite territory, better known as Almon-diblathaim, between Dibon-gad and the mountains of Abarim, one of the last stops before Israel reached the plains of Moab opposite Jericho (Num. 33:46-47).

entries.title: Alpheus (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Father of the apostle James, which is how that James is told apart from James the son of Zebedee.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Alphaeus was the father of James, one of the twelve apostles, distinguishing him as James the son of Alphaeus from James the son of Zebedee.

entries.title: Alush
entries.summary: Israel camped here between Dophkah and Rephidim, close to the end of the march to Mount Sinai.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Wilderness campsite between Dophkah and Rephidim, one of the last stops before Israel reached Mount Sinai, likely along the western Sinai coastal route (Num. 33:13-14).

entries.title: Amad
entries.summary: Named once, between Alammelech and Misheal on Asher's border, and its site has not been identified.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A border town of the tribe of Asher, named only once between Alammelech and Misheal (Joshua 19:26). Its site has not been identified.

entries.title: Amal (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A son of Helem, in Asher's line at 1 Chronicles 7:35.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Amal was a son of Helem, listed among the descendants of Asher in the tribal genealogy of 1 Chronicles 7:35.

entries.title: Amalek
entries.summary: Esau's grandson. The Amalekites who came from him attacked the weak rear of Israel's column in the wilderness, and God declared war on Amalek for it. Saul's half-done obedience against them later cost him the kingdom.
entries.books: Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Judges, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Chronicles, Psalm
entries.label: 8 books
entries.dictNote: Amalek was a grandson of Esau, and the Amalekites descended from him became one of Israel's oldest and most bitter enemies, attacking the vulnerable rear of Israel's column during the exodus wilderness journey. God declared perpetual war against Amalek for that attack, a mandate Saul's incomplete obedience against them later cost him his kingdom.

witness.excerpt: Nay till Saul’s rejection of the divine commands in the war with Amalek, when he took upon him to act as he thought fit himelf.
3 Then shall perish the seed of Canaan, And a remnant shall not be unto Amalek, And all the Cappadocians shall perish, And all the Hittites shall be utterly destroyed.
Aliphaz had five legitimate sons; Theman, Omer, Saphus, Gotham, and Kanaz; for Amalek was not legitimate, but by a concubine, whose name was Thamna.

At all events, he says in another place, \"When Moses lifted up his hands Israel prevailed, and when he let them down Amalek Prevailed.\"{91}{#ex 17:11.} And this statement implies, that when the mind raises itself up from mortal affairs and is elevated on high, it is very vigorous because it beholds God; and the mind here means Israel.

entries.title: Amalek (Edomite living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Genesis names him twice, and he is a man from the patriarchs.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Amam
entries.summary: One verse of Joshua's town lists puts it in the Negev district of Judah with Shema and Moladah. That is all that survives of it, and nobody knows where it stood.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Amam was a town in the Negev district of Judah's territory, named together with Shema and Moladah in a single verse of Joshua's town lists (Josh. 15:26). No other information about it survives, and its site is unknown.

entries.title: Amana
entries.summary: Two things share the name. At 2 Kings 5:12 the Hebrew margin reads Amana for the Abana, the river of Damascus Naaman preferred to Israel's water. In the Song of Solomon it is a mountain, likely the southern summit of the Anti-Lebanon range, where the Abana rises.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Amana names two related things sharing one root. The Hebrew margin at 2 Kings 5:12 gives Amana as an alternate reading for the Abana, the river flowing through Damascus that Naaman preferred to the waters of Israel. In the Song of Solomon it names a mountain, likely the southern summit of the Anti-Lebanon range, from whose slopes the Abana's waters rise (Song 4:8).

entries.title: Amariah (Levite living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: A levite from the wilderness years, and 1 Chronicles is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Amariah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A man from the divided-kingdom years. 2 Chronicles names him once.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Amariah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 2 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Amariah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A man from the divided-kingdom years. Zephaniah names him once.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Amariah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of several priests called Amariah, this one in Nehemiah's lists at 10:3 and 12:2.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Amariah was a common name among Israel's priests, borne by several men in the high priestly genealogy as well as a chief priest appointed by King Jehoshaphat to oversee religious matters.

entries.title: Amariah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of 9 men called Amariah. This one is a man from the exile and the return, named once in Ezra.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Amariah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A man from the exile and the return, and Nehemiah is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Amariah (Priest living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 9 men called Amariah. This one is a priest from the divided-kingdom years, named twice in 1 Chronicles and Ezra.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Amariah (Priest living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him twice, and he is a priest from the united kingdom.
entries.label: 1 book

witness.excerpt: Now he set over them Amariah the Priest, and Zebadiah [both 1 ] of the tribe of Judah.

entries.title: Amasa (Ishmaelite living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: David's nephew. He led Absalom's rebel army, and afterwards David offered him command of the whole royal army to win back Absalom's supporters. Joab, jealous, stabbed him while pretending to greet him with a kiss.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Amasa was David's nephew who commanded Absalom's rebel army during the uprising, and David surprisingly offered him command of the entire royal army afterward as part of reconciling with Absalom's former supporters, a move that provoked Joab's jealousy; Joab murdered Amasa shortly after by stabbing him while pretending to greet him with a kiss.

witness.excerpt: He appointed Amasa to be captain of all his host, instead of Joab his kinsman: his father was Ithra and his mother Abigail: now she and Zeruiah, the mother of Joab, were David's sisters.

Be thou also mindful of the transgressions of Joab, (26) the captain of the host, who hath slain two generals out of envy, and those righteous and good men, Abner the son of Ner, and Amasa the son of Jether; whose death do thou avenge as shall seem good to thee, since Joab hath been too hard for me, and more potent than myself, and so hath escaped punishment hitherto.

entries.title: Amasa (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 2 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Amasai (Levite living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Named twice in the Levitical genealogy of 1 Chronicles 6, and nothing else about him is told in those verses.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Amasai was a Levitical chief who defected to David with a group of armed men while David was still an outlaw, declaring his loyalty in a burst of prophetic assurance, and he later helped oversee temple duties under David's organization.

entries.title: Amasai (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 4 men called Amasai. This one is a man from the divided-kingdom years, named once in 1 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Amasai (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A man from the divided-kingdom years, and 2 Chronicles is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Amasai (Warrior living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a warrior from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Amashai (Levite living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A priest, Azareel's son, appointed to live in Jerusalem after the exile and help with the temple work.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Amashai was a priest, son of Azareel, appointed to reside in Jerusalem after the exile and assist with the work of the temple (Nehemiah 11:13). Nothing further is recorded about him.

entries.title: Amasiah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: In Jehoshaphat's army he commanded a thousand men, and he is remembered for volunteering himself for the LORD's service. Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A commander of thousands in the army of King Jehoshaphat of Judah, listed among the officers who volunteered themselves for the LORD's service in the military reorganization of 2 Chronicles 17:16. Nothing further is recorded about him.

entries.title: Amaziah (King living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: He took Judah's throne after his father Joash was assassinated and executed the killers but spared their children, as the law said. Then he beat Edom, brought its idols home and worshipped them. A war he picked with northern Israel ended with him captured and Jerusalem's walls torn down.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Amaziah became king of Judah after his father Joash was assassinated, and he executed the assassins but spared their children, citing the law that children shouldn't be punished for their parents' sins. After a costly victory over Edom, Amaziah brought Edomite idols home and began worshiping them, and he foolishly provoked a war with northern Israel that ended in his own capture and Jerusalem's walls being torn down. A different Amaziah was the priest of the golden calf shrine at Bethel who confronted the prophet Amos and ordered him to leave the kingdom.

witness.excerpt: When Jehoash [King of Judah ] was dead, Amaziah succeeds him in the Kingdom.

826.] In the fifteenth year of the reign of Amaziah, Jeroboam, the son of Joash reigned over Israel, in Samaria forty years.19 This King was guilty of contumely against God,  and became very wicked in worshipping of idols, and in many undertakings that were absurd and fo

Upon the whole, since it appears, even by Josephus’s own account, that Amaziah, the good King of Judah, while he was a good King, was forbidden to make use of the 100000 auxiliaries he had hired of this Joash, the King of Israel; as if he and they were then idolaters; IX.9.1 .

Accordingly there were slain by the Israelites one hundred and twenty thousand of his men that day: whose general, Amaziah by name, slew Zachariah the King’s son in his conflict with Ahaz; as well as the Governor of the Kingdom, whose name was Azricam.

entries.title: Amaziah (Levite living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A levite from the divided-kingdom years, and 1 Chronicles is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Amaziah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Not the king of Judah. This Amaziah belongs to Amos 7:10–14.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Amaziah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 4 men called Amaziah. This one is a man from the divided-kingdom years, named once in 1 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ami (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: He was among the descendants of Solomon's servants who came back from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel. Nehemiah's copy of the list calls him Amon.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Listed among the descendants of Solomon's servants who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel; the parallel list in Nehemiah gives the name as Amon (Ezra 2:57; Nehemiah 7:59).

entries.title: Aminadab (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Amminadab in its Greek form. Matthew and Luke both name him as David's ancestor through Judah, and his daughter Elisheba married Aaron, so the one family runs into the priests and the kings.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Aminadab is the Greek form of Amminadab, an ancestor of David through the line of Judah, named in the genealogies of both Matthew and Luke (Matthew 1:4; Luke 3:33). In Exodus, Amminadab's daughter Elisheba married Aaron, linking this family line to Israel's priesthood as well as to its future kings (Exodus 6:23).

witness.excerpt: Of all which Eliab was the eldest: Aminadab the second: Shammah the third: Nathanael the fourth: the fifth was called Rael : and the sixth Asam .

So when the whole body of the people were come together, as they had resolved to do, the king came to the ark, which the priest brought out of the house of Aminadab, and laid it upon a new cart, and permitted their brethren and their children to draw it, together with the oxen.

entries.title: Amittai (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Jonah's father, from Gath-hepher in Galilee. Nothing else is recorded of him.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Amittai was the father of the prophet Jonah, identified as a native of Gath-hepher in Galilee (2 Kings 14:25; Jonah 1:1). Nothing else is recorded of him beyond this identification.

entries.title: Ammah
entries.summary: A hill east of Gibeon. Joab and Abishai reached it at sunset chasing Abner after the fight at the pool of Gibeon, and there Abner called out to Joab and the two agreed a truce.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Ammah was not a person but a hill east of Gibeon that Joab and Abishai reached at sunset while pursuing Abner's forces after the skirmish at the pool of Gibeon (2 Sam. 2:24). It was there that Abner called out to Joab and the two commanders agreed to a truce.

entries.title: Ammiel (Levite living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 3 men called Ammiel. This one is a Levite from the united kingdom, named once in 1 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ammiel (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Numbers names him once, and he is a man from the wilderness years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ammiel (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles 3:5 makes an Ammiel the father of Bathsheba, called Bath-shua there. The name also turns up in 2 Samuel 9 and 17, given only as a father's name.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Ammiel was a common name, including one of the twelve spies representing the tribe of Dan and the father of Bathsheba according to 1 Chronicles, where she is called Bath-shua.

entries.title: Ammihud (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Father of Ephraim's tribal leader during the wilderness census.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Ammihud was a common Old Testament name, borne by the father of a tribal leader of Ephraim during the wilderness census and by the father of a king of Geshur whose daughter Maacah married David.

entries.title: Ammihud (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Numbers names him once, and he is a man from the wilderness years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ammihud (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: One of 5 men called Ammihud. This one is a man from the wilderness years, named once in Numbers.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ammihud (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A man from the exile and the return. 1 Chronicles names him once.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ammihud (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: A man from the united kingdom, and 2 Samuel is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Amminadab (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him twice, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Amminadab (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Two great lines run back to him. Aaron married his daughter Elisheba, and his son Nahshon stands in David's ancestry, so he sits in both the priestly and the royal genealogies.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Amminadab was an ancestor of both Aaron, through his daughter Elisheba whom Aaron married, and of David, through his son Nahshon, placing him in the genealogies of both the priestly and royal lines of Israel.

entries.title: Amminadib (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Only the King James Version has this as a name, at Song of Solomon 6:12, "the chariots of Amminadib." Most modern translations read the Hebrew as a phrase like "my noble people." Whether a real person is meant has long been argued over.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A name found only in the King James Version's translation of Song of Solomon 6:12, describing chariots compared to "the chariots of Amminadib." Most modern translations, following the Hebrew more closely, render the phrase differently, as "my noble people" or "the chariots of my people, a prince," treating it as a poetic description rather than a proper name. Whether it refers to an actual individual has long been disputed among translators.

entries.title: Ammishaddai (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: The father of Dan's tribal leader in the wilderness census.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Ammishaddai was the father of the tribal leader of Dan during the wilderness census.

entries.title: Ammizabad (Warrior living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Benaiah commanded the third division of David's army, and his son Ammizabad appears to have run it on his behalf.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Son of Benaiah, David's commander over the third division of the army; Ammizabad appears to have overseen that division on his father's behalf (1 Chronicles 27:6).

entries.title: Ammon
entries.summary: A nation east of the Jordan, descended from Lot through his younger daughter and close kin to Moab. The Ammonites fought Israel again and again, from Jephthah's war in Judges to the insult to David's envoys that started a full war in David's reign.
entries.books: Genesis, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Psalm, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, Amos, Zephaniah
entries.label: 18 books
entries.dictNote: Ammon was a nation east of the Jordan descended from Lot through his younger daughter, closely related to Moab, and the Ammonites appear repeatedly as Israel's enemies, from Jephthah's war against them in Judges to their humiliating treatment of David's envoys that triggered a full-scale war under David's reign.

witness.excerpt: So the Ammonites and Philistines had them in contempt; and laid waste the countrey with a great army: and when they had taken all Perea, they were so insolent as to attempt to gain the possession of all the rest.

But now when the Ammonites, and Moabites, and Samaritans, and all that inhabited Celesyria heard that the building went on apace, they took it hainously; and proceeded to lay snares for them, and to hinder their intentions.

entries.title: Amnon (David's son living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: David's firstborn. He raped his half-sister Tamar, with a cousin's scheme to help him, and David did not punish him. Two years later her full brother Absalom had Amnon murdered, and that was the start of the road to Absalom's revolt.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Amnon was David's firstborn son, and his rape of his own half-sister Tamar, aided by a cousin's scheming advice, went unpunished by David and provoked their full brother Absalom to murder Amnon two years later in revenge, the act that eventually spiraled into Absalom's open rebellion against their father.

witness.excerpt: Now Amnon, David's eldest son, fell in love with her, and being not able to obtain his desires, on account of her virginity, and the custody she was under, was so much out of order, nay, his grief so eat up his body, that he grew
The sons whom he had were in number eleven, whose names were Amnon, Emnos, Eban, Nathan, Solomon, Jeban, Elien, Phalna, Ennaphen, Jenae, Eliphale; and a daughter, Tamar.

entries.title: Amnon (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Amok (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A priest who came back from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel and headed a priestly family. In the days of the high priest Joiakim, his descendant Eber held that place.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Amok was a priest who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel and became head of a priestly family; his descendant Eber served as head of that family in the days of the high priest Joiakim (Nehemiah 12:7, 20).

entries.title: Amon (King living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: The son of Manasseh. He followed his father's early idolatry and never turned back, and his own officials killed him after two years. The people executed the plotters and made his young son Josiah king.
entries.books: 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Nehemiah, Jeremiah, Zephaniah, Matthew
entries.label: 7 books
entries.dictNote: Amon became king of Judah after his notorious father Manasseh, and unlike his father, who eventually repented, Amon followed his father's earlier idolatry without ever turning back to God. His own officials assassinated him after only two years on the throne, and the common people executed the conspirators and installed his young son Josiah as king instead.

Then did the king give orders that they should take Micaiah away, and guard him to Amon, the governor of the city, and to give him nothing but bread and water.

entries.title: Amon (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Kings and 2 Chronicles name him twice, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Amorite (People, perhaps from Amor)
entries.summary: One of the peoples in Canaan before Israel came, traced in Genesis 10 to a son of Canaan, and sometimes used loosely for everyone in the hill country. Sihon and Og ruled an Amorite kingdom east of the Jordan that fell to Israel under Moses. Outside the Bible they are the Amurru of Mesopotamian texts, the people whose dynasty produced Hammurabi of Babylon.
entries.books: Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Psalm, Ezekiel, Amos
entries.label: 17 books
entries.dictNote: The Amorites were one of the peoples living in Canaan before Israel's conquest, traditionally traced to a son of Canaan in Genesis 10, and the Old Testament sometimes uses their name loosely for the hill country's inhabitants in general. A specific Amorite kingdom east of the Jordan, ruled by Sihon and Og, fell to Israel under Moses and became the basis for Reuben and Gad's territory in Numbers 21. Outside the Bible, Amorites, called Amurru in Mesopotamian texts, were a real West Semitic people who migrated into Mesopotamia in the early second millennium BC and founded several dynasties there, including the one that produced Hammurabi of Babylon. Their language and personal names are well documented in cuneiform archives from Mari and elsewhere.

entries.title: Amos (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A shepherd and fig farmer from Tekoa in Judah, sent north to prophesy against Israel. He said plainly he was no professional prophet and came from no prophet's family. His book goes after the wealthy who exploited the poor while keeping up empty religious ritual.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Amos was a shepherd and fig farmer from Tekoa in Judah who was sent north to prophesy against Israel, insisting he was no professional prophet and had no prophetic family background, just a farmer God pulled off the job. His book condemns Israel's wealthy for exploiting the poor while performing empty religious rituals, and its most quoted line demands that justice roll down like waters and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream. A different Amos is listed simply as an ancestor of Jesus in Luke's genealogy.

entries.title: Amos (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Luke names him once, and he is a man from the exile and the return.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Amoz (Isaiah's father living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Isaiah's father, and not the prophet Amos: the names look alike in English but come from different Hebrew names entirely.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Amoz was the prophet Isaiah's father, distinct from the prophet Amos despite the similar English spelling, which come from different Hebrew names entirely.

entries.title: Amphipolis
entries.summary: Paul and Silas passed through on the road from Philippi to Thessalonica. It was a major Macedonian city on the Strymon River and a Roman administrative centre on the Via Egnatia, and its Greek and Roman remains, a lion monument among them, have been excavated.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Amphipolis, a major Macedonian city on the Strymon River and an important Roman administrative center on the Via Egnatia, through which Paul and Silas traveled on the road from Philippi to Thessalonica (Acts 17:1). Extensive Greek and Roman remains, including a well known lion monument and a large basilica complex, have been excavated at the site.

entries.title: Amplias (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Paul greets him in the closing list of Romans as "my beloved in the Lord." The fuller form, Ampliatus, was common among slaves and freedmen, and a decorated early Christian tomb in the Catacomb of Domitilla bears it, though nobody can prove it is the same man.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Christian in Rome whom Paul greets warmly as "my beloved in the Lord" in the list of greetings that closes Romans (Romans 16:8). The fuller Greek form of the name, Ampliatus, was common among slaves and freedmen, and a decorated early Christian tomb in the Catacomb of Domitilla bears that name, though it cannot be proven to belong to the same man Paul greets.

entries.title: Amram (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Ezra names him once, and he is a man from the exile and the return.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Amram (Moses' father living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: The father of Aaron, Moses and Miriam. He was a Levite and married his father's sister Jochebed, and beyond that little is recorded about him.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Amram was Aaron, Moses, and Miriam's father, a Levite who married his father's sister Jochebed, and beyond that marriage and his children's roles, little else is recorded about him personally.

And the most (of them) returned to Egypt, but a few of them remained in the mountains of Hebron, and

[paragraph continues] Amram thy father remained with them 1.

And afterwards, when thou wast grown up, they brought thee unto the daughter of Pharaoh, and thou didst become her son, and Amram thy father taught thee writing,  and after thou hadst completed three weeks they brought thee into the royal court.

45.] So he seized upon three of their principal men, who were also the causes of this sedition, and ordered them to be bound; and afterward had one of them slain, whose name was Hannibal: and he banished the other two, Amram, and Eleazar.

entries.title: Amramite (Moses' father living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Descendants of Amram, the son of Kohath and father of Moses, Aaron and Miriam. Under David, men of this family helped oversee the treasuries of gifts dedicated for the temple.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Amramites were the descendants of Amram, son of Kohath and father of Moses, Aaron, and Miriam, one of four Levitical families descended from Kohath. Under David, men of this family served among the officials overseeing the treasuries of dedicated gifts for the temple.

entries.title: Amran (Edomite living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Dishon's son, among the clan chiefs of Edom before Israel had a king, and called Hemdan in Genesis 36:26.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Amran, called Hemdan in the parallel genealogy of Genesis 36:26, was a son of Dishon and a descendant of Seir the Horite, one of the clan chiefs of Edom recorded before Israel had a king (1 Chronicles 1:41).

entries.title: Amraphel (King living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: King of Shinar, in southern Mesopotamia, and one of the four kings who marched with Chedorlaomer of Elam against Sodom and the cities of the plain. Older scholarship tried to make him Hammurabi, and most scholars now reject the equation.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Amraphel was the king of Shinar, in southern Mesopotamia, who joined Chedorlaomer of Elam and two other kings in a campaign against the cities of the plain, including Sodom, described in Genesis 14. Older scholarship once proposed identifying him with the famous Babylonian king Hammurabi, whose law code survives on a well-known stone stele, but most scholars today consider the equation linguistically and chronologically doubtful.

witness.excerpt: And in this year came Chedorlaomer, king of Elam, and Amraphel, king of Shinar, and Arioch, king of Sêllâsar  and Têrgâl,  king of nations, and slew the king of Gomorrah, and the king of Sodom fled, and many fell through wounds in the vale of Siddim, by the Salt Sea.

entries.title: Amzi (Levite living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A Levite, and an ancestor of Ethan, one of the temple musicians David appointed.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Amzi (Priest living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A priest in the Jerusalem settlement lists after the exile.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Two men named Amzi appear in postexilic records. One was a Levite ancestor of Ethan, one of the temple musicians David appointed (1 Chronicles 6:31, 44-45). The other was a priest whose descendant resettled in Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile (Nehemiah 11:12).

entries.title: Anab
entries.summary: Joshua drove the Anakim out of this town in the Judean hill country. It still has its old name, in the ruin Khirbet Anab southwest of Hebron.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Town in the Judean hill country from which Joshua drove out the Anakim, a people remembered in Israel's tradition for their unusual height (Josh. 11:21; 15:50). It still bears its ancient name today, preserved in the ruin Khirbet Anab southwest of Hebron.

entries.title: Anah (Edomite living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: He found hot springs in the wilderness while pasturing his father's donkeys, and he sits in the Edomite genealogies of Esau's line.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Anah was an Edomite figure, described in Genesis as discovering hot springs in the wilderness while pasturing his father's donkeys, and appears in the genealogies of Esau's descendants.

entries.title: Anaharath
entries.summary: A border town of Issachar, listed with Shihon and Rabbith, tentatively placed near Mount Tabor in the Jezreel Valley.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A border town of the tribe of Issachar, listed alongside Shihon and Rabbith (Joshua 19:19). It is tentatively identified with a site near Mount Tabor in the Jezreel Valley, though the identification is not certain.

entries.title: Anaiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Nehemiah names him once, and he is a man from the exile and the return.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Anaiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: When Ezra read the law to Jerusalem from a wooden platform, Anaiah stood at his right hand. He is likely the same man who later signed Nehemiah's covenant.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Anaiah stood at Ezra's right hand on the wooden platform built for the public reading of the law in Jerusalem (Nehemiah 8:4) and is likely the same man who later signed Nehemiah's covenant of renewed obedience to the law (Nehemiah 10:22).

entries.title: Anak (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Ancestor of the Anakim, the tall people of Hebron who frightened the spies. His father was Arba, and Hebron was first called Kirjath-arba after him. Caleb drove Anak's descendants out and took the city.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Anak was the ancestor of the Anakim, a people of great stature who inhabited Hebron and struck fear into the Israelite spies sent to scout Canaan (Numbers 13:33). Joshua 15:13 identifies his father as Arba, for whom the city of Hebron was originally named Kirjath-arba. Caleb eventually drove the descendants of Anak out of Hebron and received the city as his inheritance (Joshua 15:14).

entries.title: Anakim (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: A people of unusual height living in Canaan before the conquest. Ten of the twelve spies came back afraid of them, and that fear is why Israel spent forty years in the wilderness.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: The Anakim were a race of unusually tall people living in Canaan before the conquest, and the fear they inspired in ten of the twelve spies Moses sent to scout the land was the direct cause of Israel's forty years of wilderness wandering; Caleb and Joshua alone were unafraid, trusting God to give victory regardless of the odds.

entries.title: Anamim (People, perhaps from Anam)
entries.summary: Not a person. The Table of Nations counts them among the groups descended from Mizraim, Egypt, and which real people is meant has not been identified with confidence.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Anamim was not an individual but one of the tribal groups descended from Mizraim, the biblical name for Egypt, in the Table of Nations (Genesis 10:13; 1 Chronicles 1:11). Like several names in this list, its exact historical people group has not been identified with confidence, though scholars have proposed connections to various Egyptian or Libyan populations.

entries.title: Anammelech (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A god of the people of Sepharvaim, whom the Assyrians resettled in Samaria after deporting the northern kingdom in 722 BC. The colonists burned their children in the fire to Anammelech and to Adrammelech beside it.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Anammelech was a deity worshipped by the people of Sepharvaim, a Mesopotamian population the Assyrians resettled in Samaria after deporting the northern kingdom of Israel in 722 BC (2 Kings 17:31). The colonists reportedly burned their children in fire to Anammelech and its companion god Adrammelech, a practice associated in the ancient Near East with Molech worship. Assyrian resettlement policy of this kind is well attested in Assyrian royal inscriptions, including those of Sargon II, who claims credit for Samaria's conquest.

entries.title: Anan (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: He put his name to the sealed covenant by which the community back from exile bound itself to keep the law of Moses under Nehemiah.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Anan was one of the Jewish leaders who affixed his name to the sealed covenant by which the postexilic community bound itself to keep the law of Moses under Nehemiah (Neh. 10:26).

entries.title: Anani (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Seventh of Elioenai's seven sons, at the very end of David's royal line in 1 Chronicles 3:24, generations after the return from Babylonian exile. The list shows David's family still going long after the monarchy was gone.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The seventh of seven sons of Elioenai listed at the end of the royal genealogy of David's line in 1 Chronicles 3:24, several generations after the return from Babylonian exile. The list shows David's family continuing intact well into the postexilic period, a detail later Jewish and Christian readers drew on when tracing a "son of David" even centuries after the monarchy had ended.

entries.title: Ananiah
entries.summary: Named once, in Nehemiah, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ananiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Named once, at Nehemiah 3:23. The same name belongs to a town in Benjamin, commonly identified with Beit Hanina, a few miles north of Jerusalem.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Town in Benjamin near Jerusalem, listed among the settlements Jews reoccupied after returning from exile (Neh. 11:32). It is commonly identified with the modern village of Beit Hanina, a few miles north of Jerusalem.

entries.title: Ananias (High Priest living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: One of 3 men called Ananias. This one is a high priest from the New Testament, named twice in Acts.
entries.label: 1 book

But as for the High Priest Ananias, he increased in glory every day; and this to a great degree: and had obtained the favour and esteem of the citizens in a signal manner.

At the same time Eleazar, the son of Ananias the high priest, a very bold youth, who was at that time governor of the temple, persuaded those that officiated in the Divine service to receive no gift or sacrifice for any foreigner.

entries.title: Ananias (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: He was the disciple in Damascus who restored Paul's sight and baptised him. He was afraid of the man who had been persecuting Christians, and he went anyway.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Ananias sold a piece of property along with his wife Sapphira and brought only part of the proceeds to the apostles while claiming it was the full amount, and Peter confronted the lie directly, telling Ananias he hadn't lied to people but to God; Ananias dropped dead on the spot, and Sapphira met the same fate a few hours later when she repeated the same lie without knowing her husband was already dead. A different Ananias was the disciple in Damascus who restored Paul's sight and baptized him after his conversion, despite his own fear of the man who had been persecuting Christians.

witness.excerpt: Both their names were Ananias: and they soon came to the rulers of the Idumeans.

entries.title: Ananias (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: He and his wife Sapphira sold land and brought the apostles part of the money as if it were all of it. Peter told him he had lied to God and not to people, and he dropped dead on the spot. Sapphira told the same lie a few hours later and died the same way.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Anath (Man living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: Shamgar's father. Shamgar killed six hundred Philistines with an ox goad. The name matches the Canaanite goddess Anat, but here it is just what his father was called.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Anath was the father of Shamgar, one of Israel's early judges who struck down six hundred Philistines with an ox goad (Judges 3:31; 5:6). The name is shared with the Canaanite warrior goddess Anat, but in these verses it functions as a personal or place name for Shamgar's father.

witness.excerpt: After him Shamgar, the son of Anath, was elected for their governour; but died in the first year of his government.

entries.title: Anathoth
entries.summary: A priestly town in Benjamin, about three miles north of Jerusalem, and Jeremiah's home. He bought a field there as a sign of hope while announcing Jerusalem's fall. The site is identified with the village of Anata.
entries.books: Joshua, 1 Kings, 1 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Isaiah, Jeremiah
entries.label: 7 books
entries.dictNote: Anathoth was a priestly town in Benjamin, about three miles north of Jerusalem, best known as the hometown and lifelong home of the prophet Jeremiah, who bought a field there as a sign of hope even while announcing Jerusalem's coming fall. It also produced two of David's mighty men. The site is identified with the modern village of Anata.

witness.excerpt: Now he had resolved to go elsewhere, to his own countrey, which was called Anathoth, and was twenty furlongs distant from Jerusalem.

entries.title: Anathoth (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the wilderness years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Anathoth (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of 3 men called Anathoth. This one is a man from the exile and the return, named once in Nehemiah.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Andrew (Apostle living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Peter's brother, and in John's Gospel a disciple of John the Baptist first, who followed Jesus and straight away brought Peter to meet him. He keeps turning up at practical moments: the boy with five loaves and two fish, the Greeks who came asking for Jesus. Tradition says he was crucified on an X-shaped cross.
entries.label: 5 books
entries.dictNote: Andrew was Peter's brother and, according to John's Gospel, a former disciple of John the Baptist before he followed Jesus and immediately brought Peter to meet him as well. Andrew appears at several practical moments in the Gospels, pointing Jesus to the boy with five loaves and two fish before the feeding of the five thousand and bringing a group of inquiring Greeks to Jesus in his final week. Tradition holds that he was crucified on an X-shaped cross, which became known afterward as Saint Andrew's cross.

entries.title: Andronicus (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Paul greets Andronicus, a Jewish Christian and his relative or countryman, together with Junia in Romans 16:7. He calls the pair outstanding among the apostles and says they believed in Christ before he did.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The name here is a data spelling of Andronicus, a Jewish Christian and relative or fellow countryman of Paul whom Paul greets in Romans 16:7 along with Junia, calling the pair "outstanding among the apostles" and noting that they had been believers in Christ before Paul's own conversion.

entries.title: Anem (En-gannim)
entries.summary: Levites lived in this town in Issachar. It is generally identified with En-gannim, whose name survives in the modern city of Jenin.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Anem was a Levitical town in the tribal territory of Issachar (1 Chronicles 6:73). It is generally identified with En-gannim in the earlier town list of Joshua 19:21, whose name survives in the modern city of Jenin.

entries.title: Aner (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: An Amorite chief allied with Mamre and Eshcol, who went with Abraham after the four kings who had captured Lot. 1 Chronicles also gives the name to a Levite town of Kohath's clan in Manasseh.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Aner carries two distinct senses under one name. In Genesis it names an Amorite chief allied with Mamre and Eshcol who joined Abraham in pursuing the four kings who had captured Lot (Genesis 14:13, 24). Separately, 1 Chronicles lists Aner as a town in the territory of Manasseh set aside for the Levites of Kohath's clan, alongside Taanach in the fuller parallel list at Joshua 21:25.

entries.title: Aniam (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: A son of Shemida, in Manasseh's genealogy.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Manassite, son of Shemida, listed in the tribal genealogy of Manasseh (1 Chr. 7:19).

entries.title: Anim
entries.summary: In Judah's hill country near Eshtemoa, south of Hebron, and commonly identified with the ruin of el-Ghuwein.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Anim, a town in the hill country of Judah near Eshtemoa, in the district south of Hebron (Josh. 15:50). It is commonly identified with the ruin of el-Ghuwein, southwest of Hebron.

entries.title: Anna (Woman living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: An old prophetess of the tribe of Asher. She had been widowed after seven years of marriage and spent decades in the temple praying and fasting. The day Mary and Joseph brought Jesus in, she came up just after Simeon had spoken, and she told others who were waiting for Jerusalem's redemption.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: An elderly prophetess of the tribe of Asher who, widowed after only seven years of marriage, spent decades in the Jerusalem temple in prayer and fasting (Luke 2:36-37). She arrived at the temple the same day Mary and Joseph brought the infant Jesus for presentation, just after the aged Simeon had spoken his own prophecy over the child, and she went on to speak of Jesus to others looking for Jerusalem's redemption. Luke pairs her with Simeon as a second, independent witness confirming the child's significance at the very start of his account.

entries.title: Annas (High Priest living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: High priest from AD 6 to 15, put in by the Roman legate Quirinius and removed by the procurator Valerius Gratus. Rome could take the office off him and apparently not the standing: the Gospels still call him high priest next to Caiaphas, who was his son-in-law.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Was high priest A.D. 6 to 15. In A.D. 25 Caiaphas, who had married the daughter of Annas (John 18:13), was raised to that office, and probably Annas was now made president of the Sanhedrim, or deputy or coadjutor of the high priest, and thus was also called high priest along with Caiaphas (Luke 3:2). By the Mosaic law the high-priesthood was held for life (Num. 3:10); and although Annas had been deposed by the Roman procurator, the Jews may still have regarded him as legally the high priest. Our Lord was first brought before Annas, and after a brief questioning of him (John 18:19-23) was sent to Caiaphas, when some members of the Sanhedrim had met, and the first trial of Jesus took place (Matt. 26:57-68). This examination of our Lord before Annas is recorded only by John. Annas was president of the Sanhedrim before which Peter and John were brought (Acts 4:6).
entries.checked: Dates AD 6 to 15, verified 2026-10-03 against Wikipedia's Annas article, which gives ten years, AD 6 to 15, appointed by Quirinius and deposed by Valerius Gratus. The record's own dictionary says AD 7 to 14 and is out by a year at each end.

witness.excerpt: This man deprived Ananus of the high priesthood, and appointed Ismael, the son of Phabi, to be high priest. He also deprived him in a little time… Joseph Caiaphas was made his successor.

entries.lukeNote: Luke names Annas and Caiaphas together as if there were two high priests at once (3:2), which sounds like an error until Josephus explains why: Rome deposed and replaced high priests on its own schedule through this whole period, and Annas (Ananus), long out of office, still held the real influence as Caiaphas's father-in-law.

entries.title: Antioch
entries.summary: Antioch on the Orontes, in Syria, the third largest city of the Roman Empire. Believers were first called Christians there, and its church sent Paul out on his journeys. It survives as the Turkish city of Antakya.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Antioch on the Orontes, in Syria, was the third largest city of the Roman Empire and became the base from which the early church sent missionaries to the Gentile world; it was there that believers were first called Christians. Barnabas and Paul both taught there, and the church at Antioch commissioned Paul's missionary journeys, sending him first to a different Antioch, in Pisidia, where he preached with initial success before opposition from local Jewish leaders drove him out; he returned there later to strengthen the church he had founded. Antioch on the Orontes survives today as the Turkish city of Antakya.

entries.title: Antioch
entries.summary: The other Antioch, in Pisidia. Paul preached there with some success until local Jewish leaders drove him out, and later he came back to strengthen the church.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Antipas (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Revelation 2:13 calls him a faithful martyr, killed at Pergamum, the city "where Satan's seat is." He is not Herod Antipas the tetrarch.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Antipas is named in Revelation 2:13 as a "faithful martyr" put to death at Pergamum, a city John describes as the place "where Satan's seat is," likely a reference to the imperial cult and the great altar of Zeus there. He shares his name with Herod Antipas the tetrarch, but is a distinct figure tied specifically to the church at Pergamum, not the Herodian ruler. Later Christian tradition, of uncertain reliability, identifies him as a bishop of Pergamum martyred by being burned alive inside a bronze bull under Domitian, though the New Testament itself records nothing more than his name and his faithful death.

entries.title: Antipatris
entries.summary: Herod the Great built it on the Roman road between Jerusalem and Caesarea and named it for his father Antipater. Soldiers brought Paul there by night, under guard, after a plot against his life came out. The site is Tel Aphek.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Antipatris was a city built by Herod the Great and named for his father Antipater, standing on the Roman road between Jerusalem and Caesarea. Roman soldiers brought Paul there under guard on the night march to Caesarea after a plot against his life was uncovered (Acts 23:31). The site is identified with Tel Aphek, where excavations have uncovered occupation layers running from the Bronze Age through the Roman period, including a fortress from the Hellenistic and Herodian era on the same tell.

entries.title: Antothijah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of Jeroham's sons, a Benjamite head of a family living in Jerusalem. The name is related to Anathoth, which hints at a family tie to that town, and nothing further is recorded of him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Antothijah was a Benjamite, one of the sons of Jeroham listed among the heads of families living in Jerusalem in 1 Chronicles 8:24-28. His name, meaning roughly "answers of Jehovah," is related to the place name Anathoth, suggesting a family connection to that Benjamite town near Jerusalem. Nothing further is recorded of him beyond this genealogical listing.

entries.title: Anub (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Coz's son, in Judah's genealogy, from the line of Ashhur who founded Tekoa.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A descendant of Judah listed among the sons of Coz in the genealogy of Ashhur, founder of Tekoa, in 1 Chronicles 4:8.

entries.title: Apelles (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Paul calls him "approved in Christ," which suggests faith that had been tested. Nothing else is known about him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Apelles was a Christian at Rome whom Paul greets in Romans 16:10, calling him "approved in Christ," language suggesting he had proven his faithfulness through some tested experience rather than merely holding correct belief. Nothing more is known about him.

witness.excerpt: At which Mattathias had great indignation, and ran upon him violently, with his sons, who had swords with them, and slew both the man himself that sacrificed, and Apelles the king's general, who compelled them to sacrifice, with a few of his soldiers.

entries.title: Apharsachites (Word sometimes translated as a title)
entries.summary: One of the peoples Assyria and Babylon moved into Samaria after deporting Israel. They turn up in Ezra among the officials writing to the king.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Apharsachites were one of several foreign peoples that Assyria and Babylon resettled in Samaria after deporting Israel's population, and they appear in Ezra among the officials who wrote to the Persian king opposing the rebuilding of the Jerusalem temple.

entries.title: Apharsite (Persia)
entries.summary: One of the peoples the Assyrians had resettled in Samaria. They wrote with the Dinaites, Elamites and others to the Persian king to stop Jerusalem being rebuilt.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Apharsites were among the peoples the Assyrians had resettled in Samaria who joined other groups, including the Dinaites and Elamites, in writing to the Persian king to oppose the rebuilding of Jerusalem.

entries.title: Aphek
entries.summary: The Philistines captured the ark of the covenant from Israel at Aphek. A later battle there went the other way, when Israel beat the Arameans after Elisha promised King Jehoash the victory.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Aphek
entries.summary: Two battles happened here. The Philistines took the ark from Israel at Aphek, and later Israel beat the Arameans here, exactly as Elisha had said.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Aphek was the site of at least two significant battles, one where the Philistines captured the ark of the covenant from Israel, and a later one where Israel defeated the Arameans after Elisha promised King Jehoash a resounding victory.

entries.title: Aphek
entries.summary: 2 Kings names him once, and nothing else is recorded.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Aphekah
entries.summary: A town in Judah's hill country, not one of the several places called Aphek even though the names share a root. Its site is unknown.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A town in the hill country of Judah (Joshua 15:53), distinct from the various places named Aphek elsewhere in Israel even though the names share the same root, meaning roughly "stronghold" or "enclosure." Its exact site is unknown.

entries.title: Aphiah (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of Saul's ancestors, named in the opening line of his genealogy and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: An ancestor of King Saul named in the opening of Saul's genealogy, otherwise unknown outside this one verse (1 Samuel 9:1).

entries.title: Apollonia
entries.summary: A stop on the Via Egnatia between Amphipolis and Thessalonica, passed through by Paul and Silas on the way from Philippi.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Apollonia, a Macedonian city on the Via Egnatia between Amphipolis and Thessalonica, one of the stops Paul and Silas passed through on their journey from Philippi to Thessalonica (Acts 17:1). Stretches of the Roman road itself have been traced and excavated across northern Greece.
