THE Jews also obtained honors from the kings of Asia when they became their auxiliaries; for Seleucus Nicator made them citizens in those cities which he built in Asia, and in the lower Syria, and in the metropolis itself, Antioch; and gave them privileges equal to those

entries.title: Asiel (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A Simeonite ancestor several generations back from Jehu, one of the tribal leaders in 1 Chronicles 4:35. Nothing else is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Asiel was a Simeonite ancestor named in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 4:35, appearing several generations back from Jehu, one of the tribal leaders listed there. Nothing else is recorded about him.

entries.title: Asnah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: His descendants were temple servants, Nethinim, who came back from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The ancestor of a family of temple servants, or Nethinim, who returned from Babylonian exile to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:43-50). The Nethinim were likely descended from war captives assigned to menial sanctuary duties, and their careful listing alongside priests and Levites shows how closely the returning community tracked lineage.

entries.title: Asnapper (King living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Identified with Ashurbanipal, the last powerful king of the Neo-Assyrian Empire, who resettled conquered peoples in Samaria. The opponents of the Jews name him in their letter asking the Persian king to stop Jerusalem being rebuilt. His library at Nineveh held thousands of tablets, the Epic of Gilgamesh among them.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Identified with Ashurbanipal, the last powerful king of the Neo-Assyrian Empire, who resettled conquered peoples in Samaria after putting down rebellions in his territory. Opponents of the Jews cite him by this name in a letter urging the Persian king to stop the rebuilding of Jerusalem (Ezra 4:10). Ashurbanipal's library at Nineveh, which held thousands of cuneiform tablets including the Epic of Gilgamesh, is now one of the richest surviving windows into the ancient Near East and is held largely in the British Museum.

entries.title: Aspatha (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Another of Haman's ten sons, killed after Haman's plot against the Jews fell apart.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Aspatha was one of the ten sons of Haman, the enemy of the Jews in the book of Esther, listed among those killed after Haman's plot against the Jewish people failed (Esther 9:7). Their deaths marked the reversal of Haman's plan and are still commemorated in the reading of Esther at Purim.

entries.title: Asrielites (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: The clan from Asriel, Manasseh's grandson through Gilead, in the Numbers 26 census.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Asrielites were the clan descended from Asriel, a grandson of Manasseh through Gilead, counted in the Numbers 26 census.

entries.title: Asshur (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Shem's son, whose name stuck to the land and empire of Assyria on the upper Tigris. Assyria became the great power of the eighth and seventh centuries BC, deported Israel's northern tribes after Samaria fell, and kept threatening Judah.
entries.books: Genesis, Numbers, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Psalm, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Lamentations, Ezekiel, Hosea, Micah, Nahum, Zephaniah, Zechariah
entries.label: 17 books
entries.dictNote: Asshur was a son of Shem whose name became attached to the land and empire of Assyria, centered on the upper Tigris in what is now northern Iraq. Its earliest capital, also called Asshur, later gave way to Nineveh and Calah as royal cities. Assyria grew into the dominant Near Eastern power of the eighth and seventh centuries BC, deporting Israel's northern tribes after Samaria's fall and repeatedly threatening Judah. The Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III, which depicts Israelite king Jehu bowing before the Assyrian king, is one of several royal inscriptions that corroborate Assyria's dealings with Israel and Judah as the Bible records them.

witness.excerpt: And for Asshur came forth the second portion, all the land of Asshur and Nineveh and Shinar and to the border of India, and it ascendeth and skirteth the river.
And these are the sons of Shem: Elam, and Asshur, and Arpachshad--this (son) was born two years after the flood--and Lud, and Aram.  19.
And the Lord sent a mighty wind  against the tower and overthrew it upon the earth, and behold it was between Asshur and Babylon in the land of Shinar, and they called its name 1688 A.M.

And Abram journeyed from Haran, and he took Sarai, his wife, and Lot his brother Haran's son, to the land of Canaan, and he came into †Asshur†,  and proceeded to Shechem, and dwelt near a lofty oak.  2.

entries.title: Asshurim (People, perhaps from Asshur)
entries.summary: One of the regions Abner made Ish-bosheth king over after Saul's death, with Gilead, Jezreel, Ephraim and Benjamin. Assyria was far beyond Israel's reach then, so most read it as a scribal slip for Asherites, the land of Asher.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Asshurim (also rendered Ashurites) names one of the regions over which Abner made Saul's son Ish-bosheth king after Saul's death, listed alongside Gilead, Jezreel, Ephraim, and Benjamin. Since Assyria itself lay far outside Israelite control at this date, most read the word as a scribal variant of Asherites, referring to territory belonging to the tribe of Asher, rather than to the distant Assyrian nation.

entries.title: Assir (Levite living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him twice, and he is a Levite from the wilderness years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Assir (Levite living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: A descendant of Korah, in the Levite line at Exodus 6:24 and 1 Chronicles 6:22.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Assir was a common Levitical name, borne by a descendant of Korah and by a son of Jeconiah listed in the royal genealogy after the exile.

entries.title: Assos
entries.summary: Paul walked to Assos while his companions sailed round, and he met them there on the way to Jerusalem. It was an Aegean port in Mysia, facing Lesbos. The ruins, a Doric temple of Athena among them, still stand above the Turkish village of Behramkale.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Assos was a port city on the Aegean coast of the Roman province of Asia, in the district of Mysia, facing the island of Lesbos. Paul traveled to Assos on foot while his companions sailed around by ship, and he rejoined them there to continue toward Jerusalem (Acts 20:13-14). The city's well-preserved ruins, including a Doric temple of Athena on its acropolis, still stand above the modern Turkish village of Behramkale.

entries.title: Asyncritos (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Greeted by Paul with Phlegon, Hermas, Patrobas, Hermes and others in Rome. Beyond his name and that group nothing is known.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Christian in Rome greeted by Paul along with Phlegon, Hermas, Patrobas, Hermes and others (Romans 16:14). Nothing beyond his name and membership in this Roman house-church group is known.

entries.title: Atarah (Woman living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Jerahmeel's second wife and mother of Onam.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Second wife of Jerahmeel and mother of Onam, named in the genealogies of Judah (1 Chronicles 2:26).

entries.title: Ataroth
entries.summary: Named twice, in Joshua, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ataroth
entries.summary: Reuben and Gad asked for Ataroth because the pasture was good for their livestock. Several towns east of the Jordan shared the name.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Ataroth was a town name shared by several sites east of the Jordan, requested by the tribes of Reuben and Gad for their livestock because of its good pastureland.

entries.title: Ataroth the house of Joab
entries.summary: One of the place-clans listed under Salma in Judah's genealogy, beside Bethlehem and the Netophathites. The awkward wording is probably a compound name, Atroth-beth-Joab, to tell this Ataroth from the others. Nobody has found it.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: "Ataroth the house of Joab" is one of several place-clans listed as descendants of Salma in the genealogy of Judah, alongside Bethlehem and the Netophathites (1 Chronicles 2:54). The awkward phrasing likely reflects a compound name, Atroth-beth-Joab, distinguishing this Ataroth, meaning "crowns," a name shared by several unrelated biblical towns, from those other places. Its precise location has not been identified.

entries.title: Ataroth-addar
entries.summary: A town on the line between Ephraim and Benjamin, in Joshua's boundary lists twice, and no confident modern identification has been made.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Ataroth-addar was a town on the boundary between the territories of Ephraim and Benjamin, mentioned twice in the tribal boundary descriptions of Joshua (Josh. 16:5; 18:13). Its name combines a word for crowns with a term of uncertain meaning, and it should be distinguished from other towns simply called Ataroth elsewhere in the same region. No confident modern identification has been established.

entries.title: Ater (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: He headed a family of returning exiles. Ezra's record also lists a family of temple gatekeepers by the same name.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Ater (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: He heads a family among the returning exiles. A family of gatekeepers carries the same name and is counted separately.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Ater was the head of a family among the returning exiles, and also the name of a family of temple gatekeepers listed separately in Ezra's record.

entries.title: Ater (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of 3 men called Ater. This one is a man from the exile and the return, named once in Nehemiah.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Athach
entries.summary: David sent it a share of the spoil he took back from the Amalekite raiders who hit Ziklag, a gift to the elders of Judah who had put up with him in his outlaw years. The name occurs nowhere else, and some suggest a copyist's slip for Ether.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Athach was one of the towns David sent spoil to after recovering the plunder Amalekite raiders had taken from Ziklag, a gift meant to reward the elders of Judah for tolerating his band's presence in their territory during his years as an outlaw (1 Samuel 30:26-30). Because the name occurs nowhere else in the Bible, some have suggested it is a copyist's error for Ether, a similarly spelled town in Judah's lowlands (Joshua 15:42). Its exact site, if distinct from Ether, is unidentified.

entries.title: Athaiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A descendant of Pharez, of Judah, who resettled in Jerusalem after the exile. 1 Chronicles 9:4 calls the same man, or his line, Uthai.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A descendant of Pharez, of the tribe of Judah, listed among those who resettled in Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile (Neh. 11:4). The parallel list in 1 Chronicles 9:4 calls the same man, or his line, Uthai.

entries.title: Athaliah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Athaliah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of 3 men called Athaliah. This one is a man from the exile and the return, named once in Ezra.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Athaliah (Queen living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Ahab and Jezebel's daughter, married into Judah's royal house. When her son Ahaziah was killed she took the throne and murdered nearly the whole royal family, the only woman to rule Judah in her own name. Six years later the priest Jehoiada brought out the infant Joash, who had survived, and she was executed.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Athaliah was Ahab and Jezebel's daughter, married into Judah's royal line, and when her son King Ahaziah was killed she seized the throne for herself by murdering nearly the entire royal family, the only woman to ever rule Judah in her own name. She reigned six years worshiping Baal in Jerusalem until the priest Jehoiada revealed that one grandson, the infant Joash, had survived, and staged a coup that ended with Athaliah's execution.

witness.excerpt: And it was Athaliah, the daughter of Ahab, whom he had married, who taught him to be a bad man in other respects, and also to worship foreign gods.
Jehoshaphat took for his son Jehoram to wife the daughter of Ahab, the king of the ten tribes, whose name was Athaliah.

entries.title: Athenian (Athens)
entries.summary: Luke notes that Athenians loved anything new, just before Paul's speech to the philosophers on the Areopagus, where he used their own poets and altars to speak of the God they worshipped without knowing.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Athenian designates an inhabitant of Athens, the center of Greek philosophy and learning. Luke notes the Athenians' fondness for novelty just before recounting Paul's speech to the philosophers at the Areopagus, where he engaged their own poets and altar inscriptions to introduce the God they worshipped without knowing.

witness.excerpt: Therefore the Athenian lawgiver, Solon, when he permitted men to marry their sisters by the same father, forbade them to marry those by the same mother.
Which shekel is an Hebrew money, and is equal to four Athenian drachmæ.
This hin is an ancient Hebrew measure; and is equivalent to two Athenian Choas [or Congiuses].

entries.title: Athens
entries.summary: The intellectual capital of the Greek world. Paul's sermon on the Areopagus there, quoting Greek poets and arguing with Greek philosophy while preaching the resurrection, is one of the most carefully fitted speeches in Acts.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Athens was the intellectual capital of the Greek world, and Paul's sermon there at the Areopagus, engaging Greek philosophy and quoting Greek poets while proclaiming the resurrection, is one of the most carefully adapted evangelistic speeches recorded in Acts.

witness.excerpt: In the mean time Antony abode at Athens, while Ventidius called for Silo and Herod to come to the war against the Parthians, but ordered them first to settle the affairs of Judea; so Herod willingly dismissed Silo to go to Ventidius, but he made an expedition
Its largeness was not less than the Pyrmum [at Athens], and had towards the city a double station for the ships.

About this time it was that Antony continued some time at Athens, and that Ventidius, who was now in Syria, sent for Silo, and commanded him to assist Herod, in the first place, to finish the present war, and then to send for their confederates for the war they were themselves engage
So as the pupil is to the eye, as the power of reasoning to the soul, thus is Athens in Greece.

This was done in the ninth year of Hyrcanus the high priest and ethnarch, in the month Panemus.\" Hyreanus also received honors from the people of Athens, as having been useful to them on many occasions.

entries.title: Athlai (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of Bebai's descendants who had married foreign women during the exile and agreed to separate from them under Ezra. He appears only in this list.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of the descendants of Bebai who had married foreign women during the exile and agreed to separate from them under Ezra's reforms (Ezra 10:28). He appears only in this list of names.

entries.title: Atroth
entries.summary: Short for Atroth-shophan, a town in Gilead that Gad rebuilt and fortified. Its site is unknown.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Short form of Atroth-shophan, one of the towns in Gilead that the tribe of Gad rebuilt and fortified after the conquest of the Transjordan (Numbers 32:35). Its precise site is unknown.

entries.title: Attai (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Born into a line of Judah that ran through a marriage between an Israelite woman and her Egyptian servant.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Attai was a common name, borne by one of David's Gadite warriors and by a descendant of Judah through a marriage between an Israelite woman and her Egyptian servant.

entries.title: Attai (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 3 men called Attai. This one is a man from the divided-kingdom years, named once in 2 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Attai (Warrior living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a warrior from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Attalia
entries.summary: Paul and Barnabas sailed home to Antioch from this port in Pamphylia at the end of their first journey. Attalus II Philadelphus of Pergamon founded it and named it for himself. It is Antalya now, and parts of the old harbour and wall are still standing.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A port city of Pamphylia in Asia Minor, founded in the second century BC by Attalus II Philadelphus, king of Pergamon, and named after him. Paul and Barnabas sailed from here back to Antioch at the close of their first missionary journey (Acts 14:25); the city survives today as Antalya, Turkey, where sections of the ancient harbor and city wall are still standing.

entries.title: Augustus (Emperor living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: The first Roman emperor, under whom Christ was born. His decree that all the world should be taxed is what put the birth in Bethlehem. The name is a title, majesty, first given him by the senate, and later emperors carried it too.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The cognomen of the first Roman emperor, C. Julius Caesar Octavianus, during whose reign Christ was born (Luke 2:1). His decree that “all the world should be taxed” was the divinely ordered occasion of Jesus’ being born, according to prophecy (Micah 5:2), in Bethlehem. This name being simply a title meaning “majesty” or “venerable,” first given to him by the senate (B.C. 27), was borne by succeeding emperors. Before his death (A.D. 14) he associated Tiberius with him in the empire (Luke 3:1), by whom he was succeeded.

witness.excerpt: Accordingly, he restored him his diadem again; and encouraged him to exhibit himself as great a friend to himself as he had been to Antony, and then had him in great esteem.

entries.lukeNote: Named exactly once, for the census that puts Joseph and Mary on the road to Bethlehem (2:1). Josephus's Augustus (still Octavian here) is the same emperor deciding Herod's fate after Actium, the decree in Luke and the patronage in Josephus are two small views of the same distant, absolute power over Judea.

entries.title: Ava (Avva)
entries.summary: Also Ivah, a city in Mesopotamia from which the Assyrians sent settlers to fill Samaria after 722 BC. Sennacherib's field commander later named Ava's conquered gods, with those of Hamath and Sepharvaim, to push Hezekiah into surrender.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Ava, also called Ivah, was a city in Assyria's Mesopotamian heartland from which the Assyrians deported settlers to repopulate Samaria after Israel's exile in 722 BC (2 Kings 17:24). Sennacherib's field commander later cited Ava's conquered gods, alongside those of Hamath and Sepharvaim, to taunt Hezekiah into surrendering Jerusalem (2 Kings 18:34; 19:13). It is commonly identified with Hit, an ancient town on the Euphrates known for its natural bitumen springs.

entries.title: Aven
entries.summary: A Hebrew word for nothingness, used to mock real place names. Hosea turns Bethel into Beth-aven, house of vanity, for Jeroboam's golden calf. Ezekiel 30:17 uses it for On, the Egyptian city better known as Heliopolis.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Aven is not a person but a Hebrew word meaning nothingness or vanity, used in several places as a mocking wordplay on real place names. Hosea applies it to Bethel, calling it Beth-aven, 'house of vanity,' because of the golden calf Jeroboam had set up there (Hosea 4:15; 10:8). Ezekiel 30:17 uses it for the Egyptian city of On, better known as Heliopolis, and Amos 1:5 uses it for a Syrian city usually identified with Baalbec.

entries.title: Avim
entries.summary: A town in Benjamin's territory, and not the Avvites of the coast near Gaza. Its site is unknown.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Avim was a town allotted to the tribe of Benjamin, listed among its territory's settlements (Josh. 18:23). It is a different Avim from the coastal people called the Avvites, who lived farther southwest near Gaza before being displaced by the Caphtorim (Deut. 2:23); this town's exact site is unknown.

entries.title: Avims (Avva)
entries.summary: The Avvim lived in villages around Gaza before the Caphtorim, from Crete, drove them out. 2 Kings 17:31 gives the same name to settlers from Avva placed in Samaria by the Assyrians.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: The Avvim, also spelled Avims, were a pre-Israelite people who lived in villages in the region of Gaza before being driven out and largely destroyed by the Caphtorim, migrants from Crete associated with the Philistines (Deuteronomy 2:23; Joshua 13:3). The same Hebrew name is applied in 2 Kings 17:31 to settlers from Avva whom the Assyrians relocated to Samaria after deporting the northern kingdom's population; those settlers brought their own gods, Nibhaz and Tartak, with them.

entries.title: Avith
entries.summary: The city of Hadad son of Bedad, one of the early kings of Edom before Israel had kings of its own. He beat the Midianites in the territory of Moab.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Edomite city of Hadad son of Bedad, another of the early Edomite kings who ruled before Israel's monarchy began; he defeated the Midianites in the territory of Moab (Gen. 36:35; 1 Chr. 1:46).

witness.excerpt: And ’Asâm died, and ’Adâth,  the son of Barad,  who slew Midian in the field of Moab, reigned in his stead, and the name of his city was Avith.

entries.title: Azal
entries.summary: Zechariah says that when the Mount of Olives splits in two, the valley will run as far as Azal. The same name, as Azel, belongs to a Benjamite descendant of Saul through Jonathan, listed with his six sons in Chronicles.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Azal, also spelled Azel, is used in the Hebrew Bible for both a person and a place, though it is the same underlying name. Azel was a great-great-grandson of King Saul through Jonathan, a Benjamite listed with his six sons in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 8:37-38 and 9:43-44. Separately, the prophet Zechariah uses "Azal" as a place name near Jerusalem, saying that when the Mount of Olives splits in two, the resulting valley will reach "as far as Azal" (Zechariah 14:5), though its precise location is uncertain and some translators render the phrase simply as "very near."

entries.title: Azaliah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Shaphan's father. Shaphan was the royal scribe who read the newly found Book of the Law to King Josiah.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Azaliah was the father of Shaphan, the royal scribe who read the newly discovered Book of the Law to King Josiah and helped spark Josiah's religious reforms (2 Kings 22:3; 2 Chronicles 34:8).

entries.title: Azaniah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Father of Jeshua, a Levite who set his seal to the covenant renewed under Nehemiah.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Azaniah was a Levite, the father of Jeshua, one of the Levites who set their seal to the covenant renewed under Nehemiah after the exile (Nehemiah 10:9).

entries.title: Azarael (Levite living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Chronicles names him once, among David's musicians and officers.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Azarel was a common name among Levitical musicians and military officers in David's organization, appearing in the lists of 1 Chronicles.

entries.title: Azarael (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)

entries.dictNote: Azariah was a common name shared by many Old Testament figures, most notably serving as an alternate name for King Uzziah of Judah, and also as the birth name of Abednego, one of Daniel's three friends thrown into the fiery furnace in Babylon for refusing to worship Nebuchadnezzar's golden image.

entries.title: Azaz (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A Reubenite east of the Jordan, Bela's father. Nothing further is recorded of him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Azaz was a Reubenite, father of Bela, named in the genealogy of the tribe of Reuben settled east of the Jordan (1 Chr. 5:8). Nothing further is recorded of him.

entries.title: Azaziah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of the musicians appointed under David, at 1 Chronicles 15:21.

entries.title: Azaziah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A Levitical name. One Azaziah was a musician under David; this one is an overseer in the temple stores.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Azaziah was a common Levitical name, including a musician appointed under David and the father of one of Solomon's district governors.

entries.title: Azbuk (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: There are two Nehemiahs, and Azbuk fathered the other one, who ruled half the district of Beth-zur and repaired a section of Jerusalem's wall. He is there only to name his son.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The father of a different Nehemiah than the book's main figure, this one identified as ruler of half the district of Beth-zur and credited with repairing a section of Jerusalem's wall (Neh. 3:16). He appears only to identify his son in this list of wall-builders.

entries.title: Azekah
entries.summary: A fortified town in Judah's Shephelah. Joshua routed five Amorite kings near it in a hailstorm. A Lachish ostracon written during Nebuchadnezzar's last campaign says the writer is watching for Lachish's signal fires but cannot see Azekah, which some read as Azekah already fallen and others as a line of sight he never had.
entries.label: 5 books
entries.dictNote: Azekah was a fortified town in the Shephelah of Judah, the scene of Joshua's rout of five Amorite kings during a hailstorm (Joshua 10:10-11) and later resettled by returning exiles (Nehemiah 11:30). One of the Lachish ostraca, letters written by a Judean officer during Nebuchadnezzar's final campaign against Judah, report watching for signal fires from Lachish because "we cannot see Azekah," widely read as evidence the town had already fallen, which corroborates Jeremiah 34:7's note that Azekah and Lachish were the last fortified cities of Judah still holding out. Letter 4 says the writer watches for Lachish's signals 'but we do not see Azekah'. That is often read as meaning Azekah had already fallen, but it can as easily be read geographically, that Azekah's beacons were not visible from where the writer stood. Both readings are current.
entries.checked: Lachish Letter 4 reads that the writer watches for Lachish's beacons 'but we do not see Azekah'. The fallen-city reading is one of two: others take it geographically, that the writer's position had no sight line. My line said 'widely read', which overstated it. Verified 2026-10-04.

witness.excerpt: Now the Philistines gathered themselves together again, no very long time afterward; and having gotten together a great army, they made war against the Israelites: and having seized a place between Shochoh and Azekah, they there pitched their camp.

entries.title: Azem (Ezem)
entries.summary: Also Ezem, a town in the far south of Judah later given to Simeon. Its site in the Negev has not been identified with confidence.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Azem, also spelled Ezem, was a town in the extreme south of Judah's territory (Joshua 15:29) that was later assigned to Simeon, whose inheritance was carved out from within Judah's larger allotment (Joshua 19:3; 1 Chronicles 4:29). Its exact site in the Negev has not been identified with confidence.

entries.title: Azgad (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A large family among the returning exiles carried his name, listed by household in Ezra and Nehemiah both.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Azgad was the head of a large family among the returning exiles, listed by household in both Ezra and Nehemiah's records.

entries.title: Azgad (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Nehemiah names him once, and he is a man from the exile and the return.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Aziel (Singer living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: He played the psaltery when the ark was brought up to Jerusalem. The name seems to be short for Jaaziel, two verses earlier in the same list.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Aziel was a Levite appointed by David to play a stringed instrument, the psaltery, when the ark of the covenant was brought up to Jerusalem (1 Chr. 15:20). His name appears to be a shortened form of Jaaziel, named two verses earlier in the same list.

entries.title: Aziza (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Ezra 10:27 names him in Zattu's family, one of the men who had married a foreign wife after the return and had to send her away under Ezra's reforms.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Aziza was a layman from the family of Zattu who had married a foreign wife after the return from Babylonian exile and was required to divorce her under Ezra's reforms (Ezra 10:27). He is one of over a hundred men named in this list who complied with the covenant to end intermarriage with surrounding peoples.

entries.title: Azmaveth (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him twice, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Azmaveth (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 4 men called Azmaveth. This one is a man from the divided-kingdom years, named once in 1 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Azmaveth (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A man from the divided-kingdom years, and 1 Chronicles is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Azmaveth (Warrior living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: He fought for David and made the list of David's thirty. The same name belonged to a town near Jerusalem and to several other men. His own record is a line in each of the two lists of the thirty.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Azmaveth was a town near Jerusalem, in the territory associated with Anathoth, whose residents are twice listed among those who returned from Babylonian exile. The name was also borne by several different men: one of David's thirty mighty warriors, a Benjamite archer who joined David at Ziklag, and an official who oversaw the royal storehouses under David and Solomon.

entries.title: Azmon
entries.summary: On Israel's southern border, near the Wadi el-Arish, the Brook of Egypt that marked the southwest edge of the land. Nobody has found the site.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A point on the southern boundary of the promised land, near the Wadi el-Arish, the Brook of Egypt that marked Israel's southwestern border (Num. 34:4-5; Josh. 15:4). Its exact location remains unidentified.

entries.title: Aznoth-tabor
entries.summary: The summits of Tabor, or the ears of Tabor, one of the marks on Naphtali's boundary near Mount Tabor. It may have been a cluster of hills rather than a town.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Aznoth-tabor, "the summits" or "ears of Tabor," marked one of the boundary points of the tribe of Naphtali's territory, near Mount Tabor (Joshua 19:34). It may refer to a cluster of hills rather than a town proper. Its precise location is unidentified.

entries.title: Azor (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: In Matthew's genealogy of Jesus he sits between Eliakim and Zadok, one link in the chain from Zerubbabel down to Joseph. Nothing else about him is recorded.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Azor appears in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus as the son of Eliakim and the father of Zadok, one link in the postexilic chain connecting Zerubbabel to Joseph, husband of Mary (Matthew 1:13-14). He is not mentioned elsewhere in Scripture and has no independent narrative beyond this genealogical placement.

entries.title: Azotus (Ashdod)
entries.summary: Ashdod's Greek name, and where Philip the evangelist turned up after he baptized the Ethiopian official, carrying on along the coastal road.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The Greek name for Ashdod, one of the five Philistine cities, used in the account of Philip the evangelist's ministry along the coastal road after he baptized the Ethiopian official (Acts 8:40). The city retained this Hellenized name throughout the Roman period.

witness.excerpt: For Titus went from Gischala to Cesarea, and Vespasian from Cesarea to Jamnia, and Azotus; and took them both: and when he had put garrisons into them, he came back with a great number of the people, who were come over to him, upon his giving them his right hand for their preservation.

The Danites lot included all that part of the valley which respects the sun- setting, and were bounded by Azotus and Dora: as also they had all Jamnia and Gath, from Ekron to that mountain where the tribe of Judah begins.

entries.title: Azriel (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Azriel (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A tribal leader of Manasseh, named once in Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Azriel (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A tribal leader of Manasseh carries the name, and so does the father of an official Jehoiakim sent to arrest Jeremiah.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Azriel was a common name, borne by a tribal leader of Manasseh and by the father of an official King Jehoiakim sent to arrest Jeremiah and Baruch.

entries.title: Azrikam (Levite living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: He was a palace official, killed alongside King Ahaz's son when the invasion came.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Azrikam was a common name, including a palace official executed along with King Ahaz's son during an invasion, and a descendant of David listed in the royal genealogy.

entries.title: Azrikam (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of several men with this name, this one listed twice in the same family line, at 1 Chronicles 8:38 and again at 9:44.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Azrikam (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 4 men called Azrikam. This one is a man from the divided-kingdom years, named once in 1 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Azrikam (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A man from the divided-kingdom years, and 2 Chronicles is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Azubah (Woman living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names her twice, and she is a woman from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Azubah (Woman living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Jehoshaphat's mother. Kings and Chronicles both name her in the notice of his reign and give her nothing more.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Azubah was King Jehoshaphat's mother, and also the name of a wife of Caleb listed in the genealogies of Chronicles.

entries.title: Azur (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Jeremiah names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Azur (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of 3 men called Azur. This one is a man from the exile and the return, named once in Ezekiel.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Azur (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: He signed the covenant under Nehemiah, and that is all the record holds of him. The name, properly Azzur, means he that assists.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Azur (properly Azzur, meaning “he that assists”) is the name of at least three men in the Old Testament: a covenant-signer under Nehemiah (Nehemiah 10:17), the father of the false prophet Hananiah who broke Jeremiah's symbolic yoke and predicted a swift return from exile that never came (Jeremiah 28:1), and the father of Jaazaniah, one of the corrupt princes Ezekiel saw plotting evil counsel in a vision (Ezekiel 11:1).

entries.title: Azzah (Gaza)
entries.summary: Gaza, under a more literal spelling. The southernmost of the five chief Philistine cities, it sat on the coastal road between Egypt and Canaan.
entries.books: Genesis, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, Jeremiah, Amos, Zephaniah, Zechariah
entries.label: 11 books
entries.dictNote: Azzah is the more literal transliteration of the name usually rendered Gaza in English Bibles, the southernmost of the five chief Philistine cities on the coastal road between Egypt and Canaan.

witness.excerpt: But Gaza and Ekron escaped them: for they, lying in a flat countrey, and having a great number of chariots, they sorely galled those that attacked them.
3, reckons Gaza, which had been a free city, among the cities given Herod by Augustus, and yet implies that Herod had made Costobarus a governor of it before, Antiq.
Now in the lot of this tribe there were the cities of Ascalon and Gaza.

Besides those that had been demolished, and also of the maritime cities, Gaza, and Joppa, and Dora, and Strato's Tower; which last Herod rebuilt after a glorious manner, and adorned with havens and temples, and changed its name to Caesarea.

entries.title: Azzan (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Paltiel's father, named only so we know whose son the Issachar leader was when the land of Canaan was divided.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Azzan was the father of Paltiel, the leader from the tribe of Issachar appointed to help divide the land of Canaan among the tribes after the conquest (Numbers 34:26). He is mentioned only to identify his son.

entries.title: Baal (A male deity in the Old Testament)
entries.summary: The Canaanite storm god, the power people believed sent the rain and made the crops grow. Worshipping him was the temptation Israel never shook, and the Old Testament fights it from the judges onward.
entries.books: Judges, 1 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Jeremiah, Hosea, Zephaniah, Romans
entries.label: 10 books
entries.dictNote: Baal was the chief storm and fertility god of the Canaanite pantheon, worshiped as the power behind rain, crops, and fertility, and the Old Testament treats Baal worship as Israel's most persistent and dangerous temptation, from the judges period through the divided monarchy. Elijah's contest on Mount Carmel, where fire from heaven answered his prayer while Baal's prophets got no response from their own god, is the Bible's most direct confrontation between the two.

witness.excerpt: After which they then ran to the house of Baal; which Athaliah and her husband Jehoram had built, to the dishonour of the God of their fathers, and to the honour of Ahab; and demolished it, and slew Mattan, that had his priesthood.

Spanheim takes notice here, that in the worship of Mithra (the god of the Persians) the priests cut themselves in the same manner as did these priests in their invocation of Baal (the god of the Phoenicians).

entries.title: Baal (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 3 men called Baal. This one is a man from the divided-kingdom years, named once in 1 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Baal (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him twice, and he is a man from the united kingdom.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Baal-berith (A male deity in the Old Testament)
entries.summary: Lord of the covenant. Israel went after this Canaanite god at Shechem once Gideon was dead, and his shrine there comes up again in the next chapter.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Baal-berith, meaning "lord of the covenant," was not a person but a Canaanite god worshipped at Shechem after Gideon's death, when Israel again fell into idolatry (Judges 8:33). The same shrine is later called simply the house of the god "El-berith" or "Berith," and it funded the violent bid for kingship by Gideon's son Abimelech (Judges 9:4, 46).

entries.title: Baal-gad (Mount Hermon)
entries.summary: The farthest north Joshua's conquests reached: a Canaanite town in the valley under Mount Hermon, named for the Baal worshipped there. It lay near the sources of the Jordan.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Baal-gad, named for the worship of Baal there, was a Canaanite town in the valley below Mount Hermon and marked the northernmost point Joshua's conquests reached (Joshua 11:17; 12:7). It lay near the sources of the Jordan River, in the same district later called Baal-hermon, and is often identified with the site later known as Panias or Banias, later renamed Caesarea Philippi.

entries.title: Baal-hamon (Mount Hermon)
entries.summary: Where Solomon kept a vineyard and let it out to tenants for a hefty rent, in a closing verse of the Song of Solomon.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Baal-hamon, meaning lord of a multitude, was the site of an extensive vineyard belonging to Solomon, mentioned in a closing verse of the Song of Solomon that he leased out to tenants for a substantial rent (Song of Sol. 8:11). Its location is unknown, though some have proposed identifying it with Baal-gad near Mount Hermon or with a site near Dothan in central Israel.

entries.title: Baal-hanan (King living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: An Edomite king, from the list in Genesis of rulers who reigned before Israel had a king of its own.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Baal-hanan was an early Edomite king, listed in Genesis among the rulers who governed before Israel had any king of its own.

entries.title: Baal-hanan (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Baal-hazor
entries.summary: Absalom held a sheep-shearing feast there, on the border of Ephraim and Benjamin, and used it to have his men kill Amnon. It was revenge for what Amnon had done to their sister Tamar.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Baal-hazor, on the border between Ephraim and Benjamin, was where Absalom held a sheep-shearing feast and used the occasion to have his men murder his half-brother Amnon, in revenge for Amnon's rape of their sister Tamar (2 Samuel 13:23-29). The killing set off the chain of events that led to Absalom's exile and later revolt against David. The site is generally identified with modern Tell Asur, northeast of Bethel, the highest peak in the central hill country.

entries.title: Baal-hermon (Mount Hermon)
entries.summary: Two things carry the name. One is a town near Mount Hermon where the half-tribe of Manasseh lived, maybe the same place as Baal-gad. The other is the mountain itself, on the list of Canaanite strongholds.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Two references share this name. One is a town near Mount Hermon inhabited by the half-tribe of Manasseh, possibly the same as Baal-gad (1 Chr. 5:23). The other is the mountain itself, listed among the strongholds of Canaanite peoples that Israel failed to fully conquer during the period of the judges (Judges 3:3).

entries.title: Baal-meon
entries.summary: It was rebuilt by Reuben, a town east of the Jordan known by several names, Beth-baal-meon and Beth-meon among them. The land around it changed hands more than once.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Baal-meon was a town east of the Jordan rebuilt by the tribe of Reuben and known by several related names, including Beth-baal-meon and Beth-meon (Numbers 32:38; Ezekiel 25:9). It lay in territory that passed back and forth between Israel and Moab, and the Moabite king Mesha claims on his own inscription, the Moabite Stone, to have rebuilt Baal-meon and built a reservoir there, an extrabiblical confirmation of the town's existence. It is identified with the modern site of Ma'in, southeast of Heshbon.

entries.title: Baal-peor (A male deity in the Old Testament)
entries.summary: Israel, nearly at the promised land, got drawn into worshipping this Moabite god through Moabite women. A plague followed, and it took Phinehas acting in zeal to stop it.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Baal of Peor was a Moabite deity Israel was seduced into worshiping through relationships with Moabite women shortly before entering the promised land, provoking a plague that Phinehas's zealous action finally stopped.

entries.title: Baal-perazim
entries.summary: David named it, lord of breakthroughs more or less, after beating the Philistines there early in his reign over all Israel and comparing the win to floodwater breaking through.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Baal-perazim, meaning roughly lord of breakthroughs, was the name David gave to the site where he defeated the Philistines early in his reign over all Israel, comparing the victory to a flood bursting through (2 Sam. 5:20; 1 Chr. 14:11). Isaiah later refers to the same event at Mount Perazim (Isa. 28:21). The location lay near the Valley of Rephaim southwest of Jerusalem.

entries.title: Baal-shalisha
entries.summary: A man from here brought Elisha twenty barley loaves and some fresh grain, and the prophet fed a hundred people with it. The place was in the district of Shalisha, apparently not far from Gilgal.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Baal-shalisha lay in the district of Shalisha, apparently not far from Gilgal, and is remembered for the man who brought Elisha twenty barley loaves and fresh grain, which the prophet multiplied to feed a hundred people (2 Kings 4:42-44). The episode anticipates Jesus' feeding miracles in the Gospels. It is usually located near Sirisia, north of Lydda, though the identification is not certain.

entries.title: Baal-tamar
entries.summary: Lord of the palm tree. It sat near Gibeah in Benjamin. The other tribes regrouped there for their final assault on Benjamin, in the civil war the outrage at Gibeah set off.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Baal-tamar, "lord of the palm tree," was a site near Gibeah in Benjamin's territory where the other Israelite tribes regrouped for their final assault against Benjamin during the civil war sparked by the outrage at Gibeah (Judges 20:33). The name likely refers to a Baal shrine marked by a notable palm tree, possibly the same palm associated with the judge Deborah a few chapters earlier (Judges 4:5). Its exact site has not been identified.

entries.title: Baal-zebub (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Lord of the flies, the Philistine god of Ekron. King Ahaziah of Israel sent messengers to ask him about his health. Elijah confronted it by asking whether Israel had no God of its own.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Baal-zebub, meaning lord of the flies, was the Philistine god of Ekron that King Ahaziah of Israel sent messengers to consult about his health, a decision Elijah confronted directly by asking whether Israel had no God of its own to ask instead.

entries.title: Baal-zephon
entries.summary: A landmark on the shore by the Israelites' last camp before they crossed the sea. Exodus names it in the crossing story and Numbers in the list of wilderness stops.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Baal-zephon was a site on the shore near where the Israelites camped before crossing the sea during the exodus, mentioned as a landmark in both the crossing narrative and the wilderness itinerary (Exodus 14:2, 9; Numbers 33:7). The name reflects the Canaanite storm god Baal-Zaphon, whose cult had spread into Egypt's eastern Delta, and Egyptian records of the period independently mention a place of that name near the frontier. Its exact location along the ancient shoreline is still debated.

entries.title: Baalah
entries.summary: Named once, in Joshua, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Baalah (Kiriath-jearim)
entries.summary: Another name for Kiriath-jearim, the town that kept the ark of the covenant for twenty years until David took it to Jerusalem. A second Baalah, near Beersheba, turns up later in the same chapter of Joshua.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Baalah was an alternate name for Kiriath-jearim, the town where the ark of the covenant rested for twenty years before David brought it to Jerusalem.

entries.title: Baalath
entries.summary: Dan was given this town, and Solomon later fortified it as one of his store cities. The name means mistress or lady.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Baalath was a town assigned to the tribe of Dan (Joshua 19:44) that Solomon later fortified along with other store cities as part of his building program (1 Kings 9:18; 2 Chronicles 8:6). Its name, meaning mistress or lady, reflects Canaanite goddess worship connected to the site before Israel's conquest. Its exact location is uncertain, though it lay somewhere in the Shephelah near Gezer.

witness.excerpt: Moreover, he built two other cities not far from it, Beth-horon was the name of one of them, and Baalath of the other.

entries.title: Baalath
entries.summary: Named once, in Joshua, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Baalath-beer
entries.summary: Baalah of the well, a town of Simeon's on the southern edge of Judah's land, probably the one the parallel list calls just Baal.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Baalath-beer, meaning Baalah of the well, was a town assigned to the tribe of Simeon on the southern frontier of Judah's territory (Josh. 19:8). It is likely the same town called simply Baal in the parallel list of Simeonite towns in 1 Chronicles 4:33.

entries.title: Baale of Judah (Kiriath-jearim)
entries.summary: The name 2 Samuel 6:2 uses for Kiriath-jearim, where the ark stayed for years before David brought it up to Jerusalem.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Baale of Judah, an alternate name for Kiriath-jearim, the town where the ark of the covenant rested for years before David brought it up to Jerusalem (2 Sam. 6:2; 1 Chr. 13:6). Excavations at Kiriath-jearim's traditional site, Tell Deir el-Azhar, have uncovered a massive stone platform that some archaeologists have proposed was built to support a sanctuary, consistent with the town's role as long-term keeper of the ark.

entries.title: Baalis (King living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: King of the Ammonites when Babylon took Judah. He put Ishmael son of Nethaniah up to murdering Gedaliah, the governor Babylon had left over the people still in the land.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: King of the Ammonites during the Babylonian conquest of Judah, Baalis incited Ishmael son of Nethaniah to assassinate Gedaliah, the governor Babylon had appointed over the remnant left in the land, an act that triggered further Jewish flight into Egypt (Jeremiah 40:14; 41:1-3).

witness.excerpt: Now there was of the royal family one Ishmael, a wicked man, and very crafty; who during the siege of Jerusalem fled to Baalis, the King of the Ammonites, and abode with him during that time.

entries.title: Baana (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Solomon's district officer for the Megiddo and Taanach region, one of the men who supplied the royal household.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Baana (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of Solomon's twelve district officers, over the country around Taanach and Megiddo.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Three men carry this name. Two were district officers who supplied provisions for Solomon's royal household, one stationed in the region of Megiddo and Taanach (1 Kings 4:12), the other a son of Hushai in a different district (1 Kings 4:16). A third Baana was the father of Zadok, one of those who helped repair the wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah (Nehemiah 3:4).

entries.title: Baanah (David's compatriots living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: He and his brother Rechab murdered Ish-bosheth, the son of Saul who was still alive, thinking David would thank them. David had them executed for killing an innocent man in his own bed.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Baanah, along with his brother Rechab, assassinated Ish-bosheth, Saul's surviving son, hoping to win favor with David, but David had them executed instead for murdering an innocent man in his own bed.

entries.title: Baanah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of 4 men called Baanah. This one is a man from the exile and the return, named twice in Ezra and Nehemiah.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Baanah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A man from the exile and the return, and Nehemiah is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Baanah (Warrior living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: 2 Samuel and 1 Chronicles name him twice, and he is a warrior from the united kingdom.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Baara (Woman living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Shaharaim, a Benjamite, had wives named Hushim and Baara. He sent both away, then had more children in Moab by Hodesh. Baara is named nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Baara was one of two wives of Shaharaim, a Benjamite listed in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles. Shaharaim sent her away, along with his other wife Hushim, before fathering more children in Moab by his wife Hodesh (1 Chronicles 8:8). Nothing else is recorded about her.

witness.excerpt: Nor does Josephus's strange account of the root Baara (Of the War, B.

entries.title: Baaseiah (Levite living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Further back in Asaph's line, through the Kohathite branch of Levi. Asaph was David's chief musician, and this Levite is one name in the list that traces him back.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Levite ancestor of Asaph, David's chief musician, named in the genealogy tracing Asaph's line back through the Kohathite branch of Levi (1 Chronicles 6:25-40).

entries.title: Baasha (King living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: He killed Nadab, Israel's second king, and wiped out the rest of Jeroboam's family to take the northern throne. That fulfilled a prophecy against Jeroboam's line. Baasha's own violence brought the same kind of end on his house.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Baasha assassinated Israel's second king, Nadab, and wiped out the rest of Jeroboam's family to seize the throne of northern Israel himself, fulfilling a prophecy against that dynasty even as his own violent methods brought a matching prophecy of destruction down on his own house soon after.

witness.excerpt: I now return to Baasha, the king of the multitude of the Israelites, who slew Nadab, the son of Jeroboam, and retained the government.

In these two years he made an expedition against Gibbethon, a city of the Philistines, and continued the siege in order to take it; but he was conspired against while he was there by a friend of his, whose name was Baasha, the son of Ahijah, and was slain; which Baasha took the kingdom after the other's death, and destroyed the whole house of Jeroboam.

entries.title: Babel (Babylon)
entries.summary: The plain in Shinar where people, still speaking one language after the flood, set out to build a city and a tower reaching to the heavens and make a name for themselves. God answered by confusing their language.
entries.books: Genesis, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther, Psalm, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, Micah, Zechariah
entries.label: 14 books
entries.dictNote: Babel is the plain in Shinar where humanity, still speaking one language after the flood, attempted to build a city and a tower reaching to the heavens to make a name for themselves, and God responded by confusing their language and scattering them across the earth. The name is closely tied to Babylon, built in the same region and remembered throughout Scripture as a symbol of human pride set against God.

witness.excerpt:

 countries in which Abraham had been brought up and had lived most of his time; so that we c

entries.title: Babylon
entries.summary: The Mesopotamian empire that destroyed Jerusalem and its temple in 586 BC and carried Judah off. Later Scripture, Revelation included, uses its name as shorthand for worldly power.
entries.books: Ezra, Daniel, Matthew, Acts, 1 Peter, Revelation
entries.label: 6 books
entries.dictNote: Babylon was the dominant Mesopotamian empire that destroyed Jerusalem and its temple in 586 BC and deported Judah's population, and its name became prophetic shorthand throughout Scripture, including in Revelation, for worldly power arrayed against God. The Tower of Babel narrative is set in the same region, tying Babylon's later arrogance to humanity's earliest recorded act of collective pride.

witness.excerpt:
Now Babylon and Mesopotamia, and the
 nation of the Chaldaeans, do not receive the custom of sacrificing their children; and these are the
 countries in which Abraham had been brought up and had lived most of his time; so that we c
Moreover there was now in Babylon a righteous man, and one that enjoyed a great reputation among the multitude.

entries.title: Babylonia
entries.summary: It was the region of lower Mesopotamia, around the Euphrates and Tigris, with Babylon as its capital. Its armies conquered Judah in 586 BC and destroyed Jerusalem and Solomon's temple.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Babylonia was the ancient region and empire of lower Mesopotamia, centered on the Euphrates and Tigris valleys with Babylon as its capital. Its armies conquered the kingdom of Judah in 586 BC, destroyed Jerusalem and Solomon's temple, and deported much of the population, an event corroborated by Babylonian ration tablets that name the exiled Judean king Jehoiachin among captives at Nebuchadnezzar's court. Babylonia's own dominance ended when it fell to Cyrus the Persian in 539 BC, an event the Cyrus Cylinder itself commemorates. In Ezra 4:9 the name refers to Babylonian officials and settlers who opposed the rebuilding of Jerusalem after the exile.

witness.excerpt: And for this reason it was that the city was called Babylon .” But as to the plan of Shinar, in the country of Babylonia, Hestiæus mentions it, when he says thus, “Such of the Priests as were saved took the sacred vessels of Jupiter Enyalius, and came to Shinar of Babylonia.”
40.] A very sad calamity now befel the Jews that were in Mesopotamia: and especially those that dwelt in Babylonia.

entries.title: Baca (Valley of Hinnom)
entries.summary: In Psalm 84:6 the dry Valley of Baca turns into a place of springs for pilgrims heading to Jerusalem, and the name probably plays on balsam or mulberry trees.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Baca, the "Valley of Baca," a dry valley pictured in Psalm 84:6 as turning into a place of springs for pilgrims traveling to Jerusalem in faith. The name likely plays on the balsam or mulberry trees mentioned elsewhere (2 Sam. 5:23-24) and probably describes any parched valley on the pilgrim road rather than one fixed, identifiable site.

entries.title: Bachrites (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Becher's clan, from a son of Ephraim, counted in the Numbers 26 census.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Bachrites were the clan descended from Becher, a son of Ephraim, counted in the Numbers 26 census.

entries.title: Baharumite (Bahurim)
entries.summary: It tells you where a man came from. Azmaveth, one of David's mighty men, was from Bahurim, a Benjaminite village east of Jerusalem on the road to the Jordan. The parallel list in 2 Samuel 23:31 spells it Barhumite.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Baharumite marks Azmaveth, one of David's mighty men, as a native of Bahurim, a Benjaminite village east of Jerusalem on the road to the Jordan. The same man appears in the parallel list in 2 Samuel 23:31 under the spelling Barhumite, an alternate form of the same place name.

entries.title: Bahurim
entries.summary: A village east of Jerusalem, on the road down to the Jordan Valley. Shimei the Benjamite lived there. When David fled during Absalom's revolt, Shimei came out to curse him and throw stones.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Bahurim was a village east of Jerusalem on the road down to the Jordan Valley, home to the Benjamite Shimei, who cursed David and pelted him with stones as he fled Jerusalem during Absalom's revolt (2 Samuel 16:5-13). It was also where Jonathan and Ahimaaz hid in a well to avoid Absalom's search party while carrying intelligence back to David (2 Samuel 17:18-21).

witness.excerpt: When David was at Bahurim, a place so called, there came out a kinsman of Saul's, whose name was Shimei, and threw stones at him, and gave him reproachful words; and as his friends stood about the king and protected him, he persevered still more

entries.title: Bakbakkar (Levite living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A Levite who settled in Jerusalem after the exile, apparently of Asaph's line. Nothing further is known about him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Bakbakkar was a Levite, apparently descended from Asaph, listed among those who resettled in Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile (1 Chronicles 9:14-15). Nothing further is known about him.

entries.title: Bakbuk (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: The name means bottle or flask. His descendants were temple servants, Nethinim, who came back from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Bakbuk's descendants were among the families of temple servants (Nethinim) who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:51; Nehemiah 7:53). The name means “bottle” or “flask,” possibly an occupational designation from an ancestor's trade. Nothing more is known of him.

entries.title: Bakbukiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A Levite in Jerusalem after the exile, serving among the temple musicians and gatekeepers.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Bakbukiah was a Levite who served among the temple musicians and gatekeepers in Jerusalem during the postexilic period.

entries.title: Balaam (Prophet living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: A prophet, but not an Israelite. Balak of Moab hired him to curse the Israelites. On the way his donkey saw an angel blocking the road that Balaam himself missed, and God made the animal speak to rebuke him.
entries.books: Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, 1 Chronicles, Nehemiah, Micah, 2 Peter, Jude, Revelation
entries.label: 9 books
entries.dictNote: Balaam was a non-Israelite prophet hired by the Moabite king Balak to curse the invading Israelites, and God famously made Balaam's own donkey speak to rebuke him after the animal saw an angel blocking their path that Balaam himself couldn't see. Every time Balaam opened his mouth to curse Israel as instructed, blessing came out instead, and his oracles include a famous prophecy of a star that would rise out of Jacob. Later biblical writers remember Balaam as a corrupting influence who advised Balak on how to seduce Israel into idolatry through Moabite women, and he is killed in the resulting conflict.

witness.excerpt: Concerning Balaam the Prophet, and what kind of man he was.

entries.curatedNote: The prophet hired to curse Israel who blesses them instead, famous for the talking donkey (Numbers 22-24). Josephus gives him his own chapter title and treats him as a real, complicated figure, genuinely gifted, genuinely compromised, rather than a folk-tale villain.

entries.title: Balac (King living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Balak in Greek, brought up in Revelation 2:14 when Christ rebukes the church at Pergamum for tolerating teaching that echoes Balaam's.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Balac is the Greek form of Balak, the Moabite king who hired the prophet Balaam to curse Israel in Numbers 22-24. The name appears in Revelation 2:14, where Christ rebukes the church at Pergamum for tolerating teaching that echoes Balaam's counsel to Balak, luring Israelites into idolatry and sexual immorality.

entries.title: Baladan (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: His son was the Babylonian king who sent envoys to Hezekiah after his illness. About Baladan himself nothing else is recorded.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Baladan appears only as the father of Merodach-baladan, the Babylonian king who sent envoys to Hezekiah after his illness (2 Kings 20:12; Isaiah 39:1). Nothing else about him is recorded in the biblical text; his son's rebellions against Assyria are independently attested in Assyrian and Babylonian chronicle records of the period.

witness.excerpt: 709.] At this time it was that the dominion of the Assyrians was overthrown by the Medes.  But of these things I shall treat elsewhere.1 But the King of Babylon, whose name was Baladan, sent ambassadors to Hezekiah, with presents; and desired he would be his ally, and his friend.

entries.title: Balah
entries.summary: Bilhah in 1 Chronicles 4:29, Baalah in Joshua 15:29, Balah here: three spellings of one town of Simeon's inside Judah's territory.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A town assigned to the tribe of Simeon within Judah's territory (Josh. 19:3), called Bilhah in 1 Chronicles 4:29 and Baalah in Joshua 15:29, three spellings of the same place.

entries.title: Balak (King living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: The Moabite king who paid Balaam to curse Israel and got blessings instead, oracle after oracle. His temper fraying each time is one of the darkly comic threads in Numbers.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Balak was the Moabite king who hired the prophet Balaam to curse the invading Israelites, and his growing frustration as Balaam's oracles kept turning into blessings instead of curses is one of the more darkly comic threads in the Pentateuch.

witness.excerpt: When Balak, the King of the Moabites, who had from his ancestors a friendship and league with the Midianites, saw how greatly the Israelites were grown, he was much affrighted on account of his own and his kingdom’s danger.

entries.title: Bamah (Gibeon)
entries.summary: Bamah just means high place, and Ezekiel turns the word on Israel, asking what this high place is that they keep going to.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A generic Hebrew term for a hilltop shrine, used by Ezekiel in a pointed wordplay against Israel's idolatry: the prophet asks what this high place is that the people keep going to, noting that it is called Bamah, high place, to this very day (Ezek. 20:29).

entries.title: Bamoth
entries.summary: Heights. That was the name of one of Israel's wilderness camps, in Moabite country. It is likely tied to Bamoth-baal, the high place where Balak later took Balaam to curse Israel.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Wilderness campsite of Israel in Moabite territory, its name meaning "heights" (Num. 21:19-20). It is likely connected to Bamoth-baal, a nearby Moabite high place to which Balak later took Balaam in hopes of cursing Israel (Num. 22:41).

entries.title: Bani (Levite living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A levite from the divided-kingdom years, and 1 Chronicles is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Bani (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A common name after the return, carried by several Levites and returning exiles in Ezra and Nehemiah. This one appears at Nehemiah 8:7 and twice in chapter 9.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Bani was a common name in the postexilic period, borne by several Levites and returning exiles listed in Ezra and Nehemiah.

entries.title: Bani (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A man from the exile and the return, and Nehemiah is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Bani (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Ezra names him twice, and he is a man from the exile and the return.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Bani (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A man from the exile and the return. Ezra names him once.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.summary: Ezra names him once, and he is a man from the exile and the return.

entries.title: Bani (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A man from the exile and the return. Nehemiah names him once.

entries.title: Bani (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Nehemiah names him once, and he is a man from the exile and the return.

entries.title: Bani (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of 10 men called Bani. This one is a man from the exile and the return, named once in Nehemiah.
