entries.title: Bilhan (Edomite living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: A Horite clan chief, in Edom's genealogies.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Bilhan was a Horite clan chief in Edom's genealogies, and also the name of a descendant of Benjamin listed separately in Chronicles.

entries.title: Bilhan (Warrior living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a warrior from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Bilshan (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of the leaders who came back to Judah from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel around 538 BC. His name means something like eloquent, or man of the tongue.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Bilshan was one of the leaders who returned to Judah from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel around 538 BC (Ezra 2:2; Nehemiah 7:7). His name, meaning roughly “eloquent” or “man of the tongue,” suggests he may have served as a spokesman for the returning community, though nothing further is recorded of his role.

entries.title: Bimhal (Man living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: Japhlet's son, in Asher's genealogy, and that is the only place he appears.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Bimhal was one of the sons of Japhlet, listed in the genealogy of the tribe of Asher in 1 Chronicles 7:33. He appears only in this genealogical record.

entries.title: Binea (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Saul's line ran down through Jonathan and Mephibosheth to Binea, and Chronicles keeps his name in the genealogy of Benjamin.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Binea was a descendant of King Saul through the line of Jonathan and Mephibosheth, preserved in the genealogy of Benjamin (1 Chronicles 8:37; 9:43).

entries.title: Binnui (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A common Levitical name. Men called Binnui turn up among the wall builders under Nehemiah and among the men confronted over foreign marriages under Ezra.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Binnui was a common Levitical name among those who helped rebuild Jerusalem's walls under Nehemiah and among those confronted for foreign marriages under Ezra.

entries.title: Binnui (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Ezra names him once, and he is a man from the exile and the return.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Binnui (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of 4 men called Binnui. This one is a man from the exile and the return, named once in Ezra.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Binnui (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A man from the exile and the return, and Nehemiah is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Birsha (King living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: King of Gomorrah, one of the five kings who rebelled against Chedorlaomer and lost.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: King of Gomorrah at the time Chedorlaomer's coalition invaded the cities of the plain, named alongside Bera of Sodom in Genesis 14:2 as one of the five kings who rebelled against Chedorlaomer's overlordship and were defeated.

entries.title: Birzaith (Man or town at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: In Asher's genealogy he is a descendant of Malchiel. Some translations read the Hebrew as a place name instead, and nobody has settled which it is.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Appears in the genealogy of Asher as a descendant of Malchiel; some translations treat the underlying Hebrew as a place name rather than a person's name, and the identification remains uncertain (1 Chronicles 7:31).

entries.title: Bishlam (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A Persian official in Samaria. He joined in writing to King Artaxerxes against the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls. Some scholars think the Aramaic word behind his name may not be a name at all.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Persian official in Samaria named among those who wrote to King Artaxerxes opposing the Jews' rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls (Ezra 4:7). Some scholars think the Aramaic word behind this name may not be a personal name at all but a phrase meaning "in peace," leaving his exact identity uncertain.

entries.title: Bithiah (Woman living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Pharaoh's daughter, married to Mered, a man of Judah. Her name means daughter of the LORD. That suggests she was seen as a convert to Israel's faith.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Bithiah was the daughter of an unnamed Pharaoh who became the wife of Mered, a man of Judah, according to 1 Chronicles 4:18. Her name, meaning 'daughter of the LORD,' suggests she was regarded as a convert to Israel's faith. Jewish tradition sometimes identifies her with the Egyptian princess who rescued the infant Moses, though the Bible itself does not make that connection.

entries.title: Bithron
entries.summary: Abner and his men marched through it by night on their way back to Mahanaim, after Asahel was killed chasing Abner. It was a district or ravine in the Jordan Valley on the east side of the river.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Bithron was a district or ravine in the Jordan Valley on the eastern side of the river, through which Abner and his men marched by night on their retreat to Mahanaim after Asahel was killed while pursuing Abner (2 Samuel 2:29). Its exact boundaries and location are unknown.

entries.title: Bithynia
entries.summary: A Roman province on the south shore of the Black Sea. Paul tried to go there and the Spirit stopped him. By the time Peter wrote his first letter there were Christians there anyway.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Bithynia was a Roman province on the southern shore of the Black Sea where Paul attempted to go but was prevented by the Spirit (Acts 16:7), and where a Christian community had taken root by the time Peter addressed his first letter to believers scattered across the region (1 Peter 1:1). Bithynia's Christian population is independently confirmed a generation or two later by the governor Pliny the Younger's letter to Trajan, in which he describes interrogating believers there and asks the emperor how to handle prosecutions for the name alone.

witness.excerpt: But when Caesar and Antony had slain Cassius near Philippi, and Caesar was gone to Italy, and Antony to Asia, amongst the rest of the cities which sent ambassadors to Antony unto Bithynia, the great men of the Jews came also, and accused Phasaelus and Herod, that they kept the government by force, and that Hyrcanus had no more than an honorable name.

Now Antonius and Caesar had beaten Cassius near Philippi, as others have related; but after the victory, Caesar went into Gaul, [Italy,] and Antony marched for Asia, who, when he was arrived at Bithynia, he had ambassadors that met him from all parts.

entries.title: Bizjothjah (Biziothiah)
entries.summary: In the Negev, near Beersheba, one of the towns given to Judah.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A town in the Negev of Judah, listed near Beersheba among the towns allotted to Judah's tribe (Josh. 15:28).

entries.title: Biztha (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Another of the seven eunuchs at the court of Ahasuerus, likely Xerxes I, sent for Queen Vashti, who would not come.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of the seven eunuchs who served in the court of the Persian king Ahasuerus, likely Xerxes I, sent to bring Queen Vashti before the king's banquet, a summons she refused (Esther 1:10-12). Nothing further is recorded about him individually.

entries.title: Blastus (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Herod Agrippa I's chamberlain. The people of Tyre and Sidon won him over and got him to help patch things up with the angry king.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Blastus was the personal chamberlain of King Herod Agrippa I, whom the people of Tyre and Sidon persuaded to help reconcile them with the angry king (Acts 12:20).

entries.title: Boanerges (Apostle living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Sons of thunder. Jesus gave the nickname to two brothers together, James and John, and it fits their hot temper.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Boanerges, meaning sons of thunder, is not an individual but a nickname Jesus gave jointly to the brothers James and John (Mark 3:17). The name reflects their fervent and sometimes impetuous temperament, seen when they wanted to call down fire on a Samaritan village that rejected Jesus (Luke 9:54).

entries.title: Boaz (A pillar in the temple)
entries.summary: Named twice, in 1 Kings and 2 Chronicles, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Boaz (Man living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: A wealthy landowner in Bethlehem, related to Naomi's dead husband Elimelech. He noticed Ruth, the widowed Moabite, gleaning behind his harvesters, and he agreed to act as kinsman-redeemer.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Boaz was a wealthy landowner in Bethlehem and a relative of Naomi's late husband Elimelech, and he first noticed the widowed Moabite Ruth gleaning grain behind his harvesters. He agreed to exercise the right of a kinsman-redeemer, marrying Ruth and buying back her deceased husband's property after a closer relative declined the responsibility, and their son Obed became the grandfather of David. Boaz also became the name given to one of the two bronze pillars Solomon set up at the entrance of the temple.

witness.excerpt: How under Eli's government of the Israelites, Booz married Ruth: from whom came Obed, the grandfather of David.

entries.lukeNote: David's great-grandfather, one line in Luke's genealogy (3:32). Josephus retells the whole Book of Ruth as its own episode (spelling the name 'Booz'), explicitly naming the payoff Luke's genealogy is really built toward: the line running straight to David.

entries.title: Bocheru (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Azel's son, from Saul's family through Jonathan, kept in the genealogies of Benjamin.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Bocheru was a son of Azel, a descendant of King Saul through Jonathan's line, listed in the genealogies of Benjamin preserved in Chronicles (1 Chronicles 8:38; 9:44).

entries.title: Bochim (Bethel)
entries.summary: Here the angel of the Lord confronted Israel for making treaties with the Canaanites. The people wept bitterly, and the weeping gave the place its name. Nobody has identified the site, though it was likely near Bethel or Shiloh.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Unidentified site, likely near Bethel or Shiloh, where the angel of the Lord confronted Israel for making treaties with the Canaanites in defiance of God's command. The people wept bitterly at the rebuke, which gave the place its name, meaning "weepers," and offered sacrifices there (Judges 2:1-5).

entries.title: Bohan (Man living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: A Reubenite. The stone of Bohan, named after him, marked part of the border between Judah and Benjamin.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Bohan was a Reubenite whose name was given to a boundary stone, "the stone of Bohan," marking part of the border between the territories of Judah and Benjamin (Joshua 15:6; 18:17).

entries.title: Bosor (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Beor in Greek. Second Peter 2:15 calls Balaam the son of Bosor, and nowhere else uses this form.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Bosor is the Greek transliteration of Beor, the father of the prophet Balaam, and appears only in 2 Peter 2:15, where Balaam is called the son of Bosor. Numbers 22:5 gives the more familiar Hebrew form of the same name, Beor. The variant spelling likely reflects a regional Aramaic pronunciation.

witness.excerpt: To this exhortation Judas hearkened, and returned to the wilderness; and in the first place fell upon the inhabitants of Bosor, and took the city, and beat the inhabitants, and destroyed all the males, and all that were able to fight, and burnt the city.

entries.title: Bozcath (Bozkath)
entries.summary: A town in the Shephelah of Judah near Lachish and Eglon. Adaiah came from there. His daughter Jedidah was the mother of King Josiah.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Bozcath was a town in the Shephelah of Judah, listed among the cities near Lachish and Eglon (Josh. 15:39). It is remembered chiefly as the hometown of Adaiah, whose daughter Jedidah was the mother of King Josiah, noted in the record of Josiah's accession (2 Kings 22:1).

entries.title: Bozez
entries.summary: It is a rock, not a man. Bozez and Seneh were the two crags on either side of the pass where Jonathan and his armor-bearer climbed up to surprise the Philistine garrison at Michmash.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Bozez was not a person but one of two rocky crags, the other named Seneh, that flanked the narrow pass through which Jonathan and his armor-bearer climbed to surprise the Philistine garrison at Michmash (1 Sam. 14:4-5). The steep terrain around Michmash still matches the description in the text.

entries.title: Bozrah
entries.summary: Edom's capital, the city of the early Edomite king Jobab. The prophets kept coming back to it in their oracles against Edom. Isaiah pictures the Lord coming from Bozrah in stained garments.
entries.books: Genesis, 1 Chronicles, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Amos, Micah
entries.label: 6 books
entries.dictNote: Bozrah was the capital of Edom, the city of the early Edomite king Jobab, and became a favorite target of prophetic oracles against Edom for its treatment of Israel and Judah. Isaiah pictures the Lord coming from Bozrah with garments stained red from judgment on Edom. Excavations at Buseirah in Jordan, which preserves the ancient name, have uncovered a fortified Iron Age citadel with monumental buildings, confirming its role as Edom's political center. A different town also called Bozrah lay in the plains of Moab.

entries.title: Bukki (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Numbers names him once, and he is a man from the wilderness years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Bukki (Priest living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A priest in the high priestly line from Aaron to Zadok, named in 1 Chronicles 6 and again in Ezra's own ancestry at Ezra 7:4.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Bukki was a common name, borne by a leader from the tribe of Dan who helped divide the conquered land and by a priest in the high priestly genealogy connecting Aaron to Zadok.

entries.title: Bukkiah (Levite living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Heman's son, a Kohathite Levite. He led one of the divisions of temple musicians set up under David.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Bukkiah was a Kohathite Levite, one of the sons of Heman, and headed one of the divisions of temple musicians organized under David (1 Chronicles 25:4, 13).

entries.title: Bul (Name of the 8th month)
entries.summary: Eighth month, October into November, and Solomon finished the temple in it.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Bul was not a person but the name of the eighth month of the ancient Israelite calendar, corresponding roughly to October-November, in which Solomon completed construction of the temple (1 Kings 6:38). The name reflects a Canaanite term tied to the rainy season, and it was later replaced in common use by the Babylonian-derived name Marcheshvan after the exile.

entries.title: Bunah (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Jerahmeel's son, in Judah's line through Pharez. Nothing else is recorded of him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A son of Jerahmeel, listed in the genealogy of Judah through the line of Pharez (1 Chronicles 2:25). Nothing else is recorded of him.

entries.title: Bunni (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Nehemiah names him once, and he is a man from the exile and the return.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Bunni (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of 3 men called Bunni. This one is a man from the exile and the return, named once in Nehemiah.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Bunni (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: This Bunni was among those who signed Nehemiah's covenant renewal and helped lead worship after the law was read out.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Bunni was a common Levitical name among those who signed Nehemiah's covenant renewal and helped lead worship after the law was read publicly.

entries.title: Buz
entries.summary: The name means contempt. Nahor's second son carried it, and Jeremiah uses it for a people out in the desert.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Buz's name means “contempt” or “scorn.” The first Buz was the second son of Nahor, Abraham's brother, and an ancestor of Elihu, one of Job's counselors (Genesis 22:21; Job 32:2). A second Buz was a leading man of the tribe of Gad (1 Chronicles 5:14). The name is also attached to a region in Arabia denounced alongside Dedan and Tema in Jeremiah's oracle against foreign nations (Jeremiah 25:23), likely named for the same family line.

entries.title: Buz (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Buz (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: It means contempt. This Buz was the second son of Abraham's brother Nahor, and Elihu, one of Job's counsellors, came from his line.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Buzi (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Ezekiel's father. The book opens with Ezekiel the priest, the son of Buzi, and says nothing more about him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Buzi was the father of the prophet Ezekiel, who is introduced as "Ezekiel the priest, the son of Buzi" (Ezek. 1:3). Buzi himself was likely also a priest, since the office was hereditary in Israel, though the text does not say so directly.

entries.title: Buzite
entries.summary: Elihu, the younger man whose speeches close the dialogue in Job, was a Buzite: of the family of Ram, from the kindred of Buz. Buz was a son of Nahor and brother of Uz.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Buzite identifies Elihu, the younger man whose speeches close the dialogue in Job, as belonging to the family of Ram, of the kindred of Buz. Buz was a son of Nahor and brother of Uz, from whom Job's own homeland likely took its name, making Elihu a distant relation of Job.

entries.title: Cabbon
entries.summary: A lowland town of Judah in the district that held Lachish and Eglon. It is not mentioned anywhere else and remains unidentified.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Cabbon, a lowland town of Judah in the district that included Lachish and Eglon (Josh. 15:40). It is not mentioned elsewhere and remains unidentified.

entries.title: Cabul
entries.summary: Named once, in 1 Kings, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Cabul
entries.summary: A town on the eastern border of Asher. Another Cabul, a district of twenty towns in Galilee, got the name later.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Cabul refers to two places, not a person. One was a town on the eastern border of Asher (Joshua 19:27). The other was the name given, apparently disparagingly, to a district of twenty towns in Galilee that Solomon ceded to King Hiram of Tyre in payment for building materials and labor; Hiram was displeased with them and called the land “Cabul,” meaning roughly “good for nothing” (1 Kings 9:10-13).

entries.title: Caesar (Emperor living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Not one man. Caesar is the New Testament's title for whoever was Roman emperor, Augustus when Jesus was born and Tiberius when he was crucified.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Caesar is used throughout the New Testament as the standard title for the reigning Roman emperor rather than one specific man, covering at least Augustus, under whom Jesus was born, and Tiberius, during whose reign Jesus was crucified. Jesus's famous instruction to render to Caesar what is Caesar's and to God what is God's was a direct response to a politically loaded question about paying imperial taxes.

witness.excerpt: Caesar was also the forwarder to raise Herod's dignity, and to give him his assistance in what he desired, on account of the toils of war which he had himself undergone with Antipater his father in Egypt, and of the hospitalit

SO Caesar was now reconciled to Herod, and wrote thus to him: That he was grieved for him on account of his sons; and that in case they had been guilty of any profane and insolent crimes against him, it would behoove him to punis
But Caesar, who knew perfectly well the lineaments of Alexander's face, because he had been accused by Herod before him, discerned the fallacy in his countenance, even before he saw the man.

NOW Caesar took this wall there on the fifth day after he had taken the first; and when the Jews had fled from him, he entered into it with a thousand armed men, and those of his choice troops, and this at a place where were the m
As for Caesar himself, he could not, however, but commiserate those that thus perished, although they got up thither without any order for so doing, since there was no way of giving the many relief.

entries.title: Caesar (Emperor living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: In Acts the title stands for the emperor of the day, the authority whose court the appeal in Acts 25 went to.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Caesar (Emperor living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Luke puts names to the title: Augustus, under whom Jesus was born, and Tiberius after him.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Caesar (Emperor living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: A man from the New Testament, and Philippians is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Caesarea
entries.summary: Herod the Great built it as a Roman port on the Mediterranean coast, and it served as the administrative capital of Roman Judea. Cornelius the centurion lived there. Paul spent two years there in prison.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Caesarea was a Roman port city built by Herod the Great on the Mediterranean coast, serving as the administrative capital of Roman Judea, and it's where the centurion Cornelius lived and where Paul was imprisoned for two years before his voyage to Rome.

witness.excerpt: But Sabinus, Caesar's steward for Syrian affairs, as he was making haste into Judea to preserve Herod's effects, met with Archclaus at Caesarea; but Varus (president of Syria) came at that time, and restrained him from meddling with them, for he was there as sent for by Archceaus, by the means of Ptolemy.

entries.title: Caiaphas (High Priest living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: The high priest who presided over the council that condemned Jesus. Beforehand he argued it was better for one man to die for the people than for the whole nation to suffer, and John's Gospel reads those words as more than he knew.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Caiaphas was the Jewish high priest who presided over the council that condemned Jesus, arguing beforehand that it was better for one man to die for the people than for the whole nation to suffer, words John's Gospel treats as an unwitting prophecy of what Jesus's death would actually accomplish. He held the high priesthood for eighteen years under Roman oversight, an unusually long tenure that suggests he was skilled at managing the delicate relationship between Jewish religious life and Roman power. An ornate limestone ossuary discovered south of Jerusalem in 1990, inscribed with the name Joseph son of Caiaphas, is widely believed to be his family burial box.

witness.excerpt: which office, when he had held for a year, Gratus deprived him of it, and gave the high priesthood to Simon, the son of Camithus; and when he had possessed that dignity no longer than a year, Joseph Caiaphas was made his successor.

entries.curatedNote: The sitting high priest at 3:2, named in the same breath as Annas. Josephus's list of rapid Roman-appointed replacements just before him, three high priests in as many years, makes Caiaphas's own unusually long eighteen-year tenure  look like the exception, not the rule

entries.title: Cain (Man living at the time before the Flood)
entries.summary: Adam and Eve's firstborn, a farmer. God accepted his brother Abel's offering and not his, and Cain killed Abel out of jealousy. God marked him and sent him off to wander rather than putting him to death.
entries.books: Genesis, Numbers, Judges, Hebrews, 1 John, Jude
entries.label: 6 books
entries.dictNote: Cain was Adam and Eve's firstborn son, a farmer who murdered his shepherd brother Abel out of jealousy after God accepted Abel's offering but not his own, and God marked him and exiled him to a life of wandering rather than executing him. Cain went on to build the first city mentioned in the Bible, naming it after his son Enoch, and his descendants are credited with early advances in livestock, music, and metalworking before the line disappears from the narrative.

witness.excerpt: 3 Therefore was Cain also delivered over to seven vengeances by God, for in every hundred years the Lord brought one plague upon him.
Adam and Eve had two sons: the elder of them was named Cain; which name, when it is interpreted, signifies a Possession.

entries.title: Cainan (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Two men in the genealogies. One descends from Seth several generations before Noah; the other is a son of Arphaxad in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, a name missing from the Genesis Hebrew text but present in the Greek.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Cainan appears twice in the genealogies, once as a descendant of Seth several generations before Noah, and again in Luke's genealogy of Jesus as a son of Arphaxad, a name absent from the Genesis Hebrew text but present in the Greek Old Testament Luke drew from.

witness.excerpt: Cainan, when he had lived nine hundred and ten years, had his son Malaleel, who was born in his hundred and seventieth year.

entries.title: Calah
entries.summary: Nimrod is said to have built it in Assyria, along with Nineveh and Resen, and it is identified with Nimrud on the east bank of the Tigris south of Mosul.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Calah was one of the ancient cities Nimrod is said to have built in Assyria, along with Nineveh and Resen (Genesis 10:11-12). It is identified with Nimrud, on the east bank of the Tigris south of Mosul, which Ashurnasirpal II rebuilt as his royal capital in the ninth century BC, complete with palaces, temples, and a garden watered by canal from the Great Zab. British and Iraqi excavations there since the 1840s, most extensively under Max Mallowan in the 1950s, uncovered colossal winged bulls, palace reliefs, and a rich hoard of carved ivories that now count among the finest surviving examples of Assyrian art.

entries.title: Calcol (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Known for his wisdom, and named with Ethan, Heman and Darda as wise men Solomon outdid.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Calcol was renowned for wisdom among the sons of Zerah, or possibly of Mahol, and is named alongside Ethan, Heman, and Darda as men whose wisdom Solomon's surpassed (1 Kings 4:31; 1 Chronicles 2:6).

entries.title: Calcol (Man living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the years before the monarchy.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Caleb (Joshua's compatriot living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness and Conquest)
entries.summary: One of the twelve spies Moses sent into Canaan. He and Joshua were the only two who came back telling Israel to trust God and take the land, and the rest of that generation paid for ignoring them with forty years in the wilderness.
entries.books: Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, 1 Chronicles
entries.label: 6 books
entries.dictNote: Caleb was one of twelve spies Moses sent to scout Canaan, and along with Joshua he was the only one who returned urging Israel to trust God and take the land, a minority report that cost the rest of that generation forty years of wandering as punishment for their fear. Because of his faith, Caleb was promised he would personally enter the promised land, and at eighty-five, decades later, he asked for and received the hill country of Hebron specifically because it was still occupied by fortified cities and giants, wanting the hardest ground rather than the easiest.

witness.excerpt: But the land thereto belonging they gave as a free gift to Caleb; according to the injunctions of Moses.

But of the spies there were Joshua the son of Nun, of the tribe of Ephraim; and Caleb of the tribe of Judah, that were afraid of the consequence, and came into the midst of them, and stilled the multitude; and desired them to be of good courage; and neither to condemn God, as having told them lies; neith

entries.title: Caleb (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Not the spy. This Caleb heads his own branch of the family lines in 1 Chronicles 2, with wives and sons listed at 2:18–19 and again from 2:42.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Caleb-ephrathah
entries.summary: The Hebrew of 1 Chronicles 2:24 is hard, and some translations do not read Caleb-ephrathah as a single place at all. It turns up in connection with Hezron's clan and the district of Ephrathah near Bethlehem.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Caleb-ephrathah, a name occurring in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 2:24 in connection with Hezron's clan and the district of Ephrathah near Bethlehem. The Hebrew text is difficult, and some translations render it not as a single place name but as two separate clauses describing Caleb going in to Ephrathah; either way, it ties Hezron's line to the Bethlehem region associated with Caleb's descendants.

entries.title: Camon (Kamon)
entries.summary: Jair was buried here, the judge who led Israel for twenty-two years. Where it was is disputed: tradition puts it in Gilead east of the Jordan, or else near Mount Carmel.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The burial place of Jair, a minor judge of Israel who led the nation for twenty-two years (Judg. 10:5). Its location is disputed; tradition has placed it both in Gilead east of the Jordan and, alternatively, near Mount Carmel in the west.

witness.excerpt: He kept the government twenty two years; 13 and died an old man: and he was buried in Camon, a city of Gilead.

entries.title: Cana
entries.summary: A village in Galilee, likely a few miles north of Nazareth. At a wedding there Jesus turned water into wine, his first recorded miracle. Nathanael came from Cana.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Cana was a village in Galilee, likely a few miles north of Nazareth, where Jesus turned water into wine at a wedding, his first recorded miracle (John 2:1-11). It was also the hometown of the disciple Nathanael (John 21:2) and the site where Jesus healed a royal official's son from a distance (John 4:46-54). Its precise location is debated between two candidate ruins, Khirbet Qana and Kafr Kanna, both north of Nazareth.

witness.excerpt:
When Antiochus was fallen, his army fled to the village Cana, where the greatest part of them perished by famine.
2.
But afterward there were gotten together another numerous army of the Arabians, at Cana, which is a place of Celesyria.

entries.title: Canaan
entries.summary: The land promised to Abraham and his descendants, roughly modern Israel and the land around it. The conquest under Joshua is that promise, centuries old by then, being kept.
entries.books: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 1 Chronicles, Psalm, Isaiah, Ezekiel, Hosea, Zephaniah
entries.label: 13 books
entries.dictNote: Canaan was the land promised to Abraham and his descendants, roughly corresponding to modern Israel and the surrounding region, and the conquest of Canaan under Joshua is the fulfillment of that centuries-old promise. Canaan is also the name of Ham's son, cursed by Noah, and the Canaanite peoples descended from him are the nations Israel was commanded to dispossess.

entries.title: Canaanite
entries.summary: They were the people living in the land promised to Israel. The biblical genealogy traces them to Canaan, son of Ham. The Old Testament repeatedly orders them driven out because of their idol worship and other practices.
entries.books: Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, Ezra, Nehemiah, Job, Proverbs, Ezekiel, Obadiah, Zechariah
entries.label: 15 books
entries.dictNote: Canaanites were the inhabitants of the land promised to Israel, descended in the biblical genealogy from Canaan, son of Ham, and the Old Testament repeatedly commands their displacement because of practices like idol worship and child sacrifice associated with them. The term also became attached to the apostle Simon, called "the Canaanite" in Matthew and Mark, though this actually transliterates an Aramaic word for "zealot" rather than marking Canaanite ancestry; Luke's Gospel calls him Simon the Zealot instead. Canaanite religion and culture are well documented outside the Bible through the Ugaritic tablets found at Ras Shamra in Syria, which describe the god Baal and the goddess Asherah, both named elsewhere in the Old Testament as objects of Israelite idolatry. The Merneptah Stele, an Egyptian inscription from about 1208 BC, is the earliest known text to mention Canaan by name.

entries.title: Cananaean (Political group in the New Testament)
entries.summary: Simon's byname in the lists of the Twelve, in Matthew 10:4 and Mark 3:18. Older translations render it Canaanite, but it has nothing to do with Canaan.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: “Canaanite,” more precisely rendered “Cananaean” in modern translations, is a byname for the apostle Simon, one of the Twelve, appearing in the disciple lists of Matthew 10:4 and Mark 3:18. Despite its appearance, the word does not mean a descendant of Canaan; it transliterates an Aramaic term for the Jewish nationalist movement known as the Zealots, matching Luke's designation of the same man as “Simon the Zealot” (Luke 6:15).

entries.title: Candace (Title of a leader)
entries.summary: A title the ruling queens of Kush carried, the way Egypt's kings were all Pharaoh. The official Philip met served one of them.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A hereditary title, not a personal name, carried by the ruling queens of the Kushite kingdom centered at Meroe in Nubia, comparable to "Pharaoh" for Egypt's kings. The treasury official of one such queen was converted and baptized by Philip on the road from Jerusalem to Gaza (Acts 8:27). The power of these Kushite queens is corroborated outside the Bible: Roman sources describe a war between Rome and a Kushite army led by one of them around 24 BC, and archaeologists later recovered a bronze head of Augustus that Kushite forces had looted and buried beneath the steps of a Meroe temple as an act of triumph, now held in the British Museum.

entries.title: Canneh (Calneh)
entries.summary: Ezekiel lists it once among Tyre's trading partners, with Haran and Eden, somewhere in upper Mesopotamia or northern Syria. It is generally taken as the same place as Calno or Calneh.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Canneh appears only once, in Ezekiel's list of Tyre's trading partners, grouped with Haran and Eden in the region of upper Mesopotamia and northern Syria (Ezek. 27:23). It is generally taken as the same place as Calno or Calneh, likely to be identified with Kullani, a north Syrian city named in Assyrian annals as conquered by Tiglath-pileser III in 738 BC.

entries.title: Capernaum
entries.summary: Jesus left Nazareth and made this fishing town on the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee his base, and it is called his own city. Several of his best known miracles and teachings happened there.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Capernaum was a fishing town on the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee that Jesus made his base of operations after leaving Nazareth, calling it “his own city.” Several of his best known miracles and teachings took place there, including the healing of a centurion's servant and the bread of life discourse in its synagogue, yet Jesus also pronounced judgment on the town for its unbelief. The site, Tell Hum, has been excavated to reveal a limestone synagogue built over the basalt foundations of an earlier first century structure, along with an octagonal Byzantine church built over a house identified by ancient graffiti as Peter's, matching the Gospels' description of Jesus staying at Peter's house there.

entries.title: Caphtor (Crete)
entries.summary: Where the Philistines came from before they settled on Canaan's coastal plain, generally taken to be Crete or somewhere near it in the Aegean.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Caphtor is identified in the Old Testament as the original homeland of the Philistines before they migrated to Canaan's coastal plain, generally understood to be Crete or a nearby Aegean region.

entries.title: Cappadocia
entries.summary: A large province in eastern Asia Minor. Jews from there were in Jerusalem at Pentecost, and later Peter wrote to the scattered believers there among others.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Cappadocia was a large province in eastern Asia Minor, home to Jewish pilgrims present in Jerusalem at Pentecost (Acts 2:9) and later to one of the churches Peter addressed as scattered exiles (1 Peter 1:1). The region's connection to Mesopotamian trade networks goes back at least to the early second millennium BC, when Assyrian merchants from Ashur ran a trading colony at Kanesh, modern Kultepe, and left behind thousands of cuneiform tablets documenting their business. By the first century it was a Roman province with an active Jewish diaspora community.

entries.title: Carcas (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of the seven eunuchs Ahasuerus sent to bring Queen Vashti before his guests, which she refused.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of the seven eunuchs of the Persian king Ahasuerus sent to bring Queen Vashti before his banquet guests, a command she refused (Esther 1:10).

entries.title: Carchemish
entries.summary: A major city on the west bank of the Euphrates. For a long time it was a Hittite provincial capital, and later the seat of a Neo-Hittite kingdom of its own. Nebuchadnezzar crushed Pharaoh Necho's army there.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Major city on the west bank of the Euphrates, long a Hittite provincial capital and later the seat of an independent Neo-Hittite kingdom after the Hittite empire's collapse. Pharaoh Necho's army was crushed there by Nebuchadnezzar in 605 BC, a battle Jeremiah cites as the turning point that handed regional power to Babylon (Jer. 46:2; 2 Chr. 35:20), while Isaiah names the city among those already conquered by Assyria a century earlier (Isa. 10:9). Excavations begun in 1911 by David Hogarth and continued by Leonard Woolley, with T. E. Lawrence assisting, uncovered Hittite and Luwian hieroglyphic inscriptions confirming the city's long history as recorded in the biblical text.

entries.title: Careah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)

entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Careah was the father of Johanan, the military commander who warned Gedaliah of an assassination plot against him after Jerusalem's fall.

entries.label: 9 books
entries.dictNote: Mount Carmel is a mountain ridge on Israel's Mediterranean coast, most famous as the site of Elijah's contest against the prophets of Baal, where fire from heaven answered Elijah's prayer and exposed Baal's powerlessness before the assembled nation.

entries.title: Carmelite
entries.summary: Here it means someone from Carmel in Judah's hill country, not Mount Carmel in the north. Nabal was a Carmelite, the rich fool who insulted David, and so was his wife Abigail, who married David after Nabal died.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Carmelite here means someone from the town of Carmel in Judah's hill country, not from Mount Carmel further north. Nabal, the wealthy but foolish Carmelite who insulted David, and his wife Abigail, who became David's wife after Nabal's death, are the best known Carmelites in the Bible.

entries.title: Carshena (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: He was one of the seven top princes of Persia and Media, advisers with direct access to King Ahasuerus. They were consulted after Queen Vashti refused to appear. Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of the seven highest-ranking princes of Persia and Media, advisers with direct access to King Ahasuerus who were consulted after Queen Vashti refused to appear before him (Esther 1:14). Nothing further is recorded about him individually.

entries.title: Casiphia
entries.summary: A place in Babylonia, apparently a centre of Jewish community life. None of the returning party were Levites, so Ezra sent messengers there to find Levites and temple servants for the journey to Jerusalem.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Casiphia was a place in Babylonia, apparently a center of Jewish community life, where Ezra sent messengers to secure Levites and temple servants for the journey back to Jerusalem, since none had volunteered from among the returning exiles (Ezra 8:15-20). Its exact site is unknown, but its existence fits what cuneiform records from Babylonia itself have since confirmed: archives such as the so-called Al-Yahudu, or "Judah-town," tablets document real communities of Judean exiles and their descendants living under Persian rule, exactly the kind of Jewish settlement Ezra would have needed to draw Levites from.

entries.title: Casluhim (People, perhaps from Casluch)
entries.summary: A people, not a person. They descend from Mizraim, the ancestor of Egypt, in the Table of Nations, and Genesis says the Philistines came from them.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Casluhim was not an individual but one of the peoples descended from Mizraim, the biblical ancestor of Egypt, in the Table of Nations (Genesis 10:13-14; 1 Chronicles 1:11-12). Genesis names the Philistines as coming from this group, placing their origin somewhere along the eastern Nile delta or the Mediterranean coast near Egypt's border with Canaan.

entries.title: Cedron (Kidron)
entries.summary: The Kidron in Greek spelling, the brook and ravine between Jerusalem and the Mount of Olives. Jesus crossed it with his disciples on the night he was arrested.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Not a person but the Greek spelling of the Kidron, the brook and ravine running along the eastern side of Jerusalem between the city and the Mount of Olives. John 18:1 records that Jesus crossed the Kidron with his disciples on the night of his arrest, on the way to the garden of Gethsemane. Excavations along the valley have uncovered tombs and monuments dating back to the First Temple period, confirming its long use as a boundary and burial ground for the city.

entries.title: Cencrea (Cenchreae)
entries.summary: Corinth's eastern harbour on the Saronic Gulf, about seven miles from the city. Paul cut his hair there for a vow before he sailed, and the town had a church of its own.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Cenchreae was the eastern harbor town of Corinth, on the Saronic Gulf, roughly seven miles from the city. Paul sailed from there after cutting his hair in fulfillment of a vow (Acts 18:18), and the town had its own church, in which Phoebe served as a deacon and patron whom Paul commends to the Romans (Romans 16:1). Excavations at the site have uncovered its ancient harbor works, confirming its role as one of Corinth's two ports.

entries.title: Cephas (Apostle living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Rock, in Aramaic. Jesus gave Simon the name, and Peter is the same word in Greek. Paul generally uses the Aramaic form in his letters.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Cephas is the Aramaic name Jesus gave Simon, meaning rock, translated into Greek as Peter; Paul uses the Aramaic form when referring to him in several of his letters.

entries.title: Chaldean
entries.summary: Originally a tribal people of southern Mesopotamia who went on to found the Neo-Babylonian Empire under Nabopolassar and his son Nebuchadnezzar II. Their armies destroyed Jerusalem and its temple in 586 BC.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Chaldeans were originally a tribal people of southern Mesopotamia who rose to found the Neo-Babylonian Empire under Nabopolassar and his son Nebuchadnezzar II, the king whose armies destroyed Jerusalem and its temple in 586 BC. By the time of Daniel, "Chaldean" had also become a general term for Babylonian scholars, astrologers, and diviners. Nebuchadnezzar's own building inscriptions and the Babylonian Chronicles, which record his campaigns against Judah, corroborate the broad outline of the biblical account of Jerusalem's fall.

entries.title: Chaldeans
entries.summary: They started as one tribal group in southern Mesopotamia and ended up ruling the whole Babylonian empire. In the Old Testament the name came to mean Babylonians in general.
entries.books: Genesis, 2 Kings, 2 Chronicles, Nehemiah, Job, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, Habakkuk
entries.label: 10 books
entries.dictNote: The Chaldeans were originally a specific tribal group in southern Mesopotamia who eventually came to rule the entire Babylonian empire, and the name became a general term in the Old Testament for Babylonians broadly, especially in Daniel, where it also refers specifically to a professional class of astrologers and diviners at the Babylonian court.

entries.title: Chanaan (Canaan)
entries.summary: The King James spelling of Canaan in Acts, where Stephen's speech looks back on the land promised to Abraham's descendants.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Chanaan is the King James Version's transliteration of “Canaan” as it appears in the Greek text of Acts, referring to the land promised to Abraham's descendants rather than to a person. Stephen's speech recalls God giving Israel no inheritance there before the conquest (Acts 7:11), while Paul's synagogue sermon at Pisidian Antioch recounts God destroying seven nations in the land of Canaan to give it to Israel (Acts 13:19).

entries.title: Charran (Haran)
entries.summary: Haran, in the Greek form Stephen uses before the Sanhedrin. Abraham settled there with his father Terah after leaving Ur, and moved on to Canaan once Terah had died.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Charran is the Greek form of Haran used in Stephen's speech before the Sanhedrin, where he recounts that Abraham settled there with his father Terah after leaving Ur, before God called him onward to Canaan following Terah's death (Acts 7:2, 4). The city of Harran in northern Mesopotamia is well attested outside the Bible as a major trade and religious center devoted to the moon god Sin, important enough that Babylon's last king, Nabonidus, rebuilt its temple there some fifteen centuries after Abraham's time.

witness.excerpt: But first of all we will examine what Charran is, and what is meant by the departure from this country to go and live in another.

entries.title: Chebar
entries.summary: A river or canal in Babylonia. Jewish exiles like Ezekiel were settled near it after Jerusalem fell. By the Chebar Ezekiel saw his first vision of God's glory and the living creatures.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The Chebar was a river or canal in Babylonia, in the region where Jewish exiles including Ezekiel were settled after Jerusalem's fall. It was by the Chebar that Ezekiel received his inaugural vision of God's glory and the living creatures, and several of his later visions are likewise dated to this location. Some scholars identify it with a great irrigation canal branching off the Euphrates near Nippur, where cuneiform tablets have since documented a Jewish exile community.

entries.title: Chedorlaomer (King living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: An Elamite king. His coalition raided Sodom and carried off Lot along with the city's goods. Abraham got everything back in a surprise night attack.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Chedorlaomer was an Elamite king who led a coalition that raided Sodom and captured Lot along with the city's goods, a raid Abraham reversed with a surprise night attack that rescued Lot and recovered everything taken.

entries.summary: Of the sons of Pahath-moab, he had married a foreign wife and agreed to divorce her under Ezra's reform.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Chelal was one of the sons of Pahath-moab who had married a foreign wife and agreed to divorce her under Ezra's reform after the return from exile (Ezra 10:30).

entries.title: Chelluh (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Another of Bani's men in the foreign-marriage list of Ezra 10, who agreed to divorce his wife in Ezra's covenant reform.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Chelluh was one of the men of Bani who had married a foreign wife and agreed to divorce her as part of Ezra's covenant reform after the exile (Ezra 10:35).

entries.title: Chelub (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)

entries.title: Chelub (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Shuhah's brother and Mehir's father, in the tribe of Judah.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Chelub is a name given to two different men in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles. One was the brother of Shuhah and father of Mehir, in the tribe of Judah (1 Chronicles 4:11). The other was the father of Ezri, who oversaw the farm workers in David's administration (1 Chronicles 27:26).

entries.title: Chelubai (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Hezron's son, also called Caleb, and the head of a branch of Judah's family tree in Chronicles. He is a different man from Caleb son of Jephunneh, the spy who went into Canaan with Joshua.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Son of Hezron and also called Caleb, this figure heads a branch of Judah's genealogy in Chronicles; he is a different man from the more famous Caleb son of Jephunneh, the spy who entered Canaan with Joshua (1 Chronicles 2:9, 18, 42).

entries.title: Chemosh (A male deity in the Old Testament)
entries.summary: Moab's national god. Solomon built him a shrine to please one of his foreign wives, and that is among the reasons given for the enemies God raised against Solomon late in his reign.
entries.label: 5 books
entries.dictNote: Chemosh was the national god of Moab, and Solomon's construction of a shrine to Chemosh to please one of his foreign wives is listed among the reasons God raised up adversaries against his kingdom late in his reign.

entries.title: Chenaanah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: His son Zedekiah was a false prophet who promised King Ahab victory and struck the true prophet Micaiah in the face for saying otherwise.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Chenaanah was the father of Zedekiah, a false prophet who confidently but wrongly predicted victory for King Ahab and mockingly struck the true prophet Micaiah for contradicting him.

entries.title: Chenani (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A Levite who stood on the stairs with others and cried out to the LORD in the great public confession of Nehemiah 9, after the Law had been read. Nothing further is recorded of him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Levite who stood on the stairs with several others and cried out to the LORD during the great public confession and covenant renewal described in Nehemiah 9, following the reading of the Law under Ezra. Nothing further is recorded about him.

entries.title: Chenaniah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: David put this Levite in charge of the music when the ark was brought up to Jerusalem, because he was good at it.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Chenaniah was a Levite David placed in charge of music for the ark's procession into Jerusalem, chosen specifically for his skill.

entries.title: Chephirah
entries.summary: With Gibeon, Beeroth and Kiriath-jearim, one of the four Hivite towns whose people tricked Joshua into a peace treaty by posing as travellers from a far country.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Chephirah was one of four Hivite towns, along with Gibeon, Beeroth, and Kiriath-jearim, whose inhabitants tricked Joshua into a treaty of peace by disguising themselves as travelers from a distant country (Joshua 9:3-17). It fell within Benjamin's territory, and its people are later listed among those who returned from Babylonian exile (Ezra 2:25; Nehemiah 7:29). It is identified with Khirbet Kefireh, west of Jerusalem near Ajalon.

entries.title: Cheran (Edomite living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Dishon's son, from the Horite clans of Seir. The Horites lived in the region before Edom's kings arose and were later pushed out or absorbed.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Cheran was one of the sons of Dishon, a Horite chief listed among the clans of Seir before Edom's kings arose (Genesis 36:26; 1 Chronicles 1:41). The Horites were the region's earlier inhabitants, later displaced or absorbed by Esau's descendants.

entries.title: Cherethims (A military group in the Old Testament)
entries.summary: David's bodyguard, with the Pelethites, under Benaiah's command. They were tied closely to the Philistines and likely came from Crete.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: The Cherethites were a group closely associated with the Philistines, likely originally from Crete, and along with the Pelethites they formed David's personal bodyguard under the command of Benaiah.

entries.title: Cherethims (People, perhaps from Chereth)
entries.summary: The people themselves, close neighbours of the Philistines and likely from Crete. Ezekiel and Zephaniah both name them in oracles of judgment.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Cherith
entries.summary: It was a ravine with a seasonal stream. Elijah hid there and ravens fed him in the early part of the three-year drought under King Ahab, and its exact location is uncertain.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Cherith was not a person but a ravine with a seasonal stream where the prophet Elijah hid and was fed by ravens during the early part of a three-year drought under King Ahab (1 Kings 17:2-6). Its exact location is uncertain; proposals range from the Wadi Qelt near Jericho to ravines further east in Gilead.

entries.title: Cherub
entries.summary: A place in Babylonia, not the winged beings. With Tel-harsa and Addan it was one of the settlements some returning exiles came from who could not prove their descent.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Cherub, along with Tel-harsa and Addan, was one of the Babylonian settlements named among the returning exiles who could not prove their Israelite ancestry after the exile (Ezra 2:59; Neh. 7:61). Its exact location is unknown; it was apparently a community of Judean deportees living in southern Mesopotamia during the Babylonian captivity.

entries.title: Chesalon
entries.summary: On Judah's northern border, on the slope of Mount Jearim. It is identified with the village of Kesla in the hill country west of Jerusalem.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Chesalon marked a point on the northern border of Judah's tribal territory, on the slope of Mount Jearim (Joshua 15:10). It is identified with the modern village of Kesla in the hill country west of Jerusalem, which preserves the ancient name.

entries.title: Chesed (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Nahor's son, one of the descendants of Abraham's brother listed in Genesis 22:22. Some scholars connect the name with the Hebrew word for the Chaldeans, Kasdim.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A son of Abraham's brother Nahor, listed among his descendants in Genesis 22:22. Some scholars connect his name to the Hebrew term for the Chaldeans (Kasdim), suggesting later tradition saw him as an ancestor of that people, though the text itself states only his place in Nahor's family.

witness.excerpt: Now Nahor had eight sons by Milcha; Uz, and Buz, Kemuel, Chesed, Azau, Pheldas, Jadelph, and Bethuel.

entries.title: Chesil
entries.summary: A Negev town of Judah, likely the place Joshua 19:4 calls Bethul and 1 Chronicles 4:30 calls Bethuel.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A town in the Negev of Judah (Josh. 15:30), likely the same place called Bethul in Joshua 19:4 and Bethuel in 1 Chronicles 4:30, all apparently variant spellings of one settlement.

entries.title: Chesulloth
entries.summary: Named once, in 1 Chronicles, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

witness.excerpt: And the Romans received all the fortresses and the cities, excepting Gischala and those that had seized upon mount Tabor; Gamala also, which is a city over-against Taricheæ, but on the other side of the lake, conspired with them.
And after these was Issachar; which had its limits in length, mount Carmel, and the river: but its limit in breadth was mount Tabor.

However, thirty thousand still continued with Alexander, who was himself eager to fight also; accordingly, Gabinius went out to fight, when the Jews met him; and as the battle was fought near Mount Tabor, ten thousand of them were slain, and the rest of the multitude dispersed themselves, and fled away.

entries.title: Chesulloth
entries.summary: Issachar's town on the slopes between Jezreel and Shunem. It is usually taken to be the same place as Chisloth-tabor on Zebulun's boundary, at modern Iksal near Mount Tabor, which would put the two tribal lines meeting at one town.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Chesulloth was a town of Issachar on the slopes between Jezreel and Shunem (Joshua 19:18). It is usually equated with Chisloth-tabor, named a few verses earlier on Zebulun's boundary, and identified with modern Iksal near Mount Tabor. The overlap suggests the two tribal boundaries met close to the same town.

entries.title: Chezib (Achzib)
entries.summary: The town where Shelah, Judah's third son by his Canaanite wife, was born, generally taken as another name for Achzib in the Shephelah, though nobody has found the site.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Chezib was the town where Judah's third son by his Canaanite wife, Shelah, was born (Genesis 38:5). It is generally taken as another name for, or an early form of, Achzib, a town later listed among the Shephelah towns of Judah (Joshua 15:44) that the prophet Micah plays on for its meaning "deceitful" (Micah 1:14). Its exact site is unidentified.

entries.title: Chidon (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: The threshing floor where Uzzah put his hand on the ark and died, on the road toward Jerusalem; 2 Samuel calls the same spot Nachon's threshing floor.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Chidon, the threshing floor where Uzzah touched the ark of the covenant and died as it was being carried toward Jerusalem (1 Chr. 13:9). The parallel account in 2 Samuel 6:6 calls it Nachon's threshing floor; it stood along the route from Kiriath-jearim, northwest of Jerusalem.

witness.excerpt: But as they were come to the threshing-floor of Chidon, a place so called, Uzzah was slain by the anger of God; for as the oxen shook the ark, he stretched out his hand, and would needs take hold of it.

entries.title: Chileab (David's son living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the united kingdom.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Chileab (David's son living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: David's second son, by Abigail, born after Nabal died and David married her. Chronicles calls him Daniel. After the birth notice he never appears again, and since he plays no part in the fight over who would succeed David, he is generally thought to have died young.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Chileab was David's second son, born to Abigail after David married her following the death of her first husband Nabal (2 Samuel 3:3). He is called Daniel in 1 Chronicles 3:1. He is never mentioned again after his birth notice and is generally thought to have died young, since he plays no role in the succession disputes among David's other sons.

entries.title: Chilion (Man living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: Naomi's son. He died in Moab with his father and his brother, and his widow was one of the two left with Naomi when the men were gone.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Chilion was Naomi's son and one of Ruth's brothers-in-law, who died in Moab along with his father and brother, leaving both Israelite widows before Ruth's eventual return to Bethlehem with Naomi.

entries.title: Chilmad
entries.summary: Ezekiel lists it once among Tyre's trading partners, next to Sheba and Asshur. Some put it near Assyria. Others read the Hebrew as a phrase, not a place at all, and no location has been settled.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Chilmad appears once, among the trading partners of Tyre listed in Ezekiel's lament over the city's commercial empire, grouped with Sheba and Asshur (Ezekiel 27:23). Its identity is uncertain; some read it as a place near Assyria, while others take it not as a place name at all but as a Hebrew phrase meaning something like "as a pupil," referring to Tyre's trading apprenticeship. No location has been established with confidence.

entries.title: Chimham (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: The son of Barzillai, the old Gileadite who stood by David in Absalom's rebellion. David took Chimham back to Jerusalem as the reward. Property near Bethlehem seems to have carried his name for generations.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Chimham was the son of Barzillai, the elderly Gileadite who supported David during Absalom's rebellion, and David brought Chimham back with him to Jerusalem as a reward, apparently granting him property near Bethlehem that carried his name for generations.

witness.excerpt: When he entreated for this so earnestly, the king said, \"I dismiss thee, but thou shalt grant me thy son Chimham, and upon him I will bestow all sorts of good things.\" So Barzillai left his son with him, and worshipped the king, and wished him a prosperous conclusion of all his affairs according to his own mind, and then returned

entries.title: Chinnereth (Sea of Galilee)
entries.summary: Before anyone called it Gennesaret or Tiberias, the lake was the Sea of Chinnereth, named for a fortified Canaanite city on its northwest shore. The town fell inside Naphtali's land. Under the plural Chinneroth it named the whole district, which Ben-hadad of Syria raided in Baasha's reign.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Chinnereth was a fortified Canaanite city near the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee that gave the lake its earliest biblical name, "the Sea of Chinnereth" (Numbers 34:11; Joshua 13:27), later known by its Greco-Roman names Gennesaret and Tiberias. It marked part of Naphtali's territory (Joshua 19:35), and in its plural form, Chinneroth, it named the surrounding district raided by Ben-hadad of Syria in the reign of Baasha (1 Kings 15:20).

entries.title: Chios
entries.summary: A big Aegean island off Asia Minor, still called Chios, that Paul's ship sailed past on the way home from the third missionary journey.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Not a person but a large island in the Aegean Sea off the coast of Asia Minor, past which Paul's ship sailed on his return from the third missionary journey (Acts 20:15). The island, still called Chios today, was known in antiquity for its wine and later for the mastic resin harvested from its trees.

entries.title: Chisleu (Name of the 9th month)
entries.summary: Ninth month, late November into December, also spelled Kislev and taken from the Babylonian calendar.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Chisleu, also spelled Kislev, is not a person but the name of the ninth month of the Hebrew religious calendar, roughly corresponding to late November and December, adopted from the Babylonians after the exile (Nehemiah 1:1; Zechariah 7:1). It marks the season in which Nehemiah heard the report of Jerusalem's broken walls and Zechariah received several of his visions. The later festival of Hanukkah also falls in this month, though it is not mentioned in these particular passages.

entries.title: Chislon (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: The father of Elidad, the leader from the tribe of Benjamin picked to help divide Canaan, and nothing else is known of him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Chislon was the father of Elidad, the leader from the tribe of Benjamin chosen to help apportion the land of Canaan among the tribes after the conquest (Numbers 34:21). Nothing further is known of him.

entries.title: Chisloth-tabor (Chesulloth)
entries.summary: The name means the loins of Tabor, a point on Zebulun's boundary near the mountain. Usually placed at the village of Iksal, about two and a half miles west of Tabor, and it may be the town called Chesulloth a few verses on.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Chisloth-tabor, "the loins of Tabor," marked a point on Zebulun's boundary near Mount Tabor (Joshua 19:12). It is usually identified with the village of Iksal, about two and a half miles west of the mountain, and may be the same town called Chesulloth a few verses later in the description of Issachar's territory.

entries.title: Chittim (Cyprus)
entries.summary: Kittim was a son of Javan, and the name stretched to cover the islands and coasts of the eastern Mediterranean, Cyprus most of all. In prophecy it stands for far-off peoples who come by sea.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Kittim was a son of Javan, and the name became a general biblical term for the peoples and islands of the eastern Mediterranean, particularly Cyprus, used in prophecy for distant maritime nations.

entries.title: Chittim (People from Kittim)
entries.summary: Named twice, in Genesis and 1 Chronicles, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Chiun (A male deity in the Old Testament)
entries.summary: A star god, likely the planet Saturn, whose image Amos says Israel carried in the wilderness. The Septuagint turned the name into Rephan, and that is the form Stephen quotes in Acts 7:43.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Chiun was an astral deity, likely identifying the planet Saturn, whose image the prophet Amos says the Israelites carried and worshipped during the wilderness period (Amos 5:26). The Septuagint rendered the name as Rephan or Remphan, the form Stephen uses when quoting the verse in Acts 7:43. Star worship of this kind was widespread across the ancient Near East, and Assyrian astrological texts record Saturn's association with an underworld deity under a related name.

entries.title: Chloe (Woman living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Her people brought Paul word that the church at Corinth was splitting into factions, and nothing further is known about her.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Chloe was a Christian woman, probably of Corinth or Ephesus, whose household members reported to Paul the factional disputes dividing the Corinthian church (1 Corinthians 1:11). Nothing further is known about her.

entries.title: Chorashan (Bor-ashan)
entries.summary: After he rescued the Ziklag captives from the Amalekites, David sent gifts from the plunder to a string of towns, and this was one. It is generally identified with Ashan, a town of Simeon in the Negev of Judah.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Chorashan, one of the towns to which David sent gifts from the plunder he took after rescuing the captives of Ziklag from the Amalekites (1 Sam. 30:30). It is generally identified with Ashan, a town of Simeon in the Negev of Judah.

entries.title: Chorazin
entries.summary: Jesus did many of his miracles in this Galilee town and then pronounced a woe on it, alongside Bethsaida and Capernaum, because it did not repent. It is identified with Khirbet Karazeh about two miles north of Capernaum, where a black basalt synagogue has been dug up.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Chorazin was one of the towns around the Sea of Galilee where Jesus performed many of his miracles, yet he pronounced a woe against it for failing to repent, grouping it with Bethsaida and Capernaum (Matt. 11:21; Luke 10:13). It is identified with Khirbet Karazeh, about two miles north of Capernaum, where archaeologists have excavated an ancient synagogue built of black basalt, standing on a site of much older settlement.

entries.title: Choseba (Achzib)
entries.summary: One terse line in 1 Chronicles about men of Judah's line who had authority in Moab. It may be the same place as Achzib or Chezib, Shelah's birthplace, but the wording is too thin to be sure.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Choseba, also spelled Cozeba, appears in a brief and difficult genealogical note in 1 Chronicles about men of Judah's line who lived long before and reportedly had authority in Moab (1 Chron. 4:22). It may be the same place as Achzib or Chezib in the Shephelah of Judah, birthplace of Judah's son Shelah in Genesis 38:5, though the connection is uncertain given the terse wording of the Chronicles text.

entries.title: Christ (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: A title, not a surname. It is the Greek for the Hebrew Messiah, the anointed one, and the New Testament gives it to Jesus of Nazareth as the king, priest and deliverer the Old Testament promised. His life and ministry are under Jesus.
entries.books: Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, Acts, Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, 1 Thessalonians, 2 Thessalonians, 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, Titus, Philemon, Hebrews, James, 1 Peter, 2 Peter, 1 John, 2 John, Jude, Revelation
entries.label: 26 books
entries.dictNote: Christ is not a surname but a title, the Greek translation of the Hebrew word Messiah, meaning anointed one, and the New Testament applies it to Jesus of Nazareth as the fulfillment of Old Testament promises of a coming anointed king, priest, and deliverer. See the entry for Jesus for his life and ministry.

entries.title: Christian (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Outsiders at Antioch coined the word, possibly as mockery, for people who followed Christ. The believers called each other brethren, disciples and saints. It turns up only three times in the New Testament, the last in 1 Peter 4:16, which tells them not to be ashamed of suffering under that name.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: “Christian” is not a person but the title given to followers of Jesus, first used at Antioch according to Acts 11:26. Believers themselves used terms like “brethren,” “disciples,” and “saints,” while outsiders, likely the Greek-speaking population of Antioch, coined “Christian” as a label, possibly in mockery, marking them as partisans of Christ. The word appears only three times in the New Testament: Acts 11:26, Acts 26:28, where Agrippa uses it in his reply to Paul, and 1 Peter 4:16, which tells believers not to be ashamed of suffering under that name.

entries.title: Chub (Libya)
entries.summary: A people named once in Ezekiel's oracle against Egypt, among the allies who would fall by the sword. Many suspect a copying slip for Lub, which would make it Libya. That reading is disputed.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Chub is not a person but a people named once, in Ezekiel's oracle against Egypt, among the nations allied with Egypt that would fall by the sword (Ezekiel 30:5). Their identity is uncertain; many scholars suspect textual corruption and would read "Lub," meaning Libya, already named in the same list, though the reading is disputed.

entries.title: Chun (Berothah)
entries.summary: David took bronze from this city of Hadadezer, king of Zobah, and the bronze later went into Solomon's temple. 2 Samuel calls it Berothai. It probably lay somewhere in the Beqaa Valley of Lebanon.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A city belonging to Hadadezer, king of Zobah, from which David took bronze later used in Solomon's temple (1 Chr. 18:8). The parallel account in 2 Samuel 8:8 calls it Berothai, likely the same town as Berothah in Ezekiel 47:16, somewhere in the Beqaa Valley of Lebanon.

entries.title: Chush (Cush)
entries.summary: Cush as a land. It lay south of Egypt, roughly modern Sudan and Ethiopia, and the Old Testament keeps coming back to it as a distant, exotic country.
entries.books: Genesis, 2 Kings, Esther, Job, Psalm, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Nahum, Zephaniah
entries.label: 10 books
entries.dictNote: Cush was Ham's eldest son, and his descendants are associated with the region south of Egypt, roughly modern Sudan and Ethiopia, an area the Old Testament refers to repeatedly as a distant and exotic land.

entries.title: Chush (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Ham's eldest son, whose descendants are tied to the country south of Egypt that carries his name.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Chush (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 3 men called Chush. This one is a man from the united kingdom, named once in Psalm.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Chushan-rishathayim (King living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: God let this king of Aram-naharaim hold Israel down for eight years, the first foreign oppression in Judges. Othniel, Caleb's younger kinsman, beat him, and the land had forty years of peace. The name means something like doubly wicked Cushan, which may be a Hebrew jab rather than what he was really called.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Chushan-rishathayim was a king of Aram-naharaim (Mesopotamia) whom God allowed to oppress Israel for eight years during the period of the judges, the first of the foreign oppressions recorded in Judges. Israel cried out to the LORD, who raised up Othniel, Caleb's younger kinsman, to defeat him and secure forty years of peace (Judges 3:8-11). His title, which means something like “doubly wicked Cushan,” may be a Hebrew wordplay on his actual name rather than his given name.

entries.title: Chuza (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Steward of Herod Antipas's household. He is mainly known through his wife Joanna, who had been healed by Jesus, put her own money toward him and the disciples, and was later among the women at the empty tomb.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Chuza was the household manager, or steward, of Herod Antipas, the tetrarch who ruled Galilee during Jesus' ministry. His wife Joanna was one of the women who had been healed by Jesus and who used their own resources to support him and the disciples, and she was later among the women who discovered the empty tomb (Luke 8:3; 24:10).

entries.title: Cilicia
entries.summary: Paul was born in Tarsus, Cilicia's chief city, on the southeastern coast of Asia Minor. Cilician Jews had their own synagogue in Jerusalem and argued with Stephen there. The province was known for the goat's hair cloth used in tentmaking, which was Paul's trade.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Cilicia was a Roman province on the southeastern coast of Asia Minor, whose chief city Tarsus was Paul's birthplace and a noted center of Greek philosophy and learning. Jews from Cilicia had their own synagogue in Jerusalem, where members disputed with Stephen before his martyrdom. Paul revisited the region strengthening the churches on his second missionary journey, and the province is also famous for the goat's-hair cloth used in tentmaking, the trade Paul practiced.

entries.title: Cis (Saul's father living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Kish, Saul's father, in the Greek form Paul uses once in his sermon at Pisidian Antioch.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The Greek form of Kish, father of King Saul, mentioned by Paul in his synagogue sermon at Pisidian Antioch summarizing Israel's history (Acts 13:21). See Kish for the fuller Old Testament account.

entries.title: Clauda (Cauda)
entries.summary: Paul's ship got into the lee of this little island off Crete in the storm, long enough to haul in the boat and lash ropes round the hull. It is modern Gavdos, the southernmost point of Europe.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Clauda, also spelled Cauda, was a small island off the southwest coast of Crete that Paul's ship passed under the shelter of during the storm that eventually wrecked it on Malta (Acts 27:16). Sailors used its lee to haul in the ship's boat and undergird the vessel with ropes before running before the wind. The island is identified with modern Gavdos, the southernmost point of Europe.

entries.title: Claudia (Woman living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Paul passes her greetings to Timothy from Rome, with those of Pudens, Linus and Eubulus. People have tried to match her with a Claudia in Martial's poems who married a Pudens, but the shared names are all that idea rests on.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Christian at Rome whose greetings Paul passes on to Timothy alongside those of Pudens, Linus, and Eubulus (2 Tim. 4:21). Some interpreters have tried to connect her with a Claudia mentioned in the Roman poet Martial's epigrams as the British wife of a soldier named Pudens, but the identification with Paul's Claudia is speculative and rests only on the shared names.

entries.title: Claudius (Emperor living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: The emperor who threw the Jews out of Rome, which is how Priscilla and Aquila came to Corinth and met Paul. A famine in his reign moved the church at Antioch to send help to the believers in Judea.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Claudius was the Roman emperor who expelled Jews from Rome, an edict that sent Priscilla and Aquila to Corinth where they met Paul, and Acts also records a famine during his reign that prompted the church at Antioch to send relief to believers in Judea.
