entries.title: Clement (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: At Philippi, Paul calls him a fellow labourer whose name is in the book of life. Later tradition sometimes made him Clement of Rome, but the New Testament gives no grounds for that beyond the name.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Clement was a Christian at Philippi whom Paul calls his 'fellow labourer,' naming him among those whose names are 'in the book of life' (Philippians 4:3). Later Christian tradition sometimes identified him with Clement of Rome, author of an early and influential epistle to the Corinthians, but the New Testament gives no basis for that identification beyond the shared name.

entries.title: Cleopas (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: One of the two disciples on the road to Emmaus. The risen Jesus walked with them and they did not know him until he broke the bread. Some make him the Clopas of John 19:25, which cannot be confirmed.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Cleopas was one of two disciples whom the risen Jesus joined on the road to Emmaus, not recognizing him until he broke bread with them (Luke 24:13-18, 30-31). Some have identified him with the Clopas mentioned in John 19:25 as the husband of one of the women at the cross, but this cannot be confirmed.

entries.title: Cleophas (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Clopas, whose wife was one of the Marys standing at the cross. Many take him for the Cleopas of the Emmaus road, though Klopas and Kleopas may be two different names, one Aramaic, one Greek.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Better known as Clopas, named by John as the husband of one of the women named Mary who stood at the cross (John 19:25). Many identify him with the Cleopas of Luke 24:18, one of the two disciples who met the risen Jesus on the road to Emmaus, though the Greek spellings Klopas and Kleopas may represent two distinct names, one Aramaic and one Greek, rather than the same man.

entries.title: Cnidus
entries.summary: Paul's ship struggled to get past this harbour city at the tip of the Cnidian peninsula, in Caria, with the wind against it, and then ran for Crete. Its temple of Aphrodite was famous, and the theatre and harbour works have been excavated.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A city and harbor at the southwestern tip of the Cnidian peninsula in Caria, Asia Minor, famous in antiquity for its temple of Aphrodite. Paul's ship passed it with difficulty in adverse winds on the voyage to Rome, just before running for shelter at Crete (Acts 27:7). Extensive ruins of the Greek and Roman city, including a theater and harbor works, have been excavated at the site.

entries.title: Col-hozeh (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Nehemiah names him once, and he is a man from the exile and the return.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Col-hozeh (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: His son Shallun repaired the Fountain Gate and a stretch of wall in Nehemiah's rebuilding. He was of Judah, and a descendant named Baruch shows up among Jerusalem's returned residents.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Col-hozeh was a man of the tribe of Judah whose son Shallun repaired the Fountain Gate and part of Jerusalem's wall during Nehemiah's rebuilding project (Nehemiah 3:15). A descendant, Baruch, is also listed among Jerusalem's returned residents (Nehemiah 11:5).

entries.title: Colosse (Colossae)
entries.summary: Paul wrote Colossians to the church here, in Phrygia on the Lycus River near Laodicea and Hierapolis, without ever having visited. Epaphras, a local man, had brought the gospel. The mound is unexcavated, near modern Honaz in Turkey.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A city of Phrygia in Asia Minor, on the Lycus River near Laodicea and Hierapolis, and the destination of Paul's letter to the Colossians. Paul had apparently never visited the city himself; its church was founded through Epaphras, a native of Colossae who carried the gospel there (Col. 1:2, 7; 2:1). Archaeological survey has located the unexcavated mound of the ancient city near modern Honaz, Turkey.

entries.title: Conaniah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A Levite in charge of the tithes and offerings that came into the temple under Hezekiah's reforms.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Conaniah was a Levite entrusted with overseeing the tithes and offerings brought into the temple during Hezekiah's religious reforms.

entries.title: Coniah (King living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: The short form of Jehoiachin that Jeremiah uses, for the king of Judah carried off to Babylon. In that prophecy he is written down as childless, meaning none of his line would rule from David's throne.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Coniah is a shortened form of the name Jehoiachin, the king of Judah taken captive to Babylon, used by Jeremiah in a prophecy declaring him childless as far as ruling on David's throne was concerned.

entries.title: Core (Aaron's adversary living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: The Greek form of Korah, the Levite who rose against Moses and Aaron and went down when the ground opened. Jude puts him beside Cain and Balaam as a warning about teachers who reject authority and chase gain.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Core is the Greek form of Korah, the Levite who led a rebellion against Moses and Aaron's authority in the wilderness and was destroyed along with his followers when the ground opened beneath them (Numbers 16). Jude 1:11 cites Korah's rebellion as a warning against false teachers who reject authority and pursue gain, grouping him with Cain and Balaam as examples of corrupted faith.

entries.title: Corinth
entries.summary: Paul stayed eighteen months in this rich trading city on the isthmus, and the church he planted got two of his longest letters. He stood before the proconsul Gallio there, whose dated term helps fix Paul's timeline. An inscription found at Corinth names an Erastus who paid for a pavement, likely the city treasurer of Romans 16:23.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Corinth was a major commercial city on the isthmus connecting the Peloponnese to mainland Greece, rebuilt by Rome after its earlier destruction, known in the ancient world for its wealth and loose morals. Paul spent eighteen months there founding the church that would receive two of his most substantial letters, and appeared before the Roman proconsul Gallio, whose recorded term of office helps anchor the chronology of Paul's ministry (Acts 18:1-17). A pavement inscription discovered at Corinth naming a civic official called Erastus who paid for it at his own expense is widely thought to refer to the same Erastus, the city treasurer, whom Paul mentions in Romans 16:23.

entries.title: Corinthian
entries.summary: Anyone from Corinth. Crispus, the synagogue ruler who believed with his household, is one Acts names, and Paul speaks straight to them as Corinthians in his second letter.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Corinthian designates an inhabitant of Corinth, the wealthy Roman colony and trade hub where Paul founded a church during an eighteen-month stay. Acts names Crispus, a synagogue ruler who believed with his whole household, among the Corinthians converted there, and Paul later addresses the congregation directly by that name in his second letter to them.

entries.title: Cornelius (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: A Roman centurion at Caesarea, devout, generous, and not a Jew. An angel told him to send for Peter while a vision got Peter ready to come. When the Holy Spirit fell on his household as it had at Pentecost, the Jerusalem church accepted that Gentiles did not have to become Jews first.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Cornelius was a Roman centurion in Caesarea, devout and generous despite not being Jewish, and an angel told him to send for Peter, while a vision simultaneously prepared Peter to accept the invitation despite Jewish law's restrictions on entering a Gentile's home. Cornelius and his household became the first Gentile converts, and the Holy Spirit visibly fell on them the same way it had on the Jewish believers at Pentecost, convincing the Jerusalem church that the gospel extended to Gentiles without requiring them to become Jews first.

entries.title: Cos
entries.summary: A small island near Rhodes that Paul's ship passed heading back toward Jerusalem. In the first century it was a centre of Hellenistic culture and medicine, with a Jewish community of its own.

entries.dictNote: A small island in the Aegean Sea near Rhodes, off the coast of southwest Asia Minor, that Paul's ship passed on the voyage back toward Jerusalem after his third missionary journey (Acts 21:1). In the first century it was a noted center of Hellenistic culture and medicine, with a Jewish community documented in other ancient sources.

entries.title: Cosam (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A name in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, son of Elmodam and father of Addi, and nothing more than that.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Cosam appears in Luke's genealogy of Jesus as the son of Elmodam and father of Addi, one of the ancestors in the line traced through Joseph back to David (Luke 3:28).

entries.title: Cozbi (Woman living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Daughter of Zur, a Midianite chief. Phinehas the priest killed her and the Israelite Zimri together at Baal-peor, and the plague that came with it was remembered as a warning.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Cozbi was a Midianite woman, daughter of a tribal chief named Zur, who was killed along with the Israelite man Zimri by Phinehas the priest for their open immorality at Baal-peor (Numbers 25:6-18). The incident, and the plague that followed it, was remembered afterward as a warning against intermarriage that led Israel into idolatry.

entries.summary: A title for God, not a name. Peter uses it telling people who are suffering to hand themselves over and keep doing good.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Not a personal name: "Creator" in 1 Peter 4:19 is a title for God, urging suffering believers to entrust their souls to their "faithful Creator" while continuing to do good.

entries.title: Crescens (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: By the time Paul wrote his last letter from prison, Crescens had gone to Galatia; tradition, not Scripture, has him founding churches in Gaul.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Crescens was a coworker of Paul who had gone to Galatia by the time Paul wrote his final letter from Roman imprisonment, one of several companions Paul mentions as having departed (2 Tim. 4:10). Later church tradition, not attested in scripture, associates him with founding churches in Gaul.

entries.title: Cretan (Crete)

entries.dictNote: Crete is the large Mediterranean island where Paul left Titus to organize the churches and appoint elders, and Paul's ship also stopped there during the storm-tossed voyage to Rome recorded in Acts.

entries.title: Crispus (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: He ran the synagogue at Corinth, believed under Paul's preaching, and was one of the few Corinthians Paul baptised himself.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Crispus was the leader of the Jewish synagogue in Corinth who came to believe in Christ under Paul's preaching there (Acts 18:8). Paul later recalled personally baptizing him, one of the few Corinthian converts Paul baptized himself (1 Corinthians 1:14).

entries.title: Cushan
entries.summary: In Habakkuk's poem the tents of Cushan tremble alongside Midian as the Lord approaches. Probably a Cushite group in northwest Arabia, not African Cush, and no relation to the king Cushan-rishathaim. Where exactly it lay is not established.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Cushan appears once, in Habakkuk 3:7, paired poetically with Midian as a nomadic people or territory trembling before the Lord's approach. It most likely refers to a Cushite group in northwest Arabia rather than African Cush, and should not be confused with Cushan-rishathaim, the Mesopotamian king who oppressed Israel for eight years in Judges 3:8-10, despite the similar name. Its precise territory is not established.

entries.title: Cushi (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: The name means the Cushite, and at least two men carry it. One was the father of Shelemiah, whose son was sent to fetch Baruch after Jeremiah's scroll was burned. Another is in Zephaniah's family line, a few generations below Hezekiah.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Cushi (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Zephaniah names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Cuth
entries.summary: The Assyrians conquered the northern kingdom and moved people from this Babylonian city into Samaria, and they brought their god Nergal with them. It is identified with Tell Ibrahim northeast of Babylon. Later Jews used Cuthites, often as an insult, for Samaritans.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Cuth, or Cuthah, was a Babylonian city whose deported inhabitants the Assyrians resettled in Samaria after conquering the northern kingdom; these settlers brought the worship of their god Nergal with them (2 Kings 17:24, 30). The city has been identified with Tell Ibrahim northeast of Babylon, and “Cuthites” became a term Jews later used, often disparagingly, for Samaritans.

entries.title: Cyprus
entries.summary: The island Barnabas came from, where the first missionary journey started and the proconsul Sergius Paulus became an early convert.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Cyprus was a Mediterranean island, Barnabas's home region, and Paul and Barnabas's first missionary journey began there, where the Roman proconsul Sergius Paulus became an early convert.

entries.title: Cyrene
entries.summary: Greek colonists founded it in North Africa around 630 BC, and its temple of Apollo and theatre still stand near Shahhat in Libya. Simon of Cyrene carried Jesus's cross. Cyrenian believers helped start the mixed church at Antioch, and Lucius of Cyrene taught there.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A prominent city in North Africa, in the region later called Libya, founded by Greek colonists around 630 BC; its extensive ruins, including a temple of Apollo and a well-preserved theater, still stand near the modern town of Shahhat in Libya. Cyrene had a large Jewish population, and its people appear repeatedly in the New Testament: Simon of Cyrene was compelled to carry Jesus's cross (Matthew 27:32; Mark 15:21), Cyrenian Jews had their own synagogue in Jerusalem (Acts 6:9), Cyrenian believers helped found the mixed Jewish-Gentile church at Antioch (Acts 11:20), and Lucius of Cyrene was among the prophets and teachers serving that church (Acts 13:1).

entries.title: Cyrus (Emperor living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: The Persian king who took Babylon and let the deported peoples, the Jews among them, go home and rebuild their temples. Isaiah calls him by name long before he was born, God's shepherd and anointed. The Cyrus Cylinder, found in Babylon in 1879, records the same policy.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Cyrus the Great was the Persian king who conquered Babylon and, in a sharp break from earlier imperial policy, allowed the exiled peoples Babylon had deported, including the Jews, to return home and rebuild their temples. Isaiah names Cyrus by name generations before his birth and calls him God's anointed, a shepherd who would carry out God's purposes without even knowing the God he served. The Cyrus Cylinder, a clay artifact discovered in Babylon in 1879, independently records Cyrus's policy of returning exiled peoples and restoring their temples, closely matching the biblical account in Ezra.

witness.excerpt: I have also sent my treasurer Mithridates, and Zorobabel, the governor of the Jews, that they may lay the foundations of the temple, and may build it sixty cubits high, and of the same latitude.

entries.curatedNote: The Persian king Isaiah names by name roughly a century and a half before he was born: 'my shepherd' (Isaiah 44:28), who then actually issues the decree letting the exiles go home and rebuild the temple. Josephus preserves what he presents as the decree's own wording, the same funding order behind Zerubbabel's return.

entries.title: Dabareh (Daberath)
entries.summary: Also called Daberath, on Zebulun's border near Mount Tabor, and later given to the Gershonite Levites. The Arab village of Deburiyeh at the western foot of Tabor still carries the name.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Dabareh, also called Daberath, was a town on the border of Zebulun near Mount Tabor (Joshua 19:12) that was later assigned to the Gershonite Levites (Joshua 21:28; 1 Chronicles 6:72). It survives in the name of the Arab village Deburiyeh, which still sits at the western foot of Tabor.

entries.title: Dabbesheth
entries.summary: One of the towns marking Zebulun's border; nothing else is recorded and the site has not been found.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Dabbesheth was a town marking part of the border of the tribal allotment of Zebulun (Joshua 19:11). Nothing further is recorded of it, and its exact site has not been identified.

entries.title: Dagon (A male deity in the Old Testament)
entries.summary: The Philistines set the captured ark in Dagon's temple at Ashdod. His statue was found face down before the ark, and the second time it had lost its head and hands.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Dagon was the chief god of the Philistines, and when the captured ark of the covenant was placed in Dagon's temple at Ashdod, his statue was found fallen face down before the ark twice, the second time with its head and hands broken off, a humiliating sign of Yahweh's superiority the Philistines couldn't ignore.

entries.title: Dalaiah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: He told King Jehoiakim not to burn Jeremiah's scroll, and the king burned it anyway.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Delaiah was a common postexilic name, including an official who urged King Jehoiakim not to burn Jeremiah's prophetic scroll, a plea the king ignored.

entries.title: Dalaiah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A man from the divided-kingdom years, and 1 Chronicles is the only book that names him.

entries.title: Dalaiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Named in the returnee lists of Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7, a family head from after the exile. It was a common name in that period, and the record gives this one nothing more.

entries.title: Dalmanutha (Magadan)
entries.summary: Mark says Jesus went there by boat after feeding the four thousand. Matthew's account of the same trip says Magdala, so the two names probably cover neighbouring ground. No site has been matched to it.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Dalmanutha, on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee, is named only in Mark's account of Jesus withdrawing there by boat after feeding the four thousand (Mark 8:10). Matthew's parallel account of the same trip names the destination as the region of Magdala instead (Matthew 15:39), suggesting the two names referred to neighboring or overlapping areas rather than two different events. No archaeological site has been confidently matched to the name.

entries.title: Dalmatia
entries.summary: Titus had gone to Dalmatia by the time Paul wrote from his last imprisonment in Rome. It was the rough coast along the eastern Adriatic, part of the province of Illyricum, roughly modern Croatia and Montenegro. Rome had put down a big revolt there under Tiberius in AD 9.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Dalmatia was the rugged coastal region along the eastern Adriatic, part of the Roman province of Illyricum, corresponding roughly to the coast of modern Croatia and Montenegro. Paul mentions it once, noting that his companion Titus had gone there during Paul's final imprisonment in Rome (2 Timothy 4:10); Paul himself claims earlier to have preached as far as Illyricum (Romans 15:19). Rome fought several wars to subdue the Dalmatian tribes, finally crushing a major revolt under Tiberius in AD 9, decades before Paul's letter.

entries.title: Dalphon (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: The second of Haman's ten sons, killed by the Jews of Susa once his father's plot had failed.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Dalphon was the second named of Haman's ten sons, all of whom were killed by the Jews of Susa after Haman's plot against them failed and were afterward hanged on gallows (Esther 9:7-10).

entries.title: Damaris (Woman living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: An Athenian woman who believed after Paul spoke at the Areopagus, one of the very few converts from that speech named at all. Dionysius the Areopagite is named in the same verse, and nothing ties the two together beyond that.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: An Athenian woman who became a believer after hearing Paul's speech at the Areopagus (Acts 17:34), one of very few individuals named as converts from that address. She is mentioned alongside Dionysius the Areopagite, though there is no evidence connecting the two beyond their both being named in the same verse.

entries.title: Damascene (Damascus)
entries.summary: Paul uses the word for the people of Damascus when he tells how King Aretas's ethnarch had the city guarded to catch him, and he got out in a basket let down over the wall.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Damascene designates an inhabitant of Damascus, used by Paul when he recalls how the ethnarch under King Aretas guarded the city to arrest him, forcing Paul to escape by being lowered over the wall in a basket. Damascus is among the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world, and Aretas IV, the Nabatean king in view, is well attested on coins and inscriptions from the period.

entries.title: Damascus
entries.summary: A city has stood here, on a fertile plain watered by the Barada northwest of Mount Hermon, since before the patriarchs. It was the Aramean capital that fought Israel through the ninth and eighth centuries BC. Saul was converted on the road into it, and the street called Straight was a real colonnaded street whose columns have been found.
entries.books: Genesis, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 2 Chronicles, Song of Solomon, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Amos, Zechariah, Acts, 2 Corinthians, Galatians
entries.label: 13 books
entries.dictNote: Damascus sits in a fertile plain northwest of Mount Hermon, watered by the river Barada, which is why a city has stood on this spot without a real break since before the patriarchs. It served as the capital of the Aramean kingdom that fought Israel through the ninth and eighth centuries BC, and centuries later it was on the road into this same city that Saul was converted (Acts 9). The street the New Testament calls Straight was a real colonnaded thoroughfare running through Roman Damascus, and remains of its columns have been found.

entries.title: Dan
entries.summary: The tribe of Dan and the town it took. Squeezed in its first allotment near the Philistines, the tribe went north, captured Laish and renamed it Dan, Israel's northernmost town and the far end of from Dan to Beersheba. Jeroboam I put one of his golden calves there, and a stele from Tel Dan found in 1993 names the House of David.
entries.books: Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Jeremiah, Ezekiel
entries.label: 14 books
entries.dictNote: Dan is both Jacob's fifth son, by Bilhah, and the tribe and northern city that carry his name. Squeezed out of its first allotment near the Philistines, the tribe migrated north, took Laish and renamed it Dan, and the phrase 'from Dan to Beersheba' came to mean the whole length of the land. Jeroboam later set one of his two golden calves there.

entries.title: Dan (Jacob's son living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Jacob's son by Bilhah, Rachel's servant, and the ancestor of the tribe that carries his name.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Dan-jaan (Ijon)
entries.summary: Joab's census party passed through here on the way round the land, somewhere near Dan by the sources of the Jordan. The name may just mean Dan in the forest, and some old translations read it that way, not as a separate place.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Dan-jaan, meaning Dan in the forest, is named in the route of Joab's census-taking journey through the tribal territories east and north of Israel, somewhere near the town of Dan by the sources of the Jordan (2 Sam. 24:6). Some ancient translations read the phrase simply as Dan in the forest rather than treating it as a distinct place name.

entries.title: Daniel (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of 3 men called Daniel. This one is a man from the exile and the return, named twice in Ezra and Nehemiah.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Daniel (Prophet living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Carried off to Babylon as a young noble of Judah and renamed by his captors, he rose to high office under three empires without giving up his faith. That refusal got him a night in the lions' den. The visions he received run to the book's last chapter.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Two men named Daniel appear in the Old Testament. The one people usually mean is the prophet carried off to Babylon as a young noble of Judah, who rose to high office under three different empires while refusing to compromise his faith, surviving a night in a lion's den for it and receiving visions that stretch to the book's final chapter. The other Daniel was David's second son, born in Hebron to Abigail and also called Chileab, a figure who otherwise disappears from the record entirely.

witness.excerpt: Among these there were four of the family of Zedekiah; of most excellent dispositions: the one of whom was called Daniel… And the King of Babylon changed their names… Daniel he called Baltasar.
And when the book of Daniel was shewed him, wherein Daniel declared that one of the Greeks should destroy the empire of the Persians, he supposed that himself was the person intended.
And what things befel Daniel in Media : and what prophecies he delivered there.

entries.curatedNote: Taken to Babylon as a young noble and renamed by his captors (Daniel 1:6-7). Josephus tells the exact same scene, the deportation, the new Babylonian name, Daniel becoming Belteshazzar, as straight political history, no different in kind from any other royal hostage of the era.

entries.title: Dannah
entries.summary: One of the towns in Judah's hill country south of Hebron. It is sometimes put near modern Idhna, southwest of Hebron, but that is not certain.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Dannah was a town in the hill country of Judah, listed among the settlements south of Hebron in Joshua's account of Judah's inheritance (Josh. 15:49). It is sometimes associated with the area near the modern town of Idhna, southwest of Hebron, though the identification is not certain.

entries.title: Dara (Man living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: Probably the same man as Darda, a son of Zerah. He is one of the wise men, with Heman, Chalcol and Ethan, whose wisdom Solomon's outdid.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Dara is likely the same figure as Darda, listed among the sons of Zerah in 1 Chronicles 2:6 and named in 1 Kings 4:31 as one of the wise men, alongside Heman, Chalcol, and Ethan, whose renowned wisdom Solomon's was said to surpass.

entries.title: Darda (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Solomon's wisdom is measured against four famous wise men, and he is one of them. The name turns up again among the sons of Zerah.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of four men renowned for wisdom before Solomon's time, named as a standard of proverbial wisdom that Solomon was said to exceed (1 Kings 4:31); the same name appears again among the sons of Zerah in 1 Chronicles 2:6.

witness.excerpt: He also excelled and distinguished himself in wisdom above those who were most eminent among the Hebrews at that time for shrewdness; those I mean were Ethan, and Heman, and Chalcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol.

entries.title: Darius
entries.summary: Darius the Great, the Persian emperor in Ezra. Temple building in Jerusalem had stalled, and his decree let it start again. Ezra keeps the text of it.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Two Persian kings named Darius appear in the Old Testament. Darius the Mede is named in Daniel as ruling Babylon immediately after its fall, the king who reluctantly signed the decree that landed Daniel in the lion's den. Darius the Great, a later and better-attested Persian emperor, authorized the resumption of temple construction in Jerusalem after work had stalled, and his decree is preserved in the book of Ezra.

witness.excerpt: Now there was one Sanballat , who was sent by Darius, the last King [of Persia], into Samaria.
Against him did Cyrus, the King of Persia, and Darius, the King of Media, make war.

entries.title: Darius (Emperor living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A Persian king named once, in Nehemiah. Darius was a title several kings carried, and the verse leaves it there.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Darius (Ruler living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: In Daniel he rules Babylon right after it falls, and he is the king who signed, without wanting to, the decree that put Daniel in the lions' den. Daniel calls him Darius the Mede.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Darkon (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: His descendants came back from Babylon with Zerubbabel among the servants of Solomon, a class of temple workers.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Darkon was the ancestral head of a family among the 'servants of Solomon,' a class of temple workers, whose descendants returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:56; Nehemiah 7:58).

entries.title: Dathan (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: He and Abiram joined Korah against Moses, and the ground opened under their tents and took them and their families.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Dathan, along with Abiram, joined Korah's rebellion against Moses's leadership, and the ground opened beneath their tents and swallowed them along with their families.

witness.excerpt: And now Moses sent messengers for Abiram and Dathan; and ordered them to come to the assembly, and wait there for the holy offices that were to be performed.
But if God had determined to bestow it on the eldest tribe; that of Reubel might have it most justly: and then Dathan, and Abiram, and [On the son of] Peleth would have it.

entries.title: David (King living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: The shepherd from Bethlehem who killed Goliath and became Israel's second king, ruling the largest territory Israel ever held, which Solomon then inherited. Solomon was one of his sons. Nearly half the psalms carry his name, and the Tel Dan inscription, where an enemy king boasts over the house of David, put his dynasty outside the Bible as well.
entries.books: Ruth, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Psalm, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Song of Solomon, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Hosea, Amos, Zechariah, Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, Acts, Romans, 2 Timothy, Hebrews, Revelation
entries.label: 28 books
entries.dictNote: David was Israel's second king and its most consequential one, a shepherd from Bethlehem who killed Goliath as a young man and eventually inherited a kingdom that stretched further than anything before or after it under a single native ruler. He married at least eight women and fathered at least twenty children, among them Solomon, and nearly half the biblical psalms carry his name. For most of the twentieth century critics treated David as a legend with no life outside the text, until a broken Aramaic inscription surfaced at Tel Dan naming the "house of David" as a real dynasty, one an enemy king thought worth boasting about defeating.
entries.dictSource: study-bible (ACAI + Tyndale); Logos Factbook (Tel Dan Stele)

witness.excerpt: But David fell now into a very grievous sin, though he were otherwise naturally a righteous and a religious man, and one that firmly observed the laws of our fathers.

entries.lukeNote: Luke opens on the promise of ‘the throne of his father David’ (1:32) and closes the point with Jesus's own riddle about David's son and David's Lord (20:41-44). Josephus, introducing the Bathsheba affair, pauses to say the sin was out of character, the same tension Luke's own ‘son of David’ title leans on without ever mentioning the affair at all.

entries.title: Debir
entries.summary: Othniel took this town in Judah's hill country and won Caleb's daughter Achsah as his wife for it. Debir is also the name of a Canaanite king Joshua defeated.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Debir refers to both a Canaanite king Joshua defeated and a town in the hill country of Judah that Othniel captured, winning Caleb's daughter Achsah in marriage as a reward.

entries.title: Debir (King living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: Joshua names him once, and he is a king from the years before the monarchy.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Deborah (Judge living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: Prophetess and the one woman among Israel's judges. She sat under a palm tree between Ramah and Bethel and Israel came to her for judgment. Barak would not go against Sisera without her, so she went and told him a woman would get the credit, and Jael killed Sisera in her own tent.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Deborah was a prophetess and the only woman among Israel's judges, and she held court under a palm tree between Ramah and Bethel where Israelites came to her for judgment. When she summoned the military commander Barak to lead an attack against the Canaanite general Sisera, he refused to go unless she came with him, so she agreed but told him the credit for the victory would go to a woman instead, a prophecy fulfilled when a woman named Jael killed Sisera in her own tent with a tent peg. Deborah is also named as the nurse of Rebekah in Genesis, an earlier figure who has nothing to do with the judge.

entries.title: Deborah (Nurse living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Rebekah's nurse, who went with her from Haran and stayed with the family for life. Genesis 35:8 records her death and burial under an oak below Bethel, which was named the oak of weeping.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Decapolis
entries.summary: The name is Greek for ten cities, a loose league of Hellenistic towns mostly east and southeast of the Sea of Galilee, Gerasa and Philadelphia among them. Crowds from there followed Jesus. The man freed from Legion near Gerasa went round the whole Decapolis telling what had happened to him.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: The Decapolis, Greek for ten cities, was a loose league of Hellenistic cities mostly east and southeast of the Sea of Galilee, including Scythopolis, the only one west of the Jordan, along with Gerasa and Philadelphia. Crowds from the region followed Jesus (Matthew 4:25), and the man he freed from a legion of demons near Gerasa went on to proclaim what had happened to him throughout the Decapolis (Mark 5:20). Extensive ruins still stand at cities like Jerash and Beth Shean, among the best preserved Roman-era cities in the region.

witness.excerpt: So he sent away his son Titus to [the other] Cesarea, that he might bring the army that lay there to Seythopous, which is the largest city of Decapolis, and in the neighborhood of Tiberias, whither he came, and where he waited for his son.

entries.title: Dedan
entries.summary: An Arabian trading people, known in the prophets for caravans and goods. Their ancestor Dedan was a son of Abraham through Keturah.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Dedan was a son of Abraham through Keturah and the ancestor of an Arabian trading people associated with caravans and merchandise in the prophetic books.

entries.title: Dedan (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Genesis and 1 Chronicles name him twice, and he is a man from the patriarchs.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Dedan (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: One of 3 men called Dedan. This one is a man from the patriarchs, named twice in Genesis and 1 Chronicles.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Dedanim
entries.summary: Isaiah pictures their caravans camping in the desert thickets, and Ezekiel has them supplying Tyre. They are generally placed at the oasis of al-Ula in northwest Arabia, where Dedanite and Lihyanite inscriptions confirm a real trading kingdom.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Dedanim were the descendants of Dedan, an Arabian people whose caravans Isaiah pictures lodging in the desert thickets, and whom Ezekiel later lists among the merchants supplying Tyre with goods. Dedan is generally located at the oasis of al-Ula in northwest Arabia, where excavated inscriptions in the ancient Dedanite and Lihyanite scripts confirm the existence of a real trading kingdom by that name.

entries.title: Dehavites (Word sometimes translated as a name)
entries.summary: One of the peoples the Assyrians had settled in Samaria, who later wrote to the Persian king against rebuilding the temple. Where they came from is uncertain; some point east of the Caspian Sea.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Dehavites were among the foreign peoples the Assyrians settled in Samaria who later wrote to the Persian king opposing the rebuilding of Jerusalem's temple. Their exact origin is uncertain; some scholars connect them with a nomadic tribe from the region east of the Caspian Sea.

entries.title: Dekar (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Father of Ben-Dekar, one of Solomon's twelve district officers, whose region took in Shaalbim and Beth-shemesh.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Father of Ben-Dekar, one of Solomon's twelve district officers, responsible for supplying the royal household from the region including Shaalbim and Beth-shemesh (1 Kings 4:9).

entries.title: Delilah (Woman living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: Samson loved her, and the Philistine rulers paid her well to find out where his strength came from. He lied three times and each answer failed. She kept at him until he told her about his uncut Nazirite hair, and she had it shaved while he slept.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Delilah was a Philistine woman Samson loved, and Philistine rulers paid her heavily to discover the secret of his strength. She pressed him repeatedly, and after he lied to her three times with false answers that each failed, she wore him down until he finally admitted his strength depended on his uncut Nazirite hair, and she had it shaved off while he slept, delivering him powerless into his enemies' hands.

witness.excerpt: For he fell in love with a woman that was an harlot among the Philistines: her name was Delilah ; and he lived with her.

entries.title: Demas (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: With Paul in his imprisonment, and then gone. Paul writes that Demas deserted him because he loved this present world.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Demas was a companion of Paul during his imprisonment who later abandoned him, and Paul writes with evident disappointment that Demas deserted him because he loved this present world.

entries.title: Demetrius (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: A silversmith in Ephesus who made shrines of Artemis. He saw Paul's preaching killing his trade and started a riot, and the crowd chanted for two hours before the city officials calmed it.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Demetrius was a silversmith in Ephesus who made shrines of the goddess Artemis, and his fear that Paul's preaching was destroying his trade sparked a citywide riot that lasted two hours of continuous chanting before city officials calmed the crowd.

witness.excerpt: SO Demetrius came with an army, and took those that invited him, and pitched his camp near the city Shechem; upon which Alexander, with his six thousand two hundred mercenaries, and about twenty thousand Jews, who were of his party,

BUT when Demetrius was informed of the death of Nicanor, and of the destruction of the army that was with him, he sent Bacchides again with an army into Judea, who marched out of Antioch, and came into Judea, and pitched his camp at Arbel

But as for king Demetrius, who had a mind to make war against Hyrcanus, there was no opportunity nor room for it, while both the Syrians and the soldiers bare ill-will to him, because he was an ill man.

He also accused Demetrius, who was governor of those places, of many crimes, and turned him out; and after he had spent three years in this war, he returned to his own country, when the Jews joyfully received him upon this his good success.
4.
ABOUT the same time Demetrius, the son of Seleucus, fled away from Rome, and took Tripoli, a city of Syria, and set the diadem on his own head.

entries.title: Derbe
entries.summary: Paul and Barnabas fled here from Lystra after Paul was stoned, and Paul came back later. It was a small town in the Lycaonian highlands near modern Karaman, and the hometown of Gaius. An inscription found in 1956 at Kerti Höyük fixed the site.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Derbe was a small town in the Lycaonian highlands of Asia Minor, near modern Karaman in Turkey. Paul and Barnabas fled there from Lystra during the first missionary journey after being stoned, and Paul revisited it later; it was the hometown of his traveling companion Gaius. Its exact site was uncertain until 1956, when an inscription dated to AD 157 found at the mound of Kerti Höyük identified it as Derbe, a location now widely accepted by archaeologists.

entries.title: Deuel (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: The father of Gad's tribal leader during the wilderness census, and that is all of him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Deuel was the father of the tribal leader of Gad during the wilderness census.

entries.title: Diana (A female deity in the New Testament)
entries.summary: The Latin name for Artemis, goddess of Ephesus. When silversmiths feared Paul was ruining the shrine trade, the city chanted for two hours that great is Artemis of the Ephesians.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Diana is the Latin name for Artemis, the patron goddess of Ephesus, and a riot broke out there when silversmiths who made her shrines feared Paul's preaching was destroying their trade, chanting for two hours that great is Artemis of the Ephesians.

witness.excerpt: Now I found a very fit place in a castle that hath its name from the country Diana; this place is full of materials of several sorts, and replenished with sacred animals; I desire therefore that you will grant me leave to purge this holy place, which belongs to no master, and is fallen down, and to bu

ABOUT this time it was that king Antiochus, as he was going over the upper countries, heard that there was a very rich city in Persia, called Elymais; and therein a very rich temple of Diana, and that it was full of all sorts of donations dedicated to it; as also weapons and breastplates, which, upon inquiry, he found had been left there by Alexander, the son of Philip, king of Macedonia.

entries.title: Diblaim (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Gomer's father. Hosea married her at God's command as a picture of Israel's unfaithfulness, and nothing further is known of Diblaim.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Diblaim was the father of Gomer, the woman the prophet Hosea married at God's command as a living symbol of Israel's unfaithfulness (Hosea 1:3). Nothing further is known of Diblaim.

entries.title: Diblath (Riblah)
entries.summary: Ezekiel's judgment runs from the wilderness to Diblah, meaning the whole length of the land. It is most likely a copyist's form of Riblah on the Orontes in Syria, the Babylonian headquarters where Zedekiah was blinded after watching his sons killed.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Diblah is most likely a scribal variant of Riblah, a strategic town on the Orontes River in Syria that served as the Babylonian army's military headquarters during the fall of Jerusalem. Ezekiel 6:14 uses it as one boundary marker in a judgment oracle stretching "from the wilderness to Diblah," meaning the whole length of the land. Nebuchadnezzar's field headquarters at Riblah is where the captured king Zedekiah was blinded after watching his sons executed (2 Kings 25:6-7).

entries.title: Dibon
entries.summary: A Moabite city Israel took and rebuilt. King Mesha names it on the Moabite Stone as one of his own building projects.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Dibon was a Moabite city Israel captured and later rebuilt, mentioned on the Moabite Stone itself as one of King Mesha's building projects, corroborating the biblical record of the region's contested history.

witness.excerpt: And the seed of them shall perish, from Heshbon even to Dibon.

entries.title: Dibon
entries.summary: Named once, in Nehemiah, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Dibri (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: A Danite whose daughter Shelomith had a son by an Egyptian. The son was stoned for blasphemy in the wilderness, and the episode brought in the law on blasphemy in Leviticus.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Danite, father of Shelomith, whose son by an Egyptian father was stoned for blasphemy in the wilderness, an episode that prompted the law on blasphemy recorded in Leviticus (Leviticus 24:10-11).

entries.title: Didymus (Apostle living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Greek for twin, and John's byname for the apostle Thomas. John probably translates it because some readers knew Thomas by the nickname. No one says who the other twin was.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Didymus is the Greek word for “twin,” used in John's Gospel as a byname for the apostle Thomas (John 11:16; 20:24; 21:2). John likely includes the translation because some readers knew Thomas primarily by this descriptive nickname rather than his Aramaic name. No biblical tradition identifies who his twin sibling was.

entries.title: Diklah (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: A son of Joktan in the table of nations, more likely a tribal territory than one man. The name means palm grove, which points to a date-growing district of Arabia, but where is uncertain.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Diklah appears in the table of nations as a son of Joktan, one of the Arabian clans descended from Shem (Genesis 10:27; 1 Chronicles 1:21). Like most of Joktan's other sons, the name almost certainly designates a tribal territory rather than a single historical individual, and its meaning, palm grove, points to a district of Arabia known for date palm cultivation, though its exact location remains uncertain.

entries.title: Dilean
entries.summary: A town in the Shephelah of Judah, listed with Migdal-gad and Mizpeh, whose site has not been identified with confidence.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Dilean was a town in the lowland district, or Shephelah, of Judah's territory, listed among a group of towns that included Migdal-gad and Mizpeh (Josh. 15:38). Its site has not been identified with confidence.

entries.title: Dimnah
entries.summary: Zebulun gave this town to the Merari clan of Levites. The list in 1 Chronicles calls it Rimmon, either a copying variant or a real change of name. Nobody knows where it stood.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Dimnah was a town of the tribe of Zebulun assigned to the Levite clan of Merari for their residence (Joshua 21:35). The parallel list in 1 Chronicles 6:77 gives the same town's name as Rimmon instead, suggesting either a scribal variant or a genuine name change. Its exact site is unidentified.

entries.title: Dimon (Dibon)
entries.summary: Isaiah sees the waters of Dimon, east of the Dead Sea, turning to blood in his oracle against Moab. Many take it as another name for the waters of Dibon, the Moabite capital where Mesha's stone was found.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Dimon, the "waters of Dimon," a stream or pool east of the Dead Sea that Isaiah pictures turning to blood in his oracle of judgment against Moab (Isa. 15:9). Many read it as another name for the waters of Dibon, the Moabite capital where the Moabite Stone, King Mesha's own inscription, was later discovered.

entries.title: Dimonah
entries.summary: A town in the far south of Judah, in the Negev, generally taken as the Dibon resettled after the exile in Nehemiah 11:25.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A town in the far south of Judah, in the Negev (Joshua 15:22). It is generally taken as the same place as Dibon mentioned in Nehemiah 11:25 among the towns resettled by Judahites after the exile.

entries.title: Dinah (Jacob's daughter living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Jacob and Leah's only daughter. After Shechem raped her, Simeon and Levi made the men of his city agree to be circumcised and then killed them all while they were still recovering. On his deathbed Jacob condemned it as reckless cruelty.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Dinah was Jacob and Leah's only daughter, and her rape by a local prince named Shechem triggered one of Genesis's most violent episodes: Dinah's brothers Simeon and Levi pretended to negotiate a marriage settlement requiring the men of Shechem's city to be circumcised, then slaughtered the entire incapacitated population while they were recovering, an act of vengeance Jacob condemned on his deathbed as reckless cruelty.

entries.title: Dinaite (Word sometimes translated as a name)
entries.summary: They were among the peoples the Assyrians resettled in Samaria, and they signed the letter to Artaxerxes against rebuilding Jerusalem, which stopped the work for a time.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Dinaites were among the peoples the Assyrians had resettled in Samaria who later wrote to the Persian king Artaxerxes opposing the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls and temple, a complaint that succeeded in halting the work for a time.

entries.title: Dinhaban (Dinhabah)
entries.summary: A place, not a person, and a variant spelling of Dinhabah, the capital of Bela son of Beor, first on Edom's list of early kings. It lay somewhere south and east of the Dead Sea; the site is unknown.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: The name here is a data variant of Dinhabah, which is a place, not a person: the capital city of Bela son of Beor, the first king listed in Edom's roster of early rulers (Genesis 36:32; 1 Chronicles 1:43). Its location is unknown, though it lay somewhere in the region later called Edom, south and east of the Dead Sea.

entries.title: Dionysius (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: A member of the Areopagus, the council of Athens, who believed after hearing Paul speak there.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A member of the Areopagus, the council of Athens, who believed after hearing Paul's speech there and is named as one of the few converts from that address (Acts 17:34).

entries.title: Diotrephes (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: John rebukes him for loving to be first. He would not welcome the travelling missionaries, spread malicious talk about John, and threw out the members who did welcome them.

entries.title: Dishan (Edomite living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Youngest of the sons of Seir, a Horite chief among Edom's earlier people.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Dishan was a Horite chief, the youngest listed among the sons of Seir, whose descendants are counted among Edom's earlier inhabitants.

entries.title: Dishon (Edomite living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: One of the Horite chiefs who held Edom's land before Esau's descendants settled it.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Dishon was a Horite chief listed among the earlier inhabitants of Edom's territory before Esau's descendants settled there.

entries.title: Dishon (Edomite living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Genesis names him once, and he is a man from the patriarchs.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Dizahab
entries.summary: Place of gold, in the wilderness near where Moses gave his last addresses. Often identified with Dahab on the east coast of Sinai, which keeps the old name, though it cannot be proven.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Dizahab, meaning "place of gold," is named in Deuteronomy 1:1 as one of the wilderness locations near which Moses delivered his final addresses to Israel. It is often identified with modern Dahab on the eastern coast of the Sinai Peninsula, whose name preserves the ancient one, though the identification cannot be proven with certainty.

entries.title: Dodai (Warrior living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: An Ahohite who led David's army division in the second month, one of twelve divisions that took turns. He may be the father of Eleazar, one of David's three chief warriors.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Dodai was an Ahohite who commanded the army division serving King David during the second month of the year, one of twelve divisions that rotated monthly military duty (1 Chr. 27:4). He may be the father of Eleazar, one of David's three chief warriors (2 Sam. 23:9).

entries.title: Dodanim (People, perhaps from Dodan)
entries.summary: A seafaring people descended from Javan, not a single man. Chronicles spells the name Rodanim, which many connect to Rhodes or to the Dardanians of northwest Asia Minor.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of the peoples descended from Javan in the Table of Nations (Genesis 10:4), representing a seafaring group of the eastern Mediterranean rather than a single individual. The parallel list in 1 Chronicles 1:7 spells the name Rodanim, which many connect to Rhodes or to the Dardanians of northwest Asia Minor.

entries.title: Dodavah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A man of Mareshah. His son Eliezer rebuked Jehoshaphat for joining Ahaziah of Israel in a shipbuilding venture, and God destroyed the ships.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A man of Mareshah in Judah whose son Eliezer rebuked King Jehoshaphat for allying with the wicked King Ahaziah of Israel in a shipbuilding venture that God then destroyed, as recorded in 2 Chronicles 20:37.

entries.title: Dodo (Man living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 3 men called Dodo. This one is a man from the years before the monarchy, named once in Judges.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Dodo (Warrior living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: 2 Samuel and 1 Chronicles name him twice, and he is a warrior from the united kingdom.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Dodo (Warrior living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Father of one of David's mighty men, named only so that his son can be.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Dodo was the name of the father or grandfather of two of David's mighty warriors, listed among the elite fighters in his service.

entries.title: Doeg (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Saul's chief herdsman, an Edomite, who told Saul that the priest Ahimelech had helped David. Saul's own men would not kill the priests of Nob. Doeg did it himself, eighty-five priests and the whole town with them.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Doeg was an Edomite serving as Saul's chief herdsman who reported to Saul that the priest Ahimelech had helped David while David was fleeing, and when Saul's own men refused to kill the priests of Nob for it, Doeg carried out the massacre himself, killing eighty-five priests along with the entire town's population.

entries.title: Dophkah
entries.summary: A wilderness camp in Sinai between the desert of Sin and Alush. The name is related to a word for smelting, and some connect it with the Egyptian turquoise and copper mines at Serabit el-Khadim.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Wilderness encampment in the Sinai peninsula, between the desert of Sin and Alush (Num. 33:12-13). Its name, related to a word for smelting or forging, has led some scholars to connect it with ancient Egyptian turquoise and copper mining operations at Serabit el-Khadim, a site in the Sinai with inscriptions documenting mining expeditions from the Egyptian New Kingdom period.

entries.title: Dor
entries.summary: A royal Canaanite port on the coast south of Mount Carmel. Joshua beat its king, but its people were never fully driven out, and it later went into one of Solomon's districts. Excavation at Tel Dor traces the shift from Canaanite to Phoenician on that coast.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Dor was an ancient port city on the Mediterranean coast south of Mount Carmel, a royal Canaanite city whose king Joshua defeated (Joshua 11:1-2; 12:23) though its original inhabitants were never fully expelled (Judges 1:27); it was later assigned to one of Solomon's administrative districts (1 Kings 4:11). Decades of excavation at Tel Dor have made it one of the best sites anywhere for tracing the transition from Bronze Age Canaanite culture to Iron Age Phoenician civilization on the coast.

entries.title: Dorcas (Woman living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Tabitha in Aramaic, a woman at Joppa who made clothes for the widows. When she died the disciples sent for Peter and he raised her, and many in Joppa believed because of it.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Dorcas, called Tabitha in Aramaic, was a Christian woman at Joppa remembered for her charity; she made clothing for the widows in her care. When she died, the disciples sent for Peter, who raised her back to life, and the miracle led many in Joppa to believe (Acts 9:36-41).

witness.excerpt: This man was also called the son of Dorcas , in the language of our country.

entries.title: Drusilla (Woman living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: The youngest daughter of Herod Agrippa I. Felix, governor of Judea, talked her into leaving her first husband, the king of Emesa, and she was sitting beside Felix when Paul spoke about righteousness, self-control and judgment to come. Josephus says she died in the eruption of Vesuvius in AD 79, which some historians doubt.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The youngest daughter of Herod Agrippa I, part of the well documented Herodian dynasty known from Josephus and from coins minted under various family members. Felix, the Roman governor of Judea, persuaded her to leave her first husband, the king of Emesa, and marry him instead, and she was sitting beside Felix when Paul spoke to him of righteousness, self-control, and coming judgment (Acts 24:24-25). Josephus reports that she and a son from her marriage to Felix later died in the eruption of Vesuvius in AD 79, though some historians question whether he has confused her with another Herodian relative.

entries.title: Dumah (Arabian living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: A son of Ishmael, and the Arabian tribe and region that came from him, usually tied to the oasis of Dumat al-Jandal.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Dumah was a son of Ishmael and, by extension, the Arabian tribe and region descended from him (Genesis 25:14; 1 Chronicles 1:30). The name is generally connected to the oasis of Dumat al-Jandal in northern Arabia, an important caravan stop. Isaiah's brief oracle against Dumah (Isaiah 21:11-12) uses the name, meaning silence, as a play on words, and most read it as directed at Edom or its Arabian neighbors rather than the Ishmaelite region itself.

entries.title: Dura
entries.summary: Nebuchadnezzar set up his golden image on this plain near Babylon, and Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego refused to bow to it. The name probably comes from an Akkadian word for a walled enclosure, so it is more a kind of place than one spot, and no site has been fixed.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The plain of Dura, near Babylon, was where Nebuchadnezzar set up the golden image that all his officials were summoned to worship, the scene of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego's refusal and their deliverance from the furnace (Daniel 3:1-30). "Dura" likely derives from a common Akkadian word for a walled enclosure, which would make it more a type of place than a single proper name, and several sites near Babylon carried variants of it. No firm identification of this particular plain has been established.

entries.title: Ebal (Edomite living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: The mountain of the curses, opposite Mount Gerizim near Shechem. Moses ordered six tribes onto Ebal to speak the covenant's curses while six on Gerizim spoke its blessings, and Joshua built an altar there and wrote the law on stones. A Horite chief descended from Seir carried the name too.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Mount Ebal stands opposite Mount Gerizim near Shechem; Moses instructed that after entering Canaan, six tribes would stand on Ebal to pronounce the covenant's curses while six stood on Gerizim for its blessings, and Joshua built an altar and inscribed the law on stones there. The name also belonged to a chief of the Horites descended from Seir and, in a variant spelling, to a descendant of Eber in Shem's genealogy.

entries.title: Ebed-melech (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: When officials left Jeremiah to die in a muddy cistern, this Cushite court official got him out. Through Jeremiah, God promised Ebed-melech his own life when Jerusalem fell.

entries.dictNote: Ebed-melech was a Cushite court official who rescued the prophet Jeremiah from a muddy cistern where officials had left him to die, and God promised through Jeremiah that Ebed-melech would be spared when Jerusalem fell, a rare note of personal deliverance amid the city's destruction.

entries.title: Ebenezer
entries.summary: Stone of help. The Philistines first beat Israel near here and took the ark. Years later, after a win over the Philistines in the same area, Samuel set up a stone between Mizpah and Shen and gave it that name for the Lord's help.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Ebenezer, meaning stone of help, names a site near Aphek where the Philistines first defeated Israel and captured the ark (1 Samuel 4:1). Years later, after Israel routed the Philistines in the same general area under Samuel's leadership, Samuel set up a memorial stone there between Mizpah and Shen, naming it Ebenezer to commemorate the Lord's help (1 Samuel 7:12).

entries.title: Edar (Levite living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: A Levite, named twice in the Levite rolls of 1 Chronicles 23 and 24. The tower of Eder near Bethlehem, where Jacob camped after Rachel died, shares the name and nothing more.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The tower of Eder was a landmark near Bethlehem where Jacob camped after Rachel's death, later invoked poetically by Micah as an image of Jerusalem's coming restoration.

entries.title: Eden
entries.summary: The garden where God put the first humans. A river ran out of it and split into four, the Tigris and the Euphrates among them, which is why most people look for it in the lowlands of ancient Mesopotamia. Its exact site cannot be fixed.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Eden was the garden where God placed the first humans, watered by a river that divided into four branches including the Tigris and Euphrates, a location most often placed somewhere in the fertile lowlands of ancient Mesopotamia though its exact site cannot be fixed. The same word also denotes a trading region supplying richly worked cloth to Tyre's merchants, likely the same district referred to elsewhere as a territory conquered by Assyria, and separately belongs to a Levite who helped reform temple worship under Hezekiah.

entries.title: Eden
entries.summary: A region in northern Mesopotamia, not the garden. It sold richly worked cloth to Tyre, and the Rabshakeh named it outside Jerusalem among lands Assyria had already taken. Many identify it with Bit-Adini on the middle Euphrates, which Shalmaneser III annexed.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: This is a region in northern Mesopotamia, distinct from the garden of Eden in Genesis, though the two share a name. Ezekiel lists it among the trading partners that supplied Tyre with richly worked cloth (Ezek. 27:23), and it is named alongside other conquered territories in the Assyrian king's taunt relayed by the Rabshakeh outside Jerusalem's walls (2 Kings 19:12; Isa. 37:12). Many scholars identify it with Bit-Adini, an Aramean state on the middle Euphrates that Assyria annexed in the ninth century BC, a conquest recorded in the royal inscriptions of Shalmaneser III.

entries.title: Edom
entries.summary: Esau got the byname Edom over a bowl of red stew, and it stuck to the mountain country his descendants settled southeast of the Dead Sea. Bozrah was its old capital and Sela, the Greeks' Petra, its rock fortress. Edom refused Israel passage in the exodus and later helped Babylon sack Jerusalem, and the prophets did not let that go.
entries.books: Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Psalm, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Lamentations, Ezekiel, Daniel, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Malachi
entries.label: 21 books
entries.dictNote: Edom was the byname given to Esau after he traded his birthright for red stew, and it became the name of the mountainous territory his descendants settled southeast of the Dead Sea, stretching from the Gulf of Aqabah north toward Moab. Its old capital was Bozrah, and its rock cut stronghold Sela, later called Petra by the Greeks, still stands. The Edomites refused Israel passage during the exodus and remained hostile neighbors for centuries, eventually assisting Babylon's sack of Jerusalem, an act the prophets condemned at length. Excavations at the copper smelting site of Khirbet en Nahas and at Busayra, ancient Bozrah, have revealed an organized Edomite kingdom emerging by the tenth and ninth centuries BC, broadly consistent with the biblical timeline for Edom's rise.

entries.title: Edomite
entries.summary: Esau's descendants, living in Seir south and east of the Dead Sea. Kin to Israel and at odds with it for most of the record. Egyptian texts mention Edom as early as the thirteenth century BC, and its capital Busayra and the copper works at Khirbat en Nahas have both been excavated.
entries.books: Deuteronomy, 1 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 2 Chronicles, Psalm
entries.label: 6 books
entries.dictNote: Edomites were the descendants of Esau, Jacob's brother, settled in the rugged region south and east of the Dead Sea known as Seir, and Israel's relationship with them was marked by recurring conflict despite their shared ancestry. Edom is attested in Egyptian records from as early as the thirteenth century BC and later developed into an organized kingdom whose capital, Busayra, and copper mining sites at Khirbat en Nahas have been excavated, confirming a real Edomite state during the period the Bible describes.

entries.title: Eglah (Woman living at the time of United Monarchy)

entries.title: Eglaim
entries.summary: Isaiah's oracle says Moab's wailing carries as far as Eglaim. It is probably the En-eglaim of Ezekiel 47:10.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Moabite town named in Isaiah's oracle against Moab, where the wailing of the people is said to reach (Isa. 15:8). It is probably the same place as En-eglaim, mentioned in Ezekiel 47:10.

entries.title: Eglon
entries.summary: A royal Canaanite city in the Shephelah. Its king joined the five Amorite kings Joshua crushed at Gibeon, and the city was destroyed and given to Judah.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Two distinct figures and places share this name. Eglon king of Moab allied with Ammon and Amalek to seize Jericho and oppress Israel for eighteen years, until the left-handed judge Ehud assassinated him and led Israel to defeat the Moabites. Separately, Eglon was a Canaanite royal city in the Shephelah of Judah whose king joined the coalition of five Amorite kings crushed by Joshua at Gibeon; the city was later destroyed and its territory assigned to Judah.

entries.title: Eglon (King living before Israel's Monarchy)

entries.title: Egypt
entries.summary: Joseph rose to power there and kept his family alive through the famine. A later pharaoh enslaved their descendants, and that set up the exodus. For the rest of the Old Testament Egypt stands for the slavery Israel was brought out of, and Matthew has Jesus's family flee there from Herod as if living that story again.

entries.label: 33 books
entries.dictNote: Egypt was Israel's neighbor to the south and, across different periods, both its refuge and its oppressor: Joseph rose to power there and saved his family from famine, but generations later a new pharaoh enslaved their descendants, setting up the exodus. Egypt reappears throughout the Old Testament as a byword for the old life of slavery Israel was delivered from, and Matthew records that Jesus's own family fled there briefly to escape Herod's massacre of infants, framing Jesus as reliving Israel's own exodus story.

entries.title: Ehud (Judge living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: A left-handed judge from the tribe of Benjamin. He strapped a dagger to his right thigh, where nobody checks a right-handed man, killed the fat Moabite king Eglon, and locked the doors behind him on the way out. Israel then routed the Moabites and had eighty years of rest, the longest in Judges.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Ehud was a left-handed judge from the tribe of Benjamin who assassinated the obese Moabite king Eglon by strapping a hidden dagger to his right thigh, where guards wouldn't expect a weapon from a right-handed man, then walked out and locked the doors before anyone discovered the body. His subsequent rout of the leaderless Moabite army gave Israel eighty years of peace, the longest period of rest recorded in the book of Judges.

entries.title: Ekron
entries.summary: Northernmost of the five Philistine cities, given to Judah and then Dan but never firmly held. The ark's last stop before the Philistines sent it back. Ahaziah of Israel sent there to ask Baal-zebub about his health, and an inscription at Tel Miqne naming Ikausu, or Achish, son of Padi settles the site.
entries.books: Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, 2 Kings, Jeremiah, Amos, Zephaniah, Zechariah
entries.label: 8 books
entries.dictNote: Ekron was the northernmost of the five Philistine city states, assigned to Judah and then Dan but never securely held by Israel, and it was the last stop for the ark before the Philistines returned it after being struck with plagues. It also housed a shrine of Baal-zebub famous enough that Israel's king Ahaziah sent messengers there to inquire about his health. Excavations at Tel Miqne, identified as Ekron, uncovered a temple dedication inscription naming a king called Ikausu, or Achish, son of Padi, matching the royal name pattern used for Philistine kings of Gath and Ekron in the Bible and confirming the site's identity beyond reasonable doubt.

entries.dictNote: El-paran was not a person but a place name, "the oak (or terebinth) of Paran," marking a site on the edge of the wilderness bordering the territory of the Horites in the hill country of Seir. It marks the farthest point reached by the invading kings under Chedorlaomer before they turned back toward the Dead Sea cities (Genesis 14:6), and its name incorporates the wilderness of Paran, covered separately, through which Israel later traveled during the exodus.

entries.title: Elah (King living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: David killed Goliath in the Valley of Elah, the terebinth valley in Judah's lowlands, with the two armies on opposite slopes. The name also belongs to Elah son of Baasha, king of Israel, murdered while drunk by Zimri, his own chariot commander. Khirbet Qeiyafa above the valley has a tenth century BC fort and one of the earliest Hebrew inscriptions.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: The Valley of Elah, named for the terebinth trees that grew there, lies in the lowlands of Judah and is where the young David killed Goliath while the Israelite and Philistine armies faced off on opposite slopes. The same word names an Edomite chief in Genesis, a son of Caleb, and two kings of Israel: Elah son of Baasha, assassinated while drunk by his own chariot commander Zimri, and Elah father of Hoshea, Israel's last king before Assyria's conquest. Excavations at Khirbet Qeiyafa, a fortified site overlooking the valley, have uncovered a tenth century BC settlement with one of the earliest known Hebrew inscriptions, physical evidence of an organized kingdom in Judah near the time and place tradition assigns to David.

entries.dictNote: Elamites came from Elam, an ancient civilization centered on Susa in what is now southwestern Iran, one of the oldest urban cultures in the Near East and extensively documented in Mesopotamian and Persian records. Its site is preserved in the name of the modern Israeli city of Eilat.

entries.dictNote: Eldad was one of the seventy elders Moses appointed to help bear the burden of leading Israel. When the Spirit rested on the elders at the tent of meeting, Eldad and his companion Medad, who had remained in the camp, also prophesied there; when Joshua urged Moses to stop them, Moses responded by wishing that all the LORD's people were prophets (Numbers 11:24-29).

entries.title: Elealeh
entries.summary: Reuben rebuilt this town on the grazing plateau east of the Jordan for its herds. By Isaiah's and Jeremiah's time Moab had it back, and both name it in their oracles. The ruin el-Al, just northeast of Heshbon, is the site.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Elealeh was a town in the pastoral plateau east of the Jordan that the tribe of Reuben rebuilt for its herds after the conquest (Numbers 32:3, 37). It reappears centuries later in Isaiah's and Jeremiah's oracles against Moab, which had reclaimed the region by their time (Isaiah 15:4; 16:9; Jeremiah 48:34). The site survives as the ruin el-Al, just northeast of Heshbon in modern Jordan.

entries.label: 8 books
entries.dictNote: Eleazar was Aaron's third son and successor as high priest after his two older brothers, Nadab and Abihu, died for offering unauthorized fire before the Lord. He assisted Moses in the second census of Israel, helped Joshua divide the conquered land among the tribes, and his descendants controlled the high priesthood for most of Israel's history afterward.

entries.dictNote: Eli was the high priest and judge at Shiloh who raised the boy Samuel after his mother Hannah dedicated him to the Lord's service, but Eli's own sons abused their priestly position, stealing sacrificial meat and sleeping with women who served at the tabernacle entrance, and Eli rebuked them only mildly despite God's repeated warnings. Both sons died in the same battle where the Ark of the Covenant was captured by the Philistines, and Eli himself died of a broken neck falling backward from his seat when he heard the news, at ninety-eight years old.

entries.dictNote: Eliam appears in two contexts that may describe the same man: as the father of Bathsheba, David's wife (2 Samuel 11:3, where Chronicles gives his name as Ammiel), and as the son of David's counselor Ahithophel and one of David's elite thirty warriors (2 Samuel 23:34). entries.title: Elijah (Prophet living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A prophet from Tishbe in Gilead who took on Ahab and Jezebel over Baal worship and beat 450 prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel with fire from heaven. Straight after, he ran into the wilderness sure he was the last faithful man left, and God met him in a quiet voice, not in wind or earthquake or fire. He did not die; a whirlwind took him up while Elisha watched.
entries.books: 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 2 Chronicles, Malachi, Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, Romans, James
entries.label: 10 books
entries.dictNote: Elijah was a prophet from Tishbe in Gilead who confronted King Ahab and Queen Jezebel over Israel's slide into Baal worship, most famously by challenging 450 prophets of Baal to a fire-from-heaven contest on Mount Carmel and winning outright. He fled into the wilderness in despair immediately afterward, convinced he was the last faithful Israelite left, until God met him not in wind or earthquake or fire but in a quiet voice. Elijah never died in the ordinary sense: 2 Kings ends his story with a whirlwind and a chariot of fire that carried him up to heaven while his successor Elisha watched.

witness.excerpt: After a little while Elijah came to king Ahab, according to God's will, to inform him that rain was coming.
