entries.title: Elisabeth
entries.summary: Elizabeth was old and childless, married to the priest Zechariah, when Gabriel said she would bear a son. When Mary came to visit, the child in Elizabeth's womb leapt. She was the first in the Gospels to call Mary blessed and to see by the Spirit whom Mary was carrying.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Elizabeth was a priest's wife and a relative of Mary, and she and her husband Zechariah were both old and childless when the angel Gabriel announced she would bear a son who would prepare the way for the Messiah. When the pregnant Mary visited her, Elizabeth's own unborn child, John the Baptist, leapt inside her, and Elizabeth was the first person in the Gospels to call Mary blessed and to recognize by the Spirit that Mary carried her Lord.

entries.title: Elisha (Prophet living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A farmer's son who was ploughing when Elijah threw his cloak over him. He left the oxen, followed, and asked for a double portion of Elijah's spirit when the older man was taken up. His miracles run from poisoned water made clean to Naaman healed of leprosy, and a dead man thrown into his tomb came back to life when he touched the bones.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Elisha was a wealthy farmer's son who left his oxen in the field to follow Elijah after the older prophet threw his cloak over him, and he inherited Elijah's ministry, and by his own request a double portion of his spirit, when Elijah was taken up in the whirlwind. He performed roughly twice as many miracles as Elijah, from purifying poisoned water and multiplying a widow's oil to raising a dead boy and healing the Aramean general Naaman of leprosy, and his ministry spanned the reigns of four different kings of Israel. Even his bones kept working after his death: 2 Kings records a corpse tossed into Elisha's tomb coming back to life the moment it touched his remains.

witness.excerpt: One of the servants of Joram said, that he had seen there Elisha, the son of Shaphat, the disciple of Elijah… they asked him, ‘What would become of the army?’

entries.lukeNote: Paired with Elijah in Jesus's own synagogue sermon (4:27), the same pairing Josephus uses to introduce him: 'Elisha, the son of Shaphat, the disciple of Elijah,' called on by three kings stranded without water in the wilderness.

entries.title: Elkanah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 8 men called Elkanah. This one is a man from the divided-kingdom years, named once in 1 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Elkanah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A man from the divided-kingdom years, and 2 Chronicles is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Elkanah (Warrior living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a warrior from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Elkanan (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Elhanan, a warrior in David's army. 2 Samuel credits him with killing Goliath the Gittite, and 1 Chronicles says it was Goliath's brother Lahmi, which takes the clash out of David's story.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Elkanan (Warrior living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: 2 Samuel credits him with killing Goliath the Gittite. 1 Chronicles says it was Goliath's brother Lahmi. That is how the two accounts are usually squared.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Elhanan was a warrior in David's army credited in 2 Samuel with killing Goliath the Gittite, and 1 Chronicles clarifies he killed Goliath's brother Lahmi instead, resolving what would otherwise be a direct contradiction with David's more famous duel.

entries.title: Elkoshite
entries.summary: Nahum's home town, Elkosh. Nobody knows where it was now; tradition has tried Galilee, Judah and northern Iraq.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Elkoshite identifies the prophet Nahum as being from Elkosh, a town whose location is no longer known, though tradition has variously placed it in Galilee, Judah, and northern Iraq.

entries.title: Ellasar
entries.summary: A kingdom, not a person. Arioch ruled it and marched with Chedorlaomer against Sodom. Many connect it with Larsa, between Ur and Uruk, a city that has been well excavated.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Ellasar was not a person but the kingdom ruled by Arioch, one of the four kings who campaigned against Sodom and its allies alongside Chedorlaomer of Elam (Genesis 14:1, 9). Many scholars connect it with Larsa, an ancient Mesopotamian city between Ur and Uruk that has been extensively excavated and whose ruins preserve royal inscriptions from its own line of kings.

entries.title: Elmodam (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Son of Er in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, in the line that runs back to David's son Nathan.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Elmodam was the son of Er, listed among the ancestors of Jesus in Luke's genealogy, in the line descended from David's son Nathan (Luke 3:28).

entries.title: Elnaam (Warrior living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: His two sons, Jeribai and Joshaviah, are on the longer roll of David's warriors in Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Father of two of David's mighty men, Jeribai and Joshaviah, named in the expanded roster of David's warriors in 1 Chronicles 11:46.

entries.title: Elnathan (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A royal official. He went down to Egypt to bring the prophet Uriah back to be executed. Later he was one of those who begged Jehoiakim not to burn Jeremiah's scroll, and the king burned it anyway.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Elnathan was a royal official sent to retrieve the prophet Uriah from Egypt to be executed for prophesying against Jerusalem, and later one of the officials who unsuccessfully urged King Jehoiakim not to burn Jeremiah's scroll.

entries.title: Elnathan (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 2 Kings names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Elnathan (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of 3 men called Elnathan. This one is a man from the exile and the return, named once in Ezra.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Eloi (The Deity)
entries.summary: The cry from the cross in Mark 15:34, kept in the sound it was spoken in. It means my God.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Elon
entries.summary: Named once, in Joshua, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Elon (Edomite living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: A Hittite whose daughter Basemath married Esau; the name means oak.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Elon (Judge living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: Hebrew for oak, which is why it lands on a town and on several men. This one is in the family lists.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Elon, Hebrew for "oak," is applied in the Old Testament to one place and several distinct men. It names a town allotted to the tribe of Dan (Joshua 19:43); a Hittite whose daughter Basemath married Esau (Genesis 26:34; 36:2); one of the sons of Zebulun who founded the clan of the Elonites (Genesis 46:14; Numbers 26:26); and Elon the Zebulunite, a minor judge who led Israel for ten years and was buried in his own territory (Judges 12:11-12).

entries.title: Elon (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Genesis and Numbers name him twice, and he is a man from the wilderness years.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Elon-bethhanan
entries.summary: Joined with two towns of Dan to make one of Solomon's twelve supply districts, the one Ben-deker ran. Nothing more is recorded about it.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Elon-bethhanan was grouped with two towns of Dan to form one of the twelve administrative districts Solomon set up to supply his royal household, this one overseen by Ben-deker (1 Kings 4:9). Nothing more is recorded about it.

entries.title: Elonites (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: The clan from Elon, a son of Zebulun, counted in the wilderness census and not to be mixed up with the later judge.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Elonites were the clan descended from Elon, a son of Zebulun, counted among the tribe's families in Israel's wilderness census, distinct from the later judge of the same name.

entries.title: Elpaal (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A descendant of Benjamin whose line is credited in Chronicles with building Ono and Lod.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Elpaal was a descendant of Benjamin credited in Chronicles with building several towns, including Ono and Lod.

entries.title: Eltekeh
entries.summary: A town given to Dan and then set aside as a Levitical city for Kohath's descendants. Sennacherib's own annals say he beat an Egyptian and Ethiopian relief army near Eltekeh in 701 BC, on the same campaign in which he shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Eltekeh was a town allotted to the tribe of Dan and later set apart as a Levitical city for the descendants of Kohath (Josh. 19:44; 21:23). The site is significant beyond the biblical text because Sennacherib's own annals record a battle fought near Eltekeh in 701 BC, in which the Assyrian king defeated an Egyptian and Ethiopian relief force during the same campaign in which he besieged Jerusalem under Hezekiah.

entries.title: Eltekon
entries.summary: One of eleven towns in Judah's hill country, listed with Halhul, Beth-zur and Gedor. Its site has not been found and nothing else is recorded about it.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Eltekon was one of eleven towns in the hill country of Judah listed alongside Halhul, Beth-zur, and Gedor in Joshua's allotment to Judah's tribe (Joshua 15:58-59). Nothing else is recorded about it, and its site has not been identified.

entries.title: Eltolad
entries.summary: Judah got it first and then passed it to Simeon, since Judah had more land than it needed. It is Tolad in Chronicles, still held by Simeonite families. Somewhere in the southern Negev, but the site is not settled.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Eltolad was a town in the southern Negev of Judah, listed among the towns allotted to Judah in Joshua 15:30 and then reassigned to Simeon in Joshua 19:4 since Judah's territory was larger than that tribe needed. It appears again as Tolad in 1 Chronicles 4:29, still held by Simeonite families generations later. Its exact site has not been securely identified.

entries.title: Elul (Name of the 6th month)
entries.summary: Sixth month, August into September, and Nehemiah finished the wall in it.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Elul is not a person but the sixth month of the Hebrew religious calendar and twelfth of the civil calendar, falling in August and September. Nehemiah completed Jerusalem's wall on the twenty-fifth day of Elul, a project that took fifty-two days (Nehemiah 6:15).

witness.excerpt:
This was executed on the sixth day of the month Gorpieus [Elul].
9.
These prisoners were taken on the eighth day of the month Gorpiaeus [Elul].
And now were the banks finished on the seventh day of the month Gorpieus, [Elul,] in eighteen days' time, when the Romans brought their machines against the wall.
AND thus was Jerusalem taken, in the second year of the reign of Vespasian, on the eighth day of the month Gorpeius [Elul].
And thus was Gamala taken, on the three and twentieth day of the month Hyperbereteus, [Tisri], whereas the city had first revolted on the four and twentieth day of the month Gorpieus [Elul].

entries.title: Eluzai (Warrior living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A Benjamite who came over to David at Ziklag while David was still an outlaw. He was one of the fighters who could use bow and sling with either hand.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of the Benjamite warriors who defected to David's side while he was still an outlaw at Ziklag, listed among skilled fighters able to use bow and sling with either hand (1 Chronicles 12:5-6).

entries.title: Elymas (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Bar-Jesus, a Jewish false prophet on Cyprus, also called Elymas, which means sorcerer. He tried to turn the proconsul Sergius Paulus away from the faith. Paul struck him blind for a time, and the proconsul believed.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Elymas, meaning "magician" or "sorcerer," was the surname of the Jewish false prophet Bar-Jesus, who attended the Roman proconsul Sergius Paulus on Cyprus and tried to turn him from the faith. Paul struck him with temporary blindness, and the proconsul believed as a result (Acts 13:6-12).

entries.title: Elzabad (Levite living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A son of Shemaiah, counted among the able men of his family of gatekeepers.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Elzabad was the name of two different men in Chronicles. One was a Gadite warrior who joined David's band at Ziklag before he became king (1 Chronicles 12:8-13), and the other was a son of Shemaiah, a Korahite Levite serving as a gatekeeper of the temple (1 Chronicles 26:7).

entries.title: Elzabad (Warrior living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A Gadite who joined David at Ziklag before he was king, sharing the name with a Korahite gatekeeper in Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Emims (People, perhaps from Em)
entries.summary: A people of unusual height who lived in Moab's land before they were pushed out, remembered in Deuteronomy alongside the Anakim.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: The Emim were an ancient race of unusually tall people who once lived in Moabite territory before being displaced, remembered in Deuteronomy alongside other giant clans like the Anakim.

entries.title: Emmanuel (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: God with us. Matthew quotes Isaiah 7:14 and gives the name to Jesus at his birth, more as a title than what anyone called him day to day.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The Greek form of Immanuel, God with us, the name Matthew applies to Jesus by quoting Isaiah 7:14 to interpret his virgin birth (Matthew 1:23). It functions as a theological title rather than a name Jesus was actually called day to day; see the separate Immanuel entry for the Isaiah oracle it draws on.

entries.title: Emmaus
entries.summary: Two disciples were walking home here, about seven miles from Jerusalem, when the risen Jesus joined them and opened the Scriptures, and they knew him when he broke the bread. Where it was is still argued. Amwas, el-Qubeibeh and Qaloniyeh all have backers and none has won.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Emmaus was the village, about seven miles from Jerusalem by Luke's count, where the risen Jesus joined two disciples walking home on Easter Sunday, explaining the Scriptures to them before they recognized him in the breaking of bread (Luke 24:13-31). Its location has been disputed for centuries: candidates include Amwas/Nicopolis, roughly twenty miles from Jerusalem, which fits an alternate ancient manuscript reading of the distance; el-Qubeibeh, closer to Luke's stated distance but lacking clear first-century remains; and Qaloniyeh, a Roman veteran colony just west of the city. No site has won full scholarly consensus, and the debate remains active in current archaeological literature.

entries.title: Emmor (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Hamor, in Greek. Stephen names him as the man Abraham bought a tomb from, where Genesis gives that purchase to Jacob, and many read it as Stephen folding two land purchases into one.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Emmor is the Greek form of Hamor, the father of Shechem and prince of the Canaanite city of Shechem in Genesis 33-34. Stephen refers to him in Acts 7:16 as the one from whom Abraham purchased a burial site, though Genesis attributes that purchase to Jacob, a detail many read as Stephen collapsing two separate patriarchal land purchases from Genesis 23 and 33 into one for the sake of a concise speech.

entries.title: En-dor
entries.summary: Home of the medium Saul went to in disguise the night before his last battle. It lay in Issachar's land, near where Deborah and Barak beat Sisera. Endur, southeast of Mount Tabor, keeps the name.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: En-dor was a town in Issachar's territory, near the site of Deborah and Barak's victory over Sisera's army, which Psalm 83 recalls when praying for Israel's enemies to meet the same fate. It is best known as the home of the medium Saul consulted in disguise the night before his final, fatal battle with the Philistines (1 Samuel 28:7). The name survives in the modern village of Endur, southeast of Mount Tabor.

entries.title: En-eglaim
entries.summary: In Ezekiel's vision the healed Dead Sea will have fishermen spreading nets from En-gedi to En-eglaim. The name means spring of the two calves, and it has never been firmly located.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: En-eglaim, "spring of the two calves," is named in Ezekiel's vision of the river flowing from the restored Temple, marking one end of a stretch of Dead Sea shore where fishermen will spread their nets once the water is healed, with En-gedi marking the other (Ezekiel 47:10). Its precise location is unresolved; some place it near the Jordan's mouth at the sea's northern end, others near Ain Feshkha close to En-gedi itself, but no identification has been firmly established.

entries.title: En-gannim
entries.summary: Fountain of gardens. This one sat on Issachar's border and went to the Gershonite Levites, and it is generally identified with Jenin, which still has the name and its springs.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: En-gannim, fountain of gardens, names two separate towns. One lay in the lowlands of Judah, between Zanoah and Tappuah (Joshua 15:34). The other sat on the border of Issachar and was assigned to the Gershonite Levites (Joshua 19:21; 21:29); it is generally identified with the modern city of Jenin, which still preserves the name and its springs.

entries.title: En-gannim
entries.summary: Named once, in Joshua, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: En-gedi
entries.summary: An oasis on the western shore of the Dead Sea, fed by a spring that drops some 600 feet down the cliffs. David hid in its caves from Saul and spared Saul's life there. A Chalcolithic temple on the site is far older than Israel in Canaan.
entries.books: Joshua, 1 Samuel, 2 Chronicles, Song of Solomon, Ezekiel
entries.label: 5 books
entries.dictNote: En-gedi was an oasis on the western shore of the Dead Sea, famous for its vineyards (Song of Solomon 1:14) and fed by a freshwater spring dropping some 600 feet down the cliffs above it. David hid in its caves while fleeing Saul and there spared Saul's life when he crept up on him unseen (1 Samuel 24); excavations at the site have uncovered a Chalcolithic-era temple predating Israel's settlement of Canaan by well over a thousand years.

entries.title: En-haddah
entries.summary: A town on Issachar's border, next to Engannim in the list, with no site found.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A town on the border of the tribe of Issachar, named next to Engannim (Joshua 19:21). Its precise site is unidentified.

entries.title: En-hakhore (En-hakkore)
entries.summary: Spring of the one who called, the water God opened at Lehi for Samson after the jawbone fight.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: En-hakhore, the spring God opened at Lehi to revive Samson after his victory over the Philistines with a donkey's jawbone, its name meaning "spring of the one who called" (Judg. 15:18-19). The King James Version itself spells the name Enhakkore.

entries.title: En-hazor
entries.summary: A fortified town of Naphtali, not the big city of Hazor, named once with its site lost.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: En-hazor, a fortified town of Naphtali named in Joshua 19:37, distinct from the larger and better known city of Hazor despite the shared element in its name. It appears only once and its precise location has not been recovered.

entries.title: En-mishpat (Kadesh-barnea)
entries.summary: Spring of judgment, the old name for Kadesh in the wilderness south of Canaan. Chedorlaomer's kings hit it on the campaign that ended with Abram chasing them to get Lot back.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: An older name, meaning "spring of judgment," for the place later known as Kadesh, in the wilderness south of Canaan (Genesis 14:7). The coalition of eastern kings led by Chedorlaomer struck this place, along with the Amalekites and the Amorites, in the campaign that later drew Abram into battle to rescue Lot.

entries.title: En-rimmon (Ain)
entries.summary: Spring of the pomegranate, a Negev town resettled after the exile. It likely joins Ain and Rimmon, which the older tribal lists name separately.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: En-rimmon, "spring of the pomegranate," was one of the towns in the Negev of Judah reoccupied by returning exiles, listed in Nehemiah 11:29. It likely combines two towns named separately in the earlier tribal lists, Ain and Rimmon, among the southernmost cities of Judah and Simeon (Joshua 15:32; 19:7).

entries.title: En-rogel
entries.summary: A spring just south of Jerusalem where the Kidron and Hinnom valleys meet. Jonathan and Ahimaaz waited there to carry news to David in Absalom's revolt, and Adonijah held his feast there to make himself king. Many put it at Bir Ayyub, Job's Well.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: En-rogel was a spring just south of Jerusalem, near where the Kidron and Hinnom valleys meet, likely used by fullers treading cloth in its waters. Jonathan and Ahimaaz hid there to relay intelligence to David during Absalom's revolt (2 Samuel 17:17), and it was the site where David's son Adonijah held a feast to proclaim himself king, a bid for the throne undone when Solomon was anointed at Gihon instead (1 Kings 1:5-53). Many identify it with the deep shaft known as Bir Ayyub, "Job's Well," south of the Pool of Siloam.

entries.title: En-tappuah
entries.summary: The spring by Tappuah that marked the line between Ephraim and Manasseh. The town went to Ephraim though it stood on Manasseh's land.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A spring associated with the town of Tappuah, marking a point on the boundary between the tribal territories of Ephraim and Manasseh (Joshua 17:7). The town itself belonged to Ephraim even though it stood on land otherwise allotted to Manasseh, and the spring served as the dividing landmark between the two.

entries.title: Enaim
entries.summary: Tamar sat veiled at Enaim and waited for Judah, who had not given her his youngest son. The name means two springs, or two eyes, and the spot is usually placed between Adullam and Timnah.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Enaim was the town gate or crossroads where Tamar sat veiled, disguised as a prostitute, and waited for her father-in-law Judah after he had failed to give her his youngest son in marriage (Genesis 38:14, 21). The name means two springs or two eyes, and the site is usually placed somewhere along the road between Adullam and Timnah in the Judean foothills, though it has not been identified with certainty.

witness.excerpt:
Testament of Judah, Chapter 12

12 1 And after these things, while Tamar was a widow, she heard after two years that I was going up 2 to shear my sheep, and adorned herself in bridal array, and sat in the city Enaim by the gate.

entries.title: Enan (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Father of Naphtali's tribal leader in the wilderness census, and nothing else is recorded.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Enan was the father of the tribal leader of Naphtali during the wilderness census.

entries.title: Enoch (Man living at the time before the Flood)
entries.summary: Seventh from Adam. Genesis says he walked with God, and then he was not, for God took him, with no death notice like the others. Jude quotes a prophecy in his name, and a whole later body of Jewish apocalyptic writing carries it too, though written centuries after him.
entries.label: 5 books
entries.dictNote: Enoch was the seventh generation from Adam, and Genesis says simply that he walked with God, and he was not, for God took him, the only patriarch in the genealogy who doesn't get a death notice, understood ever since as a bodily removal to heaven without dying. Jude quotes a prophecy attributed to Enoch condemning the ungodly, and Enoch became the namesake of an extensive body of later Jewish apocalyptic literature, though that literature was not written by him and dates many centuries after his lifetime. A different Enoch was Cain's son, for whom Cain named the first city built after his exile.

witness.excerpt: Enoch, thou scribe of righteousness, go, declare to the Watchers of the heaven who have left the high heaven, the holy eternal place, and have defiled themselves with women…

entries.lukeNote: Named once, in passing, in Luke's genealogy, the same figure who narrates an entire other book. All of 1 Enoch is framed as his own testimony, starting with the Watchers calling him ‘scribe of righteousness’ and sending him to confront the fallen angels.

entries.title: Enoch (Man living at the time before the Flood)
entries.summary: Named twice, in Genesis, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Enos (Man living at the time before the Flood)
entries.summary: Seth's son. In his days, Genesis says, people began to call on the name of the Lord.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Enosh was Seth's son and Adam's grandson, and Genesis notes that it was in his days that people began to call on the name of the Lord, marking an early point of organized worship in the biblical timeline.

witness.excerpt:
And in his seed shall my name be blessed, and the name of my fathers, Shem, and

[paragraph continues] Noah, and Enoch, and Mahalalel, and Enos, and Seth, and Adam.  25.

entries.title: Enshemesh
entries.summary: A spring on the road down toward Jericho, not far from Bethany, marking the line between Judah and Benjamin. The name means fountain of the sun, and a spring still flows on that route.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Enshemesh, fountain of the sun, was a spring that served as a boundary marker between the territories of Judah and Benjamin, situated on the road down toward Jericho not far from Bethany (Joshua 15:7; 18:17). It is usually identified with a spring still flowing today along that route.

entries.title: Epaphras (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: A Colossian who probably planted the church there and then brought Paul word of how it was doing, which is what set Colossians going. Paul says he was always wrestling in prayer for them.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Epaphras was a native of Colossae who likely founded that church and reported its condition to Paul, prompting Paul's letter to the Colossians, and Paul describes him as always wrestling in prayer for the Colossian believers.

entries.title: Epaphroditus (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: The church at Philippi sent him to Rome with money for Paul in prison. He fell badly ill there and nearly died. Once he was well, and homesick, Paul sent him back carrying the letter we call Philippians, with warm words about him in it.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Epaphroditus was a member of the church at Philippi whom the congregation sent to Rome carrying financial support for the imprisoned Paul. He fell seriously ill while there, and Paul, moved by his recovery and homesickness, sent him back to Philippi bearing the letter now known as Philippians, commending him warmly to the church (Philippians 2:25-30; 4:18).

entries.title: Epenetus (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Paul greets him in Rome as beloved, the first convert to Christ from the province of Asia.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Epenetus was a Christian at Rome whom Paul greeted as his "beloved," calling him the first convert to Christ from the province of Asia (Romans 16:5).

entries.title: Ephah
entries.summary: Named once, in Isaiah, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ephah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 4 men called Ephah. This one is a man from the divided-kingdom years, named once in 1 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ephah (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Midian's son and Abraham's grandson through Keturah. His people settled in northern Arabia, and Isaiah pictures the land of Ephah bringing gold and incense to Zion.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Ephah is a name shared by a tribal ancestor and two other individuals. Ephah was a son of Midian and grandson of Abraham through Keturah, whose descendants settled in northern Arabia and gave their name to a region that Isaiah pictures bringing gold and incense to Zion (Genesis 25:4; Isaiah 60:6); the same name belonged to a concubine of Caleb (1 Chronicles 2:46) and to a descendant of Judah through Jahdai (1 Chronicles 2:47).

entries.title: Ephah (Woman living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names her once, and she is a woman from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ephai (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A Netophathite. After Jerusalem fell, his sons were among the commanders who came to Gedaliah at Mizpah and at first accepted the government Babylon had set up. Nothing else is recorded of him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Netophathite whose sons came to Gedaliah at Mizpah after the fall of Jerusalem, part of the remnant of Judean military commanders who initially submitted to Gedaliah's Babylonian-appointed government (Jeremiah 40:7-8). Nothing else is recorded of him.

entries.title: Epher (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Epher (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: A son of Midian, named in the two lists of Midian's sons and nowhere else.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Epher was a common name, borne by a son of Midian, a descendant of Judah, and a military leader from the half-tribe of Manasseh east of the Jordan.

entries.title: Epher (Warrior living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 3 men called Epher. This one is a warrior from the divided-kingdom years, named once in 1 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ephes-dammim
entries.summary: The Philistines camped here in the Valley of Elah when Goliath came out and David killed him. Chronicles calls it Pas-dammim, and it is generally placed near Socoh in the Shephelah.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The site of the Philistine camp in the Valley of Elah when Goliath challenged Israel's army and was killed by David (1 Sam. 17:1). It is also called Pas-dammim in 1 Chronicles 11:13, and is generally located near Socoh in the Shephelah of Judah.

entries.title: Ephesus
entries.summary: The chief city of Roman Asia, with the temple of Artemis and a theatre for some twenty five thousand. Paul stayed about three years and the silversmiths rioted over lost trade. Later it was one of the seven churches of Revelation, and tradition says John died and was buried there.
entries.books: Acts, 1 Corinthians, Ephesians, 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, Revelation
entries.label: 6 books
entries.dictNote: Ephesus was the leading city of Roman Asia and home to the temple of Artemis, one of the ancient world's Seven Wonders, along with a theater that could seat some twenty five thousand spectators. Paul made it the center of his third missionary journey, staying about three years and sparking a riot among silversmiths whose idol trade suffered from his preaching; he later addressed a moving farewell to the Ephesian elders at Miletus. It is one of the seven churches addressed in Revelation, and tradition holds that the apostle John spent his final years and was buried there. Excavations have uncovered much of the ancient city, including the Library of Celsus and the massive theater, still among the best preserved Roman ruins in the eastern Mediterranean.

witness.excerpt: As I was dispensing justice at Ephesus, on the Ides of February, the Jews that dwell in Asia demonstrated to me that Augustus and Agrippa had permitted them to use their own laws and customs, and to offer those their first-fruits, which every one of them fre

But still, when Antony was come to Ephesus, Hyrcanus the high priest, and our nation, sent an embassage to him, which carried a crown of gold with them, and desired that he would write to the governors of the provinces, to set those Jews free who had been carrie

But Lucius the consul's decree ran thus: \"I have at my tribunal set these Jews, who are citizens of Rome, and follow the Jewish religious rites, and yet live at Ephesus, free from going into the army, on account of the superstition they are under.

entries.title: Ephlal (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: In Jerahmeel's line, the branch of Judah that ran through Jarha, a servant who married into the family.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A descendant of Judah in the line of Jerahmeel, listed in a genealogy that traces the family through a servant, Jarha, who married into the household (1 Chronicles 2:34-37).

entries.title: Ephod (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Father of Hanniel, Manasseh's leader in dividing Canaan. Nothing else is recorded of him, and he has nothing to do with the priest's garment.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Ephod was the father of Hanniel, the leader chosen from the tribe of Manasseh to help apportion the land of Canaan among the tribes after the conquest (Numbers 34:23). Nothing else is recorded of him; his name is distinct from the priestly garment of similar spelling, which is a common word rather than this man's proper name.

witness.excerpt: Besides these, the High Priest put on a third garment, which was called the Ephod : which resembles the Epomis of the Greeks.

entries.title: Ephphatha
entries.summary: Aramaic for be opened, which Jesus says while healing a deaf man near the Decapolis. Mark keeps several of these words untranslated.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Not a person but an Aramaic word meaning "be opened," spoken by Jesus when he healed a deaf man with a speech impediment near the Decapolis (Mark 7:34). Mark is noted for preserving several of Jesus's actual Aramaic words in transliterated form, including talitha cumi (Mark 5:41) and his cry from the cross, eloi eloi lama sabachthani (Mark 15:34), details that reflect the eyewitness texture of his gospel.

entries.title: Ephraim
entries.summary: Named twice, in 2 Samuel and John, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Ephraim (Joseph's son living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Joseph's younger son. When Jacob blessed the two boys he crossed his hands on purpose and gave Ephraim the bigger blessing over Manasseh. The tribe came to dominate the north so much that the prophets use Ephraim for the whole northern kingdom.
entries.books: Genesis, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Nehemiah, Psalm, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Hosea, Obadiah, Zechariah
entries.label: 19 books
entries.dictNote: Ephraim was Joseph's younger son, given the greater blessing over his older brother Manasseh when their grandfather Jacob deliberately crossed his hands to bless the younger first. Ephraim's tribe became so dominant in the northern kingdom that Ephraim is often used as a poetic stand-in for the whole northern kingdom of Israel in the prophetic books.

witness.excerpt: The tribe of Ephraim had by lot the land that extended in length, from the river Jordan, to Gezer; but in breadth, as far as from Bethel till it ended at the great plain.
However, the tribe of Ephraim, when they besieged Bethel, made no advance; nor performed any thing worthy of the time they spent, and of the pains they took about that siege.
Those of the tribe of Ephraim were twenty thousand and eight hundred, and these mighty men of valor, and eminent for their strength.

Now the tribe of Ephraim fought against him, because he did not take them along with him in his expedition against the Ammonites; but because he alone had the prey, and the glory of what was done to himself.

entries.title: Ephraimite (Joseph's son living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Someone of the tribe of Ephraim. In Judges 12 the men of Gilead caught Ephraimites at the fords by making them say shibboleth, and killed those who could not get the first sound right.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Ephraimite designates a member of the tribe of Ephraim. The word is central to one grim episode in Judges 12, where Gilead's forces used the pronunciation of the word "shibboleth" to identify and kill fleeing Ephraimites who could not say the initial sound correctly.

entries.title: Ephraimite (Woman living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Ruth and 1 Samuel name him twice, and she is a woman from the wilderness years.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Ephron (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: The Hittite who sold Abraham the cave of Machpelah to bury Sarah. It was the first piece of the promised land Abraham owned, and Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and their wives were all buried there.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Ephron was the Hittite from whom Abraham purchased the cave of Machpelah as a burial site for Sarah, the first piece of the promised land Abraham actually owned, and it became the family tomb for Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and their wives.

witness.excerpt: Which piece of ground Abraham bought for four hundred shekels, of Ephron an inhabitant of Hebron.

Wherefore bury me near Abraham my father, in the double cave in the field of Ephron the Hittite, where Abraham purchased a sepulchre to bury in; in the sepulchre which I digged for myself, there bury me.

entries.title: Epicurean (Philosophical group in the New Testament)
entries.summary: Followers of Epicurus, who taught that the best thing in life is pleasure, meaning freedom from pain and worry, and that the gods, if there are any, leave people alone. Some of them argued with Paul in Athens, along with Stoics.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Not a person but a follower of the philosophy founded by Epicurus, who taught that pleasure, understood as freedom from pain and disturbance, was the chief good, and that the gods, if they existed, took no active interest in human affairs. Acts 17:18 records Epicurean philosophers debating Paul in Athens alongside Stoics after he preached about Jesus and the resurrection, part of the setting for his address on the Areopagus.

witness.excerpt: Now there was one Pompedius, a senator, and one who had gone through almost all posts in the government, but otherwise an Epicurean, and for that reason loved to lead an inactive life.

entries.title: Er
entries.summary: Judah's firstborn. Genesis says only that he was wicked in the Lord's sight and God put him to death, and his widow Tamar's story starts from there.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Er was Judah's firstborn son, and Genesis records simply that he was wicked in the Lord's sight and that God put him to death, leaving his widow Tamar to eventually conceive a child through Judah himself.

entries.title: Er
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the wilderness years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Er (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 3 men called Er. This one is a man from the divided-kingdom years, named once in Luke.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Eran (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Son of Shuthelah and grandson of Ephraim, and the ancestor of the Eranites in the wilderness census.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Eran was a son of Shuthelah and grandson of Ephraim, ancestor of the Eranite clan counted in the wilderness census of Numbers 26:36.

entries.title: Eranites (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: The clan from Eran, Ephraim's grandson through Shuthelah, as the census counted them.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Eranites were the clan descended from Eran, a grandson of Ephraim through Shuthelah, counted in Israel's wilderness census.

entries.title: Erastus (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Paul's companion, and in Romans the city treasurer of Corinth. An inscription found at Corinth names an Erastus who paid for a pavement in return for an aedileship.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Erastus was a companion of Paul and, according to Romans, held the position of city treasurer of Corinth, a detail confirmed by a first-century inscription found in Corinth naming an Erastus who paid for a public pavement in exchange for an aedileship, a civic office.

entries.title: Erech
entries.summary: Nimrod's kingdom took in Erech, with Babel and Akkad, in the plain of Shinar. It is Uruk, modern Warka in Iraq, among the oldest cities anywhere and probably where cuneiform writing began.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of the cities of Nimrod's kingdom in the plain of Shinar, alongside Babel and Akkad (Gen. 10:10). It is the great Sumerian city of Uruk, modern Warka in Iraq, one of the oldest cities in the world and the probable birthplace of cuneiform writing in the late fourth millennium BC; its excavated temple precincts and monumental architecture remain among the most important archaeological witnesses to early Mesopotamian civilization.

entries.title: Eri (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: A son of Gad who went down to Egypt with Jacob's family. His descendants were the Erites of the wilderness census.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Eri was a son of Gad who went down to Egypt with Jacob's family, and his descendants became the clan of the Erites counted in the wilderness census (Genesis 46:16; Numbers 26:16).

witness.excerpt: And these are the names of their sons who went with him into Egypt: the sons of Gad: Ziphion, and Haggi, and Shuni, and Ezbon, (and Eri) and Areli, and Arodi--eight.

entries.title: Erites (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Eri's descendants, a clan of Gad counted in the census.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Erites were the clan descended from Eri, a son of Gad, counted in Israel's wilderness census.

entries.title: Esar-haddon (King living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Sennacherib was murdered and Esarhaddon took the Assyrian throne after him. He carried Manasseh of Judah off to Babylon, and his own inscriptions list Manasseh among the vassal kings paying him tribute.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Esarhaddon was the Assyrian king who succeeded Sennacherib after his assassination, and he was the one who took Judah's King Manasseh captive to Babylon, an episode confirmed by Esarhaddon's own inscriptions listing Manasseh among the vassal kings who paid him tribute.

entries.title: Esau (Edomite living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Isaac and Rebekah's elder twin, born red and hairy just ahead of Jacob. He sold his birthright for a bowl of stew, and Jacob later tricked him out of the blessing too, and only after years apart did the two make up in tears. His descendants were the Edomites.
entries.books: Genesis, Deuteronomy, Joshua, 1 Chronicles, Jeremiah, Obadiah, Malachi, Romans, Hebrews
entries.label: 9 books
entries.dictNote: Esau was Isaac and Rebekah's elder twin, born moments before his brother Jacob and covered in reddish hair, and he sold his birthright to Jacob for a bowl of stew after coming in from the field exhausted and hungry, a decision Hebrews later holds up as an example of trading something sacred for immediate gratification. Jacob later stole Esau's father's blessing as well, through deception, and Esau's fury forced Jacob to flee for over a decade, though the two brothers reconciled tearfully when Jacob finally returned. Esau, also called Edom, became the ancestor of the Edomites, a nation whose long hostility toward Israel runs through much of the Old Testament.

witness.excerpt: And on that day Esau, his brother, came to him, and he was reconciled to him, and departed from him unto the land of Seir, but Jacob dwelt in tents.
And the words of Esau, her elder son, were told to Rebecca in a dream, and Rebecca sent and called Jacob her younger son, and said unto him: 2.

entries.title: Esau (Edomite living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: A man from the patriarchs. Genesis and 1 Chronicles name him 7 times.
entries.label: 2 books

witness.excerpt: And when the Edomites about that time had revolted from him, and slain their former King, who was in subjection to his father, and had set up one of their own chusing, Jehoram fell upon the land of Edom, with the horse-men that were about him, and the chariots, by night; and destroyed those that lay near to his own Kingdom: but did not proceed farther.
And Esau went to the land of Edom, to the mountains of Seir, and dwelt there.

He was a child of the stock of the Edomites, and of the blood royal; and when Joab, the captain of David's host, laid waste the land of Edom, and destroyed all that were men grown, and able to bear arms, for six months' time, this Hadad fled away, and came to Pharaoh the king of Egypt, who received him kindly, and assigned him a house to dwell in, and a coun

entries.title: Esek
entries.summary: A well, not a person. Isaac's herdsmen dug it in the valley of Gerar and the herdsmen of Gerar claimed the water, so he called it contention. Sitnah came next, and then Rehoboth, which nobody fought over.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Esek is not a person but a well that Isaac's herdsmen dug in the valley of Gerar; the name means "contention" or "quarrel," because Philistine herdsmen from Gerar disputed Isaac's claim to the water (Genesis 26:20). It was the first of three wells dug during that dispute, the others being Sitnah and the uncontested Rehoboth.

entries.title: Eshbaal (Saul's son living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Saul's fourth son, whose name means man of Baal. 2 Samuel calls him Ish-bosheth, man of shame, because later Israel did not like Baal even inside a name. Abner made him king over the northern tribes after Saul died, and his short reign ended in murder.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Eshbaal, "man of Baal," was the fourth son of King Saul (1 Chronicles 8:33; 9:39). He is better known by the name Ish-bosheth, "man of shame" (2 Samuel 2:8), a substitution that reflects later Israelite discomfort with the word "Baal" even inside personal names. After Saul's death, Abner made Eshbaal king over the northern tribes for a brief, troubled reign that ended in his assassination, clearing the way for David to rule over a united Israel (2 Samuel 2-4).

entries.title: Eshban (Edomite living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: One of Dishon's four sons, a Horite among the clan chiefs of Seir.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Eshban was a Horite, one of the four sons of Dishon listed among the clan chiefs of Seir in Edom's genealogy (Genesis 36:26; 1 Chronicles 1:41).

entries.title: Eshcol (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: An Amorite ally who helped Abraham get Lot back from Chedorlaomer. The Valley of Eshcol near Hebron, probably named for him or his clan, is where the twelve spies cut the huge cluster of grapes.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Eshcol is a name shared by a place and a person. Eshcol was an Amorite ally of Abraham who helped rescue Lot from Chedorlaomer's coalition (Genesis 14:13, 24), and the Valley of Eshcol near Hebron, likely named for him or his clan, is where the twelve spies cut the enormous cluster of grapes they carried back as proof of Canaan's fertility (Numbers 13:23-24).

entries.title: Eshean (Eshan)
entries.summary: A town in Judah's hill country whose site is not secure, though some put it near Dumah, south of Hebron.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A town in the hill country of Judah (Joshua 15:52). Its site is not securely identified, though some have proposed a location near Dumah, south of Hebron.

entries.title: Eshek (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Saul's descendant through Jonathan, in Benjamin's royal line.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A descendant of Saul through Jonathan, listed in the genealogy of Benjamin's royal line (1 Chronicles 8:39).

entries.title: Eshkalonites (Ashkelon)
entries.summary: The people of Ashkelon, one of the five Philistine cities still unconquered when Joshua was old. Digs on the coast there have found a large Philistine cemetery, which gave archaeologists the Philistines' own bones.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Eshkalonites were the inhabitants of Ashkelon, one of the five Philistine lord-cities listed in Joshua 13:3 among the territory still unconquered when Joshua was old. Ashkelon has been extensively excavated on Israel's Mediterranean coast, uncovering both Canaanite and Philistine occupation layers, including a large Philistine cemetery discovered in the 2010s that has given archaeologists direct skeletal evidence of the Philistine population.

entries.title: Eshtaol
entries.summary: Samson grew up here, and here the Spirit of the Lord first began to stir him. It was a Shephelah town that went to Dan, and the Danites sent their spies north from it. Samson was buried between Zorah and Eshtaol in his father's tomb.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Eshtaol was a town in the Shephelah of Judah later allotted to Dan (Joshua 15:33; 19:41), remembered chiefly as the place where Samson grew up and where the Spirit of the Lord first began to stir him (Judges 13:25). From here the Danites sent spies north to find territory to settle (Judges 18:2, 8, 11), and Samson was buried nearby, between Zorah and Eshtaol, in his father's tomb (Judges 16:31).

entries.title: Eshtaulites (Eshtaol)
entries.summary: One of the families of the Kiriath-jearim clans in Judah's genealogy, tied to the town of Eshtaol.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Eshtaulites were one of the families descended from the clans of Kiriath-jearim in Judah's genealogy, associated with the town of Eshtaol, the same district from which Samson's parents came and where he was first stirred by the Spirit of the Lord.

entries.title: Eshtemoa
entries.summary: David sent some of the Amalekite plunder to the elders of Eshtemoa, a priestly town south of Hebron, for standing by him in his outlaw years. It survives as es-Samu, where old ruins have been found.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Eshtemoa was a priestly town in the hill country of Judah south of Hebron, allotted with its pastureland to the Kohathite priests (Joshua 21:14); David sent part of the plunder from his raid on the Amalekites to its elders as a gift for their friendship during his years as an outlaw (1 Samuel 30:28). It survives as the Palestinian village of es-Samu, where ancient ruins have been found.

entries.title: Eshton (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A descendant of Chelub in Judah's genealogy, father of Beth-rapha, Paseah and Tehinnah. The names are probably clans or towns now lost.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Eshton appears in the genealogy of Judah as a descendant of Chelub, credited with fathering Beth-rapha, Paseah, and Tehinnah, the father of Ir-nahash (1 Chronicles 4:11-12). The list preserves little more than these family names, likely tied to towns or clans that no longer survive.

entries.title: Esli (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Son of Naggai and father of Nahum in Luke's genealogy, in the line through Nathan, and nothing else is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: An ancestor of Jesus in Luke's genealogy, listed as the son of Naggai and father of Nahum, in the line descending through Nathan rather than Solomon (Luke 3:25). Nothing else is recorded about him.

entries.title: Esrom (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Hezron, in the Greek form. He was Judah's grandson through Perez and is in both Matthew's and Luke's genealogies of Jesus.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Esrom is the Greek New Testament form of Hezron, a grandson of Judah through Perez, listed as an ancestor of Jesus in both Matthew's and Luke's genealogies (Matthew 1:3; Luke 3:33).

witness.excerpt: Judas had three sons - Sala, Phares, Zerah; and by Phares two grandchildren, Esrom and Amar.

entries.title: Esther (Woman living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: An orphan raised by her cousin Mordecai in Susa, she became queen when Ahasuerus put away his first wife. When Haman plotted to wipe out the Jews she went to the king uninvited, at the risk of her life, and Haman ended on his own gallows. The book never names God, and Purim still keeps the day.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Esther was a Jewish orphan raised by her cousin Mordecai in the Persian capital of Susa who became queen after King Ahasuerus, usually identified with Xerxes, deposed his previous wife. When the king's official Haman plotted to exterminate the Jewish people, Esther risked her life by approaching the king uninvited, and her intervention saved her people and got Haman executed on the gallows he had built for Mordecai. The book that bears her name never mentions God directly, but Jews still celebrate the deliverance every year at Purim.

witness.excerpt: Concerning Esther, and Mordecai, and Haman. And how, in the reign of Artaxerxes, the whole nation of the Jews was in danger of perishing.

entries.curatedNote: The orphaned Jewish girl who becomes queen of Persia and saves her people from Haman's plot (Esther 2-9), in a book that famously never names God once. Josephus retells the whole story at length under his own chapter title, the same three names, Esther, Mordecai, Haman, in the same order.

entries.title: Etam
entries.summary: Named twice, in 1 Chronicles, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Etam
entries.summary: The rock of Etam, where Samson went down into a cleft and stayed after he had cut down the Philistines.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Etam is the name of two Judean towns. One was a village of Simeon near a rocky refuge where Samson hid in a cleft of rock after slaughtering a group of Philistines (Judges 15:8, 11); the other, near Bethlehem and Tekoa, was fortified by Rehoboam among his network of defensive cities (2 Chronicles 11:6) and sat near the springs that fed Solomon's pools and gardens.

entries.title: Etam
entries.summary: 2 Chronicles names him once, and nothing else is recorded.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Etham
entries.summary: Israel's third camp out of Egypt, on the edge of the wilderness. From there God turned Moses back toward Pi-hahiroth to draw Pharaoh after them. It was near the north end of the Gulf of Suez, but nobody knows exactly where.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Etham was the third encampment of the Israelites after leaving Egypt, on the edge of the wilderness near the eastern fortification line known as the Wall of Egypt (Exodus 13:20; Numbers 33:6-8). From there God directed Moses to turn back toward Pi-hahiroth, a change of route intended to lure Pharaoh into pursuit (Exodus 14:1-4). Its exact location is unknown, though it lay somewhere near the northern end of the Gulf of Suez.

witness.excerpt: He thought the Israelites had proceeded as far as the desert of Etham, Exodus 13:20, when they were commanded by God to return back, Exodus 14:2, and to pitch their camp between Migdol and the sea; and that when they were not able to fly, unless by sea, they were shut in on each side by m

There was a certain place about fifty furlongs distant from Jerusalem, which is called Etham, very pleasant it is in fine gardens, and abounding in rivulets of water; (19) thither did he use to go out in the morning, sitting on high [in his chariot.]
4.

entries.title: Ethan (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: In 1 Kings Ethan is one of the wise men Solomon outdid, and Psalm 89 is credited to Ethan the Ezrahite, possibly the same man. The name also turns up among the singers of Chronicles.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Ethan was renowned for wisdom in his own right, mentioned in 1 Kings as a standard of comparison Solomon's wisdom exceeded, and Psalm 89 is attributed to an Ethan the Ezrahite, possibly the same man.

witness.excerpt: He also excelled and distinguished himself in wisdom above those who were most eminent among the Hebrews at that time for shrewdness; those I mean were Ethan, and Heman, and Chalcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol.

entries.title: Ethan (Man living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him twice, and he is a man from the years before the monarchy.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ethanim (Name of the 7th month)
entries.summary: Seventh month in the Canaanite reckoning, September into October, and Solomon's temple was dedicated in it.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Not a person but the Canaanite name for the seventh month of the Hebrew calendar, corresponding to parts of September and October, used once in 1 Kings 8:2 to date the dedication of Solomon's temple during the feast of Tabernacles. After the Babylonian exile this month came to be called Tishri, the name that stuck in later Jewish usage.

entries.title: Ethbaal (King living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: King of Sidon and Jezebel's father. Her marriage to Ahab brought Baal worship into the northern kingdom. Josephus, using Menander of Ephesus, makes him Ithobalus, a priest of Astarte who murdered King Pheles and took the throne.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: King of Sidon and father of Jezebel, whose marriage to Ahab of Israel sealed a political alliance that brought Baal worship into the northern kingdom (1 Kings 16:31). Josephus, drawing on the Tyrian historian Menander of Ephesus, identifies him with Ithobalus, a priest of Astarte who seized the throne of Tyre and Sidon after murdering King Pheles and reigned there for over three decades in the early ninth century BC. This Tyrian king list preserved through Josephus is one of the few extrabiblical anchors for the chronology of Phoenician kings in this period.

witness.excerpt: As does Philostratus, in his accounts both of India and of Phenicia say, that “this King besieged Tyre thirteen years: while at the same time Ethbaal reigned at Tyre.” These are all the histories that I have met with concerning this King.

entries.title: Ether
entries.summary: A lowland town of Judah, near Lachish in the list, later counted among Simeon's towns. The site has not been identified with confidence.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Ether was a town in the lowland district of Judah, first listed among Judah's towns near Lachish (Josh. 15:42) and then again as one of the cities allotted to Simeon within Judah's larger territory (Josh. 19:7). Its exact site has not been identified with confidence.

entries.title: Ethiopian (Cush)
entries.summary: The Candace's treasurer, a eunuch, reading Isaiah in his chariot on the road from Jerusalem to Gaza. Philip told him the passage was about Jesus and baptised him there and then.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Ethiopian here refers to the treasury official of the Ethiopian queen known as the Candace, an Ethiopian eunuch whom Philip met on the road from Jerusalem to Gaza while he was reading the prophet Isaiah (Acts 8:27). Philip explained that the passage pointed to Jesus, and the official was baptized on the spot, one of the earliest signs in Acts of the gospel reaching beyond Jewish and Samaritan boundaries.

witness.excerpt: But there was one of the King’s servants,13 who was in esteem with him; an Ethiopian by descent; who told the King what a state the Prophet was in; and said, that his friends and his rulers had done evil in putting the Prophet into the mire, and by that means contriving against him, that he should suffe

entries.title: Ethnan (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Son of Helah, one of Ashur's wives, in the genealogy of Judah. Ashur founded Tekoa, and nothing else is known of Ethnan.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Ethnan was one of the sons of Helah, a wife of Ashur, listed in the genealogy of Judah in 1 Chronicles 4:7. Ashur was the founder of Tekoa, and this brief notice is part of a longer set of family records preserving the descendants of Judah's clans. Nothing else is known of him.

entries.title: Ethni (Levite living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A Gershonite Levite in the ancestry of Asaph the musician.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Ethni was a Gershonite Levite listed in the genealogy of the musician Asaph in 1 Chronicles 6:41. Nothing further is recorded about him.

entries.title: Eubulus (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: One of the Christians in Rome whose greetings Paul sends Timothy, with Pudens, Linus and Claudia.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Christian in Rome whose greetings Paul sends to Timothy near the end of his final letter, alongside Pudens, Linus, and Claudia (2 Timothy 4:21). Nothing else is recorded of him.

entries.title: Eunice (Woman living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Timothy's mother, a Jewish believer married to a Greek. Paul says her faith was real, and that she and Lois, Timothy's grandmother, raised him on the Scriptures from a child.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Eunice was the mother of Timothy, a Jewish believer married to a Greek man (Acts 16:1). Paul commends her sincere faith and credits her, along with Timothy's grandmother Lois, with raising him in the Scriptures from childhood (2 Timothy 1:5; 3:15).

entries.title: Euodias (Woman living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Paul begs her and Syntyche at Philippi to be of the same mind, so the two had fallen out. Both had worked beside him in the gospel. The King James spelling hides that the name is a woman's.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A woman in the church at Philippi whom Paul urges to "be of the same mind" as another woman, Syntyche, indicating the two had fallen into some disagreement (Philippians 4:2). Paul says both women had struggled alongside him in spreading the gospel, evidence that women held visible, active roles in the Philippian church. The King James Version's spelling "Euodias" obscures that the name is feminine in the Greek.

entries.title: Euphrates
entries.summary: The great river. It rises in the Armenian highlands and runs some seventeen hundred miles to the Persian Gulf. Genesis has it as one of Eden's four rivers, the promise to Abraham reaches to it, and later Assyria and Babylon came from beyond it.
entries.books: Genesis, Deuteronomy, Joshua, 2 Samuel, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Jeremiah, Revelation
entries.label: 9 books
entries.dictNote: The Euphrates is the longest river of Western Asia, rising in the Armenian highlands and flowing some seventeen hundred miles to the Persian Gulf, and the Bible names it among the four rivers of Eden and repeatedly as “the great river” marking the northeastern edge of the land promised to Abraham's descendants. It served as the effective boundary of David's kingdom at its widest extent and later as a symbol of Mesopotamian imperial power, first Assyrian, then Babylonian, threatening Israel and Judah from beyond it.

witness.excerpt: Euphrates also, as well as Tigris, goes down into the Red Sea.  Now the name Euphrates, or Phrath, denotes either a Dispersion, or a Flower: by Tigris or Diglath, is signified what is swift, with narrowness: and Geon runs through

He also came over Euphrates, and left those who greatly honored him beyond that river, though he were to be entirely under Herod's government; and that it was a most incredible thing that he should enterprise any thing by way of innovation, and no

But Demetrius passed over [Euphrates], and came into Mesopotamia, as desirous to retain that country still, as well as Babylon; and when he should have obtained the dominion of the upper provinces, to lay a foundation for recovering his entire kingdom; for
So he passed over the river Euphrates; and came over Taurus, the Cilician mountain: and at Issus of Cilicia he waited for the enemy, as ready there to give him battel.

entries.title: Euroklydon
entries.summary: The wind that drove Paul's ship off course near Crete. Many manuscripts read Eurakylon instead.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Not a person but the name of the violent wind that drove Paul's ship off course near Crete on the voyage to Rome (Acts 27:14). Many manuscripts instead read Eurakylon, a Greco-Latin hybrid naming a wind roughly equivalent to what modern sailors call a gregale, a fierce northeasterly common in the eastern Mediterranean.

entries.title: Eutychus (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Asleep in a third-storey window at Troas while Paul preached late, he fell to the ground and was taken up for dead. Paul went down, held him and said he was alive, and they went back up and ate and talked until daybreak.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Eutychus was a young man at Troas who sat in a third-story window during one of Paul's late-night sermons and, overcome by drowsiness, fell asleep and dropped to the ground below, apparently dead. Paul went down, embraced him, and announced that he was alive, after which the gathering continued and shared a meal before Paul left at daybreak (Acts 20:9-12).

witness.excerpt: Agrippa praying [to God] (for they two sat by themselves), that “Tiberius might soon go off the stage, and leave the government to Caius, who was in every respect more worthy of it.” Now Eutychus, who was Agrippa’s freed man, and drove his chariot, heard these words: and at that time said nothing of them.

When they were in these circumstances, Cherea was not able to contain the anger he had, and promised, that if they desired an emperor, he would give them one, if any one would bring him the watchword from Eutychus.

entries.title: Eve (Woman living at the time before the Flood)
entries.summary: The first woman, made from Adam's rib as a fit companion, and named the mother of all the living. The serpent deceived her into eating from the one forbidden tree, and Adam ate too. Paul later sets that against the obedience of Christ.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Eve was the first woman, formed by God from Adam's rib as a companion suited to him, and Genesis names her mother of all the living. She was deceived by the serpent into eating fruit from the one forbidden tree, and Adam ate as well after she offered it to him, an act that brought sin and death into the world and that Paul later contrasts with the obedience of Christ.

witness.excerpt: Adam and Eve had two sons: the elder of them was named Cain; which name, when it is interpreted, signifies a Possession.
And Adam knew Eve his wife and she bare yet nine sons.  225-231 A.M.

Now a woman is called in the Hebrew tongue Issa: but the name of this woman was Eve: which signifies the Mother of all living.
