Let us mark its mode of dealing with the Sacred Text in salient instances.
The story of the creation of Eve, we are told, is not meant to be taken literally.

entries.title: Evi (King living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: One of five Midianite kings killed in the war against Midian that followed Baal-peor. His land is recalled in Joshua among what was later allotted. Nothing more is known of him.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Evi was one of five Midianite kings, described elsewhere as princes vassal to the Amorite king Sihon, killed by Israel's forces in the war of vengeance against Midian (Numbers 31:8), and his territory is recalled among the lands allotted afterward (Joshua 13:21). The campaign was ordered in response to Midian's role in luring Israel into idolatry and immorality at Baal-peor (Numbers 25; 31:1-2). Nothing more is known of Evi individually.

witness.excerpt: And among them fell all their Kings, five in number: Evi , and Zur , and Reba , and Hur , and Rekem , the fifth; who was of the same name with a city, the chief and capital of all Arabia, which is till now so called, by the whole Arabian nation, Arecem , from the name of the

entries.title: Evil-merodach (King living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Nebuchadnezzar's son, Amel-Marduk in Babylonian records. In his first year he let Jehoiachin out of prison and gave him a seat at the royal table for life. He lasted only about two years before he was overthrown.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Evil-merodach, known in Babylonian records as Amel-Marduk, succeeded his father Nebuchadnezzar II as king of Babylon around 562 BC. In the year he began to reign he released the exiled Judean king Jehoiachin from prison, showed him favor, and gave him a regular place at the royal table for the rest of his life (2 Kings 25:27-30; Jeremiah 52:31-34). Babylonian sources confirm him as Nebuchadnezzar's son and successor, though he reigned only about two years before being overthrown.

entries.title: Ezbai (Warrior living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Father of Naarai, one of David's mighty men, and nothing further is recorded.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Ezbai was the father of Naarai, one of David's mighty men listed in 1 Chronicles 11:37. Nothing further is recorded about him.

entries.title: Ezbon (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the wilderness years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ezbon (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: A son of Gad who went down to Egypt with Jacob's family. Numbers calls him Ozni.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Two men are named Ezbon in the genealogies. One was a son of Gad, also called Ozni, who went down to Egypt with Jacob's family (Genesis 46:16; compare Numbers 26:16). The other was a son of Bela and grandson of Benjamin, listed as a head of a family in that tribe (1 Chronicles 7:7).

entries.title: Ezekias (King living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Hezekiah, in the Greek of Matthew's genealogy. He was the reforming king of Judah who outlasted Sennacherib's siege in 701 BC, and Sennacherib's Prism boasts of shutting him up like a bird in a cage without claiming the city.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Ezekias is the Greek form of Hezekiah, used in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:9-10). Hezekiah was a reforming king of Judah who removed idolatrous shrines and survived the Assyrian king Sennacherib's siege of Jerusalem in 701 BC, an episode corroborated outside the Bible by Sennacherib's own Prism, which boasts of shutting Hezekiah up "like a bird in a cage" but stops short of claiming the city itself was captured.

witness.excerpt: There was also Judas, (16) the son of that Ezekias who had been head of the robbers; which Ezekias was a very strong man, and had with great dificulty been caught by Herod.

entries.title: Ezekiel (Prophet living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A priest taken to Babylon with the first exiles. Five years in, he saw God's throne, wheels within wheels and four living creatures, and started prophesying. He acted out a lot of it, lying on his side for over a year. His valley of dry bones coming back to life is the picture of Israel restored.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Ezekiel was a priest deported to Babylon in the first wave of exiles who began prophesying five years into his captivity after a vision of God's throne, described in famously strange imagery of wheels within wheels and four living creatures. He acted out many of his prophecies physically, lying on his side for over a year to symbolize the years of Israel's sin, and his most famous vision is a valley of dry bones brought back to life, a picture of national restoration after exile.

witness.excerpt: This King would not believe what was predicted by Jeremiah and Ezekiel.

entries.curatedNote: The priest-prophet exiled to Babylon whose visions open with the famous wheels-within-wheels (Ezekiel 1:3). Josephus mentions him more briefly than Jeremiah here, the honest gap in this particular chapter, but places him exactly where Scripture does: warning King Zedekiah, unheeded, right before the final fall of Jerusalem.

entries.title: Ezel
entries.summary: A stone near Saul's house at Gibeah where David hid while Jonathan found out what his father meant to do. It was the last time the two met before David fled for good.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Ezel was not a person but a stone or landmark near Saul's residence in Gibeah, mentioned only in 1 Samuel 20:19 as the spot where David hid while Jonathan tested his father's intentions toward him. It marks the site of David and Jonathan's last meeting before David fled from Saul for good. The Hebrew name likely means 'departure' or 'separation,' fitting the scene it names.

entries.title: Ezer (Edomite living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: A chieftain of Seir, named in Edom's early lists of clan heads.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Ezer was a common name, borne by a chieftain of Seir, a son of Ephraim killed raiding cattle from Gath, and one of David's mighty warriors from Gad.

entries.title: Ezer (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 5 men called Ezer. This one is a man from the divided-kingdom years, named once in 1 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ezer (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Named once, in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 4. The Seirite chief and the Ephraimite with the same name are other men.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ezer (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the wilderness years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ezer (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A man from the exile and the return. Nehemiah names him once.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ezer (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A Levite who repaired a stretch of Jerusalem's wall under Nehemiah.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A different Ezer, distinct from the Seirite chieftain and Ephraimite of the same name, was a Levite who helped repair a section of Jerusalem's walls under Nehemiah.

entries.title: Ezion-geber
entries.summary: Solomon built his fleet here, at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba near Elath, to sail for Ophir, and Jehoshaphat's ships were wrecked here later. Nelson Glueck dug Tell el-Kheleifeh in the 1930s and called it the site, though later work on the pottery has kept the question open.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Ezion-geber was a port city at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba, near Elath, where Solomon built his fleet of ships to trade with Ophir (1 Kings 9:26) and where Jehoshaphat's ships were later wrecked (1 Kings 22:48). Archaeologist Nelson Glueck excavated the mound of Tell el-Kheleifeh in the 1930s and identified it with the site, though later reanalysis of the pottery narrowed its date range and location debates continue.

witness.excerpt: Moreover, the king built many ships in the Egyptian Bay of the Red Sea, in a certain place called Ezion-geber: it is now called Berenice, and is not far from the city Eloth.

entries.title: Ezra (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: He is not the famous scribe but a priest in Nehemiah's list of those who came back earlier under Zerubbabel, and he is named only there.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ezra (Priest living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: The priest and scribe who led a second return from exile, from Babylon to Jerusalem. In Nehemiah 8 he reads the law aloud to the whole assembled people, and they weep.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Two priests named Ezra appear in the Old Testament. The famous one led a second wave of exiles back from Babylon to Jerusalem and is remembered as the scribe who restored the law's central place in Jewish worship after the exile, reading it aloud to the assembled people in Nehemiah 8. A different priest by the same name is listed simply among those who returned earlier under Zerubbabel.

witness.excerpt: Upon the death of Darius, Xerxes his son took the Kingdom; who, as he inherited his father's Kingdom, so did he inherit his piety towards God, and honour of him.

entries.curatedNote: The priest-scribe who leads a second return from exile and reads the Law aloud to a weeping crowd (Ezra 7-8, Nehemiah 8). Josephus's chapter on the Persian king Xerxes' favor toward the Jews is the political backdrop that makes Ezra's whole mission possible in the first place.

entries.title: Ezrah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Father of Jether, Mered, Epher and Jalon, in a Judah genealogy that also names Mered's wives and some descendants tied to Egypt, and nothing more is recorded of Ezrah himself.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Ezrah was a descendant of Judah listed in 1 Chronicles 4:17 as the father of Jether, Mered, Epher, and Jalon, part of a genealogical unit that also names Mered's wives and descendants, some associated with Egypt. Nothing more is recorded about Ezrah himself beyond this listing of his sons.

entries.title: Ezrahite (Judah's son living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: What Ethan and Heman are called. Both were wise men, counted as sons of Zerah in Chronicles, and the headings of Psalms 89 and 88 name them as the authors.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Ezrahite is the title given to Ethan and Heman, two wise men credited as sons of Zerah in Chronicles and named as authors in the headings of Psalms 89 and 88.

entries.title: Ezri (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: He was Chelub's son, and David put him over the workers who farmed the royal land; that one line in Chronicles is the whole of him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The son of Chelub, appointed overseer of the workers who farmed the royal land under David, part of the administrative list of officials Chronicles preserves for David's kingdom (1 Chr. 27:26).

entries.title: Felix (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Paul sat in custody at his court for two years. Antonius Felix was the Roman governor of Judea before Festus. He seems to have hoped Paul would pay a bribe, then left him locked up to keep the Jewish leaders happy.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Antonius Felix was the Roman governor of Judea before Festus, and Paul was held in custody at his court for two years; Felix reportedly hoped for a bribe from Paul and left him imprisoned to please the Jewish leadership rather than release him.

witness.excerpt: After this Caesar sent Felix, (16) the brother of Pallas, to be procurator of Galilee, and Samaria, and Perea, and removed Agrippa from Chalcis unto a greater kingdom; for he gave him the tetrarchy which had belonged to Philip, which contained Bata
NOW it was that Festus succeeded Felix as procurator, and made it his business to correct those that made disturbances in the country.

entries.title: Festus (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: He took over Judea from Felix and inherited Paul as a prisoner. At the hearing Paul used his right as a Roman citizen and appealed to Caesar, so Porcius Festus sent him to Rome.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Porcius Festus was the Roman governor of Judea who succeeded Felix and held a hearing for the imprisoned Paul, ultimately sending him to Rome after Paul exercised his right as a Roman citizen to appeal directly to Caesar.

witness.excerpt: NOW it was that Festus succeeded Felix as procurator, and made it his business to correct those that made disturbances in the country.
61.] And now Cesar, upon hearing the death of Festus, sent Albinus into Judea, as procurator.

entries.title: Fortunatus (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: He came from Corinth with Stephanas and Achaicus to Paul at Ephesus, probably carrying the letter that 1 Corinthians answers, and Paul says the three of them refreshed him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Fortunatus was a Christian of Corinth who, with Stephanas and Achaicus, traveled to Paul at Ephesus and refreshed him, likely delivering the letter that prompted 1 Corinthians (1 Cor. 16:17-18). Paul urges the Corinthian church to recognize such men for their service.

witness.excerpt: 22 And as soon as he heard they set sail, he sent Fortunatus, one of his freed men, to Rome; to carry presents to the Emperor, and letters against Herod; and to give Caius a particular account of those matters, if he should have any opportunity.

entries.title: Gaal (Man living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: He talked the people of Shechem into rising against Abimelech. When Abimelech brought his forces against the city, Gaal was beaten and driven out.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Gaal was an agitator who stirred up the citizens of Shechem to rebel against Abimelech's rule, but he was defeated and driven out once Abimelech brought his forces against the city.

witness.excerpt: Now it happened that there had come to them a man of authority, one Gaal, that sojourned with them; having his armed men, and his kinsmen with him.

entries.title: Gaash
entries.summary: Joshua was buried near this hill in Ephraim, close to Timnath-heres.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Mount Gaash was a hill in Ephraim's territory near which Joshua was buried after his death.

witness.excerpt:
Testament of Judah, Chapter 7

7 1 And the next day it was told us that the king of the city of Gaash with a mighty host was coming 2 against us.

entries.title: Gaba (Geba)
entries.summary: Another English spelling of Geba, a Levitical city in Benjamin by the pass of Michmash. Jonathan raided a Philistine garrison there, and later it marked the line between the northern and southern kingdoms.
entries.books: Joshua, 1 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Isaiah, Zechariah
entries.label: 10 books
entries.dictNote: Gaba is an alternate English rendering of Geba, a Levitical city in Benjamin near the pass of Michmash, notable as the site of Jonathan's raid on a Philistine garrison and later as a border marker separating the northern and southern kingdoms.

entries.summary: Named once, in Judges, and nowhere else.

entries.title: Gaba (Gibeon)
entries.summary: Named once, in 2 Samuel, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gaba (Maareh-geba)
entries.summary: Judges names him once, and nothing else is recorded.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gabbai (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Nehemiah's census of Jerusalem after the exile lists him as head of a family of Benjamin, and nothing else is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Head of a prominent family of Benjamin living in Jerusalem after the exile, listed in Nehemiah's census of the city's resettled population (Nehemiah 11:8). Nothing else is recorded about him.

entries.title: Gabbatha
entries.summary: An Aramaic word, raised place, for the paved platform outside Pilate's headquarters where he sat in judgment and sentenced Jesus. John gives the Greek too, lithostroton, a stone pavement. Some put it at a courtyard in the Antonia Fortress, but whether that pavement is old enough is disputed.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Gabbatha, an Aramaic word meaning "raised place" or "ridge," was the paved platform outside Pilate's headquarters in Jerusalem where he set up the judgment seat and sentenced Jesus (John 19:13). John pairs it with the Greek term lithostroton, describing a mosaic or tiled stone pavement; a paved courtyard at the Antonia Fortress has been proposed as the site, though its dating to Jesus's era remains disputed among archaeologists.

entries.title: Gabriel (An angel)
entries.summary: Daniel meets him first, explaining the visions of coming empires. In Luke he announces two births, John's to Zechariah and Jesus's to Mary, and tells Zechariah he is the one who stands in the presence of God. He is one of only two angels the Bible names.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Gabriel is one of only two angels named directly in the Bible, and he appears as God's messenger for major turning points: interpreting Daniel's visions of coming empires in the Old Testament, then announcing the births of both John the Baptist to Zechariah and Jesus to Mary in Luke's Gospel. He introduces himself to Zechariah simply as the one who stands in the presence of God.

witness.excerpt: Gabriel, one of the holy angels, who is over Paradise and the serpents and the Cherubim.
And to Gabriel said the Lord: ‘Proceed against the bastards and the reprobates, and against the children of fornication…’
Then Michael, Uriel, Raphael, and Gabriel looked down from heaven and saw much blood being shed upon the earth…

entries.lukeNote: The only named archangel in Luke's infancy narrative is also one of the four archangels in Enoch's Watchers narrative, same figure, two very different documents, about two centuries apart.

entries.title: Gad (Jacob's son living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Jacob's seventh son, born to Leah's servant Zilpah. His tribe asked for good pasture east of the Jordan and got it. The condition was that Gad's fighting men still crossed over and helped the other tribes take their land first.
entries.books: Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Chronicles, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Revelation
entries.label: 11 books
entries.dictNote: Gad was Jacob's seventh son, born to Leah's servant Zilpah, and his tribe requested and received territory east of the Jordan rather than in Canaan proper, valued for its good pasture land, on the condition that Gad's fighting men still crossed over to help the other tribes conquer their own territory first.

entries.title: Gad (Prophet living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: A prophet of the united monarchy, and nothing to do with Jacob's son. He first turns up in 1 Samuel 22:5, comes back in 2 Samuel 24, and Chronicles names him again.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Gadarene
entries.summary: Matthew sets the healing here, in the country around Gadara, one of the Decapolis cities east of the Sea of Galilee, where the spirits went into a herd of pigs. Other manuscripts and the parallels read Gerasene or Gergesene. Gadara itself is Umm Qais in Jordan now, with its Roman ruins dug out.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Gadarene identifies the region around Gadara, one of the cities of the Decapolis east of the Sea of Galilee, as the setting where Jesus healed a demon-possessed man, or two men in Matthew's account, and sent the spirits into a herd of pigs. Some manuscripts and Gospel parallels instead read Gerasene or Gergesene, reflecting the difficulty of pinning the miracle to one of several towns in the area; Gadara itself, modern Umm Qais in Jordan, preserves an impressive set of excavated Roman ruins.

entries.title: Gaddi (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Manasseh's man among the twelve spies Moses sent into Canaan.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The man chosen to represent the tribe of Manasseh among the twelve spies Moses sent to scout out Canaan (Numbers 13:10-11).

entries.title: Gaddiel (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Zebulun sent him as its spy into Canaan. After the report that scared Israel off the land, his name never comes up again, the same as every spy except Caleb and Joshua.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The representative of the tribe of Zebulun among the twelve spies Moses sent to scout Canaan (Numbers 13:10). Along with all his fellow spies except Caleb and Joshua, his name is not mentioned again after the report that discouraged Israel from entering the land.

entries.title: Gadi (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Only ever named as the father of Menahem, who killed Shallum, took the throne of Israel and ruled brutally.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Gadi was the father of Menahem, a king of Israel who seized the throne by assassinating Shallum and ruled with notable brutality (2 Kings 15:14, 17).

entries.title: Gaham (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: One of the sons Nahor, Abraham's brother, had by his concubine Reumah. Nothing further is recorded.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A son of Abraham's brother Nahor by his concubine Reumah, listed among Nahor's descendants in Genesis 22:24. Nothing further is recorded about him.

entries.title: Gahar (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: They came back from Babylon with Zerubbabel, the descendants of Gahar, one of the families of temple servants called the Nethinim.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Gahar headed a family of temple servants, the Nethinim, whose descendants returned from Babylonian exile to Jerusalem under Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:47; Nehemiah 7:49).

entries.title: Gaius (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: This Gaius was Paul's host when Romans was written, and one of the few Paul baptised himself in Corinth. The name was common, and at least three men carry it across Paul's circle, so which references belong to the same man is hard to say.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Gaius was a common name among Paul's traveling companions and hosts, borne by at least three different men across Acts, Romans, and Paul's letters, making it difficult to know for certain which references describe the same person.

witness.excerpt: He had stood well with Tiberius, but the accession of Gaius in 37 endangered his position, for he had been a partisan of Tiberius Gemellus, the rival candidate for the succession, had been concerned in the steps taken to prosecute Agrippina, Gaius's mother, and was friendly with

entries.title: Gaius (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: A man from the New Testament, and 3 John is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gaius (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Acts names him once, and he is a man from the New Testament.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gaius (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: One of 4 men called Gaius. This one is a man from the New Testament, named once in Acts.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Galal (Levite living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A Levite among those who settled back in Jerusalem after the exile, listed in Chronicles and Nehemiah.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Galal was a common Levitical name among those who resettled Jerusalem after the exile, listed in the genealogies of Chronicles and Nehemiah.

entries.title: Galal (Levite living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a Levite from the exile and the return.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Galatia
entries.summary: Gaulish tribes from Europe settled this part of central Asia Minor in the third century BC, and Rome made it a province in 25 BC. Paul wrote one of his sharpest letters to its churches, against teachers who wanted Gentile believers circumcised.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Galatia was a region and later Roman province in central Asia Minor, named for the Gaulish tribes who settled there after migrating from Europe in the third century BC. Rome annexed it as a province in 25 BC, and Paul addressed one of his sharpest letters to churches there, arguing against teachers who wanted Gentile believers to adopt circumcision and the Jewish law. Peter's first letter and Paul's note that Crescens had departed for Galatia (2 Timothy 4:10) show the region remained a center of early Christian activity.

witness.excerpt: And when he was dead, the people bestowed the high priesthood on Judas; who hearing of the power of the Romans, and that they had conquered in war Galatia, and Iberia, and Carthage, and Libya; and that, besides these, they had subdued Greece, and their kings, Perseus, and Philip, and Antiochus the Great also; he resolved to enter into a league of friendship with them.

entries.title: Galatian
entries.summary: It means someone from Galatia. Paul uses it once, sharply, in Galatians 3:1, to the churches turning from grace toward circumcision.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Galatian designates an inhabitant of Galatia, a Roman province in central Asia Minor settled centuries earlier by migrating Celtic tribes. Paul rebukes the Galatian churches sharply for turning from the gospel of grace toward a law-based requirement of circumcision.

entries.title: Galeed (Ramoth-gilead)
entries.summary: Not a person but a heap of stones. Jacob and Laban piled it up to seal their covenant. Laban called it Jegar-sahadutha in Aramaic, and Jacob's Hebrew name for it means heap of witness.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Galeed was not a person but the name Jacob gave to a heap of stones he and his father-in-law Laban raised in the hill country to mark a covenant of peace between them (Genesis 31:45-48). Laban called the same pile Jegar-sahadutha in Aramaic, while Jacob's Hebrew name, meaning "heap of witness," gave the surrounding region, Gilead, its lasting name.

entries.title: Galilee
entries.summary: Jesus grew up here and did most of his public work around the Sea of Galilee. Judeans thought the north provincial and mixed, which is the edge on Nathanael's question about whether anything good could come out of Nazareth.
entries.books: Joshua, 1 Kings, 1 Chronicles, Isaiah, Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, Acts
entries.label: 9 books
entries.dictNote: Galilee was the northern region of Israel where Jesus grew up and conducted most of his public ministry, centered around the Sea of Galilee, and its population was regarded by many in Judea as provincial and religiously mixed, which is part of why Nathanael's skeptical question about whether anything good could come out of Nazareth carried real social weight.

witness.excerpt: Now no place of Galilee remained to be taken but the small city of Gischala, whose multitude yet were desirous of peace; for they were generally husbandmen, and always applied themselves to cultivate the fruits of the earth.
It also appears that Galilee then paid no more than one hundred talents, or the seventh part of the entire sum to be levied in all the country.

And now the affairs of Galilee were put in such disorder after this victory of Antigonus's, that those of Antigonus's party brought the principal men that were on Herod's side to the lake, and there drowned them.

entries.title: Gallim
entries.summary: Michal was given to Palti of Gallim after Saul took her away from David. Isaiah lists the town, in Benjamin north of Jerusalem, among the places panicking as the Assyrian army comes on.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Town in Benjamin north of Jerusalem, home of Palti, the man to whom Saul gave his daughter Michal after taking her away from David (1 Sam. 25:44). Isaiah names it among the towns thrown into panic as the Assyrian army advances on Jerusalem (Isa. 10:30).

witness.excerpt: 17 For as to Michal, the daughter of King Saul, who had been David’s wife, her father had given her in marriage to Phalti, the son of Laish, who was of the city of Gallim.

entries.title: Gallio (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: The proconsul of Achaia threw out the case the Jews of Corinth brought against Paul, calling it an internal religious quarrel and no business of his court. An inscription from Delphi naming Gallio dates the scene closely enough to anchor the chronology of Paul's whole ministry.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Gallio was the Roman proconsul of Achaia who dismissed a case Corinthian Jews brought against Paul, ruling it a matter of internal Jewish religious dispute rather than a genuine legal charge. An inscription found at Delphi naming Gallio as proconsul fixes the date of this episode precisely enough to anchor the chronology of Paul's entire ministry.

entries.title: Gamaliel (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: He turns up five times in Numbers, always in the wilderness lists of tribal leaders, and he is not the Pharisee who taught Paul.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Gamaliel was a highly respected Pharisee and legal scholar who persuaded the Jewish council to release the apostles rather than execute them, arguing that if their movement wasn't from God it would collapse on its own. He was also the teacher under whom the young Saul, later Paul, studied the law.

witness.excerpt: And now Jesus, the son of Gamaliel, became the successor of Jesus, the son of Damneus, in the High Priesthood; which the King had taken from the other.

And indeed they were Gorion the son of Josephus, and Symeon the son of Gamaliel, who encouraged them, by going up and down when they were assembled together in crowds, and as they saw them alone, to bear no longer; but to inflict punishment upon these pests and plagues of their freedom: and to purg

The names of these High-priests, or rather ridiculous and profane persons, were Jesus the son of Damneus; Jesus the son of Gamaliel; Matthias the son of Theophilus; and that prodigious ignoramus Phannias, the son of Samuel.

entries.title: Gamaliel (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Acts names him twice, and he is a man from the New Testament.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gammadims (Gamad)
entries.summary: Soldiers in the towers of Tyre, beside the men of Arvad, in Ezekiel's oracle. Who they were is debated: a place called Gammad, or just a word for brave warriors.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The Gammadims were not an individual but a group of soldiers stationed in the towers of Tyre, mentioned alongside the men of Arvad as part of the city's military garrison in Ezekiel's oracle against Tyre (Ezekiel 27:11). Their exact identity is debated: some connect the name to a place called Gammad, while others take it simply as a Hebrew term for valiant or brave warriors.

entries.title: Gamul (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: The twenty-second of the twenty-four priestly divisions David set up for the temple went by his name.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Gamul headed the twenty-second of the twenty-four priestly divisions David organized for rotating temple service (1 Chronicles 24:17).

entries.title: Gareb
entries.summary: Named once, in Jeremiah, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gareb (Warrior living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of David's mighty warriors. There is also a hill near Jerusalem called Gareb, in Jeremiah, which is a different thing entirely.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Gareb was one of David's mighty warriors, and also the name of a hill near Jerusalem mentioned in Jeremiah's prophecy of the city's future rebuilding.

entries.title: Garmite (People, perhaps descended from the area of Garem)
entries.summary: The word is tied to Keilah in Judah's genealogy, 1 Chronicles 4:19, and what it means is uncertain. The text never explains it.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Garmite is an epithet attached to Keilah in the genealogy of Judah in 1 Chronicles 4:19, in a passage listing descendants connected to the towns of Keilah and Eshtemoa. The meaning of the term itself is uncertain, and it is not explained elsewhere in the text.

entries.title: Gatam (Edomite living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Esau's grandson through Eliphaz, and one of the chiefs of Edom, the dukes of the old translations, heading a clan and otherwise only a name in the lists.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Gatam was a son of Eliphaz and grandson of Esau who became one of the clan chiefs, or “dukes,” of Edom (Genesis 36:11, 16; 1 Chronicles 1:36). Like his brothers, he is remembered only as the eponymous head of an Edomite clan in the genealogical lists.

entries.title: Gath
entries.summary: Goliath's hometown, one of the five Philistine cities. The captured ark brought disaster on it, David later hid there with King Achish while running from Saul, and in the end David took it. Most identify it with Tell es-Safi, where a potsherd turned up carrying two names related to Goliath.
entries.books: Joshua, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Psalm, Amos, Micah
entries.label: 10 books
entries.dictNote: Gath was one of the five chief Philistine cities and the hometown of Goliath, whom David killed, though David himself later took refuge there with its king Achish while fleeing Saul. The ark caused disaster among the Philistines after they captured it and brought it to Gath, and David eventually conquered the city outright. It is usually identified with Tell es-Safi, where excavations have uncovered a massive siege system and a potsherd inscribed with two names philologically related to “Goliath,” evidence that such names were genuinely in use at Gath around the era described in Samuel.

witness.excerpt: Then did Achish, the King of Gath, desire David to assist them with his armed men against the Hebrews.
So the governours of the five cities, Gath, and Ekron, and Askelon; as also of Gaza and Ashdod met together, and considered what was fit to be done.
Accordingly he came with the six hundred men that were with him to Achish, the King of Gath: which was one of their five cities.
For when Hazael, King of Syria, made an irruption into his countrey, and when he had overthrown Gath, and spoiled it, he made an expedition against Jerusalem.

entries.title: Gath-kephr (Gath-hepher)
entries.summary: Jonah was born here, in Zebulun's territory, though the town is better known as Gath-hepher. Local tradition puts his tomb in the village of Mashhad by a hill called Nebi Yunus, near Nazareth.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Town in Zebulun's territory (Josh. 19:13), better known as Gath-hepher, birthplace of the prophet Jonah (2 Kings 14:25). Local tradition places Jonah's tomb near the site, in the village now called Mashhad next to a hill called Nebi Yunus, close to Nazareth.

entries.title: Gath-rimmon
entries.summary: In Dan's territory, and given to the Kohathite Levites. A second Gath-rimmon shows up in the Manasseh list, but 1 Chronicles 6:70 has Bileam there instead, which looks like a copying slip rather than two towns with one name.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Gath-rimmon was a Levitical city in the territory of Dan, given to the Kohathite Levites (Joshua 19:45; 21:24). A second town of the same name appears in the list of Levitical cities within the territory of the half tribe of Manasseh (Joshua 21:25), but the parallel list in 1 Chronicles 6:70 names the town there as Bileam instead, suggesting a copying error duplicated the Danite town's name into the Manasseh list rather than two identical town names actually existing.

entries.title: Gath-rimmon (Ibleam)
entries.summary: Named once, in Joshua, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gaza
entries.summary: Samson pulled down the temple of Dagon here, and Philip met the Ethiopian official on the desert road toward it. It was one of the five Philistine cities, assigned to Judah and never fully held, and Egyptian records already name it in the second millennium BC.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of the five great Philistine cities and a major stop on the coastal trade route between Egypt and the Levant, among the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world. It was assigned to Judah but never fully held (Josh. 15:47; Judg. 1:18), and it is remembered as the city where a captured Samson pulled down the temple of Dagon (Judg. 16:21-30); Philip the evangelist later met the Ethiopian official on the desert road leading toward it (Acts 8:26). Egyptian records from the second millennium BC, including the Amarna letters, already name the city as an administrative center under Egyptian control, confirming its antiquity.

witness.excerpt: But Gaza and Ekron escaped them: for they, lying in a flat countrey, and having a great number of chariots, they sorely galled those that attacked them.
3, reckons Gaza, which had been a free city, among the cities given Herod by Augustus, and yet implies that Herod had made Costobarus a governor of it before, Antiq.
Now in the lot of this tribe there were the cities of Ascalon and Gaza.

Besides those that had been demolished, and also of the maritime cities, Gaza, and Joppa, and Dora, and Strato's Tower; which last Herod rebuilt after a glorious manner, and adorned with havens and temples, and changed its name to Caesarea.

entries.title: Gazathite
entries.summary: A man of Gaza. Judges uses it for the men who waited at the gate to kill Samson, and he carried the gate off.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Gazathite designates an inhabitant of Gaza, one of the five Philistine lordships along the coastal plain. Judges uses the term for the men of Gaza who waited at the city gate to kill Samson, only for him to tear the gate from its posts and carry it off.

entries.title: Gazer (Gezer)
entries.summary: The same city as Gezer. Pharaoh took it and gave it to his daughter when she married Solomon, and Solomon fortified it along with Hazor and Megiddo. The Gezer Calendar, a little tablet of farming seasons in early Hebrew script, was found there.
entries.label: 5 books
entries.dictNote: Gazer is an alternate spelling of Gezer, a Canaanite royal city on the border of Philistia and Israel's central hill country that an Egyptian pharaoh captured and gave to his daughter as a dowry when she married Solomon, after which Solomon fortified it along with Hazor and Megiddo. Excavations there uncovered the Gezer Calendar, a small inscribed tablet from around the tenth century BC listing the agricultural seasons in early Hebrew script, among the oldest known Hebrew inscriptions.

entries.title: Gazez
entries.summary: Two men in one verse. One is Caleb's son by his concubine Ephah, the other is a son of Haran, Ephah's son, and so the first one's nephew. Some think the second is a scribe repeating himself, but the text as it stands has two.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Gazez is a name that appears twice within a single verse, 1 Chronicles 2:46: first as a son Caleb had by his concubine Ephah, and second as a son of Haran, who was himself Ephah's son, making the second Gazez the first one's nephew. Some read the second occurrence as a scribal repetition of the first rather than a distinct person, but the text as it stands names two.

entries.title: Gazzam (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Temple servants, the Nethinim, who came home from Babylon with Zerubbabel, counted under his name. Nothing further is known of him.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Gazzam's descendants, the Bene-Gazzam, were among the families of temple servants (Nethinim) who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:48; Nehemiah 7:51). Nothing further is known of him.

entries.title: Gebal
entries.summary: Byblos, to the Greeks, a Phoenician port north of Beirut. Ezekiel says its craftsmen caulked the ships of Tyre. The ruins gave up the Ahiram sarcophagus, carrying one of the earliest examples of the Phoenician alphabet.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: This Gebal was the great Phoenician port city the Greeks called Byblos, north of Beirut on the Lebanese coast, named in Ezekiel's oracle as the source of skilled craftsmen who caulked Tyre's ships (Ezek. 27:9). Byblos is one of the longest continuously inhabited cities in the world, and its excavated ruins have produced the Ahiram sarcophagus, inscribed with one of the earliest known examples of the Phoenician alphabet, as well as Bronze Age letters to Egypt in which its king begged Pharaoh for military help against invaders.

witness.excerpt:
Testament of Levi, Chapter 6

6 1 And when I was going to my father, I found a brazen shield; wherefore also the name of the 2 mountain is Aspis, which is near Gebal, to the south of Abila And I kept these words in my 3 heart.

entries.title: Geber (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Among Solomon's twelve district governors, each feeding the court for a month, two entries carry this name. The son of Geber was at Ramoth-gilead, and Geber son of Uri had Gilead itself, the old lands of Sihon and Og. Whether that is one man or two is unclear.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Two officials named Geber appear among Solomon's twelve district governors responsible for supplying the royal court: “the son of Geber” was stationed at Ramoth-gilead, and Geber son of Uri administered the region of Gilead itself (1 Kings 4:13, 19). Each governor supplied provisions for one month of the year, and Uri's son's territory corresponded to the conquered kingdoms of Sihon and Og east of the Jordan. It is unclear whether these two references describe one man or two.

witness.excerpt: So that Josephus’s copy differed from our other copies: as is farther plain from his own words, which render what we read, that the ships were broken at Ezion Geber , ὑπὸ μεγέθους, from their unwieldy greatness .

entries.title: Gebim
entries.summary: A village just north of Jerusalem, and the name probably means cisterns. Isaiah pictures its people running as an invading army closes on the city.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Gebim was a village just north of Jerusalem whose people are pictured fleeing as an invading army draws near, in the same poetic list of towns in Isaiah's oracle that includes Madmenah (Isa. 10:31). Its name likely comes from a Hebrew word for cisterns or pits, and it is sometimes located near the modern Jerusalem neighborhood of al-Isawiya.

entries.title: Gedaliah (Governor living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: After Jerusalem fell, Babylon made him governor of Judah over the poor left in the land, and he told them to settle down and submit. Ishmael, of the royal line, murdered him within months, and the rest fled to Egypt in spite of Jeremiah telling them not to go.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Gedaliah was appointed governor of Judah by the Babylonians after Jerusalem's destruction, tasked with governing the peasants left behind, and he urged the remaining population to settle down and submit peacefully to Babylonian rule. A royal descendant named Ishmael assassinated him within months, and fearing Babylonian reprisal for the governor's murder, the remaining population fled to Egypt against Jeremiah's direct warning not to go.

entries.title: Gedaliah (Levite living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him twice, and he is a Levite from the united kingdom.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gedaliah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A man from the divided-kingdom years, and Jeremiah is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gedaliah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A man from the divided-kingdom years. Zephaniah names him once.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gedaliah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of 5 men called Gedaliah. This one is a man from the exile and the return, named once in Ezra.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gedeon (Judge living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: The Greek form of Gideon, who beat the Midianites with three hundred men. Hebrews 11:32 has no room to tell his story and just names him with Barak, Samson and Jephthah.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Gedeon is the Greek form of Gideon, the judge who delivered Israel from Midianite oppression with a force of three hundred men (Judges 6-8). Hebrews 11:32 lists him among the heroes of faith too numerous to describe in full, alongside Barak, Samson, and Jephthah.

entries.title: Geder (Gedor)
entries.summary: Joshua beat its king. Whether it is the same place as Gedor or Gederah is possible, not certain.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Geder, a Canaanite city whose king Joshua defeated during the conquest (Josh. 12:13). It is possibly identified with Gedor or Gederah, other towns in Judah's hill country, though this is not certain.

entries.title: Gederah
entries.summary: It sat in the Shephelah, Judah's lowland, and Chronicles names potters of Judah's line who lived there and worked for the king.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Fortified town in the Shephelah, the lowland region of Judah (Josh. 15:36). A related genealogical note in Chronicles names potters descended from Judah's line who worked at Gederah, apparently a center of pottery production in the king's service (1 Chr. 4:23).

entries.title: Gederathite (Gederah)
entries.summary: Josabad was one, a Benjaminite warrior who joined David at Ziklag while Saul was still hunting him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Gederathite marks Josabad, one of the Benjaminite warriors who joined David at Ziklag while he was still fleeing Saul, as a native of Gederah in the Judean lowlands.

entries.title: Gederite (Gederah)
entries.summary: Baal-hanan, who looked after David's olive and sycamore trees in the lowlands, is called this because he came from Geder or Gederah.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Gederite marks Baal-hanan, the official David placed in charge of the royal olive and sycamore groves in the lowlands, as a native of Geder or Gederah in Judah.

entries.title: Gederoth
entries.summary: The Philistines took it in the reign of Ahaz, while Judah was worn down by war with Israel and Syria. It was a Shephelah town, and the name means sheepfolds.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Gederoth was a town in the Shephelah, the low hill country of Judah (Josh. 15:41). During the reign of Ahaz it was one of several Judean towns seized by the Philistines while Judah was weakened by war with Israel and Syria (2 Chr. 28:18). Its name, meaning sheepfolds, suggests it began as a pastoral settlement.

entries.title: Gederothaim
entries.summary: Listed right after Gederah in Joshua 15:36. The ending can mean two, so some read it as the two Gederahs rather than a town of its own, and if it was separate nobody has found where.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Gederothaim was a town in the lowland district of Judah, listed immediately after Gederah in Joshua's territorial allotment (Joshua 15:36). The "-ayim" ending is the same dual suffix found in names like Kiriathaim, "double city," which has led some scholars to read it as "the two Gederahs" rather than an independent town, though others take it as its own settlement. Its site, if independent, is unidentified.

entries.title: Gedor
entries.summary: A town in the hill country of Judah between Jerusalem and Hebron, whose founders Chronicles traces through Hur and Ephrathah. The same name belongs to another place and to a man in Saul's family.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Gedor is a Hebrew name used for at least two places and a man in the Old Testament. It names a town in the hill country of Judah between Jerusalem and Hebron, whose founding lineage the Chronicler traces through Hur and Ephrathah (Joshua 15:58; 1 Chronicles 4:4, 18), and a second place, likely near Gerar, where a band of Simeonites drove out its peaceful, prosperous residents to make room for their flocks in the days of Hezekiah (1 Chronicles 4:39-41). The same name also belongs to a man in the genealogy of Benjamin connected to the family of Saul (1 Chronicles 8:31; 9:37).

entries.title: Gedor
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and nothing else is recorded.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gedor (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him twice, and he is a man from the united kingdom.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gehazi (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Elisha's servant. When Elisha turned down Naaman's payment, Gehazi ran after the general and lied his way into silver and clothes, and Elisha, who knew without being there, gave him Naaman's leprosy for good.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Gehazi was Elisha's servant, and after Elisha refused any payment from the healed general Naaman, Gehazi secretly chased Naaman down and lied to get silver and clothing for himself. Elisha, who somehow knew exactly what Gehazi had done even though he wasn't there, transferred Naaman's leprosy onto Gehazi and his descendants forever as punishment for the deception.

entries.title: Geliloth (Gilgal)
entries.summary: On Benjamin's border, near the Jordan. It is generally taken as another name for the Gilgal of Joshua 15:7, though which Gilgal is uncertain, since the name just means circles.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Geliloth marked a point on the border of the tribal territory of Benjamin, near the Jordan (Joshua 18:17). It is generally taken as another name for Gilgal in the parallel description of Judah's border at Joshua 15:7, though whether it refers to the well-known Gilgal near Jericho or a different site of the same common name (meaning "circles") is uncertain.

entries.title: Gemalli (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Ammiel's father, and Ammiel was Dan's spy; Numbers 13:12 is the only place Gemalli appears.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Father of Ammiel, the representative of the tribe of Dan among the twelve spies Moses sent to scout Canaan (Numbers 13:12).

entries.title: Gemariah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A royal scribe, and Baruch read Jeremiah's scroll aloud from his chamber; later his son tried and failed to stop King Jehoiakim burning it.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Gemariah was a royal scribe in whose chamber Baruch read Jeremiah's scroll of prophecies aloud, and Gemariah's son later tried unsuccessfully to stop King Jehoiakim from burning it.

entries.title: Gemariah (Priest living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Jeremiah names him once, and he is a priest from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gennesaret
entries.summary: The fertile plain on the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee, and by extension the lake itself, which the Old Testament calls Chinnereth. Josephus said almost every kind of tree and crop grew there most of the year. In 1986 a first-century fishing boat came out of the mud near Kibbutz Ginosar on that shore.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Gennesaret refers both to a fertile plain on the northwestern shore of the Sea of Galilee and, by extension, to the lake itself, also called the Sea of Galilee or Chinnereth in the Old Testament (Matthew 14:34; Mark 6:53; Luke 5:1). The first-century historian Josephus praised the plain's exceptional fertility, describing it as supporting nearly every kind of tree and crop through most of the year. A first-century fishing boat recovered from the mud near Kibbutz Ginosar on the lakeshore in 1986 has illustrated the fishing economy the Gospels describe in this same area.

entries.title: Gentile (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Anyone who is not Jewish. The Greek word behind it means nation or people, and Paul's gospel turns on Gentiles being grafted into God's covenant people without first becoming Jews, the position defended at the Jerusalem council in Acts 15.
entries.books: John, Acts, Romans, 1 Corinthians, Galatians, Colossians
entries.label: 6 books
entries.dictNote: Gentile is the English rendering of a Greek word meaning "nation" or "people," used throughout the New Testament for anyone who is not Jewish. Paul's letters make the status of Gentiles central to his gospel, arguing that through Christ they are grafted into God's covenant people alongside Jews without first needing to become Jews themselves, a position defended at the Jerusalem council in Acts 15.

entries.title: Genubath (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: He was born to the Edomite prince Hadad and the sister of Tahpenes, Pharaoh's wife, and grew up in Pharaoh's own house with the royal children.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Son of the Edomite prince Hadad and an Egyptian princess, sister of Pharaoh's wife Tahpenes; he was raised in Pharaoh's own household alongside the royal children (1 Kings 11:20).

entries.title: Gera (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: The name ran in the Benjamite tribe. This Gera is in Genesis 46:21 and in 1 Chronicles 8:5, and Judges 3:15 makes a Gera the father of Ehud, the left-handed judge.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Gera (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: One of 4 men called Gera. This one is a man from the wilderness years, named once in 1 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gera (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: He is only ever named as Shimei's father, and Shimei is the Benjamite who cursed David during Absalom's rebellion.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Gera was a common Benjamite name, the father of both Ehud, the left-handed judge, and Shimei, the man who cursed David during Absalom's rebellion.

witness.excerpt: And Shimei, the son of Gera, came with a thousand men, which he brought with him out of the tribe of Benjamin; and Ziba, the freed-man of Saul, with his sons, fifteen in number, and with his twenty servants.

There is also Shimei the son of Gera, of the tribe of Benjamin, who, after he had cast many reproaches upon me, when, in my flight, I was going to Mahanaim, met me at Jordan, and received assurances that he should then suffer nothing.
And the sons of Benjamin: Bela and Becher, and Ashbel, Gera, and Naaman, and Ehi, and Rosh, and Muppim, and Huppim, and Ard--eleven.

There was a young man of the tribe of Benjamin, whose name was Ehud , the son of Gera: a man of very great courage in bold undertakings; and of a very strong body, fit for hard labour: but best skilled in using his left hand; in which was his whole strength: and he also dwelt at Jericho.

entries.title: Gera (Man living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: A man from the years before the monarchy, and 1 Chronicles is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gerar
entries.summary: Abraham and Isaac both stayed in this Philistine town in the Negev under a king called Abimelech, and both passed their wives off as sisters out of fear. Isaac reaped a hundredfold there and dug out his father's wells again until quarrels over water moved him on toward Beersheba. Tel Haror is a leading candidate for the site.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Gerar was a Philistine town and its surrounding district in the Negev, ruled by a king named Abimelech, where both Abraham and later Isaac sojourned and both, in turn, misrepresented their wives as sisters out of fear. Isaac prospered greatly at Gerar, reaping a hundredfold harvest and reopening wells his father had dug, before disputes over water led him to move on toward Beersheba. Excavations at Tel Haror in the western Negev, a leading candidate for the site, have uncovered a substantial Middle Bronze Age fortified city consistent with the patriarchal setting.

witness.excerpt: Abraham now removed to Gerar of Palestine, leading Sarah along with him, under the notion of his sister: using the like dissimulation that he had used before, and this out of fear.
When there was a famine in the land, Isaac resolved to go into Egypt: the land there being good: but he went to Gerar as God commanded him.
And in this month Abraham moved from Hebron, and departed and dwelt between Kadesh and Shur in the mountains  of Gerar.
And the famine was over the land, and Isaac departed to go down into Egypt in the second year of this week, and went to the king of the Philistines to Gerar, unto Abimelech.

God gave him a signal of victory, and joining battle cheerfully on account of what God had foretold about it, he slew a great many of the Ethiopians; and when he had put them to flight, he pursued them to the country of Gerar; and when they left off killing their enemies, they betook themselves to spoiling them, (for the city Gerar was already taken,) and to spoiling their camp, so that they carried off much gold, and much silver, and a grea

entries.title: Gergesene
entries.summary: They lived east of the Sea of Galilee, where Jesus sent a legion of demons out of a tormented man and into a herd of pigs that ran into the water and drowned. The same people are also called Gadarenes.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: The Gergesenes, also called Gadarenes, were the inhabitants of a region east of the Sea of Galilee where Jesus cast a legion of demons out of a tormented man and into a herd of pigs that then rushed into the water and drowned.

entries.title: Gerizim
entries.summary: Opposite Mount Ebal, near Shechem. Six tribes stood on Gerizim to speak the blessings while six on Ebal spoke the curses, as Moses had ordered and Joshua carried out. The Samaritans later built a temple on top as a rival to Jerusalem, which is what the Samaritan woman is asking Jesus about in John 4:20.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Mount Gerizim rises opposite Mount Ebal near Shechem in Samaria, and Moses commanded that after entering Canaan, six tribes should stand on its slopes to pronounce blessings for obedience while six tribes on Ebal pronounced curses, a ceremony Joshua carried out at the site (Deuteronomy 27:12; Joshua 8:33). Centuries later the Samaritans built their own temple on Gerizim as a rival to Jerusalem's, the practice behind the Samaritan woman's question to Jesus about the proper mountain of worship in John 4:20. Archaeological excavations on the summit have uncovered the remains of that Samaritan sacred precinct, including a large temple platform dated to the Persian or early Hellenistic period, confirming the site's long use as a rival cultic center to Jerusalem.

witness.excerpt: , and when they had destroyed the whole multitude of its inhabitants, as they ought to do, they should erect an altar that should face the rising sun; not far from the city of Shechem; between the two mountains, that of Gerizim situate on the right hand; and that called Ebal on the left: and that the army should be so divided, that six tribes should stand upon each of the two mountains; and with them the Levites, and the Priests.

entries.title: Gershom
entries.summary: These verses are the census ones, Genesis 46:11, Exodus 6:16 and Numbers 3 and 4, where his family is counted and given its share of the tabernacle work. The note filed with them describes Moses's firstborn, born in Midian and named for a stranger there, who is a different man.
entries.label: 5 books
entries.dictNote: Gershom was Moses's firstborn son, born during Moses's exile in Midian, and his name, meaning a stranger there, reflects Moses's own description of himself as a foreigner in a foreign land.

entries.title: Gershon (Levite living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Levi's eldest son. His descendants carried the tabernacle's coverings, curtains and hangings by cart through the wilderness. Exodus 2:22 and 18:3 carry the same name but belong to a different man.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Gershon was Levi's eldest son, and his descendants were assigned responsibility for the tabernacle's coverings, curtains, and hangings, transported by cart during Israel's wilderness travels.

witness.excerpt: Levi and his sons; and these are the names of his sons: Gershon, and Kohath, and Merari--four.

entries.title: Geshan (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Caleb's line, through his son Jahdai, in the genealogy of Judah.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A descendant of Caleb through his son Jahdai, listed in the genealogy of Judah (1 Chronicles 2:47).

entries.title: Geshem (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: An Arab official. With Sanballat and Tobiah he mocked Nehemiah and tried to stop the walls of Jerusalem going back up.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Geshem was an Arab official who joined Sanballat and Tobiah in opposing and mocking Nehemiah's rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls.

entries.title: Geshur
entries.summary: It was a small Aramean kingdom northeast of Galilee, and Absalom ran there after murdering his brother Amnon and stayed three years under his grandfather the king.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Geshur was a small Aramean kingdom northeast of Galilee where Absalom fled and lived for three years after murdering his brother Amnon, protected there by his grandfather, the local king.

witness.excerpt:
However, their were tears on both sides; they lamenting their brother who was killed, and the king lamenting his son, who was killed also; but Absalom fled to Geshur, to his grandfather by his mother's side, who was king of that country, and he remained with him three whole years.
4.

The eldest was by Ahinoam, and he was called Arenon; the second was Daniel, by his wife Abigail; the name of the third was Absalom, by Maacah, the daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur; the fourth he named Adonijah, by his wife Haggith; the fifth was Shephatiah, by Abital; the sixth he called Ithream, by Eglah.

entries.title: Geshuri
entries.summary: David married Maacah, daughter of Talmai, the king of Geshur, and so these people were Absalom's family on his mother's side. Their small Aramean kingdom lay east of the Sea of Galilee.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Geshurites were the people of Geshur, a small Aramean kingdom east of the Sea of Galilee. David married Maacah, daughter of Geshur's king Talmai, and their son Absalom fled to his grandfather's court there after murdering his half brother Amnon.

witness.excerpt: 19 And now he privately attacked those Geshurites and Amalekites that were neighbours to the Philistines; and laid waste their countrey; and took much prey of their beasts and camels; and then returned home.

entries.title: Gether (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: A son of Aram in Genesis 10:23, most likely standing for an Aramean clan rather than one ancestor, and no later trace of it has been found.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Gether is listed in the Table of Nations as one of the sons of Aram (Gen. 10:23; 1 Chr. 1:17). As with the other names in this list, it most likely stands for an Aramean clan or tribal group rather than a single ancestor, and no later trace of a people by this name has been identified.

entries.title: Gethsemane
entries.summary: An olive grove at the foot of the Mount of Olives, across the Kidron Valley from Jerusalem, where Jesus often went with his disciples and where he prayed in anguish the night he was arrested. The garden has been honoured roughly there since at least the fourth century. The olive trees standing now date to the medieval period.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Gethsemane was not a person but an olive grove at the foot of the Mount of Olives, just across the Kidron Valley from Jerusalem, where Jesus often withdrew with his disciples and where he agonized in prayer the night he was betrayed and arrested (Matthew 26:36-46; John 18:1-2). The garden has been venerated at roughly this location since at least the fourth century, though the olive trees standing there today have been radiocarbon-dated to the medieval period rather than to the first century.

entries.title: Geuel (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Machi's son, the spy for Gad when Moses sent twelve men into Canaan.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Son of Machi, chosen to represent the tribe of Gad among the twelve spies Moses sent into Canaan (Numbers 13:15).

entries.title: Gezrites (People, perhaps from Girzit)
entries.summary: David raided them from Ziklag along with the Geshurites and Amalekites. Most read the name as Girzites, an otherwise unknown desert tribe in the Negev toward Egypt, and not the people of Gezer.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Gezrites, named alongside the Geshurites and Amalekites as targets of David's raids while he lived among the Philistines at Ziklag, are usually read as the Girzites, an otherwise unknown desert tribe in the Negev toward Egypt, rather than the inhabitants of the well-known city of Gezer in central Canaan.

entries.title: Giah
entries.summary: It exists in the record only to locate the hill of Ammah, where Joab gave up chasing Abner in the war between the houses of David and Saul. Its site has never been identified.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Giah is named only to fix the location of the hill of Ammah, near which Joab called off his pursuit of Abner during the civil war between the houses of David and Saul (2 Samuel 2:24-28). Nothing more is known of it beyond this one topographical note, and its site has never been identified.

entries.title: Gibbar (Gibeon)
entries.summary: The family came back from Babylon with Zerubbabel, ninety-five of them. Nehemiah 7:25 gives the name as Gibeon.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Gibbar's descendants numbered ninety-five among the family heads who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:20); the parallel list in Nehemiah 7:25 gives the family name as Gibeon instead.

entries.title: Gibbethon
entries.summary: In Dan's territory and assigned to the Kohath family, but the Philistines held it most of the time. Nadab was besieging it when his officer Baasha killed him and took the throne. A generation later Elah went the same way while his army was at the same city again.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Gibbethon was a Philistine city in Dan's territory that had been assigned to the Levite family of Kohath (Joshua 19:44; 21:23), though it evidently remained under Philistine control for much of Israel's history. King Nadab of Israel was besieging it when his own officer Baasha assassinated him and seized the throne (1 Kings 15:27), and a generation later King Elah met the same fate while his army was again besieging the city (1 Kings 16:15-17).

witness.excerpt: In these two years he made an expedition against Gibbethon, a city of the Philistines, and continued the siege in order to take it; but he was conspired against while he was there by a friend of his, whose name was Baasha, the son of Ahijah, and was slain; which Baasha took the

entries.title: Gibeah (Woman or town of the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Not Saul's Gibeah in Benjamin. This one is a Judahite settlement in 1 Chronicles 2:49, founded by a descendant of Caleb, and nothing more is recorded about it.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: This entity's one canonical reference, 1 Chronicles 2:49, names Gibea as a Judahite clan or settlement founded by a descendant of Caleb, in the genealogical style where Chronicles calls a clan's founder "father of" the town he settled. It should not be confused with the far better known Gibeah of Benjamin, Saul's hometown and later royal residence, site of the outrage against a Levite's concubine that nearly destroyed the tribe of Benjamin (Judges 19-20); that is a different town in a different tribal territory, even though both carry the common Hebrew word for "hill." Nothing more is recorded about this Judahite Gibea, and its site is unidentified.

witness.excerpt: Saul also went away to Gibeah, where he was born; and many good men there were who paid him the respect that was due to him: but the greater part were ill men, who despised him, and derided the others: who neither did bring him presents; nor did the
Accordingly he obtained his purpose, and came to Gibeah, a city of the tribe of Benjamin, when it was just dark.

Now Saul being sensible of the miserable condition he had brought himself into; and that he had made God to be his enemy; he went up to his royal palace at Gibeah: which name denotes an Hill : and after that day he came no more into the presence of the Prophet.

entries.title: Gibeathite (Gibeah)
entries.summary: Benjaminite archers and slingers from Gibeah, Saul's own town, who went over to David at Ziklag while he was still an outlaw.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Gibeathite marks a family of Benjaminite archers and slingers, kinsmen of Saul who nonetheless joined David while he was still an outlaw at Ziklag, as natives of Gibeah, Saul's own hometown.

entries.title: Gibeon
entries.summary: They tricked Joshua into a treaty by dressing as travellers from far away, the Hivites of this city northwest of Jerusalem, and so they lived but served at Israel's sanctuary. The tabernacle stood at Gibeon for years, and Solomon had his dream there. At el-Jib dozens of jar handles stamped with the name have settled where it was.
entries.books: Joshua, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Nehemiah, Isaiah, Jeremiah
entries.label: 8 books
entries.dictNote: Gibeon was a major Hivite city northwest of Jerusalem whose inhabitants tricked Joshua into a peace treaty by posing as distant travelers, a ruse that spared them destruction but bound them to servitude in Israel's sanctuary. The city later hosted the tabernacle for years before Solomon built the temple, and it was there that Solomon offered sacrifices and received his famous dream. It was also the scene of a battle between the forces of David and Ish-bosheth. Excavations at el-Jib uncovered dozens of jar handles stamped with the name “Gibeon” in ancient Hebrew script, confirming the site's identification beyond doubt.

witness.excerpt: Now when he met Abner at a certain fountain, in the city of Gibeon, he prepared to fight.

So they stood in the midst of the people, and said that they were sent by the people of Gibeon, and of the circumjacent cities, which were very remote from the land where they now were; to make such a league of friendship with them, and this on such conditions as were customary among their forefathers.

entries.title: Gibeonite
entries.summary: Saul broke the old treaty and killed some of them. Under David a famine followed, and it ended only when seven of Saul's descendants were handed over to the Gibeonites for execution.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Gibeonites were the inhabitants of Gibeon, a Hivite city that secured a peace treaty with Israel in Joshua 9 by disguising themselves as travelers from a distant land. Centuries later Saul violated that treaty by killing some Gibeonites, and the resulting famine under David was only resolved by handing over seven of Saul's descendants for execution. Excavations at el-Jib, identified with biblical Gibeon, have turned up wine jar handles inscribed with the city's name, confirming the site.

entries.title: Giddalti (Levite living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of Heman's sons, and Heman was a Levite musician in David's court. Giddalti led one of the twenty-four divisions of temple musicians.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Giddalti was one of the sons of Heman, a Levite musician in David's court. He headed one of the twenty-four divisions of temple musicians organized under David to lead worship with song and instruments (1 Chronicles 25:4, 29).

entries.title: Giddel (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Head of a family of temple servants, the Nethinim, in the lists of exiles coming home.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Giddel (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Head of a family among the temple servants, and separately among Solomon's servants, both counted in the return lists.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Giddel was the head of a family among the temple servants and, separately, among Solomon's servants, listed together among the returning exiles.

entries.title: Gideon (Judge living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: An angel found him threshing wheat in a winepress, hiding it from the Midianites, and called him a mighty man of valour. Gideon asked for the fleece to be wet and then dry before he believed it. God cut his army from thirty-two thousand to three hundred, and they took the Midianite camp at night with torches, trumpets and empty jars.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Gideon was threshing wheat in a winepress to hide it from raiding Midianites when an angel found him and called him a mighty man of valor, a title Gideon immediately questioned given that his clan was the weakest in Manasseh and he was the least in his father's house. He asked God to prove the call was real with the sign of a fleece left out overnight, wet with dew while the ground stayed dry and then dry while the ground stayed wet, and God still whittled his army down from thirty-two thousand men to three hundred before letting him attack the Midianite camp with torches, trumpets, and empty jars in the middle of the night.

witness.excerpt: That the Judges who succeeded Gideon made war with the adjoining nations for a long time.
And these things have been atchieved under the conduct of Jephtha and Gideon.

entries.title: Gideoni (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Abidan was Benjamin's leader in the wilderness census, and Gideoni is only ever named as his father.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Gideoni was the father of Abidan, the tribal leader of Benjamin during the wilderness census.

entries.title: Gidom
entries.summary: Judges 20:45 names it once, as a point on the road where the retreating Benjamite army was cut down. It lay somewhere between Gibeah and the rock of Rimmon, and nobody knows exactly where.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Gidom, a site in Benjamite territory named only in Judges 20:45, marking a point along the road where the retreating Benjamite army was cut down during Israel's civil war. Its exact location between Gibeah and the rock of Rimmon is not known.

entries.title: Gihon
entries.summary: Two waters carry the name. One is a river out of Eden that circles Cush and has never been matched to a known river. The other is Jerusalem's only natural spring, in the Kidron Valley, which Hezekiah ran underground into the city before Sennacherib's siege, and the tunnel can still be walked.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Gihon is a name shared by two waters in the Old Testament. It is listed as one of the four rivers flowing out of Eden, encircling the land of Cush (Genesis 2:13), a description scholars have never matched with confidence to a known river. It is also the name of Jerusalem's only natural spring, in the Kidron Valley, whose water Hezekiah rerouted underground into the city ahead of Sennacherib's siege (2 Chronicles 32:30); the resulting tunnel is still walkable today, and the Siloam Inscription carved near its outlet by Hezekiah's workmen is one of the longest surviving inscriptions from ancient Judah.

witness.excerpt: And the name of the second river is Gihon; this is that which encircles the whole land of Ethiopia.

And it turneth from here towards the south towards the mouth of the great sea  on the shore of (its) waters, and it extendeth to the west to ‘Afrâ  and it extendeth till it reacheth the waters of the river Gihon, and to the south of the waters of Gihon,  to the banks of this river.

entries.title: Gilalai (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: In the procession at the dedication of Nehemiah's walls he was one of the priests' sons playing instruments. Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of the priests' sons who played musical instruments in the procession at the dedication of Jerusalem's rebuilt walls under Nehemiah (Neh. 12:36). Nothing further is recorded about him.

entries.title: Gilboa
entries.summary: Saul died on these hills above the Jezreel Valley. The Philistines broke his army, three of his sons fell, Jonathan among them, and Saul, badly wounded, took his own life. David's lament curses Gilboa never to have dew or rain.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Mount Gilboa is a low mountain range bordering the Jezreel Valley where the Philistines defeated Saul's army; three of Saul's sons, including Jonathan, were killed there, and Saul himself, badly wounded, took his own life rather than be captured. David's lament over Saul and Jonathan, "how the mighty have fallen," opens by cursing Gilboa's slopes to remain barren of dew and rain.

witness.excerpt: And when he was come to a certain mountain called Gilboa , he pitched his camp over against the enemy.

entries.title: Gilead
entries.summary: Hill country east of the Jordan, split by the Jabbok between Og in the north and Sihon in the south before the conquest. Gad, Reuben and half of Manasseh got it, and its rough ground made it a refuge for Jacob running from Laban and David running from Absalom. Jeremiah's question about balm in Gilead comes from its trade in balm and spices.
entries.books: Genesis, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, Psalm, Song of Solomon, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Hosea, Amos, Obadiah, Micah, Zechariah
entries.label: 19 books
entries.dictNote: Gilead was the mountainous region east of the Jordan, bounded by Bashan to the north and Moab and Ammon to the south, split by the Jabbok river into a northern half ruled by Og and a southern half ruled by Sihon before Israel's conquest. It was allotted to Gad, Reuben, and half of Manasseh, and its rugged terrain made it a natural refuge, most famously for Jacob fleeing Laban and later for David fleeing Absalom. Its forests and pastures were known for balm and spices, giving rise to Jeremiah's question, “Is there no balm in Gilead?”

Whence that hill is called Gilead, and from thence they call that land, The land of Gilead at this day.
