entries.title: Gilead (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A man from the divided-kingdom years, and 1 Chronicles is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gilead (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: The man, not the region. Numbers 26 and Joshua 17 put him in Manasseh's family, and Chronicles lists him there again.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Gilead (Man living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 4 men called Gilead. This one is a man from the years before the monarchy, named twice in Judges.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gileadite
entries.summary: Someone from Gilead, east of the Jordan, or of the clan named after Machir's son. Jephthah is the best known, the judge who beat the Ammonites and made the rash vow about his daughter.
entries.books: Numbers, Judges, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, Ezra, Nehemiah
entries.label: 7 books
entries.dictNote: Gileadite designates someone from Gilead, the hill country east of the Jordan, and names both a Manassite clan descended from Machir's son Gilead and individuals from that region, most notably Jephthah, the judge who defeated the Ammonites and later fulfilled a rash vow involving his own daughter.

witness.excerpt: These were Barzillai the Gileadite, and Siphar the ruler among the Ammonites, and Machir the principal man of Gilead; and these furnished him with plentiful provisions for himself and his followers, insomuch that they wanted no beds nor blankets for them
Now it was that Jair the Gileadite, of the tribe of Manasseh, took the government.

But David desired Barzillai the Gileadite, that great and good man, and one that had made a plentiful provision for him at Mahanaim, and had conducted him as far as Jordan, to accompany him to Jerusalem, for he promised to treat him in his old age with all mann

I also commit to thee the son of Barzillai the Gileadite, whom, in order to gratify me, thou shalt have in great honor, and take great care of; for we have not done good to him first, but we only repay that debt which we owe to his father for what he did to me in my flight.

entries.title: Gilgal
entries.summary: Israel's first camp after crossing the Jordan. The people were circumcised there and kept their first Passover in the land, and later Samuel judged at Gilgal and Saul was confirmed as king there.
entries.books: Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, Hosea, Amos, Micah
entries.label: 7 books
entries.dictNote: Gilgal was Israel's first camp in the promised land after crossing the Jordan, the site where the nation was circumcised and celebrated its first Passover in Canaan, and later a religious center where Samuel judged and Saul was confirmed as king.

witness.excerpt: And when he had numred them in Gilgal, he found them to be about four hundred thousand of the Israelites: besides the tribe of Judah.
Thou shalt also come when I send for thee to Gilgal; that we may offer thank-offerings to God for these blessings.” When Samuel had said this, and foretold these things, he sent the young man away.
Now the place where Joshua pitched his camp was called Gilgal : which denotes liberty.

When Saul, the King of the Hebrews, was informed of this, he went down to the city Gilgal, and made proclamation over all the countrey, that they should try to regain their liberty; and called them to the war against the Philistines: diminishing their forces, and despising them, as not very considerable; and

entries.title: Gilgal
entries.summary: Named once, in 2 Kings, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Giloh
entries.summary: Ahithophel came from Giloh, in Judah's hill country southwest of Hebron. When Absalom took Hushai's advice over his, he went home to Giloh and hanged himself.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Giloh was a town in the hill country of Judah southwest of Hebron (Josh. 15:51), remembered as the home of Ahithophel, David's counselor who defected to Absalom's rebellion (2 Sam. 15:12). When his advice was rejected in favor of Hushai's, Ahithophel returned to Giloh and hanged himself (2 Sam. 17:23).

entries.title: Gilonite (Giloh)
entries.summary: It is what Ahithophel is called, since he came from Giloh. He was David's trusted counsellor, then Absalom's, and he hanged himself when his advice was turned down.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Gilonite identifies Ahithophel, David's trusted counselor, as being from Giloh, a town in the Judean hill country. Ahithophel defected to Absalom's rebellion and gave him shrewd advice, but when it was rejected in favor of Hushai's counsel, he went home and hanged himself.

witness.excerpt: Among them came Ahithophel the Gilonite, a counsellor of David's, and two hundred men out of Jerusalem itself, who knew not his intentions, but were sent for as to a sacrifice.

entries.title: Gimzo
entries.summary: The Philistines took it and its villages in the reign of Ahaz. It was a lowland town known for sycamores, and the name survives in Jimzu, a village southeast of Lydda.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Gimzo was a town in the Judean lowlands noted for its sycamore trees, seized along with its surrounding villages by the Philistines during the reign of the unfaithful King Ahaz (2 Chronicles 28:18). It survives in the name of the modern village Jimzu, southeast of Lydda.

entries.title: Ginath (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: He is named as Tibni's father, and for four years Tibni's supporters fought Omri for the throne of Israel until Omri won.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Ginath was the father of Tibni, the man whose supporters contended for the throne of Israel against Omri for four years before Omri prevailed (1 Kings 16:21-22).

entries.title: Ginnetho (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A priest who came back from Babylon with Zerubbabel, and his family is one of the priestly houses Nehemiah lists.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Ginnethoi was a priest who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel, and his family is listed among the priestly houses in Nehemiah.

entries.title: Girgashite (People, perhaps from Girgas)
entries.summary: Descended from Canaan in Genesis 10, and one of the peoples on the list Israel was to drive out. Where exactly they lived is unclear, though they are generally placed in the central hill country.
entries.label: 5 books
entries.dictNote: Girgashites were among the Canaanite peoples descended from Canaan in Genesis 10 and are regularly listed among the nations Israel was to dispossess. Their exact territory is not clearly identified, though they are generally placed somewhere in the central hill country of western Palestine.

entries.title: Gispa (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: With Ziha he was over the Nethinim, the temple servants living on the hill of Ophel after the return. Nothing more is known of him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Gispa was, along with Ziha, one of the overseers of the Nethinim, the temple servants who lived on the hill of Ophel in Jerusalem after the return from exile, as recorded in Nehemiah 11:21. The Nethinim performed menial temple duties and are traditionally traced back to Gibeonites and war captives assigned to that service in earlier generations. Nothing more is known of Gispa beyond this administrative role.

entries.title: Gittaim
entries.summary: The people of Beeroth fled to Gittaim, probably a Benjamin town, and after the exile Benjaminite families settled it again.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Gittaim was a town, probably in Benjamin, to which the people of Beeroth fled after the assassins of Ish-bosheth were traced there (2 Samuel 4:2-3). Like Beeroth itself, it was resettled by Benjaminite families after the Babylonian exile (Nehemiah 11:33).

entries.title: Gittite (Gath)
entries.summary: A man from Gath. Obed-edom the Gittite kept the ark in his house before David brought it up to Jerusalem, and Ittai the Gittite brought his foreign troops to David's side when Absalom rebelled.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Gittite means a native of Gath, one of the five major Philistine cities. Obed-edom the Gittite kept the ark of the covenant in his house before David brought it to Jerusalem, and Ittai the Gittite led a contingent of loyal foreign troops who stood by David when Absalom rebelled.

entries.title: Gittith (A musical term)
entries.summary: Three psalms carry it in their heading. It may be a tune, an instrument or a style, and the name points at Gath.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Gittith is a musical or instrumental term appearing in the superscriptions of three psalms, possibly referring to a tune, instrument, or style associated with the Philistine city of Gath, rather than the name of a person.

entries.title: Gizonite (People, perhaps from Gizon)
entries.summary: Hashem, whose sons were among David's mighty men, came from Gizoh, a place in Judah's hill country otherwise unknown. In 2 Samuel 23:32 the same family is listed as Jashen.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Gizonite marks Hashem, whose sons appear among David's mighty men, as a native of Gizoh, a place otherwise unknown in the hill country of Judah; the parallel account in 2 Samuel 23:32 lists the same family under the name Jashen.

entries.title: Goath (Goah)
entries.summary: The hill Gareb to Goath is how far Jeremiah's measuring line runs for the rebuilt city, and where Goath was is unknown.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A place near Jerusalem named only in Jeremiah's vision of the city's future rebuilding, where the measuring line would run out from the hill Gareb to Goath (Jer. 31:39). Its exact location is unknown.

entries.title: Gob (Gezer)
entries.summary: Two fights with Philistine champions happened here. Sibbecai killed Saph, and Elhanan killed a brother of Goliath. Chronicles calls the place Gezer, and whether that is a copying difference or a nearby site is unclear.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Gob was the site of two battles between David's men and Philistine champions descended from the giants of Gath, in which Sibbecai killed Saph and Elhanan killed a brother of Goliath (2 Sam. 21:18-19). The parallel account in Chronicles calls the location Gezer instead (1 Chr. 20:4), and it is unclear whether this reflects a scribal variation or two nearby sites known by different names.

entries.title: God (The Deity)
entries.summary: The Bible never argues that he exists; it assumes it, and Psalm 14:1 calls the man who denies it a fool. The Hebrew is El, from a word meaning strong, or Eloah, far more often in the plural Elohim. The personal name is the four Hebrew letters YHWH, printed LORD in small capitals in most English Bibles; Jehovah is a later hybrid of those letters with the vowels of another word.
entries.books: Genesis, Exodus, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, Psalm, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Amos, Obadiah, Micah, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Zechariah
entries.label: 17 books
entries.dictNote: (A.S. and Dutch God; Dan. Gud; Ger. Gott), the name of the Divine Being. It is the rendering (1) of the Hebrew ’El, from a word meaning to be strong; (2) of ’Eloah_, plural _’Elohim. The singular form, Eloah, is used only in poetry. The plural form is more commonly used in all parts of the Bible, The Hebrew word Jehovah (q.v.), the only other word generally employed to denote the Supreme Being, is uniformly rendered in the Authorized Version by “LORD,” printed in small capitals. The existence of God is taken for granted in the Bible. There is nowhere any argument to prove it. He who disbelieves this truth is spoken of as one devoid of understanding (Ps. 14:1). The arguments generally adduced by theologians in proof of the being of God are: (1.) The a priori argument, which is the testimony afforded by reason. (2.) The a posteriori argument, by which we proceed logically from the facts of experience to causes. These arguments are, (a) The cosmological, by which it is proved that there must be a First Cause of all things, for every effect must have a cause. (b) The teleological, or the argument from design. We see everywhere the operations of an intelligent Cause in nature. (c) The moral argument, called also the anthropological argument, based on the moral consciousness and the history of mankind, which exhibits a moral order and purpose which can only be explained on the supposition of the existence of God. Conscience and human history testify that “verily there is a God that judgeth in the earth.” The attributes of God are set forth in order by Moses in Ex. 34:6, 7. (see also Deut. 6:4; 10:17; Num. 16:22; Ex. 15:11; 33:19; Isa. 44:6; Hab. 3:6; Ps. 102:26; Job 34:12.) They are also systematically classified in Rev. 5:12 and 7:12. God’s attributes are spoken of by some as absolute, i.e., such as belong to his essence as Jehovah, Jah, etc.; and relative, i.e., such as are ascribed to him with relation to his creatures. Others distinguish them into communicable, i.e., those which can be imparted in degree to his creatures: goodness, holiness, wisdom, etc.; and incommunicable, which cannot be so imparted: independence, immutability, immensity, and eternity. They are by some also divided into natural attributes, eternity, immensity, etc.; and moral, holiness, goodness, etc.

witness.excerpt: God also commanded them to send colonies abroad, for the through peopling of the earth; that they might not raise seditions among themselves, but might cultivate a great part of the earth, and enjoy its fruits after a plent
God confound thee, thou vile wretch; do not thou touch me, till thou hast cleared thyself of these crimes that are charged upon thee.
But God put a stop to his unjust inclinations, by sending upon him a distemper, and a sedition against his government.

entries.title: Gog
entries.summary: Ezekiel's enemy from the land of Magog, leading a huge coalition against restored Israel, and God himself destroys him. Revelation uses the name again for the nations gathered in a last rebellion.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Gog is a mysterious future enemy in Ezekiel's prophecy, leader of a massive coalition from the land of Magog that invades restored Israel and is destroyed by God's direct intervention, and the same name reappears symbolically in Revelation representing the nations gathered for a final rebellion against God.

entries.title: Gog (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the wilderness years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Golan
entries.summary: One of the three cities of refuge east of the Jordan, in Bashan, where someone who had killed by accident could run from revenge. It went to the Gershonite Levites and later gave its name to the region, which is why there are Golan Heights today. The exact site is not known.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Golan was a city in Bashan, east of the Sea of Galilee, designated one of Israel's three cities of refuge east of the Jordan, where a person who killed someone accidentally could flee for protection from revenge (Deuteronomy 4:43; Joshua 20:8). It was given to the Gershonite Levites and later gave its name to the surrounding region of Gaulanitis, the origin of the modern name Golan Heights. Its precise site has not been conclusively identified.

witness.excerpt: However, when he fought with Obodas, king of the Arabians, who had laid an ambush for him near Golan, and a plot against him, he lost his entire army, which was crowded together in a deep valley, and broken to pieces by the multitude of camels.
Now the cities which were set apart for this flight were these: Bezer , at the borders of Arabia; Ramoth , of the land of Gilead; and Golan , in the land of Bashan.

entries.title: Golgotha
entries.summary: The name is Aramaic for place of a skull, Calvary in Latin, where Jesus was crucified outside Jerusalem's walls. The Church of the Holy Sepulchre and the Garden Tomb both have their advocates, and neither can be confirmed.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Golgotha, meaning “place of a skull” in Aramaic, was the site outside Jerusalem's walls where Jesus was crucified, known by its Latin equivalent, Calvary (Matthew 27:33; Mark 15:22; John 19:17). All four Gospels place it near a public road and close to a garden containing a tomb, yet outside the city gate, details that complicate several traditional identifications of the site. Its exact location remains debated; the traditional site under the Church of the Holy Sepulchre and the rocky knoll known as the Garden Tomb both have modern advocates, though neither can be confirmed with certainty.

entries.title: Goliath (Giant living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: The Philistine champion from Gath whom the young David killed in the valley of Elah. The traditional Hebrew text makes him over nine feet, while the Dead Sea Scrolls and the earliest Greek give about six foot nine. One later passage credits Elhanan, and Chronicles makes Elhanan's man Goliath's brother.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Goliath was a Philistine champion from Gath, over nine feet tall by the traditional Hebrew text, though the Dead Sea Scrolls and the earliest Greek translation give a shorter reading of about six foot nine, which is why some modern translations describe him as closer to seven feet. He came from a family of giants that included his brothers Ishbi-benob and Saph, both killed later by David's men. His duel with the young David in the valley of Elah is the single scene that defines him in Scripture, and one later passage even credits a different soldier, Elhanan, with killing him, though Chronicles resolves this by making Elhanan's victim Goliath's brother instead.
entries.dictSource: Tyndale Bible Dictionary; NET Bible translator notes; Logos Factbook (Baker Encyclopedia)

witness.excerpt: And how they were overcome by David ’s slaying Goliath , in a single combat.
The High Priest said that he had no such weapon: but he added, “Here is the sword of Goliath; which, when thou hadst slain the Philistine thou didst dedicate 11 to God.” 2.

entries.title: Gomer (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Genesis 10 makes him a son of Japheth, and the name stands for his descendants too, which is how Ezekiel 38:6 can list Gomer as a nation. Hosea's wife has the same name and is a different person.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Gomer was the promiscuous woman God commanded the prophet Hosea to marry as a living illustration of Israel's unfaithfulness, and Hosea's persistent love and eventual repurchase of Gomer after she left him for other men became the book's central picture of God's relentless pursuit of an unfaithful people.

witness.excerpt: For Gomer founded those whom the Greeks now call Galatians [Galls], but were then called Gomerites.
The sons of Japheth: Gomer and Magog and Madai and Javan, Tubal and Meshech and Tiras: these are 1324-1372 A.M.

And the first portion came forth for Gomer to the east from the north side to the river Tînâ; and in the north there came forth for Magog all the inner portions of the north until it reacheth to the sea of Mê’at.

entries.title: Gomer (Woman living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Hosea names her once, and she is a woman from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gomorrah
entries.summary: Destroyed with Sodom for its wickedness, and the two became shorthand for a people ripe for judgment, from Moses through Jesus and the apostles. No remains have been confirmed. It is generally placed near the southern basin of the Dead Sea.
entries.books: Genesis, Deuteronomy, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Amos, Zephaniah
entries.label: 6 books
entries.dictNote: Gomorrah was one of the cities of the plain destroyed alongside Sodom for its wickedness, and the pair became the Bible's standard shorthand for a society ripe for divine judgment, invoked from Moses through Jesus and the apostles. No confirmed remains of the city have been found, though it is generally placed, like Sodom, somewhere near the Dead Sea's southern basin.

witness.excerpt: And in this month the Lord executed his judgments on Sodom, and Gomorrah, and Zeboim,  and all the region of the Jordan, and He burned them with fire and brimstone, and destroyed them until this day, even as [lo] I have declared unto thee all their works, that they are wicked and sinners exc

And in this year came Chedorlaomer, king of Elam, and Amraphel, king of Shinar, and Arioch, king of Sêllâsar  and Têrgâl,  king of nations, and slew the king of Gomorrah, and the king of Sodom fled, and many fell through wounds in the vale of Siddim, by the Salt Sea.

entries.title: Gomorrha (Gomorrah)
entries.summary: The Greek spelling, used in the New Testament. Jesus says it will go easier for Sodom and Gomorrha than for a town that turns his messengers away, and Peter and Jude both point to it as proof that God punishes the ungodly.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Gomorrha is the Greek form of Gomorrah, one of the cities of the plain that God destroyed with fire and sulfur alongside Sodom because of their wickedness (Genesis 19:24-25). New Testament writers invoke the memory of its destruction as a warning of certain divine judgment, whether Jesus warning towns that reject his messengers (Matthew 10:15) or Peter and Jude citing it as proof that God punishes the ungodly (2 Peter 2:6; Jude 1:7). Its exact site is unknown, though archaeologists have proposed locations near the southern end of the Dead Sea, including Bab edh-Dhra and Numeira, without any confirmed identification.

entries.title: Goshen
entries.summary: Joseph settled Jacob and the family here, in the eastern Nile delta, and Israel lived and multiplied there until the exodus. Pithom and Rameses were inside it, and it is generally identified with the Wadi Tumilat.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Goshen was the fertile district in northeastern Egypt, along the eastern Nile delta, where Joseph settled his father Jacob and the rest of his family, and where the Israelites lived and multiplied until the exodus. Its cities Pithom and Rameses lay within its borders, and it is generally identified with the Wadi Tumilat. Two lesser places in Canaan's south also bore the name Goshen.

witness.excerpt: And Israel sent Judah before him to his son Joseph to examine  the Land of Goshen, for Joseph had told his brothers that they should come and dwell there that they might be near him.

photo.description: panorama of a plain in Goshen 1

entries.title: Goshen
entries.summary: Not the Goshen in Egypt but a stretch of Canaan's south that Joshua took, along with a town of the same name in the hill country.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gozan
entries.summary: When Assyria took the northern kingdom, it resettled Israelite captives in this region of northern Mesopotamia.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Gozan was a region in northern Mesopotamia where the Assyrians resettled Israelite captives after conquering the northern kingdom.

entries.title: Grecian (Javan)
entries.summary: Greek-speaking Jews, as against Hebrew-speaking ones. They complained that their widows were losing out in the daily food, and that is how Stephen and six others came to be appointed.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Grecian in the New Testament refers to Greek-speaking Jews, distinct from Hebrew-speaking Jews, and a dispute between the two groups over the fair distribution of food to widows led directly to the appointment of Stephen and six others as the first deacons.

witness.excerpt: These retired to Ctesiphon, a Grecian city, and situate near to Seleucia: where the King [of Parthia] lives in winter every year: and where the greatest part of his riches are reposited.
I think it also very just that no Grecian city should be deprived of such rights and privileges, since they were preserved to them under the great Augustus.

Nor did he abstain from the plunder of any of the Grecian temples, and gave order that all the engravings and sculptures, and the rest of the ornaments of the statues and donations therein dedicated, should be brought to him, saying that the best things ought to be set no wher
Whence it is that we may see the greatest part of the Grecian Historiographers mention that river, and the adjoining country, by the apellation of Phut.
However, what Josephus here says more than once, that the Grecian King should smite the Persian twice , is wanting in our other copies.

entries.title: Grecian (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Joel names him once, and he is a man from the patriarchs.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Greece (Javan)
entries.summary: Paul spent three months here near the end of his third journey. The Old Testament calls the region and its people Javan. Athens, Corinth and Philippi were Greek cities where Paul planted churches.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Greece is not a person but the region Paul traveled through and stayed in for three months near the end of his third missionary journey (Acts 20:2-3). In the Old Testament the region and its people are called Javan (Genesis 10:2; Daniel 8:21), and Greek cities such as Athens, Corinth, and Philippi became major centers of Paul's church-planting work in the New Testament.

witness.excerpt: But Titus, by a divine impulse, sailed back from Greece to Syria, and came in great haste to Cesarea, to his father.
Yet, though the latter be rare, they do exist, as Greece testifies with its Seven Wise Men.

While those Athenians, who, in order to preserve the liberty of Greece, did once set fire to their own city; who pursued Xerxes, that proud prince, when he sailed upon the land, and walked upon the sea, and could not be contained by the seas, but conducted such an army as was too broad for
He was so corrupt a man, that out of the desire of getting money, he chose to live under a king, for Greece could not suffice his luxury.

entries.title: Greek (A language)
entries.summary: Here it means the language, not the people. It is one of the three on the sign Pilate had nailed above Jesus.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: This form of “Greek” functions as an adjective describing the Greek language itself. It appears in the sign Pilate had placed above Jesus on the cross, written in Hebrew, Latin, and Greek (John 19:20), and in the Roman tribune's surprised question to Paul in Acts 21:37 asking whether he could speak Greek, since the tribune had assumed Paul was an Egyptian agitator.

witness.excerpt: This, if it be expounded in the Greek language, may signify, Αριθμὸς, a Number : because God hath numbred so long a time for thy life, and for thy government: and that there remains but a small portion.
This calculation from all Josephus’s Greek copies, is exactly right.

entries.title: Greek (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Used of a woman. Mark calls the Syrophoenician mother who begged Jesus to heal her daughter a Greek, meaning a Gentile, not Greek by birth. The honourable Greek women at Berea who believed Paul get the same word.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: This form of “Greek” specifically denotes a Greek woman, and is used of the Syrophoenician woman who asked Jesus to heal her daughter, identified by Mark as “a Greek, a Syrophoenician by nation” (Mark 7:26), meaning a Gentile rather than an ethnic Greek by descent. It is also used of the “honourable women” among the Greeks in Berea who believed Paul's message alongside many Jews (Acts 17:12).

witness.excerpt: I have also taken a great deal of pains to obtain the learning of the Greeks; and understand the elements of the Greek language: although I have so long accustomed my self to speak our own tongue, that I cannot pronounce Greek with sufficient exactness.

Two of the principal Syrians in Cesarea persuaded Burrus, who was Nero’s tutor, and secretary for his Greek epistles, by giving him a great sum of money, to disanul that equality of the Jewish privileges of citizens which they hitherto injoyed.

For the Jews that dwelt at Cesarea had a synagogue near the place, whose owner was a certain Cesarean Greek: the Jews had endeavored frequently to have purchased the possession of the place, and had offered many times its value for its price; but as the owner overlooked their offers, so did he raise other buildings upon the p

entries.title: Gudgodah (Hor-haggidgad)
entries.summary: A wilderness stop in Deuteronomy 10:7, just after Moserah where Aaron died. Numbers 33 calls it Hor-haggidgad, and its place in Sinai has not been found.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Gudgodah appears in the wilderness itinerary of Deuteronomy 10:6-7, listed immediately after Moserah, where Aaron died and was buried, and before Jotbathah. It corresponds to Hor-haggidgad in the fuller itinerary of Numbers 33:32-33, and like most of the stations listed there, its precise location in the Sinai Peninsula has not been identified.

entries.title: Guni (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Guni (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: One of Naphtali's sons, and a clan of the tribe came from him.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Guni was a son of Naphtali, and his descendants formed one of the clans counted among Naphtali's tribe.

witness.excerpt: And these are the names of the sons of Naphtali: Jahziel, and Guni, and Jezer, and Shallum, and ‘Îv.  31.
He had besides by Bilhah, the handmaid of Rachel, Dan and Nephtliali; which last had four sons that followed him - Jesel, Guni, Issari, and Sellim.

entries.title: Gunites (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: The clan from Guni, Naphtali's son. They were counted in the census of Numbers 26 on the plains of Moab, before Israel crossed into Canaan.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Gunites were the clan descended from Guni, one of the sons of Naphtali, counted in the wilderness census of Numbers 26 taken on the plains of Moab before Israel entered Canaan.

entries.title: Gur
entries.summary: Jehu's servants caught King Ahaziah of Judah on the ascent of Gur, near Ibleam, as he ran, and wounded him fatally.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: An ascent near Ibleam in the Jezreel Valley, the place where the servants of Jehu overtook and mortally wounded King Ahaziah of Judah as he fled (2 Kings 9:27).

entries.title: Gur-baal
entries.summary: God helped King Uzziah beat the people of Gur-baal, along with the Philistines and the Meunites. The name means sojourn of Baal, so it was probably an Arabian settlement where Baal was worshipped, and nobody knows where.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Gur-baal appears once, in 2 Chronicles 26:7, among the peoples God helped King Uzziah defeat, alongside the Philistines and the Meunites. Its name, "sojourn of Baal," suggests it was an Arabian settlement associated with the worship of Baal, though its exact location is unknown.

entries.title: Habaiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: His family were priests who came back from Babylon and could not prove their descent from Aaron. They were kept out of the priesthood until a high priest could settle it with the Urim and Thummim, and the record never says that happened.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Habaiah headed a priestly family that returned from Babylonian exile but could not produce genealogical records proving descent from Aaron. As a result its members were barred from serving as priests and from eating the priests' portion of offerings until the matter could be settled by the high priest using the Urim and Thummim, a resolution the record does not describe as ever occurring (Ezra 2:61-63; Nehemiah 7:63-65).

entries.title: Habakkuk (Prophet living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: He argued with God. Why does Judah's injustice go unpunished, he asks, and when the answer is Babylon, he asks how God can use a nation worse than Judah to do it. The book ends with him choosing to trust and rejoice with his questions still open, and his line that the righteous will live by faith is one Paul built on.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Habakkuk was a prophet who openly questioned God, asking why he tolerated Judah's injustice and then, when told Babylon would be the instrument of judgment, asking how God could use a nation even more wicked than Judah to punish it. The book records God's answer and ends with Habakkuk choosing to trust and even rejoice in God despite having no resolution to his questions, famously declaring that the righteous will live by faith, a line Paul later builds an entire theology of salvation around.

entries.title: Habazaniah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Grandfather of Jaazaniah, the Rechabite leader Jeremiah tested with wine. Nothing else is recorded of Habazaniah himself.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The grandfather of Jaazaniah, the Rechabite leader whom Jeremiah tested by offering wine to the wine-abstaining Rechabite clan as an object lesson in obedience (Jeremiah 35:3-6). Nothing else is recorded of Habazaniah himself.

entries.title: Habor
entries.summary: After Samaria fell in 722 BC, the Assyrians deported the northern kingdom's people to this river and its district. It is the Khabur, a big tributary of the Euphrates in what is now northeastern Syria.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: River, and the district around it, in Assyrian territory to which the Assyrians deported the population of the northern kingdom of Israel after Samaria fell in 722 BC (2 Kings 17:6; 18:11; 1 Chr. 5:26). It is identified with the Khabur, a major tributary of the Euphrates in what is now northeastern Syria.

entries.title: Hachaliah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Nehemiah's father, and that is the only reason he is named.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Hachaliah was the father of Nehemiah, the cupbearer to the Persian king Artaxerxes who obtained leave to return to Jerusalem and rebuild its walls (Nehemiah 1:1; 10:1).

entries.title: Hachilah
entries.summary: David hid from Saul on this hill in the wilderness. From here he and Abishai crept into Saul's camp at night and took his spear and water jug instead of killing him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The hill of Hachilah was a wilderness stronghold where David hid from Saul, and it's the site of the episode where David and Abishai snuck into Saul's camp at night and took his spear and water jug rather than kill him while he slept.

witness.excerpt: So he came to them with three thousand armed men: and upon the approach of the night he pitched his camp at a certain place called Hachilah .

entries.title: Hachmoni (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: The Hachmonite family name stands behind Jashobeam, one of David's chief warriors, and Jehiel, who attended David's sons, is called his son.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Hachmoni, or "the Hachmonite," is named as the father of Jehiel, a court official who attended David's sons, and as the family name behind Jashobeam, one of David's chief mighty warriors, whose immediate father was Zabdiel (1 Chronicles 11:11; 27:32).

entries.title: Hadad (Arabian living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: A son of Ishmael, in the list of Genesis 25:15. Nothing else is told of him.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Hadad (King living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: One of the kings of Edom, in Genesis 36 and the matching list in Chronicles. The name was common among them.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Hadad (King living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: One of 3 men called Hadad. This one is a king from the patriarchs, named twice in 1 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hadad (King living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: An Edomite prince who fled to Egypt as a child when David's men conquered Edom, and came back grown to trouble Solomon's reign.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Hadad was a common name among Edomite kings and also the name of an Edomite prince who fled to Egypt as a child when David's forces conquered Edom, later returning as an adversary who troubled Solomon's reign.

witness.excerpt: Now when Hadad, king of Damascus and of Syria, heard that David fought against Hadadezer, who was his friend, he came to his assistance with a powerful army, in hopes to rescue him; and when he had joined battle with David at the rive

It deserves here to be remarked, that this Hadad, being a very great king, was conquered by David, whose posterity yet for several generations were called Benhadad, or the son of Hadad, till the days of Hazael, whose son Adar or Ader is also in our Hebrew copy (2 King

WHEN the affairs of Ahab were thus, at that very time the son of Hadad, [Benhadad,] who was king of the Syrians and of Damascus, got together an army out of all his country, and procured thirty-two kings beyond Euphrates to be his auxiliaries: so he made an expedition against Ahab; but bec

entries.title: Hadad-rimmon
entries.summary: Named for two Syrian storm gods, Hadad and Rimmon, and it lay in the plain of Megiddo. King Josiah was fatally wounded near Megiddo and mourned here, and Zechariah uses that grief to picture Jerusalem's.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Hadad-rimmon, a place in the plain of Megiddo named for the Syrian storm-deities Hadad and Rimmon. It became proverbial for mourning after King Josiah was fatally wounded near Megiddo and the land lamented him there (2 Chr. 35:22-25); Zechariah draws on that memory to picture Jerusalem's future grief (Zech. 12:11).

entries.title: Hadadezer (King living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: David fought this Aramean king in campaign after campaign, and the wins pushed Israel's borders out and brought in tribute and a great deal of captured bronze.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Hadadezer was a powerful Aramean king David defeated in a series of campaigns that expanded Israel's territory and brought substantial tribute and captured bronze into David's kingdom.

witness.excerpt: Now when Hadad, king of Damascus and of Syria, heard that David fought against Hadadezer, who was his friend, he came to his assistance with a powerful army, in hopes to rescue him; and when he had joined battle with David at the river Euphrates, he failed of his purpose, and lost in the battle a great numb

entries.title: Hadar (King living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: The last of the Edomite kings listed before Israel had a king. He ruled from Pau and his wife was Mehetabel. Chronicles calls him Hadad, so Hadar may only be a copying variant.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Hadar appears twice in Edom's early history, and both times the parallel genealogy in 1 Chronicles calls him Hadad instead, suggesting Hadar may simply be a copying variation of that name. The first was a son of Ishmael (Genesis 25:15; 1 Chronicles 1:30), and the second was the last of the Edomite kings listed before Israel had a monarchy, ruling from the city of Pau and married to Mehetabel (Genesis 36:39; 1 Chronicles 1:50-51).

entries.title: Hadashah
entries.summary: A lowland town of Judah, in the district with Lachish. The name means new, and it is never mentioned again.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Hadashah, a lowland town of Judah in the district that included Lachish, its name meaning "new" (Josh. 15:37). It is not mentioned again in scripture.

entries.title: Hadassah (Woman living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Esther's Hebrew name, before she took the Persian one she was known by as queen. She was an orphan, raised by her cousin Mordecai in Susa.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Hadassah was the Hebrew name of Esther before she took the Persian name by which she became known as queen to King Ahasuerus. Orphaned young, she was raised by her cousin Mordecai in Susa (Esther 2:7).

entries.title: Hadid
entries.summary: Exiles back from Babylon resettled it, a Benjamin town grouped with Lod and Ono in the lists. It is el-Haditheh, a few miles east of Lydda.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Hadid was a town in the territory of Benjamin, grouped in the census lists with the nearby towns of Lod and Ono among the places resettled by Jews returning from Babylonian exile (Ezra 2:33; Nehemiah 7:37; 11:34). It is identified with the modern site of el-Haditheh, a few miles east of Lydda.

entries.title: Hadlai (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: An Ephraimite, named only as father of Amasa, one of four Ephraimite chiefs who stood in front of the returning army and made them release and care for the Judean captives.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Hadlai was an Ephraimite and the father of Amasa, one of four Ephraimite chiefs who confronted returning Israelite soldiers and insisted that Judean captives and plunder taken in a war against Ahaz be released and cared for rather than enslaved (2 Chronicles 28:9-15). He is mentioned only to identify his son.

entries.title: Hadoram (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Genesis 10:27 makes him one of Joktan's sons. Under the same name Chronicles has a prince sent to congratulate David on a victory, and the official over Solomon's forced labour who was stoned to death when the kingdom split under Rehoboam.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Hadoram was a son of Joktan in the genealogies of Genesis, and also the name of a Syrian prince sent to congratulate David on a military victory and of Solomon's forced-labor official, stoned to death when the kingdom split under Rehoboam.

entries.title: Hadrach
entries.summary: A region in Syria between Hamath and Damascus, first on the list in Zechariah 9:1. The Zakkur Stele, an eighth-century BC inscription, names a capital called Hazrach that is almost certainly the same place.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Hadrach was not a person but a region in Syria, named as the opening target of a prophetic oracle in Zechariah 9:1, which continues on to name Damascus, Hamath, Tyre, and Sidon in the same sweep. The Aramaic Zakkur Stele, an eighth-century BC inscription of King Zakkur of Hamath and Luash found in northern Syria, names his capital city Hazrach, almost certainly the same place, and describes it withstanding a siege by a coalition of Aramean kings, giving real archaeological corroboration to the place name. Its exact borders are no longer certain, but it lay in the region between Hamath and Damascus.

entries.title: Hagab (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: His descendants were temple servants, the Nethinim, who came back from Babylon with Zerubbabel. Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Hagab's descendants, the Bene-Hagab, were among the temple servants, the Nethinim, who returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel to Jerusalem (Ezra 2:43-46). Nothing further is recorded about him.

entries.title: Hagaba (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Hagabah in Nehemiah's copy of the list. The family were temple servants, the Nethinim, home from exile with Zerubbabel.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Hagaba, called Hagabah in Nehemiah's parallel list, was the ancestral head of a family of temple servants (Nethinim) who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:45; Nehemiah 7:48).

entries.title: Hagar (Woman living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Sarah's Egyptian servant, given to Abraham to have the child Sarah could not, and she bore Ishmael. After Isaac came, Sarah had her and the boy sent into the wilderness, and God met her there. She is the only person in Genesis who gives God a name of her own, the God who sees me.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Hagar was Sarah's Egyptian servant, given to Abraham to bear a child when Sarah's own infertility made God's promise seem impossible, and she gave birth to Ishmael. After Isaac's birth, Sarah had Hagar and Ishmael sent away into the wilderness, where God met Hagar directly, promising that Ishmael too would become a great nation, and she is the only person in Genesis recorded giving God a name of her own, calling him the God who sees me.

witness.excerpt: And Sarai advised her husband Abram, and said unto him: "Go in unto Hagar, my Egyptian maid: it may be that I shall build up seed unto thee by her." 23.

As for Sarah, she at first loved Ismael, who was born of her own handmaid Hagar, with an affection not inferior to that to a son of her own; for he was brought up in order to succeed in the government.

entries.title: Hagarene (Warrior living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: They were nomads east of Gilead, beaten by Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh in a war Chronicles records.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: The Hagrites were a nomadic people east of Gilead, likely descended from Hagar's broader family line, defeated by the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh in a war recorded in Chronicles.

entries.title: Haggai (Prophet living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: The exiles were back and building their own houses while God's temple stayed a ruin, and Haggai told them that was why they were struggling. His short book is dated to the month and day in 520 BC. He got the building going again, and Zerubbabel and the high priest Joshua finished it a few years later.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Haggai was a prophet who confronted the returned exiles for rebuilding their own houses while leaving God's temple in ruins, arguing that their economic struggles were a direct result of that misplaced priority. His short book is dated with unusual precision to specific months and days in 520 BC, and his preaching successfully restarted construction on the temple, which the governor Zerubbabel and high priest Joshua completed a few years later.

witness.excerpt: The reason why the Christians here followed the Jews is, because of the prophecy of Haggai, 2:6-9, which they expound of the Messiah's coning to the second or Zorobabel's temple, of which they suppose this of Herod to be only a continuation; which is meant, I think, of his coming to the fourth and last temple

But as the Jews were now under terror, and afraid lest the King should change his resolution, as to the building of Jerusalem, and of the temple, there were two Prophets at that time among them, Haggai and Zachariah, who encouraged them, and bid them be of good chear, and to suspect no discouragement from the Persians: for that God foretold this to them.

entries.title: Haggi (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Gad's second son, one of the seventy who went down into Egypt. The Haggite clan in the wilderness census came from him, and nothing else is recorded.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Haggi was the second son of Gad and grandson of Jacob, one of the seventy who went into Egypt with the family (Genesis 46:16). He became the ancestor of the Haggite clan counted in the wilderness census (Numbers 26:15). Nothing else is recorded of him.

witness.excerpt: And these are the names of their sons who went with him into Egypt: the sons of Gad: Ziphion, and Haggi, and Shuni, and Ezbon, (and Eri) and Areli, and Arodi--eight.

entries.title: Haggiah (Levite living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A Merarite Levite, in the line of Levi's descendants who served in the temple.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Levite of the Merarite clan, listed in the genealogy of Levi's descendants who served in the temple (1 Chronicles 6:30).

entries.title: Haggith (Woman living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: She was one of David's wives and Adonijah's mother, and her son tried to take the throne while David was dying.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Haggith was one of David's wives and the mother of Adonijah, the son who tried to seize the throne while David was dying.

witness.excerpt: Now the fourth son of David was a beautiful young man, and tall, born to him of Haggith his wife.

entries.title: Hakkatan (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Johanan, who led the family of Azgad back to Jerusalem with Ezra, was his son.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Hakkatan was the father of Johanan, a leader of the family of Azgad who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra (Ezra 8:12).

entries.title: Hakupha (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: They were temple servants, the Nethinim, back from Babylon with Zerubbabel around 538 BC, and they are counted under his name. Nothing is known of Hakupha beyond the listing.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Hakupha's descendants, the Bene-Hakupha, were among the families of temple servants (Nethinim) who returned from Babylonian captivity with Zerubbabel around 538 BC (Ezra 2:51; Nehemiah 7:53). Like most Nethinim family heads, nothing is known of Hakupha beyond this listing. The parallel lists in Ezra and Nehemiah preserve slightly different numbers for the returning families, reflecting the difficulty of transmitting census figures across generations of copying.

entries.title: Halah
entries.summary: A district in Assyria, probably near Nineveh, where Israelites were deported after Samaria fell. Sargon II boasts in his own inscriptions of taking tens of thousands from Samaria around 722 BC.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Halah was a district in Assyria, likely near Nineveh, to which the Assyrians deported Israelites from both the northern kingdom and the Transjordan tribes after conquering Samaria (2 Kings 17:6; 18:11; 1 Chronicles 5:26). Sargon II's own inscriptions boast of deporting tens of thousands of people from Samaria around 722 BC, independently confirming the mass deportation the Bible describes, even though Halah itself is known mainly from the biblical text and from later geographers who placed a district by a similar name in the same general area.

entries.title: Halak
entries.summary: The bare mountain rising toward Seir, the southern edge of what Joshua took. Several barren ridges south of the Dead Sea have been suggested and none is certain.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Mount Halak marked the southernmost point of the territory Joshua conquered, described as the bare mountain that rises toward Seir on the border with Edom (Josh. 11:17; 12:7). It functions in the text purely as a boundary marker, and while various barren ridges south of the Dead Sea have been suggested as its location, none is certain.

entries.title: Halhul
entries.summary: Joshua 15:58 lists it in Judah's hill country, and it still goes by almost the same name, Halhul, a Palestinian town just north of Hebron.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A town in the hill country of Judah (Joshua 15:58). Its ancient name survives almost unchanged in Halhul, a Palestinian town just north of Hebron, making it one of the relatively few biblical place names in the region still in continuous use today.

entries.title: Hali
entries.summary: On Asher's border, between Helkath and Beten in the lists.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A border town of the tribe of Asher, named between Helkath and Beten in the tribal allotment lists (Josh. 19:25).

entries.title: Hallohesh (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: He set his seal on Nehemiah's covenant to keep God's law. Shallum, his son or descendant, helped repair the wall of Jerusalem.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Hallohesh was one of the leaders who set his seal on the covenant Nehemiah drew up, committing the returned exiles to obey God's law (Nehemiah 10:24). His son or descendant Shallum is also named among those who helped repair Jerusalem's wall (Nehemiah 3:12).

entries.title: Ham
entries.summary: The eastern kings under Chedorlaomer beat the Zuzim here, on the campaign that ended with Lot captured at Sodom. If the Zuzim are the Zamzummim, Ham lay east of the Jordan in what became Ammon. It has nothing to do with Noah's son.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Ham appears in Genesis 14:5 as the place where the coalition of eastern kings led by Chedorlaomer defeated the Zuzim, during the campaign that culminated in the capture of Lot at Sodom. The Zuzim are usually identified with the Zamzummim of Deuteronomy 2:20, an earlier people later dispossessed by the Ammonites, which would place Ham somewhere in the region later known as Ammon, east of the Jordan. It is unrelated to Noah's son Ham, despite the identical English spelling.

entries.title: Ham (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Noah's son. He saw his father drunk and naked in the tent and told his brothers instead of covering him, and when Noah woke he cursed Ham's son Canaan, not Ham. Egypt and Cush are among the peoples Genesis 10 traces to him.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Ham was Noah's son who saw his father drunk and naked inside his tent and told his brothers instead of covering him discreetly, and when Noah woke and learned what happened, he cursed not Ham himself but Ham's son Canaan to a future of servitude. Ham's other descendants, listed in Genesis 10, became the ancestors of Egypt, Cush, and several other ancient peoples.

witness.excerpt: And Ham saw Noah his father naked, and went forth and told his two brethren without.

And Ham divided amongst his sons, and the first portion came forth for Cush  towards the east, and to the west of him for Mizraim,  and to the west
.

of him for Put,  and to the west of him [and to the west thereof] on the sea
Now the sons of Noah were three, Shem and Japhet, and Ham, born one hundred years before the deluge.

Be thou ware, my son Jacob, of taking a wife from any seed of the daughters of Canaan;
For all his seed is to be rooted out of the earth. 
21, For, owing to the transgression of Ham,  Canaan erred, 
And all his seed will be destroyed from off the earth and all the residue thereof,
And none springing from him will be saved on the day of judgment.
22.

entries.title: Haman (Persian living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: The Persian king's top official. Mordecai would not bow to him, and Haman's rage grew into a plot to kill every Jew in the empire on one day, until Queen Esther exposed it and he was hanged on the gallows he had built for Mordecai.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Haman was the Persian king's highest official, and his rage at Mordecai's refusal to bow to him escalated into a plot to exterminate the entire Jewish population of the empire on a single day. Queen Esther's intervention exposed the plot, and Haman was hanged on the very gallows he had built for Mordecai, with his ten sons later executed as well.

entries.title: Hamath
entries.summary: An Aramean capital on the Orontes in Upper Syria, the old northern limit of the land promised to Israel. Its king Toi was David's ally. Inscribed stones from the site, set up by a king the Assyrians called Irhuleni, were among the first Hieroglyphic Luwian texts European scholars saw, and reading his name gave them some of the script's first sign values.
entries.books: Numbers, Joshua, Judges, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Amos, Zechariah
entries.label: 13 books
entries.dictNote: Hamath was the capital of an Aramean kingdom on the Orontes River in Upper Syria, marking the traditional northern boundary of the land promised to Israel. Its king Toi allied with David, and centuries later Assyria conquered the city, deported part of its population to Samaria after Israel's fall, and crushed a revolt there under a rebel named Yahu-bihdi. Excavations at the site, modern Hama, uncovered Hittite hieroglyphic inscriptions carved into building stones, evidence that the city had earlier been under Hittite cultural influence; these “Hamath stones” helped nineteenth century scholars begin deciphering Luwian hieroglyphic script.
entries.checked: The Hamath stones, inscriptions of Urhilina and his son Uratami, were collected in 1872 and published in 1873. Urhilina is the Irhuleni of Shalmaneser III's records, 853 to 845 BC, and reading the name yielded the sign values hu, li, na, ma and tu. Verified 2026-10-04.

witness.excerpt: But when the king of Hamath was informed of the ill success of Hadadezer, and had heard of the ruin of his army, he was afraid on his own account, and resolved to make a league of friendship and fidelity with David before he should come against hi
But he did not hearken unto them, and dwelt in the land of Lebanon from Hamath  to the entering of Egypt,  he and his sons until this day.
And he saw, and, behold, the land was very pleasant from the entering of Hamath to the lofty oak. .

But as the King of Egypt returned from the battel, he sent for Jehoahaz to come to him, to the city called Hamath ; which belongs to Syria; and when he was come, he put him in bands, and delivered the Kingdom to a brother of his by the father’s side, whose name was Eliakim ; and changed his name to Jehoiakim ; and laid a tribute up

entries.title: Hamath-Dor (Hammath)
entries.summary: Given to the Gershonite clan in Naphtali, it is usually taken as Hammath, the hot springs by Tiberias, and Chronicles calls it Hammon, which makes three spellings for one town.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Levitical city of Naphtali assigned to the Gershonite clan (Joshua 21:32). It is usually taken as the same town as Hammath, a hot-springs site near the Sea of Galilee close to Tiberias; the parallel list of Levitical cities in 1 Chronicles 6:76 gives this town's name as Hammon instead, showing the same site circulating under at least three spellings.

entries.title: Hamath-Zobah
entries.summary: Solomon captured it and rebuilt it as a store city, and whether it is Hamath on the Orontes or a separate stronghold tied to Zobah is disputed.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Hamath-zobah is not a person but a fortified city or region that Solomon captured and rebuilt as a store city (2 Chronicles 8:3). Its exact location is disputed; some identify it with Hamath on the Orontes River, while others take it as a separate Aramean stronghold associated with the kingdom of Zobah.

entries.title: Hamathite (People, perhaps from Hamath)
entries.summary: The people of Hamath, counted among Canaan's descendants. Their city on the Orontes kept marking Israel's northern border, and Assyrian records put its king Irhuleni beside Ahab against Shalmaneser III at Qarqar in 853 BC.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Hamathites descended from Canaan and were named for Hamath, a major city on the Orontes River in Syria that repeatedly marked Israel's northern border in the Old Testament. Hamath's king Toi sent gifts to congratulate David on defeating a common enemy, and Assyrian records name Hamath's later king Irhuleni as part of the coalition, including Ahab of Israel, that fought Shalmaneser III at the battle of Qarqar in 853 BC.

entries.title: Hammath
entries.summary: Its name means hot springs, and it was a fortified town of Naphtali on the Sea of Galilee. The thermal baths just south of Tiberias are the site, where a synagogue with a zodiac mosaic floor has been dug up.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Hammath was one of the fortified towns allotted to the tribe of Naphtali, on the shore of the Sea of Galilee (Josh. 19:35). Its name means hot springs, and it is identified with the thermal baths still found just south of Tiberias, a site known in Roman times as Hammat Tiberias, where excavations have uncovered an ancient synagogue with an elaborate zodiac mosaic floor.

entries.title: Hammath (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hammedatha (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Haman's father. Esther calls him the Agagite, which may tie the family to the old Amalekite royal line.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Hammedatha was Haman's father, identified in the book of Esther by the title the Agagite, possibly linking his family to the ancient Amalekite royal line.

entries.title: Hammoleketh
entries.summary: Gilead's sister, from Manasseh, and the mother of Abiezer, Ishod and Mahalah. Her name means the queen, and nothing else is recorded about her.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A woman of the tribe of Manasseh, sister of Gilead and mother of Abiezer, Ishod, and Mahalah, named in the genealogical record of 1 Chronicles 7:17-18. Her name means "the queen," though nothing further is recorded of any royal role.

entries.title: Hammon (Hammath)
entries.summary: Two towns. One was in Asher near Sidon, probably Umm el-Amoud, and the other a Levitical city in Naphtali, likely Hammath by the Sea of Galilee.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Hammon refers to two separate towns in the Old Testament: one in the territory of Asher near Sidon (Joshua 19:28), likely identified with modern Umm el-Amoud, and a Levitical city assigned to the tribe of Naphtali (1 Chronicles 6:76), probably the same place as Hammath near the Sea of Galilee (Joshua 19:35). The name, meaning “warm” or “hot spring,” likely reflects a nearby thermal spring, a natural feature found along both stretches of coast and lakeshore in the region.

entries.title: Hamon-gog
entries.summary: Ezekiel's valley where Gog's dead armies are buried. The name means multitude of Gog. It takes Israel seven months to clear the land.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Symbolic name, meaning "multitude of Gog," for a valley in Ezekiel's apocalyptic vision where the defeated armies of Gog would be buried, so thickly filled with graves that it would take Israel seven months to clear the land of bodies (Ezek. 39:11-15). It represents a future scene of judgment rather than a known geographic site.

entries.title: Hamonah
entries.summary: A city name in Ezekiel's vision, meaning multitude, set beside the valley where Gog's hordes are buried so that the place itself remembers them. It belongs to the vision, not to any map of his day.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Hamonah is not a person but a symbolic name, meaning "multitude," that Ezekiel assigns to the site in Israel where the defeated hordes of Gog would be buried, so numerous that a whole valley would be renamed for them (Ezekiel 39:11-16). The prophecy pictures the burial taking seven months and the valley being renamed the Valley of Hamon-gog, with a nearby city called Hamonah standing as a permanent marker of the event. Like Hamon-gog, the name functions within Ezekiel's vision of judgment rather than naming an actual place already on the map in his day.

entries.title: Hamor (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: The Canaanite ruler of Shechem. His son raped Dinah, and while Hamor tried to arrange a marriage, Simeon and Levi talked the men of the city into circumcision and killed them while they were still in pain.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Hamor was the Canaanite ruler of Shechem whose son raped Jacob's daughter Dinah, and his attempt to negotiate a peaceful marriage settlement ended in a massacre when Dinah's brothers Simeon and Levi tricked the city's men into circumcision and slaughtered them while they were incapacitated.

witness.excerpt: But when Shechem, the son of Hamor the King saw her, he defiled her by violence: and being greatly in love with her, he desired of his father that he would procure the damsel to him for a wife.
And I destroyed at 5 that time the sons of Hamor, as it is written in the heavenly tables.
And after this I counselled my father, and Reuben my brother, to bid the sons of Hamor not to be circumcised; for I was zealous because of the abomination which they had wrought on 4, 5 my sister.

And I was young, about
3 twenty years of age, when, with Simeon, I wrought vengeance on Hamor for our sister Dinah.

entries.title: Hamuel (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Simeonite, among Shaul's descendants in 1 Chronicles 4:26. No other information about him survives.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Hamuel was a Simeonite listed in 1 Chronicles 4:26 among the descendants of Shaul, within the tribal genealogy of Simeon. No other information about him survives.

entries.title: Hamul (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Perez's son and Judah's grandson. One of Judah's clans came from him.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Hamul was a son of Perez, Judah's grandson, and his descendants formed one of the clans counted in Judah's tribal genealogy.

entries.title: Hamulites (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Counted in the Numbers 26 census, the clan of Hamul, Judah's grandson through Pharez.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Hamulites were the clan descended from Hamul, a grandson of Judah through Pharez, counted in the Numbers 26 census.

entries.title: Hamutal (Woman living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: She was one of Josiah's wives, and two kings of Judah were her sons, Jehoahaz and Zedekiah, who both reigned after Josiah died.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Hamutal was one of King Josiah's wives and the mother of two kings of Judah, Jehoahaz and Zedekiah, who both reigned after their father's death.

witness.excerpt: He reigned in Jerusalem: and his mother was Hamutal , of the city Libnah.

entries.title: Hanameel (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Jeremiah's cousin. Babylon's army was round Jerusalem when Jeremiah bought Hanamel's field in Anathoth. He did it on purpose, as a sign that land would be bought and sold in Judah again.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Hanamel was Jeremiah's cousin, and Jeremiah's purchase of Hanamel's field in Anathoth, even as Babylon's army besieged Jerusalem, was a deliberate prophetic sign that Judah would one day be restored and land would again be bought and sold normally.

entries.title: Hananeel (Tower of Hananel)
entries.summary: A tower on Jerusalem's north wall. Nehemiah lists it among the stretches rebuilt, and Jeremiah and Zechariah use it as a landmark when they describe the city to come.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: The Tower of Hananeel was a fortification along Jerusalem's northern wall, mentioned by Nehemiah among the sections rebuilt and by Zechariah and Jeremiah as a landmark in prophecies about the city's future.

entries.title: Hanani (Levite living at the time of Divided Monarchy)

entries.title: Hanani (Prophet living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: The prophet who went to King Asa and told him he had leaned on a foreign alliance instead of on God.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Hanani was a common Old Testament name, borne by a prophet who confronted King Asa for relying on a foreign alliance instead of God, and by Nehemiah's own brother, who first brought him the news of Jerusalem's ruined walls that prompted his return.

entries.title: Hananiah (Daniel's compatriot living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A prophet who told the exiles the yoke of Babylon would break in two years. Jeremiah told him he was wrong and he died that same year.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hananiah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: He broke the wooden yoke off Jeremiah's neck and announced that Babylon's hold on Judah would be gone in two years. Jeremiah came back with word that God would put an iron yoke in its place, and that Hananiah would die within the year. He died two months later.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Hananiah was a false prophet who publicly contradicted Jeremiah, breaking a wooden yoke off Jeremiah's neck to symbolize Judah's coming freedom from Babylon within two years. Jeremiah returned with a message that God would replace the wooden yoke with an iron one, and predicted Hananiah would die within the year for prophesying rebellion God had not authorized, a prediction fulfilled two months later.

entries.title: Hanes
entries.summary: An Egyptian city in Isaiah's warning to the envoys Judah sent looking for an alliance with Egypt. It is generally identified with Herakleopolis Magna, near Ihnasiya el-Medina, south of Cairo.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Hanes was an Egyptian city named in Isaiah's warning against Judah's envoys seeking an alliance with Egypt (Isa. 30:4). It is generally identified with Herakleopolis Magna, known in Egyptian as Henen-nesut, near modern Ihnasiya el-Medina south of Cairo, an ancient regional capital with its own long dynastic history.

entries.title: Hannah (Woman living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Elkanah loved her, and she had no children, and his other wife Peninnah made sure she felt it. She prayed so hard and so silently at Shiloh that Eli thought she was drunk. Samuel was the answer, and she gave him to the Lord's service once he was weaned.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Hannah was Elkanah's beloved but childless wife, tormented by her husband's other wife Peninnah for her infertility, and she prayed so fervently and silently at the tabernacle at Shiloh that the priest Eli initially mistook her for drunk. God answered her vow with the birth of Samuel, whom she dedicated to the Lord's service as soon as he was weaned, and her prayer of thanksgiving in 1 Samuel 2 anticipates themes and language that echo later in Mary's song in Luke.

witness.excerpt: Elcanah, a Levite, one of a middle condition among his fellow citizens; and one that dwelt at Ramathaim, a city of the tribe of Ephraim, married two wives, Hannah and Peninnah.

entries.title: Hannathon
entries.summary: It lay on Zebulun's border in Galilee, and the Amarna letters of the fourteenth century BC already name it, as Hinnatuna, a garrison town fought over on the road through Galilee.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A border town of the tribe of Zebulun in Galilee (Joshua 19:14). It is widely identified with Tell el-Bedeiwiyeh in the Beth-netofa valley, and a town of the same name, Hinnatuna, appears in the fourteenth-century BC Amarna letters as a garrison town fought over along a key route through Galilee, giving this minor biblical town a genuine extrabiblical attestation centuries before Joshua's conquest narrative.

entries.title: Hanniel (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hanniel (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Moses picked him to speak for Manasseh when the land was divided.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Two men named Hanniel appear in the Pentateuch and Chronicles. One was a chief of the tribe of Manasseh whom Moses appointed to help divide the land of Canaan among the tribes (Numbers 34:23). The other was a chief of the tribe of Asher, listed among mighty warriors and heads of families (1 Chronicles 7:39-40).

entries.title: Hanochites (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Reuben's eldest son was Hanoch, and this clan, counted in the wilderness census, came from him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Hanochites were the clan descended from Hanoch, the eldest son of Reuben, counted in Israel's wilderness census.

entries.title: Hanun (King living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: David sent men to comfort him when his father died, and the Ammonite king shaved off half their beards and cut their clothes short. It started a full war between Israel and Ammon with its Aramean allies.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Hanun was the Ammonite king who humiliated David's envoys of condolence by shaving off half their beards and cutting their garments short, an insult that triggered a full-scale war between Israel and the combined forces of Ammon and its Aramean allies.

entries.title: Hanun (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Nehemiah names him once, and he is a man from the exile and the return.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hanun (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of 3 men called Hanun. This one is a man from the exile and the return, named once in Nehemiah.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Haphraim (Ophrah)
entries.summary: Issachar's town near Shunem in Joshua 19:19. El-Afuleh in the Jezreel Valley is the tentative match, on geography more than evidence.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Haphraim was a town of Issachar named near Shunem in Joshua's allotment list (Joshua 19:19). It is tentatively identified with the village of el-Afuleh in the Jezreel Valley, near ancient Shunem, though the identification rests mainly on geographic fit rather than direct evidence.

entries.title: Happizzez (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Head of the eighteenth of the twenty-four priestly divisions, chosen by lot. Some English versions spell it Aphses, and nothing else is recorded of him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The head of the eighteenth of the twenty-four priestly divisions David organized for temple service, chosen along with the other course heads by lot (1 Chronicles 24:15). Some English translations render the name Aphses. Nothing else is recorded of him.

entries.title: Hara
entries.summary: Members of Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh were deported here by the Assyrians. It seems to have lain along the Khabur River, and Tiglath-pileser III's own annals record the deportation.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A region of Assyria, apparently along the Khabur River between the Tigris and Euphrates, to which the Assyrians deported members of the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh (1 Chr. 5:26). Assyrian royal annals from Tiglath-pileser III independently record the mass deportation of Israelite populations from Transjordan, corroborating the biblical account of this resettlement policy.

entries.title: Haradah
entries.summary: The name means fright, and it was the twenty-fifth stop on the wilderness route. Numbers 33:24-25 is all there is.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Haradah, meaning fright or fear, was the twenty-fifth stop in Israel's wilderness itinerary, mentioned only in Numbers 33:24-25. Its location is unknown and nothing beyond its name and place in the list has survived.

entries.title: Haran
entries.summary: Abraham's family stopped and settled here for a while on the way toward Canaan, and Abraham set out again from Haran in Genesis 12:4. The city was likely named after his brother.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Haran was Abraham's brother, Lot's father, who died young in Ur before the rest of the family migrated toward Canaan, and the city of Haran where the family later settled temporarily was likely named after him.

entries.title: Haran (Levite living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a Levite from the divided-kingdom years.
