entries.title: Hermes (A male deity in the New Testament)
entries.summary: In Acts 14:12 a crowd decides Paul must be Hermes, the messenger of the Greek gods, because he was the one doing the talking. The Roman Christian of the same name in Romans 16:14 is someone else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hermes (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Paul greets him at the end of Romans, among a list of believers in Rome. He shares a name with the Greek messenger god, and that is all anyone knows.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Hermes, sharing his name with the Greek messenger god, was a Roman Christian Paul greets among a list of believers in Rome at the end of his letter to the Romans (Romans 16:14). Nothing further is known of him; the shared name with the deity was common among slaves and freedmen in the Roman world and carries no religious significance for its bearer here.

entries.title: Hermogenes (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: He deserted Paul. Paul names him with Phygellus in Asia Minor and sets them against Onesiphorus, who did not.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Christian in Asia Minor whom Paul names, along with Phygellus, as one who deserted him, part of a wider abandonment Paul laments in 2 Timothy 1:15. He contrasts their desertion with the loyalty of Onesiphorus, mentioned in the very next verse.

entries.title: Hermon
entries.summary: On Israel's northern border, and the snowmelt off it gives the Psalms their picture of dew. It is near Caesarea Philippi, which makes it a likely site for Jesus's transfiguration.
entries.books: Deuteronomy, Joshua, 1 Chronicles, Psalm, Song of Solomon
entries.label: 5 books
entries.dictNote: Mount Hermon is a prominent peak on Israel's northern border, likely the traditional site of Jesus's transfiguration given its proximity to Caesarea Philippi, and its abundant snowmelt is a recurring image in the Psalms for refreshing dew.

witness.excerpt:
10.  And their habitation was from the land of the children of Ammon to Mount Hermon, and the seats of their kingdom were Karnaim and

[paragraph continues] Ashtaroth,  and Edrei, and Mîsûr,  and Beon.  11.

And they were in all two hundred; who descended in the days of Jared on the summit of Mount Hermon, and they called it Mount Hermon, because they had sworn and bound themselves by mutual imprecations upon it.
And I went off and sat down at the waters of Dan, in the land of Dan, to the south of the west of Hermon: I read their petition till I fell asleep.

entries.title: Herod
entries.summary: King when Jesus was born. When the magi did not come back to him, Herod the Great ordered the boys of Bethlehem killed. He also enlarged the Jerusalem temple, and Josephus tells his story at length.
entries.label: 3 books

witness.excerpt: a fire glowed in him slowly, which did not so much appear to the touch outwardly, as it augmented his pains inwardly… his privy-member was putrefied, and produced worms; and when he sat upright, he had a difficulty of breathing.

entries.lukeNote: Luke's Herod (Antipas, the tetrarch who mocks Jesus in 23:7-15) is Herod the Great's son, not the dying king in this passage, but it's the same dynasty, and Josephus's account of the father's final illness is one of the most infamous death scenes in ancient historiography, read by generations as divine judgment on the family.

entries.title: Herod (Tetrarch living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Herod Antipas, the son of Herod the Great. He ruled Galilee through Jesus's ministry and beheaded John the Baptist for condemning his marriage, and Luke has him mock Jesus before the crucifixion.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Several different rulers named Herod appear across the New Testament, all from the same Roman-appointed dynasty. Herod the Great, king when Jesus was born, ordered the massacre of infant boys in Bethlehem after failing to trick the magi into revealing the child's location. His son Herod Antipas ruled Galilee during Jesus's ministry, beheaded John the Baptist for condemning his marriage, and briefly interrogated Jesus before his crucifixion. A grandson, Herod Agrippa the First, executed the apostle James and imprisoned Peter, and Agrippa's own son, Herod Agrippa the Second, later heard Paul's defense before his final voyage to Rome. Josephus records the same dynasty in detail outside the Bible, confirming their reigns and building projects, including Herod the Great's expansion of the Jerusalem temple.

entries.title: Herod (Tetrarch living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Herod Agrippa the First, the grandson. He executed the apostle James and put Peter in prison.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Herodians (Political group in the New Testament)
entries.summary: Partisans of Herod, in the plainest sense of the name. They backed Herod's dynasty and Roman rule, and still joined the Pharisees, whose views they did not share, to try to trap Jesus over paying taxes to Caesar.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: The Herodians were a Jewish political faction supportive of Herod's dynasty and Roman rule, and they occasionally allied with the Pharisees, despite otherwise opposing views, in attempts to trap Jesus, most notably over the question of paying taxes to Caesar.

entries.title: Herodias (Woman living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Granddaughter of Herod the Great. She left her first husband for his half-brother, Herod Antipas, and when John the Baptist called the marriage unlawful she had her daughter dance at a banquet and ask for his head. Josephus gives a different reason for John's death, a political execution.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Herodias was the granddaughter of Herod the Great who left her first husband to marry his half-brother Herod Antipas, a marriage John the Baptist publicly condemned as unlawful. Her resentment of John's criticism led her to orchestrate his execution, having her daughter dance for Antipas at a banquet and then demand John's head on a platter as the reward, a request Antipas granted reluctantly to avoid breaking an oath made in front of his guests.

witness.excerpt: Herod slew him… who was a good man, and commanded the Jews to exercise virtue, both as to righteousness towards one another, and piety towards God… Herod, who feared lest the great influence John had over the people might put it into his power… to raise rebellion… thought it best, by putting him to death, to prevent any mischief he might cause.

entries.lukeNote: Luke names her only as the reason John rebukes Herod and gets imprisoned for it (3:19), the marriage itself. Josephus, independent of any Gospel and with no Christian interest at stake, confirms John's death under Herod Antipas and gives his own reason: not the dinner-party beheading of the later Gospel account, but a preemptive political execution, fear of a popular movement Herod couldn't control.

entries.title: Herodion (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: He gets a greeting from Paul in Rome, who calls him "kinsman", most likely meaning a fellow Jew. The name comes from the Herod family, so he may have belonged to a Herodian household.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Christian in Rome whom Paul greets as his "kinsman," likely meaning a fellow Jew rather than a blood relative, near the end of his letter to the Romans (Rom. 16:11). His name, derived from the Herod family, suggests he may have belonged to the household of a member of the Herodian dynasty.

entries.title: Hesed (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: His son Ben-hesed was one of the twelve district officers who fed Solomon's household, a month each in turn, and Sochoh and the land of Hepher fell in that district. Of Hesed himself, nothing else is recorded.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The father of Ben-hesed, one of twelve district officers Solomon appointed to supply provisions for the royal household, each responsible for one month of the year (1 Kings 4:7-10). Ben-hesed's district included Sochoh and the land of Hepher.

entries.title: Heshbon
entries.summary: Sihon's capital, east of the Jordan near the northern edge of Moab. Moses took it before Israel crossed into Canaan, and it became a Levitical city in Reuben. Moab later had it back, which is why the prophets name it in their judgments on Moab, and the ruins, still called Hesban, lie about twenty miles east of the Jordan.
entries.books: Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 1 Chronicles, Nehemiah, Song of Solomon, Isaiah, Jeremiah
entries.label: 9 books
entries.dictNote: Heshbon was the capital of Sihon, king of the Amorites, situated east of the Jordan near the northern edge of Moab. Moses captured it and the surrounding territory before Israel entered Canaan, and it later became a Levitical city within the tribe of Reuben. After the Israelite monarchy declined the Moabites reoccupied it, and the prophets accordingly pronounce judgment on Heshbon alongside the rest of Moab. Its ruins, still called Hesban, lie about twenty miles east of the Jordan, and excavations there have traced occupation across many centuries, though matching specific layers to the biblical conquest period remains debated among archaeologists.

witness.excerpt: \"For then,\" says Moses, \"the expounders of riddles will say, Come to Heshbon, that the city of Sihon may be built and furnished.

entries.title: Heshmon
entries.summary: One of the southernmost towns given to Judah in the Negev, toward the border of Edom, and nobody has found where it was.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Heshmon was a town in the Negev district assigned to the tribe of Judah, listed among the southernmost settlements toward the border of Edom (Josh. 15:27). Its location has not been identified with any confidence.

entries.title: Heth (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Canaan's son and the father of the Hittites, the people Abraham bought Sarah's burial cave from and the people Uriah, Bathsheba's husband, came from generations later.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Heth was Canaan's son and the ancestor of the Hittites, the people from whom Abraham purchased a burial cave for Sarah and among whom Uriah, Bathsheba's husband, was numbered generations later.

witness.excerpt: For in patience of spirit he conversed with the children of Heth, to the intent that they should give him a place in which to bury his dead.

And Rebecca went in and said to Isaac: "I loathe my life because of the two daughters of Heth, whom Esau hath taken him as wives; and if Jacob take a wife from among the daughters of the land such as these, for what purpose

do I further live; for the daughters of Canaan are evil."  9.

entries.title: Hethlon
entries.summary: It sits on the northern border of the restored land in Ezekiel's vision, on the road toward "the entrance of Hamath", likely a pass through the Lebanon range.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Place marking part of the northern boundary of the land in Ezekiel's vision of restored Israel, associated with "the entrance of Hamath" (Ezek. 47:15; 48:1), likely a mountain pass through the Lebanon range leading toward the plain of Hamath.

entries.title: Hezeki (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A Benjamite descended from Elpaal, in the Chronicles genealogy, and that is the whole entry.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Benjamite listed among the descendants of Elpaal in the tribal genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8:17. Nothing else is recorded about him.

entries.title: Hezekiah (King living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of Judah's few good kings. He came after Ahaz, reopened the temple, tore down the high places, and broke up the bronze serpent Moses had made once people began worshipping it. When Sennacherib besieged Jerusalem in 701 BC, Hezekiah prayed, Isaiah promised deliverance, and the siege broke overnight. His seal impression has been dug up near the Temple Mount, and his tunnel still runs under the city.
entries.books: 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Proverbs, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Hosea, Micah
entries.label: 8 books
entries.dictNote: Hezekiah was one of Judah's few genuinely good kings, coming to the throne amid the wreckage his father Ahaz had left and immediately reopening the temple, restoring proper worship, and destroying the high places and idols his people had accumulated, even smashing the bronze serpent Moses had made centuries earlier once it became an object of worship in its own right. When the Assyrian king Sennacherib besieged Jerusalem in 701 BC after Hezekiah stopped paying tribute, Hezekiah prayed in the temple and the prophet Isaiah promised deliverance, and the siege broke overnight. A royal seal impression reading belonging to Hezekiah son of Ahaz king of Judah, found in excavations near the Temple Mount, is the first archaeological find naming a biblical king that was also excavated under controlled conditions rather than bought on the antiquities market, and the tunnel Hezekiah dug to secure Jerusalem's water supply during that same siege still runs beneath the city today.

witness.excerpt: How Sennacherib made an expedition against Hezekiah… How Isaiah the Prophet encouraged him: How Sennacherib, having failed of success in Egypt, returned thence to Jerusalem: and how, upon his finding his army destroyed, he returned home.

entries.curatedNote: The reforming king who survives Assyria's siege of Jerusalem (2 Kings 18-19). Josephus's whole chapter title is basically a recap of the crisis: Sennacherib's threats, Isaiah's reassurance, the army's destruction, confirming the same sequence of events from outside the biblical text.

entries.title: Hezekiah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A man from the divided-kingdom years, and Zephaniah is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hezekiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Ezra and Nehemiah name him twice, and he is a man from the exile and the return.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Hezekiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of 4 men called Hezekiah. This one is a man from the exile and the return, named once in Nehemiah.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hezion (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: King of Aram-Damascus. He was father of Tabrimon and grandfather of the Ben-hadad whom Asa paid to attack Israel. Some identify him with Rezon, who set up the Damascus kingdom against Solomon, but the link is not certain.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Hezion was an early king of Aram-Damascus, father of Tabrimon and grandfather of Ben-hadad I, the Syrian king whom Asa of Judah paid to attack Israel (1 Kings 15:18). He is sometimes identified with Rezon, who established the Damascene kingdom that opposed Solomon (1 Kings 11:23-25), though the connection is not certain.

entries.title: Hezir (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Head of the seventeenth of the priestly divisions David set up for temple service. A first-century BC tomb in the Kidron Valley names a priestly family called the Sons of Hezir, so the name stayed in Jerusalem's priesthood a long time.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hezir (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A leader who sealed Nehemiah's covenant. The seventeenth priestly division under David carries the name too.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Two men named Hezir appear in the postexilic records: the head of the seventeenth division of priests organized by David for temple service (1 Chronicles 24:15), and a leader who sealed Nehemiah's covenant of reform after the exile (Nehemiah 10:20). Whether the two are related is not stated. A first-century BC tomb in Jerusalem's Kidron Valley, known as the Tomb of the Sons of Hezir, bears an inscription naming a priestly family by this name, showing it remained in use among Jerusalem's priesthood for centuries.

entries.title: Hezro (Warrior living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Called the Carmelite, he stands among David's mighty warriors in both lists of them. Nothing else is recorded about him.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Hezro the Carmelite was one of David's mighty warriors, the elite fighters who distinguished themselves in David's service (2 Samuel 23:35; 1 Chronicles 11:37).

entries.title: Hezron (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Perez's son, and the line that ends in David runs through him; Ruth closes with it and Matthew picks it up. The same name marks a spot on Judah's southern border, west of Kadesh-barnea.
entries.label: 5 books
entries.dictNote: Hezron most often names two of Judah's ancestors in Genesis and Chronicles' genealogies, a son of Reuben and, more significantly, the son of Perez through whom the line runs down to David and eventually to Jesus in Matthew's genealogy. The same word also marks a plain on Judah's southern border, west of Kadesh-barnea, listed among the towns on the tribe's frontier in Joshua.

witness.excerpt: 12.  Reuben, the first-born of Israel; and these are the names of his sons: Enoch, and Pallu, and Hezron and Carmi--five.  13.

entries.title: Hezron (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Reuben's son, listed with the family that went down to Egypt and again in Reuben's line in Exodus and Chronicles. He is a different man from Perez's son of the same name.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Hezronites (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Two clans in the wilderness census carried this name. One came from Reuben's son Hezron, the other from Judah's line through Perez, and that second one is David's own family.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Hezronites was the name given to two distinct clans in Israel's wilderness census, both descended from men named Hezron. One family traced to a son of Reuben; the other, listed separately among Judah's descendants, traced to a different Hezron, grandson of Judah through Perez and an ancestor in David's own line.

entries.title: Hiddai (Warrior living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: From the ravines of Gaash and one of David's thirty, though Chronicles spells him Hurai.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of David's elite thirty warriors, from the ravines of Gaash (2 Samuel 23:30). The parallel list in 1 Chronicles 11:32 names him Hurai instead, one of several small spelling variants between the two rosters.

entries.title: Hiddekel (Tigris)
entries.summary: The Tigris, under its Hebrew name. It is one of the four rivers out of Eden, running east of Assyria, and Daniel is standing on its bank when his last vision comes.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Hiddekel is the Hebrew name for the Tigris, one of the four rivers described as flowing out of Eden, said to run east of Assyria (Gen. 2:14). It appears again as the setting for Daniel's final vision, where he stood on its bank (Dan. 10:4). The Tigris rises in the mountains of eastern Turkey and flows more than a thousand miles before joining the Euphrates near the Persian Gulf, its banks home to major Mesopotamian cities including Nineveh and Asshur.

entries.title: Hiel (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: He rebuilt Jericho in Ahab's reign, and it cost him both ends of his family: Abiram, his firstborn, died when he laid the foundation and Segub, the youngest, when he set up the gates. Joshua had cursed whoever rebuilt the city, and Kings tells it as that word coming true.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Hiel of Bethel rebuilt Jericho during the reign of Ahab, centuries after Joshua had destroyed the city and pronounced a curse on whoever would rebuild it (Joshua 6:26). The curse was fulfilled literally: 1 Kings 16:34 records that Hiel lost his firstborn son Abiram when he laid the city's foundation and his youngest son Segub when he set up its gates. The episode is presented as proof that the word spoken through Joshua, like the word spoken through Elijah in the surrounding narrative, held true.

entries.title: Hierapolis
entries.summary: In the Lycus Valley of Phrygia, alongside Colossae and Laodicea, and Epaphras worked hard for the church there. Its hot springs left white terraces that still draw people, at modern Pamukkale in Turkey. Early tradition says the apostle Philip died in the city.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Hierapolis was a city in the Lycus Valley of Phrygia, paired with Colossae and Laodicea as one of three churches Paul addresses through his letter to the Colossians, though he had not visited any of them personally; Epaphras is named as the one who worked hard on behalf of all three (Colossians 4:12-13). The city was famous in antiquity, as it still is today, for the white travertine terraces formed by its mineral hot springs, now the site of modern Pamukkale in Turkey. In 2011 archaeologists excavating there identified what they believe are the remains of a martyrium built over the tomb of the apostle Philip, who according to early Christian tradition died in the city.

photo.description: panorama of the theater at Hierapolis

entries.title: Hilen (Holon)
entries.summary: Joshua's list calls it Holon. It was a town of Judah handed over, with its pasturelands, to Aaron's descendants among the Levites, and nobody knows where it stood.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Hilen was a town of Judah given, along with its surrounding pasturelands, to the Levite clan descended from Aaron for their residence (1 Chronicles 6:43). The parallel list in Joshua 21:15 gives the same town's name as Holon. Its site is unidentified.

entries.title: Hillel (Man living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: Father of Abdon, the judge who came after Jephthah, and a Pirathonite from the hill country of Ephraim. He has nothing to do with the later rabbi of the same name.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Hillel was a Pirathonite from the hill country of Ephraim, the father of Abdon, one of the minor judges who governed Israel after Jephthah (Judges 12:13, 15). Nothing more is recorded about him, and he is not related to the later rabbinic sage of the same name who taught in Jerusalem centuries afterward.

witness.excerpt: Abdon also, the son of Hillel, of the tribe of Ephraim, and born at the city Pyrathon, was ordained their supreme governor after Helon.

entries.title: Hillkiah (High Priest living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: The high priest under Josiah who found a forgotten scroll of the law while the temple was being repaired. What he found set off Judah's last great reform.
entries.books: 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Jeremiah
entries.label: 6 books
entries.dictNote: Hilkiah was the high priest during King Josiah's reign who discovered a forgotten scroll of the law while the temple was being repaired, a find that triggered Judah's last great religious reform. A different Hilkiah was the father of the prophet Jeremiah.

entries.title: Hillkiah (Levite living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A levite from the divided-kingdom years, and 1 Chronicles is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hillkiah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Known through his son, the palace official who went out to meet the enemy's envoys at the wall, in 2 Kings 18 and again in Isaiah 36. Nothing else is recorded about him.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Hillkiah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A man from the divided-kingdom years. 1 Chronicles names him once.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hillkiah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 7 men called Hillkiah. This one is a man from the divided-kingdom years, named once in Jeremiah.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hillkiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of 7 men called Hillkiah. This one is a man from the exile and the return, named twice in Nehemiah.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hillkiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Nehemiah names him once, and he is a man from the exile and the return.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hirah (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Judah's friend from Adullam. He was there when Judah married a Canaanite woman. Later Judah sent him with a goat to pay the woman he had slept with, who was Tamar in disguise.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Hirah was an Adullamite and close friend of Judah, present when Judah married a Canaanite woman and later sent by Judah to deliver a goat to Tamar in payment for what he did not realize was a disguised encounter with his own daughter-in-law (Genesis 38:1, 12, 20).

entries.title: Hiram (King living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: He was king of Tyre and a friend to both David and Solomon, sending cedar and craftsmen for David's palace and for the temple and keeping up the trade with Israel through both reigns.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Hiram was the king of Tyre who supplied cedar wood, craftsmen, and skilled labor for both David's palace and Solomon's temple, maintaining a friendly trade relationship with Israel across both reigns. A different Hiram, also called Huram-abi, was a master bronzeworker Hiram the king sent to cast the temple's bronze pillars, sea, and other furnishings.

witness.excerpt: Hiram also, the king of the Tyrians, sent ambassadors to him, and made a league of mutual friendship and assistance with him.
Moreover Hiram, king of Tyre, when he had heard that Solonion succeeded to his father's kingdom, was very glad of it, for he was a friend of David's.

When Solomon had completed all this in twenty years' time, because Hiram king of Tyre had contributed a great deal of gold, and more silver to these buildings, as also cedar wood and pine wood, he also rewarded Hiram with rich presents; corn he sent him also year by year, and wine and oil, w

This country belonged formerly to the Jews, and became useful for shipping from the donations of Hiram king of Tyre; for he sent a sufficient number of men thither for pilots, and such as were skillful in navigation, to whom Solomon gave this command: That they should go along with his own stewards to the land that was o

Now that year on which the temple began to be built was already the eleventh year of the reign of Hiram; but from the building of Tyre to the building of the temple, there had passed two hundred and forty years.
2.

entries.title: Hiram (Syrian living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: A bronzeworker, also called Huram-abi, sent by the king of Tyre to Solomon. He cast the temple's bronze pillars, the sea and the rest of the bronze furnishings.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hittite (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Ephron the Hittite sold Abraham the cave of Machpelah at Hebron, and Uriah, the soldier whose wife David took, was a Hittite too. Critics once doubted there was ever a Hittite nation, until digs at Boghazkoy in Turkey found its capital. The Hittites in Canaan were probably a smaller offshoot, or the name used loosely.
entries.books: Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Ezekiel
entries.label: 15 books
entries.dictNote: Hittites appear in the Old Testament as one of the peoples native to Canaan, most famously at Hebron, where Abraham bought the cave of Machpelah from Ephron the Hittite as a burial site for Sarah, and later as individuals such as Uriah, the Hittite soldier whose wife Bathsheba David took. For a long time critics doubted a Hittite nation ever existed, but nineteenth and twentieth century excavations at Boghazkoy in Turkey uncovered the capital and royal archives of a genuine Hittite Empire, a major Bronze Age power that rivaled Egypt and fought Ramesses II at Kadesh. The biblical Hittites of Canaan were likely a smaller offshoot, or simply a name borrowed loosely from that larger Anatolian people, rather than the imperial Hittites themselves.

witness.excerpt: Wherefore bury me near Abraham my father, in the double cave in the field of Ephron the Hittite, where Abraham purchased a sepulchre to bury in; in the sepulchre which I digged for myself, there bury me.

When the king heard that the Philistines were gathered together at the city Gazara, he sent an army against them, when Sibbechai the Hittite, one of David's most courageous men, behaved himself so as to deserve great commendation, for he slew many of those that bragged they were the posterity of the giants, and vaunted themselves highly on that account, and

And when they told him that he was at Hachilah, he concealed his going away from his own companions, and came to Saul’s camp: having taken with him Abishai, his sister Zeruiah’s son; and Abimelech the Hittite.

entries.title: Hivite (People, perhaps from Hiv)
entries.summary: One of the peoples in the land before Israel. At Shechem a Hivite's son raped Dinah, and at Gibeon Hivites tricked Joshua into a treaty by pretending to come from far off, which put the city under Israel's protection.
entries.books: Genesis, Exodus, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles
entries.label: 9 books
entries.dictNote: Hivites were one of the Canaanite peoples occupying the land before Israel's arrival, associated in Genesis 34 with the city of Shechem, where Hamor the Hivite's son violated Jacob's daughter Dinah, and in Joshua 9 with Gibeon, whose inhabitants tricked Joshua into a treaty by pretending to come from a distant country. That treaty later brought Gibeon under Israelite protection even though the city was never conquered outright.

witness.excerpt: And there they carried off Dinah, the daughter of Jacob, into the house of Shechem, the son of Hamor, the Hivite, the prince of the land, and he lay with her and defiled her, and she was a little girl, a child of twelve years.

entries.title: Hobab (Midianite living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Moses asked him to be Israel's guide out of Sinai, since he knew the wilderness. He was a Kenite related to Jethro, and Judges uses a word for him that has led some to think he was Jethro himself. His descendants settled near Jericho and later around Arad.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Hobab was Moses' brother-in-law, a Kenite and relative of the Midianite priest Jethro, whose knowledge of the wilderness terrain Moses sought when Israel set out from Sinai, asking him to serve as guide (Numbers 10:29-32). Judges 4:11 uses the same relational term for him as for Moses' father-in-law, an ambiguity in the Hebrew word for in-law that has led some to identify Hobab with Jethro himself rather than as a separate individual. His descendants, the Kenites, settled among the Israelites, first near Jericho and later in the Negev around Arad (Judges 1:16).

entries.title: Hobah
entries.summary: North of Damascus. It marks how far Abram chased the four kings who had taken Lot, after routing them at night near Dan. Nobody has matched it to a modern site.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Hobah lay north of Damascus and marks the farthest point of Abram's pursuit of the four eastern kings who had captured his nephew Lot, after Abram's night attack routed them near Dan (Genesis 14:15). Nothing else is known of the site, and it has not been identified with any modern location.

entries.title: Hod (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Son of Zophah, of Asher, and one verse is all there is.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Hod was a son of Zophah, listed among the descendants of Asher in the tribal genealogy of 1 Chronicles 7:37.

entries.title: Hodaiah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: After the exile the royal line of Judah keeps going in a list, and Hodaiah is in it, a son of Elioenai. Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A descendant of the royal line of Judah listed among the sons of Elioenai in the genealogies following the Babylonian exile (1 Chr. 3:24). Nothing further is recorded about him.

entries.title: Hodaviah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A chief of the half-tribe of Manasseh, east of the Jordan. The name means "praise the LORD", and no story goes with it.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hodaviah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the exile and the return.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hodaviah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: The name means praise the LORD, and several men carry it in the genealogies. This one is in the return lists.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Hodaviah, meaning “praise the LORD,” is the name of several distinct men in the Old Testament genealogies, including a chief of the half-tribe of Manasseh east of the Jordan (1 Chronicles 5:24), a descendant of the royal line of David listed after the exile (1 Chronicles 3:24), and the ancestor of a Levitical family that returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:40). None of the individuals bearing the name has a recorded narrative beyond their place in these lists.

entries.title: Hodesh (Woman living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Shaharaim sent away two wives, Hushim and Baara, and had sons in Moab by others. Hodesh was one of them, and she is named so her sons, heads of Benjamite families, could be recorded.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A wife of Shaharaim, a Benjamite clan head listed in 1 Chronicles 8:8-9 among the men who bore children in Moab after he had sent away his first two wives, Hushim and Baara. She and Shaharaim's other wives are named only to record the sons who became heads of Benjamite families.

entries.title: Hodevah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Another spelling of Hodaviah. He headed a family of Levites that came back from Babylon with Zerubbabel.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Hodevah is an alternate spelling of Hodaviah, head of a family of Levites who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Neh. 7:43). Nothing further is recorded of him.

entries.title: Hodijah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: The name turns up among those who helped the people understand the law after Ezra read it out, and again among the signers of the covenant under Nehemiah; it was a common Levitical name.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Hodijah was a common Levitical name among those who helped explain the law to the people after Ezra's public reading and who signed the covenant renewal under Nehemiah.

entries.title: Hodijah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Nehemiah names him once, and he is a man from the exile and the return.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hodijah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of 3 men called Hodijah. This one is a man from the exile and the return, named once in Nehemiah.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hoglah (Woman living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: One of Zelophehad's five daughters. They asked Moses for their father's land, got it, and set a precedent for Israel.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Hoglah was one of five daughters of Zelophehad whose successful petition to Moses for the right to inherit their father's land set a new legal precedent for Israel.

entries.title: Hoham (King living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: King of Hebron, and an Amorite. He joined four other kings to besiege Gibeon for making peace with Israel, which brought Joshua on a forced march, and afterwards he was found hiding with the others in a cave at Makkedah and executed.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The Amorite king of Hebron who joined four other Canaanite kings in besieging Gibeon after it made peace with Israel, prompting Joshua's forced march and the battle in which the sun and moon reportedly stood still (Josh. 10:1-27). He and his allied kings were later found hiding in a cave at Makkedah, captured, and executed.

entries.title: Holon
entries.summary: In the hill country of Judah, and later one of the towns given to the Levites.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Holon was a town in the hill country of Judah, later designated as one of the cities given to the Levites.

entries.title: Holon
entries.summary: Named once, in Jeremiah, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Homam (Edomite living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: The name is Edomite, from the line of Seir the Horite, and Genesis spells it Hemam.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: An Edomite name in the genealogy of Esau's descendants through Seir the Horite; the parallel list in Genesis gives the form Hemam (1 Chronicles 1:39; Genesis 36:22).

entries.title: Hophni (Priest living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Eli's son, a priest at Shiloh, and a corrupt one. He and his brother Phinehas died in the battle where the Philistines took the Ark.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Hophni was one of Eli's two corrupt priestly sons, condemned for abusing his position at the Shiloh tabernacle, and he died alongside his brother Phinehas in the battle where the Philistines captured the Ark of the Covenant.

witness.excerpt: The occasion was this: Eli the High Priest had two sons, Hophni and Phineas.

entries.title: Hor
entries.summary: Aaron died on Mount Hor, at the edge of Edom near the end of the wandering. His priestly garments were taken off him in sight of the people, and they buried him on the mountain.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Mount Hor is where Aaron died, stripped of his priestly garments in sight of the people and buried on the mountain, at the edge of the land of Edom near the end of Israel's wilderness wandering.

entries.title: Hor
entries.summary: Named twice, in Numbers, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hor-hagidgad (Hor-haggidgad)
entries.summary: A wilderness camp in the list of stations in Numbers, usually taken to be the Gudgodah of Deuteronomy. Its site south of Kadesh has not been fixed.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Hor-hagidgad was a desert encampment in Israel's wilderness itinerary, generally taken to be the same place called Gudgodah in Deuteronomy 10:7 (Numbers 33:32-33). Its location among the stations south of Kadesh has not been fixed.

entries.title: Horam (King living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: Gezer's king. He came to help Lachish while Joshua had it under siege, and Joshua wiped out him and his army. Gezer itself stayed Canaanite until Solomon.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: King of Gezer at the time of Joshua's southern campaign. He marched to relieve Lachish while Joshua besieged it, but Joshua defeated him and his army, leaving no survivors (Josh. 10:33). Gezer itself remained a Canaanite enclave for generations afterward and was not fully absorbed into Israel until Solomon's reign.

entries.title: Horeb (Mount Sinai)
entries.summary: Another name for Sinai, where Moses met God at the burning bush and Israel received the law, and where Elijah later ran and heard God in a still, small voice after the wind, earthquake and fire.
entries.books: Exodus, Deuteronomy, 1 Kings, 2 Chronicles, Psalm, Malachi
entries.label: 6 books
entries.dictNote: Horeb is another name for Mount Sinai, the mountain where Moses first encountered God at the burning bush and later where Israel received the law, and it's also where Elijah later fled and heard God speak in a still, small voice after the fire, earthquake, and wind.

witness.excerpt: The other name of it, Horeb , is never used by Josephus: and perhaps was its name among the Egyptians only, whence the Israelites were lately come; as Sinai was its name among the Arabians, Canaanites, and other nations.

entries.title: Horem
entries.summary: A fortified town of Naphtali, listed with Iron and Migdal-el. The name means roughly "sacred place", and the site is unknown.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of the fenced cities of the tribe of Naphtali, listed in Joshua 19:38 alongside Iron and Migdal-el. Its exact site is unknown; the name means roughly "consecrated" or "sacred place."

entries.title: Hori (Edomite living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: In Edom's genealogies he is one of the Horite clan chiefs, and that is all the record gives.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Hori was a Horite clan chief in Edom's genealogies, and also the name of the father of the spy who represented the tribe of Simeon.

entries.title: Hori (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Numbers names him once, and he is a man from the wilderness years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Horims (Edomite living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: They lived in the region that became Edom before Esau's descendants pushed them out. Genesis records them as the land's earlier people.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: The Horites were the original inhabitants of the region that became Edom before Esau's descendants displaced them, mentioned in Genesis's genealogical record of the land's earlier population.

entries.title: Hormah (Zephath)
entries.summary: Its name means "devoted to destruction", and it was first called Zephath. Israel was beaten there after going into Canaan without the Lord, following the spies' report. Later Israel vowed to destroy the cities of the region, and the vow, kept under Joshua, gave the town its name.
entries.books: Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, 1 Chronicles
entries.label: 6 books
entries.dictNote: Hormah, meaning "devoted to destruction," was a town in the Negev originally called Zephath. Israel was first routed there by the Amalekites and Canaanites after presuming to invade Canaan without the Lord's presence following the spies' report. Later, after a Canaanite king attacked and took Israelite captives, Israel vowed to destroy the region's cities in retaliation, a vow finally fulfilled under Joshua, giving the site its lasting name.

entries.title: Horonaim
entries.summary: A Moabite town south of the Arnon, and Isaiah and Jeremiah both name it among the towns that would fall. The name means "two hollows". Where it was is not known for sure.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Horonaim was a Moabite city south of the Arnon River, cited repeatedly in Isaiah's and Jeremiah's oracles of judgment against Moab as one of the towns that would fall and mourn in the coming disaster (Isaiah 15:5; Jeremiah 48:3, 5, 34). Its name, meaning "two caverns" or "two hollows," suggests it sat in a valley or ravine setting. Its precise location has not been identified with confidence.

entries.title: Horonite (People, perhaps from Horon)
entries.summary: Sanballat's label, and the man was one of Nehemiah's chief opponents over the wall. It probably means he came from Horonaim in Moab or from one of the Beth-horons. The Elephantine papyri name him as governor of Samaria.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Horonite identifies Sanballat, one of the chief opponents of Nehemiah's project to rebuild Jerusalem's walls, probably from Horonaim in Moab or one of the two towns called Beth-horon. Sanballat's role as governor of Samaria is independently confirmed by the Elephantine papyri, a cache of Jewish letters from Egypt that name him, lending solid historical grounding to Nehemiah's account.

entries.title: Hosah
entries.summary: Named once, in Joshua, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hosah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A Levite of Merari's family whom David made a gatekeeper, and his family kept the post after him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Hosah is a name shared by a place and a person. It marks a town on the border of Asher near Tyre (Joshua 19:29) and, more prominently, a Levite of the family of Merari whom David appointed as one of the gatekeepers of the sanctuary, a post his family continued to hold (1 Chronicles 16:38; 26:10-16).

entries.title: Hosea (King living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: God told Hosea to marry Gomer, a woman who would be unfaithful, and his taking her back again and again became his book's picture of God with Israel. He prophesied to the north in the decades before it fell to Assyria. The same name, spelled Hoshea, belongs to four other men.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Hosea was a prophet to northern Israel whom God commanded to marry a promiscuous woman named Gomer as a living picture of Israel's unfaithfulness to God, and Hosea's repeated forgiveness and pursuit of Gomer even after she left him for other men became the book's central metaphor for God's relentless love toward an unfaithful people. He prophesied in the decades leading up to Israel's fall to Assyria, and his book is full of marriage and family imagery, naming his children symbolic names that doubled as warnings to the nation.

entries.title: Hosea (Prophet living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A prophet from the divided-kingdom years, and Hosea is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hoshaiah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: He is known only as the father of one of the leaders who took the survivors down to Egypt and forced Jeremiah along against his warnings.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Hoshaiah was the father of a group of Jewish refugees who forced Jeremiah to go with them into Egypt against his warnings, and also the name of a leader who took part in the dedication of Jerusalem's rebuilt walls.

entries.title: Hoshaiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Nehemiah names him once, and he is a man from the exile and the return.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hoshama (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Son of Jeconiah, the king of Judah taken to Babylon, and probably born while his father was a prisoner there. Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Hoshama was a son of King Jeconiah (Jehoiachin) of Judah, listed among the royal descendants in 1 Chronicles 3:18, likely born during his father's long imprisonment in Babylon. Nothing further is recorded about him.

entries.title: Hoshea (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hoshea (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of 4 men called Hoshea. This one is a man from the exile and the return, named once in Nehemiah.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hotham (Man living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: Heber's son, of Beriah's clan and a chief in Asher; another Hotham turns up among David's warriors.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Hotham was a chief of the tribe of Asher, son of Heber of the clan of Beriah (1 Chronicles 7:32). A second Hotham, the Aroerite, is listed among David's mighty warriors (1 Chronicles 11:44).

entries.title: Hotham (Warrior living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a warrior from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hothir (Levite living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Heman had fourteen sons, and Hothir was one of them. Heman was David's seer and a lead Levite musician, and Hothir led one of the divisions of temple musicians chosen by lot.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Hothir was one of the fourteen sons of Heman, David's seer and a chief Levite musician, and was appointed with his brothers to lead one of the divisions of temple musicians organized by lot (1 Chronicles 25:4, 28).

entries.title: Hukkok
entries.summary: A Levitical town near the border of Naphtali and Asher, not far from the Jordan. It may be the village of Yakuk near the Sea of Galilee.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Hukkok was a town near the border of Naphtali and Asher, not far from the Jordan, that appears in the list of Levitical cities given to the Gershonite Kohathites (1 Chronicles 6:60). It has been tentatively identified with the village of Yakuk near the Sea of Galilee.

entries.title: Hul (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Aram's son, Shem's grandson, in the Table of Nations. Like the other names there it probably means a clan or district. Its location is not known.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Hul appears in the Table of Nations as one of the sons of Aram and a grandson of Shem (Gen. 10:23; 1 Chr. 1:17). Like other names in this genealogy, it most likely designates an Aramean clan or district rather than a single individual, though its location has not been identified with confidence.

entries.title: Huldah (Prophetess living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Josiah's officials took the scroll found in the temple to her, a prophetess in Jerusalem, and not to any of the men prophesying at the time. She told them it was genuine. Judgment was coming on Judah, she said, though not in Josiah's lifetime.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Huldah was a prophetess in Jerusalem during King Josiah's reign, and when workers repairing the temple discovered a forgotten scroll of the law, Josiah sent his officials directly to Huldah rather than to any of the male prophets active at the time, and she confirmed the scroll's authority and predicted the coming judgment on Judah, though not within Josiah's own lifetime.

entries.title: Humtah
entries.summary: A hill-country town of Judah, grouped with Hebron in Joshua's list, and its site has not been found.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Humtah was a town in the hill country of Judah, grouped with Hebron in the town list of Joshua 15:54. Nothing further is known of it, and its exact site remains unidentified.

entries.title: Hupham (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Benjamin's son, and the Huphamite clan in the wilderness census comes from him. Genesis and Chronicles call him Huppim.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Hupham was a son of Benjamin and founder of the Huphamite clan, counted in the wilderness census of Numbers 26:39. He is also called Huppim in Genesis 46:21 and 1 Chronicles 7:12.

entries.title: Huphamites (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: They were Hupham's clan, counted in the census of Numbers 26.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Huphamites were the clan descended from Hupham, a son of Benjamin, counted in the Numbers 26 census.

entries.title: Huppah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: In David's reign the priests served by rota, and Huppah headed the thirteenth of the twenty-four divisions.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A priest in David's reign, head of the thirteenth of the twenty-four priestly divisions organized for rotating temple service (1 Chr. 24:13).

entries.title: Huppim (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Another of Benjamin's sons, whose descendants became one of the tribe's clans in the genealogies.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Huppim was a son of Benjamin, and his descendants formed one of the clans counted among Benjamin's tribe in Israel's genealogies.

witness.excerpt: And the sons of Benjamin: Bela and Becher, and Ashbel, Gera, and Naaman, and Ehi, and Rosh, and Muppim, and Huppim, and Ard--eleven.

entries.title: Huppim (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Genesis names him once, and he is a man from the wilderness years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hur (Aaron's compatriot living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: He helped Aaron hold up Moses's arms while Israel fought Amalek, since Israel won as long as those hands stayed up. When Moses went up Sinai for the law, Hur was left in charge with Aaron.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Hur assisted Aaron in holding up Moses's tired arms during the battle against Amalek, a task that kept Israel winning as long as Moses's hands stayed raised, and he was left in charge alongside Aaron while Moses was on Mount Sinai receiving the law.

witness.excerpt: But Moses not being able to sustain his hands thus stretched out, (for as often as he let down his hands, so often were his own people worsted:) he had his brother Aaron, and Hur, their sister Miriam’s husband, to stand on each side of him, and take hold of his hands, and not permit his weariness to prevent it, but to assist him in the extension of his hands.

entries.title: Hur (King living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Numbers and Joshua name him twice, and he is a king from the wilderness years.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Hur (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of 3 men called Hur. This one is a man from the exile and the return, named once in Nehemiah.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hurai (Warrior living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Chronicles' name for one of David's thirty, from the valley by Mount Gaash in Ephraim. Samuel's list calls him Hiddai.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Hurai was one of David's thirty mighty warriors, a native of the valley near Mount Gaash in the hill country of Ephraim (1 Chronicles 11:32). The parallel list in 2 Samuel 23:30 gives his name as Hiddai.

entries.title: Huram (King living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Chronicles spells the king of Tyre this way. He is the Hiram who sent materials for Solomon's temple.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Huram is an alternate spelling of Hiram, covered under that entry; it refers to the king of Tyre who supplied materials for Solomon's temple and a skilled bronzeworker of the same name Hiram sent to craft the temple's furnishings.

entries.title: Huram (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: One of 3 men called Huram. This one is a man from the wilderness years, named once in 1 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Huram (Syrian living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: The bronzeworker the king of Tyre sent to make the temple's furnishings, spelled Huram in Chronicles and Hiram elsewhere.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Huri (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A Gadite in Bashan, east of the Jordan, and father of Abihail. Gad's genealogy runs through him down to family heads in the days of Jotham of Judah and Jeroboam II of Israel. Nothing else is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Huri was a Gadite, father of Abihail, listed in the genealogy of the tribe of Gad that settled in Bashan east of the Jordan (1 Chronicles 5:14). The chapter traces this branch of Gad's descendants down to family heads living in the region during the reigns of Jotham of Judah and Jeroboam II of Israel. Beyond his place in this genealogical chain, nothing else is recorded about him.

entries.title: Hushah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One name in Judah's genealogy, tied to the descendants of Ezer.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A name appearing in the genealogies of Judah, associated with the descendants of Ezer (1 Chronicles 4:4).

entries.title: Hushai (David's compatriot living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: David's friend, who stayed behind when Absalom rebelled so he could work from inside Absalom's court. Ahithophel gave Absalom sound advice, Hushai talked him into a worse plan, and the time it bought saved David.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Hushai was David's loyal friend who stayed behind during Absalom's rebellion specifically to infiltrate Absalom's court and counter Ahithophel's sound military advice with a deliberately worse plan, a deception that bought David crucial time to regroup and ultimately saved his life.

entries.title: Husham (King living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: He was king of Edom in the days before Israel had any king.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Husham was an early king of Edom, listed among the rulers who governed there before Israel had a king of its own.

entries.title: Hushathite (Warriors, perhaps from Hushath)
entries.summary: Two of David's mighty men carry this label, Sibbecai and Mebunnai, and it ties them to Hushah in Judah's genealogy. Sibbecai is also the one who killed a Philistine giant in a later battle at Gob.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Hushathite marks two of David's mighty men, Sibbecai and Mebunnai, as coming from Hushah, a town associated with Judah's descendants. Sibbecai is separately credited with killing a Philistine giant during a later battle at Gob.

entries.title: Hushim (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 3 men called Hushim. This one is a man from the divided-kingdom years, named once in 1 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hushim (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Genesis names him once, and he is a man from the wilderness years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hushim (Woman living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of the wives of a Benjamite clan leader in the Chronicles genealogy. The same name belongs to a son of Dan.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Hushim was the name of a son of Dan and also of one of the wives of a Benjamite clan leader listed in the genealogies of Chronicles.

witness.excerpt: And the sons of Dan were Hushim, and Sâmôn, and Asûdî, and ’Îjâka, and Salômôn--six.

entries.title: Hymenaeus (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Paul names him twice, both times as a warning. In one letter he and Alexander are handed over to Satan for blasphemy; in the other he and Philetus are teaching that the resurrection has already happened, and some have lost their faith over it. He was probably at Ephesus.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Hymenaeus was a man in the early church, probably at Ephesus, whom Paul names twice as an example of shipwrecked faith. In 1 Timothy 1:20 Paul says he handed Hymenaeus and Alexander over to Satan for blasphemy, and in 2 Timothy 2:17-18 he links Hymenaeus with Philetus for teaching that the resurrection had already taken place, a claim Paul says overturned the faith of some believers.

entries.title: I-chabod (Levite living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: His mother named him as she died giving birth, having just heard that the ark was taken and that her husband Phinehas and his father Eli were both dead. The name means "no glory".
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Ichabod was born to the wife of Phinehas, Eli's son, just as she was dying in childbirth after hearing that the ark of the covenant had been captured by the Philistines and that both her husband and father-in-law had been killed in the same battle. She named the child Ichabod, meaning "no glory," saying that Israel's glory had departed since the ark was gone (1 Samuel 4:19-22).

entries.title: Ibhar (David's son living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Born to David in Jerusalem, after he was king, and nothing more.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Ibhar was one of David's sons born in Jerusalem after he became king.

entries.title: Ibleam
entries.summary: A town given to Manasseh inside Issachar's borders, where the Canaanites were never driven out. King Ahaziah of Judah took his death wound near there, running from Jehu. It is generally identified with Khirbet Bel'ameh, near Jenin.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Ibleam was a town assigned to Manasseh that lay within Issachar's borders, though the Canaanites there were never fully driven out (Joshua 17:11; Judges 1:27). It is best known as the place where King Ahaziah of Judah was mortally wounded while fleeing Jehu's purge of Ahab's dynasty (2 Kings 9:27). It is generally identified with Khirbet Bel'ameh, near Jenin.

entries.title: Ibneiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Jeroham's son, a Benjamite, among the family heads who settled in Jerusalem after the exile.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Son of Jeroham, a Benjamite listed among the heads of families who resettled in Jerusalem after the exile, named in 1 Chronicles 9:8.

entries.title: Ibnijah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: After the exile he was one of the Benjamite family heads living in Jerusalem, and that is the extent of him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Benjamite listed among the family heads who resettled in Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile, in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 9:8. Nothing further is recorded about him.

entries.title: Ibri (Levite living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A Merarite Levite of Jaaziah's family, in the Levitical divisions of David's time. Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Ibri was a Merarite Levite of the family of Jaaziah, listed among the Levitical divisions organized in the time of David (1 Chronicles 24:27). Nothing further is recorded about him.

entries.title: Ibzan (Judge living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: He judged Israel from Bethlehem for seven years and had thirty sons and thirty daughters. Nothing else of his rule is recorded.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Ibzan was the tenth judge of Israel, ruling for seven years from his hometown of Bethlehem (Judges 12:8-10). The text notes that he had thirty sons and thirty daughters, but records nothing else of his rule.

witness.excerpt: Now when Jephtha was dead, Ibzan took the government; being of the tribe of Judah, and of the city of Bethlehem.

entries.title: Iconium
entries.summary: Modern Konya, in central Asia Minor. Paul and Barnabas came here after being thrown out of Antioch in Pisidia, and a crowd of Jews and Gentiles turned on them, so they fled to Lystra and Derbe. Paul came back later to strengthen the church.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Iconium was the capital of ancient Lycaonia in central Asia Minor, modern Konya, visited by Paul and Barnabas on their first missionary journey after they were expelled from Antioch in Pisidia (Acts 13:51-14:1). A mixed crowd of Jews and Gentiles turned against them there too, forcing them to flee to Lystra and Derbe, though Paul returned to strengthen the young church on his way back (Acts 14:19-21).

entries.title: Idalah
entries.summary: On Zebulun's border, listed with Shimron and the Bethlehem of Zebulun. It is often placed near the Kishon valley, though nobody is sure.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Idalah, a town on the border of the tribe of Zebulun, listed with Bethlehem of Zebulun and Shimron in Joshua 19:15. It is often identified with a site near the Kishon valley, though the location is not certain.

entries.title: Idbash (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: One of three sons of "the father of Etam", in Judah's genealogy, with a sister named Hazelelponi.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of three sons of the father of Etam, listed in the tribal genealogy of Judah alongside his sister Hazelelponi (1 Chronicles 4:3).

entries.title: Iddo (Levite living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A levite from the divided-kingdom years. 1 Chronicles names him once.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Iddo (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Named once, in a list of tribal officers in Chronicles, and that is all the record holds.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Iddo (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Zechariah the prophet is called his grandson in Zechariah's opening lines and his son in Ezra, so the family is remembered through him.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Iddo was a common name in the postexilic period, most notably the prophet Zechariah's grandfather, and also a seer whose otherwise lost records are cited as sources in Chronicles for the reigns of Solomon, Rehoboam, and Abijah.

entries.title: Iddo (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of 5 men called Iddo. This one is a man from the exile and the return, named twice in Nehemiah.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Iddo (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: A man from the united kingdom, and 1 Kings is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Iddo (Prophet living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A seer whose writings Chronicles cites for the reigns of Solomon, Rehoboam and Abijah. The writings themselves are lost.
entries.label: 1 book

witness.excerpt: Since Zachariah the prophet was really the son of Barachiah, and grandson of Iddo : Zach.

entries.title: Iddo (Prophet living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Ezra's company was short of temple ministers, so Ezra sent to this Iddo, the leader at the place where they could be found.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Idumaea (Idumea)
entries.summary: Edom, under its Greek and Roman name, south of Judea. John Hyrcanus had forced it into Judea, and Herod the Great's family came from its people. Mark lists it among the places crowds came from to see Jesus.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The Greek and Roman name for Edom, the region south of Judea named for Esau's descendants. By the New Testament era its Idumean population had been forcibly incorporated into Judea under the Hasmonean ruler John Hyrcanus, and it was from this Idumean stock that the family of Herod the Great descended; Mark 3:8 lists Idumea among the regions from which crowds came to Jesus.

entries.title: Igal (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 3 men called Igal. This one is a man from the divided-kingdom years, named once in 1 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Igal (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Issachar's man among the twelve spies Moses sent into Canaan.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Igal was one of the twelve spies Moses sent to scout Canaan, representing the tribe of Issachar, and also the name of one of David's mighty warriors.

entries.title: Igal (Warrior living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: 2 Samuel names him once, and he is a warrior from the united kingdom.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Igdaliah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: "The man of God", Jeremiah calls him, and gives nothing else. His son Hanan had a room in the temple, and that room is where Jeremiah tested the Rechabites.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Igdaliah was called "the man of God," an otherwise unknown prophet or holy figure whose son Hanan had a chamber in the temple where Jeremiah gathered the Rechabites to test their obedience to their ancestral vow (Jer. 35:1-4).

entries.title: Iim
entries.summary: The name means ruins, and two places carry it. One is a town in the far south of Judah near Edom; the other is a late stop in the wilderness, just before Israel reached Moab's border.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Iim, meaning ruins, is used of two separate places in the record. The first is a town in the far south of Judah near the Edomite border (Joshua 15:29). The second is one of the late stations in Israel's wilderness itinerary, mentioned just before the arrival at the border of Moab (Numbers 33:45). The two are unrelated beyond sharing a common Hebrew word for heaps of ruins.

entries.title: Ije-abarim (Iye-abarim)
entries.summary: They camped here on the border of Moab late in the journey from Egypt. The name means "ruins of Abarim", after the range east of the Jordan, and the camp itself has not been found.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Ije-abarim, ruins of Abarim, was a wilderness station on the border of Moab where Israel camped late in the journey from Egypt (Numbers 21:11; 33:44). Its name recalls the Abarim mountain range east of the Jordan, though the precise campsite has not been located.

entries.title: Ijon
entries.summary: In Naphtali, in Israel's far north. Ben-hadad took it at Asa's request, and later Tiglath-pileser III took it in Pekah's reign, a conquest his own inscriptions also list. It is usually identified with Tell Dibbin.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Ijon was a city in the tribe of Naphtali in Israel's far north, captured by the Aramean king Ben-hadad at Asa's request (1 Kings 15:20; 2 Chronicles 16:4) and later by Assyria's Tiglath-pileser III during Pekah's reign (2 Kings 15:29). Tiglath-pileser's own summary inscriptions list the conquest of this same cluster of Galilean towns, an independent confirmation of the biblical account. It is usually identified with the site of Tell Dibbin in the Marj Ayyun valley.

witness.excerpt: So they went and burnt some of them, and spoiled others; Ijon, and Dan, and Abelmain (33) and many others.

entries.title: Ikkesh (Warrior living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: His son Ira, from Tekoa, was one of David's mighty warriors.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Ikkesh was the father of Ira, one of David's mighty warriors from Tekoa.

entries.title: Ilai (Warrior living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: An Ahohite among David's chief warriors. Samuel's list has Zalmon in his place.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: An Ahohite counted among David's chief warriors, called Zalmon in the parallel list in Samuel (1 Chronicles 11:29; 2 Samuel 23:28).

entries.title: Illyricum
entries.summary: Paul says he preached as far as Illyricum, and that was the farthest he went. It lay along the eastern Adriatic, roughly modern Albania and the Dalmatian coast.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A region along the eastern Adriatic coast, corresponding roughly to modern Albania and the Dalmatian coast, marking the farthest extent of Paul's preaching according to Romans 15:19. Paul traveled through Macedonia toward its border on his third missionary journey.

photo.description: panorama of a coastline in Illyricum

entries.title: Imla (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Micaiah's father. Micaiah was the one prophet at Ahab's court who would contradict the four hundred and say Ahab would die in battle.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Imlah was the father of Micaiah, the one prophet at Ahab's court willing to contradict four hundred court prophets and correctly predict Ahab's death in battle.

entries.title: Immanuel (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: "God with us." Isaiah gave the name to King Ahaz as a sign that the danger to Judah would pass before a child called by it was old enough to know right from wrong. Matthew applies it to Jesus' birth, and which child Isaiah first had in view is still argued over.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Immanuel, meaning "God with us," is not a historical individual but a prophetic name. Isaiah gave it as a sign to King Ahaz, promising that before a child bearing this name grew old enough to know right from wrong, the threat facing Judah would pass (Isaiah 7:14), and used it again as a rallying cry against Judah's enemies (Isaiah 8:8). Matthew's Gospel applies the name to Jesus' birth as its ultimate fulfillment (Matthew 1:23), while the identity of the child originally in view in Isaiah's own day is still debated among interpreters.

entries.title: Immer
entries.summary: Ezra and Nehemiah name him twice, and nothing else is recorded.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Immer (Levite living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles and Nehemiah name him twice, and he is a Levite from the exile and the return.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Immer (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Head of one of David's twenty-four priestly divisions, and his family name comes back with the returning exiles.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Immer was the head of a priestly family, one of the twenty-four divisions of priests King David organized for rotating temple service, and descendants bearing his family name appear among the postexilic returnees.

entries.title: Immer (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A man from the exile and the return, and Nehemiah is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Imna (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A later man of Asher's line, in Chronicles, distinct from Asher's own son of the same name.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Imna (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 2 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Imna (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: A son of Asher. Genesis, Numbers and Chronicles all list him. Numbers counts a clan from him.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Imnah was a son of Asher, listed among the tribal genealogies in Genesis and Numbers.

witness.excerpt: And the sons of Asher: Imnah, and Ishvah, (and Ishvi), and Beriah, and Serah, their one sister--six.

entries.title: Imrah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Zophah's son, in Asher's family lines in Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A descendant of Asher through the family of Zophah, listed among the heads of households in the tribal genealogy of 1 Chronicles 7:36.

entries.title: Imri (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: His family, from Judah, was among those who resettled Jerusalem after the exile. Chronicles gives his name as an ancestor and nothing about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Imri (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Father of Zaccur, who repaired a stretch of the wall under Nehemiah.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Two men named Imri appear in postexilic records: an ancestor of a family from the tribe of Judah listed among those who resettled Jerusalem after the exile (1 Chronicles 9:4), and the father of Zaccur, who helped rebuild a section of Jerusalem's wall under Nehemiah (Nehemiah 3:2). Whether they are the same person is not stated.

entries.title: India
entries.summary: Not a person. Esther marks the eastern edge of Ahasuerus's empire with it, with Cush at the other end and 127 provinces in between, and it most likely means the Indus region.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: India is not a person but the eastern limit of the Persian Empire under King Ahasuerus (Xerxes), named alongside Cush (Ethiopia) to mark the vast extent of his dominion, stretching over 127 provinces (Esther 1:1; 8:9). It likely refers to the Indus River region rather than the full subcontinent.

witness.excerpt: And Phison, which denotes a Multitude, running into India, makes its exit into the sea; and is by the Greeks called Ganges.
