entries.title: Jehoiachin (King living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Three months on Judah's throne, then he surrendered to Nebuchadnezzar and went to Babylon with much of Jerusalem's upper class. He spent thirty-seven years a prisoner. A new Babylonian king let him out and fed him at the royal table for the rest of his life, and 2 Kings ends there.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Jehoiachin was a king of Judah who reigned only three months before surrendering to Nebuchadnezzar's siege and being taken captive to Babylon along with much of Jerusalem's elite. He remained a prisoner for thirty-seven years until a new Babylonian king released him and gave him a regular place at the royal table for the rest of his life, a small note of hope that closes out 2 Kings.

witness.excerpt: He also reproached him for his ingratitude; that when he had received the Kingdom from him, who had taken it from Jehoiachin, and given it him, he had made use of the power he gave him against him that gave it.

entries.title: Jehoiada (David's compatriot living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Known through his son, the commander of David's bodyguard who carried out the killings after David's death, in Samuel and Kings.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Jehoiada (High Priest living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: After Athaliah killed the royal family, this priest hid the baby Joash in the temple for six years and then led the coup that put him on the throne. While Jehoiada lived, Joash ruled well. They buried him among the kings.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Jehoiada was the priest who hid the infant king Joash in the temple for six years after Queen Athaliah massacred the rest of the royal family, then staged a coordinated coup that overthrew Athaliah and installed Joash as Judah's rightful king. As long as Jehoiada lived he guided Joash toward faithful reform, and Judah's leadership honored him at his death with burial among the kings, an honor no other priest received.

witness.excerpt: So he called Jehoiada, and bid him send the Levites and Priests through all the countrey to require half a shekel of silver for every head, towards the rebuilding and repairing of the temple, which was brought to decay by Jehoram, and Athali
Out of the tribe of Levi came four thousand and seven hundred, having Jehoiada for their leader.
He also made Seisan the scribe, and committed the command over the guards of his body to Benaiah; the son of Jehoiada.

entries.title: Jehoiakim (King living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Pharaoh Necho put him on Judah's throne. When Jeremiah's scroll was read to him, he cut it off a section at a time and burned it in the fire pot, while his advisors begged him to stop. Jeremiah had it written out again, with more added.
entries.label: 5 books
entries.dictNote: Jehoiakim was installed as king of Judah by the Egyptian pharaoh Necho and later switched allegiance to Babylon under pressure, and he is remembered mainly for his contempt toward the prophet Jeremiah's warnings: when a scroll of Jeremiah's prophecies was read to him, Jehoiakim cut off each section with a knife and burned it in a fire pot as it was read, unmoved even as advisors begged him to stop. Jeremiah had the entire scroll rewritten, with additional judgments added specifically because of what Jehoiakim had done to the first copy.

Now Zedekiah was twenty and one years old when he took the government; and had the same mother with his brother Jehoiakim: but was a despiser of justice, and of his duty.

entries.title: Jehoram (King living at the time of Divided Monarchy)

entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Two kings named Jehoram appear in the Old Testament, one ruling northern Israel as Ahab's son, killed by Jehu in the coup that ended his family's dynasty; the other ruling Judah, who murdered all his own brothers to secure the throne and married Ahab's daughter Athaliah, importing Baal worship into Judah before dying of a prolonged and painful intestinal disease the prophet Elijah had predicted for him.

entries.title: Jehoshabeath (Woman living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: King Jehoram's daughter and the priest Jehoiada's wife. When Athaliah set out to kill the royal family, she hid the baby Joash and his nurse in a temple storeroom, and Kings calls her Jehosheba.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Daughter of King Jehoram of Judah and sister of King Ahaziah, married to the priest Jehoiada. When the queen mother Athaliah moved to kill off the royal family after Ahaziah's death, Jehoshabeath hid the infant Joash and his nurse in a temple storeroom, preserving the Davidic line (2 Chronicles 22:11). She appears as Jehosheba in the parallel account in 2 Kings 11.

entries.title: Jehoshaphat (King living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A king of Judah who sent officials and Levites through the land to teach the law. His alliance with Israel kept going wrong, and in one battle enemy soldiers took him for Ahab and nearly killed him. When Moab, Ammon and Edom invaded together, he sent singers ahead of the army, and the invaders destroyed each other.
entries.label: 5 books
entries.dictNote: Jehoshaphat was a king of Judah remembered for his religious reforms, sending officials and Levites throughout the kingdom to teach the law, and for an alliance with the northern kingdom of Israel that repeatedly went badly, including a joint military campaign that nearly got him killed when enemy soldiers mistook him for the wicked king Ahab. His greatest crisis came when Moab, Ammon, and Edom invaded together; rather than fight, Jehoshaphat sent singers ahead of his army to praise God, and the invading coalition turned on itself and destroyed its own forces before Judah ever engaged. Several minor figures elsewhere in the Old Testament also share the name.

entries.title: Jehoshua (Judge living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness and Conquest)
entries.summary: Joshua, in the longer spelling. Moses's attendant and successor, and one of two from the generation out of Egypt who lived to enter the land. He took Israel over the Jordan, brought down Jericho and divided the land among the tribes. The name means Yahweh saves, the same name Greek renders Jesus.
entries.books: Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 1 Kings, 1 Chronicles
entries.label: 7 books
entries.dictNote: Jehoshua, better known as Joshua, was Moses's attendant and eventual successor, one of only two men from the generation that left Egypt who lived to enter the promised land. He led Israel across the Jordan on dry ground, brought down the walls of Jericho, and directed the campaign that broke Canaanite resistance, dividing the conquered territory among the twelve tribes before his death. His name, meaning Yahweh saves, is the same Hebrew name later rendered Jesus in Greek.

entries.title: Jehu (King living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Anointed king by one of Elisha's students with a single job, to wipe out Ahab's family, and he did it thoroughly: Joram, Jezebel, every descendant left, then Baal's priests tricked into one building and killed together. The Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III shows an Israelite bowing and paying tribute, named as Jehu, though whether the figure is the king himself or his envoy is argued either way.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Jehu was a military commander anointed king of Israel by one of Elisha's prophetic students specifically to destroy Ahab's dynasty, and he carried out that mission with notorious thoroughness, killing King Joram, Queen Jezebel, and every remaining descendant of Ahab's house, then tricking Baal's priests into a fake sacrifice so he could slaughter them all at once. An Assyrian relief, the Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III, depicts Jehu bowing before the Assyrian king and paying tribute, the only known image of an Israelite king in ancient art. The Black Obelisk names the tribute as Jehu's. Whether the prostrate figure on it is Jehu himself or one of his envoys is open, so calling it a picture of an Israelite king goes further than the object does.

Many interpreters identify her with Bithiah, Pharaoh's daughter, named in the same verse, whose marriage into Judah's line made her "the Jewess" by adoption rather than birth.

entries.title: Jephthah (Judge living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: Son of a prostitute, thrown out by his half-brothers, and leading a gang of raiders when Gilead's elders came begging him to fight the Ammonites. He vowed to sacrifice whatever came out of his house first after the victory, and it was his daughter, his only child. Judges tells it without approving the vow or explaining why he kept it.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Jephthah was the son of a prostitute, driven out by his half-brothers and living as a bandit leader until Gilead's elders begged him to lead their fight against the Ammonites. He made a reckless vow that whatever came out of his house first to greet him after victory would be sacrificed to God, and that turned out to be his own daughter, his only child, a story Judges records without endorsing the vow or explaining why Jephthah felt bound to keep it.

entries.title: Jeremiah (Prophet living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A priest's son from Anathoth, called as a young man in Josiah's thirteenth year. For four decades he told Judah Babylon was coming, and for that he was jailed, dropped in a cistern, and had his scroll burned. He saw Jerusalem fall as he had said, then was dragged off to Egypt against his will. His scribe Baruch may be the Berekhyahu on a clay seal from his lifetime.
entries.label: 5 books
entries.dictNote: Jeremiah was a priest's son from Anathoth called to prophesy as a young man in the thirteenth year of King Josiah, and he spent the next four decades warning Judah of the coming Babylonian conquest while the nation's leaders imprisoned him, threw him in a cistern, and burned his prophecies rather than listen. He watched Jerusalem fall exactly as he had predicted and was forced into exile in Egypt against his will after the city's remaining leadership was assassinated. A clay seal impression reading Berekhyahu son of Neriyahu the scribe, found in Jerusalem and dated to Jeremiah's own lifetime, is widely identified with Baruch, the scribe who wrote down Jeremiah's dictated prophecies in Jeremiah 36. Several minor figures elsewhere in the Old Testament share the name Jeremiah but have no connection to the prophet.

entries.title: Jericho
entries.summary: Israel crossed the Jordan and Jericho was the first city it took, walled and gated, with its own king. Achan died for what he stole from the plunder there, a Babylonian robe and silver that belonged to God. By then the place was already ancient: digging at the site has turned up remains about ten thousand years old.
entries.books: Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Jeremiah, Matthew, Mark, Luke, Hebrews
entries.label: 15 books
entries.dictNote: Jericho sat on the west bank of the Jordan, close enough to the cliffs behind it that the site is traditionally linked to Christ's temptation centuries later. Walled and gated, ruled by its own king, it was the first city Israel took after crossing the Jordan, and the plunder found inside it, Babylonian robes and hoarded silver, became the reason Achan was executed for taking what belonged to God. Long before any of that, Jericho had already been standing for millennia: archaeologists have found remains at the site predating the Neolithic period, roughly ten thousand years old, making it one of the oldest continuously occupied settlements ever excavated.
entries.dictSource: International Standard Bible Encyclopedia (1915); Logos Factbook (Baker Encyclopedia)

To stop his people going back to Jerusalem to worship, he set up golden calves at Bethel and Dan with a priesthood of his own. Every northern king after him gets measured against that sin.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Jeroboam was an official under Solomon who led the ten northern tribes in breaking away to form a separate kingdom of Israel after Solomon's son Rehoboam refused to ease his father's harsh labor policies. To keep his new subjects from returning to Jerusalem to worship and possibly switching allegiance back to Judah, Jeroboam set up golden calves at Bethel and Dan and installed his own priesthood, a decision the Old Testament treats as the original sin that doomed every king of northern Israel after him. A later king of Israel, Jeroboam the second, ruled generations afterward during a period of unusual prosperity and military success.

entries.title: Jerusalem
entries.summary: David took it from the Jebusites and made it his capital, and once Solomon's temple stood there it was the centre of Israel's worship for a thousand years. Babylon destroyed it, the exiles rebuilt it, Rome destroyed it again in AD 70. Jesus died and rose just outside its walls, and Revelation ends with a new Jerusalem coming down from heaven.
entries.books: Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther, Psalm, Ecclesiastes, Song of Solomon, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Lamentations, Ezekiel, Daniel, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Micah, Zephaniah, Zechariah, Malachi, Matthew, Luke, Acts, Romans, 1 Corinthians, Galatians, Hebrews, Revelation, Mark, John
entries.label: 36 books
entries.dictNote: Jerusalem was Israel's capital under David, who captured it from the Jebusites and made it his political and religious center, and Solomon's temple there made it the focal point of Israelite worship for a thousand years, through destruction by Babylon, rebuilding under the returned exiles, and a final destruction by Rome in AD 70. Jesus's death and resurrection took place just outside its walls, and its name became synonymous throughout Scripture with God's dwelling among his people, extended in Revelation into the vision of a new Jerusalem descending from heaven. It remains one of the most excavated cities in the world, and finds ranging from Hezekiah's tunnel to the Pilate-era Pool of Siloam continue to confirm details from the biblical account.

entries.dictNote: Jeshua is a shortened, post-exilic spelling of the name Joshua, “the LORD saves,” and in Ezra-Nehemiah it belongs to several different people as well as to a resettled town. entries.title: Jesus (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Born in Bethlehem to Mary and raised in Nazareth in Galilee. Around thirty he began teaching in parables, healing, and gathering twelve disciples, until he was arrested in Jerusalem at Passover, tried before the council and Pontius Pilate, and crucified. His followers said he rose bodily three days later, and the New Testament names him the Messiah, God's own Son become human.
entries.books: Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, Acts, Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, 1 Thessalonians, 2 Thessalonians, 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, Titus, Philemon, Hebrews, James, 1 Peter, 2 Peter, 1 John, 2 John, Jude, Revelation
entries.label: 26 books
entries.dictNote: Jesus of Nazareth is the central figure of the New Testament, born in Bethlehem to Mary, a virgin engaged to Joseph, and raised in Nazareth in Galilee. He began a public ministry around age thirty, teaching in parables, gathering twelve core disciples, and performing miracles of healing and provision that the Gospels present as signs of God's kingdom breaking into the present. His growing following and his direct challenges to the religious establishment led to his arrest in Jerusalem during Passover, a rushed trial before the Jewish council and the Roman governor Pontius Pilate, and execution by crucifixion, a Roman method of execution independently confirmed by archaeology, including a first-century heel bone found in Jerusalem still pierced by an iron nail. Christian faith rests on the claim that Jesus rose bodily from the tomb three days later, an event his earliest followers testified to at the cost of their own lives, and the New Testament identifies him as the promised Messiah, God's own Son become human.

entries.title: Jew (Jacob's son living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: The word comes from Judah. At first it meant someone from the kingdom of Judah, and after the exile it came to cover the whole covenant people descended from Abraham, whatever tribe they came from.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Jew derives from Judah and originally meant a citizen of the kingdom of Judah, later broadening after the exile into the standard term for the entire covenant people descended from Abraham, regardless of which of the twelve original tribes they came from.

entries.title: Jezabel (Queen living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: This is a woman in the church at Thyatira, not the old queen. She called herself a prophetess and taught believers to commit sexual immorality and eat food sacrificed to idols, and John hangs the queen's name on her to say what kind of influence she was.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: This Jezebel is not the Old Testament queen but a woman in the church at Thyatira whom Christ rebukes in Revelation for calling herself a prophetess and teaching believers to commit sexual immorality and eat food sacrificed to idols (Revelation 2:20). John applies the notorious name as a label for her corrupting influence, deliberately recalling the Old Testament queen who promoted Baal worship in Israel, rather than naming an actual descendant or namesake of hers.

entries.title: Jezaniah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Hoshaiah's son, the Maachathite, led one of the bands of Judean soldiers who got out into the countryside when Babylon besieged Jerusalem. He submitted to Gedaliah, Babylon's governor. After Gedaliah was murdered he was one of the leaders who, against Jeremiah's warning, took the people left in Judah off to Egypt.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Jezaniah, son of Hoshaiah the Maachathite, commanded one of the bands of Judean soldiers who had escaped into the countryside during the Babylonian siege of Jerusalem. He submitted to Gedaliah, the governor Babylon installed over Judah, but after Gedaliah's assassination he was among the leaders who, against Jeremiah's warning, forced the remaining Judeans to flee to Egypt (2 Kings 25:23; Jeremiah 40:8; 42:1; 43:2).

entries.title: Jezebel (Queen living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A princess of Sidon, married to Ahab to seal an alliance. As queen she pushed Baal worship and hunted down Yahweh's prophets, and when Naboth would not sell his vineyard she had him framed and stoned. Elijah said dogs would eat her. When Jehu came, she did her makeup and her hair and met him at a window, and he had her thrown down.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Jezebel was a Phoenician princess, daughter of the king of Sidon, whom Ahab married to cement a political alliance, and she used her position as queen to aggressively promote Baal worship and hunt down Yahweh's prophets across Israel. When Naboth refused to sell Ahab a vineyard, Jezebel arranged false charges that got Naboth stoned to death so Ahab could take the land, a crime Elijah confronted directly, prophesying that dogs would eat her body. Years later, when Jehu seized the throne in a violent coup, Jezebel put on makeup and dressed her hair before facing him from a window, and Jehu had her thrown down and left for the dogs, exactly as Elijah had said.

entries.title: Jezerite (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: In the Numbers 26 census, the clan of Jeezer, also called Abiezer, Gilead's son, in Manasseh. It is the same Abiezrite family Gideon was born into, and his hometown Ophrah belonged to it.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Jezerite marks the clan descended from Jeezer, also spelled Abiezer, a son of Gilead within the tribe of Manasseh, counted in the Numbers 26 census. This is the same Abiezrite family into which Gideon was born, and Ophrah, his hometown, belonged to this clan.

entries.title: Jezerites (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: The fourth of twenty-four divisions of temple singers under Asaph, the turn falling by lot to Izri, whose name is elsewhere spelled Zeri.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Jezerites here names the fourth division of the Levitical singers organized under Asaph for temple worship, assigned by lot to Izri, also spelled Zeri, in 1 Chronicles 25:11. Twenty-four such divisions of musicians, each serving in rotation, are listed in the chapter.

entries.title: Jeziah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of the descendants of Parosh in Ezra's long list of men who had married foreign wives and agreed to put them away. Nothing beyond this single mention is known of him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Jeziah was one of the descendants of Parosh named in Ezra 10:25 among the men who had married foreign wives during the exile and agreed, under Ezra's reform, to put them away. He appears in a long list of names grouped by ancestral family, reflecting the scale of the intermarriage crisis Ezra addressed after the return from Babylon. Nothing beyond this single mention is known of him.

entries.title: Jeziel (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Azmaveth's son, a Benjamite archer who could sling stones and shoot arrows with either hand. He came over to David at Ziklag while David was still hiding from Saul, one of the early men from Saul's own tribe.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A son of Azmaveth and one of the skilled Benjamite archers, able to sling stones and shoot arrows with either hand, who joined David at Ziklag while he was still hiding from Saul (1 Chronicles 12:1-3). These early recruits from Saul's own tribe were a notable sign of David's growing support.

entries.title: Jezliah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A Benjamite family head in Jerusalem, one of Elpaal's sons, and nothing else is recorded of him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Benjamite, one of the sons of Elpaal, listed among the family heads who lived in Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 8:18). Nothing else is recorded of him.

entries.title: Jezreel
entries.summary: A valley and town in northern Israel. Naboth's vineyard was there, the one Ahab and Jezebel stole, and it was there that Jehu wiped out Ahab's whole house. Hosea named one of his children Jezreel to say judgment was coming.
entries.books: Joshua, Judges, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 2 Chronicles, Hosea
entries.label: 7 books
entries.dictNote: Jezreel was a strategic valley and town in northern Israel, site of Naboth's vineyard that Ahab and Jezebel stole, and later the site of Jehu's bloody purge of Ahab's entire dynasty, an event the prophet Hosea later named one of his own children after as a symbol of coming judgment.

entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Jezreelite marks a person as being from Jezreel, a town in the fertile valley of the same name. Naboth the Jezreelite is the best known example, the vineyard owner whom Ahab and Jezebel falsely accused and executed to seize his land, a crime the prophet Elijah confronted head on.

entries.title: Jibsam (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)

entries.title: Jidlaph (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: He was Nahor's son by Milcah, and Nahor was Abraham's brother. Jidlaph is one name in the list of his children and nothing more.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Jidlaph was a son of Nahor, Abraham's brother, listed among Nahor's children by his wife Milcah in Genesis 22:22. Nothing further is recorded about him.

entries.title: Joab (David's compatriot living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: David's nephew, and the commander of his army for most of the reign. He was loyal to what David needed rather than what David said: he arranged Uriah's death when asked, killed Absalom when told not to, and murdered Abner and Amasa under cover of friendship. David never forgave him. On David's word Solomon had Joab killed, even holding on to the altar.
entries.label: 5 books
entries.dictNote: Joab was David's nephew and the commander of his army for most of his reign, fiercely loyal to David's interests even when that meant acting against David's explicit wishes, as when he had Absalom killed against David's direct order to spare him. Joab also arranged Uriah's death in battle at David's request to cover up David's affair with Bathsheba, and he murdered two rival commanders, Abner and Amasa, in acts of personal vengeance disguised as reconciliation. David never forgave him for Absalom's death and left instructions for Solomon to have Joab executed, which Solomon carried out even after Joab fled to the altar for sanctuary.

entries.title: Joanna (Woman living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: She was the wife of Chuza, a steward of Herod Antipas, and she helped pay for Jesus' ministry out of her own means. She was also one of the women who found the tomb empty and went to tell the apostles.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Joanna was the name of two figures connected to Luke's Gospel. One was an ancestor of Jesus in Luke's genealogy, apparently the same man Chronicles calls Hananiah, a descendant of Zerubbabel (Luke 3:27; 1 Chronicles 3:19). The other Joanna was the wife of Chuza, a steward of Herod Antipas; she helped support Jesus' ministry financially, and she was among the women who found the empty tomb and reported it to the apostles (Luke 8:3; 24:10).

entries.title: Joannas (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: The genealogy in Luke puts him among Zerubbabel's descendants, through Nathan's line, and Matthew leaves him out. Nothing further about him is recorded.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Listed in Luke's genealogy of Jesus as a descendant of Zerubbabel, in the line traced through Nathan rather than Solomon (Luke 3:27). He does not appear in Matthew's parallel genealogy, and nothing further about him is recorded.

entries.title: Joash (King living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Seven years old when he was made king of Judah, after six years hidden in the temple from his grandmother Athaliah, who had killed the rest of the royal family. While Jehoiada the priest lived, Joash ruled well and repaired the temple. Afterwards he let it go, and when Jehoiada's son stood up to him he had the man stoned in the temple court. His own murder followed.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Joash became king of Judah at seven years old, the only survivor of a massacre his grandmother Athaliah carried out against the rest of the royal family, hidden in the temple for six years by his aunt until the priest Jehoiada staged a coup that killed Athaliah and installed Joash on the throne. Joash ordered the temple repaired and reigned well while Jehoiada lived, but after the priest died he abandoned the reforms, and when Jehoiada's own son confronted him for it, Joash had the man stoned to death in the temple courtyard, a betrayal that led to Joash's own assassination not long after.

entries.summary: Matthew's spelling of Jotham, king of Judah, who stands in the genealogy between his father Uzziah and his son Ahaz. He strengthened Jerusalem's defences and brought the Ammonites under.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The Greek New Testament form of Jotham, king of Judah, named in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus between his father Uzziah and his son Ahaz (Matt. 1:9). Jotham himself ruled Judah in the eighth century BC and is credited in 2 Kings and 2 Chronicles with strengthening Jerusalem's defenses and subduing the Ammonites.

entries.title: Job (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: One of the seventy who went down to Egypt, a son of Issachar. He shares the name with the man in the book of Job only in most English versions. Numbers and Chronicles call him Jashub.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Not the patriarch of the book of Job, despite sharing his name in most English translations. This Job, more often rendered Jashub in the parallel lists of Numbers 26:24 and 1 Chronicles 7:1, is one of the sons of Issachar listed among the seventy descendants of Jacob who went down to Egypt (Gen. 46:13). The overlap in spelling is a known point of confusion between two otherwise unrelated figures.

entries.title: Job (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Uz was his country, and he was rich and righteous until God let Satan take his children, his wealth and his health to see whether his faith was only about the good life. He never curses God, but he does demand an answer. When God speaks from the whirlwind he gives no reason, only the size of creation, and Job goes quiet and gets back double.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Job was a wealthy and righteous man from the land of Uz whose story opens with a wager in the divine council: God allows Satan to strip Job of his children, his wealth, and his health to test whether Job's faith depends on his prosperity. Job never curses God, but he does demand an explanation, and most of the book is a long argument between Job and three friends who insist his suffering must be punishment for hidden sin. When God finally answers from a whirlwind, he never actually explains why Job suffered, instead overwhelming Job with the scale of creation, and Job's response is to fall silent and be restored with double what he had before.

entries.title: Jobesh (-Gilead)
entries.summary: Better known as Jabesh-gilead, a town in Gilead east of the Jordan. Its men stayed home from the war against Benjamin and were nearly wiped out for it, and their daughters were handed to Benjamin's survivors as wives. When Nahash the Ammonite besieged it, Saul rescued it. Years later its men took his body down from the walls of Beth-shan and buried it.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Town in Gilead east of the Jordan, better known as Jabesh-gilead. Its men failed to join Israel's coalition against Benjamin and were nearly wiped out as punishment, until the tribe's survivors were given Jabesh-gilead's surviving virgin daughters as wives to preserve Benjamin's line (Judges 21:8-14). Generations later the Ammonite king Nahash besieged the town, and Saul's rescue of it was his first act as king, one that secured his authority over Israel (1 Sam. 11). After Saul's death in battle, the town's men risked their lives to recover his body from the walls of Beth-shan and gave it honorable burial (1 Sam. 31:11-13; 1 Chr. 10:11-12).

entries.title: Jochebed (Woman living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)

entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Jochebed was the wife of Amram and the mother of Miriam, Aaron, and Moses (Numbers 26:59). She hid the infant Moses for three months and then placed him in a basket on the Nile to save him from Pharaoh's decree, and later nursed him as his hired wet nurse after Pharaoh's daughter drew him from the water (Exodus 2:1-10).

entries.title: Joel (Levite living at the time of United Monarchy)

entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Joel was a prophet whose short book uses a locust plague that had devastated Judah as a picture of an even more terrible coming day of the Lord, calling the nation to repentance and fasting in response. His prophecy that God would pour out his Spirit on all people, sons and daughters, old and young, slave and free, is quoted directly by Peter in Acts to explain what was happening at Pentecost. Several minor figures elsewhere in the Old Testament also share the name.

entries.summary: The prophet who comes out of the wilderness in Matthew 3, preaching repentance and baptising. Jesus came to him to be baptised. Later, from prison, he sent his own disciples to ask whether Jesus was the one.
entries.label: 5 books
entries.dictNote: John was a fisherman, the son of Zebedee and younger brother of James, and part of Jesus's innermost circle along with Peter and James, present at moments the other disciples weren't, including the transfiguration and Gethsemane. Tradition identifies him as the disciple whom Jesus loved in the fourth Gospel, and it was John whom Jesus entrusted with the care of his mother Mary from the cross. He went on to become a leading figure in the Jerusalem church, and early Christian tradition credits him with writing the Gospel of John, three New Testament letters, and the book of Revelation while exiled on the island of Patmos.

entries.dictNote: Jokneam was a Canaanite royal city defeated by Joshua, situated near Mount Carmel by the Kishon River (Joshua 12:22). It fell within Zebulun's territory and was later assigned, with its pasturelands, to the Merarite Levites (Joshua 19:11; 21:34). entries.title: Joktheel

entries.dictNote: Two places carry this name, meaning "subdued by God." One was a town in Judah near Lachish (Josh. 15:38). The other was the new name Amaziah, king of Judah, gave to Sela after conquering Edom and slaughtering its army (2 Kings 14:7); Sela, meaning "rock," is often linked to the Edomite highlands south of the Dead Sea, where a rock outcrop near Bozrah bears a carved relief and inscription of the Babylonian king Nabonidus, evidence that the region's strongholds remained significant for centuries after Amaziah's campaign.

entries.title: Jonah (Prophet living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: God told him to preach to Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, Israel's enemy, and he took a ship the other way. A storm, three days in a great fish, and then he did preach, and the whole city repented and God spared it. That made Jonah furious. The book stops with God questioning his anger and leaves it there.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Jonah was a prophet ordered to preach repentance to Nineveh, the capital of Israel's enemy Assyria, and he ran the opposite direction by ship instead, prompting the storm and the famous three days inside a great fish that eventually vomited him onto dry land. When he finally preached to Nineveh, the entire city repented and God spared it, which made Jonah furious rather than pleased, and the book ends with God gently confronting Jonah's anger rather than resolving it. A different man named Jonah is listed as the father of the apostle Peter in the Gospels.

witness.excerpt: It is also reported that Jonah was swallowed down by a whale, and that when he had been there three days, and as many nights, he was vomited out upon the Euxine Sea, and this alive, and without any hurt upon his body; and there, on his prayer to God, he obtained pardon for his sins, and went to the city Nineveh…

entries.lukeNote: Jesus calls his own coming death and resurrection ‘the sign of Jonah’ (11:29-30) and rates Nineveh's repentance above his own generation's (11:32), both times treating the whale story as settled history, not metaphor. Josephus tells it the same way a century later, adding a detail Jonah itself never states: which sea he surfaced in.

entries.title: Jonathan (David's compatriot living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Saul's eldest son, heir to the throne, and David's friend. He made a covenant with David knowing it cost him the crown. Once, with only his armour-bearer, he climbed a cliff and started a rout of the Philistine army. He died with Saul and two brothers on Mount Gilboa, and David's lament for him says his love was "surpassing the love of women."
entries.label: 5 books
entries.dictNote: Jonathan was Saul's eldest son and heir to Israel's throne, best remembered for his loyal friendship with David, a friendship sealed with a covenant even though Jonathan knew it meant giving up his own claim to the kingship. Early in his father's reign he single-handedly triggered a rout of the Philistine army by climbing a cliff with only his armor-bearer and trusting that God could win with few as easily as with many. He died alongside Saul and two brothers at the battle of Mount Gilboa, and David's lament over him, "your love to me was wonderful, surpassing the love of women," is one of the most quoted lines in the Old Testament.

entries.title: Joppa
entries.summary: Judea's main seaport, a point of land on the Mediterranean. Jonah sailed from there running from Nineveh, and cedar for Solomon's and Zerubbabel's temples came ashore there. In Acts, Peter raised Tabitha at Joppa and, staying with Simon the tanner, had the vision that opened the gospel to Gentiles.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Joppa was Judea's principal seaport, a promontory on the Mediterranean coast from which Jonah once boarded a ship to flee his commission to Nineveh, and through which cedar for both Solomon's and Zerubbabel's temples was floated ashore. In Acts, Peter raised Tabitha from the dead at Joppa and, while staying in the house of Simon the tanner there, received the vision that opened the gospel to Gentiles. The city's capture is recorded in an Egyptian tale from the reign of Thutmose III, describing a general smuggling soldiers inside baskets, evidence of Joppa's strategic importance more than a thousand years before Peter's visit.

entries.title: Jordan
entries.summary: It runs from the slopes of Mount Hermon through the Sea of Galilee and down the Rift Valley to the Dead Sea, about sixty five miles in a straight line and nearer two hundred as the river winds. Israel crossed it on dry ground under Joshua, Elijah and Elisha each parted it, and John the Baptist baptised Jesus in it.
entries.books: Genesis, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Job, Psalm, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Zechariah, Matthew, Mark, Luke, John
entries.label: 21 books
entries.dictNote: The Jordan is the chief river of Palestine, running north to south from the slopes of Mount Hermon through the Sea of Galilee and down the Rift Valley to the Dead Sea, a straight-line distance of about sixty five miles that the river's winding course stretches to roughly two hundred. Its principal sources are the Dan, Banias, and Hasbany springs, all fed by Hermon's snowmelt. The Israelites crossed it on dry ground to enter Canaan under Joshua, Elijah and Elisha each parted its waters, and John the Baptist used it for the baptisms that included Jesus. Excavations at Bethany beyond the Jordan, on the river's east bank, have uncovered Byzantine era churches and baptismal pools marking the traditional site of that baptism.

entries.title: Joseph (Jacob's son living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Jacob's eleventh son and Rachel's first. His father's favouritism and his own tactless dreams got him sold into Egypt by his brothers, and there he rose from slave to prisoner to second in the land by reading Pharaoh's dreams of famine. When the famine drove his brothers down for grain, he told them who he was and forgave them.
entries.books: Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 1 Chronicles, Psalm, Ezekiel, Amos, Obadiah, Zechariah, John, Acts, Hebrews, Revelation
entries.label: 18 books
entries.dictNote: Joseph was Jacob's eleventh son and Rachel's firstborn, sold into Egyptian slavery by his jealous brothers after his father's obvious favoritism and his own tactless dreams made him a target. In Egypt he rose from slave to prison to the second-highest office in the land by correctly interpreting Pharaoh's dreams of coming famine, and when that famine drove his brothers to Egypt for grain, he revealed himself and forgave them, reuniting the family that would become the nation of Israel. His deathbed instructions to carry his bones back to Canaan were kept literally, centuries later, during the exodus.

entries.title: Joseph (Mary's husband living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: A descendant of David from Nazareth, engaged to Mary when she turned out to be pregnant. An angel in a dream talked him out of quietly ending it, and he raised Jesus as his legal father. Scripture says nothing of him after Jesus's boyhood.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: A different Joseph, a descendant of David from the town of Nazareth, was engaged to Mary when she was found to be pregnant before their marriage, and an angel convinced him in a dream to go through with the wedding rather than quietly break the engagement. He raised Jesus as his legal father, and Scripture gives no record of him after Jesus's boyhood, which is usually taken to mean he had died before Jesus's public ministry began.

entries.title: Joses (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Mark names him only to say whose mother she was: one of the women who watched the crucifixion from a distance and saw where Jesus was laid.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Joses was the name of one of Jesus's brothers, and also of Barnabas, whose birth name was Joses before the apostles nicknamed him Barnabas, meaning son of encouragement.

entries.title: Joshah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A chief of the tribe of Simeon. In Hezekiah's reign his family drove the Hamite and Meunite people out of a good valley near Gedor and took it for themselves.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Joshah was a chief of the tribe of Simeon whose family, during Hezekiah's reign, drove out the Hamite and Meunite inhabitants of a fertile valley near Gedor and settled there in their place (1 Chr. 4:34-41).

entries.title: Joshaphat (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A priest who blew a trumpet in front of the ark when David brought it up to Jerusalem.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Joshaphat, called "the Mithnite," is listed among David's mighty warriors in the record of his elite fighting men (1 Chronicles 11:43).

entries.title: Joshaphat (Warrior living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: The Mithnite, one of David's mighty warriors.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Joshaviah (Warrior living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Elnaam's son, and on the roster of David's mighty warriors.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Son of Elnaam, listed among David's mighty warriors in the roster of his elite fighting men (1 Chronicles 11:46).

entries.title: Joshbekashah (Levite living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Heman, David's seer, had a son by this name, and the seventeenth of the twenty-four courses of temple musicians was his.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Joshbekashah was a son of Heman, David's seer, and headed the seventeenth of the twenty-four courses of temple musicians David organized for worship (1 Chronicles 25:4, 24).

entries.title: Josiah (King living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Made king of Judah at eight after his father Amon was murdered. In his eighteenth year workmen repairing the temple found a forgotten scroll of the law, and its reading set off Judah's last great reform: pagan altars torn down, the priests of the high places killed, and a Passover like none since the judges. He died young at Megiddo, trying to stop the Egyptian army reaching Assyria.
entries.books: 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Jeremiah, Zephaniah
entries.label: 6 books
entries.dictNote: Josiah became king of Judah at eight years old after his father Amon was assassinated, and in the eighteenth year of his reign workers repairing the temple found a forgotten scroll of the law, whose reading triggered Judah's last great religious reform: Josiah tore down pagan altars across the kingdom, reinstated Passover on a scale not seen since the days of the judges, and executed the priests of the high places he destroyed. He died young, killed in battle at Megiddo trying to block the Egyptian army from reinforcing Assyria, and Judah's slide toward Babylonian exile resumed almost immediately under his successors. The Babylonian Chronicle, a cuneiform tablet recording the same Egyptian campaign, confirms the military situation that cost Josiah his life.

witness.excerpt: After Amon reigned Josiah. He was both righteous, and religious. As also concerning Huldah the Prophetess.

entries.curatedNote: The boy-king whose reforms follow the rediscovery of the Law scroll in the temple (2 Kings 22-23). Josephus's chapter groups him with Huldah the prophetess, the same pairing 2 Kings makes, the king who acts, and the prophetess he consults to be sure the scroll is genuine.

entries.title: Josiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Zechariah names him once, and he is a man from the exile and the return.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Josias (King living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Matthew's Greek spelling of Josiah, the boy king of Judah who launched a reform after a scroll of the law turned up during temple repairs, and who died in battle against Pharaoh Necho.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Josias is the Greek form of Josiah, the reforming king of Judah, used in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:10-11). Josiah came to the throne as a boy and later launched a sweeping religious reform after a scroll of the law was discovered during temple repairs, purging idolatrous worship from Judah before his death in battle against Pharaoh Necho.

entries.title: Josibiah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Jehu's father. Jehu was one of the Simeonite family heads who pushed out the Hamite people of Gedor under Hezekiah, and nothing else is recorded about Josibiah himself.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Father of Jehu, one of the Simeonite family heads listed in 1 Chronicles 4:35 among clans that expanded their pasturelands by displacing the Hamite inhabitants of Gedor in Hezekiah's reign. Nothing else is recorded about him.

entries.title: Josiphiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: His son Shelomith brought about 160 men back to Jerusalem with Ezra.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Josiphiah was the father of Shelomith, who led a company of about 160 men among the exiles who returned to Jerusalem with Ezra around 459 BC (Ezra 8:10).

entries.title: Jotbah
entries.summary: Meshullemeth came from there, King Manasseh's wife and mother of Amon. Where it was has been lost. It is a different place from Jotbathah in the wilderness.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Jotbah, the hometown of Meshullemeth, wife of King Manasseh and mother of King Amon of Judah (2 Kings 21:19). Its precise location is not preserved, and it should not be confused with Jotbathah, a wilderness stopping point during the exodus.

entries.title: Jotbath
entries.summary: They camped here in the wilderness, between Hor-hagidgad and Ebronah. Moses remembered it as a land of brooks of water, which in that desert stood out. Nobody knows for sure where it was.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Jotbathah was one of the stations where the Israelites camped during the wilderness wanderings, between Hor-hagidgad and Ebronah (Numbers 33:33-34). Moses later recalled it in Deuteronomy 10:7 as a land of brooks of water, a notable contrast to the surrounding desert. Its exact location in the Sinai peninsula is not known with certainty.

entries.title: Jotham (King living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: He carried on his father Uzziah's steady rule in Judah, building up Jerusalem's defences and bringing the Ammonites under, and Scripture counts him one of the few kings who did right in the Lord's eyes. The high places stayed, though.
entries.books: 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Isaiah, Hosea, Micah
entries.label: 6 books
entries.dictNote: Jotham was a king of Judah who continued his father Uzziah's competent rule, strengthening Jerusalem's defenses and subduing the Ammonites, and Scripture credits him as one of the few kings who did right in the Lord's eyes, though it also notes the high places of unauthorized worship were never removed during his reign.

entries.title: Jotham (Man living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: The youngest son, and the only one who got away when his half-brother murdered the other seventy. He stood on a mountain and told the town a fable about trees choosing a bramble for king, then ran for it. By the end of Judges 9 his curse had come true.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jozachar (Ammonite living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of two court officials who killed King Joash of Judah at Beth-millo. Chronicles says it was revenge for the priest Zechariah, and calls him Zabad.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of two court officials who assassinated King Joash of Judah at Beth-millo, in retaliation, according to Chronicles, for the killing of the priest Zechariah (2 Kings 12:20-21); the parallel account in 2 Chronicles 24:26 calls him Zabad.

entries.title: Jozadak (High Priest living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A high priest taken into exile in Babylon. His son Joshua led the priesthood when the exiles came back and rebuilt the temple. Most of his story sits under Jehozadak.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Jozadak was a high priest taken into Babylonian exile, and his son Joshua led the priesthood during the return and rebuilding of the temple, covered more fully under the entry for Jehozadak.

entries.title: Jozadak (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Ezra names him once, and he is a man from the exile and the return.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jubal (Man living at the time before the Flood)
entries.summary: Lamech and Adah's son, in Cain's line, and father of everyone who plays the lyre and pipe. He is the first musician the Bible names.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Son of Lamech and Adah, in the line of Cain, remembered as the ancestor of all who play the lyre and pipe, making him the Bible's first named musician (Genesis 4:21).

witness.excerpt: But Jubal, who was born of the same mother with him, exercised himself in musick;  and invented the psaltery and the harp.

entries.title: Jucal (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of Zedekiah's officials who had Jeremiah dropped into a cistern for weakening the defenders of Jerusalem. He belonged to the party at court that wanted to keep fighting Babylon, and earlier in the same crisis he is called Jehucal.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Son of Shelemiah and one of the officials of King Zedekiah who had Jeremiah thrown into a cistern for discouraging the defenders of Jerusalem (Jeremiah 38:1), also named Jehucal earlier in the same crisis (Jeremiah 37:3). He represents the faction at court pushing for continued resistance against Babylon.

entries.title: Juda(-h (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: They named a lot of men Judah. This one sits in Luke 3:30, in Jesus's line of ancestors, generations after the patriarch, and nothing else is said of him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: This covers the Greek form of Judah used in the New Testament. Judah, son of Jacob and Leah, gave his name to the tribe from which both David and Jesus descended, and the genealogies of Matthew and Luke trace Jesus' ancestry through him; Hebrews notes that Jesus came from this tribe rather than the priestly line of Levi. Revelation draws on Jacob's blessing over Judah to call Jesus "the Lion of the tribe of Judah." The same Greek name also belongs to Jude, the writer of the short New Testament letter that opens by identifying himself as a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James, a different man from the patriarch despite sharing the underlying name.

entries.title: Judaea (Judea)
entries.summary: The Roman name for the southern part of the land around Jerusalem, roughly old Judah. Client kings of Herod's family ruled it, then Roman procurators like Pontius Pilate. John the Baptist preached in its wilderness and the Passion happened there. After the revolt of AD 66 to 70 Rome struck coins reading "Judaea Capta."
entries.books: Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, Acts, Romans, 2 Corinthians, Galatians, 1 Thessalonians
entries.label: 9 books
entries.dictNote: Judaea was the Roman name for the southern portion of Palestine centered on Jerusalem, corresponding roughly to the old territory of Judah and, in a broader New Testament usage, sometimes standing for the whole of Jewish Palestine. It was governed for much of the New Testament period by client kings of the Herodian dynasty and then directly by Roman procurators such as Pontius Pilate. John the Baptist preached in its wilderness, and it was the setting for the Passion narratives and much of Acts. After the Jewish revolt of AD 66 to 70, Rome commemorated its conquest of the province with coins stamped “Judaea Capta.”

entries.title: Judah (Jacob's son living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Leah's fourth son, and the brother who ends up leading. He talked the others into selling Joseph rather than killing him, and later offered himself as a hostage in Benjamin's place. His tribe produced David's royal line and gave its name to the southern kingdom, and Jacob's dying blessing promised the sceptre would not leave him.
entries.books: Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, Ruth, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther, Psalm, Proverbs, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Lamentations, Ezekiel, Daniel, Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Micah, Nahum, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi, Matthew, Luke, Hebrews, Jude, Revelation
entries.label: 38 books
entries.dictNote: Judah was Jacob and Leah's fourth son, and though not the firstborn, he emerges as the de facto leader among his brothers, proposing they sell Joseph into slavery rather than kill him and later offering himself as a hostage in Benjamin's place to protect his father. His tribe became the dominant one in Israel's history, producing David's royal line and giving its name to the southern kingdom of Judah after the nation split, and Jacob's dying blessing over Judah promises that the scepter will not depart from his line until the coming of one to whom obedience belongs.

entries.title: Judith (Woman living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Beeri the Hittite's daughter, one of two Hittite wives Esau took at forty, and the marriage grieved Isaac and Rebekah. She is usually matched with Oholibamah in the later list in Genesis 36, but the two lists name the wives differently and the match has long been argued over.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Judith, daughter of Beeri the Hittite, was one of two Hittite wives Esau married at age forty (Genesis 26:34). She is usually identified with Oholibamah, daughter of Anah, in the later list of Esau's wives in Genesis 36:2, though the two genealogies name his Canaanite wives differently and the harmonization has long been debated. Her marriage, like Esau's other foreign marriages, grieved Isaac and Rebekah.

entries.title: Julia (Woman living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Paul greets her at the end of Romans, alongside Philologus, Nereus and his sister. The name was common in Rome and may tie her to a household of the Julian family, as a freedwoman or slave. Nothing else about her is recorded.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Julia was a Christian in Rome greeted by Paul in his closing salutations in Romans 16:15, grouped together with Philologus, Nereus, and his sister. The common Roman name suggests she may have been a freedwoman or slave connected to a household of the imperial Julian family, a pattern typical of many names in Paul's list. Nothing else about her is recorded beyond this single mention, though her inclusion shows women held recognized places in the earliest Roman house churches.

entries.title: Julius (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: The Roman centurion of the Augustan Cohort who took Paul and other prisoners to Rome. He was kind to Paul all the way, let him see friends at Sidon, and after the wreck at Malta stopped the soldiers from killing the prisoners.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Julius was the Roman centurion of the Augustan Cohort assigned to escort Paul and other prisoners to Rome. He treated Paul with notable kindness throughout the voyage, allowing him to visit friends at Sidon and later protecting him from soldiers who wanted to kill the prisoners after the shipwreck at Malta (Acts 27:1-3, 43).
