entries.title: Junias (Woman living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Paul calls Andronicus and Junias his relatives and fellow prisoners, "outstanding among the apostles." Whether the name is the masculine Junias or the much more common feminine Junia is argued, and most modern scholars now read Junia, a woman.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Junias, or Junia, is a name Paul greets alongside Andronicus in Romans 16:7, calling the pair his relatives and fellow prisoners who were 'outstanding among the apostles.' Whether the Greek name is the masculine Junias or the far more common feminine Junia has been debated, and most modern scholars now favor Junia, which would make her a woman recognized in the earliest church in a role connected to the apostles.

entries.title: Jupiter (A male deity in the New Testament)
entries.summary: At Lystra, after Paul healed a man lame from birth, the crowd decided Barnabas was Jupiter and Paul was Mercury. The priest of Jupiter brought oxen to sacrifice to them, and the two tore their clothes to stop it. Jupiter was the Greeks' Zeus, the chief god.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Jupiter, known to the Greeks as Zeus, was the chief god of the Greco-Roman pantheon, ruler of the sky and the other gods. At Lystra the crowd, astonished when Paul healed a man lame from birth, hailed Barnabas as Jupiter and Paul as Mercury and the local priest of Jupiter, whose temple stood before the city, brought oxen to sacrifice to them until Paul and Barnabas tore their clothes and stopped the crowd (Acts 14:11-18).

witness.excerpt: Those above him being Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars; then comes the Sun himself, and next to him Mercury, Venus, and the Moon, which last is close to the air.
He also frequented that temple of Jupiter which they style the Capitol, which is with them the most holy of all their temples, and had boldness enough to call himself the brother of Jupiter.

Now the last part of this pompous show was at the temple of Jupiter Capitolinus, whither when they were come, they stood still; for it was the Romans' ancient custom to stay till somebody brought the news that the general of the enemy was slain.

entries.title: Jushab-hesed (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of Zerubbabel's sons, in the royal genealogy of Judah after the exile.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of the sons of Zerubbabel, the governor who led the first group of exiles back from Babylon to rebuild the temple, listed in the royal genealogy of Judah after the exile (1 Chronicles 3:20).

entries.title: Justus (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: A second name several early Christians carried. One was a man in Corinth whose house stood next door to the synagogue, and Paul used it as a meeting place.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Justus was a common secondary name among several early Christians, including a man in Corinth whose house neighbored the synagogue and became a meeting place for Paul, and a Jewish coworker of Paul mentioned in Colossians.

entries.title: Justus (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Colossians names him once, and he is a man from the New Testament. The verse is Colossians 4:11.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Juttah
entries.summary: A hill-country town of Judah given to Aaron's line. It survives as the village of Yatta, a few miles south of Hebron, and an old tradition makes it John the Baptist's birthplace.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Juttah was a town in the hill country of Judah assigned to the Levites descended from Aaron (Josh. 15:55; 21:16). It survives as the modern village of Yatta, a few miles south of Hebron, and a long tradition, based on Luke's description of Zechariah and Elizabeth's home as a city of Juda in the hill country, identifies it as the birthplace of John the Baptist (Luke 1:39).

entries.title: Kabzeel
entries.summary: The far south of Judah's land, out by the border with Edom. Benaiah came from there, one of David's best-known warriors and later head of his bodyguard. After the exile it seems to have been lived in again as Jekabzeel.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Kabzeel was a town in the extreme south of Judah's territory, near the border with Edom (Joshua 15:21), and the birthplace of Benaiah, one of David's most celebrated warriors and later commander of his bodyguard (2 Samuel 23:20; 1 Chronicles 11:22). After the exile it appears to have been resettled under the related name Jekabzeel (Nehemiah 11:25).

entries.title: Kadesh
entries.summary: Kadesh-barnea, Israel's main camp in the wilderness of Zin. Moses sent the twelve spies from there, Miriam died there, and there he struck the rock and lost his way into Canaan. It is usually identified with Ain el-Qudeis or Ain el-Qudeirat, where a fortress of the Israelite period has been dug up.
entries.books: Genesis, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Judges, Psalm, Ezekiel
entries.label: 6 books
entries.dictNote: Kadesh, or Kadesh-barnea, was Israel's main encampment in the wilderness of Zin on the southern edge of Canaan, the base from which Moses sent twelve spies into the land and where, decades later, Miriam died and Moses struck the rock in disobedience that cost him entry into Canaan. It is usually identified with the oasis of Ain el-Qudeis or nearby Ain el-Qudeirat, where excavations have uncovered an Israelite period fortress. A different Kadesh, on the Orontes River in Syria, was a Hittite stronghold and the site of a major battle between Ramesses II of Egypt and the Hittite king Muwatalli II, an inconclusive clash later settled by one of the oldest surviving peace treaties in history.

witness.excerpt: And in this month Abraham moved from Hebron, and departed and dwelt between Kadesh and Shur in the mountains  of Gerar.

entries.title: Kadesh
entries.summary: Named once, in Joshua, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Kadeshbarnea
entries.summary: An oasis in the wilderness of Zin, on Canaan's southern edge, where Israel camped for much of the wandering years. The spies went out from here, and the people's fear at their report got that whole generation sentenced to die in the desert. Later it marked the southern boundary of the land.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Kadesh-barnea was an oasis in the wilderness of Zin on the southern border of Canaan where Israel camped for much of the wanderings. It was from here that Moses sent twelve spies into Canaan, and the people's fearful response to their report led God to sentence that generation to die in the wilderness. Kadesh-barnea later marked the southern boundary of the promised land in the tribal allotments.

entries.title: Kadmiel (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A Levite who led worship and helped oversee the rebuilding when the exiles came back, under Zerubbabel and later under Nehemiah.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Kadmiel was a Levite who led temple worship and helped oversee the reconstruction efforts among the returning exiles under Zerubbabel and later Nehemiah.

entries.title: Kadmonites (People, perhaps from Kadmon)
entries.summary: "Easterners." God named them among the peoples in the land when he promised it to Abram. They never turn up again, and nobody knows who they were.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Kadmonites, meaning easterners, were one of the peoples living in Canaan when God promised the land to Abram in Genesis 15:19. They are named alongside better known groups such as the Hittites and Amorites but are not mentioned elsewhere in the Bible, and their exact territory and identity remain unknown.

witness.excerpt: And on that day the Lord made a covenant with Abram, saying: "To thy seed will I give this land, from the river of Egypt unto the great river, the river Euphrates, the Kenites, the Kenizzites, the Kadmonites, the Perizzites, and the Rephaim, the Phakorites,  and the Hivites,  and the Amorites, and the Canaanites, and the Girgashites, and the Jebusites."  19.

entries.title: Kallai (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: He was a priest in Joiakim's time, head of the family of Sallai, in a list of priestly family heads.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A priest in the days of the high priest Joiakim, head of the priestly family of Sallai (Nehemiah 12:20). He appears only in this list of priestly family heads from the generation after the return from exile.

entries.title: Kanah
entries.summary: The name means reedy, and this one is a stream on the border between Ephraim and Manasseh, running from the hill country to the Mediterranean. Another Kanah, a town up in Asher, is a separate place.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Kanah names two separate places sharing one word for reedy. One is a stream that formed part of the border between Ephraim and Manasseh, running from the hill country to the Mediterranean (Joshua 16:8; 17:9). The other is a town in the northern part of Asher's territory (Joshua 19:28), distinct from the stream and generally located further north toward Tyre.

entries.title: Kanah (Cana)
entries.summary: Named once, in Joshua, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Karkaa
entries.summary: On Judah's southern boundary, between Adar and Azmon in the wilderness of Zin. Its exact site is unknown.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A landmark on the southern boundary of Judah's territory, between Adar and Azmon, in the wilderness of Zin toward the Egyptian border (Joshua 15:3). Its exact site is unknown.

entries.title: Karkor
entries.summary: Desert country east of the Jordan, past Succoth and Penuel. Gideon caught the Midianite kings Zebah and Zalmunna there and broke what was left of their army, ending seven years in which Israel had hidden in mountain caves.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Karkor lay in the desert country east of the Jordan, beyond Succoth and Penuel, where Gideon finally caught up with the fleeing Midianite kings Zebah and Zalmunna and routed their remaining forces (Judges 8:10-12). The rout there ended the Midianite oppression that had driven Israel to hide in mountain caves for seven years. Its precise site is unidentified.

entries.title: Kartah (Kitron)
entries.summary: Zebulun's town given to the Levites of Merari's clan, and probably the Kattath of the earlier boundary list.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Kartah, a town of the tribe of Zebulun given to the Levites of Merari's clan (Josh. 21:34). It is likely the same town called Kattath in the earlier boundary list of Joshua 19:15.

entries.title: Kartan
entries.summary: In Naphtali, given to the Gershonite clan. Chronicles calls the same town Kirjathaim, "double city," which is probably the full name behind the short one.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Levitical city of Naphtali given to the Gershonite clan (Joshua 21:32). The parallel list in 1 Chronicles 6:76 gives the name of this same town as Kirjathaim, "double city," which is likely the fuller form of the name Kartan represents in abbreviated form.

entries.title: Kattath (Kitron)
entries.summary: It was a town allotted to Zebulun. It may be Kitron, one of the places where Zebulun never drove out the Canaanites, though nobody is sure of the site.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Kattath was a town allotted to the tribe of Zebulun (Josh. 19:15). It may be the same place as Kitron, mentioned in Judges 1:30 as a town Zebulun failed to fully drive its Canaanite inhabitants from, though its exact site remains disputed and older proposals linking it to Cana of Galilee are no longer widely accepted.

entries.title: Kedar (Arabian living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Ishmael's son, and the father of a desert tribe known for dark tents and good archers. Poets use Kedar for far-off wilderness living, and the Song of Solomon uses it for dark beauty.
entries.books: Genesis, 1 Chronicles, Psalm, Song of Solomon, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel
entries.label: 7 books
entries.dictNote: Kedar was a son of Ishmael and the ancestor of a nomadic Arabian tribe known for their dark tents and skilled archers, used poetically in the Old Testament as an image of both remote wilderness life and, in Song of Solomon, of striking dark beauty.

witness.excerpt: Of this wife were born to Ishmael twelve sons: Nabaioth, Kedar, Abdeel, Mabsam, Idumas, Masmaos, Massaos, Chodad, Theman, Jetur, Naphesus, Kadmas.

entries.title: Kedemah (Arabian living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: He was the youngest of Ishmael's twelve sons, and his name means "eastward," which suits sons who settled east of Canaan. Nothing else is recorded about him individually.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Kedemah was the youngest of the twelve sons of Ishmael, listed among the tribal chiefs whose descendants became the Ishmaelite peoples of the Arabian desert (Genesis 25:15-16). His name, meaning “eastward,” fits the pattern of Ishmael's sons settling in the region east of Canaan. Nothing else is recorded about him individually.

entries.title: Kedemoth
entries.summary: A town in Reuben's land, given to the Merarite Levites. Moses sent messengers from its wilderness to Sihon, king of the Amorites, asking to pass through, and Sihon's refusal led to war.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Kedemoth was a town in the territory of Reuben, assigned to the Merarite Levites, that gave its name to the surrounding wilderness from which Moses sent messengers to Sihon, king of the Amorites, requesting safe passage before Sihon's refusal led to war (Deuteronomy 2:26; Joshua 13:18; 21:37). Its precise site east of the Jordan has not been securely identified.

entries.title: Kedesh
entries.summary: A city of refuge in Galilee, one of six where someone who had killed by accident could run and be safe. Barak came from there, the commander Deborah called up.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Kedesh was a city of refuge in Galilee, one of six towns designated where someone who killed accidentally could flee for protection from vengeance, and also the hometown of Barak, the military commander Deborah summoned.

entries.title: Kehelathah
entries.summary: A stop on the wilderness march, between Rissah and Mount Shepher. The name is related to the Hebrew word for assembly, and the site cannot be found today.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Kehelathah was one of the stations in Israel's wilderness itinerary, listed between Rissah and Mount Shepher (Num. 33:22-23). Its name is related to the Hebrew word for assembly or congregation, though the text gives no further detail and the site cannot be located today.

entries.title: Keilah
entries.summary: David saved this walled town from a Philistine raid while Saul was hunting him. Then he learned they would have handed him over if Saul came, and he moved on into the wilderness of Ziph.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Keilah was a walled town in Judah's lowlands that David rescued from a Philistine raid while he was still a fugitive from Saul, only to learn its residents would have handed him over had Saul come for him, prompting David to move on into the wilderness of Ziph.

witness.excerpt: When he was at Keilah still but 400 both in Josephus and in the LXXII; but 600 in our Hebrew copies: 1 Sam.
About this time it was that David heard how the Philistines had made an inroad into the country of Keilah, and robbed it.

entries.title: Kelaiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A man from the exile and the return. Ezra names him once.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Kelaiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: He was a Levite who had married a foreign wife and agreed under Ezra to send her away. He is also called Kelita, and is probably the Kelita who helped people understand the reading of the law.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Kelaiah, also called Kelita, was a Levite among those who had married foreign wives during the postexilic period and agreed to separate from them under Ezra's reform (Ezra 10:23). A Levite named Kelita later helped the people understand the reading of the law in Nehemiah 8:7, likely the same man.

entries.title: Kelita (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: The law was read out in public, and he was one of the Levites who explained it to the people. He also signed the covenant renewal under Nehemiah.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Kelita was a Levite who helped explain the law to the people after Ezra's public reading and who signed Nehemiah's covenant renewal.

entries.title: Kemuel (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 3 men called Kemuel. This one is a man from the divided-kingdom years, named once in 1 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Kemuel (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: A tribal leader of Ephraim, appointed to help divide the land under Joshua.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Kemuel was Abraham's nephew through his brother Nahor, and also the name of a tribal leader of Ephraim appointed to help divide the conquered land under Joshua.

entries.title: Kemuel (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Nahor's son, and so Abraham's nephew.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Kenath
entries.summary: In Bashan, east of the Jordan, taken when Israel moved in and renamed Nobah after the man who took it. It is generally identified with Qanawat on the slopes of Jebel Hauran, where Roman ruins still stand, a theatre among them.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Kenath was a town in the region of Bashan, east of the Jordan, captured during Israel's advance into the territory and renamed Nobah after its conqueror (Num. 32:42). It is also listed among towns taken from Geshur and Aram by the descendants of Machir (1 Chr. 2:23). The site is generally identified with Qanawat, an ancient city on the slopes of Jebel Hauran whose Roman-era ruins, including a theater and temple remains, are still visible today.

entries.title: Kenath
entries.summary: Named once, in Judges, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Kenaz (Edomite living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: One of Edom's clan chiefs, in Genesis 36 and again in Chronicles. The Kenizzites are counted among the Edomite clans.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Kenaz (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 3 men called Kenaz. This one is a man from the divided-kingdom years, named once in 1 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Kenaz (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Caleb's younger brother, and father of Othniel, Israel's first judge.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Kenaz was Caleb's younger brother and the father of Othniel, Israel's first judge, and his descendants, the Kenizzites, are counted among the Edomite clans in Genesis.

entries.title: Kenezite (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Caleb, one of the two spies who stayed faithful, is called a Kenizzite. The clan came from Kenaz and was tied to Edom in Genesis, then folded into Judah.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Kenizzites were a clan descended from Kenaz, associated with Edom in Genesis but later absorbed into Judah. Caleb, one of the two faithful spies who entered Canaan, is called a Kenizzite, showing how outsiders could be fully incorporated into an Israelite tribe.

entries.title: Kenezite (People, perhaps from Keniz)
entries.summary: Named once, in Genesis, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

witness.excerpt: And on that day the Lord made a covenant with Abram, saying: "To thy seed will I give this land, from the river of Egypt unto the great river, the river Euphrates, the Kenites, the Kenizzites, the Kadmonites, the Perizzites, and the Rephaim, the Phakorites,  and the Hivites,  and the Amorites, and the Canaanites, and the Girgashites, and the Jebusites."  19.

entries.title: Kenite
entries.summary: They were a wandering clan close to Midian, outside the twelve tribes but mostly friendly to Israel. Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, was a Kenite priest, and Jael, Heber the Kenite's wife, killed Sisera.
entries.label: 5 books
entries.dictNote: Kenites were a nomadic clan closely tied to Midian, generally friendly to Israel even though they stood outside the twelve tribes. Moses' father in law Jethro was a Kenite priest, and Heber the Kenite's wife Jael killed the fleeing Canaanite general Sisera in the days of the judges.

witness.excerpt: At last Sisera, as soon as he saw himself beaten, fled away, and came to a woman whose name was Jael , a Kenite; who received him, when he desired to be concealed; and when he asked for somewhat to drink, she gave him sour milk.

entries.title: Keren-happuch (Woman living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Job's youngest daughter, born after God restored him. Her name means "horn of eye paint." She and her sisters got an inheritance alongside their brothers, which was unusual.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Keren-happuch, whose name means "horn of eye paint," was the youngest of Job's three daughters, born to him after God restored his fortunes at the end of his ordeal (Job 42:14). Job gave his daughters an inheritance alongside their brothers, an unusual provision for that culture (Job 42:15).

entries.title: Kerioth
entries.summary: Named once, in Joshua, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Kerioth (Kiriathaim)
entries.summary: God's judgment on Moab, in Jeremiah and Amos, names this Moabite city. Judas Iscariot's name may mean "man of Kerioth."
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Kerioth was a Moabite city named in Jeremiah's and Amos's prophecies of judgment against Moab, and possibly the hometown implied in the name Judas Iscariot, meaning man of Kerioth.

entries.title: Keros (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Ancestor of a family of temple servants, the Nethinim, who came back from Babylon with Zerubbabel.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Keros was the ancestral head of a family of temple servants (Nethinim) whose descendants returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:44; Nehemiah 7:47).

entries.title: Keturah (Woman living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: The wife Abraham took after Sarah died. Her six sons became Arabian and Midianite peoples, and Abraham sent them away with gifts so Isaac would stand alone as heir.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Keturah was the wife Abraham married after Sarah's death, and she bore him six sons who became the ancestors of various Arabian and Midianite peoples, though Abraham sent them away from Isaac with gifts to secure Isaac's position as sole heir.

witness.excerpt: For the children by Keturah were gone to their own remote habitations.
And Abraham took to himself a third wife, and her name was Keturah, from among the daughters of his household servants, for Hagar had died before Sarah.  12.
These are by Herodotus called Barbarians, and perhaps were derived from the Syrians and Arabians, the posterity of Abraham by Keturah.

entries.title: Kezia (Woman living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: The second of Job's three daughters, born after God restored him, and given an inheritance with her brothers.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The second of Job's three daughters, born after God restored his fortunes at the end of the book, and one of the daughters given an inheritance alongside their brothers (Job 42:14-15).

entries.title: Keziz
entries.summary: Emek-keziz in full Hebrew, a town in Benjamin's eastern district by the Jordan valley, listed with Jericho and Beth-hoglah. No one knows exactly where it was.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Keziz, fuller in Hebrew as Emek-keziz, was one of the towns assigned to the tribe of Benjamin in the eastern district near the Jordan valley (Josh. 18:21). It is grouped in the list with Jericho and Beth-hoglah, but its precise location is unknown.

entries.title: Kibroth-hattaavah
entries.summary: "The graves of craving." The people were sick of manna and demanded meat, and God sent quails in a huge flock. A plague broke out while they ate, and the dead were buried where they fell, so the camp was named for what they had wanted. Moses brought it up again years later when he listed the times they had provoked God.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Kibroth-hattaavah, "the graves of craving," marks the wilderness camp where the Israelites, weary of manna, demanded meat and were sent a massive flock of quails by God. Their gluttony brought on a plague that killed many, and the dead were buried there and the place named for their craving (Numbers 11:31-34). It was one of the stations on Israel's route from Sinai toward Canaan, mentioned again in the itinerary of Numbers 33 and in Moses' later rebuke in Deuteronomy 9:22.

entries.title: Kibzaim
entries.summary: A Levitical town in Ephraim, given to the Kohathites, which Chronicles calls Jokmeam.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Levitical city in the territory of Ephraim, assigned to the Kohathites (Josh. 21:22). The parallel list in 1 Chronicles 6:68 gives its name as Jokmeam.

entries.title: Kidron
entries.summary: The valley along Jerusalem's east side, between the city and the Mount of Olives. Reforming kings dumped smashed idols and temple rubbish into it, and Jesus crossed it with his disciples on the way to Gethsemane the night he was arrested.
entries.label: 5 books
entries.dictNote: The Kidron Valley runs along Jerusalem's eastern edge, between the city and the Mount of Olives, and it served as a dumping ground for the idols and debris of successive religious reforms, as well as the path Jesus and his disciples crossed on the way to Gethsemane the night of his arrest.

entries.title: Kinah
entries.summary: Far south in Judah, near the border with Edom, in the dry country below Beersheba.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A town in the extreme south of Judah, near the border with Edom, in the arid district south of Beersheba (Josh. 15:22).

entries.title: Kir
entries.summary: Amos says God brought the Arameans from Kir the way he brought Israel out of Egypt, and he warns that Damascus will be sent back there. Tiglath-pileser III did exactly that in 732 BC, and his own annals record it. Isaiah's Kir, set beside Elam in a scene of soldiers arming, may or may not be the same place.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Two different places share this name. Kir of Moab, one of Moab's two chief cities alongside Ar, appears in Isaiah's oracle against Moab and is usually identified with Kerak, a fortress town east of the Dead Sea (Isa. 15:1). The other Kir was the original homeland of the Arameans; Amos says God brought Aram from Kir just as he brought Israel from Egypt (Amos 9:7), and elsewhere warns that the Arameans of Damascus would be sent back there in judgment (Amos 1:5), a threat fulfilled when Tiglath-pileser III deported Damascus's population after conquering it in 732 BC, an episode recorded in his own Assyrian annals. Isaiah pairs a Kir with Elam in a separate scene of soldiers preparing for battle (Isa. 22:6), though scholars debate whether it is the same place.

entries.title: Kir
entries.summary: Named once, in Isaiah, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Kir-haraseth (Kir of Moab)
entries.summary: Moab's fortress capital, modern Kerak in Jordan. When Mesha of Moab rebelled after Ahab died, Israel, Judah and Edom besieged him there, and he sacrificed his own son on the wall, which ended the siege. His own account of the revolt survives on the Moabite Stone, found in 1868.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Kir-haraseth, also called Kir-heres or Kir-hareseth and identified with modern Kerak in Jordan, was the fortress capital of Moab. When King Mesha of Moab rebelled against Israel after Ahab's death, the combined armies of Israel, Judah, and Edom besieged him there, driving him to sacrifice his own son on the city wall in a desperate act that ended the siege (2 Kings 3:25-27). Mesha's own account of his revolt survives on the Moabite Stone, a black basalt inscription discovered in 1868 that corroborates the biblical narrative of Moab's struggle against Israelite rule. Isaiah and Jeremiah both lament the city's fall in their oracles against Moab (Isaiah 16:7-11; Jeremiah 48:31-36).

entries.title: Kiriathaim
entries.summary: It started out as a town of Reuben's and ended up in Moab, on Jeremiah's list of the cities God's judgment would fall on.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Kiriathaim was a Moabite town, originally allotted to the tribe of Reuben, later listed by Jeremiah and Ezekiel among the cities God's judgment on Moab would fall upon.

entries.title: Kiriathaim
entries.summary: Named once, in 1 Chronicles, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Kirjath (Kiriath-jearim)
entries.summary: Kirjath-jearim, also called Baalah, a Gibeonite town on the line between Judah and Benjamin. The ark sat there twenty years after the Philistines gave it back, until David brought it up to Jerusalem. The prophet Uriah, whom Jehoiakim had killed, came from there.
entries.books: Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Jeremiah
entries.label: 6 books
entries.dictNote: This is Kirjath-jearim, a Gibeonite town on the border of Judah and Benjamin also known as Baalah. The ark of the covenant rested there for twenty years after the Philistines returned it, until David had it brought up to Jerusalem. Kirjath-jearim was also the home of the prophet Uriah, whom King Jehoiakim had executed for prophesying against Jerusalem.

entries.title: Kirjath-arba (Hebron)
entries.summary: "Arba's city," Hebron's older name, after a great man among the Anakim. Sarah died there and Abraham bought the cave of Machpelah close by to bury her. Joshua gave it to Caleb for the faithful report he brought back as a spy.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Kirjath-arba, "city of Arba," was the earlier name of Hebron, named for a great man among the Anakim. Sarah died there, and Abraham purchased the cave of Machpelah nearby as a family burial site. Joshua later gave the city to Caleb as his inheritance for his faithful report as one of the twelve spies.

entries.title: Kirjath-huzoth (Kiriath-huzoth)
entries.summary: Balak, king of Moab, met Balaam in this town, "city of streets," after sending to the Euphrates to have him curse Israel. It lay near the high places where Balaam later looked down on the camp.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Moabite town, "city of streets," where King Balak met and entertained Balaam after summoning him from the Euphrates region to curse Israel (Numbers 22:39). It stood near the high places from which Balaam later viewed the Israelite camp, and is generally placed in the plains of Moab near Kirjathaim.

entries.title: Kirjath-sannah (Debir)
entries.summary: Another name for Debir, also called Kirjath-sepher, a royal Canaanite city in the hills southwest of Hebron. Caleb promised his daughter Achsah to whoever took it, and his nephew Othniel did.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Kirjath-sannah is an alternate name for the town also called Kirjath-sepher and, after Israel's conquest, Debir, a royal Canaanite city in the hill country southwest of Hebron thought to have been a center of learning among its Canaanite inhabitants (Joshua 15:15-16, 49). Caleb offered his daughter Achsah in marriage to whoever captured it, a prize claimed by his nephew Othniel, later Israel's first judge (Judges 1:11-13).

entries.title: Kirjathbaal (Kiriath-jearim)
entries.summary: They also called Kirjath-jearim by this name, and Baalah, a boundary town between Judah and Benjamin and one of the Gibeonite towns. The ark stayed there about twenty years before David brought it up to Jerusalem.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Kirjath-baal is another name for Kirjath-jearim, listed alongside it as a boundary town of Judah and Benjamin (Joshua 15:60; 18:14). Also called Baalah, it was one of the four Gibeonite league towns and later held the ark of the covenant for about twenty years before David brought it up to Jerusalem.

entries.title: Kish (Levite living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: He is a Levite, not Saul's father. His sons married their cousins because their uncle died with only daughters, and the temple rota in Chronicles counts his family.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Kish (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 4 men called Kish. This one is a man from the divided-kingdom years, named once in 2 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

witness.excerpt: This reflection is openly confirmed to us from the example of Saul, the son of Kish: who was the first King who reigned after our aristocracy, and government under the judges were over: and that by his slaughter of three hundred Priests and Prophets, on occasion of his suspicion about Ahimelech; and by

entries.title: Kish (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A man from the exile and the return, and Esther is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Kish (Saul's father living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Saul's father, a Benjamite of some standing. He lost his donkeys, sent Saul to find them, and the search ended with Samuel anointing Saul as Israel's first king.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Kish was King Saul's father, a Benjamite of standing whose lost donkeys sent Saul on the search that led him to Samuel and his anointing as Israel's first king.

witness.excerpt: There was one of the tribe of Benjamin, a man of a good family, and of a virtuous disposition; his name was Kish.

entries.title: Kishi (Levite living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Kishi, or Kushaiah, was the Merarite Levite whose son Ethan was one of the three chief musicians David put to serve before the ark.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Kishi, also called Kushaiah (1 Chronicles 15:17), was a Levite of the Merarite clan and the father of Ethan, one of the three chief musicians David appointed for service before the ark (1 Chronicles 6:44; 15:17).

entries.title: Kishion
entries.summary: A town in Issachar given to the Gershonite Levites, spelled Kishon in the second list, its exact site unknown.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Kishion was a town in Issachar assigned to the Gershonite Levites, listed among their cities in Joshua 19:20 and again, spelled Kishon, in Joshua 21:28. Its exact site is unknown.

entries.title: Kishion
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and nothing else is recorded.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Kishon
entries.summary: It is a winter stream that drains the Jezreel Valley into the Mediterranean below Mount Carmel, and it floods fast. It swept away Sisera's chariots when Deborah and Barak fought the Canaanites, and in its valley Elijah had the prophets of Baal killed after the contest on Carmel.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: The Kishon is a winter stream draining the Jezreel Valley into the Mediterranean at the foot of Mount Carmel, prone to flash flooding. Its swollen waters swept away Sisera's chariots during Deborah and Barak's battle against the Canaanites (Judges 4:7, 13; 5:21), and it was in its valley that Elijah had the prophets of Baal put to death after the contest on Mount Carmel (1 Kings 18:40).

entries.title: Kithlish (Chitlish)
entries.summary: In the Judean lowlands, listed with Lahmam and Gederoth. It has traditionally been placed near Jelameh, though the identification is not firmly established.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Kithlish was a town in the Judean lowlands, listed among the towns of Judah's inheritance alongside Lahmam and Gederoth (Joshua 15:40). It has traditionally been located near Jelameh, though the identification is not firmly established.

entries.title: Kitron
entries.summary: Zebulun never drove out the Canaanites of this town, so they stayed on as forced labour, and Joshua 19:15 probably lists it as Kattath.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Kitron was a Canaanite town within Zebulun's allotted territory that the tribe failed to drive out, so its inhabitants remained and were put to forced labor instead (Judges 1:30). Joshua 19:15 lists the same town's territory under the name Kattath. Its exact site is unidentified; the older proposal equating it with Cana of Galilee is not widely accepted today.

entries.title: Koa
entries.summary: Ezekiel names Koa once, with Shoa and Pekod, among the peoples coming with Babylon against Jerusalem. Many scholars take it to be Gutium, a land east of the Tigris that turns up in Sumerian, Babylonian and Assyrian records.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A name occurring only in Ezekiel 23:23, paired with Shoa and Pekod as peoples or territories allied with Babylon against Jerusalem. Many scholars identify it with Gutium, a region and people named repeatedly in Sumerian, Babylonian, and Assyrian records as lying east of the Tigris, rather than a single city.

entries.title: Kohath (Levi's son living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Levi's second son. His descendants had the holiest work in the tabernacle, carrying the ark and the sacred furniture on poles, and even they would die if they touched those things.
entries.label: 5 books
entries.dictNote: Kohath was Levi's second son, and his descendants, the Kohathites, were assigned the most sacred tabernacle duties, carrying the ark of the covenant and other holy furnishings on their shoulders using poles, since even they were forbidden to touch the sacred objects directly on penalty of death.

witness.excerpt: And the sons of Kohath, 3, 4 Ambram, Issachar, Hebron, and Ozeel.
Levi and his sons; and these are the names of his sons: Gershon, and Kohath, and Merari--four.

And she conceived and bare a son, and I called his name Gersam, for we were sojourners in our land 3, 4 And I saw concerning him, that he would not be in the first rank, And Kohath was born in the 5 thirty-fifth year of my life, towards sunrise.

entries.title: Kohathites (Levi's son living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: One of the three Levitical divisions, descended from Kohath. They carried the holiest furnishings, the ark among them, on poles and not in a cart, and 2 Samuel 6 shows what happened when that rule was broken. They camped south of the tabernacle. Moses, Aaron and Samuel were all Kohathites.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: The Kohathites were the descendants of Kohath, one of Levi's three sons, and formed one of the three Levitical divisions responsible for the tabernacle. Their specific charge was the most sacred furnishings, including the ark of the covenant, which they carried on poles rather than in a cart so that no one would touch it directly, a rule broken with fatal results in 2 Samuel 6. In the wilderness camp they pitched south of the tabernacle, and Moses, Aaron, and Samuel all belonged to this line.

entries.title: Kolaiah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Jeremiah names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Kolaiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Benjamite ancestor of one of the exiles who came back and settled in Jerusalem. He is a different man from the Kolaiah whose son Ahab was a false prophet in Babylon.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Kolaiah was the father of the false prophet Ahab, who along with Zedekiah prophesied lies to the exiles in Babylon and was condemned by Jeremiah; Nebuchadnezzar had both men roasted in the fire as a warning (Jeremiah 29:21-22). A separate Kolaiah was a Benjamite ancestor of one of the returned exiles who resettled Jerusalem (Nehemiah 11:7).

entries.title: Korah (Aaron's adversary living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: A Levite who led a revolt against Moses and Aaron, with more than two hundred fifty leading Israelites behind him, all saying the whole community was holy and Moses had no special claim. The ground opened and took Korah and his family alive, and fire burned up the rest. Israel complained about it the very next day.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Korah was a Levite who led a rebellion against Moses and Aaron's leadership, joined by over two hundred fifty prominent Israelites who argued the whole community was holy and Moses had no special claim to authority. The ground opened and swallowed Korah and his family alive, and fire consumed the other rebels, a judgment severe enough that Israel complained about it the very next day.

entries.title: Korah (Edomite living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: An Edomite chief in Genesis 36 and Chronicles, with nothing to do with the Levite who rebelled.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Korah (Edomite living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: One of 4 men called Korah. This one is a man from the patriarchs, named once in Genesis.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Korah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A man from the divided-kingdom years, and 1 Chronicles is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Kore (Levite living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: There was a family of temple gatekeepers who traced themselves to him, and Chronicles names him at the head of their line.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Kore was a common Levitical name, borne by an ancestor of a group of temple gatekeepers and by a Levite placed in charge of freewill offerings under King Hezekiah.

witness.excerpt: Thus some have deified the four elements earth (Kore, Demeter, Pluto), water (Poseidon), air (Hera), and fire (Hephaestus); others the sun (Apollo), moon (Artemis), and the stars fixed and the planets (e.

entries.title: Kore (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 2 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Koz (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Ancestor of a priestly family that came back from exile and could not prove its descent, and until that was settled they were kept out of the priesthood.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Koz was the head of a priestly family among the returning exiles who couldn't initially prove their priestly genealogy and were excluded from serving until the matter could be resolved.

entries.title: Kushaiah (Levite living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Ethan's father, a Merarite Levite, and Ethan sang among the musicians David appointed for bringing the ark up to Jerusalem. The other genealogy calls him Kishi.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Levite of the Merarite clan, father of the singer Ethan whom David appointed among the musicians for the ark's procession to Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 15:17). He is called Kishi in the parallel genealogy at 1 Chronicles 6:44.

entries.title: Laadah (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Shelah's line, Judah's son, and the father of the clan at Mareshah.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Laadah was a descendant of Judah through Shelah, named as father of the clan of Mareshah in the tribal genealogy of Judah (1 Chr. 4:21).

entries.title: Laadan (Levite living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: One of the founders of the Gershonite Levite families in Chronicles, though a man of Ephraim has the name too.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Laadan was a common name, borne by an ancestor of the Gershonite Levites and by a descendant of Ephraim in the genealogies of Chronicles.

entries.title: Laadan (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the wilderness years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Laban
entries.summary: Named once, in Deuteronomy, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Laban (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Rebekah's brother and Jacob's uncle, and then his father-in-law twice, after he slipped Leah in where Rachel should have been and got fourteen years of work out of him. He kept changing Jacob's wages as the flocks grew. Jacob finally slipped away with his family, and the two parted under a covenant, not with a fight.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Laban was Rebekah's brother and Jacob's uncle, and later his father-in-law twice over after tricking Jacob into marrying Leah before Rachel, then extracting fourteen years of labor from him. Laban repeatedly changed Jacob's wages as Jacob's flocks prospered, and Jacob eventually fled with his family and God's blessing rather than continue negotiating with him, though the two men parted with a formal covenant rather than open violence.

witness.excerpt: And he was taken captive and was bought by Laban; and he gave him Euna his handmaid to wife, and she bore a daughter, and called her name Zilpah, after the name 12 of the village in which he had been taken captive.
I have heard before that daughters have been born to Laban, thy brother, and I have set my heart on them to take a wife from amongst them.

And he went on his journey, and came to the land of the east, to Laban, the brother of Rebecca, and he was with him, and served him for Rachel his daughter one week.  2.  And in the first year of the third week he said unto him: "Give 2122 A.M.

entries.title: Lachish
entries.summary: A heavily fortified Canaanite royal city in Judah's lowlands. Joshua took it, Rehoboam rebuilt it into one of Judah's strongest fortresses, and in 701 BC Sennacherib's Assyrians took it again. Assyria carved the siege on wall reliefs now in the British Museum. The ruins at Tell ed-Duweir also gave up the Lachish Letters, written during Babylon's last siege, just before Jerusalem fell.
entries.books: Joshua, 2 Kings, 2 Chronicles, Nehemiah, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Micah
entries.label: 7 books
entries.dictNote: Lachish was a heavily fortified Canaanite royal city in Judah's lowlands, captured and destroyed by Joshua and later rebuilt into one of Judah's strongest fortresses under Rehoboam. Sennacherib's Assyrian army besieged and captured it in 701 BC, an episode Assyria commemorated in a series of relief carvings, now in the British Museum, depicting the siege ramp, battle, and deportation of captives in detail. Excavations at Tell ed-Duweir, the city's ruins, also uncovered the Lachish Letters, a set of Hebrew ostraca written during the final Babylonian siege of Judah shortly before Jerusalem's fall, a rare firsthand military correspondence from the very end of the kingdom.

witness.excerpt: Now these things happened to the people of Jerusalem in the fourteenth year of the reign of Amaziah, who after this had a conspiracy made against him by his friends, and fled to the city Lachish; and was there slain by the conspirators, who sent men thither to kill him.

entries.title: Lael (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Eliasaph's father, named only to say whose son the leader of the Gershonite Levites in the wilderness was.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The father of Eliasaph, chief of the Gershonite Levites during the wilderness wandering (Num. 3:24). He is named only to identify his son.

entries.title: Lahad (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of Jahath's sons, in Judah's line through Shobal. Nothing else is recorded of him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A son of Jahath, listed among the descendants of Judah through the line of Shobal in 1 Chronicles 4:2. Nothing else is recorded of him.

entries.title: Lahmam
entries.summary: Listed with Kithlish and Gederoth in the lowland district of Judah, at a site nobody has identified.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Lahmam was a town in the lowland district of Judah, listed alongside Kithlish and Gederoth in Joshua's territorial allotment (Joshua 15:40). Nothing else is recorded about it, and its site is unidentified.

entries.title: Lahmi (Giant living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Goliath's brother, killed by Elhanan son of Jair in a fight between David's men and the Philistines.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Brother of the Philistine giant Goliath, killed by Elhanan son of Jair during a battle between David's men and the Philistines (1 Chronicles 20:5).

entries.title: Laish (Dan)
entries.summary: Peaceful, cut off, and Canaanite. The tribe of Dan, having failed to settle the land it was given, took the city and renamed it Dan.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Laish was a peaceful, isolated Canaanite city that the tribe of Dan conquered and renamed Dan after failing to fully settle their originally assigned territory.

witness.excerpt: 17 For as to Michal, the daughter of King Saul, who had been David’s wife, her father had given her in marriage to Phalti, the son of Laish, who was of the city of Gallim.

entries.title: Laish (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Samuel and 2 Samuel name him twice, and he is a man from the united kingdom.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Lakum (Lakkum)
entries.summary: On Naphtali's border, listed with Adami and Jabneel, and never mentioned again.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Lakum was one of several places marking the border of the tribal territory of Naphtali, listed alongside Adami and Jabneel in Joshua 19:33. It is not mentioned elsewhere in the Bible, and its site has not been identified.

entries.title: Lamech (Man living at the time before the Flood)
entries.summary: Noah's father, from Seth's line. He named his son Noah in the hope that the boy would bring relief from farming the cursed ground. Luke's genealogy keeps him as one link in the chain.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Two men named Lamech appear in Genesis. One was a descendant of Cain notorious for boasting to his two wives that he had killed a young man for merely wounding him, escalating the violence Cain's own murder had introduced. The other Lamech was Noah's father, from the righteous line through Seth, and he named his son Noah expressing hope that he would bring relief from the painful labor of farming cursed ground.
entries.lukeNote: One line in Luke's chain of ‘son of.’ In the Book of Noah fragment he's a frightened new father who flees his own son's birth and needs Methuselah and Enoch to talk him down.

entries.title: Lamech (Man living at the time before the Flood)
entries.summary: He was Cain's descendant. He boasted to his two wives that he had killed a young man just for wounding him. Cain's violence came down to him and got worse.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Laodicea
entries.summary: A rich banking and cloth city in the Lycus Valley. It had no water of its own and piped it in from the hot springs at Hierapolis and the cold springs at Colossae, so it arrived lukewarm, and Revelation's "neither cold nor hot" plays on that. Its church gets the sharpest rebuke of the seven.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Laodicea was a wealthy banking and textile city in the Lycus Valley of Asia Minor, addressed in Revelation as the last and most sharply rebuked of the seven churches (Revelation 3:14-22), and mentioned by Paul alongside Colossae (Colossians 2:1; 4:15-16). The city had no natural water source and piped water in by aqueduct from the hot springs at Hierapolis and the cold springs at Colossae, which arrived lukewarm and mineral-laden; John's rebuke that the church was "neither cold nor hot" plays directly on that well-known local water supply.

And because, upon the taking of Laodicea by Cassius, the men of power were gotten together from all quarters, with presents and crowns in their hands, Herod allotted this time for the punishment of Malichus.

Antony was persuaded by these arguments; and when he came to Laodicea, he sent and commanded Herod to come and make his defense, as to what he had done to Aristobulus, for that such a treacherous design was not well done, if he had any hand in it.

photo.description: ruins at Laodicea on the Lycus

entries.title: Laodicean
entries.summary: Someone from Laodicea, and Paul tells the Colossians to swap letters with the Laodicean church.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Laodicean designates an inhabitant of Laodicea, a wealthy city in the Lycus valley of Asia Minor near Colossae. Paul instructs the Colossians to exchange letters with the Laodicean church, and Revelation later rebukes that same congregation for being lukewarm, an image that likely plays on the city's famous aqueduct system, which delivered water that arrived neither hot nor cold.

entries.title: Lappidoth (Woman living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: Deborah's husband, and Scripture says nothing more about him. The name means "torches", and some older readers took it as a word about Deborah herself. The plain reading makes it his name.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The husband of Deborah, the prophetess and judge who led Israel against the Canaanite general Sisera (Judges 4:4). Scripture says nothing about Lappidoth himself beyond identifying him as Deborah's husband; some older interpreters have suggested the name, meaning "torches" or "flashes," was actually an epithet for Deborah's own fiery character rather than her husband's given name, though the plain reading takes it as his name.

entries.title: Lasea
entries.summary: On Crete's south coast, near the harbour called Fair Havens where Paul's ship took shelter. Its ruins were found again in the nineteenth century a few miles east of Fair Havens, just where Luke's account puts it.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Lasea was a city on the south coast of Crete, named in Luke's detailed account of Paul's voyage to Rome as lying near the harbor called Fair Havens where the ship sheltered (Acts 27:8). Its ruins were rediscovered in the nineteenth century a few miles east of Fair Havens, confirming the precise geography behind Luke's narrative, a detail often cited as evidence of Luke's care as a historian of the voyage.

entries.title: Lasha
entries.summary: The eastern corner of Canaan in the Table of Nations, with Sidon at the north. Jewish tradition put it at Callirhoe, the hot springs on the east shore of the Dead Sea where Herod the Great is said to have gone in his last illness.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Lasha marks the eastern boundary point of Canaanite territory in the Table of Nations, paired with Sidon in the north and the cities of the plain in the south (Genesis 10:19). Jewish tradition identified it with Callirhoe, a resort on the eastern shore of the Dead Sea famous in the Roman period for its hot mineral springs, which Herod the Great reportedly visited during his final illness. If that identification is correct, the name preserves a memory of the region's thermal springs long before Roman writers described them.

entries.title: Lasharon
entries.summary: "Belonging to Sharon." Joshua beat a king of Lasharon, but most of these verses are about the Sharon plain, the rich coast between Joppa and Mount Carmel, with royal pasture and some of Gad living there. Its beauty became a byword, "the rose of Sharon," and Isaiah pictures it blooming again.
entries.books: Joshua, 1 Chronicles, Song of Solomon, Isaiah
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Lasharon, meaning "belonging to Sharon," appears once as the name of a Canaanite town or district whose king Joshua defeated (Joshua 12:18), and most of the other references gathered under the name belong instead to the famous Sharon plain, the fertile coastal region between Joppa and Mount Carmel. Sharon supplied excellent royal pastureland (1 Chronicles 27:29) and part of the tribe of Gad settled there (1 Chronicles 5:16); its beauty became proverbial, celebrated as "the rose of Sharon" (Song of Solomon 2:1) and pictured by Isaiah blossoming in the age of restoration (Isaiah 35:2).

entries.title: Latin (A language)
entries.summary: Rome's official language, and one of the three on the sign above the cross.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Latin, not a person, was the official language of Rome and one of three languages, along with Aramaic and Greek, used in the inscription Pilate ordered placed over Jesus on the cross, reading "Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews" (John 19:19-20). Its inclusion reflects Rome's administrative presence in Judea.

witness.excerpt: The Latin, from which our carbuncle is derived, carbunculus, a diminutive of carbo, which also means a coal.} because, I imagine, when it becomes inflamed it burns; from which fact it has derived that appellation.

entries.title: Lazarus (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: The beggar in Jesus's parable, covered in sores at a rich man's gate and wanting scraps from his table. After death he is comforted and the rich man is not. He is the only character in any of the parables with a name.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Lazarus (Mary's brother living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Mary and Martha's brother in Bethany, and a close friend of Jesus. He had been four days in the tomb when Jesus raised him, the last miracle in John's Gospel and the one that made the authorities decide to finish Jesus off.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Lazarus of Bethany was the brother of Mary and Martha and a close friend of Jesus, and his death and resurrection after four days in the tomb is the last and greatest of the miracles recorded in John's Gospel, the one that finally convinced the religious authorities to move against Jesus for good. A different Lazarus is the beggar in one of Jesus's parables, covered in sores and longing for scraps from a rich man's table, who ends up comforted in the afterlife while the rich man suffers, the only character in any of Jesus's parables given a name.

witness.excerpt: And, indeed, why do I relate these particular calamities? while Manneus, the son of Lazarus, came running to Titus at this very time, and told him that there had been carried out through that one gate, which was intrusted to his care, no fewer than a hundred and fifteen thousand eight hundred and eighty dead b

entries.title: Leah (Woman living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Jacob's first wife, given to him by her father Laban in place of Rachel, and Jacob only found out in the morning. He never loved her the way he loved Rachel. Genesis says God gave her children because she was unloved, and she bore six of the twelve sons, Judah among them.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Leah was Jacob's first wife, given to him by her father Laban in place of her younger sister Rachel through a deception Jacob only discovered the morning after the wedding. Though Jacob never loved her the way he loved Rachel, Leah bore six of his twelve sons, including Judah, ancestor of David and ultimately Jesus, and Genesis notes that God gave her children specifically because she was unloved.

witness.excerpt: And had not Leah my mother paid the two apples for the sake of his company, she would have borne eight sons; for this reason she bare six, and Rachel bare the two: for on account of the mandrakes the Lord 3 visited her.

entries.title: Lebana (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Ancestor of a family of temple servants, the Nethinim, who came back from Babylon with Zerubbabel.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Lebana, also spelled Lebanah, was the ancestor of a family of temple servants, or Nethinim, who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:45; Nehemiah 7:48). Nothing further is recorded of him.

entries.title: Lebanon
entries.summary: Two mountain ridges along the coast, Lebanon proper to the west and the Anti-Lebanon rising to Mount Hermon, with the Beqaa Valley between. Solomon's temple and palace were built of its cedar, cut and floated south under a deal with Hiram of Tyre. Israel was promised it and never took all of it.
entries.books: Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Psalm, Song of Solomon, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Hosea, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zechariah
entries.label: 16 books
entries.dictNote: Lebanon is the mountain range running along Syria's Mediterranean coast, its western ridge, Lebanon proper, and eastern ridge, the Anti-Lebanon culminating in Mount Hermon, enclosing the long Beqaa Valley between them. Its cedar forests supplied timber for Solomon's temple and palace, cut and floated south under an agreement with Hiram of Tyre, and its snow capped peaks and springs made it a recurring image of grandeur and freshness in the Psalms and Song of Solomon. Israel was promised the territory but never fully conquered it. Egyptian records such as the Tale of Wenamun describe the same cedar trade with the Lebanese coast that the Bible attributes to Solomon and Hiram.

entries.title: Lebaoth
entries.summary: "Lionesses." One of Judah's southernmost towns, by the Edom border, and probably the same as Beth-lebaoth, which went to Simeon.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Lebaoth, meaning "lionesses," was one of the southernmost towns of Judah's tribal allotment, near the border with Edom (Joshua 15:32). It is probably identical with Beth-lebaoth, assigned to Simeon in Joshua 19:6.

entries.title: Lebonah
entries.summary: Judges 21:19 uses it to say where Shiloh was, on the road between Bethel and Shechem, when the men of Benjamin grabbed wives from the girls dancing at the festival. It is generally identified with Lubban, south of Nablus, which still keeps the name.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Lebonah was a town near Shiloh, used in Judges 21:19 as a landmark to describe Shiloh's location relative to the annual festival where the men of Benjamin seized wives from among the dancing women. It lay along the road between Bethel and Shechem and is generally identified with the modern village of Lubban, south of Nablus, which still preserves the ancient name.

entries.title: Lecah (Man or town at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Named once among the descendants of Shelah, Judah's son by Bath-shua, and probably a clan or the town it founded. Nothing further is known of it.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Lecah is named once, in the genealogy of Judah, among the descendants of Shelah, Judah's third son by his Canaanite wife Bath-shua (1 Chronicles 4:21). As with several other names in this genealogical passage, it likely denotes a clan or the town it founded rather than a single individual. Nothing further is known of it.

entries.title: Lehabim (People from Lehab)
entries.summary: A people descended from Mizraim, the ancestor of Egypt, in the Table of Nations. The name is widely tied to the Lebu of Egyptian inscriptions, ancestors of the Libyans on the coast west of Egypt.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Lehabim appears in the Table of Nations as one of the peoples descended from Mizraim, the biblical ancestor of Egypt (Genesis 10:13; 1 Chronicles 1:11). The name is widely connected to the Rebu or Lebu people known from Egyptian inscriptions, generally identified as ancestors of the Libyans, who lived along the North African coast west of Egypt.

entries.title: Lehi
entries.summary: "Jawbone." The Philistines gathered here to take Samson, and he broke his ropes and killed a thousand of them with a donkey's jawbone. Afterwards, parched, he called on God, and a spring opened in a hollow there.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Lehi, meaning jawbone, was a place in Judah where the Philistines gathered to capture Samson after he had been burning their fields, only for him to break free of his ropes and strike down a thousand of them with the jawbone of a donkey (Judges 15:9-15). Samson then named the site Ramath-lehi and, when thirsty afterward, called on God, who split open a hollow place there that became known as En-hakkore, the spring of the caller (Judges 15:17-19).

entries.title: Lemuel (King living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Proverbs 31 opens with what his mother taught him, to stay off wine and stand up for the poor and needy. Which kingdom he ruled nobody knows. Later Jewish tradition sometimes made him Solomon under another name, but that cannot be confirmed.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Lemuel was a king whose mother's wise instruction is recorded in Proverbs 31:1-9, advice about avoiding wine and defending the poor and needy. Nothing certain is known about which kingdom he ruled, and later Jewish tradition sometimes identified him with Solomon under a symbolic name, though this cannot be confirmed.

entries.title: Leshem (Dan)
entries.summary: An older form of Laish, the Canaanite city Dan took and renamed after leaving its assigned land on the coast. Tel Dan, the site, produced the Tel Dan Stele, where an Aramean king boasts of beating the "house of David," the earliest mention of David's dynasty outside the Bible.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Leshem is an older form of the name Laish, the Canaanite city that the tribe of Dan captured and resettled after abandoning their assigned coastal territory, renaming it Dan after their ancestor (Joshua 19:47; compare the fuller account in Judges 18). The site, at Tel Dan in northern Israel, has been extensively excavated and is best known for producing the Tel Dan Stele, a ninth-century BC inscription in which an Aramean king boasts of defeating the "house of David," the earliest extrabiblical reference to David's dynasty.

entries.title: Letushim (People, perhaps from Letush)
entries.summary: A tribe, not a person. They were one of three groups from Dedan, Abraham's grandson through Keturah, with Asshurim and Leummim, and who they were in history is uncertain.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Letushim was not an individual but one of three tribal groups, alongside Asshurim and Leummim, descended from Dedan, a grandson of Abraham through Keturah (Genesis 25:3). Like the other two, its plural Hebrew form marks it as the name of a clan or people rather than a single ancestor, and its historical identity is uncertain.

entries.title: Leummim (People, perhaps from Leumm)
entries.summary: The word means "peoples." It names a group of Arabian tribes from Dedan, Abraham's grandson through Keturah, listed with Asshurim and Letushim.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Leummim designates a group of Arabian tribes rather than a single ancestor, listed among the descendants of Dedan, grandson of Abraham through Keturah, in the genealogy of Genesis 25:3. The Hebrew word itself means peoples or nations, marking it as a collective term for related clans rather than one man's name. Like the neighboring Asshurim and Letushim named in the same verse, it names a tribal confederation that settled in the Arabian peninsula along routes later associated with Midian and Sheba.

entries.title: Levi (Apostle living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: The tax collector better known as Matthew. One verse after Jesus called him from his booth, Levi threw a big dinner for him, full of tax collectors and other outcasts, and the Pharisees complained.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A second mention, one verse later, of the same Levi named in Luke 5:27, the tax collector better known as Matthew, who left his post to follow Jesus and then hosted a banquet for him attended by fellow tax collectors and other social outcasts, drawing sharp criticism from the Pharisees (Luke 5:27-32).

entries.title: Levi (Jacob's son living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Jacob's third son. He and Simeon massacred the men of Shechem after their sister Dinah was raped, and Jacob cursed them both for it on his deathbed. Even so, Levi's descendants became Israel's priestly tribe, given service at the tabernacle instead of land, partly for their zeal against the golden calf at Sinai.
entries.books: Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, 1 Kings, 1 Chronicles, Ezra, Ezekiel, Zechariah, Malachi, Hebrews, Revelation
entries.label: 13 books
entries.dictNote: Levi was Jacob's third son, and his violent participation in the massacre at Shechem after his sister Dinah's rape earned Jacob's deathbed condemnation alongside his brother Simeon. Levi's descendants nonetheless became Israel's priestly tribe, set apart for temple and tabernacle service instead of receiving a normal territorial inheritance, a role the Levites earned in part by their zeal in punishing the golden calf idolatry at Sinai. A few minor figures in Jesus's genealogy also carry the name Levi.

witness.excerpt: Levi and his sons; and these are the names of his sons: Gershon, and Kohath, and Merari--four.
And Levi and Dan and Asher went forth on the east side of the tower, and fifty (men) with them, and they slew the fighting men of Moab and Ammon.
And Levi and Judah were glorified by the Lord even among the sons of Jacob; for the Lord gave them an inheritance, and to Levi He gave the priesthood, and to Judah the kingdom.

entries.title: Levi (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: This is Matthew the tax collector. Mark and Luke call him Levi when they tell the story of his calling.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: This Greek-language Levi entry refers to Matthew the tax collector, called Levi in Mark and Luke's accounts of his calling; see the entry for Matthew.

entries.title: Levi (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A Levi in Luke's genealogy, and not Levi the tax collector.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Leviite (Jacob's son living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: An old spelling of Levite, found in a few manuscripts and translations for the tribe of Levi.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Leviite is an alternate spelling of Levite found in a handful of biblical manuscripts and translations, referring to the same tribe of Levi set apart for tabernacle and temple service.

entries.title: Levite (Jacob's son living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: They belonged to the tribe of Levi and served at the tabernacle and later the temple, helping the priests, who came from Aaron's branch of the same tribe. Their work was religious, so they got no tribal land, only forty eight towns among the other tribes and the tithes of Israel. Over time they carried and guarded the holy things, sang, kept the gates, and taught the law.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Levites were members of the tribe of Levi set apart to serve in Israel's tabernacle and later temple, assisting the priests, who came from Aaron's branch of the same tribe. Because their work was religious rather than agricultural, they received no tribal land allotment; instead they were given forty eight designated cities scattered among the other tribes and lived on tithes from the rest of Israel. Their duties ranged from carrying and guarding the sacred furnishings during the wilderness journey to serving later as temple musicians, gatekeepers, and teachers of the law.

witness.excerpt: Elcanah, a Levite, one of a middle condition among his fellow citizens; and one that dwelt at Ramathaim, a city of the tribe of Ephraim, married two wives, Hannah and Peninnah.
There was a Levite, a man of a vulgar family, that belonged to the tribe of Ephraim, and dwelt therein.

In this city lived one Abinadab , by birth a Levite, and who was greatly commended for his righteous and religious course of life: so they brought the ark to his house, as to a place fit for God himself to abide in, since therein did inhabit a righteous man.

entries.title: Levitical (Jacob's son living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Not a person. The word describes the hereditary priesthood from Levi, and Hebrews 7:11 uses it to argue that this priesthood could never make anything perfect, since Scripture speaks of another priest "after the order of Melchizedek."
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: "Levitical" is not a person but an adjective describing the hereditary priesthood descended from the tribe of Levi under the law of Moses. Hebrews 7:11 uses the term to argue that the Levitical priesthood could not bring about lasting perfection, since Scripture later speaks of a different priest arising "after the order of Melchizedek" rather than after Levi's line.

entries.title: Libertine (Group of Jews in the New Testament)
entries.summary: Members of the Synagogue of the Freedmen in Jerusalem, Jews once enslaved in Rome and later set free, possibly taken there after Pompey conquered Judea in 63 BC. Some of them argued with Stephen and helped bring the false charges that got him killed.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: "Libertine" in Acts 6:9 does not name an individual but describes members of the Synagogue of the Freedmen in Jerusalem, a congregation of Jews or their descendants who had once been enslaved in Rome, likely deported there after Pompey's conquest of Judea in 63 BC, and later manumitted. Members of this synagogue were among those who disputed with Stephen and helped bring the false charges that led to his execution (Acts 6:9-14).

entries.title: Libnah
entries.summary: A royal Canaanite city near Lachish that Joshua took and gave to the Levites in Judah. It held out against Sennacherib's Assyrians. Hamutal, Josiah's wife and mother of two of Judah's last kings, came from there.
entries.books: Joshua, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Isaiah, Jeremiah
entries.label: 6 books
entries.dictNote: Libnah was first one of Israel's wilderness campsites and later a royal Canaanite city near Lachish that Joshua captured and assigned to the Levites within Judah. It withstood a siege by Sennacherib's Assyrian forces and was the hometown of Hamutal, wife of Josiah and mother of two of Judah's last kings.

witness.excerpt: He reigned in Jerusalem: and his mother was Hamutal , of the city Libnah.
However, this expedition did him no service: for they all revolted from him, with those that dwelt in the countrey of Libnah.

entries.title: Libnah
entries.summary: Named twice, in Numbers, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Libni (Levite living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Gershon's son, Levi's grandson, and the head of one of the Levitical clans.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Libni was a son of Gershon, Levi's grandson, and his descendants formed one of the Levitical clans.

entries.title: Libni (Levite living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a Levite from the wilderness years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Libnites (Levite living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Libni's clan, Levites from Gershon's line, who looked after the coverings and hangings of the tabernacle on the march.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Libnites were a Levitical clan descended from Libni, a son of Gershon, and were among the families given responsibility for the tabernacle's coverings and hangings during Israel's wilderness travels.

entries.title: Libya
entries.summary: North Africa west of Egypt, with Cyrene its main city in the Greco-Roman period. People from Libya were in Jerusalem at Pentecost.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The region of North Africa west of Egypt, associated in Genesis 10:13 with the Ludim among the descendants of Mizraim (Egypt). Cyrene was its most prominent city in the Greco-Roman period, and Jews from Libya were present in Jerusalem at Pentecost (Acts 2:10).
