entries.title: Likhi (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Shemidah's son, of Manasseh, and a family head in that tribe.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A descendant of Manasseh through Shemidah, listed among the family heads of that tribe (1 Chronicles 7:19).

entries.title: Linus (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Paul passes on his greeting to Timothy from Rome. Irenaeus records a tradition that he was the first bishop of Rome after Peter and Paul, though the New Testament says nothing about any office he held.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Christian in Rome whom Paul names in his greetings to Timothy (2 Timothy 4:21). Early church tradition, recorded by Irenaeus, identifies him as the first bishop of Rome after Peter and Paul, though the New Testament itself says nothing about any church office he held.

entries.title: Lo-ammi (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: "Not my people." God told Hosea to give his second son by Gomer that name, to say Israel's northern kingdom was being cast off. Later in the book it is turned round, and those called "not my people" are to be called sons of the living God. Paul reads that reversal as the Gentiles coming in.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Lo-ammi, meaning “not my people,” was the symbolic name God commanded the prophet Hosea to give his second son by Gomer, representing God's coming rejection of the northern kingdom of Israel for its unfaithfulness (Hosea 1:9). The name is deliberately reversed later in the book, where God promises that those once called “not my people” will be called “sons of the living God” (Hosea 1:10; 2:23), a reversal Paul later applies to the inclusion of Gentiles among God's people (Romans 9:25-26). Hosea's children's names function as a set of acted prophecies rather than ordinary personal names.

entries.title: Lo-debar
entries.summary: A town where, in 2 Samuel 9, a lame son of the old royal house is found living in another man's home. Amos plays on its name, which sounds like "nothing."
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Debir refers to both a Canaanite king Joshua defeated and a town in the hill country of Judah that Othniel captured, winning Caleb's daughter Achsah in marriage as a reward.

witness.excerpt: So when he had learned where and by whom he was brought up, he sent messengers to Machir, to the city of Lodebar, for with him was the son of Jonathan brought up, and sent for him to come to him.

entries.title: Lo-ruhamah (Woman living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: "Not pitied." Hosea's daughter carried the name as a sign that God would stop showing mercy to the northern kingdom, and when Hosea 2:23 turns it to "loved," Paul hears in it the Gentiles brought in.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Lo-ruhamah, meaning “not pitied” or “not loved,” was the symbolic name God commanded the prophet Hosea to give his daughter, signifying that God would no longer show mercy to the northern kingdom of Israel (Hosea 1:6-8). The name's reversal in Hosea 2:23, where God promises to call her “loved,” became a picture of future restoration that Paul later applies to the inclusion of Gentiles (Romans 9:25).

entries.title: Lod
entries.summary: They called it Lydda in New Testament Greek. Over seven hundred people came back from exile to this town of Benjamin, on the plain along the road from Jerusalem to Joppa. Modern Lod, by Tel Aviv's airport, keeps the name.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Lod is the Hebrew name for the town known in the New Testament by its Greek name, Lydda. It is listed among the towns of Benjamin resettled by Jews returning from Babylonian exile, its population numbering over seven hundred according to the lists in Ezra and Nehemiah (Ezra 2:33; Nehemiah 7:37; 11:35). It lay on the coastal plain along the road from Jerusalem to Joppa, and modern Lod, near Tel Aviv's international airport, preserves the ancient name.

entries.title: Lois (Woman living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Timothy's grandmother. Paul says the faith he sees in Timothy lived first in her and then in her daughter Eunice.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The grandmother of Timothy, commended by Paul for the sincere faith she passed down through her daughter Eunice to her grandson (2 Timothy 1:5), making her one of the few New Testament figures named specifically for her role in a family's spiritual formation.

entries.title: Lot (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Abraham's nephew, who came with him from Ur. When their herdsmen started fighting and they split, Lot took the green Jordan valley and ended up living by Sodom. Angels dragged him out before it burned, and his wife looked back and became a pillar of salt. Afterwards his two daughters got him drunk and had sons by him, the fathers of Moab and Ammon.
entries.label: 5 books
entries.dictNote: Lot was Abraham's nephew who traveled with him from Ur and eventually settled near Sodom, choosing the fertile Jordan valley for himself when he and Abraham split up to avoid conflict between their herdsmen. When God destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah, angels physically dragged Lot and his family out of the city, and Lot's wife was turned into a pillar of salt for looking back against their explicit instructions. Lot's two daughters, believing no other men were left alive, later got their father drunk and conceived children by him, and those sons became the ancestors of the Moabites and Ammonites.

witness.excerpt: He gave Lot his option, or leave to chuse which lands he would take… Lot possessed the land of the plain, and the river Jordan, not far from the city of Sodom.

entries.curatedNote: Jesus uses him three times in one breath as a warning, eating, drinking, building, right up until the fire fell (17:28-32), ending in the single starkest line in the passage: 'Remember Lot's wife.' Josephus tells the same land-division story Genesis does, the ordinary choice that put Lot next door to Sodom in the first place.

entries.title: Lotan (Edomite living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: He was a Horite chief whose sister Timna made him Esau's brother-in-law, and his people were living in Edom's land before Edom.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Lotan was a Horite chief and Esau's brother-in-law through his sister Timna, listed among the earlier inhabitants of Edom's territory.

entries.title: Lucas (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: The Latin form of Luke, Paul's travelling companion and doctor. Early tradition gives him the Gospel of Luke and Acts, which would make him the one Gentile writer in the New Testament.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Lucas is the Latin form of Luke, Paul's traveling companion and physician, and early church tradition credits him with writing both the Gospel of Luke and the book of Acts, making him the only Gentile author in the New Testament.

entries.title: Lucius (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: One of the prophets and teachers in the church at Antioch, from Cyrene, there when the Holy Spirit set Barnabas and Saul apart. Paul sends greetings from a Lucius he calls his kinsman in Romans 16:21, and whether that is the same man is uncertain.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Lucius of Cyrene was one of the prophets and teachers at the church in Antioch who, along with Barnabas and Saul, was set apart by the Holy Spirit for missionary work (Acts 13:1-2). Paul later calls a Lucius his kinsman in his greetings from Corinth, though it is uncertain whether this is the same man (Romans 16:21).

entries.title: Lud (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Shem's son. His people are usually taken to be the Lydians of Asia Minor. Some later passages may mean a people in Africa instead.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Lud was a son of Shem, and his descendants are generally associated with the Lydians of Asia Minor, though some later biblical uses of the name possibly point toward peoples in Africa instead.

witness.excerpt: And there came forth for Lud  the fifth portion, the mountains of Asshur and all appertaining to them till it reacheth the Great Sea, and till it reacheth the east of Asshur his brother.
And these are the sons of Shem: Elam, and Asshur, and Arpachshad--this (son) was born two years after the flood--and Lud, and Aram.  19.

entries.title: Luhith
entries.summary: In Isaiah and Jeremiah, refugees climb the road up to Luhith in Moab weeping. It was somewhere between Zoar and Horonaim, exactly where is unknown.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: The ascent of Luhith was a road in Moab that refugees are pictured fleeing up while weeping, in the oracles of judgment against Moab shared by Isaiah and Jeremiah in nearly identical language (Isa. 15:5; Jer. 48:5). It lay somewhere between Zoar and Horonaim, though its exact location is unknown.

entries.title: Luz
entries.summary: Named once, in Judges, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Luz (Bethel)
entries.summary: It was the old Canaanite name of Bethel, where Jacob dreamed of the stairway to heaven, and it hung on in a nearby town after Bethel was renamed.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Luz was the original Canaanite name for Bethel, the site where Jacob had his dream of a stairway to heaven, and the name persisted for a nearby town even after Bethel itself was renamed.

entries.title: Lycaonia
entries.summary: Inland Asia Minor, between Cappadocia and Galatia, with Iconium, Lystra and Derbe in it. Paul and Barnabas preached through it on the first journey. The crowd at Lystra shouted in "the speech of Lycaonia" when they took the two for Hermes and Zeus, and an inscription found near Lystra shows those two gods really were worshipped together there.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Lycaonia was an inland region of Asia Minor bordered by Cappadocia and Galatia, home to the cities of Iconium, Lystra, and Derbe. Paul and Barnabas preached across the region on Paul's first missionary journey, and Paul revisited it later (Acts 14:6-21; 16:1-6). Luke notes that the crowd at Lystra shouted in "the speech of Lycaonia" when they mistook Paul and Barnabas for Hermes and Zeus (Acts 14:11-12); an inscription discovered near the site of ancient Lystra referring to priests of Hermes alongside a stone image of Zeus shows this pairing of gods was a genuine local cult, giving real background to Luke's account.

photo.description: panorama of a hill in Lycaonia

entries.title: Lycia
entries.summary: Mountains and coast in southwest Asia Minor, across from Rhodes. Paul's ships put in at its ports, Patara and Myra.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Lycia was not a person but a mountainous region and Roman province on the southwestern coast of Asia Minor, opposite Rhodes. Paul's ship touched its ports of Patara and Myra on voyages to and from Jerusalem (Acts 21:1-2; 27:5), and its cities have yielded substantial Greek and native Lycian-language inscriptions documenting the region's distinct pre-Roman culture.

entries.title: Lydda (Lod)
entries.summary: About nine miles southeast of Joppa on the coastal plain. Peter healed a paralysed man named Aeneas there, and many in the plain of Sharon turned to the Lord. Today it is Lod, where Ben Gurion Airport is.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Lydda was a town on the coastal plain about nine miles southeast of Joppa, known in the Old Testament as Lod (1 Chronicles 8:12). Peter healed a paralyzed man named Aeneas there, a miracle that led many in the surrounding plain of Sharon to turn to the Lord (Acts 9:32-35). The Romans later destroyed and rebuilt the city under the name Diospolis; today it is the Israeli city of Lod, home to Ben Gurion Airport.

entries.title: Lydia (Woman living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: She sold purple cloth, came from Thyatira, and lived in Philippi when Paul arrived. She already worshipped God, and after hearing Paul by the river she and her household were baptised, apparently the first converts in Europe. Then she put Paul and his companions up in her house.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Lydia was a merchant from Thyatira dealing in purple cloth who was living in Philippi when Paul arrived there. She was already a worshiper of God, and after hearing Paul preach by the riverside she and her household were baptized, making her apparently the first convert in Europe; she then hosted Paul and his companions in her home (Acts 16:14-15, 40).

There is another witness to the same point in Croesus, the king of Lydia, the wealthiest of all monarchs, who, having conceived the hope of destroying the kingdom of the Persians, not only lost all his men, but was taken prisoner, and was at the point of being burnt alive.

entries.title: Lysanias (Tetrarch of Abilene living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Tetrarch of Abilene, on the eastern slope of the Anti-Lebanon near Damascus, and one of the rulers Luke uses to date his story. Josephus confirms the tetrarchy was real.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Tetrarch of Abilene (Luke 3:1), on the eastern slope of Anti-Lebanon, near the city of Damascus.

witness.excerpt: After which he put a diadem upon his head, and appointed him to be King of the tetrarchy of Philip. He also gave him the tetrarchy of Lysanias, and changed his iron chain for a golden one of equal weight.

entries.lukeNote: The most minor name in Luke's whole list of rulers (3:1), tetrarch of Abilene, otherwise unattested in the Gospels. Josephus confirms the tetrarchy was real and names its later fate: folded into Herod Agrippa I's kingdom a few years after Luke's date, exactly the kind of small-print detail a fabricated list would be unlikely to get right.

entries.title: Lysias (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Claudius Lysias, the Roman tribune over the garrison at the Antonia Fortress. He pulled Paul out of a mob in the temple and then sent him under armed guard to Felix in Caesarea with a letter about the case.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Lysias, more fully Claudius Lysias, was the Roman tribune who commanded the garrison at the Antonia Fortress in Jerusalem. He rescued Paul from a mob in the temple, had him examined under guard, and later sent him under armed escort to the governor Felix in Caesarea with a letter explaining the case (Acts 21:31-33; 23:26-30). He is not the same person as the Hellenistic-era Syrian regent of the same name mentioned in the books of Maccabees, who lived roughly two centuries earlier.

entries.summary: Acts names him once, and he is a man from the New Testament.

entries.title: Lystra
entries.summary: A Roman colony in the wild hills of Lycaonia, and Timothy's hometown. Paul healed a man lame from birth there and the crowd tried to sacrifice to him and Barnabas as Hermes and Zeus. Then Paul's opponents turned the same crowd, and they stoned him and left him for dead.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Lystra was a Roman colony in the wild, mountainous district of Lycaonia in Asia Minor, established under Augustus and settled with military veterans; it was Timothy's hometown (2 Timothy 3:10-11; Acts 16:1). Paul preached there after being driven from Iconium and healed a man lame from birth, so impressing the crowd that they tried to offer sacrifices to Paul and Barnabas as Hermes and Zeus, an episode matched by inscriptions found near Lystra dedicating statues to that same local pairing of gods; the same crowd, stirred up by Paul's opponents, then stoned him and left him for dead (Acts 14:8-19).

entries.title: Maachah (Maacath)
entries.summary: A small Aramean kingdom near Geshur, east of the Sea of Galilee. Israel never managed to drive it out.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Maachah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Maachah (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Genesis names him once, and he is a man from the patriarchs.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Maachah (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 10 men called Maachah. This one is a man from the united kingdom, named once in 1 Kings.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Maachah (Woman living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Absalom's granddaughter, married to Rehoboam, and queen mother after him. Her grandson Asa took the title away because she promoted idol worship.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Maachah was a small Aramean kingdom near Geshur, east of the Sea of Galilee in the region later called Batanea, mentioned among the peoples Israel failed to fully dispossess in Joshua's day. The same Hebrew name was borne by several people connected to the royal court: Maacah daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur, became one of David's wives and the mother of Absalom, while another Maacah, also called Michaiah, a granddaughter of Absalom, married Rehoboam and later served as queen mother until her grandson Asa removed her for promoting idol worship. A third Maacah fathered Achish, king of Gath, in Saul's day.

witness.excerpt: And after he had married a woman of his own kindred, and had by her three children born to him, he married also another of his own kindred, who was daughter of Absalom by Tamar, whose name was Maachah, and by her he had a son, whom he named Abijah.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Maai (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Maarath
entries.summary: Hill-country Judah, near Hebron. It is often placed near Beit Ummar, a few miles north of Hebron, though the identification is not certain.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Maarath was a town in the hill country of Judah, listed among the settlements near Hebron in Joshua's account of Judah's inheritance (Josh. 15:59). It is often placed near the modern village of Beit Ummar, a few miles north of Hebron, though the identification is not certain.

entries.title: Macedonia
entries.summary: The Roman province over northern Greece. Paul crossed into it after a vision of a man pleading, "Come over into Macedonia and help us," and went on through Philippi, Thessalonica and Berea, where Christian mission in Europe is usually said to begin. He came back at least twice and praised its churches for giving out of their poverty.
entries.books: Acts, Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians, 1 Timothy
entries.label: 7 books
entries.dictNote: Macedonia was the Roman province covering northern Greece, governed by a proconsul, that Paul entered after receiving a vision of a man pleading, “Come over into Macedonia and help us.” His journey through its cities, including Philippi, Thessalonica, and Berea, marks the traditional start of Christian mission in Europe, and Lydia of Philippi, a seller of purple dye, was his first recorded convert there. Paul revisited the province at least twice more and later praised the Macedonian churches for their generosity despite their own poverty. Travel through the province followed the Via Egnatia, the Roman road linking the Adriatic to Byzantium, whose paved remains can still be traced in parts of modern Greece and North Macedonia.

entries.title: Machbenah (Woman or town of at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Sheva is said to have "fathered" it in Caleb's genealogy, which probably means he founded the settlement. Where it was is unknown.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Machbenah appears in the genealogy of Caleb in 1 Chronicles 2:49, said to be "fathered" by Sheva. As with several other names in this list, it most likely stands for a town or clan settlement rather than a literal individual, following the Chronicler's habit of expressing tribal and geographic relationships in father-son language. Its location is unknown.

entries.title: Machi (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)

entries.dictNote: Machi was the father of Geuel, the Gadite who was one of the twelve spies Moses sent to scout the land of Canaan (Numbers 13:15).

entries.label: 6 books
entries.dictNote: Machir was Manasseh's son, and his descendants, the Machirites, were notable enough as a fighting clan that Machir's name is sometimes used to represent the entire half-tribe of Manasseh that settled east of the Jordan.

entries.title: Machpelah
entries.summary: The cave near Hebron that Abraham bought from Ephron the Hittite, with its field, to bury his family. Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Rebekah, Jacob and Leah all ended up there. Herod's massive stone enclosure still stands over the traditional site, now a mosque and a synagogue.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Machpelah was the cave near Hebron that Abraham bought from Ephron the Hittite, together with the field around it, as a family burial ground (Genesis 23), later holding the bodies of Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Rebekah, Jacob, and Leah (Genesis 49:31; 50:13). A massive Herodian-era stone enclosure still stands over the traditional site in Hebron, one of the best-preserved large structures anywhere from Herod's building program, now shared as a mosque and synagogue.

entries.title: Madian (Midian)
entries.summary: Midian, in Greek. Moses ran there after killing an Egyptian and kept sheep for his father-in-law until God called him at the burning bush.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Madian, the Greek form of Midian, the region east of the Gulf of Aqaba where Moses fled after killing an Egyptian and where he lived as a shepherd for his father-in-law until God called him at the burning bush (Acts 7:29-30; see Exod. 2:15-22).

entries.title: Madmannah
entries.summary: Down in the Negev, in Judah's south, and later held by Caleb's descendants. One proposed site is southwest of Gaza and another northeast of Beersheba, and neither is certain.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Madmannah was a town in the southern Negev of Judah, later held by descendants of Caleb (Joshua 15:31; 1 Chronicles 2:49). Two different modern sites have been proposed for it, one southwest of Gaza and another northeast of Beersheba, and neither identification is certain.

entries.title: Madmen
entries.summary: Jeremiah names this Moabite town in his judgment on Moab and puns on it: it sounds like the Hebrew for "be silenced," and Moab would be silenced.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Moabite town named in Jeremiah's oracle of judgment against Moab, threatened with destruction by an invading army (Jer. 48:2). The prophet plays on the town's name, which sounds like the Hebrew for be silenced, to declare that Moab itself would be silenced.

entries.title: Madmenah
entries.summary: Its people run in Isaiah's picture of an army coming down on Jerusalem from the north, one village in a list with Anathoth and Nob.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Madmenah was a town near Jerusalem named in Isaiah's vivid poetic sketch of an invading army's advance, whose inhabitants flee before it reaches the city (Isa. 10:31). It appears in a short list of villages north of Jerusalem, alongside Anathoth and Nob, tracing the imagined approach route of an Assyrian force.

entries.title: Madon
entries.summary: Its king joined Jabin of Hazor's coalition against Joshua at the Waters of Merom and was killed. It has been tentatively placed at a ruin near Hattin, west of Tiberias.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Madon was a Canaanite city in northern Palestine whose king joined the coalition Jabin of Hazor assembled against Joshua at the Waters of Merom; the alliance was defeated and its king killed (Joshua 11:1; 12:19). It has been tentatively located at a ruin near Hattin, west of Tiberias.

entries.title: Magbish
entries.summary: One hundred fifty-six men came back from Babylon with Zerubbabel under this name. Whether it is a town or an ancestor is argued, and if a town, no one has found it.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Magbish appears once, in the list of families and towns whose people returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel, a group of 156 men identified by it (Ezra 2:30). Whether Magbish names a place or an ancestor is debated, since most of the surrounding entries in that list are towns but a few are clearly clan names. Its location, if a place, has not been identified.

entries.title: Magdala (Magadan)
entries.summary: The home town that gave Mary Magdalene her name, on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee. Matthew says Jesus went to the region of Magdala after feeding the four thousand, where Mark calls the same area Dalmanutha. Digging there since 2009 has turned up a first-century synagogue and the carved Magdala Stone, one of the earliest pictures of the Temple's menorah.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Magdala, from the Hebrew Migdal meaning tower, sat on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee and is remembered chiefly as the hometown of Mary Magdalene. Matthew 15:39 names it as the region Jesus reached after feeding the four thousand; Mark's parallel account calls the same area Dalmanutha. Excavations at the site since 2009 have uncovered a first-century synagogue and the intricately carved "Magdala Stone," one of the earliest known depictions of the Jerusalem Temple's menorah, likely carved by someone who had seen the Temple standing before its destruction in AD 70.

entries.title: Magdalene (Magadan)
entries.summary: It means "from Magdala," the town on the Sea of Galilee, and it keeps this Mary apart from the other Marys in the Gospels. She watched the crucifixion and was the first to see the risen Jesus. The old idea that she was the sinful woman of Luke 7 has nothing in the text behind it.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Magdalene identifies Mary as coming from Magdala, a town on the Sea of Galilee, distinguishing her from the Gospels' other women named Mary. She is best known as a witness to the crucifixion and the first person to see the risen Jesus, and the long standing tradition identifying her with the unnamed sinful woman of Luke 7 has no basis in the biblical text itself.

entries.title: Magdiel (Edomite living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: One of the chiefs of Edom descended from Esau, in the lists at Genesis 36:43 and 1 Chronicles 1:54. The name may mark a clan territory more than a single ruler.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Magdiel was one of the tribal chiefs (“dukes”) of Edom descended from Esau, listed in the Edomite king-and-chief records of Genesis 36:43 and 1 Chronicles 1:54. Nothing else is recorded of him individually; his name marks a clan territory rather than necessarily one ruler.

entries.title: Magog
entries.summary: Ezekiel makes it the homeland of Gog, who leads a great army against a restored Israel. Revelation picks the name up again for the nations gathered in the last rebellion against God. In the genealogies Magog is a son of Japheth.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Magog was a son of Japheth and, in Ezekiel's prophecy, the homeland of Gog, the leader of a future coalition invading restored Israel, a name later reused symbolically in Revelation for the nations gathered in final rebellion against God.

entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Mahalalel was a descendant of Seth in the genealogy leading to Noah, four generations before Enoch.

entries.title: Mahalath (A musical term)
entries.summary: Two psalms are set upon Mahalath. What that means is not settled.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Mahalath here is not a person but a musical or liturgical term in the headings of Psalms 53 and 88, both of which are set "upon Mahalath." Its exact meaning is uncertain; suggestions include a tune name, a wind instrument, or a word related to sickness or suffering fitting the psalms' somber content, but no consensus survives from antiquity.

entries.title: Mahalath (Woman living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 2 Chronicles names her once, and she is a woman from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mahalath (Woman living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Ishmael's daughter, and the wife Esau took to please his parents after his Canaanite wives had upset them. Genesis seems to call her Bashemath as well.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Two women named Mahalath appear in the genealogies. One was a daughter of Ishmael whom Esau married, apparently also called Bashemath, in an attempt to please his parents after his earlier marriages to Canaanite women displeased them (Genesis 28:9; 36:3). The other was a granddaughter of David, daughter of Jerimoth, who became one of Rehoboam's wives (2 Chronicles 11:18).

entries.title: Mahanaim
entries.summary: "Two camps." Jacob met the angels of God here near the Jabbok River on his way home, and split his household in two before facing Esau. After Saul died, Ishbosheth ruled the northern tribes from Mahanaim while David held Hebron, and years later David fled there himself from Absalom and heard there that his son was dead.
entries.label: 5 books
entries.dictNote: Mahanaim, meaning "two camps," was the place near the Jabbok River where Jacob was met by angels of God on his return from Paddan-aram and divided his household into two companies before facing Esau. The town later became a Levitical city and, after Saul's death, served as the capital where Ishbosheth reigned over the northern tribes while David ruled from Hebron. Decades later David himself took refuge at Mahanaim during Absalom's rebellion, and it was there he received news of Absalom's death.

entries.title: Mahaneh-dan
entries.summary: The camp of Dan, behind Kirjath-jearim. Samson first felt the Spirit stirring him here, and later six hundred armed Danites camped on the same ground on their way north to take Laish.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Mahaneh-dan, meaning camp of Dan, names the place behind Kirjath-jearim where the Spirit began to stir Samson in his youth (Judg. 13:25) and where, later, six hundred armed Danites camped on their way north to conquer the city of Laish and resettle it as Dan (Judg. 18:12).

entries.title: Maharai (Warrior living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: From Netophah, one of David's mighty warriors, and later the commander of one of David's monthly army divisions.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Maharai was one of David's mighty warriors, from the town of Netophah, and he also commanded one of the monthly military divisions David organized.

entries.title: Mahath (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A Kohathite Levite, named among the men who worked on cleaning out the temple.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Mahath was a Levite involved in the religious reforms under both Hezekiah, overseeing dedicated offerings, and generations earlier in the genealogies of the Kohathite line.

entries.title: Mahath (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 2 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mahavite (Warriors, perhaps from Mahav)
entries.summary: An epithet, and it belongs to Eliel, one of David's mighty men. Nobody knows what place it points to.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Mahavite identifies Eliel, one of David's mighty men; the place the epithet refers to is otherwise unknown.

entries.title: Mahazioth (Levite living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Heman's son, one of the Kohathite Levites David set over the temple music. He led the twenty-third of the twenty-four courses. His name means "visions," which suits a family whose playing was called prophesying.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Mahazioth was a Kohathite Levite, one of the sons of Heman appointed by David to lead temple music, and he headed the twenty-third of the twenty-four courses of musicians who served on a rotating schedule (1 Chronicles 25:4, 30-31). His name means “visions,” fitting a family whose musical service was described as prophesying with instruments (1 Chronicles 25:1). Nothing else is recorded of him.

entries.title: Maher-sha-lal-bash-baz (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Isaiah's son, and the name was the message: "quick to the plunder, swift to the spoil." Before the boy could say father or mother, Assyria would strip Damascus and Samaria. Isaiah had the name written on a large tablet, with two reliable men as witnesses, before the child was born.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Maher-shalal-hash-baz, meaning “quick to the plunder, swift to the spoil,” was the son of the prophet Isaiah, given this deliberately ominous name as a sign to King Ahaz that Assyria would plunder Damascus and Samaria before the child could say “father” or “mother” (Isaiah 8:1-4). Isaiah had the name publicly recorded on a large tablet before the boy's birth, witnessed by two reliable men, underscoring the prophecy's certainty. The prediction was fulfilled within a few years when Tiglath-Pileser III of Assyria conquered Damascus and stripped Israel of territory.

entries.title: Mahlah (Woman living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names her once, and she is a woman from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mahlah (Woman living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Zelophehad had five daughters and no son, and Mahlah was one of them; their plea to Moses to inherit his land changed the law.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Mahlah was one of five daughters of Zelophehad whose successful petition to Moses for the right to inherit their father's land in the absence of a son set a new legal precedent.

entries.title: Mahli (Levite living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Merari's son and Levi's grandson. His family became one of the Levitical clans with work at the tabernacle.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Mahli was a son of Merari, Levi's grandson, and his descendants formed one of the Levitical clans responsible for tabernacle duties.

entries.title: Mahli (Levite living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: A second Mahli, under Merari's line in the Levite lists of Chronicles, and nothing more is known of him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mahlites (Levite living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: The Levites from Mahli, son of Merari. With the Mushites they looked after the frame of the tabernacle.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Mahlites were the Levitical clan descended from Mahli, son of Merari, counted alongside the Mushites among the families responsible for the tabernacle's structural components.

entries.title: Mahlon (Man living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: Naomi's son, and Ruth's first husband. He died in Moab with his brother and father, which left Ruth a widow with no child before she went back to Bethlehem with Naomi and married Boaz.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Mahlon was Naomi's son and Ruth's first husband, who died in Moab along with his brother and father, leaving Ruth a childless widow before her return to Bethlehem with Naomi and her eventual marriage to Boaz.

entries.title: Mahol (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Four wise men, Ethan, Heman, Chalcol and Darda, are called his sons in 1 Kings 4:31, and Solomon was wiser than all of them. The same men appear elsewhere as sons of Zerah of Judah, so "sons of Mahol" may be a guild or family name rather than a real father.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Mahol was the father of four men, Ethan, Heman, Chalcol, and Darda, renowned for their wisdom, whom 1 Kings 4:31 says Solomon surpassed. Some read 'sons of Mahol' as a guild or family name rather than a literal father, since these same men appear elsewhere as sons of Zerah of Judah (1 Chronicles 2:6). Either way, the comparison shows how far Solomon's proverbial wisdom was thought to exceed even the most gifted of his contemporaries.

witness.excerpt: He also excelled and distinguished himself in wisdom above those who were most eminent among the Hebrews at that time for shrewdness; those I mean were Ethan, and Heman, and Chalcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol.

entries.title: Mainan (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A name in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, from David's son Nathan, a few generations above Mattatha and Melea. The Old Testament never mentions him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Mainan appears in Luke's genealogy of Jesus as an ancestor descended from David's son Nathan, several generations before Mattatha and Melea (Luke 3:31). He is not otherwise mentioned in the Old Testament and nothing beyond his place in the list is known.

entries.title: Makaz
entries.summary: Solomon had twelve officers feeding his household, and Ben-deker's district took in Makaz, Shaalbim and Beth-shemesh. That one verse is all there is, and the site has never been found.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Makaz appears once, in the list of twelve district officers who supplied provisions for Solomon's royal household, naming the territory under Ben-deker's charge alongside Shaalbim and Beth-shemesh (1 Kings 4:9). Nothing else is known of it, and its site has not been discovered.

entries.title: Makheloth
entries.summary: Somewhere between Haradah and Tahath on Israel's march, in the list of camps in Numbers 33.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Wilderness campsite of Israel, named only in the travel itinerary of Numbers 33 between Haradah and Tahath (Num. 33:25-26). Nothing further is recorded of it.

entries.title: Makkedah
entries.summary: Five Amorite kings ran from the battle at Gibeon and hid in a cave near this royal city in the Shephelah. Joshua sealed them in until the fighting was over, then brought them out, killed them, and hung their bodies on trees. Then he took the city.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Makkedah was a royal Canaanite city in the Shephelah near a cave where five allied Amorite kings hid after their defeat by Joshua at Gibeon. Joshua had the kings sealed inside the cave until the battle was finished, then had them brought out, executed, and their bodies hung on trees before the city itself was captured and destroyed.

witness.excerpt: Insomuch that Joshua took the Kings, which were hidden in a certain cave at Makkedah, and put them to death.

entries.title: Maktesh (Mortar)
entries.summary: "The mortar," a hollow in or near Jerusalem where merchants and silversmiths worked. Zephaniah calls out to its people when he announces judgment on the city's trade. It is generally thought to be a low market quarter, maybe in the Tyropoeon Valley.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Maktesh, meaning the mortar or hollow, named a district in or near Jerusalem inhabited by merchants and silversmiths, addressed directly in Zephaniah's prophecy of coming judgment on the city's commercial quarter (Zeph. 1:11). It is generally thought to refer to a low-lying market area, possibly within the Tyropoeon Valley, though its exact bounds are not known.

entries.title: Malachi (Prophet living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Almost nothing is known about the man. Even his name may be a title, "my messenger." His book is the last of the prophets in the usual order, written to a Judah after the exile where priests offered blemished animals and people held back their tithes, and it ends looking for a messenger who will prepare the way before the Lord.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Malachi is the last prophetic book in the Old Testament's traditional ordering, and almost nothing is known about the man himself beyond his name, which may even be a title meaning my messenger rather than a personal name. The book confronts a post-exilic Judah that had grown spiritually lazy, priests offering blemished sacrifices and the people withholding tithes, and it closes the Old Testament looking forward to a coming messenger who would prepare the way before the Lord.

entries.title: Malcham
entries.summary: The national god of the Ammonites, also called Milcom. Solomon went after him in his old age, and the high place built for him stood near Jerusalem until a later king tore it down.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Malcham was a descendant of Benjamin listed among the tribal genealogies of Chronicles, and the name is also an alternate rendering of Milcom, the Ammonite deity elsewhere called Molech.

entries.title: Malchiah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Several men carried this name, many of them priests or from Levitical families. Their verses run from the lists in Chronicles through the men who rebuilt sections of Jerusalem's wall under Nehemiah, and on into Jeremiah.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Malchiah was a common priestly and Levitical name in the postexilic period, borne by several men who helped rebuild sections of Jerusalem's walls under Nehemiah.

entries.title: Malchiel (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: He was Asher's son, and his descendants made up one of the clans of Asher in the genealogies.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Malchiel was a son of Asher, and his descendants formed one of the clans counted among Asher's tribe in Israel's genealogies.

entries.title: Malchielite (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: The clan from Malchiel, of the tribe of Asher, counted in the wilderness census.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Malchielites were the clan descended from Malchiel, a grandson of Asher, counted among the tribe's families in Israel's wilderness census.

entries.title: Malchijah (Levite living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A levite from the divided-kingdom years. 1 Chronicles names him once.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Malchijah (Levite living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles and Nehemiah name him twice, and he is a Levite from the exile and the return.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Malchijah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 12 men called Malchijah. This one is a man from the divided-kingdom years, named once in 1 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Malchijah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A man from the exile and the return, and Nehemiah is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Malchijah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)

entries.title: Malchijah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)

entries.title: Malchijah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A man from the exile and the return. Ezra names him once.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Malchijah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Nehemiah names him once, and he is a man from the exile and the return. The verse is Nehemiah 10:3.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Malchijah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of 12 men called Malchijah. This one is a man from the exile and the return, named once in Nehemiah. The verse is Nehemiah 12:42.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Malchijah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Nehemiah names him once, and he is a man from the exile and the return. The verse is Nehemiah 3:11.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Malchijah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of 12 men called Malchijah. This one is a man from the exile and the return, named once in Nehemiah. The verse is Nehemiah 3:14.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Malchiram (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Born to King Jeconiah, also called Jehoiachin, during or after the family's time as captives in Babylon.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Malchiram was a son of King Jeconiah, also called Jehoiachin, born during or after the family's Babylonian captivity (1 Chronicles 3:18).

entries.title: Malchishua (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of Saul's sons, who died with his father and brothers when the Philistines beat Israel on Mount Gilboa.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Malchishua was one of Saul's sons, killed alongside his father and brothers in the battle against the Philistines at Mount Gilboa.

entries.title: Malchus (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Peter cut off his right ear the night Jesus was arrested. He was the high priest's servant, and Jesus healed the ear with a touch, the last miracle recorded before the crucifixion. Only John gives his name.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Malchus was the servant of the high priest present when Jesus was arrested in the garden of Gethsemane; Peter drew a sword and cut off his right ear, which Jesus then healed with a touch, the last recorded miracle before the crucifixion (John 18:10; Luke 22:51). John is the only Gospel writer who names him.

witness.excerpt: Malchus also, the king of Arabia, sent a thousand horsemen, besides five thousand footmen, the greatest part of which were archers; so that the whole army, including the auxiliaries sent by the kings, as well horsemen as footme

And indeed Alexander Polyhistor gives his attestation to what I here say: who speaks thus: “Cleodemus the Prophet, who was also called Malchus , who wrote an history of the Jews, in agreement with the history of Moses, their legislator, relates, that there were many sons born to Abraham by Keturah.

entries.title: Maleleel (Man living at the time before the Flood)
entries.summary: Luke's Greek spelling of Mahalalel, Seth's descendant before the flood, in the genealogy that runs back through Noah to Adam.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Maleleel is the Greek form of Mahalalel, a descendant of Seth before the flood, listed among the ancestors of Jesus in Luke's genealogy, which traces the line back through Noah to Adam (Luke 3:37; cf. Gen. 5:12-17).

entries.title: Mallothi (Levite living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Heman's son, one of the Levite musicians David appointed, and the lot made him head of the nineteenth of twenty-four divisions.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Mallothi was a Levite musician, one of the sons of Heman appointed by David to the temple music service (1 Chronicles 25:4). He headed the nineteenth of the twenty-four divisions of musicians chosen by lot (25:26).

entries.title: Malluch (Levite living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a Levite from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Malluch (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of those who signed the covenant renewal under Nehemiah, carrying a name common among the priests after the exile.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Malluch was a common postexilic Levitical and priestly name among those who signed the covenant renewal under Nehemiah.

entries.title: Malluch (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of 5 men called Malluch. This one is a man from the exile and the return, named once in Ezra.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Malluch (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A man from the exile and the return, and Ezra is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Malluch (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A man from the exile and the return. Nehemiah names him once.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mamre
entries.summary: Near Hebron, where Abraham settled and built an altar. The three visitors who told him Isaac was coming found him there. Mamre was also the name of an Amorite who stood with Abraham as an ally.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Mamre was an Amorite ally of Abraham and the name of the site near Hebron where Abraham settled, built an altar, and received the three visitors who announced Isaac's coming birth.

witness.excerpt: And he took all these in the middle of the month; and he dwelt at the oak of Mamre, which is near Hebron.  11.
And on the new moon of the fourth month we  appeared unto Abraham, at the oak of Mamre, and we talked with him, and we announced to him that a son would be given to him by Sarah his wife.  2.

And the Lord gave him grace before all who saw him, and he besought in gentleness the sons of Heth, and they gave him the land of the double cave  over against Mamre, that is Hebron, for four hundred pieces of silver.

entries.title: Mamre (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Genesis names him once, and he is a man from the patriarchs.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Manaen (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: A prophet and teacher in the church at Antioch, with Barnabas, Simeon called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene and Saul. That group laid hands on Barnabas and Saul and sent them out. Luke adds that Manaen grew up alongside Herod Antipas, the man who had John the Baptist killed.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Manaen was one of the prophets and teachers in the church at Antioch, listed alongside Barnabas, Simeon called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, and Saul, the group that laid hands on Barnabas and Saul to send them out on what became the first missionary journey (Acts 13:1-3). Luke notes that Manaen had been brought up together with Herod Antipas, the tetrarch who executed John the Baptist, a striking contrast between two men raised in the same household who took very different paths.

entries.title: Manahath
entries.summary: Named once, in 1 Chronicles, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Manahath (Edomite living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Shobal's son, Seir the Horite's grandson, and a clan chief of Edom in Genesis and Chronicles. The same name shows up in Benjamin's genealogy, probably for the related Manahathites, who are tied elsewhere to Zorah and Caleb's family.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Manahath was a son of Shobal and grandson of Seir the Horite, an Edomite clan chief listed in the genealogies of Genesis and Chronicles (Genesis 36:23; 1 Chronicles 1:40). The name also appears in the genealogy of Benjamin (1 Chronicles 8:6), likely referring to the related clan or town of the Manahathites, who elsewhere are connected to Zorah and the family of Caleb (1 Chronicles 2:52, 54).

entries.title: Manasseh (Joseph's son living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Joseph's elder son, whom Jacob took as his own and blessed. His name went to one of Israel's twelve tribes, and from Numbers through Joshua and Chronicles most of his verses are about that tribe and its land.
entries.books: Genesis, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 1 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Psalm, Isaiah, Ezekiel
entries.label: 11 books
entries.dictNote: Manasseh was Hezekiah's son and Judah's longest-reigning king, and also its worst: he rebuilt the high places his father had torn down, practiced sorcery, and reportedly sacrificed his own son, filling Jerusalem with innocent blood. Assyrian records confirm he was taken captive to Babylon at one point, and 2 Chronicles says that captivity broke his pride and he genuinely repented, spending his remaining years trying to undo the damage he had done, though the reforms didn't outlast him. Manasseh is also the name of Joseph's elder son, ancestor of one of Israel's twelve tribes.

witness.excerpt: Out of the half tribe of Manasseh came eighteen thousand, of the most potent men.

entries.title: Manasseh (King living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Hezekiah's son, who reigned in Judah longer than any king and did more harm than any. He rebuilt the high places, practiced sorcery, apparently sacrificed his own son, and filled Jerusalem with innocent blood. Chronicles says captivity in Babylon broke his pride and he repented, but his reforms died with him.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Manasseh (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of 4 men called Manasseh. This one is a man from the exile and the return, named once in Ezra.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Manasseh (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A man from the exile and the return, and Ezra is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Manasses (Joseph's son living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: The Greek form of Manasseh. Here it is the tribe, counted among the sealed in Revelation.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Manasses is the Greek New Testament form of Manasseh and refers to two different things. In Matthew's genealogy it names the notorious king of Judah, ancestor of Jesus, who reigned longer than any other Judean king and led the nation into idolatry (Matthew 1:10). In Revelation it instead names the tribe descended from Joseph's son Manasseh, listed among the twelve tribes sealed by God (Revelation 7:6).

entries.title: Manasses (King living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: The Greek form of Manasseh. Matthew uses it for the king of Judah in Jesus' family line, the one who reigned longest and led the nation into idols.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Manoah (Samson's father living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: Samson's father. An angel came to him and his wife, who had no children, to say a son was coming who would be a Nazirite from birth, and when Manoah realised who he had seen he was sure they would both die.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Manoah was Samson's father, and an angel appeared to him and his previously childless wife to announce Samson's birth and his lifelong Nazirite calling, an encounter so overwhelming that Manoah feared they would die for having seen God.

witness.excerpt: There was one Manoah, a person of such great virtue, that he had few men his equals; and without dispute the principal person of his countrey.

entries.title: Maoch (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Father of Achish, the Philistine king of Gath who took David in when Saul was hunting him. A later king of Gath, Achish son of Maacah, turns up in Solomon's time, and whether Maoch and Maacah are the same man or the name just ran in that royal house is uncertain.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Father of Achish, the Philistine king of Gath who sheltered David from Saul (1 Samuel 27:2). A later king of Gath also named Achish, son of Maacah, appears in Solomon's reign (1 Kings 2:39); whether Maoch and Maacah are the same figure or the name simply recurred in Gath's ruling house is uncertain.

entries.title: Maon
entries.summary: About seven miles south of Hebron, in the Judean hill country. David hid from Saul in the wilderness named after it, and Nabal, whose widow Abigail married David, kept his flocks there. The ruins, now Tell Ma'in, still mark the spot.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Maon was a hill town in the Judean hill country about seven miles south of Hebron that gave its name to the surrounding wilderness where David hid from Saul (1 Samuel 23:24-25) and where the wealthy Nabal, later married to Abigail, kept his flocks (1 Samuel 25:2). Ruins and cisterns at the site, now called Tell Ma'in, still mark its location.

witness.excerpt: For when David was apprized of the malignant intentions of the men of Ziph, and of the approach of Saul, he left the straits of that countrey; and fled to the great rock that was in the wilderness of Maon.

entries.title: Maon (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mara (Woman living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: "Bitter." Naomi came home to Bethlehem from Moab having buried her husband and both sons, and told the women to call her Mara instead, because God had dealt bitterly with her.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Mara, meaning "bitter," was the name Naomi took for herself on returning to Bethlehem from Moab, after the deaths of her husband and two sons left her feeling that God had dealt bitterly with her (Ruth 1:20).

witness.excerpt: And when Naomi was so called by her fellow-citizens, according to her true name, she said, “You might more truly call me Mara.” Now Naomi signifies in the Hebrew tongue, Happiness: and Mara, Sorrow.

entries.title: Marah
entries.summary: Three days past the sea, the first water Israel found was too bitter to drink. Moses threw a piece of wood in at the Lord's word and it turned sweet, and God gave them a statute there and tested them. Many put it at Ain Hawarah in Sinai, a spring that is still brackish.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Marah, meaning bitterness, was the first watering stop the Israelites reached after crossing the sea, three days into the wilderness, where the water was too bitter to drink (Exodus 15:23). Moses threw a piece of wood into the water at the Lord's direction and it became drinkable, after which God gave Israel a statute and tested them there (Exodus 15:25-26). It is often identified with Ain Hawarah, a spring in the Sinai peninsula still known for brackish water.

witness.excerpt: And as they thus travelled, they came late in the evening to a place called Marah : which had that name from the badness of its water; for Mar denotes bitterness .

entries.title: Maralah (Mareal)
entries.summary: A point on the southern edge of Zebulun's land, placed at Ma'lul, a village southwest of Nazareth.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Maralah marked a point on the southern boundary of Zebulun's territory (Joshua 19:11). It has been identified with the modern village of Ma'lul, southwest of Nazareth.

entries.title: Maran-atha (A religious chant)
entries.summary: Aramaic for our Lord, come. Paul puts it at the end of 1 Corinthians, and the early church seems to have used it as a set phrase.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Maranatha is not a name but an Aramaic expression, “our Lord, come,” that Paul appends to the close of 1 Corinthians as a solemn invocation (1 Corinthians 16:22). It functioned in the early church as both a prayer for Christ's return and a formula of exclusion pronounced against those who did not love him, showing how quickly Aramaic liturgical phrases entered Greek-speaking congregations.

entries.title: Marcus (Levite living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: John Mark. He set out with Paul and Barnabas and left partway through the first journey, and that later split the two men in a sharp quarrel. Peter calls him his son, and early church tradition says he wrote the Gospel of Mark from Peter's preaching.
entries.label: 5 books
entries.dictNote: Marcus, more commonly known as John Mark, was a companion of Paul and Barnabas on part of their first missionary journey before leaving partway through, a departure that later caused a sharp disagreement between Paul and Barnabas. He was also a close associate of Peter, who calls him his son, and early church tradition credits him with writing the Gospel of Mark based substantially on Peter's own preaching and memories.

entries.title: Mareshah
entries.summary: Rehoboam fortified this Shephelah city, and Asa beat Zerah the Cushite's far larger army there. Micah mourns it among Judah's towns. Its ruins at Tell Sandahanna hold a Hellenistic underground city and painted Sidonian tombs full of exotic animals.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Mareshah was a city in the Shephelah of Judah, fortified by Rehoboam and the site where King Asa defeated a vastly larger invading army under Zerah the Cushite. Micah laments over the city in his oracle of judgment on Judah's towns. Excavations at the site, known today as Tell Sandahanna, have uncovered an extensive Hellenistic-era underground city and the painted Sidonian burial caves, whose walls depict exotic animals in a style showing strong Egyptian and Phoenician influence.

entries.title: Mareshah (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the wilderness years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mareshah (Man or town at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 3 men called Mareshah. This one is a man from the divided-kingdom years, named once in 1 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Maroth
entries.summary: Micah names it in his lament over the towns of the Judean lowlands as Assyria came, playing its name against the Hebrew for "bitterness." Nobody knows where it was, only that it sat in the same district as Lachish and Moresheth.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A town named in Micah's oracle of lament over the towns of the Judean lowlands facing Assyrian invasion (Micah 1:12), where the prophet plays on the similarity between the name Maroth and the Hebrew word for "bitterness." Its exact location is unknown, though it lay somewhere in the same district as the other towns Micah names, such as Lachish and Moresheth.

entries.title: Marsena (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of the seven princes of Persia and Media who advised Ahasuerus, men who could see the king and held the top seats in the kingdom.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of the seven princes of Persia and Media named as royal counselors to Ahasuerus, advisers who had direct access to the king and the highest seats in the kingdom (Esther 1:14).

entries.title: Martha (Woman living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Lazarus and Mary's sister, at Bethany. Jesus gently told her off for fussing over the meal while Mary sat and listened. Later, grieving her brother, she said one of the boldest things anyone says in the Gospels, that Jesus was the Christ, the Son of God, just before he raised Lazarus.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Martha was the sister of Mary and Lazarus in Bethany, and she's remembered chiefly for two contrasting moments: being gently corrected by Jesus for being distracted by her many household preparations while her sister simply sat and listened to him, and later making one of the boldest declarations of faith in the Gospels, confessing Jesus as the Christ, the Son of God, even while grieving her brother's death just before Jesus raised him.

entries.title: Mary (Barnabus' relative living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: A man from the New Testament, and Acts is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mary (Jesus' mother living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Jesus' mother. She was engaged to Joseph when Gabriel told her she would bear the Messiah, she raised Jesus in Nazareth, and she stood at the cross when he died.
entries.label: 5 books
entries.dictNote: Three different women named Mary appear around Jesus. The most important is his mother, engaged to Joseph when the angel Gabriel told her she would bear the Messiah, who raised Jesus in Nazareth and stood at the foot of the cross when he died. Mary Magdalene was a follower Jesus had healed of seven demons, and she was the first person any Gospel records seeing the risen Jesus, mistaking him for a gardener until he said her name. The third, Mary of Bethany, sister of Martha and Lazarus, is remembered for sitting at Jesus's feet to listen while Martha worked in the kitchen, and for anointing Jesus's feet with expensive perfume shortly before his death.

witness.excerpt: There was a certain woman that dwelt beyond Jordan, her name was Mary; her father was Eleazar, of the village Bethezob, which signifies the house of Hyssop.

entries.title: Mary (Lazarus' sister living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: She sat at Jesus' feet listening while Martha did the work. This is the Mary of Bethany, sister of Martha and Lazarus, who not long before his death anointed his feet with expensive perfume.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Mary (Woman living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Another Mary in the Gospels, one of the women at the cross and at the empty tomb, and not to be mixed up with Jesus' mother or the Mary of Bethany.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Maschil (A musical term)
entries.summary: Thirteen psalms carry this word in their heading. It probably marks a contemplative psalm, or a skilfully made one.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Maschil is a Hebrew term appearing in the superscriptions of thirteen psalms, likely meaning a contemplative or skillfully composed psalm, and it is a literary or musical designation rather than the name of a person.

entries.title: Mash (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: The Table of Nations lists Mash as one of Aram's four sons. Chronicles gives the name as Meshech. Some connect his people with the Mount Masius range in what is now southeastern Turkey.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Mash was one of the four sons of Aram listed in the Table of Nations, and his name attached to a tribe or region east of Mesopotamia (Genesis 10:23). The parallel genealogy in 1 Chronicles 1:17 gives the name as Meshech instead, and some geographers connect his descendants with the Mount Masius range in what is now southeastern Turkey.

entries.title: Mashal (Mishal)
entries.summary: A Levitical town in Asher, somewhere on the coastal plain. Joshua calls it Mishal in one list and Misheal in another, and the exact site is lost.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Mashal was a Levitical town within the tribal territory of Asher (1 Chronicles 6:74), called Mishal in the parallel list at Joshua 21:30 and Misheal in Asher's original town list at Joshua 19:26. Its exact site is unknown, though it lay somewhere along the Mediterranean coastal plain of Asher's territory.

entries.title: Masrekah
entries.summary: Samlah came from this town in Edom. He was one of the kings who ruled there before Israel had a king of its own.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Edomite town, home of Samlah, one of the kings who ruled Edom before Israel had a monarchy of its own, according to the parallel genealogical lists in Genesis and Chronicles (Gen. 36:36; 1 Chr. 1:47).

entries.title: Massa (Arabian living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Ishmael had twelve sons, each the head of an Arabian tribe, and Massa was one. Assyrian records of the eighth century BC name a nomad tribe called Mas'a in the same region, and many scholars take them for his descendants.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Massa was one of Ishmael's twelve sons, each the head of an Arabian tribal confederation (Genesis 25:14; 1 Chronicles 1:30). Assyrian records from the eighth century BC mention a nomadic Arabian tribe called “Mas'a” in the same general region, which many scholars identify with his descendants. Nothing further is recorded of Massa himself.

entries.title: Massah
entries.summary: "Testing." Near Rephidim the Israelites ran out of water, quarrelled with Moses and demanded a drink, testing God even as he tested them. The place was also called Meribah, and what happened there became shorthand for a hard heart, used as a warning in Psalm 95 and again in Hebrews 3.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Massah, meaning "testing," was the name given to the site near Rephidim where the Israelites, thirsty in the wilderness, quarreled with Moses and demanded water, provoking God's testing of their faith even as they tested him (Exodus 17:1-7). The same site was also called Meribah, "quarreling," and Israel's rebellion there became a byword for hardened unbelief, invoked later in Psalm 95 and Hebrews 3 as a warning against a hardened heart.

entries.title: Master (Title of a leader)
entries.summary: A title, not a name. Luke especially uses it for Jesus where the others would say teacher.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Master is a title used throughout the Gospels, especially in Luke, as a form of respectful address to Jesus, roughly equivalent to teacher or rabbi, rather than the name of a person.

witness.excerpt:
For, O Master! they are all your favours and your gifts, of which you have thought us worthy, and so enabled us to live comfortably and to rejoice in unexpected blessings which thou hast given to us, who did not expect them.\"

entries.title: Mathat (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Luke's genealogy has two men called Mathat, and this is the one further back, near Levi.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Luke's genealogy of Jesus lists two different men named Mathat among the ancestors of Joseph, one closer to Joseph's own generation and another, generations further back, near Levi and Melki (Luke 3:24, 29). Little else is recorded about either beyond their place in the genealogical line.

entries.title: Mathat (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Luke's genealogy of Joseph has two men called Mathat, one near Joseph's own generation and one much further back near Levi and Melki. Little is known of either.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Matred (Woman living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Mezahab's daughter, and the mother of Mehetabel, who married Hadar, the last king of Edom in the Genesis list. Women are rare in those lists, and nothing more is said of her.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Matred was the daughter of Mezahab and mother of Mehetabel, who married Hadar (also called Hadad), the last king of Edom named in the Genesis king-list before Israel's own kings arose (Genesis 36:39; 1 Chronicles 1:50). She is one of the few women named in these otherwise male genealogical lists. Nothing further is recorded of her.

entries.title: Matri (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: When the lot fell on Saul to be Israel's first king, it fell first on his family within Benjamin, the Matri, and that is the only time they are named.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Matri was the family within the tribe of Benjamin to which Saul belonged, named when Saul was chosen by lot to be Israel's first king (1 Samuel 10:21). Nothing further is recorded about this family beyond its role in Saul's selection.

witness.excerpt: When the Hebrews had so done, the lot fell upon the tribe of Benjamin: and when the lot was cast for the families of this tribe, that which was called Matri was taken: and when the lot was cast for the single persons of that family; Saul the son of Kish was taken, for their King.

entries.title: Mattan (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A priest of Baal, killed at his own altar when the people of Jerusalem tore Baal's worship down after Queen Athaliah was overthrown.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Mattan was a priest of Baal killed at his own altar when the people tore down Baal worship in Jerusalem after the coup that overthrew Queen Athaliah.

witness.excerpt: After which they then ran to the house of Baal; which Athaliah and her husband Jehoram had built, to the dishonour of the God of their fathers, and to the honour of Ahab; and demolished it, and slew Mattan, that had his priesthood.

entries.title: Mattan (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Jeremiah names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mattanah
entries.summary: "A gift." Israel camped here between the desert and the borders of Moab, in the same short itinerary that has the well springing up at Beer. It is generally placed in the Wadi Waleh.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Mattanah, a gift, was a wilderness station where Israel camped between the desert and the borders of Moab, mentioned in the same brief itinerary that records the springing up of the well at Beer (Numbers 21:18-19). It is generally placed somewhere in the Wadi Waleh.

entries.title: Mattaniah (Levite living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him twice, and he is a Levite from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mattaniah (Levite living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Zedekiah's name before Nebuchadnezzar made him king and changed it.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Mattaniah was the birth name of Zedekiah, Judah's last king, before Nebuchadnezzar changed his name as a sign of his subjugation to Babylon when he installed him on the throne.

entries.title: Mattaniah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A man from the divided-kingdom years, and 2 Chronicles is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mattaniah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)

entries.summary: Nehemiah names him once, and he is a man from the exile and the return.

entries.title: Mattatha (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Nathan's son and David's grandson in Luke's genealogy, which runs Jesus' line through Nathan instead of Solomon.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: An ancestor of Jesus listed in Luke's genealogy as the son of Nathan and grandson of David, part of the line traced through David's son Nathan rather than through Solomon (Luke 3:31).

entries.title: Mattathah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Of Judah, and listed in Ezra 10:33 among the men who had married foreign wives and were made to send them away. The name probably shortens Mattithiah, "gift of the LORD."
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of the men listed in Ezra 10:33 among those of the tribe of Judah who had married foreign wives during the exile and were required to separate from them under Ezra's covenant reform. The name is likely a shortened form of Mattithiah or Mattathiah, "gift of the LORD."

entries.title: Mattathias (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Two of them stand next to each other in Luke's genealogy, the son of Amos and the son of Semein, both some generations above Joseph. Neither is known otherwise. The priest who started the Maccabean revolt carried the same name, but he is a different man.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mattathias (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Luke's genealogy has two of them in consecutive generations, and neither is mentioned anywhere else.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Two men named Mattathias appear consecutively in Luke's genealogy of Jesus: the son of Amos and the son of Semein, both several generations before Joseph (Luke 3:25-26). Neither is otherwise known; the name, meaning “gift of the Lord,” was common enough to later be borne by the priest who launched the Maccabean revolt roughly a century and a half before Jesus, though that Mattathias is a different, unrelated figure.

entries.title: Mattenai (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: In Ezra's reform a Mattenai was called out for a foreign marriage. The name was common after the exile.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mattenai (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Ezra names him once, and he is a man from the exile and the return.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mattenai (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A priest in Nehemiah's lists, and the name was common after the exile.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Mattenai was a common postexilic name, including a priest listed in Nehemiah's genealogies and a man confronted for a foreign marriage under Ezra.

entries.title: Matthan (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Matthew's genealogy makes him Jacob's father and grandfather to Joseph, Mary's husband. Luke gives Joseph a different grandfather, Matthat, one of the places the two lines part, probably because they trace different lines of descent.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Matthan appears in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus as the father of Jacob and grandfather of Joseph, Mary's husband (Matthew 1:15-16). Luke's parallel genealogy names a different grandfather of Joseph, Matthat, one of several points where the two genealogies diverge, likely because they trace different lines of descent.

entries.title: Matthew (Apostle living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: A tax collector, which made him an outcast among fellow Jews for working on Rome's behalf, until Jesus called him straight from his booth to be one of the twelve. Mark and Luke call him Levi. He threw a big dinner for Jesus with other tax collectors, and early church tradition says he wrote the Gospel that carries his name, aimed at Jewish readers.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Matthew was a tax collector, a profession that made him a social outcast among fellow Jews for working on Rome's behalf, and Jesus called him directly from his tax booth to become one of the twelve apostles. Also called Levi in Mark and Luke's accounts, Matthew hosted a large dinner for Jesus with his fellow tax collectors and other social outcasts, and early church tradition credits him with writing the Gospel that bears his name, aimed especially at showing Jewish readers how Jesus fulfilled the Old Testament.

entries.title: Matthias (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: The eleven drew lots between two men who had been with Jesus since his baptism, and the lot fell on Matthias, to take Judas Iscariot's place before Pentecost. The New Testament says nothing more about him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Matthias was chosen by the remaining eleven apostles to replace Judas Iscariot, selected by casting lots between two candidates who had both been with Jesus from his baptism onward, filling out the number of twelve before Pentecost. Nothing more is recorded about him in the New Testament itself.
