He had three male children, Jonathan, and Ishui, and Melchi-shua; with Merab and Michal his daughters.

entries.title: Michmethath
entries.summary: A landmark on the line between Ephraim and Manasseh, near Shechem. Joshua uses it only to mark the border, and no one has found the site.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Michmethath was a landmark on the boundary between the territories of Ephraim and Manasseh, located near Shechem (Josh. 16:6; 17:7). It served purely as a boundary reference point in Joshua's territorial descriptions, and its precise site remains unidentified.

entries.title: Michri (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Uzzi's father, a Benjamite, among the family heads who settled in Jerusalem after the exile. Nothing more is written of him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Benjamite, father of Uzzi, listed among the family heads who resettled Jerusalem after the exile (1 Chronicles 9:8). Nothing else is recorded of him.

entries.title: Michtam (A musical term)
entries.summary: Six psalms carry it in their heading. Whether it is musical or literary, nobody is sure.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Michtam is a Hebrew term appearing in the superscriptions of six psalms, likely a musical or literary designation whose exact meaning is uncertain, rather than the name of a person.

entries.title: Middin
entries.summary: "Measures." One of the six towns in the wilderness west of the Dead Sea, listed with En-gedi.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Measures, one of the six cities “in the wilderness,” on the west of the Dead Sea, mentioned along with En-gedi (Josh. 15:61).

entries.title: Midian
entries.summary: A people descended from Abraham through Keturah, and they keep turning up in different roles. Midianite traders bought Joseph. Moses found a home and a wife, Zipporah, in Midian. Later they oppressed Israel until Gideon beat them.
entries.books: Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Joshua, Judges, 1 Kings, 1 Chronicles, Psalm, Isaiah, Habakkuk
entries.label: 10 books
entries.dictNote: Midian was a nation descended from Abraham through his wife Keturah, and Midianites appear throughout the Old Testament in shifting roles, from the merchants who bought Joseph as a slave to Moses's own adopted homeland and family through his wife Zipporah to a major oppressor of Israel that Gideon eventually defeated.

witness.excerpt: Now Moses sent an army against the land of Midian, for the causes fore­mentioned; in all twelve thousand: taking an equal number out of every tribe: and appointed Phineas for their commander.
And ’Asâm died, and ’Adâth,  the son of Barad,  who slew Midian in the field of Moab, reigned in his stead, and the name of his city was Avith.
And she bare him six sons, Zimram, and Jokshan, and Medan, and Midian, and Ishbak, and Shuah, in the two weeks of years.

entries.title: Midian (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Abraham's son by Keturah, the man the Midianites traced themselves back to.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Migdal-eder
entries.summary: "Tower of the flock," near Bethlehem. Jacob pitched his tent there after burying Rachel by the road. Micah uses the name for Jerusalem's stronghold, promising its old rule would come back to the daughter of Zion.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Migdal-eder, tower of the flock, was a place near Bethlehem where Jacob pitched his tent after Rachel's death and burial on the road there (Genesis 35:19-21). Micah later uses the same name figuratively for Jerusalem's stronghold, promising that dominion and former glory would return to the daughter of Zion (Micah 4:8). Later Jewish tradition associated the watchtower with a site where shepherds guarded flocks destined for temple sacrifice, though the Bible itself gives no more than the name and its two occurrences.

entries.title: Migdal-el
entries.summary: "Tower of God," a fortified town of Naphtali. Some scholars have tied it to Magdala, Mary Magdalene's town, but the link is not certain.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Migdal-el, tower of God, was a fortified town of Naphtali listed in Joshua 19:38. Some scholars have identified it with Magdala on the Sea of Galilee, the town associated with Mary Magdalene in the Gospels, though the connection is not certain.

entries.title: Migdal-gad
entries.summary: In the lowland district of Judah, the Shephelah. The name means "tower of Gad," and it is generally placed at el-Mejdel near Ashkelon, which still keeps the word migdal.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Migdal-gad, "tower of Gad," was a town in the lowland district (Shephelah) of Judah's tribal allotment (Joshua 15:37). It is generally identified with the site of el-Mejdel near Ashkelon, whose name preserves the biblical "migdal," meaning tower.

entries.title: Migdol
entries.summary: "Tower," a fortified point on Egypt's northeastern border. One Migdol is on Israel's route to the crossing of the sea. Jeremiah names a Migdol where Jewish refugees settled in Egypt, and Ezekiel's "from Migdol to Syene" means the whole length of the country.
entries.label: 5 books
entries.dictNote: Migdol, meaning "tower," names a fortified point on Egypt's northeastern frontier. One Migdol is mentioned in the route of Israel's crossing of the Red Sea in Exodus and Numbers, near the sea's northern end. A Migdol is also named by Jeremiah among the places where Jewish refugees settled after fleeing to Egypt, and Ezekiel uses "from Migdol to Syene" as a way of describing the whole length of Egypt in his oracles of judgment.

witness.excerpt: He thought the Israelites had proceeded as far as the desert of Etham, Exodus 13:20, when they were commanded by God to return back, Exodus 14:2, and to pitch their camp between Migdol and the sea; and that when they were not able to fly, unless by sea, they were shut in on each side by mountains.

entries.title: Migron
entries.summary: Saul camped under a pomegranate tree at Migron, near Gibeah, with about six hundred men, just before Jonathan's raid on the Philistines at Michmash. Isaiah has an invading army pass a Migron near Aiath, apparently a different spot of the same name.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Migron names two locations near the Benjamite hill country. One lay near Gibeah, where Saul was camped under a pomegranate tree with about six hundred men before Jonathan's raid on the Philistine garrison at Michmash (1 Sam. 14:2). The other, apparently a different site of the same name, appears in Isaiah's description of an invading army's march route toward Jerusalem, positioned near Aiath and Michmash (Isa. 10:28).

entries.title: Mikloth (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mikloth (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: A man of the Benjamite family that settled in Gibeon, father of Shimeah, in the line that leads to King Saul.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Mikloth is not a place but a name shared by two men in Chronicles. One Mikloth belonged to the Benjamite family that settled in Gibeon, appearing in the genealogy leading to King Saul as the father of Shimeah (1 Chronicles 8:32; 9:37-38). A different Mikloth served as a military officer under Dodai, commanding one of David's monthly divisions of twenty-four thousand troops (1 Chronicles 27:4).

entries.title: Mikmas (Michmash)
entries.summary: Michmash, a town in Benjamin north of Jerusalem. The Philistines gathered there against Saul, and Jonathan and his armour-bearer climbed across a rocky ravine to attack their garrison, which set off a rout. Isaiah pictures the Assyrian army leaving its baggage there, and families from Michmash came back from Babylon.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Michmash was a town in Benjamin north of Jerusalem where the Philistines mustered against Saul's army; it was the site of Jonathan's daring raid with his armor-bearer against a Philistine garrison across a rocky ravine, which triggered a rout that Saul's forces exploited. Isaiah pictures an invading Assyrian army storing its baggage at Michmash on its march toward Jerusalem, and families from the town were among those who returned from Babylonian exile.

entries.title: Mikneiah (Singer living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A Levite of the second rank, gatekeeper and harp player in the choir that went with the ark up to Jerusalem.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Mikneiah was a Levite of the second rank whom David appointed as a gatekeeper and musician, playing the harp in the choir that accompanied the ark's procession to Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 15:18, 21).

entries.title: Milalai (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: At the dedication of Jerusalem's rebuilt walls, Milalai was among the Levite musicians in the procession, probably from Asaph's family.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Milalai was a Levite musician, probably a descendant of Asaph, who took part in the procession of singers and instrumentalists at the dedication of Jerusalem's rebuilt walls under Nehemiah (Nehemiah 12:36). The event followed the return from Babylonian exile and marked the completion of one of Nehemiah's major building projects.

entries.title: Milcah (Woman living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: A different woman from Nahor's wife. This Milcah is one of the five sisters in Numbers 27 who asked for their father's land.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Milcah (Woman living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Nahor's wife and Abraham's niece. Through her granddaughter Rebekah, who married Isaac, her branch of the family in Mesopotamia joined back into the main line.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Milcah was Nahor's wife and Abraham's niece, and her descendants through her granddaughter Rebekah connect Abraham's extended family in Mesopotamia directly back into the patriarchal line through Isaac's marriage.

entries.title: Miletus
entries.summary: About thirty-five miles south of Ephesus, a port in Ionia. Paul, hurrying to be in Jerusalem for Pentecost, called the elders of Ephesus down to Miletus and gave them his farewell, warning of false teachers to come. He later left Trophimus there sick. Silt from the Meander River has since pushed the coast away, and the old theatre now stands miles inland.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Ionian port city about thirty-five miles south of Ephesus. Sailing past Ephesus to save time before Pentecost, Paul summoned that city's elders to Miletus and delivered his farewell address, warning them of false teachers to come (Acts 20:15-38); he later left his sick companion Trophimus there (2 Tim. 4:20). Once a leading Greek city, Miletus was already fading by the Roman period as silt from the Meander River pushed its harbor away from the coast, a well-documented process that has left its ancient theater stranded several miles inland today.

entries.title: Miniamin (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A priestly name of the years after the exile, carried by men who served in the temple and joined the dedication of the rebuilt walls.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Miniamin was a common priestly name among those who served in the temple during the postexilic period and took part in the dedication of Jerusalem's rebuilt walls.

entries.title: Miniamin (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Nehemiah names him once, and he is a man from the exile and the return.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Minni
entries.summary: A kingdom in the mountains east of Assyria, in what is now northwestern Iran, generally taken as Mannea of the Assyrian records. Jeremiah calls it out with Ararat and Ashkenaz to march on Babylon.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Not a person but a kingdom in the mountains east of Assyria, in what is now northwestern Iran, generally identified with Mannea, known from Assyrian royal annals as a frequent target of campaigns. Jeremiah 51:27 summons Minni along with Ararat and Ashkenaz as nations to muster against Babylon, part of the prophet's oracle announcing Babylon's coming fall.

entries.title: Minnith
entries.summary: Jephthah's victory over the Ammonites ran as far as this town. Ezekiel lists wheat from Minnith among the goods Judah sold to Tyre. It stood on the tableland east of the Jordan, somewhere near Heshbon and Rabbah.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Minnith was an Ammonite town that marked the extent of Jephthah's victory over the Ammonites (Judges 11:33) and later appears in Ezekiel's list of goods Judah traded with Tyre, exporting wheat from the district around Minnith (Ezekiel 27:17). It lay somewhere in the tableland east of the Jordan, in the general vicinity of Heshbon and Rabbah.

entries.title: Miphkad (Muster Gate)
entries.summary: The Muster Gate, one of Jerusalem's gates, repaired when Nehemiah rebuilt the wall. It probably stood near the northeast corner of the temple area.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Miphkad is not a person but one of the gates of Jerusalem, called "the gate Miphkad" or the Muster Gate, repaired during Nehemiah's rebuilding of the city wall (Nehemiah 3:31). Its exact location is uncertain, though it likely stood near the northeast corner of the temple area.

entries.title: Miriam (Moses' sister living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Moses and Aaron's older sister, and a prophetess. She watched over the baby Moses in the reeds of the Nile, and after the crossing of the sea she led Israel's women in song.
entries.label: 5 books
entries.dictNote: Scripture names two women Miriam. The one nearly everyone means is Moses and Aaron's older sister, a prophetess herself, who watched over the infant Moses in the Nile reeds and later led Israel's women in song after the crossing of the sea. A second, much more obscure Miriam turns up once in a genealogy of Judah, a daughter of Mered and Bithiah with no story attached to her at all.

witness.excerpt: But Miriam, the child's sister, passed along upon the bank over against him, as her mother had bid her, to see whither the ark would be carried, where God demonstrated that human wisdom was nothing, but that the Supreme Being is a
Then it was that Miriam, the sister of Moses came to her end; having completed her fortieth year since she left Egypt; on the first day of the lunar month Xanthicus.

For Aaron the word, and Miriam the outward sense, when they rose up against Moses were expressly told that \"If there shall arise a prophet to the Lord, God shall be made known to him in a vision, and in a shadow, but not Clearly.{50}{#nu 12:6.} But

Now their names are set down in writing in the sacred Books; and they were these: Besaleel , the son of Uri , of the tribe of Judah, the grandson of Miriam, the sister of their conductor; and Aholiab the son of Ahisamach , of the tribe of Dan.

entries.title: Miriam (Woman living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names her once, and she is a woman from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mirma (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Shaharaim's son, a Benjamite chief born in Moab, which suggests some Benjamites lived there for a while.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Benjamite chief, son of Shaharaim, born to him in Moab according to the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8:10, a detail suggesting some Benjamites relocated there for a time, perhaps during a period of regional instability.

entries.title: Mishael (Daniel's compatriot living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of Daniel's three friends. In Babylon he was renamed Meshach, and he lived through Nebuchadnezzar's furnace after refusing to worship the golden image.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Mishael was one of Daniel's three friends, renamed Meshach in Babylon, who survived Nebuchadnezzar's fiery furnace after refusing to worship his golden image.

entries.title: Mishael (Levite living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Exodus and Leviticus name him twice, and he is a Levite from the wilderness years.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Mishael (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of 3 men called Mishael. This one is a man from the exile and the return, named once in Nehemiah.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mishal
entries.summary: A coastal town of Asher, probably near Mount Carmel, given with its pastures to the Gershonite Levites.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Coastal town of Asher assigned, with its pasturelands, to the Gershonite Levites (Josh. 21:30; 1 Chr. 6:74), likely located near Mount Carmel along the Mediterranean coast.

entries.title: Misham (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Elpaal's son, a Benjamite in 1 Chronicles 8, and that is all.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Misham was a Benjamite, one of the sons of Elpaal, listed in the tribal genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8. Nothing further is recorded about him.

entries.title: Mishma (Arabian living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: One of Ishmael's sons, from whom one of Ishmael's twelve tribes came, a set of twelve to match Israel's.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Mishma was a son of Ishmael, and his descendants are counted among the twelve tribal leaders that came from Ishmael's line, paralleling Israel's own twelve tribes.

entries.title: Mishma (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him twice, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mishmannah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: The Gadites who went over to David at Ziklag while he was running from Saul had faces like lions and were as quick as gazelles on the hills. Mishmannah was one of them.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of the Gadite warriors, described as having faces like lions and being as swift as gazelles on the mountains, who defected to David's camp at Ziklag while he was still fleeing Saul (1 Chronicles 12:8-13). These men are singled out among David's early supporters for their skill with shield and spear.

entries.title: Mishraites (People, perhaps from Mishrait)
entries.summary: One of the families that came out of the clans of Kiriath-jearim, named with the Ithrites, Puhites and Shumathites in 1 Chronicles 2:53.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Mishraites were one of the families descended from the clans of Kiriath-jearim in Judah's genealogy, named in 1 Chronicles 2:53 alongside the Ithrites, Puhites, and Shumathites.

entries.title: Mispereth (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: He came back from Babylon among the leaders with Zerubbabel and Jeshua. Ezra's list spells him Mizpar.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Mispereth was one of the leaders who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel and Jeshua, named in the roster of returnees in Nehemiah 7:7. The parallel list in Ezra 2:2 gives the name as Mizpar, a variant spelling of the same person.

entries.title: Misrephoth-mayim (Misrephoth-maim)
entries.summary: Joshua chased the beaten northern Canaanites from the Waters of Merom as far as this place, and later it is listed as land still not taken in his old age. The name is usually read "burnings of water," maybe hot springs or lime kilns by the coast. It is generally put near the Mediterranean north of Acco, without much confidence.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Misrephoth-mayim marked the western limit of Joshua's pursuit of the northern Canaanite coalition after their defeat at the Waters of Merom (Joshua 11:8) and is later listed among territory still unconquered in Joshua's old age (Joshua 13:6). The name, usually rendered burnings of water, may refer to hot springs or to lime-burning kilns near the coast, and the site is generally placed somewhere near the Mediterranean north of Acco, though it has not been identified with confidence.

entries.title: Mithcah (Mithkah)
entries.summary: "Sweetness." One of the stops late in the forty years of wandering, in Numbers 33, with no word on why it got the name and no known site.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Mithcah appears only in the wilderness itinerary of Numbers 33:28-29, one of the unidentified stations Israel passed through late in the forty years of wandering. Its Hebrew name means sweetness, but nothing in the text explains why it was so called, and its exact location is unknown.

entries.title: Mithnite (Warriors, perhaps from Mithn)
entries.summary: Joshaphat's tag in the list of David's mighty men. The place it comes from is unknown.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Mithnite identifies Joshaphat, one of David's mighty men; the place the epithet refers to is otherwise unknown.

entries.title: Mithredath (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Cyrus's treasurer, whose name in Persian is Mithridates, "given by Mithra." At the king's order he counted out the temple vessels Nebuchadnezzar had carried off from Jerusalem and handed them to the returning exiles. Another Mithredath, an official in Samaria, signed a letter to Artaxerxes against the rebuilding.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mithredath (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: He was Cyrus's treasurer, the man who handed back the temple vessels Nebuchadnezzar had taken. The name is Persian.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Mithredath, a Hebrew form of the Persian name Mithridates meaning “given by Mithra,” was the royal treasurer of Cyrus who, at the king's command, returned the temple vessels Nebuchadnezzar had looted from Jerusalem to the returning exiles (Ezra 1:8). A different Mithredath was a Persian official in Samaria who joined other local officials in writing a letter to King Artaxerxes opposing the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls (Ezra 4:7).

entries.title: Mitspah
entries.summary: A watchtower name, which is why so many places carry it. This one is where Jacob and Laban piled stones and agreed to keep apart.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Mizpah was a common town name in Israel, most notably a site where Israel gathered for covenant renewal under Samuel and where Jacob and Laban set up a boundary stone, giving the word Mizpah its familiar meaning as a watchpost between separated parties.

entries.title: Mitylene
entries.summary: Paul's ship put in for a night at Mitylene, the chief city of Lesbos, as he hurried to reach Jerusalem before Pentecost. The classical world knew it as the home of the poets Sappho and Alcaeus.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Mitylene was the chief city of the island of Lesbos in the Aegean Sea, famous in the classical world as the home of the poets Sappho and Alcaeus. Paul's ship anchored there for a night during his third missionary journey as he hurried toward Jerusalem before Pentecost (Acts 20:14-16).

witness.excerpt: Now Agrippa was [about this time] sent to succeed Caesar in the government of the countries beyond the Ionian Sea, upon whom Herod lighted when he was wintering about Mitylene, for he had been his particular friend and companion, and then returned into Judea again.

entries.title: Mizar
entries.summary: A hill near Mount Hermon, beyond the Jordan, that the psalmist remembers in Psalm 42 while far from Jerusalem and longing to go back. Where exactly it stood is no longer known.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Mizar was not a person but a hill or lesser summit somewhere near Mount Hermon, in the region beyond the Jordan, recalled by the psalmist in Psalm 42:6 while far from Jerusalem and longing to return. Its exact location is no longer known.

entries.title: Mizpar (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Ezra's spelling of Mispereth, one of the leaders who came back from Babylon with Zerubbabel.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of the leaders who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel, counted in the roll of returnees in Ezra 2:2; the parallel list in Nehemiah 7:7 gives the name as Mispereth.

entries.title: Mizpeh
entries.summary: Another spelling of Mizpah, the watchpost name given to several places in Israel.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Mizpeh is an alternate spelling of Mizpah, a common watchpost name for several sites in Israel, covered more fully under that entry.

witness.excerpt: So Samuel gathered them together, to a certain city called Mizpeh; which signifies in the Hebrew tongue a watch tower.

entries.title: Mizzah (Edomite living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: A clan chief of Edom, from Esau's line, and the record has no more.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Mizzah was an Edomite clan chief listed among the descendants of Esau.

entries.title: Mnason (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: From Cyprus, and a disciple from the earliest days of the Jerusalem church. Paul and his companions lodged at his house in Jerusalem at the end of the third journey.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Christian from Cyprus, described as an "early disciple," meaning he had been a believer since the earliest days of the Jerusalem church; Paul and his companions stayed at his house in Jerusalem near the end of the third missionary journey (Acts 21:16).

entries.title: Moab
entries.summary: East of the Dead Sea, the nation descended from Lot through his elder daughter. Israel and Moab went back and forth between enemies and kin: Balak hired Balaam to curse Israel, and yet Ruth, a Moabite, became King David's great-grandmother. King Mesha's own inscription on the Moabite Stone records the wars with Israel that 2 Kings describes.
entries.books: Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, Ruth, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Psalm, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, Amos, Micah, Zephaniah
entries.label: 21 books
entries.dictNote: Moab was a nation east of the Dead Sea descended from Lot through the incestuous union with his elder daughter, and Israel's relationship with Moab swung between hostility, as when Balak hired Balaam to curse them, and close kinship, as in the story of Ruth, a Moabite woman who became King David's great-grandmother. The Moabite Stone, a ninth-century BC inscription by King Mesha of Moab, independently confirms the Moab-Israel conflicts described in 2 Kings.

witness.excerpt: On the second year of his reign the King of Moab fell off from his obedience; and left off paying those tributes which he before payed to his father Ahab.
And they bare sons: the son of the elder was named Moab : which denotes one derived from his father .

Now when the King of Israel was come out of the land of Moab to Samaria, he had with him Elisha the Prophet: whose acts I have a mind to go over particularly: for they were illustrious, and worthy to be related; as we have them set down in the sacred Books.

And now hearken unto us: Let us send to Aram  and Philistia  and Moab

and Ammon,  and let us choose for ourselves chosen men who are ardent for battle, and let us go against him and do battle with him, and let us exterminate him from the earth before he groweth strong." 7.

entries.title: Moab
entries.summary: Genesis names him once, and he is a man from the patriarchs.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Moadiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A priestly family head after the exile. Nehemiah spells him Moadiah in one list and Maadiah in another, and nothing more is known.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A priestly family head in the postexilic community, named Moadiah in Nehemiah 12:17 and Maadiah in the parallel list of Nehemiah 12:5. Nothing further is recorded about him.

entries.title: Moladah
entries.summary: In the Negev. Judah was given it first, then Simeon, whose land sat inside Judah's, and people moved back there after the exile. It is often placed at Tel Malhata, east of Beersheba.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Moladah was a town in the Negev originally allotted to Judah and then reassigned to Simeon, whose inheritance lay within Judah's larger territory (Joshua 15:26; 19:2). Its people resettled there after the Babylonian exile, according to the list in Nehemiah 11:26. It is often identified with Tel Malhata, east of Beersheba, a site with excavated Iron Age remains.

entries.title: Molech (A male deity in the Old Testament)
entries.summary: A god of the Canaanites and Ammonites, worshipped with the sacrifice of children. The law forbids it again and again, and still some kings did it, Ahaz and Manasseh among them.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Molech was a Canaanite and Ammonite deity associated with child sacrifice, and the Old Testament repeatedly and explicitly forbids Israelites from giving their children to Molech, a practice several kings, including Ahaz and Manasseh, were condemned for adopting anyway.

entries.title: Molid (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Abishur and Abihail's son, of Jerahmeel's line in Judah.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Molid was a son of Abishur and his wife Abihail, descended from Jerahmeel in the tribal genealogy of Judah (1 Chronicles 2:29).

entries.title: Moloch (A male deity in the Old Testament)
entries.summary: The Ammonite god, worshipped by burning children, and the same as Molech, Milcom and Malcham. Solomon built him a high place on the Mount of Olives for his foreign wives, and Josiah tore it down. Stephen quotes Amos against his worship in front of the Sanhedrin.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Not a person but the national god of the Ammonites, worshiped with child sacrifice by fire, also called Molech, Milcom, and Malcham in various Old Testament passages (Lev. 18:21, 20:2-5; 1 Kings 11:5, 33; Zeph. 1:5). Solomon built a high place for Moloch on the Mount of Olives to please his foreign wives, and the cult persisted intermittently until Josiah's reforms destroyed it (1 Kings 11:7; 2 Kings 23:10, 13). Stephen references the exile-era rebuke of Moloch worship in his speech before the Sanhedrin (Acts 7:43, quoting Amos 5:26); archaeologists have found child burial sites called tophets at Carthage and other Phoenician colonies that many scholars connect to related West Semitic child-sacrifice cults, though the practice's exact nature remains debated.

witness.excerpt: However, the general sense of both seems to be this: that there were certain chariots, with their horses, dedicated to the idol of the sun, or to Moloch: which idol might be carried about in procession, and worshipped by the people: which chariots were now taken away , as Josephus says: or, as the book of Kings says, burnt with fire by Josiah .

And to this law there is no limit of days, and no remission, nor any atonement: but the man who hath defiled his daughter shall be rooted out in the midst of all Israel, because he hath

given of his seed to Moloch,  and wrought impiously so as to defile it.

entries.title: Morashthite (Moresheth)
entries.summary: "From Moresheth," the prophet Micah's town in the Judean lowlands near Gath. Nearly a century after Micah spoke, the elders in Jeremiah's day quoted his warning against Jerusalem, and that he went unpunished, to save Jeremiah's life.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Morashthite identifies the prophet Micah as being from Moresheth, a town in the Judean lowlands near Gath. Jeremiah's elders quote Micah's prophecy against Jerusalem by this epithet nearly a century after he spoke it, citing his unpunished warning as precedent to spare Jeremiah's own life.

entries.title: Mordecai (Esther's relative living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A Benjamite in Susa who raised his orphaned cousin Esther as his daughter. He once exposed a plot to kill King Ahasuerus, and the king forgot it until a sleepless night had the records read to him. On the very day Haman had a gallows ready for him, Mordecai rode through the city in the king's robes, and he ended second in the empire.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Mordecai was a Benjamite in the Persian capital of Susa who raised his orphaned cousin Esther as his own daughter and later uncovered a plot to assassinate King Ahasuerus, a service the king had forgotten until a sleepless night sent him back through the royal records. That rediscovery reversed Mordecai's fortunes overnight: the same day his enemy Haman had built a gallows for him, Mordecai was paraded through the city in the king's own robes, and he was later elevated to the second-highest position in the empire.

witness.excerpt: Concerning Esther, and Mordecai, and Haman. And how, in the reign of Artaxerxes, the whole nation of the Jews was in danger of perishing.

entries.curatedNote: Esther's cousin and guardian, the one who refuses to bow to Haman and sets the whole plot in motion (Esther 2:5, 3:2). Josephus's retelling of the book keeps him right where Scripture does, second billing to Esther, first cause of everything that happens to her.

entries.title: Mordecai (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Ezra and Nehemiah name him twice, and he is a man from the exile and the return.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Moreh
entries.summary: The oak of Moreh, near Shechem, where Abraham stopped when he first came into Canaan, and Deuteronomy points back to it to show Israel where they would stand.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: The hill of Moreh was where the Midianite camp lay before Gideon's small force of three hundred routed them at night, and a different site called the oak of Moreh near Shechem is where Abraham first built an altar upon entering Canaan.

entries.title: Moreh
entries.summary: Named once, in Judges, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Moresheth-gath
entries.summary: Micah came from here, a town in the Shephelah near Gath. It probably lay at or near Tell el-Judeideh.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The hometown of the prophet Micah, who is called the Morasthite in Jeremiah 26:18, located in the Shephelah lowlands near Gath (Mic. 1:14). It probably lay at or near the site now called Tell el-Judeideh.

entries.title: Moriah
entries.summary: Abraham was told to take Isaac to the land of Moriah and offer him there. Chronicles puts Solomon's temple on Mount Moriah in Jerusalem, on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite. Jewish tradition has long taken the two as the same ridge.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Moriah is not a person but the name of a mountain in Jerusalem, the site where Solomon later built the temple on what had been the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite (2 Chronicles 3:1). Genesis 22:2 identifies 'the land of Moriah' as the place where Abraham was told to offer Isaac, and Jewish tradition has long linked the two locations as the same ridge, generally understood as part of the same hill as Mount Zion.

witness.excerpt: But note, that what Josephus here says of the original scantiness of this Mount Moriah, that it was quite too little for the temple, and that at first it held only one cloister or court of Solomon's building, and that the foundations were forced to be added long afterwards by degrees, to render it capable

entries.title: Mosera
entries.summary: A camp in the wilderness near Mount Hor. Deuteronomy says Aaron died and was buried there, where Numbers puts his death on Mount Hor itself and lists Moseroth nearby, and the two are usually read as the same area.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Mosera, a wilderness campsite near Mount Hor where, according to Deuteronomy's summary, Aaron died and was buried (Deut. 10:6). Numbers 33:38 places his death at Mount Hor itself and lists Moseroth as a nearby stage of the journey; the two accounts are usually read as describing the same general area.

entries.title: Moses (Levite living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Born a Hebrew slave in Egypt and raised in Pharaoh's house, he killed an Egyptian overseer and ran to Midian, where he kept sheep for forty years. God called him back from the burning bush to face Pharaoh and lead Israel out. He gave them the law at Sinai, led them forty years in the wilderness, and died at a hundred and twenty within sight of the promised land.
entries.books: Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Psalm, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Daniel, Micah, Malachi, Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, Acts, Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, 2 Timothy, Hebrews, Jude, Revelation
entries.label: 31 books
entries.dictNote: Moses was born a Hebrew slave in Egypt and raised in Pharaoh's own household, only to flee into the desert after killing an Egyptian overseer and spend the next forty years as a shepherd in Midian. God called him back through the burning bush to confront Pharaoh and lead Israel out of slavery, and Moses spent the rest of his life shaping that liberated people into a nation, delivering the law at Sinai and leading them through forty years in the wilderness before dying within sight of the promised land at a hundred and twenty. He is named more often than anyone else in the Old Testament, and archaeology confirms plenty of the world he moved through, the store cities, the Egyptian court, the route through Sinai, without ever turning up a record of Moses himself.

witness.excerpt: it is now the will of God, and the course of old age, at a hundred and twenty, requires it that I should depart out of this life.

witness.source: Philo, On the Life of Moses I.3
witness.excerpt: Accordingly as the child Moses, as soon as he was born, displayed a more beautiful and noble form than usual, his parents resolved, as far as was in their power, to disregard the proclamations of the tyrant.
Moses indeed calls this belt Abaneth ; but we have learned from the Babylonians to call it Emia ; for so it is by them called.

Moses took out the tribe of Levi from communicating with the rest of the people, and set them apart, to be an holy tribe; and purified them by water, taken from perpetual springs, and with such sacrifices as were usually offe
SO Moses, when he understood that the Pharaoh, in whose reign he fled away, was dead, asked leave of Raguel to go to Egypt, for the benefit of his own people.

entries.lukeNote: Stands beside Elijah at the Transfiguration (9:30) and anchors the risen Jesus's own Bible study on the Emmaus road (24:27, 24:44). Josephus has Moses announce his own death at 120 in his own voice, matching Deuteronomy 34:7's age note exactly, three centuries later. Philo devoted an entire two-volume biography to him alone, it opens on the same infancy-narrative beat Exodus 2 does, an unusually beautiful baby, but reads it as the first sign of what he'd become.

entries.title: Moza (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A descendant of Saul in the genealogies of Chronicles, a name also found in Caleb's family.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Moza was a common name in the genealogies of Judah and Benjamin, borne by a descendant of Caleb and by a descendant of Saul.

entries.title: Moza (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the wilderness years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mozah
entries.summary: A town of Benjamin, usually placed at Tel Moza just west of Jerusalem. Digging there has found a large Iron Age temple and a grain store.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Mozah, a town allotted to the tribe of Benjamin (Josh. 18:26), commonly identified with Tel Moza just west of Jerusalem. Excavations there have uncovered a large Iron Age temple and grain-storage complex, among the more significant recent archaeological finds in the Jerusalem region.

entries.title: Muppim (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Benjamin's son, one of Jacob's household who went down to Egypt. Numbers calls him Shupham, head of the Shuphamite clan.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of the sons of Benjamin who went to Egypt with Jacob's household, listed in Genesis 46:21; the parallel census in Numbers 26:39 gives the name as Shupham, head of the Shuphamite clan.

witness.excerpt: And the sons of Benjamin: Bela and Becher, and Ashbel, Gera, and Naaman, and Ehi, and Rosh, and Muppim, and Huppim, and Ard--eleven.

entries.title: Mushi (Levite living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Merari's son and Levi's grandson. His family became one of the Levitical clans serving at the tabernacle.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Mushi was a son of Merari, Levi's grandson, and his descendants formed one of the Levitical clans assigned to tabernacle service.

entries.title: Mushites (Levite living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: They came from Mushi, son of Merari, and with their fellow Levites they looked after the frames, bars and pillars of the tabernacle.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Mushites were the Levitical clan descended from Mushi, son of Merari, one of the families charged with caring for the tabernacle's frames, bars, pillars, and other structural furnishings.

entries.title: Myra
entries.summary: On the coast of Lycia in southwestern Asia Minor. Here the centurion moved Paul and the other prisoners onto a grain ship from Alexandria bound for Italy, the ship that later broke up off Malta. A Roman theatre and rock-cut tombs above the old harbour still stand.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Myra was a leading city of the Lycian coast in southwestern Asia Minor, where the centurion guarding Paul transferred him and the other prisoners onto an Alexandrian grain ship bound for Italy, the same ship later wrecked off Malta (Acts 27:5). The site preserves an impressive Roman theater and a cluster of rock-cut tombs carved into the cliffside above the ancient harbor.

entries.title: Mysia
entries.summary: The northwest corner of the province of Asia. The Spirit kept Paul's party from turning aside, so they passed through Mysia without preaching and came down to Troas, where Paul saw the man from Macedonia in a vision.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Mysia was a region in the northwest of the Roman province of Asia. Paul and his companions passed through it without stopping to preach, prevented by the Spirit from turning into the neighboring regions, and continued on to its port city of Troas (Acts 16:7-8), where Paul received the vision of the Macedonian man that redirected the mission into Europe.

witness.excerpt: The legions also that were in Mysia and Pannonia, who had been in commotion a little before, on account of this insolent attempt of Vitellius’s, were very glad to take the oath of fidelity to Vespasian, upon his coming to the Empire.
In the mean time Antonius Primus took the third of the legions that were in Mysia, for he was president of that province, and made haste, in order to fight Vitellius.

And are not the Athenians, and Lacedemonians, and Nicopolitans, and that Pergamus which is in Mysia, full of donations that Herod presented them withal? And as for that large open place belonging to Antioch in Syria, did not he pave it with polished marble, though it were twenty furlongs long? and this when it was shu

entries.title: Naam (Man living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: Caleb son of Jephunneh had a son named Naam. He gets one mention, in the genealogy of Judah.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Naam was one of the sons of Caleb son of Jephunneh, named in the genealogy of Judah (1 Chr. 4:15). He appears only in this single genealogical notice.

entries.title: Naamah
entries.summary: Joshua names him once, and nothing else is recorded.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Naamah (Woman living at the time before the Flood)
entries.summary: Named once, in Genesis, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Naamah (Woman living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: An Ammonite, one of Solomon's foreign wives, and the mother of Rehoboam, the only one of Solomon's wives named as a king's mother.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Naamah names two people and a place in the Old Testament. The first Naamah was the daughter of Lamech and Zillah, a descendant of Cain, and sister of the metalworker Tubal-cain (Genesis 4:22). A second Naamah was an Ammonite woman, one of Solomon's many foreign wives, and the mother of his heir Rehoboam, the only wife of Solomon's named as the mother of a king (1 Kings 14:21, 31; 2 Chronicles 12:13). A town of the same name lay in the lowland plain of Judah, listed among the cities of that region in Joshua 15:41.

witness.excerpt: Lamech was also the father of a daughter, whose name was Naamah.

entries.title: Naaman (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Numbers and 1 Chronicles name him twice, and he is a man from the wilderness years.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Naaman (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: One of 4 men called Naaman. This one is a man from the wilderness years, named once in Genesis.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Naaman (Man living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: A man from the years before the monarchy, and 1 Chronicles is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Naaman (Syrian living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Commander of the Aramean army, a great man, and a leper. A captured Israelite girl told his household about a prophet in Samaria. Elisha did not even come out, only sent word to wash seven times in the Jordan, and Naaman almost went home angry before his servants talked him round. He came out of the water clean, and Gehazi, who ran after him for a payment, got his leprosy.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Naaman was the commander of the Aramean army, a respected and successful general who also had leprosy, and it was a captured Israelite servant girl who first told him a prophet in Samaria could heal him. Naaman nearly walked away insulted when Elisha simply sent word for him to wash seven times in the Jordan River rather than perform some dramatic ritual in person, but his servants talked him into trying it, and he came out of the water completely healed. He tried to pay Elisha, who refused any reward, and Naaman left declaring his new faith in Israel's God, while Elisha's own servant Gehazi secretly chased Naaman down for a payment and was struck with the leprosy Naaman had just been cured of.

witness.excerpt: And the sons of Benjamin: Bela and Becher, and Ashbel, Gera, and Naaman, and Ehi, and Rosh, and Muppim, and Huppim, and Ard--eleven.
The other, Benjamin, had ten sons - Bolau, Bacchar, Asabel, Geras, Naaman, Jes, Ros, Momphis, Opphis, Arad.
One of those Histories, omitted at present, was evidently in his Bible: I mean that of the curing of Naaman’s leprosy: 2 Kings 5.

And when they sought to kill Ahab alone, but could not find him, there was a young nobleman belonging to king Benhadad, whose name was Naaman; he drew his bow against the enemy, and wounded the king through his breastplate, in his lungs.

entries.title: Naamathite (People, perhaps from Naamath)
entries.summary: The tag on Zophar, one of Job's three friends. Naamah, wherever it was, may have been in Arabia.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Naamathite designates Zophar, one of Job's three friends, from a place called Naamah whose location, likely somewhere in Arabia, is not otherwise known.

entries.title: Naamites (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: From Naaman, Bela's son and Benjamin's grandson. The Numbers 26 census counts them as a clan.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Naamites were the clan descended from Naaman, a grandson of Benjamin through Bela, counted in the Numbers 26 census.

entries.title: Naarah (Woman living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Ashur's second wife, in Hezron's line of Judah, and the mother of four of his sons.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The references here describe a person rather than a place, despite the place tag. Naarah was the second wife of Ashur, a descendant of Judah through Hezron, and the mother of several sons whose names are preserved in the tribal genealogy of Chronicles (1 Chr. 4:5-6). A different place called Naarah, or Naarath, near Jericho on Ephraim's border is mentioned separately in Joshua 16:7.

entries.title: Naarai (Warrior living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of David's mighty men. Second Samuel calls him Paarai the Arbite.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of David's mighty men (1 Chronicles 11:37), called Paarai the Arbite in the parallel roster in 2 Samuel 23:35.

entries.title: Naaran
entries.summary: A town of Ephraim near the border with Benjamin, linked with Jericho. It is generally taken as the Naarah of Joshua 16:7 and placed a few miles north of Jericho.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A town of Ephraim near the border with Benjamin, associated with Jericho (1 Chronicles 7:28). It is generally taken as the same place as Naarah, listed among Ephraim's towns in Joshua 16:7, and is usually placed a few miles north of Jericho.

entries.title: Naashon (Man living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: Leader of Judah in the wilderness years, and Aaron's brother-in-law. David came from his line, and so does Jesus in Matthew's genealogy.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Nahshon was a tribal leader of Judah during the wilderness years and the brother-in-law of Aaron, and he became an ancestor of both David and, through Matthew's genealogy, Jesus.

entries.title: Naasson (Man living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: The Greek spelling of Nahshon, prince of Judah in the wilderness and brother-in-law to Aaron through his sister Elisheba. Matthew and Luke both list him among Jesus' ancestors.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Naasson is the Greek New Testament form of Nahshon, a prince of the tribe of Judah during Israel's wilderness wanderings and brother-in-law of Aaron through his sister Elisheba. He is listed as an ancestor of Jesus in both Matthew's and Luke's genealogies (Matthew 1:4; Luke 3:32).

entries.title: Nabal (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: A rich, hard man. David's men had guarded his shepherds, and when David asked for food Nabal sent back insults. Only his wife Abigail, riding out with a generous gift, kept David from killing his whole household. When she told Nabal ten days later what he had nearly brought on them, he seems to have had a stroke, and he died. David married Abigail.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Nabal was a wealthy but harsh landowner who rudely refused David's request for provisions after David's men had protected Nabal's shepherds and flocks, and only his wife Abigail's quick intervention with a generous gift stopped David from slaughtering Nabal's entire household in retaliation. Nabal died of what appears to be a stroke ten days after Abigail told him what he'd nearly brought on his family, and David married Abigail soon after.

witness.excerpt: For so we see it was in this case of David: who altho’ he had sworn to destroy Nabal, and his family, yet does he here and 1 Sam.

entries.title: Naboth (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: His vineyard sat next to King Ahab's palace, and he would not sell it, because Israel's law kept family land in the family. Jezebel had false witnesses accuse him of blasphemy, he was stoned, and Ahab took the vineyard. Elijah met Ahab there and announced the end of his dynasty.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Naboth was an Israelite who owned a vineyard next to King Ahab's palace and refused to sell it, since Israelite law protected ancestral land from being permanently sold outside the family. Queen Jezebel arranged false charges of blasphemy that got Naboth stoned to death so Ahab could seize the vineyard, a crime the prophet Elijah confronted directly, prophesying doom on Ahab's entire dynasty.

witness.excerpt: Now there was one Naboth, of the city Izar, [Jezreel,] who had a field adjoining to that of the king: the king would have persuaded him to sell him that his field, which lay so near to his own lands, at what price he pleased, that he might join
And when Joram met him in the field of Naboth, he asked him, If all things were well in the camp? but Jehu reproached him bitterly; and ventured to call his mother a witch, and an harlot.

entries.title: Nachon (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: At the threshing floor of Nachon, Uzzah reached out to steady the ark and died. Chronicles calls it the threshing floor of Chidon, and scholars are split on whether that was one man with two names or whether one text named the place rather than its owner.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The owner of the threshing floor near Jerusalem where Uzzah reached out to steady the ark of the covenant and was struck dead for touching it (2 Samuel 6:6). The parallel account in 1 Chronicles 13:9 calls the same site the threshing floor of Chidon instead, and scholars are divided over whether Nachon and Chidon were two names for one man or whether one of the texts originally named the location rather than its owner.

entries.title: Nachor (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Luke's Greek spelling of Nahor, Abraham's grandfather.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Nachor is the Greek form, used in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, of the Old Testament name Nahor, grandfather of Abraham (Luke 3:34; compare Genesis 11:24-26).

entries.title: Nadab (King living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: He reigned over northern Israel two years. Then Baasha killed him and wiped out his family.
entries.label: 1 book

witness.excerpt: I now return to Baasha, the king of the multitude of the Israelites, who slew Nadab, the son of Jeroboam, and retained the government.
But Jeroboam, the king of the ten tribes, died when he had governed them two and twenty years; whose son Nadab succeeded him, in the second year of the reign of Asa.

entries.title: Nadab (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 4 men called Nadab. This one is a man from the divided-kingdom years, named twice in 1 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Nadab (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: A man from the united kingdom, and 1 Chronicles is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Nadab (Priest living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Aaron's eldest son. He and his brother Abihu offered unauthorised fire before the Lord and were struck dead.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: At least five people in the Bible and its associated writings are called Nadab. The priest is the one most people mean: Aaron's eldest son, struck dead alongside his brother Abihu for offering unauthorized fire before the Lord. A king by the same name ruled northern Israel for two years before Baasha assassinated him and wiped out his family. A third Nadab was Saul's uncle, a fourth appears only in a genealogy of Judah as the son of Shammai, and a fifth, a relative of the Ahikar of the book of Tobit, belongs to the Second Temple literature rather than the Hebrew Bible.

witness.excerpt:
He had at that time four sons; Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.

2.

entries.title: Nagge (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: In Luke's genealogy, Maath's son and the father of Esli. Nothing else is known.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Nagge appears in Luke's genealogy of Jesus as an ancestor in the line through Mary, listed as the father of Esli and son of Maath (Luke 3:25). Nothing else is known of him.

entries.title: Nahalal (Nahalol)
entries.summary: A town in Zebulun, later given with its pastures to the Merarite Levites. Zebulun never drove out the Canaanites there and put them to forced labour instead. It is sometimes linked with Tell en-Nahl near the Kishon River.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Nahalal was a town within the tribal territory of Zebulun (Joshua 19:15) later assigned, with its pasturelands, to the Merarite Levites (Joshua 21:35). Zebulun failed to drive out its Canaanite inhabitants, who instead were put to forced labor (Judges 1:30). Its exact site is uncertain, though it is sometimes linked to Tell en-Nahl near the Kishon River.

entries.title: Nahaliel (Lasha)
entries.summary: "Torrent of God," one of Israel's camps on the border of Moab. It is often placed at the Wadi Zarqa Ma'in east of the Dead Sea, known for its hot springs.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of the encampments of Israel during the wilderness journey, on the border of Moab, named in the travel itinerary of Numbers 21:19. Its name means "torrent" or "valley of God," and it is often identified with the Wadi Zarqa Ma'in east of the Dead Sea, an area known for hot springs.

entries.title: Naham (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: The brother of Hodiah's wife, in a tangled verse of Judah's genealogy that translations parse in different ways.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Named in a difficult genealogical note in 1 Chronicles 4:19 as the brother of the wife of Hodiah, in the tribe of Judah. The verse is one of the more textually obscure entries in Chronicles' genealogies, and translations vary in how they parse its relationships.

entries.title: Nahamani (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Among the leaders who came back from Babylon with Zerubbabel, in Nehemiah 7:7, and nothing more is told of him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Nahamani was one of the leaders of the Jewish community who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel, named in the roster of returnees in Nehemiah 7:7. Nothing further is recorded about him.

entries.title: Naharai (Warrior living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: From Beeroth. He carried Joab's armour and is counted among David's mighty warriors.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Naharai, from Beeroth, served as armor-bearer to Joab, David's army commander, and is listed among David's mighty warriors (2 Samuel 23:37; 1 Chronicles 11:39).

entries.title: Nahash (King living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: The Ammonite king who besieged Jabesh-gilead and offered peace only if he could put out every man's right eye. That threat rallied Israel behind Saul, newly anointed, for his first victory.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Nahash (King living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: A king of the Ammonites. When he died, Israel's king sent men to comfort his son, and 2 Samuel 10 is the war that came out of how they were received.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Nahash was an Ammonite king whose brutal siege terms against Jabesh-gilead, offering peace only if he could gouge out every resident's right eye, rallied Israel behind newly anointed King Saul for his first military victory.

entries.title: Nahash (King living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: A king from the united kingdom, and 2 Samuel is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Nahash (Woman living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Named once, at 2 Samuel 17:25, as the parent of Abigail and so of Amasa. Whether Nahash there is a man or a woman is an old question: the verse calls Abigail 'daughter of Nahash' while 1 Chronicles 2:16 makes her Jesse's daughter, and readers have squared that either by taking Nahash as another name for Jesse or as the name of Jesse's wife.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Nahath (Edomite living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: An Edomite chief from Esau's line. The name was also carried by a Levite in Chronicles.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Nahath was a common name, borne by an Edomite clan chief descended from Esau and by a Levite involved in temple administration under Hezekiah.

entries.title: Nahath (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 2 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Nahor (Abraham's brother living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Abraham's brother, Terah's son, who stayed in Mesopotamia when Abraham went to Canaan. His family there gave Isaac a wife, Rebekah, and gave Jacob his uncle and father-in-law, Laban.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Two men named Nahor appear in Genesis. Terah's father was the grandfather Abraham was named for, generations back in the genealogy from Shem. Terah's son, Abraham's brother, stayed behind in Mesopotamia when Abraham left for Canaan, and his descendants there included Rebekah, who would later marry Isaac, and Laban, Jacob's uncle and father-in-law.

witness.excerpt: And she bare him Nahor, in the first year of this week, and he grew and dwelt in Ur of the Chaldees, and his father taught him the researches of the Chaldees to divine and augur, according to the signs of heaven.
For Abraham was the son of Terah, as well as Haran and Nahor.

The son of Phaleg, whose father was Heber, was Ragau: whose son was Serug: to whom was born Nahor: his son was Terah: who was the father of Abraham: who accordingly was the tenth from Noah:  and was born in the two hundred and ninety second year after the deluge.

entries.title: Nahor (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Terah's father, Abraham's grandfather, in the line from Shem. Joshua remembers that this family served other gods beyond the river.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Nahum (Prophet living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: His short book is about one thing, the fall of Nineveh, the Assyrian capital. It had repented once under Jonah and gone back to its cruelty, and Nahum describes its end in vivid, almost gleeful detail as the price of what it did to the nations it conquered.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Nahum was a prophet whose short book announces the coming destruction of Nineveh, the Assyrian capital that had once repented under Jonah's preaching but had since returned to its cruelty, and Nahum describes Nineveh's fall in vivid, almost gleeful detail as deserved judgment for the empire's brutality toward the nations it conquered.

entries.title: Nain
entries.summary: Jesus met a funeral coming out of this village in Galilee and raised a widow's only son. It sits at the foot of the hill of Moreh and survives as the Arab village of Nein, a few miles southeast of Nazareth.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A village in Galilee at the foot of the hill of Moreh, where Jesus met a funeral procession and raised a widow's only son from death (Luke 7:11-17). It survives as the Arab village of Nein, a few miles southeast of Nazareth.

witness.excerpt: For he built a wall at a certain village called Nain , 21 and made use of that as a fortress for his own party’s security; and at the valley called Pharan he enlarged many of the caves, and many others he found ready for his purpose: these he made use of as repositories f

entries.title: Naioth
entries.summary: Near Ramah, apparently a cluster of houses where Samuel kept his company of prophets. David ran there from Saul. Saul's messengers arrived and fell to prophesying, then Saul came himself and did the same, and David got away.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Naioth was a settlement near Ramah, apparently a cluster of dwellings housing the prophetic community Samuel gathered and led. David fled there for refuge from Saul, and Saul's messengers, then Saul himself, fell into prophetic ecstasy upon arriving, giving David time to escape (1 Samuel 19:18-23; 20:1).

witness.excerpt: When the Prophet was made acquainted with the unjust proceedings of the King, he left the city Ramah, and took David with him, to a certain place called Naioth , 9 and there he abode with him.

entries.title: Nakbi (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Vophsi's son, sent by Moses to spy out Canaan for the tribe of Naphtali. He came back with the others, all but Joshua and Caleb, and their report talked the people out of going in.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of the twelve tribal representatives Moses sent to spy out the land of Canaan, representing the tribe of Naphtali and identified as the son of Vophsi (Num. 13:14). Along with all but Joshua and Caleb, he returned from the mission with the majority report that discouraged the people from entering the land. Nothing further is recorded about him.

entries.title: Naomi (Woman living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: She went to Moab with her husband Elimelech and their two sons during a famine, and all three men died there. Naomi told her Moabite daughters-in-law to go home, but Ruth would not leave her. Her bitterness turned to joy when Ruth married Boaz and had Obed, and Naomi helped raise him like her own.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Naomi was an Israelite woman who moved to Moab with her husband Elimelech and two sons during a famine, and after all three men died, she urged her Moabite daughters-in-law to return to their own families rather than follow her back to Bethlehem. Ruth refused to leave her, and Naomi's bitterness at her losses turned to joy once Ruth married Boaz and gave birth to Obed, whom Naomi helped raise as if he were her own.

witness.excerpt: Under him,21 when the countrey was afflicted with a famine, Elimelech of Bethlehem, which is a city of the tribe of Judah, being not able to support his family under so sore a distress, took with him Naomi his wife, and the children that were born to him by her, Chilion and Mahlon; and removed his habitation into the land of Moab: and upon the happy prosperity of his affairs there, he took for his sons wives of the Moabit

entries.title: Naphish (Arabian living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Ishmael's son. His people are among the tribes Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh beat in a war that Chronicles records.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Naphish was a son of Ishmael, and his descendants are counted among the tribes defeated by Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh in a war recorded in Chronicles.

entries.title: Naphtali (Jacob's son living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Jacob's sixth son, born to Rachel's servant Bilhah. His tribe settled in northern Galilee, the land Isaiah says will see a great light, and Matthew ties that to Jesus starting his work there.
entries.books: Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Psalm, Isaiah, Ezekiel
entries.label: 13 books
entries.dictNote: Naphtali was Jacob's sixth son, born to Rachel's servant Bilhah, and his tribe's territory in northern Galilee is the region Isaiah prophesies will see a great light, a prophecy Matthew connects directly to Jesus beginning his ministry in that same region.

entries.title: Naptuhim (People, perhaps from Naphtuh)
entries.summary: One of the peoples descended from Mizraim, that is Egypt, in the Table of Nations. Some put them in Lower Egypt or the Nile Delta, but there is no agreement.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: The Naphtuhim were one of the peoples descended from Mizraim, or Egypt, listed in the Table of Nations (Genesis 10:13; 1 Chronicles 1:11), representing an ethnic or tribal group associated with ancient Egypt rather than a single individual. Their precise historical identification is uncertain; proposals have linked them to Lower Egypt or the Nile Delta region, but no scholarly consensus exists.

entries.title: Narcissus (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Paul greets the believers in the household of Narcissus, not the man himself. Some guess he was a rich freedman tied to the emperor's court; the text does not say.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Roman resident whose household Paul greets in Romans 16:11, addressing believers who were part of it rather than Narcissus himself by name. Some have guessed he was a wealthy freedman connected to the imperial court, but nothing in the text confirms this.

witness.excerpt: Hudson: \"In the reign of Claudius,\" says he, \"Vespasian, for the sake of Narcissus, was sent as a lieutenant of a legion into Germany.

entries.title: Nathan (David's son living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of David's sons born in Jerusalem. Luke traces Jesus' line through him, not through Solomon.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Nathan (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A man from the divided-kingdom years, and 1 Chronicles is the only book that names him.

entries.summary: Ezra names him once, and he is a man from the exile and the return.

entries.title: Nathan (Prophet living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: The prophet who told David the story of the rich man who took a poor man's only lamb, let David condemn the man, and then turned it on him over Bathsheba and Uriah. Earlier he had brought God's promise that David's house would last forever. When David was dying, Nathan helped put Solomon on the throne ahead of a rival half-brother.
entries.label: 5 books
entries.dictNote: Nathan was the prophet who confronted King David over his affair with Bathsheba and the killing of her husband Uriah, using a parable about a rich man stealing a poor man's only lamb to trap David into condemning his own sin before he realized the story was about him. He had earlier delivered God's promise that David's dynasty would last forever, and he later helped secure the throne for Solomon over a rival half-brother when David was dying. A son of David was also named Nathan, and appears in Luke's genealogy of Jesus rather than Matthew's.
