entries.title: Nathan (Warrior living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 6 men called Nathan. This one is a warrior from the united kingdom, named twice in 2 Samuel and 1 Chronicles.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Nathanael (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Philip brought him to Jesus, and his first words were whether anything good could come out of Nazareth. Jesus told him he had seen him under the fig tree before Philip called, and Nathanael called him the Son of God. Many think he is Bartholomew, since John never names Bartholomew, the other Gospels never name Nathanael, and both are paired with Philip.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Nathanael was one of Jesus's earliest disciples, introduced to Jesus by his friend Philip and famous for his skeptical first reaction, asking whether anything good could come out of Nazareth. Jesus won him over instantly by telling him he had seen Nathanael sitting under a fig tree before Philip ever called him, a small detail that convinced Nathanael he was looking at the Son of God. Many identify Nathanael with the apostle Bartholomew, since the Synoptic Gospels never mention a Nathanael and John's Gospel never mentions a Bartholomew, and the two names always appear paired with Philip in their respective lists.

witness.excerpt: Of all which Eliab was the eldest: Aminadab the second: Shammah the third: Nathanael the fourth: the fifth was called Rael : and the sixth Asam .

entries.title: Nathanmelech (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: An official in Josiah's time. The horses earlier kings had dedicated to the sun stood near his room at the temple entrance, and Josiah took them away.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A court official under King Josiah, associated in the account of Josiah's religious reforms with the removal of horses that earlier kings had dedicated to sun worship at the entrance to the temple (2 Kings 23:11).

entries.title: Naum (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: The Greek form of Nahum, a name in Luke's genealogy, son of Esli and father of Amos. Luke's line after David runs through Nathan, which is why it parts from Matthew's.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Naum, the Greek form of Nahum, appears only in Luke's genealogy of Jesus as the son of Esli and father of Amos, one link in the chain tracing Christ's ancestry back through David to Adam (Luke 3:25). Nothing is known of him beyond his place in this list. Luke's genealogy differs substantially from Matthew's for the generations after David, most likely because the two evangelists trace descent through different sons of David, Nathan in Luke's case.

entries.title: Nazarene (Nazareth)
entries.summary: It means from Nazareth, Jesus' home town, and it became the name for his followers too, "the sect of the Nazarenes" in Acts 24:5. Matthew ties it to prophecy, possibly playing on the Hebrew word for "branch" in Isaiah 11. Arabic and Hebrew still call Christians by it.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Nazarene marks Jesus as a native of Nazareth, the small Galilean town where he grew up, and by extension became the name for his early followers, who were known in Jerusalem as "the sect of the Nazarenes" in Acts 24:5. Matthew connects the title to Old Testament prophecy, possibly playing on the Hebrew word for "branch" used of the coming Messiah in Isaiah 11. The name is still the standard Arabic and Hebrew word for Christians today.

witness.excerpt: He indeed, as then an Ebionite, must have read and believed the Nazarene gospel; as my I st Dissertation shews, § 71.

entries.title: Nazareth
entries.summary: A small village in the hills of Galilee, never named in the Old Testament and not thought much of, which is likely the edge on Nathanael's question about whether anything good could come from it. Gabriel came to Mary there, and Jesus grew up there. When he preached in its synagogue, his neighbours drove him out.
entries.label: 5 books
entries.dictNote: Nazareth was a small, obscure village in the hill country of Galilee, never mentioned in the Old Testament and generally held in low regard, which is likely the force of Nathanael's question, "can any good thing come out of Nazareth?" It was the hometown of Joseph and Mary, the place of Gabriel's announcement to Mary, and where Jesus grew up and later launched his ministry, until his neighbors drove him out after he preached in the synagogue there. Its obscurity is itself part of the gospel writers' point: Israel's Messiah came from a place nobody expected.

witness.excerpt: 48, that, \"If they let Jesus alone,\" with his miracles, \"all men would believe on him, and the Romans would come and take away both their place and nation.\" Which political crucifixion of Jesus of Nazareth brought down the vengeance of God upon them, and occasioned those very Romans, of whom they seemed so much afraid, that to prevent it they put him to death, actually to \"come and take away both their place and nation\"

entries.title: Neah (Neiel)
entries.summary: On the border of Zebulun, not far from Rimmon. The site has not been firmly found.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A border town of the tribe of Zebulun, situated not far from Rimmon (Josh. 19:13). Its site has not been securely identified.

entries.title: Neapolis
entries.summary: "New city," the port for Philippi on the coast of Macedonia. Paul, Silas, Timothy and Luke landed there from Troas, their first step in Europe, and walked the Via Egnatia about ten miles inland to Philippi. The town is Kavala in Greece today.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Neapolis, "new city," was the port of Philippi on the coast of Macedonia and the first place in Europe where Paul, Silas, Timothy, and Luke set foot, arriving by ship from Troas at the start of Paul's second missionary journey (Acts 16:11). From there the party took the Via Egnatia, the great Roman highway linking the Adriatic to the Aegean, about ten miles inland to Philippi. Neapolis survives today as Kavala, Greece, whose harbor and hillside old town still overlook the same strait Paul's ship would have crossed.

entries.title: Neariah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A descendant of David in the royal line Chronicles carries on past the exile.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Neariah was a descendant of David listed in the royal genealogy of Chronicles after the return from exile.

entries.title: Neariah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Nebai (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of the family heads who set their seal to the covenant under Nehemiah. Nothing more is recorded.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of the lay family heads who set their seal to the covenant renewal under Nehemiah (Neh. 10:19-27), a communal pledge to keep the law after the return from exile. Nothing more is recorded about him beyond his place in this list of signatories.

entries.title: Nebaioth (Arabian living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Ishmael's firstborn. His descendants were an Arabian trading people, named next to Kedar in Isaiah.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Nebaioth was Ishmael's firstborn son, and his descendants are associated with a prominent Arabian trading people mentioned alongside Kedar in Isaiah's prophecies.

witness.excerpt: And she bare him a son, and he called his name Nebaioth;  for she said, "The Lord was nigh to me when I called upon him."

entries.title: Neballat
entries.summary: Men of Benjamin resettled it after the exile, along with Hadid and Ono. The name lives on in the village of Beit Nabala, a few miles northeast of Lydda.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A town resettled by men of Benjamin after the return from exile, listed alongside Hadid and Ono (Nehemiah 11:34). It survives in the name of the village Beit Nabala, a few miles northeast of Lydda.

entries.title: Nebat (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Jeroboam's father, and he is only ever named in "Jeroboam son of Nebat," the phrase the books of Kings use again and again for the king blamed for making idol worship the habit of the north.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Nebat was the father of Jeroboam, Israel's first king after the kingdom split from Judah, and appears in the Bible only in the recurring phrase Jeroboam son of Nebat, used repeatedly to identify the king blamed for institutionalizing idolatry in the northern kingdom.

witness.excerpt: There was also one of Solomon's own nation that made an attempt against him, Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who had an expectation of rising, from a prophecy that had been made to him long before.

The Old Testament is full of the miseries of the people of the Jews derived from such court politics, especially in and after the days of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, \"who made Israel to sin;\" who gave the most pernicious example of it; who brought on the grossest corruption of religion by it; and the punishment of whose family for it was most remarkable.

entries.title: Nebo
entries.summary: The mountain in Moab where Moses looked over the promised land before he died, taken as Jebel Neba on the ridge of Pisgah east of the Dead Sea. A Reubenite town nearby had the same name, and the oracles against Moab condemn it.
entries.label: 5 books
entries.dictNote: Nebo was the Babylonian god of writing and wisdom, son of Marduk, whose worship spread into Assyria; Isaiah mocks the idol being carted off on beasts of burden as Babylon falls. The name also belonged to the mountain in Moab from which Moses viewed the promised land before his death, identified with Jebel Neba on the ridge of Pisgah east of the Dead Sea, and to a Reubenite town nearby rebuilt after the conquest and later condemned in Moab oracles for its idolatry. A separate town called Nebo in Benjamin gave its name to a family among the exiles who returned with Zerubbabel.

witness.excerpt: The names of these generals who ravaged and subdued Jerusalem, if any one desire to know them, were these; Nergal Sharezer, Samgar Nebo, Rabsaris, Sarsechim, and Rabmag.

entries.title: Nebo
entries.summary: The other Nebo, a town in Benjamin. A family from it came back from exile with Zerubbabel.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Nebo (A male deity in the Old Testament)
entries.summary: Isaiah names him once, and nothing else is recorded.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Nebuchadnezzar (Emperor living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: King of Babylon. He destroyed Jerusalem and its temple in 586 BC and carried Judah off, and the Bible still calls him the tool God used to judge his people. Daniel tells how, after boasting of his greatness, he went mad and lived like an animal for seven times, which Daniel never defines, until he gave God the glory and got his throne back.
entries.books: 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel
entries.label: 9 books
entries.dictNote: Nebuchadnezzar was the king of Babylon who destroyed Jerusalem and its temple in 586 BC and deported Judah's population, making him the central villain of Israel's exile even as the Bible also portrays him as an instrument God used deliberately to judge his people. The book of Daniel records his dramatic humiliation: driven mad and reduced to living like an animal in the fields for seven years after boasting about his own greatness, until he acknowledged God's sovereignty and was restored to his throne. Nebuchadnezzar's building projects, including the massive city walls and temples of Babylon, are extensively documented in his own inscriptions, which independently confirm the scale of the empire the Bible describes.

witness.excerpt: Now in the fourth year of the reign of Jehoiakim, one whose name was Nebuchadnezzar took the government over the Babylonians; who at the same time went up with a great army.

entries.curatedNote: The Babylonian king who besieges Jerusalem three times over a generation, the figure behind both Daniel's exile and 2 Kings' final chapters. Josephus dates his rise the same way Jeremiah does, the fourth year of Jehoiakim, and follows the same campaign against Jerusalem.

entries.title: Nebushazban (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Rab-saris, chief of the court officials, in Nebuchadnezzar's service. After Jerusalem fell he was one of the senior men sent to find Jeremiah, see he was treated well and let him out of the court of the guard. The name means something like "Nabu, save me."
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Nebushazban was a Babylonian officer holding the title Rab-saris, chief of the court officials, in the service of Nebuchadnezzar. He is named in Jeremiah 39:13 among the senior officers Nebuchadnezzar sent to Jerusalem after its fall in 586 BC, with orders to locate Jeremiah and see that he was treated well and released from the court of the guard. His Akkadian name, meaning roughly "Nabu, save me," reflects the standard Babylonian court practice of naming officials after the god Nabu.

entries.title: Nebuzaradan (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: He commanded the Babylonians who burned Jerusalem and its temple. To Jeremiah, though, he showed unusual kindness, and let the prophet choose whether to go to Babylon or stay in Judah.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Nebuzaradan was the Babylonian commander who carried out the destruction of Jerusalem and its temple under Nebuchadnezzar's orders, and he later showed unusual personal consideration toward the prophet Jeremiah, giving him the choice to go to Babylon or remain in Judah.

witness.excerpt: 588.] And now it was, that the King of Babylon sent Nebuzaradan, the general of his army, to Jerusalem, to pillage the temple: who had it also in command to burn it, and the royal palace, and to lay the city even with the ground, and to transplant the people into Babylon.

entries.title: Necho (Pharaoh living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Necho the Second, pharaoh of Egypt, killed King Josiah at Megiddo. Afterwards he removed Josiah's son Jehoahaz and set up another son, Jehoiakim, under him.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Necho the Second was the Egyptian pharaoh who killed King Josiah in battle at Megiddo and later deposed Josiah's son Jehoahaz, installing a different son, Jehoiakim, as a subject king instead.

entries.title: Nedabiah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Jeconiah's son, born before or during the king's exile in Babylon. The royal list in 1 Chronicles 3:18 is the only place he appears.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of the sons of King Jeconiah (Jehoiachin) of Judah, born either before or during his exile in Babylon, listed in the royal genealogy of 1 Chronicles 3:18. Nothing further is recorded about him.

entries.title: Nehelamite (People, perhaps from Nehel)
entries.summary: Shemaiah the Nehelamite was a false prophet among the exiles in Babylon. He wrote to the priests in Jerusalem to have Jeremiah silenced, and Jeremiah condemned him for prophesying lies. Where the name comes from is unknown; some read it as "dreamer."
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Nehelamite designates Shemaiah, a false prophet among the Judean exiles in Babylon who wrote letters urging the priests in Jerusalem to silence Jeremiah, only to be condemned by Jeremiah himself for prophesying lies. The origin of the name itself is unknown, though it has sometimes been read as related to a Hebrew word for "dreamer."

entries.title: Nehemiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Cupbearer to the Persian king Artaxerxes. He used that trust to get leave, money and safe conduct to rebuild Jerusalem's walls, and finished in fifty-two days against constant sabotage. As governor of Judah he forced debt relief for the poor and took on intermarriage and Sabbath breaking.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Nehemiah was a Jewish cupbearer to the Persian king Artaxerxes who used his position of trust to get permission, funding, and safe passage to rebuild Jerusalem's ruined walls, finishing the job in just fifty-two days despite constant opposition and sabotage attempts. He went on to serve as governor of Judah, enforcing debt relief for the poor and confronting the intermarriage and Sabbath violations that had crept back into Jewish practice. Two other men named Nehemiah appear only in passing, one in the list of returning exiles and another among those who repaired a section of the wall.

witness.excerpt: Concerning Esdras and Nehemiah.

entries.curatedNote: The cupbearer-turned-governor who rebuilds Jerusalem's walls in fifty-two days despite constant sabotage (Nehemiah 1-6). Josephus's chapter title pairs him directly with Ezra, the same pairing their two books share in most English Bibles.

entries.title: Nehemiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Ezra and Nehemiah name him twice, and he is a man from the exile and the return.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Nehemiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of 3 men called Nehemiah. This one is a man from the exile and the return, named once in Nehemiah.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Nehum (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of the leaders who came back to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel, called Rehum in Ezra's list.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Nehum, called Rehum in the parallel list of Ezra 2:2, was one of the leaders who returned from Babylonian exile to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel (Nehemiah 7:7).

entries.title: Nehushta (Woman living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Elnathan's daughter, from Jerusalem. She was King Jehoiakim's wife and the mother of Jehoiachin, who reigned three months at eighteen before Nebuchadnezzar took him, and she was carried to Babylon with him in 597 BC. The Babylonian Chronicle records that capture of Jerusalem.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Nehushta was the daughter of Elnathan of Jerusalem and the wife of King Jehoiakim of Judah, and the mother of Jehoiachin, who succeeded his father at eighteen and reigned only three months before Nebuchadnezzar deposed him (2 Kings 24:8, 15). She and her son were among the Judean elite deported to Babylon in 597 BC, an event corroborated by the Babylonian Chronicle, which records Nebuchadnezzar capturing Jerusalem and installing a king of his own choosing that same year.

witness.excerpt: And this was the end of King Jehoiakim, when he had lived thirty six years, and of them reigned eleven.12 But Jehoiachin succeeded him in the Kingdom: whose mothers name was Nehushta: she was a citizen of Jerusalem.

entries.title: Nehushtan (A male deity in the Old Testament)
entries.summary: Hezekiah's scornful name for the bronze serpent Moses had made in the wilderness. People had taken to burning incense to it, so Hezekiah broke it up, calling it a mere piece of bronze.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Nehushtan is the contemptuous name King Hezekiah gave to the bronze serpent Moses had made in the wilderness to heal those bitten by venomous snakes (Numbers 21:8-9). Over the centuries Israelites had begun burning incense to the relic as an idol, so Hezekiah destroyed it as part of his religious reforms, dismissing it as “a mere piece of bronze” (2 Kings 18:4).

entries.title: Neiel
entries.summary: On Asher's southern border. It is tentatively placed at a ruin near where the Wadi esh-Shaghur comes out, north of Kabul in western Galilee.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Neiel, a town on the southern border of the tribe of Asher (Josh. 19:27). It is tentatively identified with a ruin near the outlet of the Wadi esh-Shaghur, north of Kabul in the western Galilee.

entries.title: Nekoda (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: His family were temple servants who came back from exile and could not prove their descent.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Nekoda (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Head of a family among the temple servants who came back from exile and could not prove their descent. Several families had the same problem.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Nekoda was the head of a family among the temple servants who returned from exile but could not prove their genealogical descent, a problem shared by several other returning families.

entries.title: Nemuel (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: In the Numbers 26 census, a Nemuel is counted in Reuben's line, and the clan record says nothing more.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Nemuel was a son of Reuben, and his descendants formed one of the clans counted in Israel's wilderness census.

entries.title: Nemuel (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: A man from the wilderness years. Numbers names him once.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Nemuelite (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: The clan from Nemuel, son of Simeon, in the Numbers 26 census. Genesis calls the same man Jemuel.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Nemuelites were the clan descended from Nemuel, a son of Simeon, counted in the Numbers 26 census; the same man is called Jemuel in Genesis 46:10.

entries.title: Nepheg (David's son living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of David's sons born in Jerusalem, and nothing more is told of him.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Nepheg was a common name, borne by one of Moses and Aaron's cousins and by one of David's sons born in Jerusalem.

entries.title: Nepheg (Levite living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Exodus names him once, and he is a Levite from the wilderness years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Nephisesim (People, perhaps from Nephus)
entries.summary: A family of Nethinim, the temple servants, back from Babylon with Zerubbabel. Ezra's list spells them Nephusim.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Nephisesim, also spelled Nephushesim, names a family of Nethinim, temple servants assigned menial duties in worship, who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Nehemiah 7:52). The parallel list in Ezra 2:50 gives the family name as Nephusim, one of several small spelling variations among the Nethinim clans in these overlapping census lists.

entries.title: Nephthalim (Jacob's son living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: The Greek spelling of Naphtali. Matthew uses it for the land where a people in darkness see a great light, as Jesus begins his work there.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Nephthalim is the Greek New Testament form of Naphtali, the tribe whose territory Matthew cites as fulfilling Isaiah's prophecy of a people in darkness who would see a great light when Jesus began his ministry there.

witness.excerpt: And after him Nephthalim: as it were unconquerable in stratagems: since Rachel tried to conquer the fruitfulness of her sister by this stratagem.

entries.title: Nephusim (People, perhaps from Nephus)
entries.summary: The margin's spelling of a family of temple servants, or Nethinim, who returned with Zerubbabel; Nehemiah calls them Nephushesim.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Nephusim is an alternate spelling, preserved in the margin, of Nephishesim, the ancestral head of a family of temple servants, or Nethinim, who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:50; called Nephushesim in Neh. 7:52).

entries.title: Neptoah (Nephtoah)
entries.summary: The waters of Neptoah are a point on the border between Judah and Benjamin, named twice in Joshua. They are commonly linked to the spring at Lifta, just northwest of Jerusalem.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The waters of Neptoah mark a point on the boundary between the tribal territories of Judah and Benjamin, mentioned twice in the border descriptions of Joshua (Josh. 15:9; 18:15). The name is commonly linked to the spring at Lifta, just northwest of Jerusalem, whose modern Arabic name preserves a similar sound. Beyond its role as a landmark in Judah's border survey, nothing else is recorded about it.

entries.title: Ner (Saul's uncle living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Father of Abner, Saul's army commander. Ner was Saul's grandfather or great-uncle, depending on how the genealogies are fitted together.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Ner was King Saul's grandfather, or great-uncle depending on how the genealogies are reconciled, and the father of Abner, Saul's army commander.

witness.excerpt: He had also Abner his uncle’s son for the Captain of his host: that uncle’s name was Ner .

But as soon as Abner, the son of Ner, who was general of Saul's army, and a very active man, and good-natured, knew that the king, and Jonathan, and his two other sons, were fallen in the battle, he made haste into the camp; and taking away with him the re

Be thou also mindful of the transgressions of Joab, (26) the captain of the host, who hath slain two generals out of envy, and those righteous and good men, Abner the son of Ner, and Amasa the son of Jether; whose death do thou avenge as shall seem good to thee, since Joab hath been too hard for me, and more potent than myself, and so hath escaped punishment hitherto.

entries.title: Nereus (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Paul greets him and his sister in Rome at the end of the letter to the Romans, and nothing else is known.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Nereus was a Christian in Rome whom Paul greeted by name, along with his sister, at the close of his letter to the Roman church (Romans 16:15). Nothing further is known about him.

entries.title: Nergal (A male deity in the Old Testament)
entries.summary: A Mesopotamian god of war, plague and the underworld, worshipped at Cuthah. When Assyria moved people from Cuthah into Samaria after 722 BC, they brought him with them.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Nergal was a Mesopotamian god of war, plague, and the underworld, worshipped at the city of Cuthah; when Assyria deported Cuthites to resettle Samaria after 722 BC, they brought his cult with them into the mixed religion the transplanted population practiced there (2 Kings 17:24, 30). Mesopotamian temple records confirm his cult center at Cuthah, modern Tell Ibrahim, naming him alongside his consort Ereshkigal.

witness.excerpt: The names of these generals who ravaged and subdued Jerusalem, if any one desire to know them, were these; Nergal Sharezer, Samgar Nebo, Rabsaris, Sarsechim, and Rabmag.

entries.title: Nergal-sharezer (Babylonian official living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of Nebuchadnezzar's officers at the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC; a man of this name with the title Rab-mag helped get Jeremiah out of prison. Scholars generally take him for Neriglissar, who later killed his brother-in-law Evil-Merodach and ruled Babylon from about 560 to 556 BC.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Nergal-sharezer (Babylonian official of Samgar living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of Nebuchadnezzar's officers at the fall of Jerusalem. The name belongs to the Babylonian god Nergal.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Nergal-sharezer, named for the Babylonian god Nergal, appears among the officials of Nebuchadnezzar's army at the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC, and one bearing the additional title “Rab-mag” helped release Jeremiah from prison (Jeremiah 39:3, 13). Scholars generally identify this official with Neriglissar, the Babylonian general who later murdered his brother-in-law Evil-Merodach (Amel-Marduk) and reigned as king from about 560 to 556 BC. Neriglissar's short reign and violent seizure of the throne are independently confirmed by Babylonian chronicles and king lists.

entries.title: Neri (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Shealtiel's father in Luke's genealogy, on the line through David's son Nathan.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Father of Shealtiel in Luke's genealogy of Jesus (Luke 3:27), part of the line traced through David's son Nathan rather than through Solomon as in Matthew's genealogy.

entries.title: Neriah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Baruch was his son, Jeremiah's scribe, and so was a royal official, which made Neriah's a family of some weight in Judah's last years before Babylon.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Neriah was the father of Baruch, Jeremiah's scribe, and also of a royal official, making his family prominent in the administration of Judah's final years before Babylon's conquest.

Accordingly Jeremiah abode in a city of that countrey which was called Mispah ; and desired of Nebuzaradan that he would set at liberty his disciple Baruch, the son of Neriah; one of a very eminent family; and exceeding skilful in the language of his countrey.

entries.title: Nethaneel (David's brother living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the united kingdom.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Nethaneel (Levite living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: A levite from the united kingdom. 1 Chronicles names him once.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Nethaneel (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 10 men called Nethaneel. This one is a man from the divided-kingdom years, named once in 1 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Nethaneel (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A man from the divided-kingdom years, and 1 Chronicles is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Nethaneel (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 2 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.

entries.title: Nethaneel (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 10 men called Nethaneel. This one is a man from the divided-kingdom years, named once in 2 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Nethaneel (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Leader of Issachar during the wilderness census. The name was common, and later priests and Levites carried it too.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Nethaneel was a common name in the Old Testament, borne by a tribal leader of Issachar during the wilderness census and by several priests and Levites in later generations.

entries.title: Nethaneel (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Nehemiah names him once, and he is a man from the exile and the return.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Nethaneel (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A man from the exile and the return, and Ezra is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Nethaneel (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A man from the exile and the return. Nehemiah names him once.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Nethaniah (Levite living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him twice, and he is a Levite from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Nethaniah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Father of Ishmael, the man of royal blood who murdered Gedaliah, the governor Babylon set over Judah after Jerusalem fell.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Nethaniah was the father of Ishmael, the royal descendant who assassinated Gedaliah, the Babylonian-appointed governor of Judah, after Jerusalem's fall.

entries.title: Nethaniah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 4 men called Nethaniah. This one is a man from the divided-kingdom years, named once in 2 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Nethaniah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A man from the divided-kingdom years, and Jeremiah is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Nethinims
entries.summary: Temple servants, probably war captives to begin with, given the heavy work around the Levites. Groups of them come back from Babylon in the return lists.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: The Nethinim were temple servants, likely originally war captives, assigned to assist the Levites with menial temple labor, and groups of them are listed among those who returned from Babylonian exile to serve at the rebuilt temple.

entries.title: Nethinims
entries.summary: The same temple servants, here under the tax exemption the king grants them.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Netophah
entries.summary: "Dripping," probably for a spring, the name of a town near Bethlehem. Some of its people came back from Babylon with Zerubbabel, and two of David's best soldiers were Netophathites.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Town near Bethlehem in Judah. Some of its residents, called Netophathites, returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:22; Neh. 7:26), and two Netophathites served among David's elite soldiers (2 Sam. 23:28-29; 1 Chr. 27:13, 15). Its name, meaning "dripping" or "distillation," likely refers to a local spring.

entries.title: Netophathite (Netophah)
entries.summary: From Netophah, a small town near Bethlehem. Several of David's mighty men carried the name, and later some Levitical singers did too.
entries.label: 5 books
entries.dictNote: Netophathite marks a person as coming from Netophah, a small town near Bethlehem. Several of David's mighty men and, later, Levitical singers appointed to temple service are identified by this name in Chronicles and Ezra.

entries.title: Neziah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Head of a family of Nethinim, temple servants whose descendants came back with Zerubbabel. Nothing more survives.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Neziah headed a family of Nethinim, temple servants whose descendants returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:54; Nehemiah 7:56). Nothing further is recorded about him.

entries.title: Nezib
entries.summary: In Judah's Shephelah, at the ruin of Khirbet Beit Nasib southwest of Hebron.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A town in the Shephelah lowlands of Judah (Josh. 15:43), identified with the ruin of Khirbet Beit Nasib southwest of Hebron.

entries.title: Nibhaz (A male deity in the Old Testament)
entries.summary: An idol the Avite settlers brought to Samaria when the Assyrians moved them there. Old tradition says it was shaped like a dog.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Nibhaz is not a person but an idol the Avite settlers brought to Samaria after the Assyrians deported them there following the fall of the northern kingdom (2 Kings 17:31). Ancient tradition describes it as having the form of a dog, though little else is known of this god.

entries.title: Nibshan
entries.summary: Six towns stood in Judah's wilderness by the western shore of the Dead Sea, and Nibshan was one. It is often put near En-gedi, without a firm site.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Nibshan was one of six towns Joshua's allotment places "in the wilderness" of Judah, near the western shore of the Dead Sea (Joshua 15:61-62). It is often located near En-gedi, though no firm identification has been established.

entries.title: Nicanor (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: The Jerusalem church picked seven men to run the daily food for widows after the Hellenistic and Hebrew believers fell out, and Nicanor was one of them. That is all the New Testament says.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of the seven men chosen by the Jerusalem church to oversee the daily distribution of food to widows, a role created to resolve a dispute between Hellenistic and Hebrew believers (Acts 6:5). Nothing else is recorded of him in the New Testament.

entries.title: Nicodemus (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: A Pharisee on the ruling council who came to Jesus at night, afraid to be seen, and heard that a person must be born again to see the kingdom of God. Later he spoke up, carefully, against arresting Jesus without a hearing. After the crucifixion he helped Joseph of Arimathea bury the body, bringing enough spices for a king.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Nicodemus was a Pharisee and member of the Jewish ruling council who came to Jesus secretly at night, afraid of being seen, and received the famous teaching that a person must be born again to see the kingdom of God. He later spoke up cautiously in Jesus's defense when the council wanted to arrest him without a hearing, and after the crucifixion he helped Joseph of Arimathea bury Jesus's body, bringing a burial spice mixture heavy enough for a king.

entries.title: Nicolaitane (Religious group in the New Testament)
entries.summary: Christ condemns them twice in the letters of Revelation, once to Ephesus and once to Pergamum. Their teaching or practice was tied to idolatry and sexual immorality, and that is about all the text gives us.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The Nicolaitans were a group active in the churches of Ephesus and Pergamum in the late first century, condemned twice by Christ in the letters of Revelation for teaching or practices linked to idolatry and sexual immorality (Revelation 2:6, 15). Some early church writers connected the name to Nicolas, one of the seven men chosen to serve the Jerusalem church in Acts 6:5, though the link is disputed and little else is known of the group's actual teaching.

entries.title: Nicolaus (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: One of the seven the Jerusalem church picked to oversee the daily food for widows, and called a proselyte of Antioch, a Gentile who had converted to Judaism before he came to Christ.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Nicolaus was one of the seven men chosen by the Jerusalem church to oversee the daily distribution of food to widows, described as a proselyte of Antioch, meaning a Gentile convert to Judaism before becoming a Christian (Acts 6:5). Later Christian writers linked his name to the Nicolaitans condemned in Revelation 2, though the New Testament itself does not connect him to that group.

entries.title: Nicopolis
entries.summary: Paul wanted Titus to come and spend the winter with him here (Titus 3:12). The name means city of victory, and the likeliest candidate is the one in Epirus, on Greece's northwestern coast.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Nicopolis, meaning city of victory, was where Paul asked Titus to join him for the winter (Titus 3:12). The most likely candidate is the Nicopolis in Epirus, on Greece's northwestern coast, founded by Augustus to commemorate his naval victory over Antony and Cleopatra at nearby Actium in 31 BC; extensive Roman ruins there, including a theater and a monument to the Actium victory itself, have been excavated.

entries.title: Niger (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Simeon's Latin surname, meaning "black." He was one of the prophets and teachers at Antioch who sent Paul and Barnabas off on their first missionary journey.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The Latin surname, meaning "black," of Simeon, one of the prophets and teachers of the church at Antioch who helped commission Paul and Barnabas for their first missionary journey (Acts 13:1). The name likely reflects a dark complexion, and some have suggested an African origin, though the text gives no further detail.

They also chose other generals for Idumea; Jesus, the son of Sapphias, one of the high priests; and Eleazar, the son of Ananias, the high priest; they also enjoined Niger, the then governor of Idumea, (32) who was of a family that belonged to Perea, beyond Jordan, and was thence called the Peraite, that he should be obedient to those fore-named commanders.

entries.title: Nimrah
entries.summary: Reuben and Gad wanted this ground east of the Jordan for their herds because it was good cattle land, and it is usually identified with Beth-nimrah.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Nimrah was a well-watered site east of the Jordan that the tribes of Reuben and Gad requested as pastureland for their large herds because of its suitability for cattle (Numbers 32:1-3). It is usually identified with Beth-nimrah, mentioned a few verses later as one of the towns Gad rebuilt (Numbers 32:36), and its name survives in the modern Wadi Nimrin near the Jordan.

entries.title: Nimrim
entries.summary: Isaiah and Jeremiah both name the waters of Nimrim, a once-fertile spot in Moab, in their oracles of judgment against that country.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: The waters of Nimrim were a stream or spring-fed area in Moabite territory, cited by both Isaiah and Jeremiah in their oracles of judgment against Moab as a once-fertile place reduced to desolation (Isa. 15:6; Jer. 48:34). It is usually located southeast of the Dead Sea, in the plain of Moab proper.

entries.title: Nimrod (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Noah's great-grandson through Ham, called a mighty hunter before the Lord. Genesis credits him with founding a run of Mesopotamian cities, Babel among them. Micah later uses his name for the land of Assyria itself.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Nimrod was a great-grandson of Noah through Ham, described in Genesis as a mighty hunter before the Lord and the founder of a series of major Mesopotamian cities including Babel, the site of the later tower and scattered languages. His name became proverbial enough that later Old Testament writers refer to Assyria itself as the land of Nimrod.

witness.excerpt: But Nimrod, the son of Chus, stayed and tyrannized at Babylon; as we have already informed you.
Now it was Nimrod who excited them to such an affront and contempt of God.

entries.title: Nimshi (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Jehu's grandfather, who survives almost entirely inside the phrase "Jehu son of Nimshi."
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Nimshi was Jehu's grandfather, remembered mainly in the recurring phrase Jehu son of Nimshi used to identify the king who destroyed Ahab's dynasty.

So he returned to have his wound healed in Jezreel; but left his whole army in Ramoth, and Jehu the son of Nimshi for their General: for he had already taken the city by force: and he proposed, after he was healed, to make war with the Syrians.

entries.title: Nineve
entries.summary: Luke's Greek spelling of Nineveh. Jesus says the men of Nineve will rise up in judgment against his own generation, since they repented at Jonah's preaching and someone greater than Jonah was now standing in front of them.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The Greek form of Nineveh, used in Luke's account of Jesus warning that "the men of Nineve" will rise up in judgment against his own unrepentant generation, because Nineveh repented at the preaching of Jonah while someone greater than Jonah stood unheeded before Israel (Luke 11:32). Nineveh, once the capital of the Assyrian Empire on the Tigris opposite modern Mosul, is richly documented archaeologically, including Sennacherib's palace reliefs and the library of Ashurbanipal recovered from its ruins.

witness.excerpt: Ashur lived at the city Nineve; and named his subjects Assyrians: who became the most fortunate nation, beyond others.
Jonah had been commanded by God to go to the Kingdom of Nineve: and when he was there, to publish it in that city, how it should lose the dominion it had over the nations.

entries.title: Nineveh
entries.summary: The capital of the Assyrian empire. Jonah preached there against his will and watched the city repent, and Nahum later announced its destruction once it had gone back to its old cruelty.
entries.books: Genesis, 2 Kings, Isaiah, Jonah, Nahum, Zephaniah
entries.label: 6 books
entries.dictNote: Nineveh was the capital of the Assyrian empire, the city Jonah reluctantly preached to and watched repent, and later the target of Nahum's prophecy of destruction once it had returned to its old cruelty. Extensive archaeological excavation of Nineveh has recovered the Assyrian royal library and detailed records of the empire's military campaigns, including Sennacherib's own account of his siege of Jerusalem.

So the King was in a great dread, and in a terrible agony at this calamity; and being in great fear for his whole army, he fled with the rest of his forces to his own Kingdom, and to his city Nineveh.

entries.title: Nisan (Name of the 1st month)
entries.summary: First month of the religious year, March into April. The older texts call it Abib, and Nehemiah and Esther both date by it.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Nisan is not a person but the first month of the Hebrew religious calendar, corresponding roughly to March-April, also called Abib in earlier texts. It is named in Nehemiah as the month in which he approached King Artaxerxes about rebuilding Jerusalem's walls (Nehemiah 2:1), and in Esther as the month in which Haman cast lots to fix the date for the destruction of the Jews (Esther 3:7).

entries.title: Nisroch (A male deity in the Old Testament)
entries.summary: Sennacherib, king of Assyria, was killed by his own sons in the temple of Nisroch, an Assyrian god and not a man at all.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Nisroch was not a person but a god in the Assyrian pantheon, worshiped with the head of an eagle, in whose temple King Sennacherib of Assyria was assassinated by his own sons (2 Kings 19:37; Isaiah 37:38). The god's name does not correspond cleanly to any deity known from surviving Assyrian records, and it may be a scribal corruption of another god's name such as Nusku. Sennacherib's murder itself is corroborated outside the Bible: the Babylonian Chronicle and later Assyrian records confirm he was killed by one of his own sons in a palace coup.

entries.title: No (Thebes)
entries.summary: Nahum points to the fall of No, the Hebrew name for the Egyptian city of Thebes, as a warning to Nineveh that no city is too strong for God's judgment.
entries.label: 5 books
entries.dictNote: No, also called No-amon, is the Hebrew name for the great Egyptian city of Thebes, and the prophet Nahum cites its historical destruction as a warning to Nineveh that no city, however powerful, is beyond God's judgment.

entries.title: Noadiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: When Ezra's company reached Jerusalem, the temple silver and gold were weighed out, and Noadiah was one of the Levites on hand (Ezra 8:33). Nothing else is said about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Noadiah (Woman living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A prophetess who worked with those trying to frighten Nehemiah off the wall.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Noadiah is the name of two different figures. One was a Levite who returned from Babylon with Ezra and helped weigh out the temple treasures (Ezra 8:33). The other was a prophetess who, together with the enemies Tobiah and Sanballat, tried to intimidate and discourage Nehemiah while he was rebuilding Jerusalem's walls (Nehemiah 6:14).

entries.title: Noah (Flood survivor living at the time before the Flood)
entries.summary: God picked him as the one righteous man of his generation and told him to build an ark. His family came through the flood with him, along with pairs of every kind of animal. Afterward God made a covenant with him.
entries.books: Genesis, 1 Chronicles, Isaiah, Ezekiel, Matthew, Luke, Hebrews, 1 Peter, 2 Peter
entries.label: 9 books
entries.dictNote: Noah was the only righteous man of his generation, chosen to build an ark and preserve his family and pairs of every kind of animal through a catastrophic flood God sent to judge human wickedness. After the flood, God made a covenant with Noah never to destroy the earth by flood again, sealed with the sign of the rainbow, and Noah's three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth, became the ancestors of all the nations listed in Genesis 10.
entries.lukeNote: Jesus cites ‘the days of Noah’ twice as the pattern for his own return (Luke 17:26-27), the same Noah whose birth a separate, non-canonical tradition (the Book of Noah fragment preserved inside 1 Enoch) renders as something closer to a portent than an ordinary delivery.

entries.title: Noah (Woman living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Not the man of the flood. This Noah was one of the five daughters of Zelophehad who went to Moses and won the right to inherit their father's land, since there was no son.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: A different Noah, unrelated to the flood, was one of five daughters of Zelophehad who successfully petitioned Moses for the right to inherit their father's land in the absence of a son.

entries.title: Nob
entries.summary: A town of priests near Jerusalem. David came here running from Saul, and the priest Ahimelech gave him the consecrated bread and Goliath's sword. Saul had the priests of Nob killed for it.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Nob was a city of priests near Jerusalem where the tabernacle stood during part of Samuel and Saul's era. David, fleeing from Saul, came to the priest Ahimelech there and received the consecrated bread and Goliath's sword, an act Saul's informant Doeg the Edomite reported back to the king (1 Samuel 21:1-9). In retaliation, Saul had Doeg slaughter Nob's entire priestly population, eighty-five priests along with the town's other inhabitants, one of the darkest episodes of his reign (1 Samuel 22:9-19). Isaiah later references Nob's proximity to Jerusalem in his description of an invading army's approach (Isaiah 10:32).

entries.title: Nobah (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: He took the Amorite town of Kenath east of the Jordan and renamed it after himself, and the town turns up again as a landmark on Gideon's route.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Nobah was the name a Manassite warrior gave to the Amorite town of Kenath after he captured it during Israel's advance east of the Jordan (Num. 32:42). The renamed town reappears as a landmark on the route Gideon took while pursuing the Midianite kings Zebah and Zalmunna (Judg. 8:11), suggesting the new name endured at least into the period of the judges.

entries.title: Nod (Near Eden)
entries.summary: It lay east of Eden, and Cain went there after he killed Abel. Nod means wandering, which fits the sentence God had just passed on him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Nod, "wandering," was the land east of Eden where Cain settled after murdering his brother Abel and being driven from the ground he had farmed (Genesis 4:16). The name plays on the sentence God had just pronounced over him, that he would be "a fugitive and a wanderer" for the rest of his life (Genesis 4:12). No geographic identification is intended or possible; the name functions as commentary on Cain's condition rather than a real place on any map.

witness.excerpt: And when Cain had travelled over many countries, he, with his wife, built a city, named Nod: which is a place so called: and there he settled his abode: where also he had children.

entries.title: Nodab (Arabian living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: A tribal group, not a single man, descended from Ishmael. Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh went to war against them, according to 1 Chronicles 5:19.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Nodab is not an individual but the name of a tribal group descended from Ishmael, listed in 1 Chronicles 5:19 among the peoples the trans-Jordanic tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh went to war against, along with Jetur and Naphish. The Ishmaelite tribes named there correspond broadly to Arab groups listed in Genesis 25:15. No further information about this particular clan survives outside this one battle notice.

entries.title: Nogah (David's son living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Born to David in Jerusalem after he became king there. He is on two lists of David's sons and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Nogah was one of David's sons born in Jerusalem after David became king there, listed among his children by unnamed wives (1 Chronicles 3:7; 14:6).

entries.title: Nohah (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Listed as Benjamin's fourth son in 1 Chronicles 8:2, though the lists in Genesis and Numbers do not have him. Nothing more is known.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The fourth son of Benjamin listed in the tribal genealogies of 1 Chronicles 8:2. He does not appear in the earlier lists of Benjamin's sons in Genesis or Numbers, and nothing further is recorded about him.

entries.title: Non (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Joshua's father, of the tribe of Ephraim, more usually spelled Nun and hardly ever seen outside the phrase "Joshua son of Nun."
entries.books: Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 1 Kings, 1 Chronicles, Nehemiah
entries.label: 8 books
entries.dictNote: Non, more commonly spelled Nun, was Joshua's father, from the tribe of Ephraim, and appears in the Bible almost exclusively in the recurring phrase Joshua son of Nun.

entries.title: Noph (Memphis)
entries.summary: Memphis, under its Hebrew name, which several prophets use when they speak of Egypt's coming judgment.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Noph is the Hebrew name for the Egyptian city of Memphis, mentioned by several prophets as a city that would share in Egypt's coming judgment.

entries.title: Nophah (Kenath)
entries.summary: An old victory song in Numbers 21:27-30 celebrates the Amorite king Sihon taking Moabite land, and Nophah is one of the towns it names. Israel then defeated Sihon.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Moabite town captured by the Amorite king Sihon and mentioned in an ancient victory song quoted in Numbers 21:27-30, celebrating Sihon's conquest of Moabite territory before Israel in turn defeated Sihon.

entries.title: Nymphas (Woman living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: A church met in this believer's house, probably in or near Laodicea, and Paul sends greetings in Colossians 4:15. The manuscripts disagree on whether the name is Nymphas, a man, or Nympha, a woman.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A believer, probably in or near Laodicea, whose house served as a meeting place for a local church, greeted by Paul in Colossians 4:15. Ancient manuscripts differ on whether the name is masculine, Nymphas, or feminine, Nympha, a point still debated by textual critics.

entries.title: Obadiah (Levite living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of 12 men called Obadiah. This one is a Levite from the exile and the return, named twice in 1 Chronicles and Nehemiah.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Obadiah (Levite living at the time of Exile and Return)

entries.title: Obadiah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Ahab's palace manager, a man who feared the Lord. While Jezebel was killing the prophets he hid a hundred of them in caves and kept them fed. When the drought was at its worst he was out searching for grass for the king's horses and mules.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Obadiah's short prophetic book, the shortest in the Old Testament, is directed entirely against Edom for gloating over and looting Jerusalem's destruction instead of helping their relative nation Israel, despite Edom's own descent from Esau, Jacob's brother. Almost nothing is known about Obadiah himself, and the name was common enough that at least a dozen other men in the Old Testament share it, including a righteous official under Ahab who hid a hundred prophets from Jezebel's persecution.

entries.title: Obal (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: First Chronicles spells him Ebal, but in Genesis 10:28 he is Obal, one of the thirteen sons of Joktan.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Obal was a son of Joktan listed in the Table of Nations in Genesis 10:28, one of thirteen sons whose descendants populated Arabia. The parallel genealogy in 1 Chronicles 1:22 gives his name as Ebal. Like his brothers, he represents an Arabian tribal group rather than being remembered for any individual deed.

entries.title: Obed (Levite living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A levite from the divided-kingdom years, and 1 Chronicles is the only book that names him.

entries.title: Obed (Man living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: Boaz and Ruth's son, and Naomi helped raise him. He was David's grandfather, which puts Ruth's story inside the royal line.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Obed was the son of Boaz and Ruth, and his birth restored hope and lineage to Naomi, who helped raise him; he became the grandfather of David, making Ruth's story a direct link in the ancestry that leads to both David and, through Matthew's genealogy, Jesus.

entries.title: Obed (Warrior living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 5 men called Obed. This one is a warrior from the divided-kingdom years, named once in 1 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Obed-edom (Singer living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: After Uzzah died, David would not take the ark any further and left it in Obed-edom's house for three months. It brought blessing on his whole household, and that was what got David moving again.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Obed-edom was a Levite in whose house the ark of the covenant stayed for three months after Uzzah's death, and rather than bringing disaster the way it had for the Philistines, the ark brought blessing to Obed-edom's entire household, encouraging David to finally bring it the rest of the way to Jerusalem.

entries.title: Obil (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: An Ishmaelite in charge of King David's camels, one of the officials over the royal herds and estates in 1 Chronicles 27:30.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: An Ishmaelite appointed over King David's camels, one of several officials named in 1 Chronicles 27:30 who managed the royal herds and estates.

entries.title: Oboth
entries.summary: Israel camped at Oboth after the bronze serpent. Where exactly it sat along the route is not known.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Oboth was a wilderness campsite of the Israelites, the first stop after they left the site where Moses raised the bronze serpent to heal those bitten by venomous snakes (Numbers 21:9-10; 33:43-44). Its precise location along the route east of Edom is unknown.

entries.title: Ocran (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Father of the man who led Asher in the wilderness census, and that is the whole of him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Ocran was the father of the tribal leader of Asher during the wilderness census.

entries.title: Oded (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: His son Azariah was the prophet who encouraged King Asa's reforms. Oded himself is only ever a father's name in 2 Chronicles 15.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Oded was the father of the prophet Azariah, who encouraged King Asa's religious reforms, and a different Oded was a prophet who successfully persuaded northern Israel's army to release Judean captives taken in battle rather than enslave them.

entries.title: Oded (Prophet living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 2 Chronicles names him once, and he is a prophet from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Og (King living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: King of Bashan and, in Deuteronomy, the last of the Rephaim, with a bed over thirteen feet long. Israel beat him and took his whole kingdom.
entries.books: Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, 1 Kings, Nehemiah, Psalm
entries.label: 6 books
entries.dictNote: Og was the king of Bashan, remembered in Deuteronomy as the last of the Rephaim, a race of giants, with a bed reportedly over thirteen feet long. Israel defeated him and took his entire kingdom without losing a man, and his conquest became a standing example, repeated throughout the Old Testament, of God's power to defeat overwhelming odds.

entries.title: Ohad (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: The third son of Simeon, one of Jacob's family who went down into Egypt. He is missing from the Simeonite clan lists in Numbers 26, so his line may have died out or been folded into another clan.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Ohad was the third son of Simeon who went down to Egypt with Jacob's family (Genesis 46:10). He does not reappear in the later Simeonite clan lists in Numbers 26, so his line may have died out or been absorbed into another clan. Nothing else is known of him.

and Jachin, and Zohar, and Shaul, the son of the Zephathite  woman--seven.

entries.title: Ohel (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of Zerubbabel's sons, in the list at 1 Chronicles 3:20, and nothing further.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Ohel was one of the sons of Zerubbabel, the governor who led the returning exiles and rebuilt the Jerusalem temple, listed among his children in 1 Chronicles 3:20. Nothing further is recorded about him.

entries.title: Olivet (Mount of Olives)
entries.summary: The ridge east of Jerusalem. Jesus taught his disciples there about what was coming, and he wept over the city from it. Gethsemane sits at its foot, and Luke and Acts put the ascension here too.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Olivet, or the Mount of Olives, is the ridge east of Jerusalem where Jesus taught his disciples privately about the future, wept over the city, prayed the night of his arrest in the garden of Gethsemane at its base, and ascended into heaven after his resurrection.

entries.title: Olympas (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Paul greets him by name at the end of Romans, a Christian in Rome about whom nothing more is known.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Olympas was a Christian in Rome whom Paul greets by name at the close of his letter to the Romans (Romans 16:15). Nothing further is known about him.

entries.title: Omar (Edomite living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Esau's grandson and an Edomite clan chief, listed in the genealogies of Genesis 36.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Omar was a grandson of Esau and an Edomite clan chief listed in Genesis's genealogies.

entries.title: Omega (Name of a letter)
entries.summary: Last letter of the Greek alphabet, paired with Alpha. Revelation puts the pair in God's own mouth, three times over.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Omega is the final letter of the Greek alphabet, paired with Alpha, the first letter, in the divine self-description “I am Alpha and Omega,” found three times in Revelation (1:8; 21:6; 22:13). The phrase functions as a title, not a name, declaring God, and in 22:13 Christ, as the beginning and end of all things, encompassing everything in between. The imagery draws on a common ancient rhetorical device of using the first and last letters of an alphabet to signify totality.

entries.title: Omri (King living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: An army commander who took the northern throne after a civil war. He founded a dynasty. Assyrian records went on calling Israel the House of Omri long after he was dead.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Omri was a military commander who seized the throne of northern Israel after a civil war and founded a dynasty significant enough that Assyrian records refer to Israel as the House of Omri for generations after his death, even though the Bible itself gives his reign only a brief summary, noting mainly that he built the city of Samaria as his new capital and did more evil than all who were before him.

entries.title: Omri (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Omri (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the wilderness years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Omri (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of 4 men called Omri. This one is a man from the exile and the return, named once in 1 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: On
entries.summary: Joseph's wife Asenath was the daughter of Potipherah, priest of On. The city stood on the east bank of the Nile near modern Cairo and was the center of Egyptian sun worship, which is why the Greeks called it Heliopolis.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: On was a major Egyptian city on the east bank of the Nile near modern Cairo, the center of Egyptian sun worship and known to the Greeks as Heliopolis. Joseph married Asenath, daughter of Potipherah, priest of On (Genesis 41:45, 50; 46:20), tying Egypt's highest religious office to Joseph's own household. A granite obelisk raised by the pharaoh Senusret I still stands at the site today, the oldest standing obelisk in Egypt and one of the few visible remains of the ancient temple complex.

entries.title: On (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: He joined Dathan and Abiram in their rebellion against Moses and Aaron, and then vanishes from the story after one verse. A Reubenite, son of Peleth.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Reubenite, son of Peleth, named as one of the men who joined Dathan and Abiram in the rebellion against Moses and Aaron (Numbers 16:1). He disappears from the story immediately after this verse; Jewish tradition holds that his wife talked him out of taking part before judgment fell on the rest of the conspirators, though the biblical text itself says nothing more about him.

entries.title: Onam (Edomite living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: A Horite clan name in Edom's genealogies, listed in Genesis 36:23 and again in 1 Chronicles 1:40.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Onam was a Horite clan name in Edom's genealogies and also the name of a descendant of Judah through Jerahmeel's line.

entries.title: Onam (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him twice, and he is a man from the united kingdom.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Onan (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Judah's second son. Custom required him to father a child for his dead brother through the widow Tamar. He made sure it never happened, and God put him to death for it.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Onan was Judah's second son, and when custom required him to father a child with his deceased brother's widow Tamar to preserve his brother's line, he deliberately avoided completing the act, a refusal God put him to death for.
