entries.title: Onesimus (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: A runaway slave who ended up with Paul in prison and became a Christian there. Paul sent him back to his owner. The letter to Philemon is Paul's request that Philemon take him in as a brother.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Onesimus was a runaway slave who ended up with Paul during one of Paul's imprisonments and became a Christian there, and Paul sent him back to his owner Philemon along with a personal letter, tactfully asking Philemon to receive Onesimus back not as a slave but as a beloved brother.

entries.title: Onespiphorus (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: The spelling is a slip in the source data for Onesiphorus. He was a believer from Ephesus who went looking for Paul in his Roman imprisonment and looked after him without being ashamed of the chains.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The name here is a misspelling of Onesiphorus in the source data; the person intended is Onesiphorus, a believer from Ephesus who sought Paul out and ministered to him during Paul's Roman imprisonment, unashamed of his chains (2 Timothy 1:16-18). Paul later sends greetings to Onesiphorus's household and recalls his service at Ephesus (2 Timothy 4:19).

entries.title: Ono
entries.summary: Nehemiah's enemies Sanballat and Tobiah asked him four times to come down and meet them in the plain of Ono, and he would not go. The town belonged to Benjamin, in a fertile plain northwest of Jerusalem, and returning exiles settled it again.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Ono was a town of Benjamin in a fertile plain northwest of Jerusalem, resettled by returning exiles (Ezra 2:33; Nehemiah 11:35). Nehemiah's enemies Sanballat and Tobiah tried four times to lure him to a meeting in the plain of Ono, intending to harm him while he rebuilt Jerusalem's walls, but he refused each invitation (Nehemiah 6:2-4).

entries.title: Ophel
entries.summary: Temple servants lived on the Ophel, the fortified stretch of Jerusalem between the temple mount and the city of David, while Nehemiah was rebuilding the wall.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: The Ophel was a fortified section of Jerusalem between the temple mount and the city of David, and Nehemiah records temple servants living there during the wall-rebuilding project.

entries.title: Ophir
entries.summary: It was the gold that made Ophir famous across the ancient world. Solomon's ships, sailing with Hiram of Tyre, brought it back in quantity, and the place itself was likely in southern Arabia or along the Red Sea.
entries.books: 1 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Job, Psalm, Isaiah
entries.label: 6 books
entries.dictNote: Ophir was a region, likely in southern Arabia or along the Red Sea, famed throughout the ancient world for its fine gold. Solomon's ships, sailing in partnership with Hiram of Tyre, brought back large quantities of gold, precious stones, and rare wood from Ophir, and later biblical poetry uses "gold of Ophir" as shorthand for the finest wealth imaginable. The name also belonged to a son of Joktan in the table of nations, likely the ancestor of a people associated with the region.

witness.excerpt: Now Joctan, one of the sons of Heber, had these sons, Elmodad, Saleph, Asermoth, Jera, Adoram, Aizel, Decla, Ebal, Abimael, Sabeus, Ophir, Euilat, and Jobab.

; for he sent a sufficient number of men thither for pilots, and such as were skillful in navigation, to whom Solomon gave this command: That they should go along with his own stewards to the land that was of old called Ophir, but now the Aurea Chersonesus, which belongs to India, to fetch him gold.

entries.title: Ophir (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Genesis and 1 Chronicles name him twice, and he is a man from the patriarchs.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Ophni
entries.summary: A town given to Benjamin, listed in Joshua 18:24 with Geba and other places north of Jerusalem. Its site is uncertain.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Ophni is not actually a clan or people group but a town allotted to the tribe of Benjamin, listed in Joshua 18:24 alongside Geba and other Benjaminite settlements north of Jerusalem. Its exact site is uncertain, though some identify it with the later village of Gophna mentioned by Josephus.

entries.title: Ophrah
entries.summary: Gideon's hometown. The angel of the Lord first appeared to him there, and later he set up a golden ephod in the same place, which Israel ended up worshipping.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Ophrah was Gideon's hometown, where the angel of the Lord first appeared to him and where he later set up a golden ephod that became, ironically, an object of idolatrous worship for Israel.

witness.excerpt: And when Gideon was come to his own countrey of Ophrah, he slew the Kings of the Midianites.

entries.title: Ophrah
entries.summary: Named twice, in Joshua and 1 Samuel, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Ophrah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 3 men called Ophrah. This one is a man from the divided-kingdom years, named once in 1 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Oreb (Man living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: He was one of two Midianite commanders the men of Ephraim killed during Gideon's rout, and the rock where he died took his name.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Oreb was one of two Midianite commanders killed by the men of Ephraim during Gideon's rout of the Midianite army, and the rock where he died was afterward named for him.

entries.title: Oren (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: In the genealogy of Judah he is one of Jerahmeel's sons (1 Chronicles 2:25). Nothing further is known about him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Oren was one of the sons of Jerahmeel, listed in the genealogy of Judah in 1 Chronicles 2:25. Nothing further is known about him.

entries.title: Ornan (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: The Jebusite who owned the threshing floor David bought to build an altar and stop the plague, the ground where Solomon's temple later stood. Ornan offered it for nothing, and David insisted on paying. He is also called Araunah.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Ornan, also called Araunah, was the Jebusite who owned the threshing floor David purchased to build an altar and stop a plague, a site that later became the location of Solomon's temple. Ornan offered to give David the land for free, but David insisted on paying full price, unwilling to offer God a sacrifice that cost him nothing.

entries.title: Orpah (Woman living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: She was Ruth's sister-in-law, a Moabite married to Naomi's son Chilion. When Naomi headed back to Bethlehem, Orpah wept, kissed her, and stayed in Moab.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Orpah was a Moabite woman married to Chilion, one of Naomi's sons, and sister-in-law to Ruth. When Naomi decided to return to Bethlehem after her husband and sons died, Orpah wept and, after Naomi's urging, chose to stay in Moab with her own people, unlike Ruth who famously clung to Naomi (Ruth 1:4-14).

entries.title: Osee (Prophet living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Paul quotes Hosea in Romans 9:25, God calling a people not his own "my people," and the King James renders the prophet's name Osee, from the Greek.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Osee is the Greek form of the prophet Hosea's name as it appears in the King James rendering of Romans 9:25, where Paul quotes Hosea's prophecy that God would call a people not his own "my people." The reference points to the same eighth-century BC prophet known from the book of Hosea, not a separate individual.

entries.title: Othni (Levite living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A gatekeeper's son. His father was Shemaiah, and the family kept the temple gates in David's reign.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Son of Shemaiah, a temple gatekeeper of notable ability during David's reign (1 Chronicles 26:6-7).

entries.title: Othniel (Judge living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: Caleb's younger relative, who won Caleb's daughter Achsah by taking a Canaanite city. He became Israel's first judge and broke eight years of oppression under a Mesopotamian king.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Othniel was Caleb's younger relative, who won Caleb's daughter Achsah in marriage by capturing a Canaanite city, and he later became Israel's first judge, delivering the nation from eight years of oppression under a Mesopotamian king.

witness.excerpt: When Othniel was dead, the affairs of the Israelites fell again into disorder: and while they neither payed to God the honour due to him; nor were obedient to the laws, their afflictions increased: till Eglon, King of the Moabites,

entries.title: Ozem (David's brother living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: David's older brother, the sixth of Jesse's sons (1 Chronicles 2:15).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ozem (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: A son of Jerahmeel in Judah's genealogy, named once.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Two men carry this name. One was David's older brother, the sixth of Jesse's sons (1 Chronicles 2:15). The other belonged to a different branch of Judah's genealogy, a son of Jerahmeel (1 Chronicles 2:25).

entries.title: Ozias (King living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Matthew's spelling of Uzziah in the genealogy of Jesus, son of Joram.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Ozias is the Greek New Testament spelling of Uzziah, used in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:8-9), where he is listed as the son of Joram and ancestor of Christ. In the Old Testament, Uzziah reigned as king of Judah for over fifty years and was struck with leprosy after presumptuously burning incense in the temple, a priestly duty reserved for Aaron's line.

entries.title: Ozni (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: He was a son of Gad, and the Oznite clan counted in the wilderness census came from him. Genesis 46:16 calls him Ezbon.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A son of Gad and ancestor of the Oznite clan counted in the wilderness census (Numbers 26:16). The earlier genealogy in Genesis 46:16 gives his name as Ezbon.

entries.title: Paarai (Warrior living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of David's thirty, Paarai the Arbite. The parallel roster in Chronicles has Naarai son of Ezbai, one of several small spelling differences between the two lists.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Paarai the Arbite was one of David's thirty mighty men, listed among the elite warriors in 2 Samuel 23:35. The parallel roster in 1 Chronicles 11:37 gives his name as Naarai son of Ezbai, one of several small spelling differences between the two lists of David's champions. Beyond his inclusion in this honor roll, nothing further is recorded about him.

entries.title: Padan (Paddan-aram)
entries.summary: Short for Paddan-aram, the country around Haran in upper Mesopotamia where Abraham's brother Nahor settled. Rebekah came from there. Jacob ran there years later to get away from Esau.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Padan is a shortened form of Paddan-aram, the region of upper Mesopotamia around Haran where Abraham's brother Nahor settled. It was from Paddan-aram that Isaac's wife Rebekah came, and Jacob fled there to escape Esau's anger, working for his uncle Laban and marrying Leah and Rachel before returning to Canaan with his large family.

entries.title: Padon (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: His family were Nethinim, temple servants who came back from Babylon with Zerubbabel, and nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Padon headed a family of Nethinim, temple servants whose descendants returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:44; Nehemiah 7:47). Nothing further is recorded about him.

entries.title: Pagiel (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: He led Asher during the wilderness census, one of the twelve who stood with Moses for their tribes.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Pagiel was the tribal leader of Asher during the wilderness census, one of twelve representatives appointed to assist Moses.

entries.title: Pahathmoab (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A big family among the returning exiles, big enough that Ezra and Nehemiah both list it house by house.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Pahath-moab was the name of a prominent family among the returning exiles, large enough to be listed by household in both Ezra and Nehemiah's records.

entries.title: Pahathmoab (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of 3 men called Pahathmoab. This one is a man from the exile and the return, named once in Nehemiah.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Pahathmoab (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Nehemiah names him once, and he is a man from the exile and the return.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Pai (Pau)
entries.summary: Hadar, last of Edom's early kings in the Genesis list, ruled from Pai, also spelled Pau, and nobody knows where in Edom it stood.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Pai, also spelled Pau, was the royal city of Hadar, also called Hadad, the last king listed in the genealogy of Edom's early rulers before Israel had a monarchy of its own (Gen. 36:39; 1 Chr. 1:50). Its location within Edom is not otherwise specified in the text and has not been identified.

entries.title: Palal (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Son of Uzai. When Nehemiah rebuilt the wall of Jerusalem, Palal took the section opposite the corner and the tower that stuck out from the upper palace, by the court of the guard.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A son of Uzai who helped repair the wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah, rebuilding the section opposite the corner and the tower projecting from the upper palace near the court of the guard (Nehemiah 3:25). He is one of dozens of otherwise unknown Jerusalemites Nehemiah names by the stretch of wall each repaired.

entries.title: Palestina (Philistia)
entries.summary: The King James word for Philistia, the Philistines' strip of coast along the Mediterranean.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Palestina is the King James rendering of the Hebrew word for Philistia, the coastal territory of the Philistines along the southeastern Mediterranean. The term became attached to the wider region over the following centuries and is the ultimate source of the modern name Palestine, though in its Old Testament occurrences it refers specifically to Philistine land, which the prophets warn will share in judgment alongside Israel's other neighbors.

entries.title: Pallu (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Reuben's son. His descendants, the Palluites, were one of the clans counted in the wilderness.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Pallu was a son of Reuben, and his descendants, the Palluites, are listed among the clans counted in Israel's wilderness census.

witness.excerpt: 12.  Reuben, the first-born of Israel; and these are the names of his sons: Enoch, and Pallu, and Hezron and Carmi--five.  13.

entries.title: Palluites (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Pallu's descendants, a clan of Reuben counted in the wilderness census, and listed once.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Palluites were the clan descended from Pallu, a son of Reuben, counted in Israel's wilderness census.

entries.title: Palti (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: When Moses sent twelve spies into Canaan, Palti went for Benjamin (Numbers 13:9).
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Palti was one of the twelve spies Moses sent into Canaan, representing the tribe of Benjamin (Numbers 13:9). A different man named Palti, son of Laish, was the husband Saul gave Michal after David fled the court; when David later reclaimed her as his wife, Palti followed her weeping until Abner ordered him back home (1 Samuel 25:44; 2 Samuel 3:14-16).

entries.title: Palti (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Samuel names him once, and he is a man from the united kingdom.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Paltiel (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Two men. One was the leader from Issachar picked to help divide the land among the tribes. The other, son of Laish, was given Michal by King Saul after David fled, and he lost her again when David took her back.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Two men named Paltiel appear in the Old Testament: the prince of the tribe of Issachar appointed to help divide the promised land among the tribes (Numbers 34:26), and Paltiel son of Laish, to whom King Saul gave his daughter Michal after taking her from David; when Abner later returned Michal to David, Paltiel followed her weeping until Abner ordered him home (2 Samuel 3:15-16). The two references belong to entirely different periods and are unrelated apart from the shared name, also written “Palti” in 1 Samuel 25:44.

entries.title: Paltite (Warriors, perhaps from Pelon or Palet)
entries.summary: Helez, one of David's thirty, carries this label, which ties him to Beth-pelet in Judah's Negev. Chronicles calls him the Pelonite.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Paltite identifies Helez, one of David's thirty mighty men, as being from Beth-pelet in Judah's Negev. The parallel list in Chronicles calls him the Pelonite instead, likely a variant spelling of the same epithet.

entries.title: Pamphylia
entries.summary: Jews from Pamphylia were in Jerusalem at Pentecost. The province lay on the south coast of Asia Minor between Lycia and Cilicia. Paul and Barnabas came ashore at its capital, Perga.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Pamphylia was a coastal province of southern Asia Minor between Lycia and Cilicia; Jews from Pamphylia were present in Jerusalem at Pentecost (Acts 2:10), and Paul and Barnabas landed at its capital, Perga, at the start of their inland journey through Asia Minor (Acts 13:13). It was here that John Mark left the mission and turned back to Jerusalem, a decision that later caused Paul and Barnabas to part ways (Acts 15:38).

witness.excerpt: But as he was in peril about Pamphylia, and obliged to cast out the greatest part of the ship's lading, he with difficulty got safe to Rhodes, a place which had been grievously harassed in the war with Cassius.

So he set sail from thence to Pamphylia, and falling into a violent storm, he had much ado to escape to Rhodes, with the loss of the ship's burden; and there it was that two of his friends, Sappinas and Ptolemeus, met with him; and as he found that city very

There is a mountain called Climax, adjoins to the Sea of Pamphylia, leaving a narrow passage on the shore, which, in calm weather, is bare, so as to be passable by travelers, but when the sea overflows, it is covered to a great degree by the waves.
So he marched over Lydia, and subdued Ionia, and over-ran Caria, and fell upon the places of Pamphylia: as has been related elsewhere.

entries.title: Pannag
entries.summary: A trade good Judah and Israel sold to Tyre, listed with wheat and honey. What it actually was, nobody knows.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Pannag is not a person but a term for a trade commodity listed among the goods Judah and Israel exchanged with Tyre in Ezekiel's oracle against that city (Ezekiel 27:17), alongside wheat, honey, oil, and balm. Its exact meaning is uncertain: some take it as a type of confection or pastry, others as the name of a place whose products carried that name, similar to how other goods in the list are identified by their region of origin. The word appears only this once in the Hebrew Bible, which is part of why its meaning remains disputed.

entries.title: Paphos
entries.summary: The Roman capital of Cyprus, where the governor lived. On their first journey Paul and Barnabas came here and faced down the sorcerer Elymas in front of the proconsul Sergius Paulus.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Paphos was the Roman capital of Cyprus and residence of its governor when Paul and Barnabas visited during their first missionary journey and confronted the sorcerer Elymas before the proconsul Sergius Paulus (Acts 13:6-13). An inscription found on Cyprus names a proconsul Paulus in office around the same period Luke describes, corroborating the office and roughly the timeframe Acts assigns to Sergius Paulus's governorship.

entries.title: Parah
entries.summary: It means heifer. A town in Benjamin's lot, commonly placed at the ruins of Ain Fara, about six miles northeast of Jerusalem.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Parah, meaning heifer, was a town allotted to the tribe of Benjamin (Josh. 18:23). It is commonly identified with the ruins at Ain Fara, about six miles northeast of Jerusalem in the Wadi Qelt watershed, a spring-fed site still bearing a version of the ancient name.

entries.title: Paran
entries.summary: Ishmael grew up in this wilderness after Hagar was sent away with him, and Israel camped there for part of the long march.
entries.books: Genesis, Numbers, Deuteronomy, 1 Samuel, 1 Kings, Habakkuk
entries.label: 6 books
entries.dictNote: Paran was a wilderness region in the Sinai peninsula where Israel camped during part of their wilderness wandering, and where Ishmael later settled and grew up after being sent away with Hagar.

witness.excerpt: When Moses had led the Hebrews away from thence to a place called Paran , which was near to the borders of the Canaanites, and a place difficult to be continued in, he gathered the multitude together to a congregation: and standing in the midst of them, he said, “Of the two things that God
And Ishmael and his sons, and the sons of Keturah and their sons, went together and dwelt from Paran to the entering in of Babylon in all the land which is towards the East facing the desert.
And she  opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water, and she went and filled her bottle with water, and she gave her child to drink, and she arose and went towards the wilderness of Paran.

entries.title: Parbar
entries.summary: It is a place on the temple grounds, not a person, on the west side, probably a colonnade or open court. Gatekeepers were posted there.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Parbar is not a person but a structure or precinct on the west side of the temple complex, apparently a colonnade or open court, mentioned in connection with gatekeepers assigned there (1 Chronicles 26:18) and possibly the same area where wicked King Manasseh had placed horses dedicated to the sun (2 Kings 23:11).

entries.title: Parmasta (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Haman had ten sons, and Parmashta was one of them, killed by the Jews of Susa on the day set for their own destruction.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Parmashta was one of the ten sons of Haman killed by the Jews of Susa in self-defense on the day appointed for their destruction (Esther 9:9).

entries.title: Parmenas (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Another of the seven picked by the Jerusalem church to oversee the daily food for widows, so the apostles could keep to prayer and preaching (Acts 6:5).
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of the seven men chosen by the Jerusalem church to oversee the daily distribution of food to widows, freeing the apostles to focus on prayer and preaching (Acts 6:5).

entries.title: Parnach (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Elizaphan led Zebulun when the land of Canaan was being divided, and Parnach was his father, named only to identify the son.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Parnach was the father of Elizaphan, the leader from the tribe of Zebulun appointed to help divide the land of Canaan among the tribes (Numbers 34:25). He is mentioned only to identify his son.

entries.title: Parosh (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: The family of Parosh heads the list of lay families who came back from exile. A large house, and Ezra puts it first.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Parosh was the head of a large family among the returning exiles, prominent enough to be listed first among the lay families in Ezra's genealogical record.

entries.title: Parosh (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Ezra names him once, and he is a man from the exile and the return.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Parosh (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A man from the exile and the return, and Nehemiah is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Parosh (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of 4 men called Parosh. This one is a man from the exile and the return, named once in Nehemiah.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Parshandatha (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Haman's eldest son. He died with his nine brothers when the Jews of Susa defended themselves against the slaughter Haman had planned.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The eldest of Haman's ten sons, killed by the Jews of Susa along with his brothers when they defended themselves against the pogrom Haman had planned (Esther 9:7-10).

entries.title: Parthian (People living in Parthia)
entries.summary: At Pentecost the crowd in Jerusalem is listed nation by nation, and Parthians come first. These were Jews of the dispersion from the Parthian empire, Rome's great rival in the east, centered on Persia and Mesopotamia.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Parthians were Jews of the diaspora living within the Parthian empire, Rome's great eastern rival centered in Persia and Mesopotamia, and they are named first among the many nationalities gathered in Jerusalem to hear the apostles speak in their own languages at Pentecost.

witness.excerpt: But the Parthian King was provoked at this his behaviour; and denounced war immediately against Izates.

83, that Arsaces, who raised the Parthian empire, was of the :seed of Abraham by Chetura; and that thereby was accomplished that prediction which said, \"Kings of nations shall proceed from thee,\" Genesis 17:6.
He also sent away in a friendly manner Mithridates and Orsanes, who were Parthian deserters, and came to him, though the report went abroad that they had run away from him.
Upon this the senate was irritated; and Antony informed them further, that it was for their advantage in the Parthian war that Herod should be king.

These reasons greatly moved the senate; at which juncture Antony came in, and told them that it was for their advantage in the Parthian war that Herod should be king; so they all gave their votes for it.

entries.title: Paruah (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Father of Jehoshaphat, Solomon's district officer over Issachar.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Paruah was the father of Jehoshaphat, one of the twelve officers Solomon appointed over Israel's administrative districts to supply provisions for the royal court, with Jehoshaphat's district covering Issachar (1 Kings 4:17). He is mentioned only to identify his son.

entries.title: Parvaim
entries.summary: Solomon got gold from Parvaim to overlay the temple, and nobody is sure where that was. Guesses run from Arabia to India. Some think the word just means the east.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A region of uncertain location from which Solomon obtained gold for overlaying the temple (2 Chronicles 3:6). Suggested locations range from Arabia to India, and some scholars think the word may simply be a general term for "eastern lands" rather than a specific place name, similar to the uncertainty surrounding the gold-source Ophir elsewhere in the Old Testament.

entries.title: Pas-dammim (Ephes-dammim)
entries.summary: Eleazar son of Dodo held his ground here. It lay between Socoh and Azekah in the Valley of Elah, the same country where David killed Goliath. First Samuel calls it Ephes-dammim.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Pas-dammim, called Ephes-dammim in 1 Samuel 17:1, lay between Socoh and Azekah in the Valley of Elah, the same district where David killed Goliath. In 1 Chronicles 11:13 it is the site where Eleazar son of Dodo held his ground against the Philistines when the rest of Israel's army fled, one of the feats that earned him a place among David's three mightiest warriors.

entries.title: Pasach (Man living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: A son of Japhlet, in Asher's genealogy (1 Chronicles 7:33), and nothing more.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A son of Japhlet in the tribal genealogy of Asher (1 Chronicles 7:33). Nothing else is recorded about him.

entries.title: Paseah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Paseah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: He headed one of the families of temple servants who came back from exile.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Paseah was the head of a family among the temple servants who returned from Babylonian exile.

entries.title: Paseah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of 3 men called Paseah. This one is a man from the exile and the return, named once in Nehemiah.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Pashur (Levite living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: His name heads a family that came back from exile, counted in Ezra 2:38 and Nehemiah 7:41. He is not the temple official who had Jeremiah beaten; that man has his own entry.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Pashur was a temple official who had the prophet Jeremiah beaten and put in stocks overnight for his prophecies of coming judgment, and Jeremiah responded the next day by renaming him Magor-missabib, meaning terror on every side, and predicting Pashur would die in exile in Babylon.

entries.title: Pashur (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: He had Jeremiah beaten and locked in the stocks overnight for prophesying judgment. In the morning Jeremiah gave him a new name, Magor-missabib, terror on every side.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Pashur (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 4 men called Pashur. This one is a man from the divided-kingdom years, named twice in Jeremiah.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Pashur (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A man from the exile and the return, and Nehemiah is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Patara
entries.summary: It was a port on the Lycian coast of southwestern Asia Minor. Paul changed ships there on the way home from his third journey, taking a larger one across open water to Phoenicia.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Patara was a major port city on the Lycian coast of southwestern Asia Minor where Paul changed ships on his way back from his third missionary journey, boarding a larger vessel bound across the open sea for Phoenicia (Acts 21:1). Excavations at the site have uncovered an extensive Roman city, including a lighthouse built under Nero in the first century AD, among the oldest lighthouses known from the ancient world.

entries.title: Pathros
entries.summary: Upper Egypt. Jewish refugees fled there, and the prophets name it among the places God promised to gather his scattered people back from.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Pathros refers to Upper Egypt, and the prophets mention it as one of the regions Jewish refugees fled to and where God promised a future regathering of his exiled people.

entries.title: Pathrusim (People, perhaps from Pathrus)
entries.summary: Descendants of Mizraim, named after Pathros, the country along the Nile south of Memphis.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Pathrusim were a people descended from Mizraim named for Pathros, the region of Upper Egypt along the Nile south of Memphis. Later prophets name Pathros among the places Israelites were scattered to, and where God promises to eventually regather his exiled people.

entries.title: Patmos
entries.summary: John was on Patmos, a small rocky island in the Aegean off Asia Minor, when he saw the visions in Revelation.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A small, rocky island in the Aegean Sea, part of the Sporades group off the coast of Asia Minor, where the apostle John was in exile when he received the visions recorded in the book of Revelation (Revelation 1:9). Roman authorities used islands like Patmos as places of banishment, and John says he was there "for the word of God and for the testimony of Jesus Christ." The island still bears the name Patmos today, and a cave traditionally associated with John's vision remains a pilgrimage site.

entries.title: Patrobas (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: He is greeted in Rome along with Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes and Hermas. Nothing further about him is recorded.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Christian in Rome to whom Paul sends greetings, grouped with Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, and Hermas near the close of his letter to the Romans (Rom. 16:14). Nothing further about him is recorded.

entries.title: Paul (Apostle living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Born Saul, a Jew of the tribe of Benjamin and a Roman citizen from Tarsus. He trained as a Pharisee under Gamaliel and hunted the early church. Then the risen Christ met him in a blinding vision.
entries.books: Acts, Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, 1 Thessalonians, 2 Thessalonians, 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, Titus, Philemon, 2 Peter
entries.label: 15 books
entries.dictNote: Paul was born Saul, a Jew of the tribe of Benjamin and a Roman citizen from Tarsus, trained as a Pharisee under the respected teacher Gamaliel and an active persecutor of the early church until a blinding vision of the risen Christ on the road to Damascus turned him into its most influential missionary. He planted churches across the eastern Mediterranean on three long journeys, wrote roughly half the New Testament in letters to those churches, and was eventually imprisoned and executed in Rome. A Roman inscription found at Delphi naming the proconsul Gallio fixes the date of Paul's time in Corinth precisely enough that it anchors the chronology of his entire ministry.

witness.excerpt: Paul had said either by word of mouth, or by an epistle, or by both, that the day of Christ ἐνέστηκε was immediately at hand .
There was one of the tribe of Benjamin, a man of a good family, and of a virtuous disposition; his name was Kish. He had a son… They called him Saul.

entries.title: Paul (Apostle living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: A man from the New Testament. Acts names him 5 times.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Pavement (Gabbatha)
entries.summary: A raised stone platform outside Pilate's headquarters in Jerusalem, called Gabbatha in Aramaic. Roman governors set the judgment seat there to hear cases in public. Pilate sat there at the trial of Jesus (John 19:13).
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Not a person but an elevated, stone-paved platform outside Pilate's headquarters in Jerusalem, called Gabbatha in Aramaic, where Roman governors set up the judgment seat to hear cases in public (John 19:13). It was here that Pilate presented Jesus to the crowd and formally handed him over for crucifixion. Its precise location within ancient Jerusalem has not been conclusively identified, though several sites near the Temple Mount have been proposed.

entries.title: Pedahel (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Son of Ammihud, and the leader from Naphtali whom Moses picked to help share out Canaan among the tribes. His name means "God has redeemed."
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Pedahel son of Ammihud was the prince of the tribe of Naphtali whom Moses appointed to help apportion the land of Canaan among the tribes (Numbers 34:28). His name means "God has redeemed." Nothing else is recorded about him.

entries.title: Pedahzur (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Father of the man who led Manasseh in the wilderness census.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Pedahzur was the father of the tribal leader of Manasseh during the wilderness census.

entries.title: Pedaiah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: In the royal line after the exile, named in 1 Chronicles 3:18-19 in the same breath as Zerubbabel.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Pedaiah was a common postexilic and royal name, borne by Zerubbabel's uncle and by several officials involved in rebuilding Jerusalem's walls under Nehemiah.

entries.title: Pedaiah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 7 men called Pedaiah. This one is a man from the divided-kingdom years, named once in 1 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Pedaiah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 2 Kings names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Pedaiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Nehemiah names him once, and he is a man from the exile and the return.

entries.summary: One of 7 men called Pedaiah. This one is a man from the exile and the return, named once in Nehemiah.

entries.title: Pedaiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A man from the exile and the return. Nehemiah names him once.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Pekah (King living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: He took the northern throne by murdering the king before him. Then he joined Syria against Assyria, invaded Judah, and tried to force King Ahaz into the alliance.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Pekah seized the throne of northern Israel by assassinating his predecessor and allied with Syria against Assyria, an alliance that included invading Judah and trying to force King Ahaz into joining them. Assyria's king Tiglath-pileser the Third responded by conquering large parts of Israel's territory and deporting the population, a devastating blow from which the northern kingdom never recovered, and Pekah himself was assassinated soon after by his successor.

entries.title: Pekahiah (King living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: King of northern Israel for two years, until his own officer Pekah killed him and took the throne.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Pekahiah was a king of northern Israel who reigned only two years before his own military officer Pekah assassinated him and seized the throne.

entries.title: Pekod (Babylon)
entries.summary: Not a person. Pekod is a tribal or regional name in southern Babylonia, the Puqudu of Assyrian and Babylonian records, and both Jeremiah and Ezekiel bring it into their oracles against Babylon.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Pekod is not a person but a tribal or regional name in southern Babylonia, corresponding to the Puqudu people known from Assyrian and Babylonian records. Jeremiah and Ezekiel both invoke it in judgment oracles against Babylon, likely playing on its similarity to the Hebrew word for “punishment” (Jeremiah 50:21; Ezekiel 23:23).

entries.title: Pelaiah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Pelaiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of the Levites who helped the people understand the law when Ezra read it, and later a signer of the covenant (Nehemiah 8:7; 10:10).
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Pelaiah's name means “the LORD has distinguished.” One man of this name appears in the royal genealogy as a descendant of David after the exile (1 Chronicles 3:24). A second Pelaiah was a Levite who helped explain the law to the people after Ezra read it publicly in Jerusalem (Nehemiah 8:7) and later signed Nehemiah's covenant (Nehemiah 10:10).

entries.title: Pelaliah (Levite living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A name in the line of Adaiah, one of the priests who settled in Jerusalem after the exile. He appears in that list and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Pelaliah was a priest named in the genealogy of Adaiah, one of the priests who resettled in Jerusalem after the exile (Nehemiah 11:12). He appears only in this list of returned priestly families.

entries.title: Pelatiah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Pelatiah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 4 men called Pelatiah. This one is a man from the divided-kingdom years, named once in 1 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Pelatiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: In a vision Ezekiel saw him among the leaders giving Jerusalem false comfort. Pelatiah dropped dead while the vision was still going on, and Ezekiel cried out in fear for whoever was left.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Pelatiah was a corrupt official Ezekiel saw in a vision advising Jerusalem's leaders toward false security, and he dropped dead during the vision itself, a shock that made Ezekiel cry out in fear for the rest of the people.

entries.title: Pelatiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A man from the exile and the return, and Nehemiah is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Peleg (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: In his days the earth was divided, Genesis says. That is usually taken to mean the scattering at Babel. He came down from Shem.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Peleg was a descendant of Shem, and Genesis notes that in his days the earth was divided, generally understood as a reference to the scattering of languages and peoples at Babel occurring around his lifetime.

entries.title: Pelet (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A descendant of Judah through Jahdai, in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 2:47.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Two men named Pelet appear in the tribal genealogies of 1 Chronicles: a descendant of Judah through Jahdai (1 Chronicles 2:47), and a Benjamite warrior, skilled with bow and sling, who joined David's growing band of fighters at Ziklag while he was still fleeing Saul (1 Chronicles 12:2-3). The two belong to different tribes and are unrelated.

entries.title: Pelet (Warrior living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a warrior from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Peleth (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Peleth (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: His son On joined Korah's rebellion against Moses and Aaron. Peleth was a Reubenite, named in Numbers 16:1 and only there.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Two men named Peleth appear in the Old Testament: a Reubenite whose son On joined Korah's rebellion against Moses and Aaron in the wilderness (Numbers 16:1), and a son of Jonathan in the genealogy of Jerahmeel, of the tribe of Judah (1 Chronicles 2:33). The two belong to different tribes and different eras and are otherwise unrelated.

entries.title: Pelethites (People, perhaps from Pelath)
entries.summary: They always come paired with the Cherethites, as David's personal guard under Benaiah. The names sound foreign, and they were probably hired soldiers of Philistine or Aegean background.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Pelethites, always mentioned alongside the Cherethites, formed part of David's personal bodyguard under the command of Benaiah. Their foreign sounding names suggest they were mercenaries of Philistine or Aegean background rather than native Israelites, which made them useful as troops loyal to the king rather than to any Israelite tribe.

entries.title: Pelonite (Warriors, perhaps from Pelon or Palet)
entries.summary: Two of David's mighty men, Helez and Ahijah, carry this label. Where it points is unclear, and it may just be another spelling of Paltite.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Pelonite marks two of David's mighty men, Helez and Ahijah, whose exact place of origin is unclear; some scholars think the word is simply a variant spelling of "Paltite."

entries.title: Peniel
entries.summary: Jacob wrestled here through the night by the Jabbok River. He came away with a new name, Israel, and a limp he kept. He called the place Peniel, face of God, because he had seen God face to face and lived.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Peniel, also spelled Penuel, was the place near the Jabbok River where Jacob wrestled through the night with a mysterious figure identified as God, emerging with a new name, Israel, and a permanent limp. Jacob named the place "face of God" because, he said, he had seen God face to face and survived. The town there was later destroyed by Gideon for refusing to aid his pursuit of Midian, and Jeroboam I fortified it after Israel's kingdom split.

entries.title: Peninnah (Woman living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Elkanah's other wife. She had children while Hannah had none, and she taunted Hannah about it year after year, until Hannah's grief drove her to pray at Shiloh.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Peninnah was one of Elkanah's two wives and the mother of several children, while his other wife, Hannah, remained childless for years (1 Samuel 1:2). Peninnah taunted Hannah over her barrenness, provoking the grief that led Hannah to pray for a son at Shiloh, a prayer answered with the birth of Samuel (1 Samuel 1:4-7).

witness.excerpt: Elcanah, a Levite, one of a middle condition among his fellow citizens; and one that dwelt at Ramathaim, a city of the tribe of Ephraim, married two wives, Hannah and Peninnah.

entries.title: Pentecost (Name of a festival)
entries.summary: The harvest festival fifty days after Passover. It is the day the Spirit came down on the disciples in Jerusalem. Peter preached, and that is where the church starts.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Pentecost was a Jewish harvest festival held fifty days after Passover, and it's the day the Holy Spirit visibly descended on the gathered disciples in Jerusalem, empowering Peter's first public sermon and marking what Christians regard as the church's founding.

entries.title: Peor
entries.summary: Balak took Balaam up this peak in Moab for one last try at cursing Israel. It came out a blessing again, the one about a star and a scepter rising out of Israel.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Peor was a mountain peak in Moab from which Balak brought Balaam for one last attempt to curse Israel, only to hear him pronounce a blessing instead, including the famous prophecy of a star and a scepter rising out of Israel (Numbers 23:28; 24:2-17). The name is also attached to a local Moabite and Midianite deity worshiped there, known as Baal-peor, whose fertility rites drew Israelite men into idolatry and immorality at Shittim, provoking a plague that killed twenty-four thousand people (Numbers 25:1-9).

entries.title: Perazim
entries.summary: The prophet Isaiah warns that the Lord will rise against his own people the way he once rose up at Mount Perazim. The earlier victory there is almost certainly David's battle with the Philistines.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Mount Perazim appears once, in Isaiah 28:21, where the prophet warns that the Lord will rise against his own people as unexpectedly as he once rose against the Philistines there. That earlier victory is almost certainly the battle of Baal-perazim, where David broke through the Philistine lines in the Valley of Rephaim near Jerusalem and named the site "the Lord who breaks through" (2 Samuel 5:20). Isaiah's point is that God's coming judgment on Judah will feel just as sudden and decisive, an alien work compared to his usual saving acts.

entries.title: Peresh (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: A son of Machir by his wife Maachah, with a brother named Sheresh, and that is the whole record.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A son of Machir by his wife Maachah, listed in the genealogy of Manasseh alongside his brother Sheresh (1 Chronicles 7:16). Nothing else is recorded of him.

entries.title: Perez (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Judah's son by Tamar. He pushed out ahead of his twin Zerah, though Zerah's hand had already been marked with a scarlet thread as the firstborn. His line runs through Boaz to David.
entries.label: 5 books
entries.dictNote: Perez was Judah's son by Tamar, born pushing ahead of his twin brother Zerah in a delivery marked by a scarlet thread meant to identify the true firstborn, and Perez's line runs directly through Boaz to David and, in Matthew's genealogy, to Jesus.

witness.excerpt: Judah and his sons; and these are the names of his sons: Shela, and Perez, and Zerah--four.

entries.title: Perezuzza
entries.summary: The breach of Uzzah. David gave the threshing floor this name after Uzzah reached out to steady the ark and was struck dead.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Perez-uzzah, meaning the breach of Uzzah, was the name David gave to the threshing floor where Uzzah was struck dead for touching the ark of the covenant to steady it during its transport toward Jerusalem (2 Sam. 6:6-8; 1 Chr. 13:9-11). The episode led David to leave the ark at the house of Obed-edom for three months before resuming the journey.

entries.title: Perga
entries.summary: Capital of Pamphylia, on the Cestrus River a few miles in from the sea. Paul and Barnabas landed here on their first journey. It was at Perga that John Mark turned back and went home.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Capital of Pamphylia on Asia Minor's southern coast, on the Cestrus River a few miles inland from the sea. Paul and Barnabas landed there on their first missionary journey, and it was from Perga that John Mark turned back and returned to Jerusalem, a decision that later caused Paul and Barnabas to part ways (Acts 13:13; 15:36-39). Paul preached there again on his way home (Acts 14:25). Excavations at the site, now called Perge in Turkey, have uncovered a Hellenistic city gate, a large Roman theater and stadium, and a temple to Artemis of Perga, confirming its importance as a regional center in Paul's day.

witness.excerpt: 72, 73): Alexander removed from Phaselis, he sent some part his army over the mountains to Perga; which road the Thracians showed him.

entries.title: Pergamos (Pergamum)
entries.summary: One of the seven churches of Revelation sat here, and Christ commends it for holding fast to his name in the place Revelation calls "Satan's seat." That is likely the city's huge altar to Zeus.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Capital of the Roman province of Asia, seat of one of the seven churches of Revelation, commended for holding fast to Christ's name even where Revelation calls "Satan's seat," likely a reference to the city's massive altar to Zeus or its role as a center of emperor worship (Rev. 2:12-17). Its acropolis library was famed in antiquity as second only to Alexandria's, and the city gave its name to parchment, pergamene, a writing material its scribes are credited with popularizing after Egypt restricted papyrus exports.

entries.title: Perida (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: His family were servants of Solomon, and their descendants, the house of Perida or Peruda, came back from Babylon with Zerubbabel.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Perida, also spelled Peruda, headed a family of servants of Solomon whose descendants returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel to Jerusalem (Ezra 2:55; Nehemiah 7:57).

entries.title: Perizzite (People, perhaps from Periz)
entries.summary: They come almost every time in a list, paired with the Canaanites, as one of the peoples living in Canaan before Israel arrived.
entries.books: Genesis, Exodus, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 1 Kings, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah
entries.label: 9 books
entries.dictNote: Perizzites are listed among the peoples inhabiting Canaan before Israel's conquest, almost always paired with the Canaanites in the recurring phrase describing the land's population. Unlike most of the other named peoples, they are not listed among Canaan's sons in Genesis 10, and their name may simply describe village or open country dwellers rather than a single ethnic clan.

entries.title: Persia
entries.summary: The empire that took Babylon under Cyrus. Unlike the empires before it, Persia let the exiled Jews go home and rebuild their temple, and Ezra keeps the decree.
entries.label: 5 books
entries.dictNote: Persia was the empire that conquered Babylon under Cyrus and, in a major policy shift from earlier empires, allowed the exiled Jews to return home and rebuild their temple, a decree preserved in the book of Ezra and independently corroborated by the Cyrus Cylinder.

entries.title: Persian
entries.summary: Darius the Persian, whose reign is the marker for when the priestly and Levitical family records in Nehemiah 12 were brought up to date.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Persian here refers to Darius the Persian, the king under whose reign the priestly and Levitical family records in Nehemiah 12 were kept current, reflecting the Jewish community's continued life under Persian imperial administration after the exile.

entries.title: Persis (Woman living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Paul calls her "beloved" and says she "labored much in the Lord." She was a Christian woman at Rome, greeted in Romans 16:12, and Paul uses that kind of language for real work in ministry.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Persis was a Christian woman at Rome whom Paul greets in Romans 16:12, describing her as "beloved" and noting that she "labored much in the Lord," language he uses elsewhere for active ministry rather than mere friendship. She is one of several women Paul names by name and commends for their work in that closing chapter.

entries.title: Peter (Apostle living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: A Galilean fisherman named Simon. Jesus renamed him Cephas, or Peter, which means rock. He became the most prominent of the twelve, and in Matthew it is his confession that Jesus is the Messiah the Gospel turns on.
entries.books: Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, Acts, Galatians, 1 Peter, 2 Peter
entries.label: 8 books
entries.dictNote: Peter was a Galilean fisherman named Simon before Jesus renamed him Cephas, or Peter, meaning rock, and he became the most prominent of the twelve apostles, the first to confess Jesus as the Messiah and the one Jesus promised to build his church on. He also denied knowing Jesus three times the night of the crucifixion, exactly as Jesus had predicted, and was restored to leadership afterward in a pointed three-part exchange on the shore of Galilee. Peter preached the first Christian sermon at Pentecost, took the gospel to the first Gentile convert, and tradition holds he was crucified in Rome under Nero, upside down at his own request because he considered himself unworthy to die the same way as Jesus.

entries.title: Pethakiah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: When the priests were divided by lot into their courses, one of them fell to Pethahiah (1 Chronicles 24:16), and nothing more is said.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Pethakiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Ezra names him once, and he is a man from the exile and the return.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Pethakiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A man from the exile and the return, and Nehemiah is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Pethakiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A common name after the exile. This one heads a priestly division.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Pethahiah was a common postexilic name, including the head of one of the priestly divisions and a Levite who helped lead public confession and prayer after Ezra's reading of the law.

entries.title: Pethor
entries.summary: Balaam's hometown, by the Euphrates in northern Mesopotamia. Balak of Moab sent there to hire him. It is generally identified with Pitru.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Pethor was the hometown of Balaam, the diviner hired by Balak of Moab to curse Israel, located by the Euphrates river in northern Mesopotamia (Deut. 23:5; Num. 22:5). It is generally identified with Pitru, a town on the Sajur river near Carchemish known from Assyrian royal inscriptions, and Balaam himself is independently attested outside the Bible in a plaster inscription found at Deir Alla in Jordan naming Balaam son of Beor as a seer of the gods, dated to roughly the eighth century BC.

entries.title: Pethuel (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Joel's father, named in the book's first verse and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Pethuel was the father of the prophet Joel, named in the opening verse of the book of Joel (Joel 1:1). Nothing else about him is known, and even the dating of Joel's ministry remains uncertain among scholars.

entries.title: Peulthai (Levite living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: He was one of Obed-edom's sons, in a family of Levite gatekeepers. The ark of the covenant had rested in that household for three months and brought it blessing.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Peulthai was one of the sons of Obed-edom, a family of Levite gatekeepers noted in 1 Chronicles 26:5 as particularly capable men. His father's household had been blessed after the ark of the covenant rested there for three months under David (2 Samuel 6:11).

entries.title: Phalec (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Luke's Greek spelling of Peleg, in the genealogy of Jesus. The Hebrew name means division, and Genesis 10:25 says the earth was divided in his days.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Phalec is the Greek form of Peleg, an ancestor of Jesus listed in Luke's genealogy (Luke 3:35). Genesis 10:25 explains the Hebrew name's meaning, 'division,' noting that in Peleg's days the earth was divided, generally understood as a reference to the dispersal of peoples after Babel.

entries.title: Phanuel (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: He is named only to show that Anna, the old prophetess who knew the infant Jesus in the temple, came from the tribe of Asher.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The father of Anna, the elderly prophetess who recognized the infant Jesus in the Jerusalem temple (Luke 2:36). Nothing else is recorded about him; he is named only to establish his daughter's lineage from the tribe of Asher.

witness.excerpt: But Jacob was pleased with these things; and named the place Phanuel : which signifies The face of God .

entries.title: Pharaoh
entries.summary: The king Moses stood in front of. God sent Moses to him to bring Israel out of Egypt, and he hardened his heart through plague after plague before he let them go.
entries.books: Exodus, Deuteronomy, 1 Samuel, 2 Kings, Nehemiah, Psalm, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Romans
entries.label: 9 books
entries.dictNote: Pharaoh is the Egyptian royal title used throughout the Old Testament for a series of different, usually unnamed, kings, not one individual, spanning from the pharaoh who made Joseph second-in-command to the pharaoh who enslaved the Israelites centuries later and the pharaoh Moses confronted during the exodus. Egyptian records independently confirm many of the events and periods these unnamed pharaohs presided over, even though Egyptian royal inscriptions, understandably, never record embarrassing defeats like the exodus plagues.

witness.excerpt: Pharaoh the king had seen in his sleep the same evening two visions; and after them had the interpretations of them both given him.

And Pharaoh, king of Egypt, issued a command regarding them that they

should cast all their male children which were born into the river.

entries.title: Pharaoh
entries.summary: Joseph's Pharaoh. Potiphar was his officer, his baker and butler landed in prison with Joseph, and his dreams of fat and thin cows were what got Joseph out and set him over Egypt.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Pharaoh
entries.summary: Solomon married his daughter. Pharaoh is a title rather than a name, and the record never gives this one any other.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Pharaoh
entries.summary: The Pharaoh who put Israel to forced labour on store cities. He then ordered the Hebrew baby boys thrown into the river. His own daughter pulled one of them out.
entries.label: 3 books

witness.excerpt: But as soon as Pharaoh saw the land freed from this plague, he forgot the cause of it, and retained the Hebrews; and, as though he had a mind to try the nature of more such judgments, he would not yet suffer Moses and his people to depart, ha

entries.title: Pharaoh
entries.summary: In the divided-kingdom years this was the Egypt people were tempted to lean on, mocked as a broken reed that pierces the hand of whoever leans on it, and Isaiah warned against going down to Pharaoh for help.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Pharaoh
entries.summary: Abraham went down to Egypt in a famine and passed his wife off as his sister, and this Pharaoh took her into his house. God struck the household with plagues. Pharaoh sent them both away.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Pharaoh
entries.summary: One of 8 men called Pharaoh. This one is a man from the divided-kingdom years, named once in 1 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Pharaoh
entries.summary: A man from the divided-kingdom years, and Jeremiah is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Pharaoh-hophra (Pharaoh living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Known to history as Apries, king of Egypt from about 589 to 570 BC. He backed Zedekiah's revolt against Babylon for a while and then pulled out, and Jerusalem fell in 586 BC.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Pharaoh Hophra, known to history as Apries, ruled Egypt from about 589 to 570 BC and briefly supported King Zedekiah of Judah's revolt against Babylon before withdrawing, leaving Jerusalem to fall in 586 BC. Jeremiah predicted that Hophra, like Zedekiah, would be handed over to his enemies (Jeremiah 44:30); Egyptian records confirm he was overthrown in a civil war led by his general Amasis and later killed, a case where a specific biblical prophecy about a named foreign king's downfall is corroborated by that king's own country's records.

entries.title: Phares (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Matthew and Luke both list Perez, son of Judah and Tamar, in the genealogy of Jesus under this Greek spelling.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Phares is the Greek form of Perez, listed as an ancestor of Jesus in the genealogies of both Matthew (1:3) and Luke (3:33). He was the son of Judah and Tamar, born in the unusual circumstances recounted in Genesis 38, and became the founder of one of Judah's leading clans; Boaz and eventually David descended from him (Ruth 4:18-22). His prominent place in two independent genealogies of Jesus underlines how central the Judah-Tamar line was reckoned in Israel's royal ancestry.

witness.excerpt: Judas had three sons - Sala, Phares, Zerah; and by Phares two grandchildren, Esrom and Amar.

entries.title: Pharisee (Religious group in the New Testament)
entries.summary: A Jewish movement devoted to strict keeping of the law, the written text and a large body of oral tradition around it. They carried real weight in the religious life of the people. They argue with Jesus again and again.
entries.books: Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, Acts, Philippians
entries.label: 6 books
entries.dictNote: The Pharisees were a Jewish religious movement devoted to strict observance of the law, both the written text and an extensive body of oral tradition interpreting it, and they held significant influence over Jewish religious life in the first century despite holding no official political power. Jesus repeatedly clashed with Pharisees over his willingness to break their added traditions, particularly around Sabbath observance and ritual purity, even as the apostle Paul himself had been a Pharisee before his conversion.

witness.excerpt: Paul, a Pharisee, confesses that he had not known concupiscence, or desires, to be sinful, had not the tenth commandment said, \"Thou shalt not covet,\" Romans 7:7, the case seems to have been much the same with our Josephus, who was of

But Pollio the Pharisee, and Sameas, a disciple of his, were honored by him above all the rest; for when Jerusalem was besieged, they advised the citizens to receive Herod, for which advice they were well requited.

He endeavored also to persuade Pollio the Pharisee, and Satneas, and the greatest part of their scholars, to take the oath; but these would neither submit so to do, nor were they punished together with the rest, out of the reverence he bore to Pollio.

It seems not very improbable to me, that this Sadduc, the Pharisee, was the very same man of whom the Rabbins speak, as the unhappy, but undesigning occasion of the impiety or infidelity of the Sadducees.

Yet was there one Judas, a Gaulonite;  of a city whose name was Gamala; who, taking with him Saddouk, a Pharisee,  became zealous to draw them to a revolt: who both said that this taxation was no better than an introduction to slavery: and exhorted the nation to assert their liberty.

entries.title: Pharpar
entries.summary: It was one of the rivers of Damascus, with the Abana. Naaman did not see why he should wash in the Jordan when those were right there. It is usually identified with the Nahr al-Awaj.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Pharpar was one of the two rivers of Damascus, named by Naaman alongside the Abana when he objected to washing in the Jordan instead (2 Kings 5:12). It is usually identified with the Nahr al-Awaj, which flows through the district south of Damascus before emptying into a marsh east of the city.

entries.title: Pharzites (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: The clan of Pharez, Judah's son by his daughter-in-law Tamar, counted in the census of Numbers 26. Boaz, Jesse and David came out of this line.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Pharzites were the clan descended from Pharez (also spelled Perez), the son Judah had by his daughter-in-law Tamar, counted in the Numbers 26 census. Pharez's own line later produced Boaz, Jesse, and David.

entries.title: Phebe (Woman living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: A servant of the church at Cenchreae, the eastern port of Corinth, whom Paul commends to the Romans and who probably carried the letter to them herself.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Phoebe was a deaconess, or servant, of the church at Cenchreae, the eastern port city of Corinth, whom Paul commended to the Roman church and who likely carried his letter to the Romans to its recipients (Romans 16:1-2). Paul describes her as a benefactor who had helped many believers, including himself, making her one of the earliest named women to hold a recognized role of service in a New Testament congregation.

entries.title: Phenice (Phoenicia)
entries.summary: The King James spelling of Phoenicia, the narrow coast north of Israel where Tyre and Sidon traded. Believers scattered after Stephen's death took the gospel there.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Phenice here is the King James rendering of Phoenicia, the narrow coastal strip north of Israel that was home to the trading cities of Tyre and Sidon. Believers scattered by persecution after Stephen's death carried the gospel there (Acts 11:19), and Paul passed through the region on his way to and from Jerusalem on later journeys (Acts 15:3; 21:2). This is a different place from the harbor called Phoenix on Crete's south coast mentioned in Acts 27:12, a separate Greek word that older reference works sometimes conflated with this one under the same English spelling.

entries.title: Phenice (Phoenix)
entries.summary: Paul's ship was trying to reach this harbour on the south coast of Crete to spend the winter, and the storm drove it off toward Malta instead. More properly Phoenix.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Phenice, more accurately Phoenix, was a harbor on the south coast of Crete that the crew of Paul's ship hoped to reach for safer winter anchorage before a storm drove them off course toward Malta (Acts 27:12). Its exact site is debated between the modern bays of Loutro and Phineka, and it is a separate place from the region of Phoenicia on the Syrian coast, which older English translations render with the same spelling elsewhere in Acts.

entries.title: Phichol (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: He commanded Abimelech's army, and was there when Abimelech made peace with Abraham, and again a generation later with Isaac.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Phicol was the commander of Abimelech's army, present when Abimelech made a covenant of peace with both Abraham and, a generation later, Isaac.

entries.title: Philadelphia
entries.summary: The church in Philadelphia had little strength and kept the faith anyway, and Revelation praises it for that. The city stood in Lydia in Asia Minor, close to a fault line, and earthquakes hit it again and again.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: City in Lydia, Asia Minor, seat of one of the seven churches addressed in Revelation and commended for remaining faithful despite having little strength (Rev. 3:7-13). The city sat near a fault line and suffered repeatedly from earthquakes, including a major one in AD 17 that devastated the region and is recorded by the Roman historian Tacitus; Rome's financial help afterward led several Lydian cities to add the emperor's name to their own in gratitude. It survives today as the Turkish city of Alaşehir.

witness.excerpt: So Aretas was terrified, and retired out of Judea to Philadelphia, as did Scaurus return to Damascus again; nor was Aristobulus satisfied with escaping [out of his brother's hands,] but gathered all his forces together, and pursued his enemies, and fought them at a place called Papyro

Now the length of Perea is from Macherus to Pella, and its breadth from Philadelphia to Jordan; its northern parts are bounded by Pella, as we have already said, as well as its Western with Jordan; the land of Moab is its southern border, and its eastern limits reach to Arabia, and Silbonitis, and besid

But Fadus, as soon as he was come procurator into Judea, found quarrelsome doings between the Jews that dwelt in Perea, and the people of Philadelphia, about their borders at a village called Mia , that was filled with men of a warlike temper.

On this year, therefore, Ptolemy was freed from being besieged, and slew the brethren of John, with their mother, and fled to Zeno, who was also called Cotylas, who was tyrant of Philadelphia.

Upon which stroke that the Jews received at Cesarea, the whole nation was greatly enraged; so they divided themselves into several parties, and laid waste the villages of the Syrians, and their neighboring cities, Philadelphia, and Sebonitis, and Gerasa, and Pella, and Scythopolis, and after them Gadara, and Hippos; and falling upon Gaulonitis, some cities they destroyed there, and some they set on fire, and then went to Kedasa, belonging to

entries.title: Philemon (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: He owned Onesimus, the runaway slave who met Paul and became a believer. Philemon was a well-off Christian, likely at Colossae, and Paul's short letter to him asks that Onesimus be welcomed back without punishment.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Philemon was a wealthy Christian, likely in Colossae, whose runaway slave Onesimus encountered Paul and became a believer, and Paul's short letter to Philemon appeals for Onesimus to be welcomed back without punishment, hinting that Paul would consider it a personal favor and even offering to cover any debt Onesimus owed.

entries.title: Philetus (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Paul warns Timothy about him and Hymenaeus, who were saying the resurrection had already happened. Paul says that kind of talk spreads "like gangrene."
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A false teacher paired with Hymenaeus, whom Paul warns Timothy about for spreading the claim that the resurrection had already taken place, a teaching Paul says spreads "like gangrene" through the church (2 Tim. 2:17-18). Nothing further is known about him outside this warning.

entries.title: Philip (Apostle living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: One of the twelve, from Bethsaida like Peter and Andrew. Philip found Nathanael and brought him to Jesus, and in John's Gospel he gets asked how they were going to feed the crowd.
entries.label: 5 books
entries.dictNote: Philip was one of the twelve apostles, from Bethsaida like Peter and Andrew, and it was Philip who found Nathanael and brought him to Jesus. He appears at a few pointed moments in John's Gospel, questioned by Jesus about how to feed the crowd before the feeding of the five thousand, and later asking Jesus to simply show the disciples the Father, prompting Jesus's reply that whoever has seen him has seen the Father. A different Philip, one of seven men chosen to oversee food distribution in the early Jerusalem church, became a traveling evangelist and personally led the Ethiopian eunuch to faith on a desert road.

entries.title: Philip (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Not the apostle. This Philip was one of the seven chosen to oversee the food in the Jerusalem church. He became a traveling evangelist and led the Ethiopian eunuch to faith.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Philip (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: One of 4 men called Philip. This one is a man from the New Testament, named twice in Matthew and Mark.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Philip (Tetrarch living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: The tetrarch, one of Herod the Great's sons. Luke dates John's ministry by his rule, and Josephus credits him with building Paneas and renaming it Caesarea.
entries.label: 1 book

witness.excerpt: When Philip also had built Paneas, a city at the fountains of Jordan, he named it Cesarea. He also advanced the village Bethsaida, situate at the lake of Gennesareth, unto the dignity of a city; both by the number of inhabitants it contained, and its other grandeur…

entries.lukeNote: Luke names him only to date John's ministry, tetrarch of Ituraea and Trachonitis (3:1), Herod Antipas's half-brother, not to be confused with the apostle Philip named later in the same Gospel. Josephus catches him founding two real Gospel places under new names: Caesarea Philippi (Panias) and Bethsaida-Julias.

entries.title: Philippi
entries.summary: Paul came here after a vision of a man of Macedonia asking for help. Philippi was a Roman colony, founded by Philip II and later settled with veteran soldiers under Augustus, and it carried itself like a small Rome.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Philippi was a Roman colony in Macedonia, founded by Philip II and later resettled with veteran soldiers under Augustus, giving it the legal status and civic pride of a "miniature Rome." Paul, guided there by a vision of a Macedonian man, planted the first Christian church on European soil in the city, converting the merchant Lydia and casting a spirit of divination out of a slave girl before he and Silas were beaten and imprisoned (Acts 16:9-40). Archaeologists have excavated its well-preserved forum and theater, along with a prison traditionally associated with Paul's imprisonment, and Paul later wrote his letter to the Philippians to the congregation he founded there.

witness.excerpt: Now Antonius and Caesar had beaten Cassius near Philippi, as others have related; but after the victory, Caesar went into Gaul, [Italy,] and Antony marched for Asia, who, when he was arrived at Bithynia, he had ambassadors that met him from all parts.

But when Caesar and Antony had slain Cassius near Philippi, and Caesar was gone to Italy, and Antony to Asia, amongst the rest of the cities which sent ambassadors to Antony unto Bithynia, the great men of the Jews came also, and accused Phasaelus and Herod, that they kept the
About this time it was that King Agrippa built Cesarea Philippi larger than it was before: and in honour of Nero, named it Neronias .

But as for Titus, he marched from that Cesarea which lay by the sea-side, and came to that which is named Cesarea Philippi, and staid there a considerable time, and exhibited all sorts of shows there.

entries.title: Philippian
entries.summary: Someone from Philippi. Paul uses the word once, in Philippians 4:15, to remember that the Philippians alone helped him with money in the early days.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Not a person but a term for an inhabitant of Philippi, the Roman colony in Macedonia where Paul planted a church. Paul uses it in Philippians 4:15 to recall that the Philippians alone supported him financially in the early days of his ministry after he left Macedonia. It describes the congregation collectively rather than any individual.

entries.title: Philistine (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Seafaring people who settled the coastal plain between Gezer and Gaza, most likely from Caphtor, which the Old Testament elsewhere identifies as Crete.
entries.books: Genesis, Exodus, Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Psalm, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Amos, Obadiah, Zephaniah, Zechariah
entries.label: 18 books
entries.dictNote: The Philistines were a seafaring people who settled the coastal plain between Gezer and Gaza, most likely arriving from Caphtor, which the Old Testament elsewhere identifies as Crete. Unlike Israel's other neighbors, they never had a single king; five cities, Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Gath, and Ekron, each answered to its own lord, and together those cities gave Israel its most persistent military rival from the judges through the united monarchy.
