Excavations at Gezer, Lachish, and Ashkelon, along with the Amarna Letters, confirm a settled population in this same region going back to the time of Moses and Joshua, and Egyptian temple reliefs from a century later show the Philistines arriving as part of the larger wave the Egyptians called the Sea Peoples.

witness.excerpt: Now as David was talking with his brethren about the business for which his father had sent him, he heard the Philistine reproaching and abusing the army, and had indignation at it; and said to his brethren, I am ready to fight a single combat with this adversary.
The High Priest said that he had no such weapon: but he added, “Here is the sword of Goliath; which, when thou hadst slain the Philistine thou didst dedicate 11 to God.” 2.

entries.title: Philologus (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Greeted at the end of Romans along with Julia, Nereus and others, probably all one household or house church.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Philologus was a Christian at Rome to whom Paul sends greetings in Romans 16:15, grouped together with Julia, Nereus, and others, likely members of the same household or house church. Nothing further is known about him.

entries.title: Phinehas (High Priest living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Aaron's grandson, Eleazar's son. When Israel was being struck by a plague for idolatry and sexual sin with Moabite women, Phinehas drove a spear through an Israelite man and a Midianite woman together, and the plague stopped.
entries.books: Exodus, Numbers, Joshua, Judges, 1 Chronicles, Ezra, Psalm
entries.label: 7 books
entries.dictNote: Phinehas was Aaron's grandson and Eleazar's son, and he ended a plague God had sent on Israel for their idolatry and sexual immorality with Moabite women by personally spearing an Israelite man and a Midianite woman together in the act, a zeal God rewarded with a covenant of permanent priesthood for his descendants. A different Phinehas was one of Eli's corrupt sons, killed in battle the same day the Ark of the Covenant was captured by the Philistines.

witness.excerpt: He also appointed Zadok, of the family of Phinehas, to be high priest, together with Abiathar, for he was his friend.

entries.title: Phinehas (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of 3 men called Phinehas. This one is a man from the exile and the return, named once in Ezra.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Phinehas (Priest living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of Eli's corrupt sons, killed in battle on the same day the Philistines captured the Ark of the Covenant.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Phlegon (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Another of the names Paul greets in Rome, grouped with Asyncritus, Hermas, Patrobas and Hermes (Romans 16:14).
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Christian in Rome to whom Paul sends greetings near the close of his letter to the Romans, grouped with Asyncritus, Hermas, Patrobas, and Hermes (Rom. 16:14). Nothing further about him is recorded.

entries.title: Phrygia
entries.summary: A big inland region of Asia Minor, with Colossae, Hierapolis, Laodicea and Iconium among its cities. Jews from Phrygia heard the apostles at Pentecost. Paul went through the region more than once.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Phrygia was a large region in the interior of Asia Minor, home to cities such as Colossae, Hierapolis, Laodicea, and Iconium. Jews from Phrygia were present in Jerusalem at Pentecost (Acts 2:10), and Paul passed through the region on both his second and third missionary journeys, strengthening the churches there (Acts 16:6; 18:23). By Roman times it was divided administratively between the provinces of Asia and Galatia.

witness.excerpt: Yet was Mucianus afraid of going by sea, because it was the middle of winter; and so he led his army on foot through Cappadocia, and Phrygia.

Now as soon as those affairs of Pontus were finished, for whose sake Agrippa was sent thither, they did not think fit to return by sea, but passed through Paphlagonia and Cappadocia; they then traveled thence over great Phrygia, and came to Ephesus, and then they sailed from Ephesus to Samos.

entries.title: Phurah (Man living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: He was Gideon's servant, likely his armour-bearer. The night before the attack with three hundred men, Gideon took Phurah down to spy on the Midianite camp.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Phurah was Gideon's servant, likely his armor-bearer, who accompanied him on a night reconnaissance of the Midianite camp before Gideon's famous attack with three hundred men (Judges 7:10-11).

witness.excerpt: So he obeyed, and went and took his servant Phurah with him.

entries.title: Phut (Libya)
entries.summary: A son of Ham in the table of nations. The prophets tie his descendants to northern Africa, likely ancient Libya, and keep listing them among the hired soldiers in other people's armies.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Phut appears in the table of nations as a son of Ham, and the peoples descended from him are consistently associated in the prophets with northern Africa, likely the region of ancient Libya. Phut is repeatedly listed among the mercenary troops serving in the armies of Egypt and Tyre, reflecting a real ancient reputation as a source of soldiers for hire.

witness.excerpt: Phut also was the founder of Libya, and called the inhabitants Phutites, from himself: there is also a river in the country of Moors which bears that name.

entries.title: Phut (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Genesis and 1 Chronicles name him twice, and he is a man from the patriarchs.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Phuvah (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Issachar's son, usually spelled Puvah, in the genealogies of Genesis and Numbers.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Puvah was a son of Issachar, listed among the tribal genealogies in Genesis and Numbers.

entries.title: Phuvah (Man living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: Judges names him once, and he is a man from the years before the monarchy.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Phygellus (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: In his last imprisonment in Rome, Paul writes that everyone in Asia turned away from him, and he names Phygellus and Hermogenes.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Phygellus was a Christian in the Roman province of Asia named by Paul as one who turned away from him during his final imprisonment in Rome, alongside a man named Hermogenes (2 Tim. 1:15). Paul lists the defection among the signs of isolation in his last letter. Nothing more is known of Phygellus.

entries.title: Pi-beseth
entries.summary: Ezekiel says its young men will fall by the sword. The Greeks called it Bubastis, a city in the eastern Nile Delta and the center of worship for the cat goddess Bastet.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Pi-beseth, called Bubastis by the Greeks, was an Egyptian city in the eastern Nile Delta and the center of worship for the cat goddess Bastet. Ezekiel 30:17 pairs it with On (Heliopolis) in a prophecy that its young men would fall by the sword and the city go into captivity, part of a broader oracle against Egypt. Herodotus, writing in the fifth century BC, described Bubastis's annual festival as the most popular in all Egypt, and the site, now called Tell Basta, has been excavated since the nineteenth century, uncovering the remains of Bastet's temple that he described.

entries.title: Pi-hahiroth
entries.summary: Israel doubled back from Etham and camped here beside the sea, and Pharaoh's army came up behind them. It was here that Moses stretched out his hand over the water.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Pi-hahiroth was the campsite in Egypt where the Israelites, having doubled back from Etham, made camp beside the sea with Pharaoh's pursuing army closing in behind them (Exodus 14:1-9). It was there that Moses stretched out his hand and God parted the sea, letting Israel cross on dry ground before the waters closed over the pursuing Egyptian chariots (Exodus 14:21-28). Its exact location is disputed, since shifting Nile sediment has reshaped the Isthmus of Suez considerably since ancient times.

entries.title: Pilate (Ruler living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Pontius Pilate, Roman governor of Judea. He said three times that he found no guilt in Jesus, and then gave the crowd and the religious leaders what they wanted and had him crucified.
entries.books: Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, Acts, 1 Timothy
entries.label: 6 books
entries.dictNote: Pontius Pilate was the Roman governor of Judea who presided over Jesus's trial and, despite declaring three times that he found no guilt in Jesus, gave in to pressure from the crowd and religious leaders and had him crucified, a decision he tried to distance himself from by publicly washing his hands. A limestone block found at Caesarea Maritima in 1961, inscribed with Pilate's name and title, is the only archaeological confirmation of his existence outside literary sources, and it settled a long debate over his exact Roman rank.

witness.excerpt: Pilate was the first who brought those images to Jerusalem, and set them up there; which was done without the knowledge of the people, because it was done in the night time; but as soon as they knew it, they came in multitudes to Cesarea, and interceded with Pilate many days that he would remove the images.

witness.source: Philo, On the Embassy to Gaius 299-300
witness.excerpt: Pilate was one of the emperor's lieutenants, having been appointed governor of Judaea. He, not more with the object of doing honour to Tiberius than with that of vexing the multitude, dedicated some gilt shields in the palace of Herod, in the holy city; which had no form nor any other forbidden thing represented on them except some necessary inscription…

entries.lukeNote: Luke's trial narrative (23:1-25) shows a Pilate who tries three times to release Jesus. Josephus's Pilate, who sneaks Caesar's images into Jerusalem by night and later slaughters Samaritans, the incident that gets him recalled to Rome, is a harder, more provocative administrator, the reputation Luke's crowd would have already known him by. Philo tells a separate incident, gilded shields in Herod's old palace, no images, just an inscription, that Tiberius himself ordered taken down after Jewish protest, a second, independent witness to the same abrasive governorship.

entries.title: Pilcha (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: He set his seal to Nehemiah's covenant, one of the leaders of the people. That list is the only place he turns up.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of the leaders of the people who set their seal to the covenant of renewed obedience under Nehemiah (Nehemiah 10:24). Nothing else is known about him beyond this list of signatories.

entries.title: Pildash (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Nahor, Abraham's brother, had eight sons by Milcah, and Pildash was one.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of the eight sons born to Nahor, Abraham's brother, by his wife Milcah, part of a genealogy that connects Abraham's extended family to Aram (Genesis 22:20-22).

entries.title: Piltai (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: In the days of the high priest Joiakim, the generation after the return, he headed the priestly family of Moadiah. Nothing further is recorded.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Piltai was head of the priestly family of Moadiah in the days of the high priest Joiakim, in the generation after the return from Babylonian exile, as recorded in the priestly and Levitical family lists of Nehemiah 12. Nothing further is known of him.

entries.title: Pinon (Edomite living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: An Edomite chief in Genesis 36:41 and 1 Chronicles 1:52, whom many scholars take to be the same name as Punon.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Pinon appears among the chiefs, or 'dukes,' of Edom in the genealogical lists of Genesis 36:41 and 1 Chronicles 1:52, where each name marks the head of a clan or territory. Many scholars think Pinon is the same as Punon, an Edomite way station named in Numbers 33:42-43, associated with the copper mining region of Feinan in the Jordan valley, where archaeologists have uncovered extensive ancient smelting sites.

entries.title: Piram (King living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: King of Jarmuth, one of five Amorite kings who besieged Gibeon. Joshua beat them in the battle where the sun stood still, and the five were found hiding in a cave at Makkedah.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The Amorite king of Jarmuth, one of five Canaanite kings who besieged Gibeon and were defeated by Joshua in the battle remembered for the sun standing still (Josh. 10:3, 23). He was captured with his allies hiding in a cave at Makkedah and put to death.

entries.title: Pirathon
entries.summary: It was Abdon the judge's town, in the hill country of Ephraim, and he was buried there. Benaiah the Pirathonite, one of David's thirty, also came from it.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Pirathon was a town in the hill country of Ephraim, home to Abdon, one of the minor judges of Israel, who was buried there (Judges 12:13-15). It also gave its name to Benaiah the Pirathonite, one of David's thirty mighty warriors (2 Samuel 23:30), and is generally identified with the modern village of Far'ata, about six miles southwest of Shechem.

witness.excerpt: He died an old man; and obtained a magnificent burial in Pirathon.

entries.title: Pirathonite
entries.summary: Two men carry the label, both from Pirathon in Ephraim. Abdon son of Hillel judged Israel for eight years and is remembered for his many sons and grandsons. Benaiah was one of David's thirty.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Pirathonite names two separate figures in the Bible from the town of Pirathon in Ephraim. The first is Abdon son of Hillel, a minor judge who led Israel for eight years and is remembered mainly for his many sons and grandsons who rode donkeys in Judges 12. The second is Benaiah, one of David's thirty elite warriors, distinct from the better known Benaiah son of Jehoiada who commanded David's bodyguard.

entries.title: Pisgah
entries.summary: Moses looked out over the promised land from the top of Pisgah before he died. Balak had brought Balaam up the same ridge in Moab to curse Israel's camp. It belongs to the range called Abarim.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Pisgah was a mountain ridge in Moab, part of the range known as Abarim, from which Balak brought Balaam to view and curse Israel's camp, and from whose summit Moses looked out over the promised land before his death. Its height, Mount Nebo, is usually identified with modern Jebel Siyagha near the northeastern shore of the Dead Sea.

entries.title: Pisidia
entries.summary: Rough country north of Pamphylia, with the Taurus mountains running through it. Paul and Barnabas crossed it on their first journey and preached at Antioch of Pisidia going out and coming back.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Pisidia was a rugged district of Asia Minor north of Pamphylia, crossed by the Taurus mountains, that Paul and Barnabas passed through on their first missionary journey, preaching at Antioch of Pisidia on both the outward and return legs (Acts 13:14; 14:24). Excavations at Pisidian Antioch uncovered dozens of fragments of a Latin copy of the Res Gestae, Augustus's own account of his achievements, inscribed near the city's monumental gate, evidence of how thoroughly Rome had absorbed the district by Paul's time.

photo.description: panorama of a mountain and ancient theater at Termessos in Pisidia

entries.title: Pison (Near Eden)
entries.summary: One of four rivers that branch from the river watering Eden, said to wind around the land of Havilah, where there is gold, bdellium and onyx. Nobody has ever pinned it on a map.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Pishon was one of four rivers said to branch from the river watering the garden of Eden, described as encircling the land of Havilah, a region rich in gold, bdellium, and onyx (Genesis 2:11-12). Its location has never been convincingly fixed; proposals over the centuries have ranged from the Nile to rivers in Arabia and India, including a now-vanished paleochannel across northern Arabia detected in satellite radar imagery, but none commands consensus. Genesis pairs it with the Tigris and Euphrates, both real and identifiable rivers, which is part of why the search for the other two continues rather than being dismissed outright.

entries.title: Pispah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A son of Jether, among the family heads and warriors of Asher, with nothing else recorded of him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A son of Jether, listed among the leading warriors and family heads of the tribe of Asher (1 Chronicles 7:38-40). Nothing else is recorded of him.

entries.title: Pithom
entries.summary: The Israelites were forced to build it for Pharaoh as a store city before the exodus. The name comes from the Egyptian "Per-Atum." That means house of the sun-god Atum.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of the store-cities the Israelites were forced to build for Pharaoh in Egypt before the exodus (Exodus 1:11), its name deriving from the Egyptian "Per-Atum," house of the sun-god Atum. Excavations by Édouard Naville in 1883 at Tell el-Maskhuta in the Wadi Tumilat uncovered large storage-chamber remains and brickwork consistent with the biblical account, though some Egyptologists now argue the site lay instead a little further west, at Tell er-Retabeh; either way, the identification rests on real excavated store-city ruins in the eastern Nile Delta.

witness.excerpt: And he set over them taskmasters to afflict them with slavery; and they built strong 2 cities for Pharaoh, Pithom and Raamses, and they built all the walls and all the fortifications which had fallen in the cities of Egypt.

entries.title: Pithon (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: In the line of King Saul that runs through Jonathan, Pithon is a son of Micah and a grandson of Mephibosheth.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Pithon was a son of Micah and grandson of Mephibosheth, in the genealogy preserving the line of King Saul through his son Jonathan (1 Chronicles 8:35; 9:41).

entries.title: Pontius (Ruler living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Pilate's family name, and the reader wants the entry for Pilate.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Pontius is the family name of Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor who presided over Jesus's trial; see the entry for Pilate.

witness.excerpt:
When Gratus had done these things, he went back to Rome; after he had tarried in Judea eleven years: when Pontius Pilate came as his successor.

3.

entries.title: Pontus
entries.summary: A Roman province along the southern coast of the Black Sea. Jews from Pontus were at Pentecost in Jerusalem, and Peter wrote his first letter partly to believers scattered there.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Roman province along the southern coast of the Black Sea in northern Asia Minor. Jews from Pontus were present in Jerusalem at Pentecost (Acts 2:9), and Peter addressed part of his first letter to believers scattered across the province (1 Pet. 1:1); Paul's coworker Aquila was a native of Pontus (Acts 18:2). The region had earlier been the heartland of King Mithridates VI, whose decades-long wars against Rome in the first century BC are extensively documented in Greek and Roman historical sources.

witness.excerpt: A little after this, certain persons came out of Pontus, and informed Pompey, as he was on the way, and conducting his army against Aristobulus, that Mithridates was dead, and was slain by his son Pharmaces.

He was also in friendship with Ahab’s son, who was King of Israel; and he joined with him in the building of ships that were to sail to Pontus, and the traffick- cities of Thrace: but he failed of his gains: for the ships were destroyed by being so great [and unwieldy.] On which account he was no longer concerned about shipping.

Accordingly there came to him Antiochus, king of Commalena, Sampsigeratnus, king of Emesa, and Cotys, who was king of the Lesser Armenia, and Polemo, who was king of Pontus, as also Herod his brother, who was king of Chalcis.

photo.description: panorama of a mountain in Pontus

entries.title: Poratha (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Haman had ten sons. Poratha was one, killed by the Jews of Susa when they defended themselves against the slaughter Haman had planned, and Purim remembers it.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of the ten sons of Haman killed by the Jews of Susa when they defended themselves against the pogrom Haman had planned, as recorded in Esther 9:8. Their deaths are commemorated in the Jewish festival of Purim.

entries.title: Porcius (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Festus's family name. Porcius Festus took over from Felix as governor of Judea, and Paul made his defence in front of him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The family name, or nomen, of Porcius Festus, the Roman procurator who succeeded Felix as governor of Judea and before whom Paul defended himself (Acts 24:27). See Festus for his role in Paul's trial and appeal to Caesar.

witness.excerpt: 58.] Now when Porcius Festus was sent as successor to Felix by Nero, the principal of the Jewish inhabitants of Cesarea went up to Rome, to accuse Felix.

entries.title: Poti-pherah (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Priest of On. His daughter Asenath married Joseph after Pharaoh raised Joseph up, so Ephraim and Manasseh were his grandsons.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Potiphera was an Egyptian priest of On whose daughter Asenath married Joseph after Pharaoh elevated him to power, making Potiphera the grandfather of Ephraim and Manasseh.

entries.title: Potiphar (Egyptian living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: An Egyptian official. He bought Joseph as a slave and soon had him running the whole household. When Potiphar's wife accused Joseph falsely, Potiphar had him put in prison.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Potiphar was an Egyptian official who bought Joseph as a slave and quickly promoted him to run his entire household, until Potiphar's wife falsely accused Joseph of assault after he refused her repeated advances, and Potiphar had Joseph thrown into prison, where he would eventually rise again through interpreting dreams.

witness.excerpt: NOW Potiphar, an Egyptian, who was chief cook to king Pharaoh, bought Joseph of the merchants, who sold him to him.

That Joseph himself was laid in bonds by Potiphar, who was his head cook, as a slave; but, he said, he was one of the noblest of the stock of the Hebrews; and said further, his father lived in great splendor.
And the king called Joseph's name Sĕphânṭîphâns, 2 and gave Joseph to wife the daughter of Potiphar, the daughter of the priest of Heliopolis, the chief cook. 3 11.

entries.title: Prisca (Woman living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Paul's formal Latin form of Priscilla, used in his letters.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Prisca is the formal Latin form of the name Priscilla, used by Paul in his letters; see the entry for Priscilla.

entries.title: Priscilla (Woman living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Usually named with her husband Aquila. They were tentmakers and church leaders who worked alongside Paul in several cities and hosted a church in their home. Together they took the eloquent Apollos aside and explained the way of God to him more accurately.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Priscilla, usually named alongside her husband Aquila, was a tentmaker and early Christian leader who hosted a church in her home and helped Paul in his ministry across several cities. She and Aquila together took the eloquent but incompletely taught preacher Apollos aside and explained the way of God to him more accurately, and Paul consistently names her, unusually for the period, before her husband.

entries.title: Prochorus (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Named third among the seven picked to oversee the daily food for widows, right after Stephen and Philip.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of the seven men chosen by the Jerusalem church to oversee the daily distribution of food to widows, freeing the apostles to focus on prayer and teaching (Acts 6:5). He is named third, right after Stephen and Philip, the two best known of the seven.

entries.title: Ptolemais
entries.summary: Paul stopped here and greeted the believers on his way to Jerusalem. It is the old port of Acco under the Greek name it got after the Ptolemaic kings of Egypt took the Syrian coast.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Ptolemais was the Greek name given to the ancient port city of Acco after one of the Ptolemaic kings of Egypt took control of the Syrian coast, and it is the name Luke uses for the stop where Paul greeted the local believers on his final journey to Jerusalem (Acts 21:7). Excavations at Tel Akko, the older mound east of the modern city, and at Hellenistic-era harbor works on the coast have traced the site's occupation back to the early Bronze Age and confirmed it as one of the largest ports on the Levantine coast in the Hellenistic period.

witness.excerpt: NOW Vespasian returned to Ptolemais on the fourth day of the month Panemus, [Tamus] and from thence he came to Cesarea, which lay by the sea-side.
BY this time Herod had sailed out of Italy to Ptolemais, and had gotten together no small army, both of strangers and of his own countrymen, and marched through Galilee against Antignus.
So he was reduced to the utmost necessity: and came to Ptolemais.

Now as soon as the other body of auxiliaries were come to Ptolemais, as well as Aretas the Arabian, (who, out of the hatred he bore to Herod, brought a great army of horse and foot,) Varus sent a part of his army presently to Galilee, which lay near to Ptolemais, and Caius, one of his f

He built palaces for exercise at Tripoli, and Damascus, and Ptolemais; he built a wall about Byblus, as also large rooms, and cloisters, and temples, and market-places at Berytus and Tyre, with theatres at Sidon and Damascus.

entries.title: Puah (Woman living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Pharaoh ordered her and Shiphrah, two Hebrew midwives, to kill the Israelite baby boys at birth. They feared God more than Pharaoh, let the boys live, and God rewarded them for it.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Puah was one of two Hebrew midwives, along with Shiphrah, whom Pharaoh ordered to kill Israelite baby boys at birth during Israel's slavery in Egypt. The two women feared God rather than Pharaoh, let the boys live, and were rewarded with households of their own (Exod. 1:15-21), making their quiet refusal one of the earliest acts of civil disobedience recorded in the Bible.

entries.title: Publius (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Paul's ship wrecked on Malta, and Publius, the island's leading official, took them in for three days. Paul healed his father of fever and dysentery. Then the other sick people on the island came.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Publius was the leading official of the island of Malta who hospitably received Paul and his shipwrecked companions for three days. When Paul healed his father of fever and dysentery, and then others on the island who were sick, Publius and the islanders honored the travelers and supplied them for the rest of their voyage (Acts 28:7-10).

witness.excerpt: So he came without delay to Publius Petronius, who was then president of Syria, and accused the people of Doris.

Now after Caius was slain, when Marcus Antonius and Publius Dolabella were consuls, they both assembled the senate, and introduced Hyrcanus's ambassadors into it, and discoursed of what they desired, and made a league of friendship with them.

[Unless of course Philo is wrong and Josephus is right.] This Publius Petronius was after this still president of Syria under Claudius: and at the desire of Agrippa published a severe decree against the inhabitants of Dora, who, in a sort of imitation of Caius, had set op a statue of Clau

entries.title: Pudens (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: He sends greetings to Timothy with Claudia, Linus and Eubulus at the close of 2 Timothy. A Christian at Rome, and attempts to tie him to a Roman senator lack real proof.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Christian at Rome who joins Claudia, Linus, and Eubulus in sending greetings to Timothy at the close of Paul's second letter to him (2 Tim. 4:21). As with Claudia, some have tried, without real proof, to connect him to a Roman soldier named Pudens whom the poet Martial mentions marrying a British woman.

entries.title: Pul (King living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Another Old Testament name for the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser the Third, the one Menahem of Israel paid off to keep his own throne.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Pul is an alternate name used in the Old Testament for the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser the Third, to whom King Menahem of Israel paid tribute to secure his own throne.

witness.excerpt: 15:20, observes, that “When this Menahem is said to have exacted the money of Israel, of all the mighty men of wealth, of each man fifty shekels of silver , to give Pul the King of Assyria 1000 talents; this is the first publick money raised by any [Israelite] King by a tax on the people: that they used before to raise it out of the treasures of the house of the Lord, or of their own h

entries.title: Pul (Libya)
entries.summary: Named once, in Isaiah, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Punites (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: The clan of Puvah, Issachar's son, counted in the census of Numbers 26.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Punites were the clan descended from Puvah, also spelled Pua, a son of Issachar, counted in the Numbers 26 census.

entries.title: Punon
entries.summary: Israel camped here between Zalmonah and Oboth, and it is identified with Phaeno, where early Christian writers placed Roman copper mines.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Punon was a wilderness station on Israel's route, between Zalmonah and Oboth (Num. 33:42-43). It is identified with Phaeno, mentioned by early Christian writers as a site of Roman-era copper mines, and modern excavations at Khirbet Feinan in southern Jordan have confirmed intensive copper mining and smelting there going back millennia before the Roman period, making it one of the largest ancient metal-production sites in the region.

entries.title: Pur (Name of a festival)
entries.summary: It means a lot, the thing Haman cast to pick a date for killing the Jews. Purim takes its name from it, which reads like a joke at his expense.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Pur is the Hebrew and Akkadian word for a lot, cast by Haman to select a date for destroying the Jews, and the festival of Purim takes its name directly from this word, commemorating the reversal of Haman's plot.

entries.title: Puteoli
entries.summary: A big Roman port on the Bay of Naples, modern Pozzuoli. Paul landed here after the shipwreck and found believers already in the town. Rome's grain ships came in here.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Puteoli, a major Roman port on the Bay of Naples, modern Pozzuoli, where Paul landed after his shipwreck voyage and found a community of believers already established there (Acts 28:13-14). It served as Rome's chief harbor for grain shipped from Egypt and North Africa, and substantial Roman remains, including its amphitheater and the piers of the ancient harbor mole, survive at the site today.

witness.excerpt: So he landed at Dicearchia, [Puteoli,] and got very large presents from the Jews who dwelt there, and was conducted by his father's friends as if he were a king; nay, the resemblance in his countenance procured him so much credit, that those who had seen A

Accordingly Alexander paid them five talents at Alexandria; and promised to pay him the rest of that sum at Dicearchia [Puteoli]: and this he did out of the fear he was in that Agrippa would soon spend it.

entries.title: Putiel (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: His daughter married Eleazar, Aaron's son, and their son was Phinehas. Putiel himself is a name and nothing more.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The father of the woman who married Eleazar, Aaron's son, and became the mother of Phinehas, the priest whose zeal against idolatry at Baal-peor later secured his line a perpetual priesthood (Exod. 6:25; Num. 25:10-13). Putiel himself is named only to complete this priestly genealogy.

entries.title: Quartus (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: A Christian at Corinth who joins in Paul's greetings at the end of Romans, mentioned beside Erastus, the city treasurer.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Quartus was a Christian at Corinth whom Paul includes among those sending greetings to the Roman church at the close of his letter (Romans 16:23), alongside Erastus, the city treasurer. Nothing more is known of him.

entries.title: Quirinius (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Luke names him once, for the census that takes Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem, and the old spelling is Cyrenius. Josephus opens a book of his history with the same man arriving in Syria to take that kind of account.
entries.label: 1 book

witness.excerpt: Now Cyrenius, a Roman senator, and one who had gone through other magistracies, and had passed through them till he had been consul… came at this time into Syria… being sent by Cesar to be a judge of that nation, and to take an account of their substance.

entries.lukeNote: Named once, for the census that gets Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem (2:2): Cyrenius in the old spelling. Josephus opens the very next book of his own history with the same man's arrival in Syria to do exactly that job: take an account of the province's substance for Rome.

entries.title: Raamah
entries.summary: Named once, in Ezekiel, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Raamah (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: His sons Sheba and Dedan fathered Arabian trading peoples. Raamah himself was a son of Cush, and Ezekiel lists Raamah's merchants among those who brought Tyre its spices and precious stones.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Raamah was a son of Cush and, through his sons Sheba and Dedan, the ancestor of Arabian trading peoples (Genesis 10:7; 1 Chronicles 1:9). Ezekiel lists Raamah's merchants among those who supplied Tyre with spices, precious stones, and gold (Ezekiel 27:22). Most scholars connect the name to a city called Ragmatum known from South Arabian inscriptions in the old Sabaean kingdom of Yemen, matching the trading-nation identity the Bible gives it.

entries.title: Raamiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of the leaders who came back from Babylon with Zerubbabel, called Reelaiah in Ezra's list.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of the leaders who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel, named in Nehemiah 7:7; the parallel list in Ezra 2:2 calls him Reelaiah instead. Nothing further is recorded about him.

entries.title: Raamses
entries.summary: The Israelites built Raamses, also spelled Rameses, as a store city for Pharaoh in the eastern Nile Delta, alongside Pithom. When they left Egypt, this is where they set out from.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Raamses, also spelled Rameses, was one of the store cities the enslaved Israelites were forced to build for Pharaoh in the eastern Nile Delta, alongside Pithom (Exodus 1:11). It also served as Israel's staging point at the start of the exodus, from which the people set out toward Succoth (Exodus 12:37; Numbers 33:3, 5). Most scholars identify the site with Pi-Ramesse, the Delta capital built by Ramesses II, whose extensive remains, including monumental gateways and colossal statuary, have been excavated at Qantir.

witness.excerpt: And he set over them taskmasters to afflict them with slavery; and they built strong 2 cities for Pharaoh, Pithom and Raamses, and they built all the walls and all the fortifications which had fallen in the cities of Egypt.

entries.title: Rab-mag (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: It is a Babylonian court title, roughly chief of the magi, and not a name. Nergal-sharezer held it, one of the officials Nebuchadnezzar sent to see Jerusalem fall.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Rab-mag is not a personal name but a Babylonian court title, roughly chief of the magi or chief soothsayer, held by Nergal-sharezer, one of the officials Nebuchadnezzar sent to oversee the fall of Jerusalem and the treatment of Jeremiah (Jeremiah 39:3, 13).

entries.title: Rab-saris (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A court title, roughly chief officer, not a man's name, and officials holding it turn up at both sieges of Jerusalem.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Rab-saris was a senior Assyrian, and later Babylonian, court title, roughly chief eunuch or chief officer, rather than a personal name, held by officials present at both Sennacherib's siege of Jerusalem and Jerusalem's final fall to Babylon.

entries.title: Rab-saris (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 2 Kings names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Rabbah (Ammon)
entries.summary: Capital of Ammon. David's army besieged it, and Uriah died in that siege, put where the fighting was worst on David's orders.
entries.books: Deuteronomy, Joshua, 2 Samuel, 1 Chronicles, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Amos
entries.label: 7 books
entries.dictNote: Rabbah was the capital of Ammon, besieged and captured by David's army in the same campaign during which David arranged Uriah's death, and the city where Uriah was killed in battle.

witness.excerpt: Upon this letter of Joab's, the king accepted of his good-will and fidelity, and took with him his army, and came to the destruction of Rabbah; and when he had taken it by force, he gave it to his soldiers to plunder it; but he himself took the king of the Ammonites' crown, whose weight was a talent of gold; (13) and it had in its middle a precious stone calle

entries.title: Rabbith
entries.summary: A border town of Issachar, named once in Joshua 19:20, and nobody knows its site.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A border town of the tribe of Issachar, named once in the tribal allotment lists (Josh. 19:20). Its exact site is unidentified.

entries.title: Rabboni (Title of a leader)
entries.summary: An intensified Rabbi, closer to my great master. Blind Bartimaeus uses it, and so does Mary at the tomb, both at full stretch.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: It is an intensified, more reverential form of “Rabbi,” closer to “my great master” or “my lord and teacher.” Both speakers use it in moments of urgent personal appeal to Jesus rather than as a formal title.

entries.title: Rabshakeh (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A title, not a name: a senior Assyrian officer. During Sennacherib's siege he stood outside Jerusalem's walls and taunted the people in Hebrew, trying to break them over the heads of their leaders.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: The Rabshakeh was a senior Assyrian military official, not a personal name but a title, who delivered a taunting speech in Hebrew outside Jerusalem's walls during Sennacherib's siege, trying to demoralize the population directly and undermine Hezekiah's authority.

entries.title: Raca (Title of disrespect)
entries.summary: A term of contempt, roughly empty-head, which Jesus says is enough to answer for.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Not a person but an Aramaic term of contempt, roughly meaning "empty-headed" or "worthless," that Jesus names in the Sermon on the Mount as an insult serious enough to warrant judgment, alongside anger and the word "fool" (Matt. 5:22). His point was that contemptuous words toward another person carry real moral weight, not only physical violence.

entries.title: Rachab (Woman living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: Matthew's spelling of Rahab, in the genealogy of Jesus, wife of Salmon and mother of Boaz.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The Greek form of Rahab's name in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus, identifying her as the wife of Salmon and mother of Boaz; tradition identifies her with Rahab of Jericho, who hid Israel's spies and was spared when the city fell (Matthew 1:5; Joshua 2; 6:17).

entries.title: Rachal (Carmel)
entries.summary: David sent a share of the plunder from his Amalekite raid to the elders here, a town in Judah's Negev. Nobody has located it.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Rachal, a town in the Negev of Judah to which David sent a share of the plunder from his raid on the Amalekites, part of his effort to secure the loyalty of Judah's elders after the Ziklag raid (1 Sam. 30:29). Its location has not been identified.

entries.title: Rachel (Woman living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Jacob's favourite wife. He was tricked into marrying her older sister Leah first and had to work another seven years for Rachel. For years Leah bore son after son while Rachel had none.
entries.label: 5 books
entries.dictNote: Rachel was Jacob's favorite wife, though he was tricked into marrying her older sister Leah first and had to work another seven years for Rachel herself, and her long struggle with infertility while Leah bore son after son is one of the more painful family dynamics in Genesis. She eventually gave birth to Joseph and later died giving birth to Benjamin on the road to Bethlehem, where a pillar marking her tomb is mentioned as still standing when Genesis was written.

witness.excerpt: Rachel had two sons, the one of whom, Joseph, had two sons also, Manasses and Ephraim.
And since Rachel my mother died in giving me birth, I had 4 no milk; therefore I was suckled by Bilhah her handmaid.
And the sons of Rachel, the wife of Jacob: Joseph and Benjamin.
And in those days Rachel became pregnant with her son Benjamin.

And Reuben saw Bilhah, Rachel's maid, the concubine of his father, bathing in water in a

secret place, and he loved her.

entries.title: Raddai (David's brother living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: The fifth of Jesse's seven sons, so one of David's brothers, and named in a single verse.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The fifth of Jesse's seven sons, and so a brother of David (1 Chronicles 2:14).

entries.title: Ragau (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Reu, son of Peleg, in his Greek spelling in Luke's genealogy of Jesus.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The Greek form of Reu, son of Peleg, listed in Luke's genealogy of Jesus among the ancestors between Noah's line and Abraham (Luke 3:35). See Reu for the corresponding Old Testament genealogy in Genesis 11:18-21.

witness.excerpt: The son of Phaleg, whose father was Heber, was Ragau: whose son was Serug: to whom was born Nahor: his son was Terah: who was the father of Abraham: who accordingly was the tenth from Noah:  and was born in the two hundred and ninety second year after the deluge.

entries.title: Raguel (Edomite living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: In Genesis 36 he is an Edomite chief. The record elsewhere ties the name to Jethro, Moses's father-in-law, the Midianite priest, but these verses are the Edomite.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Raguel is another name for Jethro, Moses's father-in-law, the Midianite priest who advised Moses to appoint additional judges to share the burden of governing Israel.

witness.excerpt: Raguel, one of the holy angels who takes vengeance on the world of the luminaries.
Now when Raguel, Moses’s father-in-law, understood in what a prosperous condition his affairs were, he willingly came to meet him.
For he had a just occasion for saving them; since they were of the kindred of Raguel, Moses’s father- in- law.

entries.title: Raguel (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: One of 4 men called Raguel. This one is a man from the wilderness years, named once in Numbers.
entries.label: 1 book

witness.excerpt: And I asked saying: 'What is this which rests not?' Then Raguel, one of the holy angels who was with me, answered me and said unto me: 'This course of fire which thou hast seen is the fire in the west which persecutes all the luminaries of heaven.'

entries.title: Raguel (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A man from the exile and the return, and 1 Chronicles is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Raguel (Midianite living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Exodus and Numbers name him twice, and he is a man from the wilderness years.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Rahab (A monster)
entries.summary: Not the woman from Jericho. This Rahab is the sea monster the poets use for chaos, and by extension a nickname thrown at Egypt.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Rahab is also used poetically in the Old Testament as a name for a primeval sea monster representing chaos, and by extension as a taunting nickname for Egypt in several prophetic and poetic passages, distinct from Rahab the prostitute of Jericho.

entries.title: Rahab (Woman living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: A prostitute in Jericho. She hid the two spies Joshua sent ahead, and for that, and for the faith she declared in Israel's God, she and her family were spared when the city fell.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Rahab was a prostitute in Jericho who hid the two Israelite spies Joshua sent ahead of the conquest, and in exchange for her help and her declared faith in Israel's God she and her family were spared when the city fell. She went on to marry into Israel and became an ancestor of David and, through Matthew's genealogy, of Jesus himself, one of only a handful of women named there. The New Testament holds her up twice as an example of faith demonstrated through action.

entries.title: Raham (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A descendant of Caleb through Hebron, in Judah's genealogies at 1 Chronicles 2:44.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A descendant of Caleb through the line of Hebron, named in the genealogies of Judah (1 Chronicles 2:44).

entries.title: Rakkath (Tiberias)
entries.summary: Naphtali's fortified town on the shore of the Sea of Galilee. Jewish tradition says Herod Antipas later built Tiberias on top of it.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A fortified town of the tribe of Naphtali on the shore of the Sea of Galilee (Josh. 19:35). Jewish tradition identifies it as the earlier settlement on whose site Herod Antipas later built Tiberias.

entries.title: Rakkon
entries.summary: On the coast north of Joppa, near the mouth of the Yarkon, this town belonged to Dan. It is generally placed at Tell er-Reqqeit.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A coastal town belonging to the tribe of Dan, near the mouth of the Yarkon River north of Joppa (Josh. 19:46). It is generally located at Tell er-Reqqeit on the Mediterranean shore.

entries.title: Ram (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: One of 3 men called Ram. This one is a man from the patriarchs, named once in Job.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ram (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: In the line from Judah through Perez to Boaz, and on through Matthew's genealogy to David and Jesus.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Ram was a descendant of Judah through Perez, an ancestor of both Boaz and, through Matthew's genealogy, of David and Jesus.

entries.title: Ram (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him twice, and he is a man from the united kingdom.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Rama
entries.summary: Matthew quotes Jeremiah's Rachel weeping for her children in Rama, and applies it to Herod killing the baby boys of Bethlehem. Rama is the Greek form of Ramah.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Rama is the Greek form of Ramah, used in Matthew's Gospel to quote Jeremiah's image of Rachel weeping for her children, a passage Matthew applies to Herod's slaughter of the infant boys of Bethlehem (Matt. 2:18). The Ramah in view is the town just north of Jerusalem, near Gibeah, where, according to Jeremiah, captives from the fallen kingdom of Judah were gathered before being marched off to Babylon, making it a fitting image of a mother's grief.

entries.title: Ramah
entries.summary: Samuel's hometown, and where he was buried. The name was common enough that several towns carried it. Jeremiah's Rachel weeping for her children is set here too.
entries.books: Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Hosea
entries.label: 11 books
entries.dictNote: Ramah was a common town name in Israel, most notably Samuel's hometown and the site of his tomb, and also the town where Rachel was buried, a site Jeremiah invokes poetically as Rachel weeping for her exiled children.

witness.excerpt: They buried him in his own city of Ramah; and wept for him a very great number of days: not looking on it as a sorrow for the death of another man, but as that in which they were every one themselves concerned.

But David, when he had escaped this danger, came to the Prophet Samuel, to Ramah, and told him what snares the King had laid for him; and how he was very near to death by Saul’s throwing a spear at him; although he had been no way guilty with relation to him; nor had he been cowardly in his battels

But when his servant that followed him told him, as they were near the city of Ramah, that there was a true Prophet in that city; and advised him to go to him: for that by him they should know the upshot of the affair of their asses; he replied, that if they should go to him, they had nothing to give hi
Accordingly he gave order to slay him immediately at Gilgal: and then went away to the city Ramah.

But the people, upon these injuries offered to their former constitution, and government by the Prophet’s sons, were very uneasy at their actions; and came running to the Prophet, who then lived at the city Ramah, and informed him of the transgressions of his sons; and said, that “As he was himself old already, and too infirm by that age of his to oversee their affairs in the manner he used to do; so they begged of him, and intr

entries.title: Ramah
entries.summary: Named once, in Joshua, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ramah
entries.summary: Joshua names him once, and nothing else is recorded.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ramath-lehi
entries.summary: "Height of the jawbone." Samson named it after he killed a thousand Philistines there with a donkey's jawbone. It lay somewhere in the Shephelah.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Ramath-lehi, meaning "height of the jawbone," the name Samson gave the site where he killed a thousand Philistines using a donkey's jawbone (Judg. 15:15-17). It lay somewhere in the Shephelah near Philistine territory, though its exact site is unknown.

entries.title: Ramathaimzophim (Mizpah)
entries.summary: The fuller form of Ramah, Samuel's hometown in the hill country of Ephraim. The "Zophim" part ties it to the clan of Zuph, his family.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The fuller, formal form of the name Ramah, the hill-country town in Ephraim's territory that was the home and birthplace of the prophet Samuel (1 Samuel 1:1). The added element "Zophim" ties the town to the clan of Zuph, Samuel's ancestral family.

entries.title: Ramathite (People, perhaps from Ramath)
entries.summary: It tells you Shimei, David's man over the produce of the royal vineyards, came from Ramah.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Ramathite marks Shimei, the official David placed in charge of the royal vineyards' produce, as a native of Ramah.

entries.title: Ramiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A descendant of Parosh who had married a foreign wife and agreed to send her away under Ezra.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of the descendants of Parosh listed among the men who had married foreign wives during the postexilic community and agreed to separate from them under Ezra's reforms (Ezra 10:25). Nothing further is recorded about him.

entries.title: Ramoth
entries.summary: Ramoth in Gilead, one of the cities of refuge east of the Jordan. Israel and Aram fought over it again and again. Ahab took his death wound there in disguise, and later Jehu was anointed king in the same place.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Ramoth-gilead was a city east of the Jordan repeatedly fought over between Israel and Aram, the site where Ahab was fatally wounded in battle despite disguising himself, and later where Jehu was anointed king in a coup against Ahab's dynasty.

witness.excerpt: 886.] Now Joram, the King of Israel, after the death of Benhadad, hoped that he might now take Ramoth, a city of Gilead, from the Syrians.
Now the cities which were set apart for this flight were these: Bezer , at the borders of Arabia; Ramoth , of the land of Gilead; and Golan , in the land of Bashan.

entries.title: Ramoth-gilead
entries.summary: A city of refuge in Gad's land east of the Jordan, and too useful for Israel and Aram to leave alone. Ahab died after being wounded there trying to take it back with Jehoshaphat.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Ramoth-gilead was a city of refuge east of the Jordan in Gad's territory, strategically important enough to be repeatedly fought over between Israel and Aram. Ahab died there after being wounded while trying to retake it with Jehoshaphat's help, and it was there, years later, that Jehu was anointed king by one of Elisha's disciples while the army was stationed on the frontier. Its exact site is disputed among several candidates on the northern Gilead plateau.

entries.title: Rapha (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Rapha (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Ancestor of a clan of giants, and the Samuel narrative ties Goliath's kin to him.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Rapha was the ancestor of a clan of giants, the Rephaim, and Goliath and his brothers are identified in some passages as descendants of Rapha, connecting the most famous Philistine giant to a broader lineage of unusually large warriors.

entries.title: Raphu (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Father of Palti, the Benjamite among the twelve spies Moses sent into Canaan.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Raphu was a Benjamite, the father of Palti, one of the twelve spies Moses sent to scout the land of Canaan (Numbers 13:9).

entries.title: Reaia (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Reaia (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 3 men called Reaia. This one is a man from the divided-kingdom years, named once in 1 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Reaia (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: The head of a family of temple servants who came back from exile, listed in Ezra 2:47 and Nehemiah 7:50.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Reaiah was a common name, borne by a descendant of Judah through Shobal and by the head of a family of temple servants among the returning exiles.

entries.title: Reba (King living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: One of five Midianite kings killed in the war Moses ordered shortly before his death. His land was later counted in Reuben's share. Joshua 13:21 lists him again with the others.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Reba was one of five Midianite kings, or tribal chiefs, killed by the Israelites in the war of vengeance commanded by Moses shortly before his death (Numbers 31:8). His territory was later listed among the lands allotted to the tribe of Reuben east of the Jordan (Joshua 13:21).

witness.excerpt: And among them fell all their Kings, five in number: Evi , and Zur , and Reba , and Hur , and Rekem , the fifth; who was of the same name with a city, the chief and capital of all Arabia, which is till now so called, by the whole Arabian nation, Arecem , from the name of the King that built it: b

entries.title: Rebecca (Woman living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Paul uses her in Romans 9:10 to show that God's choosing does not hang on works or birth order. She is Rebekah, Isaac's wife, mother of Jacob and Esau.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Rebecca is the Greek form of Rebekah, Isaac's wife and the mother of Jacob and Esau. Paul cites her in Romans 9:10 as proof that God's electing purpose does not depend on human works or birth order, since she received the oracle that "the older will serve the younger" while both sons were still unborn.

witness.excerpt: For when Rebecca, that is the patient soul, proceeds to ask an oracle from God, the answers are, \"Two nations are in thy womb, and two people shall come forth from thy bowels, and one people shall be stronger than the other people, and

entries.title: Rebekah (Woman living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Abraham's servant went back to Mesopotamia to find Isaac a wife. He asked for water, and Rebekah offered to water his camels too. That was the sign he had been waiting for.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Rebekah was chosen as Isaac's wife when Abraham's servant traveled back to Mesopotamia and tested prospective brides by asking for water, and Rebekah's immediate willingness to water his camels as well identified her as the right choice. She later favored her younger son Jacob over the elder Esau and orchestrated the deception that let Jacob steal his father's dying blessing, a decision that fractured the family and sent Jacob fleeing for his life.

entries.title: Rechab (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: His son Jehonadab laid down a rule his descendants kept for generations: no wine, no permanent houses. Jeremiah held the Rechabites up as a rebuke to Judah.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Rechab was the father of Jehonadab, whose descendants, the Rechabites, kept a strict vow of nomadic simplicity for generations, refusing wine and permanent houses, and Jeremiah held their disciplined faithfulness up as a rebuke to Judah's own broken promises to God.

entries.title: Rechab (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of 3 men called Rechab. This one is a man from the exile and the return, named once in Nehemiah.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Rechab (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: He and his brother were captains of raiding bands. They killed their own master in his bed, carried the head off expecting a reward, and were put to death for it.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Rechah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: The verses gathered under this name are Jeremiah 35, where the prophet brings the Rechabites into the temple and sets wine in front of them. They refuse it, keeping their father's command.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The verses gathered here are Jeremiah 35, where the prophet sets wine before the Rechabites in the temple and they refuse it, keeping a rule their ancestor Jonadab laid down. The people in that chapter are the house of Rechab; no individual named Rechah appears in it. The place name Rechah belongs to 1 Chronicles 4:12 and has its own record.

entries.title: Rechah (Recah)
entries.summary: Named once, in 1 Chronicles, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Red Sea (Suph)
entries.summary: Between Egypt and Arabia. Israel crossed it on dry ground in the exodus. When the waters came back, the Egyptian army chasing them was destroyed.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The Red Sea is the body of water between Egypt and Arabia through which Israel crossed on dry ground during the exodus, while the pursuing Egyptian army was destroyed when the waters returned (Exod. 14-15). No Egyptian record of the crossing survives, but the event became Israel's founding national memory, recalled repeatedly in later Scripture (Neh. 9:9-11; Ps. 106:7-9; Acts 7:36).

witness.excerpt: Euphrates also, as well as Tigris, goes down into the Red Sea.  Now the name Euphrates, or Phrath, denotes either a Dispersion, or a Flower: by Tigris or Diglath, is signified what is swift, with narrowness: and Geon runs through Egypt, and denotes what arises from the East: which
These inhabited all the country from Euphrates, to the Red Sea: and called it Nabatene .
Moreover, the king built many ships in the Egyptian Bay of the Red Sea, in a certain place called Ezion-geber: it is now called Berenice, and is not far from the city Eloth.

entries.title: Reeliah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A leader of the exiles who came home from Babylon under Zerubbabel and Jeshua (Ezra 2:2).
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Reeliah is listed among the leaders of the Jewish exiles who returned to Judah from Babylon under Zerubbabel and Jeshua (Ezra 2:2). The parallel roster of leaders in Nehemiah 7:7 gives a slightly different set of names, a minor variation common between the two overlapping return lists.

entries.title: Regem (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A son of Jahdai, in Judah's genealogy through the line of Caleb, and nothing more is known of him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Regem was a son of Jahdai, listed in the tribal genealogy of Judah through the line of Caleb (1 Chronicles 2:47). Nothing more is known of him.

entries.title: Regem-melech (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: The people of Bethel sent him and Sherezer to Jerusalem in the fourth year of Darius. Their question for the priests and prophets was whether to keep on fasting for the temple's destruction.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Regem-melech was one of two men, along with Sherezer, sent by the Jewish community at Bethel to Jerusalem in the fourth year of Darius to ask the priests and prophets whether the fasts commemorating the temple's destruction should continue now that the exile had ended (Zechariah 7:2). The question sparked the series of oracles that follow in Zechariah 7 and 8. Nothing else is known of him beyond this diplomatic mission.

entries.title: Rehabiah (Levite living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Moses's grandson, through his son Eliezer. Chronicles says Rehabiah's descendants grew very many.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Rehabiah was a descendant of Moses through his son Eliezer, and his own descendants multiplied greatly according to the genealogical note in Chronicles.

entries.title: Rehob
entries.summary: The far edge of the spies' route into Canaan, up in the north. Asher was allotted a Rehob too, and Judges 1:31 says Asher never drove out the people living there.
entries.label: 5 books
entries.dictNote: Rehob names both places and people in the Old Testament. Beth-rehob was a town in the far north near Dan that marked the limit of the spies' reconnaissance of Canaan and gave its name to a small Aramean kingdom that fought alongside Ammon against David. Two other towns called Rehob belonged to Asher, one assigned to the Levites; a third Asherite town of the name was never fully cleared of its Canaanite inhabitants. The name also belonged to the father of Hadadezer, the Aramean king of Zobah whom David defeated, and to a leader who sealed Nehemiah's covenant after the exile.

witness.excerpt: He then made war against Iadadezer, the son of Rehob, king of Sophene; (10) and when he had joined battle with him at 'the river Euphrates, he destroyed twenty thousand of his footmen, and about seven thousand of his horsemen.

entries.title: Rehob
entries.summary: Joshua names him once, and nothing else is recorded.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Rehob (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A man from the exile and the return, and Nehemiah is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Rehob (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: 2 Samuel names him twice, and he is a man from the united kingdom.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Rehoboam (King living at the time of United Monarchyand Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Solomon's son, and he lost most of the kingdom in his first days on the throne. The northern tribes asked him to lighten the heavy labour his father had laid on them. He turned down the older advisers and threatened them with worse.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Rehoboam was Solomon's son and successor, and his reign began with a catastrophic miscalculation: when the northern tribes asked him to lighten the heavy labor Solomon had imposed, he rejected his older advisors' counsel and threatened even harsher treatment, provoking ten of Israel's twelve tribes to break away and form a separate kingdom under Jeroboam. The kingdom he was left with, Judah, was invaded a few years later by the Egyptian pharaoh Shishak, who stripped the temple of its treasures, an episode Shishak also recorded on his own temple wall at Karnak in Egypt.

witness.excerpt: Now Rehoboam, the son of Solomon, who, as we said before, was king of the two tribes, built strong and large cities, Bethlehem, and Etare, and Tekoa, and Bethzur, and Shoco, and Adullam, and Ipan, and Maresha, and Ziph, and Adorlam,

NOW when Solomon was dead, and his son Rehoboam (who was born of an Amntonite wife; whose name was Naamah) had succeeded him in the kingdom, the rulers of the multitude sent immediately into Egypt, and called back Jeroboam; and when he was come to them, to the city S

However, he dwelt in Jerusalem two years, and became the father of three sons, and one daughter; which daughter was of very great beauty, and which Rehoboam, the son of Solomon, took to wife afterward, and had by her a son named Abijah.

Yet did not Jeroboam lay any of these things to heart, but he brought together a very numerous army, and made a warlike expedition against Abijah, the son of Rehoboam, who had succeeded his father in the kingdom of the two tribes; for he despised him because of his age.

He also dedicated to God at Jerusalem the golden quivers, the entire armor which the guards of Hadad used to wear; which Shishak, the king of Egypt, took away when he fought with David's grandson, Rehoboam, with a great deal of other wealth which he carried out of Jerusalem.

entries.title: Rehoboth
entries.summary: It means broad places, and the name turns up in more than one spot. Genesis 10:11 puts a Rehoboth among the cities built in Assyria, and an Edomite king came from a Rehoboth by the river.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Rehoboth, meaning "broad places" or "open spaces," names at least three different locations in the Old Testament. Isaac's servants dug a well by that name in the Negev after two earlier wells provoked disputes with local herdsmen, this one finally left uncontested (Genesis 26:22). A city called "Rehoboth by the river" is listed among the descendants of Esau as the home of an Edomite king (Genesis 36:37; 1 Chronicles 1:48), likely on the Euphrates. Genesis 10:11 also names Rehoboth-Ir among the cities built in Assyria, though many translators instead render the phrase as simply the "city squares" or open spaces of Nineveh rather than a separate place name.

witness.excerpt: At length the King gave him leave to dig a well, without disturbance: he named this well Rehoboth ; which denotes a large space .

entries.title: Rehoboth
entries.summary: Named once, in Genesis, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Rehum (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A Persian official who wrote to the king against the rebuilding of Jerusalem. The letter worked, and the work stopped.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Rehum was a common postexilic name, borne by a Persian official who wrote a letter opposing the rebuilding of Jerusalem and by several Levites and returning exiles.

entries.title: Rehum (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Ezra and Nehemiah name him twice, and he is a man from the exile and the return.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Rehum (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A man from the exile and the return, and Nehemiah is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Rehum (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of 4 men called Rehum. This one is a man from the exile and the return, named once in Nehemiah.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Rei (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: When Adonijah tried to take the throne near the end of David's reign, Rei stayed loyal, alongside Zadok, Nathan and Benaiah.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of the men who remained loyal to David and refused to join Adonijah's attempt to seize the throne near the end of David's reign, named alongside Zadok, Nathan, and Benaiah in 1 Kings 1:8.

entries.title: Rekem
entries.summary: Joshua names him once, and nothing else is recorded.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Rekem (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him twice, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Rekem (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: One of the five Midianite kings Israel killed in the days of Moses. The same name belongs to a man in Manasseh's genealogy.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Rekem is a name shared by a place and several men in the Old Testament. It names a town in Benjamin (Joshua 18:27) as well as one of the five Midianite kings killed by Israel in the days of Moses (Numbers 31:8; Joshua 13:21), a son of Hebron in Caleb's line (1 Chronicles 2:43-44), and a descendant of Manasseh through Gilead (1 Chronicles 7:16).

witness.excerpt: And among them fell all their Kings, five in number: Evi , and Zur , and Reba , and Hur , and Rekem , the fifth; who was of the same name with a city, the chief and capital of all Arabia, which is till now so called, by the whole Arabian nation, Arecem , from the name of the King that built it: but is by the Greeks ca

entries.title: Remaliah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Pekah's father. Isaiah keeps calling Pekah "the son of Remaliah," and it is not meant kindly.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Remaliah was the father of Pekah, a king of northern Israel, and appears in Isaiah's prophecies mainly in the phrase son of Remaliah, used somewhat dismissively to refer to Pekah during his war against Judah.

witness.excerpt: Who followed the barbarity of his father, and so ruled but two years only: after which he was slain with his friends at a feast, by the treachery of one Pekah , the General of his horse, and the son of Remaliah, who laid snares for him.

entries.title: Remeth (Ramoth)
entries.summary: Named once, in 1 Chronicles, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

witness.excerpt: 886.] Now Joram, the King of Israel, after the death of Benhadad, hoped that he might now take Ramoth, a city of Gilead, from the Syrians.
Now the cities which were set apart for this flight were these: Bezer , at the borders of Arabia; Ramoth , of the land of Gilead; and Golan , in the land of Bashan.

entries.title: Remeth (Ramoth)
entries.summary: A town of Issachar in Joshua's allotment list. It is probably the town listed elsewhere as Ramoth and Jarmuth.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Remeth was a town of Issachar named in Joshua's allotment list (Joshua 19:21). It is probably the same town listed elsewhere as Ramoth (1 Chronicles 6:73) and Jarmuth (Joshua 21:29), Levitical cities assigned to the Gershonite clan, the name apparently shifting between these related forms in different texts. Its exact site is unidentified.

entries.title: Remmon (A male deity in the Old Testament)
entries.summary: 2 Kings names him once, and nothing else is recorded.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Remmon (Ain)
entries.summary: Named once, in Zechariah, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Remmon (Dimnah)
entries.summary: Named twice, in Joshua and 1 Chronicles, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Remmon (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Father of the two captains who murdered their master in his bed (2 Samuel 4:2), and he is named for no other reason.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Remmon (Rimmon)
entries.summary: In Judges 20 the last six hundred survivors of the tribe ran to the rock of Rimmon and held out there for four months. Later the other tribes sent word to them there and made peace.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Remmon (Rimmon)
entries.summary: A town in the far south, named in the town lists of Joshua 15:32 and 19:7 and again in 1 Chronicles 4:32.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Rimmon was the storm god of Aram-Damascus, and the Aramean commander Naaman, after being healed of leprosy by Elisha, asked forgiveness in advance for the times he would still have to bow in Rimmon's temple while assisting his king.

entries.title: Remphan (A male deity in the Old Testament)
entries.summary: A star god, not a man. Stephen, quoting Amos, said Israel carried his image in the wilderness. The name is likely another for Saturn, or for the god called Chiun.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Remphan is not a person but a pagan star god, likely an alternate name for Saturn or the deity elsewhere called Chiun, whom Stephen accused Israel of worshipping in the wilderness (Acts 7:43, quoting Amos 5:26). Stephen's speech follows the Greek Septuagint's rendering "Rephan" for the Hebrew "Kiyyun" in Amos.

entries.title: Rephael (Levite living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: The sons of Shemaiah, a Korahite gatekeeper, were marked for their "strength for service," and Rephael was one of them.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Rephael was one of the sons of Shemaiah, a Korahite gatekeeper of the temple, and was noted along with his brothers for their "strength for service" among the divisions of temple gatekeepers David organized (1 Chronicles 26:6-8). Nothing further is recorded about him individually.

entries.title: Rephah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Listed in the genealogy of Ephraim, on the line that comes down several generations later to Joshua son of Nun.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A son of Ephraim listed in the tribal genealogy of Ephraim in 1 Chronicles 7, an ancestor in the line that eventually leads down to Joshua son of Nun several generations later. Nothing else is recorded of him beyond his place in this list.

entries.title: Rephaiah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: The name of a descendant of David in the royal genealogy. It is common after the exile.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Rephaiah was a common name, borne by a descendant of David in the royal genealogy and by a leader who helped repair a section of Jerusalem's walls under Nehemiah.

entries.title: Rephaiah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Rephaiah (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: One of 4 men called Rephaiah. This one is a man from the wilderness years, named once in 1 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Rephaiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A man from the exile and the return, and Nehemiah is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Rephidim
entries.summary: Israel camped here near Sinai and ran out of water. The people nearly stoned Moses, and he struck the rock at Horeb and water came out. Amalek attacked them at the same place.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Rephidim was a wilderness campsite of the Israelites near Sinai where the people, desperate for water, nearly stoned Moses before he struck the rock at Horeb and water flowed out for them (Exodus 17:1-7). It was also the site of Israel's first battle, a victory over Amalek won as long as Moses held up his hands, supported by Aaron and Hur (Exodus 17:8-13).

witness.excerpt: As soon as they were removed thence, they came to Rephidim: being distressed to the last degree by thirst: and while in the foregoing days they had light on a few small fountains, but now found the earth entirely destitute of water, they were in an evil case: and so they again

entries.title: Resen
entries.summary: Between Nineveh and Calah, among the cities Nimrod is said to have built in Assyria. Some read the verse to mean the settlements grew into one great city.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Resen was one of the cities Nimrod is said to have built in Assyria, located between the great cities of Nineveh and Calah (Gen. 10:12). Some read the verse as implying that these separate settlements eventually grew together into the larger city later known simply as Nineveh, though Resen's precise site has not been identified.

entries.title: Resheph (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A son of Ephraim, in 1 Chronicles 7:25. The name is also a Canaanite god of plague and war. Nothing suggests a connection.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Resheph was a son of Ephraim, listed in the tribal genealogy of Ephraim in 1 Chronicles 7:25. His name is shared with a Canaanite deity associated with plague and war, though nothing suggests any connection beyond the shared word. Nothing further is recorded about him.

entries.title: Reu (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Between Noah's family and Abraham the genealogy runs through Reu, a descendant of Shem.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Reu was a descendant of Shem and an ancestor of Abraham, listed in the genealogy connecting Noah's family to the patriarchs.

entries.title: Reuben (Jacob's son living at the time of the Patriarchs)
