entries.summary: Jacob's firstborn. He slept with one of his father's concubines and lost the birthright for it, and Jacob had not forgotten it on his deathbed.
entries.books: Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 1 Chronicles, Ezekiel, Revelation
entries.label: 9 books
entries.dictNote: Reuben was Jacob's firstborn son, and Genesis records that he lost his birthright and his father's blessing after sleeping with one of Jacob's concubines, a betrayal Jacob never forgave even on his deathbed. Reuben did try, unsuccessfully, to save Joseph's life when his other brothers wanted to kill him, secretly planning to rescue Joseph later, and his tribe eventually settled east of the Jordan River rather than in the heart of Canaan.

witness.excerpt: Reuben,  on the fourteenth day of the ninth month, in the first year of the third week.
And Reuben and Issachar and Zebulon went forth on the north side of the tower, and fifty men with them, and they slew the fighting men of the Philistines.
And Reuben said: "Give him into my hand, and if I do not bring him back to thee, slay my two sons instead of his soul." And he said unto him He will not go with thee." 19.

entries.title: Reumah (Woman living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: She was the concubine of Nahor, Abraham's brother, and bore him four sons: Tebah, Gaham, Tahash and Maacah.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The concubine of Nahor, Abraham's brother, and mother of four sons named in the brief genealogical note of Genesis 22:24: Tebah, Gaham, Tahash, and Maacah. The verse rounds out the family record Genesis provides for Nahor's household alongside his principal wife Milcah's eight sons, one of whom, Bethuel, becomes the father of Rebekah.

entries.title: Rezeph
entries.summary: Sennacherib's field commander named it as proof that no god had saved anyone from Assyria. Usually identified with Rasappa.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Rezeph was an Assyrian-controlled town cited by Sennacherib's field commander as proof of Assyrian military might, one of the places its gods could not save (2 Kings 19:12; Isaiah 37:12). It is usually identified with Rasappa, a city on the middle Euphrates that Assyrian records name as the seat of its own provincial governor from the ninth century BC onward, confirming the biblical picture of a well-established administrative center under Assyrian control.

entries.title: Rezia (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: An Asherite, of the family of Ulla, among the heads of families in 1 Chronicles 7:39.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: An Asherite descendant of Ulla, listed among the heads of families in the tribal record of 1 Chronicles 7:39.

entries.title: Rezin (King living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: King of Aram-Damascus. He and Pekah of Israel came against Judah together, and Ahaz panicked and turned to Assyria instead of trusting Isaiah's word that the threat would pass.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Rezin was the king of Aram-Damascus who allied with Pekah of Israel against Judah, an alliance so threatening it prompted King Ahaz's fateful decision to seek Assyrian protection instead of trusting Isaiah's assurance that the threat would fail.

entries.title: Rezin (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Ezra and Nehemiah name him twice, and he is a man from the exile and the return.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Rezon (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: He had been an officer of Hadadezer, king of Zobah. After David beat his master, Rezon son of Eliadah ran off, gathered a band of raiders, took Damascus and made himself king. He was a thorn to Solomon for as long as Solomon reigned.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Rezon son of Eliadah was a former officer of Hadadezer, king of Zobah, who fled after David's victory over his master and gathered a band of raiders that eventually seized Damascus and made him king of Syria (1 Kings 11:23-25). He became a persistent adversary to Solomon throughout his reign, one of several troubles God raised up against Solomon for his unfaithfulness, and his kingdom in Damascus remained a rival power to Israel for generations afterward.

witness.excerpt: ; and when he was not able to make the people forsake Solomon, for it was kept under by many garrisons, and an innovation was not to be made with safety, he removed thence, and came into Syria; there he lighted upon one Rezon, who had run away from Hadadezer, king of Zobah, his master, and was become a robber in that country, and joined friendship with him, who had already a band of robbers about him.

entries.title: Rhegium
entries.summary: Modern Reggio Calabria, at the southern tip of Italy on the Strait of Messina, and Paul's ship put in briefly on the last leg to Rome.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A port city at the southern tip of Italy on the Strait of Messina, modern Reggio Calabria, where Paul's ship stopped briefly on the final leg of his voyage to Rome (Acts 28:13).

witness.excerpt: And for any great or royal work that he ever did, which might be for the present and for future ages, nobody can name any such, but only the haven that he made about Rhegium and Sicily, for the reception of the ships that brought corn from Egypt; which was indeed a work without dispute very great in itself, and of very great advantage to the navigation.

entries.title: Rhesa (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Luke lists him as a son of Zerubbabel. Some scholars think the name is really the Aramaic title "resh," meaning prince or head, and was once attached to Zerubbabel himself.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Listed in Luke's genealogy of Jesus as a son of Zerubbabel (Luke 3:27). Some scholars think "Rhesa" preserves not a separate son's name but the Aramaic title "resh," meaning "prince" or "head," attached to Zerubbabel in a source Luke used, which would mean the name does not belong to a distinct individual at all.

entries.title: Rhoda (Woman living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: A servant girl in the house of Mary, mother of John Mark, where the believers were praying for Peter. When Peter turned up at the gate after the angel freed him, she was so glad she forgot to open it.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Rhoda was a servant girl in the Jerusalem house of Mary, mother of John Mark, where believers had gathered to pray for Peter's release from prison. When Peter appeared at the gate after his angelic escape, she was so overjoyed that she ran to tell the others without opening the door, and they at first refused to believe her (Acts 12:13-15).

entries.title: Rhodes
entries.summary: A large island off the southwest coast of Asia Minor, and Paul's ship stopped there. In the ancient world it was famous for the Colossus of Rhodes, one of the Seven Wonders.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Rhodes is not a person but a large island off the southwest coast of Asia Minor, famous in antiquity for the Colossus of Rhodes, one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world, and for its naval power in the Hellenistic period. Paul's ship stopped there briefly on his return from his third missionary journey (Acts 21:1).

witness.excerpt: So when he had sailed by Rhodes and by Cos, he touched at Lesbos, as thinking he should have overtaken Agrippa there; but he was taken short here by a north wind, which hindered his ship from going to the shore; so he continued many days at Chius, and
When he had given them this charge, he made haste to Rhodes, to meet Caesar; and when he had sailed to that city, he took off his diadem, but remitted nothing else of his usual dignity.
He also gave corn to all such as wanted it, and conferred upon Rhodes large sums of money for building ships; and this he did in many places, and frequently also.

However, the king resolved to expose himself to dangers: accordingly he sailed to Rhodes, where Caesar then abode, and came to him without his diadem, and in the habit and appearance of a private person, but in his behavior as a king.

So he set sail from thence to Pamphylia, and falling into a violent storm, he had much ado to escape to Rhodes, with the loss of the ship's burden; and there it was that two of his friends, Sappinas and Ptolemeus, met with him; and as he found that city very much damaged in the war against Cassius, though he were in necessity hi

entries.title: Ribai (Warrior living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: A Benjamite from Gibeah, the father of Ittai, one of David's thirty. Nothing further is recorded.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Ribai was a Benjamite from Gibeah, the father of Ittai, one of David's thirty mighty warriors (2 Samuel 23:29; 1 Chronicles 11:31). Nothing further is recorded about him.

entries.title: Riblah
entries.summary: Twice a wartime headquarters. The town sat on the east bank of the Orontes in the land of Hamath, where the roads between Egypt, Palestine and Babylon crossed. Pharaoh Necho used it first, and later Babylon did the same.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Riblah was a town on the east bank of the Orontes River in the land of Hamath, at a strategic crossroads between Egypt, Palestine, and Babylon. It served twice as a wartime headquarters, first for Pharaoh Necho after his victory over Josiah at Megiddo (2 Kings 23:33), then for Nebuchadnezzar during his final siege of Jerusalem, where the Judean king Zedekiah was brought to be blinded after watching his sons executed (2 Kings 25:6-7; Jeremiah 39:5-6; 52:9-11). Its ruins survive at the modern village of Ribleh in Syria.

entries.title: Riblah
entries.summary: Named once, in Numbers, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Rimmon-parez (Rimmon-perez)
entries.summary: A camp in the wilderness between Rithmah and Libnah, named only in Numbers 33, and its site is unknown.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Wilderness campsite of Israel between Rithmah and Libnah, named only in the itinerary of Numbers 33 (Num. 33:19-20). Nothing further is recorded of it, and its location is unknown.

entries.title: Rinnah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of the sons of Shimon, in Judah's line.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A descendant of Judah listed among the sons of Shimon in the tribal genealogy of 1 Chronicles 4:20. Nothing else is recorded about him.

entries.title: Riphath (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Gomer's second son and Japheth's grandson. Ancient readers tied his descendants to peoples of northern Asia Minor, possibly the Paphlagonians, though nobody can be sure.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The second son of Gomer in the Table of Nations, grandson of Japheth (Genesis 10:3). Ancient interpreters connected his descendants with peoples of northern Asia Minor, possibly the Paphlagonians, but the identification is uncertain and the name otherwise disappears from the biblical record.

witness.excerpt: So did Riphath found the Ripheans, now called Paphlagonians; and Thrugramma, the Thrugrammeans, who, as the Greeks resolved, were named Phrygians.

entries.title: Rissah
entries.summary: Israel stopped here between Libnah and Kehelathah. The name may mean ruin, or dew.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Rissah was a stopping place in Israel's wilderness itinerary, between Libnah and Kehelathah (Num. 33:21-22). Its name may mean ruin or dew, but nothing beyond its place in the list has been preserved about it.

entries.title: Rithmah
entries.summary: One of the camps in the itinerary of Numbers 33. It is named for the broom shrub common in the desert.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Rithmah was one of the stations where Israel camped during the wilderness wanderings, listed in the itinerary of Numbers 33 (Num. 33:18-19). Its name comes from the Hebrew word for the broom shrub common in the desert, and the site is generally placed in the vicinity of Kadesh-barnea, though its precise location is uncertain.

entries.title: Rizpah (Woman living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Saul's concubine. When David handed seven of Saul's descendants over to be executed to end a famine, two of them her sons, she kept watch over their bodies for months. She drove off the birds by day and the animals by night.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Rizpah was one of Saul's concubines, and after David handed over seven of Saul's descendants to be executed to end a famine, Rizpah kept a lonely vigil over their exposed bodies for months, driving off birds and animals by day and night until David finally arranged a proper burial, a grief so striking it moved David to action.

entries.title: Roboam (King living at the time of United Monarchyand Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Matthew's Greek spelling of Rehoboam, Solomon's son, under whom the kingdom split.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Roboam is the Greek form, used in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus, of Rehoboam, Solomon's son who succeeded him as king and under whom the kingdom split in two (Matthew 1:7; compare 1 Kings 12).

entries.title: Rogelim
entries.summary: Barzillai's town in Gilead. He was the old, wealthy man who fed David's camp during Absalom's revolt, and afterward he turned down the king's offer of a place in Jerusalem and sent Chimham instead.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Rogelim was a town in Gilead, the home of Barzillai, the elderly and wealthy man who supplied David's camp during Absalom's revolt and later declined the king's invitation to move to Jerusalem, sending his servant Chimham in his place (2 Samuel 17:27; 19:31-40). It probably lay near Mahanaim, though its precise site is unknown.

entries.title: Rohgah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: An Asherite, son of Shamer, whom 1 Chronicles 7 counts among Asher's mighty men of valour.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Rohgah was an Asherite, one of the sons of Shamer (also called Shomer) listed in the tribal genealogy of Asher in 1 Chronicles 7:30-40. The chapter identifies this branch of Asher's descendants as mighty men of valor and heads of their fathers' houses. Nothing beyond this genealogical listing is recorded of him.

entries.title: Romamti-ezer (Levite living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: He was a son of Heman, David's seer, set apart with his brothers for music in the temple. When the lots were cast, the twenty-fourth of the twenty-four courses fell to him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Romamti-ezer was a son of Heman, David's seer, and was set apart along with his brothers for the ministry of music in the temple. He headed the twenty-fourth of the twenty-four courses assigned to lead worship by casting lots (1 Chronicles 25:4, 31).

entries.title: Rome
entries.summary: Capital of the empire that ruled Judea through the whole New Testament period. Paul wrote to the church there, and Acts ends with him in the city as a prisoner, his case appealed to Caesar.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Rome was the capital of the empire that ruled Judea throughout the New Testament period, and Paul's letter to the Roman church and his eventual voyage there as a prisoner, appealing his case to Caesar, close out the book of Acts.

witness.excerpt: But Rome itself felt the most dismal effects of what he did, while he deemed that not to be any way more honorable than the rest of the cities; but he pulled and hauled its other citizens, but especially the senate, and particul
I will myself send to Rome; and will not refuse to serve you in all things, both by myself and by my friends.” 6 .
The other Colossus of Rome was equal to that of Juno at Argos.

WHEN Herod had been at Rome, and was come back again, a war arose between him and the Arabians, on the occasion following: The inhabitants of Trachonitis, after Caesar had taken the country away from Zenodorus, and added it to Herod, had not now p

entries.title: Rosh (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Genesis 46:21 lists him among the sons of Benjamin who went down to Egypt with Jacob. He is missing from the longer lists of Benjamin's line in Numbers 26 and 1 Chronicles 7 and 8.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Rosh was one of the sons of Benjamin listed among those who went to Egypt with Jacob in Genesis 46:21, though he does not appear in the later, more detailed genealogies of Benjamin's line in Numbers 26 or 1 Chronicles 7-8. The word rosh also occurs in Ezekiel 38:2-3, where it is usually translated "chief," an unrelated term rather than a reference to this same figure or, as older commentators once speculated, to Russia.

witness.excerpt: And the sons of Benjamin: Bela and Becher, and Ashbel, Gera, and Naaman, and Ehi, and Rosh, and Muppim, and Huppim, and Ard--eleven.

entries.title: Rufus (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Mark names him and his brother Alexander as the sons of Simon of Cyrene, the man made to carry Jesus' cross. Mark expects his readers to know them.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Rufus (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Son of Simon of Cyrene, the man made to carry the cross. Mark names him as someone his readers would know.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Rufus was the son of Simon of Cyrene, the man compelled to carry Jesus' cross to Golgotha; Mark names him alongside his brother Alexander as someone his original readers would recognize (Mark 15:21). Paul later greets a Rufus in Rome and calls his mother a mother to him as well, which many take to be the same family, since Mark's Gospel is traditionally linked to the Roman church (Romans 16:13).

entries.title: Rumah
entries.summary: Named once, in 2 Kings, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Rumah (Dumah)
entries.summary: A town in the hill-country list of Judah (Joshua 15:52), and its site is uncertain.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Rumah appears in the hill-country town lists of Judah (Josh. 15:52) and, in a different context, as the hometown of Pedaiah, whose daughter Zebudah was the mother of King Jehoiakim of Judah (2 Kings 23:36). Its location is uncertain; some link it to Arumah near Shechem, mentioned in the days of the judges, while others place it farther north in Galilee.

entries.title: Ruth (Woman living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: A Moabite widow who would not leave her mother-in-law Naomi. "Where you go I will go," she said, and went with her to Bethlehem, where she married Naomi's relative Boaz.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Ruth was a Moabite woman who chose to stay with her Israelite mother-in-law Naomi after both their husbands died, famously declaring "where you go I will go" rather than return to her own people. In Bethlehem she married Naomi's relative Boaz through the ancient custom of levirate redemption, and their son Obed became the grandfather of David, making a foreign widow one of the four women named in Jesus's genealogy in Matthew.

witness.excerpt: Samson’s wife, and Ruth, when she was a widow, are called παῖδες, children , Antiq.

entries.title: Sabean (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Traders from Sheba in southern Arabia. Isaiah 45:14 says their wealth will come over to Israel's God.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Sabeans here are the wealthy traders of Sheba in southern Arabia, named in Isaiah 45:14 among the nations whose wealth will one day come to acknowledge Israel's God. Sheba's caravan trade in spices and gold is well attested, and inscriptions from the ancient South Arabian kingdom of Saba, in modern Yemen, confirm its wealth and prominence in the ancient incense trade.

entries.title: Sabta (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: A son of Cush and grandson of Ham, also spelled Sabtah, and ancestor of a people among the early tribes of Arabia or northeast Africa.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Sabta, also spelled Sabtah, was a son of Cush and grandson of Ham, and became the eponymous ancestor of a people grouped with other early tribes of Arabia or northeast Africa (Genesis 10:7; 1 Chronicles 1:9).

entries.title: Sabtecha (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Cush's fifth son, listed with Seba, Havilah, Sabtah and Raamah in the table of nations. Like his brothers' names, his almost certainly stands for a people.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Sabtecha appears in the table of nations as the fifth son of Cush, grouped with Seba, Havilah, Sabtah, and Raamah among the peoples descended from Ham (Genesis 10:7; 1 Chronicles 1:9). As with his brothers' names, Sabtecha almost certainly designates a tribal group and its territory rather than one man, generally placed somewhere in southern Arabia or the adjacent African coast, though its exact location has never been fixed.

entries.title: Sacar (Levite living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a Levite from the united kingdom.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Sacar (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Father of Ahiam, one of David's mighty warriors (1 Chronicles 11:35).
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Two men carry this name among David's fighting men. One was the father of Ahiam, listed among David's mighty warriors (1 Chronicles 11:35). The other was a Korahite gatekeeper of the temple, a son of Obed-edom (1 Chronicles 26:4).

entries.title: Sadducee (Religious group in the New Testament)
entries.summary: A party drawn mostly from the priestly aristocracy. They rejected the oral tradition the Pharisees kept, and they denied the resurrection of the body.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: The Sadducees were a Jewish religious and political party drawn mainly from the priestly aristocracy, distinguished from the Pharisees by their rejection of oral tradition, their denial of bodily resurrection, and their closer cooperation with Roman authority, and Jesus directly challenged their denial of resurrection using an argument from the Torah they themselves accepted.

entries.title: Sadoc (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: In Matthew's genealogy, between Zerubbabel's family and Joseph. Nothing further is recorded.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Listed in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus, in the line of descent between Zerubbabel's family and Joseph (Matt. 1:14). Nothing further about him is recorded in scripture.

entries.title: Sala
entries.summary: Luke's spelling of Shelah, in the genealogy of Jesus between Arphaxad and Abraham.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Sala, also spelled Shelah, appears in Luke's genealogy of Jesus as a descendant of Arphaxad and ancestor of Abraham, matching the postdiluvian Shelah of Genesis 11:12-15 and 1 Chronicles 1:18, 24.

witness.excerpt: Sala was the son of Arphaxad: and his son was Heber; from whom they originally called the Jews Hebrews.  Heber begat Joctan, and Phaleg.
Judas had three sons - Sala, Phares, Zerah; and by Phares two grandchildren, Esrom and Amar.

entries.title: Salah (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Son of Arphaxad and father of Eber. He is a link in the chain from Noah to Abraham.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Shelah was a descendant of Shem, the son of Arphaxad and father of Eber, in the genealogical chain connecting Noah to Abraham.

entries.title: Salamis
entries.summary: The first stop Paul and Barnabas made on their first journey. It was a big port on the east coast of Cyprus, and they preached in its synagogues.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Salamis was a major port city on the eastern coast of Cyprus, the first stop for Paul and Barnabas on their first missionary journey, where they preached in the Jewish synagogues of the city (Acts 13:5). Extensive Roman-era ruins have been excavated at the site, including a large gymnasium, a theater, and a forum, testifying to the city's importance in the period of Paul's visit.

entries.title: Salathiel (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Son of the exiled king Jeconiah, also called Shealtiel, and in most lines the father of Zerubbabel, who led the return from Babylon.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Salathiel (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Also spelled Shealtiel. He is Jeconiah's son and Zerubbabel's father, or his uncle, depending which genealogy you follow.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Salathiel, also called Shealtiel, was the son of the exiled king Jeconiah (Jehoiachin) and the father, or in some genealogical lines the uncle, of Zerubbabel, who led the return from Babylonian exile. He appears in both genealogies of Jesus, in Matthew through David's royal line and in Luke through Nathan (Matthew 1:12; Luke 3:27).

entries.title: Salcah (Salecah)
entries.summary: The eastern edge of Israelite settlement. Salcah was a city of Bashan, given to the half tribe of Manasseh once Og, king of Bashan, was beaten.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Salcah was a city of Bashan on the eastern edge of Israelite settlement, assigned to the half tribe of Manasseh after Og, king of Bashan, was defeated (Deuteronomy 3:10; Joshua 12:5; 13:11). It marked the furthest eastern boundary of Israelite territory in several biblical descriptions. It is identified with modern Salkhad in southern Syria, a town built around a prominent volcanic hill still crowned by a medieval citadel.

entries.title: Salem
entries.summary: The old name for Jerusalem. Melchizedek was its king when he came out to bless Abraham, and Psalm 76 uses the name again for the city where God lives.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Salem is the earlier name for Jerusalem, the city ruled by Melchizedek when he blessed Abraham in Genesis, and Psalm 76 later uses the name poetically for the city as God's dwelling place.

witness.excerpt: It was David, therefore, who first cast the Jebusites out of Jerusalem, and called it by his own name, The City of David: for under our forefather Abraham it was called (Salem, or) Solyma; (5) but after that time, some say that Homer mentions it by that name of Solyma, [for he named the temple Solyma, according to the Hebrew language, which denotes security.] Now the whole time from the warfa

entries.title: Salim
entries.summary: John the Baptist was baptizing at Aenon near Salim, because there was plenty of water there (John 3:23). Where it was is still argued over, and one view puts it in the Jordan Valley south of Beth-shean.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A place near Aenon, west of the Jordan, where John the Baptist was baptizing because water was plentiful there (John 3:23). Its exact location is debated among scholars; some place it in the Jordan Valley south of Beth-shean, others further south near ancient Shechem.

entries.title: Sallai (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A common name after the exile, and this one turns up in Nehemiah's lists of the families who came back.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Sallai was a common postexilic name among the returning exiles and priestly families listed in Nehemiah.

entries.title: Salma (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Son of Nahshon and father of Boaz, the same man Ruth and Matthew call Salmon. Chronicles lists him in the line of Judah.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Salma, also spelled Salmon, was the son of Nahshon, a leader of the tribe of Judah, and the father of Boaz through his marriage to Rahab of Jericho, according to the genealogies in Ruth 4:20-21 and Matthew 1:5. Chronicles also remembers him as the ancestor, or founding patriarch, of Bethlehem and several related Judahite clans (1 Chronicles 2:11, 51, 54). Through Boaz and Ruth, his line runs directly to David and, in Matthew's genealogy, to Jesus.

entries.title: Salmon (Man living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: He was Boaz's father, and his wife was Rahab, the woman who hid Israel's spies at Jericho, which puts him in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Salmon appears in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus as the father of Boaz by Rahab, the Canaanite woman who sheltered Israel's spies at Jericho (Matthew 1:4-5). He is the same man the book of Ruth calls Salmon or Salma, an ancestor of David through the line that runs from Judah's son Perez down to Jesse (Ruth 4:20-21).

entries.title: Salmone
entries.summary: Paul's ship, fighting the wind, rounded this cape at the eastern tip of Crete on the way to Rome. It is generally identified with Cape Sidero.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A cape at the eastern tip of Crete, rounded by the ship carrying Paul toward Rome after it ran into contrary winds (Acts 27:7). It is generally identified with the modern Cape Sidero.

entries.title: Salome (Woman living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: She was Zebedee's wife and the mother of James and John. She followed Jesus in Galilee and watched the crucifixion with the other women. On the first morning of the week she went to the tomb.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Salome was the wife of Zebedee and mother of the apostles James and John. She followed Jesus and ministered to him in Galilee, stood among the women watching the crucifixion, and came to the tomb on the first day of the week with spices to anoint his body, becoming one of the first witnesses of the empty tomb (Mark 15:40; 16:1; compare Matthew 27:56).

Salome also, besides what the king had left her in his testaments, was now made mistress of Jamnia, and Ashdod, and Phasaelis.

entries.title: Samaria
entries.summary: Omri bought a hill from a man called Shemer and built a capital on it. Samaria took over from Tirzah as the seat of the northern kingdom. Ahab and the kings after him ruled from there.
entries.books: 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 2 Chronicles, Nehemiah, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Hosea, Amos, Obadiah, Micah, Luke, John, Acts, Ezra
entries.label: 15 books
entries.dictNote: Samaria was built by Omri, king of Israel, on a hill purchased from a man named Shemer, becoming the northern kingdom's capital in place of Tirzah. Ahab and later kings ruled from its fortified summit, and the city withstood two Syrian sieges before finally falling to Assyria after a three year siege under Shalmaneser V and Sargon II in 722 BC, when much of its population was deported. Excavations there uncovered a cache of inscribed potsherds, the Samaria Ostraca, recording shipments of wine and oil to the royal court and preserving personal names that match the biblical record. Herod the Great later rebuilt the city and renamed it Sebaste in honor of Augustus; in the New Testament, Philip preached there after the persecution that followed Stephen's death.

entries.title: Samaritan (Samaria)
entries.summary: The people who lived in Samaria in Jesus' day. 2 Kings traces them back to the Israelites left behind and the foreigners Assyria brought in. They worshiped at a temple of their own.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Samaritans were the inhabitants of Samaria in Jesus' day, a population 2 Kings traces to a mixture of surviving Israelites and foreign settlers brought in after Assyria deported the northern kingdom. They worshiped at a temple on Mount Gerizim rather than Jerusalem and were generally despised by Jews of the period, which gives Jesus' parable of the good Samaritan and his conversation with the Samaritan woman at the well their sharp edge. Archaeological excavation on Mount Gerizim has confirmed the remains of the Samaritan temple the Jewish historian Josephus describes, and a small Samaritan community still exists in Israel and the West Bank today.

entries.title: Samaritans (Samaria)
entries.summary: Settlers from Babylon, Cuthah and other places, brought in after Assyria deported most of the northern kingdom in 722 BC.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Samaritans were the mixed population that settled the territory of the former northern kingdom after the Assyrians deported most of Israel's population in 722 BC and resettled the land with people from Babylon, Cuthah, and other conquered regions. Over time these settlers blended Yahweh worship with their own traditions, and by the postexilic period the returning Jews rejected their claim to a share in rebuilding the Jerusalem temple, a rift that hardened into the open hostility reflected in Jesus' encounter with the Samaritan woman at the well in John 4 and the parable of the good Samaritan. The Samaritans built their own temple on Mount Gerizim, and archaeological excavation there has uncovered its remains along with a large fortified precinct; a small Samaritan community, numbering several hundred, still lives near Mount Gerizim and in Holon, Israel, preserving its own version of the Pentateuch.

witness.excerpt: When the Samaritans saw the Jews under these sufferings, they no longer confessed that they were of their kindred, nor that the temple on Mount Gerizzim belonged to Almighty God.

Nor did the Samaritans escape their share of misfortunes at this time; for they assembled themselves together upon file mountain called Gerizzim, which is with them a holy mountain, and there they remained; which collection of theirs, as well

But when the Samaritans, who were still enemies to the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, heard the sound of the trumpets, they came running together; and desired to know what was the occasion of this tumult? And when they perceived that it was fro

entries.title: Samgar-nebo (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Listed with the Babylonian officers who sat down in Jerusalem's middle gate in 586 BC, once Nebuchadnezzar's army was through the wall. Whether Samgar-nebo is a name or a title is not settled.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A title or name listed among the Babylonian officers who took their seats at the middle gate of Jerusalem when Nebuchadnezzar's forces broke through the city wall in 586 BC (Jeremiah 39:3). Many scholars now read Samgar-nebo as part of a title attached to the following name, Nergal-sharezer, rather than as a separate individual, since several names in this list appear to be titles rather than personal names.

entries.title: Samlah (King living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Edom had kings before Israel did, and Samlah was one of them.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Samlah was an early king of Edom, listed among the rulers who governed there before Israel had a king of its own.

entries.title: Samos
entries.summary: Paul's ship passed the island on the run from Assos to Miletus. Samos sits in the Aegean off Asia Minor, and in the ancient world it was known for its temple to Hera.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: An island in the Aegean Sea near the coast of Asia Minor that Paul's ship passed on the way from Assos to Miletus during his third missionary journey (Acts 20:15). In the ancient world Samos was known for its temple to Hera and, later, as the birthplace of the philosopher Pythagoras.

entries.title: Samothracia (Samothrace)
entries.summary: A high, mountainous island in the northern Aegean, off Thrace, that sailors steered by. Paul's ship anchored there for a night on the way to Europe.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Samothracia was not a person but a mountainous island in the northern Aegean Sea, off the coast of Thrace, whose height made it a landmark and overnight anchorage for ships crossing to Europe. Paul's ship stopped there on the voyage from Troas to Neapolis at the start of his first mission on the European mainland (Acts 16:11).

entries.title: Samson (Judge living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: He was set apart before birth as a Nazirite, with the rule that his hair was never to be cut, and his strength held as long as the vow did, enough to kill a lion with his bare hands and Philistines by the score.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Samson was a judge set apart from birth as a Nazirite, forbidden to cut his hair or drink wine, and he possessed superhuman strength as long as he kept that vow, using it to kill a lion barehanded, slaughter Philistines with the jawbone of a donkey, and carry off the gates of a city on his shoulders. His fatal weakness was Philistine women, and Delilah, bribed by Philistine rulers, wore him down until he revealed that his strength was tied to his uncut hair; once shaved, he was captured, blinded, and enslaved. In his final act, Samson prayed for strength one last time and pulled down the pillars of a Philistine temple, killing more people in his death than in his entire life.

witness.excerpt: Samson’s wife, and Ruth, when she was a widow, are called παῖδες, children , Antiq.

entries.title: Samuel (Prophet living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Hannah prayed for a son and gave him to the Lord before he was born. He grew up to be the last of the judges and the first great prophet. Israel's first two kings were both anointed by him.
entries.books: Numbers, 1 Samuel, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Psalm, Jeremiah, Acts, Hebrews
entries.label: 8 books
entries.dictNote: Samuel was the last of Israel's judges and its first great prophet, born to Elkanah and Hannah after Hannah prayed for a son and dedicated him to the Lord's service before he was even conceived. He anointed Israel's first two kings, Saul and then David, and spent his final years as the nation's conscience, rebuking Saul for disobedience so sharply that the two men never met again. He had two sons of his own, Joel and Abijah, whose corruption as judges is what pushed Israel to demand a king in the first place.

witness.excerpt: So Samuel the Prophet, seeing how ready they were to do their duty, thought this a proper time to speak to them.

entries.curatedNote: The last judge and the prophet who anoints both of Israel's first two kings (1 Samuel 1:20). Josephus picks up his story as a general leading Israel against the Philistines, prophet and military leader in one, the same combination that makes his later confrontations with Saul so charged.

entries.title: Sanballat (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: The main enemy Nehemiah faced while the walls of Jerusalem went back up. A Samaritan official, Sanballat mocked the work, plotted attacks, and tried to lure Nehemiah into a trap.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Sanballat was a Samaritan official who led sustained opposition to Nehemiah's rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls, mocking the project, plotting armed attacks, and attempting to lure Nehemiah into a trap, all of which Nehemiah records himself successfully resisting.

entries.title: Sansannah
entries.summary: A town in the Negev of Judah. Joshua 19:5 calls it Hazar-susah and 1 Chronicles 4:31 calls it Hazar-susim, and the names mean roughly village of the horse.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A town in the Negev of Judah (Josh. 15:31), also called Hazar-susah in Joshua 19:5 and Hazar-susim in 1 Chronicles 4:31, all meaning roughly village of the horse.

entries.title: Saph (Giant living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: A Philistine giant of the Rephaim line, killed by Sibbechai the Hushathite in a battle at Gob, whom Chronicles calls Sippai.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Philistine giant of the line of the Rephaim, killed by Sibbechai the Hushathite during a battle with the Philistines at Gob; the parallel genealogical account in Chronicles calls him Sippai (2 Samuel 21:18; 1 Chronicles 20:4).

entries.title: Saphir (Shaphir)
entries.summary: Micah plays on the name, which means beautiful, and tells the people of Saphir to pass by naked and ashamed. The pretty name only makes the disgrace worse.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Saphir, "beautiful," was a town of Judah that Micah addresses in a wordplay-laden oracle of judgment, telling its inhabitants to pass by naked and ashamed, the town's pleasant name mocking its coming disgrace (Micah 1:11). It is generally located at es-Sawafir, southeast of Ashdod in the coastal plain. Nothing else about the town is recorded.

entries.title: Sapphira (Woman living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: She and her husband Ananias sold property and lied to the apostles about how much they were giving. Peter put the same question to her that he had put to him, and she did not know Ananias was already dead.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Sapphira conspired with her husband Ananias to sell property and lie to the apostles about donating the full proceeds, and when Peter confronted her with the same question he'd put to her husband, unaware Ananias was already dead, she repeated the lie and immediately died the same way.

entries.title: Sara (Woman living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Sarah, spelled the Greek way. Paul and the writer of Hebrews both hold her up as someone who trusted God's promise when she was far too old for it.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Sara is the Greek New Testament spelling of Sarah, Abraham's wife, referenced by both Paul and the author of Hebrews as an example of faith in God's promise despite her age.

witness.excerpt: Since Sarah, that is to say, prudence, brings forth a male child, flourishing, not according to the periodical seasons of the year, but according to those seasons and felicitous occasions which have no connection with time; for it
Aser had a daughter, Sarah, and six male children, whose names were Jomne, Isus, Isoui, Baris, Abar and Melchiel.

entries.title: Sarah (Woman living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Not Abraham's wife but a different woman, named in the family lists at Genesis 46:17, Numbers 26:46 and 1 Chronicles 7:30, from the years in Egypt and the wilderness.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Sarah (Woman living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Abraham's wife. She was ninety when Isaac was born, after decades of being unable to have children, and earlier she had doubted the promise could come through her at all.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Sarah was Abraham's wife and, after decades of infertility that made God's promise of descendants seem impossible, she gave birth to Isaac at ninety years old. Earlier, doubting the promise could ever be fulfilled through her, she had offered her servant Hagar to Abraham to produce an heir instead, a decision that created lasting tension once Isaac was born and Sarah insisted Hagar and her son Ishmael be sent away.

witness.excerpt: Since Sarah, that is to say, prudence, brings forth a male child, flourishing, not according to the periodical seasons of the year, but according to those seasons and felicitous occasions which have no connection with time; for it
Aser had a daughter, Sarah, and six male children, whose names were Jomne, Isus, Isoui, Baris, Abar and Melchiel.

entries.title: Sarai (Woman living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: It was what Sarah was called before Genesis 17, when God changed her name as part of the covenant and promised that she would be the mother of nations and kings.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Sarai was Sarah's name before God changed it as part of his covenant with Abraham in Genesis 17, promising that despite her age she would become the mother of nations and kings.
