entries.title: Saraph (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Ruled in Moab once, according to a line in Judah's genealogy that never says how. That is 1 Chronicles 4:22, and nothing more is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Saraph is listed among the descendants of Judah in 1 Chronicles 4:22, in a genealogy that also notes some of these men once ruled in Moab, a detail otherwise unexplained. Nothing further is recorded about him.

entries.title: Sardis
entries.summary: The church at Sardis got one of the seven letters in Revelation. The city had been the rich capital of Lydia in western Asia Minor, the seat of King Croesus, and known for refining gold.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Sardis was the wealthy capital of ancient Lydia in western Asia Minor, famous in earlier centuries as the seat of King Croesus and a center of gold refining. It received one of the seven letters in Revelation, rebuked for having a reputation for life while being spiritually dead (Revelation 3:1-6). Decades of excavation at the site have uncovered one of the largest ancient synagogues known and a massive temple of Artemis, confirming the city's real prominence in the Roman period.

entries.title: Sardites (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Zebulun's firstborn was Sered, and the Sardites were his clan, counted in the census of Numbers 26.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Sardites were the clan descended from Sered, the firstborn son of Zebulun, counted in the Numbers 26 census.

entries.title: Sarepta (Zarephath)
entries.summary: Luke's Greek spelling of Zarephath, a Phoenician town between Tyre and Sidon. Elijah lodged there with a widow and kept her flour and oil from running out. Later he brought her son back to life.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Sarepta is the Greek form of Zarephath, the Phoenician coastal town between Tyre and Sidon where the prophet Elijah lodged with a widow during a famine, miraculously sustaining her flour and oil and later restoring her son to life (1 Kings 17:9-24). Jesus cites the episode in his synagogue sermon at Nazareth as an example of God's mercy extended to a Gentile outsider when many widows in Israel were passed over, a comparison that provoked his hometown to try to kill him (Luke 4:25-29).

witness.excerpt: Now the famine had seized upon the whole country, and there was a great want of what was necessary for sustenance, insomuch that it was after the recovery of the widow's son of Sarepta, God sent not only men that wanted it, but the earth itself also, which did not produce enough for the horse and the other beasts of what was useful for them to feed on, by reason of the drought.

entries.title: Sargon (Emperor living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Sargon II took the Assyrian throne after Shalmaneser V died, around 722 BC. His annals from Khorsabad claim he conquered Samaria and carried off 27,290 of its people, though the Babylonian Chronicle gives the city to Shalmaneser and most historians read Sargon as taking his predecessor's credit.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Sargon II seized the Assyrian throne after Shalmaneser V's death around 722 BC and claimed the conquest of Samaria and the deportation of 27,290 of its people in his royal annals at Khorsabad, though the Babylonian Chronicle credits Shalmaneser V with taking the city, and most reconstructions have Shalmaneser besieging it and Sargon claiming the credit. He is named directly in the Bible only once, in connection with his general's siege of Ashdod (Isaiah 20:1), and he later drove the Babylonian rebel Merodach-baladan out of Babylon before being killed on campaign in Tabal in 705 BC, his body never recovered, and succeeded by his son Sennacherib. For years scholars doubted a king named Sargon had even existed, since he appeared nowhere outside Isaiah 20:1; the nineteenth-century excavation of his inscriptions at Khorsabad confirmed both his reign and his Samaria campaign.
entries.checked: Sargon's Khorsabad annals claim the conquest and the figure of 27,290 deportees. The Babylonian Chronicle says Shalmaneser V ravaged Samaria in 722, and the common reconstruction is Shalmaneser in 723/722 with Sargon suppressing the city again in 720. Verified 2026-10-04.

entries.title: Sarid
entries.summary: On Zebulun's border, west of Chisloth-tabor. Nobody has pinned down the site, though several ruins in the eastern Jezreel valley have been put forward.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Boundary landmark of the tribe of Zebulun, lying west of Chisloth-tabor (Josh. 19:10, 12). Its exact site is unidentified, though several ruins in the eastern Jezreel valley have been proposed.

entries.title: Saron (Sharon)
entries.summary: Sharon, in its Greek form. Acts 9:35 says the people of Lydda and Saron turned to the Lord when they saw the paralyzed man healed. It is the coastal plain between Joppa and Mount Carmel.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The Greek form of Sharon, the fertile coastal plain of Israel stretching between Joppa and Mount Carmel. Luke uses it in Acts 9:35 to describe the region around Lydda whose residents turned to the Lord after seeing the paralyzed Aeneas healed by Peter.

entries.title: Sarsechim (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: He sat in the middle gate with the other Babylonian officers after Jerusalem's walls were breached, and Jeremiah 39:3 names him once.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of the Babylonian officials present at the fall of Jerusalem, listed among the officers who sat in the middle gate at Nebuchadnezzar's order after the city's walls were breached (Jeremiah 39:3).

witness.excerpt: The names of these generals who ravaged and subdued Jerusalem, if any one desire to know them, were these; Nergal Sharezer, Samgar Nebo, Rabsaris, Sarsechim, and Rabmag.

entries.title: Saruch (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Serug, as Luke spells it. Son of Reu and an ancestor of Abraham, he is one of the names in Luke's genealogy of Jesus.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Saruch is the Greek form, used in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, of the Old Testament name Serug, the son of Reu and an ancestor of Abraham (Luke 3:35; compare Genesis 11:20-23).

entries.title: Satan (An angel in the Old Testament)
entries.summary: The name means adversary. In Job he questions whether Job's goodness is real, and in Zechariah he stands to accuse Joshua the high priest before the angel of the Lord.
entries.books: Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, Acts, Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, 1 Thessalonians, 2 Thessalonians, 1 Timothy, Revelation
entries.label: 12 books
entries.dictNote: Satan, meaning adversary, appears in the Old Testament as a heavenly figure who challenges Job's righteousness before God and accuses the high priest Joshua before the angel of the Lord in Zechariah. The New Testament identifies him more fully as the tempter who tested Jesus in the wilderness, the ruler of this present evil age, and the ultimate enemy of God's people, and Revelation describes his final defeat and eternal judgment.

witness.excerpt: And there was no Satan  nor any evil all the days of the life of Joseph which he lived after his father Jacob, for all the Egyptians honoured the children of Israel all the days of the life of Joseph.

7 For the spirit of hatred worketh together with Satan, through hastiness of spirit, in all things to men's death; but the spirit of love worketh together with the law of God in long-suffering unto the salvation of men.
This spirit goeth always with lying at the right hand of Satan, that with cruelty and lying his works may be wrought.

[For I have read in the book of Enoch, the righteous, that your prince is Satan, and that all the spirits of wickedness and pride will conspire to attend constantly on the sons of Levi, to cause them to sin before the Lord.

Testament of Dan, Chapter 6

6 1, 2 And now, fear the Lord, my children, and beware of Satan and his spirits.

entries.title: Saul (Apostle living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Paul's name before the road to Damascus. Acts keeps calling him Saul for some time after he turned, and the rest of his story is under Paul.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Saul is the Hebrew name the apostle Paul used before his encounter with Christ on the road to Damascus, and Acts continues to call him Saul for some time even after his conversion. See the entry for Paul for the rest of his story.

entries.title: Saul (King living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Israel's first king, found while he was out looking for his father's lost donkeys and anointed by Samuel in private before the tribes confirmed him.
entries.books: 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Chronicles, Psalm, Isaiah, Acts
entries.label: 6 books
entries.dictNote: Saul was Israel's first king, chosen almost by accident while searching for his father's lost donkeys and anointed privately by Samuel before Israel's assembled tribes confirmed him publicly. He started well, rallying Israel against the Ammonites and the Philistines, but lost God's favor through repeated disobedience, most decisively when he offered a sacrifice he had no right to offer and later spared an enemy king God had ordered destroyed. His last three decades were consumed by a jealous pursuit of David, the shepherd Samuel had already anointed to replace him, and he died by his own sword on Mount Gilboa after a defeat by the Philistines. An earlier king of Edom, generations before Israel had any king at all, carried the same name.

witness.excerpt: There was one of the tribe of Benjamin, a man of a good family, and of a virtuous disposition; his name was Kish. He had a son… They called him Saul.
Saul ’s expedition against the nation of the Ammonites , and victory over them, and the spoils he took from them.

Saul envies David for his glorious success; and takes an occasion of entrapping him, from the promise he made him of giving him his daughter in marriage; but this upon condition of his bringing him six hundred heads of the P

entries.curatedNote: Israel's first king, introduced in 1 Samuel 9:2 as tall and striking. Josephus opens his own account the same way Scripture does, through his father Kish's lost donkeys, the errand that puts Saul in Samuel's path in the first place.

entries.title: Sceva (Priest living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Acts calls him a chief priest. No high priest of that name appears in the records, so it probably means he stood high among the Jews of Ephesus.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Jew at Ephesus called a "chief priest," probably meaning he held high standing among the local Jewish community rather than an actual Jerusalem office, since no high priest of that name appears in contemporary records (Acts 19:13-16). His seven sons tried to imitate Paul's exorcisms by invoking the name of Jesus over a demon-possessed man, and the spirit turned on them instead, an episode Luke uses to contrast magical formulas with real apostolic authority.

entries.title: Scythian (People living in Scythia)
entries.summary: Not a name but a people: nomads from the steppes north of the Black Sea and Caspian Sea, and the ancient byword for distant outsiders. Paul puts the Scythian in his list in Colossians 3:11.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Not a personal name but a term for the nomadic peoples who inhabited the steppes north of the Black Sea and Caspian Sea, proverbial in the ancient world as distant and uncivilized outsiders. Paul uses the term in Colossians 3:11 to list categories erased by unity in Christ, alongside Greek, Jew, barbarian, slave, and free, making the point that the gospel's reach extends even to peoples considered furthest outside civilized society.

witness.excerpt: “The Iberians, says he, when they had taken the countrey, sent out by the Caspian road the Sarmatians [a Scythian nation] against the Armenians.” As Dr.

entries.title: Seba
entries.summary: He was a son of Cush, and his descendants are tied to a kingdom somewhere in Africa or Arabia. The Psalms have it bringing tribute.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Seba was a son of Cush, and his descendants are associated with a distant African or Arabian kingdom mentioned in the Psalms alongside Sheba as bringing tribute to Israel's king.

entries.title: Seba (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Son of Cush, whose descendants the Psalms put with Sheba, a far kingdom in Africa or Arabia bringing tribute to Israel's king.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Sebat (Name of the 11th month)
entries.summary: Eleventh month, January into February, and Zechariah dates one of his night visions to the twenty-fourth of it.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Sebat, also spelled Shevat, was the eleventh month of the Hebrew religious calendar, falling roughly in January and February. Zechariah dates one of his night visions to the twenty-fourth day of this month, in the second year of the Persian king Darius (Zechariah 1:7).

entries.title: Secacah
entries.summary: In Judah's wilderness district on the western shore of the Dead Sea, one of six towns listed with Beth-arabah, Middin and En-gedi. Its exact site is unknown.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of six towns assigned to Judah in the wilderness district along the western shore of the Dead Sea, grouped with Beth-arabah, Middin, and En-gedi (Josh. 15:61-62). Its precise site is unidentified, though it lay in the general vicinity later occupied by the Qumran community.

entries.title: Sechu (Secu)
entries.summary: Saul stopped at the great well here and asked where Samuel and David were. It lay between Gibeah and Ramah, and the site has not been identified.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A place between Gibeah and Ramah known for its "great well," where Saul asked after Samuel and David while hunting for David (1 Samuel 19:22). Its precise site has not been identified.

entries.title: Secundus (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: He came from Thessalonica and travelled with Paul through Macedonia near the end of the third missionary journey, and Acts 20:4 is the only place he is named.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Christian from Thessalonica who was part of the group accompanying Paul on his return through Macedonia near the end of his third missionary journey (Acts 20:4).

entries.title: Segub (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Kings names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Segub (Man living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: Named in 1 Chronicles 2:21 and 2:22, in a family list from before the monarchy, and that is all of him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Segub was the son a man named Hiel lost as the cost of rebuilding Jericho's gates, fulfilling a curse Joshua had pronounced centuries earlier against anyone who rebuilt the city.

entries.title: Seir
entries.summary: A rough range of mountains east of the Arabah. It runs from the bottom of the Dead Sea toward the Gulf of Aqabah. The Horites lived there first, and Esau's descendants pushed them out.
entries.books: Genesis, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Isaiah, Ezekiel
entries.label: 9 books
entries.dictNote: Seir most often refers to the rugged mountain range east of the Arabah, stretching from the southern end of the Dead Sea toward the Gulf of Aqabah, originally home to the Horites before the descendants of Esau displaced them and made it the heartland of Edom. The name also belonged to one of the Horite chiefs listed in Genesis, and separately to a lesser known ridge in the territory of Judah, distinct from the Edomite range. Its terrain of narrow valleys and red sandstone cliffs shaped Edom's reputation for natural defenses.

witness.excerpt: And Esau went to the land of Edom, to the mountains of Seir, and dwelt there.
And the sons of Jacob pursued after them to the mountains of Seir.
But Jacob pretending that the cattel were weary, Esau returned to Seir: for there was his place of habitation.
And Jacob smote Esau with an arrow, and he was taken up wounded on Mount Seir, and 4 as he went he died at Anoniram.

entries.title: Seir (Edomite living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Seir the Horite, whose sons are listed in Genesis 36:20 and again in 1 Chronicles 1:38. They were the people in the land before Esau's line took it.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Seirath (Seirah)
entries.summary: Ehud ran here after he killed Eglon, the Moabite king, and rallied Israel before going back down to attack. It was in the hill country of Ephraim, near the border of Benjamin.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A place among the hill country of Ephraim, near the border of Benjamin, where the judge Ehud took refuge after assassinating the Moabite king Eglon at Jericho (Judg. 3:26-27). He rallied Israel's forces there before attacking the leaderless Moabites.

entries.title: Sela
entries.summary: Named once, in 2 Kings, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Sela-hammalekoth (Rock of Escape)
entries.summary: Saul and David were on opposite sides of this mountain in the wilderness of Maon, and Saul was closing in. Then a messenger came with word of the Philistines, and Saul turned back. The name means rock of escape.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Sela-hammalekoth, "the rock of divisions" or "rock of escape," was a cliff in the wilderness of Maon where Saul and David's forces circled opposite sides of a mountain, Saul closing in until a messenger arrived warning of a Philistine raid and forced him to break off the chase (1 Samuel 23:24-28). The name commemorates that narrow escape. Its exact location in the rugged country south of Hebron is unknown.

entries.title: Seled (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: He died without children, according to Judah's genealogy, which traces him back to Jerahmeel through Nadab (1 Chronicles 2:30).
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A descendant of Jerahmeel through Nadab, listed in Judah's genealogy as having died without children (1 Chronicles 2:30).

entries.title: Seleucia
entries.summary: The port of Antioch, near the mouth of the Orontes River, where Paul and Barnabas set sail at the start of their first missionary journey.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Seleucia was the seaport of Antioch, situated near the mouth of the Orontes River, from which Paul and Barnabas sailed at the start of their first missionary journey (Acts 13:4). It was founded by Seleucus I Nicator, one of Alexander's successors, and later became a free city under Rome. Excavations at the site, now in southern Turkey, have uncovered its ancient harbor works and a massive Roman-era rock-cut tunnel built to divert floodwater away from the port.

witness.excerpt: He also demolished Golan, and Seleucia, and what was called the Valley of Antiochus; besides which, he took the strong fortress of Gamala, and stripped Demetrius, who was governor therein, of what he had, on account of the many crimes laid to his charge, and
This city lay upon the borders of Agrippa’s kingdom, as also did Sogana and Seleucia.
Whereupon Vonones fled away on horseback, with a few of his attendants about him, to Seleucia [Upon Tigris].

740, relates, that this Selene Cleopatra was besieged by Tigranes, not in Ptolemais, as here, but after she had left Syria, in Seleucia, a citadel in Mesopotamia; and adds, that when he had kept her a while in prison, he put her to death.

Which made those Jews so vehemently to resent the injuries they received from the Babylonians, that being neither able to fight them, nor bearing to live with them, they went to Seleucia; the principal city of those parts; which was built by Seleucus Nicator.

entries.title: Semachiah (Levite living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A Korahite Levite, son of Shemaiah, put on the gatekeeping for the tabernacle stores under David.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Levite of the Korahite line, son of Shemaiah, appointed as one of the gatekeepers responsible for the tabernacle stores under David (1 Chronicles 26:7).

entries.title: Semei (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Luke 3:26 has his name in the genealogy of Jesus, and nothing else is known about him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A name in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, listed among the ancestors between the exile and David's line (Luke 3:26). Nothing is known about him beyond his place in this list.

witness.excerpt:
Testament of Levi, Chapter 12

12 1, 2 And Gersam took a wife, and she bare to him Lomni and Semei.

entries.title: Senaah
entries.summary: Over three thousand of its people came back from exile with Zerubbabel, one of the largest single groups. Later, men from Senaah worked on Jerusalem's Fish Gate.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Clan or town whose descendants formed one of the largest single groups to return from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel, over three thousand strong (Ezra 2:35; Neh. 7:38). Men from Senaah later helped rebuild Jerusalem's Fish Gate under Nehemiah (Neh. 3:3). Its location is unknown, though some place it near Jericho.

entries.title: Senazar (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Son of Jeconiah, the exiled king also called Jehoiachin. He is in David's royal line in 1 Chronicles 3:18.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A son of Jeconiah, also called Jehoiachin, the exiled king of Judah, listed in the royal genealogy of David's line preserved after the Babylonian captivity (1 Chronicles 3:18).

entries.title: Seneh
entries.summary: The rocky cliff on the south side of the pass at Michmash, facing the crag called Bozez. Jonathan and his armor-bearer climbed it to attack a Philistine garrison.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Seneh was not a person but the rocky cliff on the south side of the pass of Michmash, opposite the crag called Bozez, which Jonathan and his armor-bearer climbed to attack a Philistine garrison (1 Samuel 14:4-5). The narrow gorge of the Wadi es-Suweinit separating the two crags northeast of Jerusalem is still identifiable in the terrain today.

entries.title: Senir (Mount Hermon)
entries.summary: The Amorite name for Mount Hermon. Ezekiel mentions its fir trees, which went into the ships of Tyre.
entries.books: Deuteronomy, 1 Chronicles, Song of Solomon, Ezekiel
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Senir is an alternate Amorite name for Mount Hermon, mentioned in Deuteronomy and in Ezekiel's description of fir trees used to build Tyre's ships.

entries.title: Sennacherib (Emperor living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: He besieged Jerusalem in Hezekiah's reign and boasted in his own inscriptions that he shut Hezekiah up like a bird in a cage. He never claims he took the city.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Sennacherib was the Assyrian king who besieged Jerusalem during Hezekiah's reign, boasting in his own inscriptions of shutting Hezekiah up like a bird in a cage, though notably never claiming to have actually captured the city, matching the biblical account of a siege that broke overnight after Hezekiah's prayer and Isaiah's promise of deliverance.

witness.excerpt: When Sennacherib, king of Assyria, brought along with him all Asia, and encompassed this city round with his army, did he fall by the hands of men? were not those hands lifted up to God in prayers, without meddling with their arms, when

Note also, that Josephus might well put the Jews in mind, as he does here more than once, of their wonderful and truly miraculous deliverance from Sennacherib, king of Assyria, while the Roman army, and himself with them, were now encamped upon and beyond that very spot of ground where the Assyrian army lay seven hundred and eighty years before, and which retained the very na

entries.title: Seorim (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Head of the fourth of the twenty-four priestly divisions David set up so the priests could take turns at the temple.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A priest in David's reign, head of the fourth of the twenty-four priestly divisions established for rotating temple service (1 Chr. 24:8).

entries.title: Sephar
entries.summary: Joktan's descendants settled as far east as Sephar, with Mesha marking the other end (Genesis 10:30). It is commonly identified with Zafar on the southern Arabian coast.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Sephar, the eastern limit of the territory settled by Joktan's descendants in the Table of Nations, paired with Mesha as a boundary marker (Gen. 10:30). It is commonly identified with Zafar (Dhofar) on the southern Arabian coast, a region later known for its frankincense trade.

entries.title: Sepharad (Sardis)
entries.summary: Obadiah names it as a place where Jerusalem's exiles were scattered. They will come back from there, he says, to the towns of the Negev. Where it was is uncertain, though some connect it with Sardis.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Sepharad is named once, as a place where Jerusalem's exiles were scattered and from which they would one day return to resettle the towns of the Negev (Obadiah 1:20). Its identity is uncertain: some scholars connect it with Sardis in Lydia, attested in a bilingual Lydian-Aramaic inscription from that city as "Sparda," while later Jewish tradition took it to mean Spain, giving rise to the term "Sephardic" for Jews of Iberian descent. Some ancient interpreters instead read the word simply as "dispersion" or "diaspora."

entries.title: Sepharvaim
entries.summary: A city the Assyrians took. They moved its people into Samaria after deporting Israel, and they became part of the mix that later made up the Samaritans.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Sepharvaim was a city the Assyrians conquered and whose displaced population they resettled in Samaria after deporting Israel's own population, part of the mixed settlement that later became the Samaritans.

entries.title: Sepharvite (Sepharvaim)
entries.summary: People from Sepharvaim, settled in Samaria by the Assyrians. 2 Kings 17:31 says they burned their children as offerings to their gods Adrammelech and Anammelech.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Sepharvites were people from Sepharvaim, one of the nations the Assyrians transplanted into Samaria after deporting Israel. 2 Kings 17:31 reports that they burned their children as offerings to their gods Adrammelech and Anammelech, and the location of Sepharvaim itself remains uncertain, variously identified with a Syrian or Babylonian site.

entries.title: Seraiah (High Priest living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: The chief priest in Jerusalem when it fell. Nebuchadnezzar had him executed, and the name runs on through several later generations of priests.
entries.label: 5 books
entries.dictNote: Seraiah was a common name among priests and officials in the Old Testament, borne by the chief priest executed by Nebuchadnezzar after Jerusalem's fall and by several others across different generations of priestly and scribal families.

witness.excerpt: Now the rulers that were over them were Johanan, the son of Kareah; and Jezaniah, and Seraiah, and others beside them.

But the general of the Babylonian King now overthrew the city, to the very foundations, and removed the people, and took for prisoners the High Priest, Seraiah; and Zephaniah the Priest that was next to him; and the rulers that guarded the temple, who were three in number; and the eunuch who was over the armed men; and seven friends of Zedekiah, and his Scribe, and sixty other

entries.title: Seraiah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 8 men called Seraiah. This one is a man from the divided-kingdom years, named twice in 2 Kings and Jeremiah.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Seraiah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A man from the divided-kingdom years. Jeremiah names him twice.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Seraiah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 8 men called Seraiah. This one is a man from the divided-kingdom years, named once in 1 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Seraiah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A man from the divided-kingdom years, and Jeremiah is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Seraiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A Seraiah from the years of the return, not the chief priest Nebuchadnezzar executed. The name sits in Ezra 2:2 and again in the Nehemiah lists.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Seraiah (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: 2 Samuel names him once, and he is a man from the united kingdom.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Seraiah (Man living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: A man from the years before the monarchy, and 1 Chronicles is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Sered (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Zebulun's son, who went down to Egypt with Jacob's family and from whom the Seredites came.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Sered was a son of Zebulun who went down to Egypt with Jacob's family and became the ancestor of the clan of the Seredites (Genesis 46:14; Numbers 26:26).

witness.excerpt: Zebulon and his sons; and these are the names of his sons: Sered, and Elon, and Jahleel--four.

entries.title: Sergius (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Sergius Paulus was the Roman proconsul of Cyprus. He sent for Barnabas and Saul because he wanted to hear the word of God, and he believed after he watched Paul strike the sorcerer Elymas blind. An inscription found on Cyprus names him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Sergius Paulus was the Roman proconsul of Cyprus who summoned Barnabas and Saul to hear the word of God, then believed after watching Paul strike the sorcerer Elymas blind (Acts 13:6-12). An inscription discovered on Cyprus names a proconsul Sergius Paulus from roughly this period, lending historical support to Luke's precise use of the title "proconsul" for the island's governor.

entries.title: Serug (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Abraham's great-grandfather, a descendant of Shem, on the line that joins Noah's family to the patriarchs.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Serug was a descendant of Shem and Abraham's great-grandfather, listed in the genealogy connecting Noah's family to the patriarchs.

witness.excerpt: For this reason he called the name of Sêrôḫ, Serug, for every one turned to do all manner of sin and transgression.

The son of Phaleg, whose father was Heber, was Ragau: whose son was Serug: to whom was born Nahor: his son was Terah: who was the father of Abraham: who accordingly was the tenth from Noah:  and was born in the two hundred and ninety second year after the deluge.

entries.title: Seth (Man living at the time before the Flood)
entries.summary: After Cain killed Abel, Eve had a third son. She named him Seth, saying God had given her another child in Abel's place. His line is the one Genesis follows forward.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Seth was Adam and Eve's third son, born after Cain murdered Abel, and Eve named him as a replacement, saying God had appointed her another child in Abel's place. Seth's line is the one Genesis traces forward through ten generations to Noah, and Luke's genealogy of Jesus runs through Seth rather than through Cain's line, which disappears from the record after a handful of generations.

witness.excerpt: Upon Adam's prediction that the world was to be destroyed at one time by the force of fire, and at another time by the violence and quantity of water, they made two pillars: the one of brick, the other of stone… Now this remains in the land of Siriad to this day.

entries.lukeNote: One more link in the genealogy (3:38). Josephus tells a story about his descendants that never made it into Genesis at all, warned of coming destruction by fire and flood, they inscribed their astronomical discoveries on two pillars, one brick and one stone, so at least one would survive. He claims the stone pillar was still standing in his own day.

entries.title: Sethur (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: He went in for Asher when Moses sent twelve spies into Canaan. Like ten of the others, he came back with a report that frightened the people, and Israel wandered forty years for it.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The representative of the tribe of Asher among the twelve spies Moses sent to scout the land of Canaan (Numbers 13:13). Along with ten of the other spies, he returned with a discouraging report that contributed to Israel's forty years of wandering.

entries.title: Shaalabbin (Shaalbim)
entries.summary: Allotted to Dan, but the Danites never fully took it, and Amorites held on there until they were put to forced labour. It is also spelled Shaalbim.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Shaalabbin, also spelled Shaalbim, was a town assigned to the tribe of Dan (Joshua 19:42) that the Danites failed to fully conquer, leaving Amorites in control until they were put to forced labor (Judges 1:35). Centuries later it fell within one of Solomon's twelve administrative districts responsible for supplying the royal court (1 Kings 4:9). It is usually located near Aijalon, in the northern Shephelah.

entries.title: Shaalbonite (Shaalbim)
entries.summary: Eliahba, one of David's thirty mighty men, came from Shaalbim in Dan, and this is what that makes him.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Shaalbonite identifies Eliahba, one of David's thirty mighty men, as being from Shaalbim, a town in the territory allotted to Dan.

entries.title: Shaaph (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Caleb's genealogy in Chronicles has two men by this name. This one is a son of Jahdai, in 1 Chronicles 2:47, and nothing else is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shaaph (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: A son Caleb had by his concubine Maacah.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shaaph was the name of two men in Caleb's genealogy in Chronicles. One was a son of Jahdai (1 Chronicles 2:47), and the other was a son Caleb had by his concubine Maacah, remembered as the founder or ruler of the town of Madmannah (1 Chronicles 2:49).

entries.title: Shaaraim
entries.summary: The name means two gates. When David killed Goliath, the Philistines fled along the road past this Shaaraim, out in the Shephelah.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Two Judean towns carried this name, which means "two gates." One lay in the Shephelah along the route the Philistines fled after David killed Goliath (1 Sam. 17:52; called Sharaim in Josh. 15:36); the other was a Simeonite town listed among that tribe's settlements (1 Chr. 4:31). Some archaeologists identify the first with Khirbet Qeiyafa, a fortified Iron Age site in the Elah Valley with two gates, an unusual feature for the period that would match the town's name and location near the Goliath battle site, though the identification remains debated.

entries.title: Shaashgaz (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: He was the eunuch over the king's concubines in the harem of Ahasuerus. Esther came under his charge after her first night with the king.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shaashgaz was the eunuch in charge of the king's concubines in the harem of Ahasuerus, responsible for the women, including Esther, after their first night with the king (Esther 2:14).

entries.title: Shabbethai (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)

entries.title: Shabbethai (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A Levite who helped explain the law to the people after Ezra read it out, and who was in the middle of the foreign-marriage crisis.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shabbethai was a Levite who helped explain the law to the people after Ezra's public reading and who was involved in addressing the crisis over foreign marriages.

entries.title: Shachia (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Born in Moab, a son of Shaharaim by his wife Hodesh, and listed among the heads of families in Benjamin's genealogy.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A son of Shaharaim by his wife Hodesh, born in Moab and listed among the heads of families in Benjamin's genealogy (1 Chronicles 8:8-10).

entries.title: Shadrach (Daniel's compatriot living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: The Chaldean name given to Hananiah. He was one of the young captives Nebuchadnezzar carried off to Babylon, and he and his two friends would not bow down to the king's image.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Aku’s command, the Chaldean name given to Hananiah, one of the Hebrew youths whom Nebuchadnezzar carried captive to Babylon (Dan. 1:6, 7; 3:12-30). He and his two companions refused to bow down before the image which Nebuchadnezzar had set up on the plains of Dura. Their conduct filled the king with the greatest fury, and he commanded them to be cast into the burning fiery furnace. Here, amid the fiery flames, they were miraculously preserved from harm. Over them the fire had no power, “neither was a hair of their head singed, neither had the smell of fire passed on them.” Thus Nebuchadnezzar learned the greatness of the God of Israel. (See ABEDNEGO.)

witness.excerpt: Daniel he called Baltasar: Ananias, Shadrach: Misael, Meshach: and Azarias, Abednego.

entries.title: Shage (Warrior living at the time of United Monarchy)

entries.title: Shaharaim (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A Benjamite who sent away two wives, Hushim and Baara. Later, in Moab, he had children by his wife Hodesh. Their descendants are listed among the heads of families back in Benjamite land.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Benjamite who divorced two wives, Hushim and Baara, and later fathered children in Moab by his wife Hodesh (1 Chronicles 8:8-11). His descendants are listed among the heads of families back in Benjamite territory.

entries.title: Shahazimah (Shahazumah)
entries.summary: A border town of Issachar. The name means toward the heights, and nobody knows where it was.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A border town of the tribe of Issachar, its name meaning toward the heights (Josh. 19:22). Its exact site is unknown.

entries.title: Shalim (Shaalim)
entries.summary: Saul came through the land of Shalim while he was hunting for his father's stray donkeys, before he was anointed king. Where exactly it lay is uncertain.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The "land of Shalim," a district Saul passed through while searching for his father's stray donkeys before his anointing as king (1 Samuel 9:4). Its location within the central hill country of Benjamin or Ephraim is uncertain.

entries.title: Shalisha
entries.summary: Saul passed through here looking for the lost donkeys too. The name means triple land, and the route puts it in the hill country of Ephraim.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shalisha, a district Saul passed through while searching for his father's lost donkeys (1 Sam. 9:4). Its name, meaning "triple land," and its position in the itinerary suggest it lay in the hill country of Ephraim, in the same general area as the later town of Baal-shalisha (2 Kings 4:42).

entries.title: Shalleketh (Shallecheth)
entries.summary: Not a person. It was a gate on the west side of the temple, on the causeway going up, and the gatekeepers Shuppim and Hosah were put in charge of it.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shalleketh was not a person but the name of a gate on the western side of the Jerusalem temple complex, assigned to the gatekeepers Shuppim and Hosah along the ascending causeway (1 Chronicles 26:16). Its name, from a root meaning 'to cast' or 'throw down,' most likely refers to the raised causeway leading up to it, though the precise sense is debated.

entries.title: Shallum (King living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: He killed the king of Israel and took the throne himself, then was killed in turn after one month.

entries.title: Shallum (Levite living at the time of Exile and Return)

entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Shallum was common enough as a name to belong to several Old Testament figures, most notably a king of northern Israel who assassinated his predecessor and was himself assassinated after only one month on the throne, the shortest reign of any king of Israel.

entries.title: Shalmai (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Head of a family of the Nethinim, the temple servants, whose descendants came back from exile with Zerubbabel. Nehemiah 7:48 spells the name Salmai.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Shalmai was the ancestral head of a family among the Nethinim, the temple servants whose descendants returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:46). The parallel list in Nehemiah 7:48 gives the name as Salmai.

entries.title: Shalman (King living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Hosea 10:14 remembers him for the brutal sack of Beth-arbel and holds it up as a warning to Israel. Most take him to be Shalmaneser V of Assyria.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shalman appears in Hosea 10:14 as the perpetrator of a brutal defeat of Beth-arbel, an event the prophet cites as a warning of the judgment coming on Israel. Most interpreters identify him with Shalmaneser V, the Assyrian king whose forces besieged Samaria and brought the northern kingdom to its end around 722 BC (2 Kings 17:3-6). A minority instead connect the name to Salamanu, a king of Moab recorded as a tribute-payer in the annals of Tiglath-pileser III, since the specific battle Hosea references is not otherwise attested for either ruler.

entries.title: Shalmaneser (King living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: King of Assyria from about 727 to 722 BC. When Hoshea of Israel held back tribute and looked to Egypt, Shalmaneser came and laid siege to Samaria.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shalmaneser V ruled Assyria from about 727 to 722 BC, succeeding his father Tiglath-Pileser III. When King Hoshea of Israel withheld tribute and sought an alliance with Egypt, Shalmaneser invaded and besieged Samaria; the siege lasted roughly three years before the city fell (2 Kings 17:3-6; 18:9-11). Assyrian records are notably silent on his own account of the conquest, since he died around the time Samaria fell and his successor, Sargon II, claimed credit for the city's capture in his own inscriptions, a discrepancy that has long puzzled historians reconciling the biblical and Assyrian records. The Babylonian Chronicle independently confirms that a king by this name reigned briefly in this period, corroborating the biblical timeframe.

entries.title: Shalthiel (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Zerubbabel's father. He came from the exiled king Jehoiachin, so through him David's royal line can be traced through the Babylonian captivity.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Shealtiel was Zerubbabel's father, listed in the genealogies as a descendant of the exiled king Jehoiachin, keeping David's royal line traceable through the Babylonian captivity and into the postexilic period.

entries.title: Shama (Warrior living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of David's mighty men, an Aroerite, named with his brother Jehiel.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of David's mighty men, an Aroerite listed among the roughly thirty warriors named in David's later roster of champions (1 Chronicles 11:44). He is named alongside his brother Jehiel.

entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shemariah was a common name, borne by one of David's warriors who defected to him at Ziklag and by a son of King Rehoboam.

entries.title: Shamgar (Judge living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: Son of Anath. He saved Israel from the Philistines by killing six hundred men with an ox goad, the long pointed pole used to drive cattle, and the Song of Deborah remembers him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shamgar, son of Anath, delivered Israel from a Philistine incursion by killing six hundred men with an ox goad, a long, sharp-tipped pole used for driving cattle (Judges 3:31). He is remembered again in the Song of Deborah as a figure from a dangerous era when travel on the main roads had become unsafe (Judges 5:6).

witness.excerpt: After him Shamgar, the son of Anath, was elected for their governour; but died in the first year of his government.

entries.title: Shamhuth (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Commander of the fifth division of David's army, which served one month each year.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Commander of the fifth division of David's army, serving one month each year in the king's rotating military schedule (1 Chronicles 27:8).

entries.title: Shamir
entries.summary: Tola, the judge, lived at Shamir in the hill country of Ephraim, and Judges 10:1 and 10:2 name it as his home.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shamir was a town in the hill country of Judah, and also the name of a judge, Tola, whose hometown of the same name is mentioned in Ephraim's territory.

entries.title: Shamir

entries.title: Shamma (Warrior living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Son of Zophar, among the leading men of Asher in 1 Chronicles 7:37. He is not Shammah son of Agee, David's warrior, though the spellings sit close.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shamma was a son of Zophar, listed among the leading men of the tribe of Asher in Israel's genealogies (1 Chronicles 7:37). He is distinct from Shammah, son of Agee, one of David's three mightiest warriors; the two names are spelled differently in Hebrew despite their similar English rendering.

entries.title: Shammah (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Genesis 36 has a Shammah among its chiefs, and 1 Samuel 16:9 and 17:13 name one as a brother of David. The name was used more than once.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Shammah was one of David's three mightiest warriors, remembered for single-handedly defending a field of lentils against a Philistine raiding party while the rest of Israel's army fled.

entries.dictNote: Shaphat was Elisha's father, and also the name of one of the twelve spies Moses sent to scout Canaan, representing the tribe of Simeon.

entries.title: Shapper (Mount Shepher)
entries.summary: Mount Shepher, a stop in the wilderness between Kehelathah and Haradah. The name means beauty or brightness. The text gives nothing more.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Mount Shepher was a wilderness station between Kehelathah and Haradah in Israel's itinerary (Num. 33:23-24). Its name means beauty or brightness, but the text gives no other details, and its location among the mountains of the Sinai peninsula has not been identified.

entries.title: Sharai (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of the sons of Bani who had married a foreign wife and agreed to send her away under Ezra's reform.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Sharai was one of the men listed in Ezra 10 who had married foreign wives during the postexilic period and agreed to separate from them as part of Ezra's covenant reform. He is identified as one of the sons of Bani.

entries.title: Sharar (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)

entries.title: Sharesh (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Sharezer (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)

entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Sharezer, along with his brother Adrammelech, assassinated their father Sennacherib, king of Assyria, an event recorded briefly in both 2 Kings and Isaiah.

witness.excerpt: The names of these generals who ravaged and subdued Jerusalem, if any one desire to know them, were these; Nergal Sharezer, Samgar Nebo, Rabsaris, Sarsechim, and Rabmag.

entries.title: Sharonite

entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Sharonite identifies Shitrai, the official David put in charge of the royal herds grazing in the plain of Sharon, the fertile coastal region between Joppa and Mount Carmel.

entries.title: Sharuhen

entries.title: Sharuhen
entries.summary: A town of Simeon inside Judah's land, called Shaaraim in 1 Chronicles 4:31. Egyptian records describe a fortress by this name that the Hyksos held.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Sharuhen, a town allotted to the tribe of Simeon within Judah's territory (Josh. 19:6), called Shaaraim in the parallel list of 1 Chronicles 4:31. Egyptian records describe a fortress by this name that the Hyksos held against a lengthy siege by Pharaoh Ahmose after their expulsion from Egypt; the biblical town is commonly identified with Tell el-Far'ah, near the Negev border with Gaza.

entries.title: Shashai (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)

entries.title: Shaulites (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)

entries.title: Shaveh
entries.summary: The king of Sodom came out to meet Abram in the Valley of Shaveh. Abram had just rescued Lot and beaten the eastern kings. It was also called the King's Valley.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The Valley of Shaveh, also called the King's Valley, was where the king of Sodom went out to meet Abram after his rescue of Lot and victory over the invading eastern kings (Gen. 14:17). The same valley is named again generations later as the site where Absalom set up a monument to himself (2 Sam. 18:18), though its precise location near Jerusalem is no longer known.

entries.title: Shaveh Kiriathaim
entries.summary: The plain around Kiriathaim, east of the Jordan. The eastern kings beat the Emim there in Genesis 14:5.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shaveh Kiriathaim was the plain surrounding Kiriathaim, a town east of the Jordan where the eastern coalition of kings defeated the Emim during the campaign described in Genesis 14:5, before Chedorlaomer moved south to strike Sodom and Gomorrah. Kiriathaim later belonged to Moab and is named in the Mesha Stele (Moabite Stone), where King Mesha claims credit for rebuilding it alongside other Moabite towns known from the Bible. The exact location of the surrounding plain is not established.

entries.title: Shavsha (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of David's royal secretaries. The same man seems to turn up as Seraiah, Sheva and Shisha in other lists, which is how court names tended to drift.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of David's royal secretaries (1 Chronicles 18:16); the same official appears under the names Seraiah in 2 Samuel 8:17, Sheva in 2 Samuel 20:25, and Shisha in 1 Kings 4:3, the variation typical of how court titles and names were transliterated across parallel records.

entries.title: Sheal (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A son of Bani who had married a foreign wife and agreed to send her away under Ezra (Ezra 10:29). Nothing more is recorded of him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Sheal was one of the sons of Bani listed among the Israelites who had married foreign wives during the exile and agreed to separate from them under Ezra's reform (Ezra 10:29). Nothing more is recorded of him.

entries.title: Shealtiel (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Zerubbabel's father, and the name means asked of God.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Asked for of God, father of Zerubbabel (Ezra 3:2, 8; Neh. 12:1).

entries.title: Shear-jashub (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Isaiah's son, whose name was a message, a remnant shall return, and Isaiah took the boy with him when he went out to meet King Ahaz.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shear-jashub, meaning "a remnant shall return," was the symbolic name Isaiah gave to his son, whom the prophet brought along when he confronted King Ahaz of Judah with a message of assurance during the Syro-Ephraimite crisis (Isaiah 7:3). The name itself functioned as a walking prophecy, promising that even after judgment a remnant of Israel would survive and return to God.

entries.title: Sheariah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of Saul's descendants through Jonathan's son Merib-baal, kept in the Chronicles genealogy of Saul's line. Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Sheariah was a descendant of Saul through Jonathan's son Merib-baal, part of the genealogy Chronicles preserves for Saul's line after the family's near destruction (1 Chronicles 8:38; 9:44). Nothing further is recorded about him.

entries.title: Sheba
entries.summary: The Queen of Sheba came a long way, probably from southern Arabia. She came to test Solomon with hard questions. She went home saying the reports she had heard did not tell the half of it.
entries.books: 1 Kings, 2 Chronicles, Job, Psalm, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel
entries.label: 7 books
entries.dictNote: Two figures named Sheba appear in the Old Testament. The Queen of Sheba traveled a great distance, likely from southern Arabia, to test Solomon's famous wisdom with hard questions, and left declaring the reports she had heard didn't do him justice. A different Sheba, a Benjamite, led a short-lived rebellion against David shortly after Absalom's revolt was crushed.

entries.title: Sheba (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)

entries.title: Shebah (Beersheba)
entries.summary: Not a person but a well. Isaac's servants dug it, and Genesis 26:33 says it gave Beersheba its name, the well of the oath, or of seven.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Not a person but the well Isaac's servants dug that gave the city of Beersheba its name, "well of the oath" or "well of seven," according to Genesis 26:33. The chapter presents it as the third in a sequence of wells contested between Isaac's household and the Philistines of Gerar, resolved this time by a covenant oath between Isaac and Abimelech rather than by further conflict.

entries.title: Shebam
entries.summary: Good grazing land east of the Jordan, taken from Sihon, which Reuben and Gad asked for because of their flocks.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Shebam was a pastoral town east of the Jordan, in territory taken from Sihon, requested by and eventually granted to the tribes of Reuben and Gad because of its excellent grazing land (Numbers 32:3-4, 38). It is likely the same place called Sibmah elsewhere, later famous for its vineyards until Moab overran it (Isaiah 16:8-9; Jeremiah 48:32).

entries.title: Shebna (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)

entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Shebna was a palace administrator under Hezekiah whom Isaiah condemned for carving himself an extravagant tomb and prophesied he would be removed from office and die in a foreign land instead, replaced by the more faithful Eliakim.

witness.excerpt: But he did not himself come out to them, for fear; but he sent three of his most intimate friends; the name of one was Eliakim, who was over the Kingdom; and Shebna, and Joah the recorder.

entries.title: Shechem
entries.summary: Abram stopped here when he first came into the land, and Joseph's brothers were grazing the flocks near it when Joseph went looking for them. The city took its name from a Canaanite prince.
entries.books: Genesis, Joshua, Judges, 1 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Psalm, Jeremiah
entries.label: 8 books
entries.dictNote: Shechem, as a person, was the Canaanite prince whose rape of Jacob's daughter Dinah triggered the massacre carried out by her brothers Simeon and Levi; the city of the same name was also where Joseph's brothers were pasturing flocks when he was sent to check on them, and later the place where Israel renewed its covenant under Joshua.

witness.excerpt: For when I went to Shechem to bring ointment for the flocks, and Reuben to Dothan, where were our necessaries and all our stores, Judah my brother sold him to the Ishmaelites.
And from thence he went to Shechem, together with all the people, and raised an altar where Moses had before­hand directed.
For from this day forward shall Shechem be 3 called a city of imbeciles; for as a man mocketh a fool, so did we mock them.

entries.title: Shelah (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Judah's third son by his Canaanite wife. Judah held him back from marrying Tamar, the widow, as custom said he should. That broken promise is what drove Tamar to disguise herself.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Shelah was Judah's third son by his Canaanite wife, and Judah withheld him from marrying his widowed daughter-in-law Tamar as custom required, a broken promise that led Tamar to disguise herself and conceive by Judah directly instead.

witness.excerpt: 6 And I wished to give Shelah also to her, but his mother did not permit it; for she wrought evil against Tamar, because she was not of the daughters of Canaan, as she also herself was.
She bare me Er, and Onan and Shelah; and two of them the Lord smote: for Shelah lived, and his children are ye.
And while I was away she went and took for 4 Shelah a wife from Canaan.
Japheth, and in the fourth year he begat a son, and called his name Shelah;  for he said: "Truly I have been sent."  6.
And Judah said unto Tamar, his daughter-in-law: "Remain in thy father's house as a widow till Shelah my son be grown up, and I shall give thee to him to wife." 7.

entries.title: Shem (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Noah's oldest son. The Semitic peoples, Abraham's line among them, all trace back to him, and Genesis 10 follows his descendants down to Eber.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Shem was Noah's oldest son and the ancestor of the Semitic peoples, including Abraham's line, and Genesis 10 traces his descendants through Elam, Asshur, and Arphaxad down to Eber, whose name is the likely source of the word Hebrew. Noah blessed Shem specifically after the flood, setting his line apart even among his brothers.

witness.excerpt: Terah begat Abram in his seventieth year. Nahor begat Haran, when he was one hundred and twenty years old… Terah: who was the father of Abraham: who accordingly was the tenth from Noah.

entries.lukeNote: Noah's son, one generation up from Terah in Luke's chain (3:36). Josephus counts out the exact same ten generations from Noah to Abraham that Luke's genealogy implies, just narrated instead of listed.

entries.title: Shema
entries.summary: A town of Judah in the Negev, among the southernmost cities near the border of Edom. It is generally identified with the Sheba of Joshua 19:2.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shema was a town allotted to the tribe of Judah in the Negev, listed in Joshua 15:26 among the southernmost cities near the border of Edom; it is generally identified with Sheba in the parallel list at Joshua 19:2, and its exact site is unidentified. Easton's dictionary lists three unrelated men also named Shema under the same headword, but the entry here, tied to Joshua 15:26, concerns only the town.

entries.title: Shema (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Caleb's line through Hebron runs to this Shema, who fathered Raham (1 Chronicles 2:43–44). At least four men carry the name in the lists.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shema is a name shared by at least four different men in the genealogical lists of Chronicles and Nehemiah, not a single figure. One Shema was a descendant of Caleb through Hebron, in the tribe of Judah, and fathered Raham (1 Chronicles 2:43-44). A second was an ancestor of Bela, a leading man among the Reubenites who lived on the plateau east of the Jordan (1 Chronicles 5:8). A third was a Benjamite clan leader who helped drive the inhabitants out of Gath (1 Chronicles 8:13), and a fourth stood on the wooden platform beside Ezra when he read the Law aloud to the assembled people at the Water Gate in Jerusalem (Nehemiah 8:4).

entries.title: Shemeber (King living at the time of the Patriarchs)
