entries.title: Sheminith (A musical term)
entries.summary: Meaning eighth, and a direction rather than a name. It sits in two psalm headings and in the record of temple worship.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Sheminith, meaning “eighth,” is a musical direction rather than a personal name, appearing in the titles of Psalms 6 and 12 and in the description of Levitical musicians in Chronicles. Its exact meaning is debated; most understand it as an instruction to play or sing in a lower octave or register (1 Chronicles 15:21).

entries.title: Shemiramoth (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 2 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shemiramoth (Singer living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: David made him one of the musicians when the ark was carried into Jerusalem. He played the harp, a Levite among the temple musicians.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shemiramoth was a Levite David appointed as a musician for the ark's procession into Jerusalem, playing the harp among the temple musicians.

entries.title: Shen
entries.summary: A landmark, apparently a rock or ridge, between Mizpah and Jeshanah. After the Philistines were beaten in 1 Samuel 7, Samuel set up a stone between Mizpah and Shen.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shen was a landmark, apparently a rock or ridge, between Mizpah and Jeshanah in the hill country of Benjamin. After Israel's victory over the Philistines described in 1 Samuel 7, Samuel set up a stone between Mizpah and Shen and named it Ebenezer, "stone of help," to commemorate the Lord's aid in battle. Its exact site has not been identified.

entries.title: Shepham
entries.summary: A point on the eastern border Israel was meant to have, between Hazar-enan and Riblah (Numbers 34:10–11). Nobody can place it exactly.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A boundary point named in the description of Israel's ideal eastern border in Numbers 34:10-11, lying on the line between Hazar-enan and Riblah. Its exact location, likely somewhere near the headwaters region north and east of the Sea of Galilee, is unknown.

entries.title: Shephatiah (David's son living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: 2 Samuel and 1 Chronicles name him twice, and he is a man from the united kingdom.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Shephatiah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A man from the divided-kingdom years. 1 Chronicles names him once.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shephatiah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shephatiah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 9 men called Shephatiah. This one is a man from the divided-kingdom years, named once in 2 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shephatiah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A man from the divided-kingdom years. Jeremiah names him once.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shephatiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A family name among the returning exiles in Ezra 2:4 and Nehemiah 7:9. Ezra 8:8 has more of the same family coming back later.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Shephatiah was a common Old Testament name, borne by one of David's sons, a royal official who wanted Jeremiah executed for his discouraging prophecies during the siege of Jerusalem, and several postexilic figures.

entries.title: Shephatiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of 9 men called Shephatiah. This one is a man from the exile and the return, named twice in Ezra and Nehemiah.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Shephatiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A man from the exile and the return, and 1 Chronicles is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shephatiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A man from the exile and the return, and Nehemiah is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shephi (Edomite living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Son of Shobal, of the line of Seir the Horite, among Edom's clan chiefs, and Genesis 36:23 spells him Shepho.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Shephi was a son of Shobal descended from Seir the Horite, listed among Edom's clan chiefs (1 Chronicles 1:40). The parallel genealogy in Genesis 36:23 gives his name as Shepho.

entries.title: Shephuphan (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Bela's son, Benjamin's grandson. The lists also call him Shupham, Shuppim and Muppim, and the Shuphamites came from him.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Shephuphan was a son of Bela and grandson of Benjamin, ancestor of the clan of the Shuphamites; the name also appears as Shupham, Shuppim, and Muppim in parallel genealogies (Numbers 26:39; 1 Chronicles 8:5).

entries.title: Sherah (Woman living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: She built both towns called Beth-horon, and a third that carries her own name, Uzzen-sherah. She was a daughter of Beriah, in Ephraim's genealogy.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A daughter of Beriah in Ephraim's genealogy, credited with building the two towns of Beth-horon, later strategically important sites on the road from the coastal plain to Jerusalem, and a third town named after her, Uzzen-sherah (1 Chr. 7:24). She is one of the rare women in Chronicles' genealogies credited directly with a building project.

entries.title: Sherebiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A Levite Ezra went out of his way to bring along on the journey back to Jerusalem, because of his skill and standing.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Sherebiah was a Levite Ezra specifically recruited to accompany the returning exiles to Jerusalem, valued for his skill and standing among the Levitical families.

entries.title: Sherebiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A Levite in the Nehemiah lists. He sealed the covenant in Nehemiah 10:12 and appears again among the Levites of Nehemiah 12.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Sheshach (Babylon)
entries.summary: Babylon in code. Swap each Hebrew letter for the one counted from the other end of the alphabet, a cipher called atbash, and Babylon comes out as Sheshach. Jeremiah uses it in his oracles.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Sheshach was not a person but a coded name for Babylon, formed by substituting each Hebrew letter with its counterpart counted from the opposite end of the alphabet, a cipher called atbash. Jeremiah used the name in oracles against Babylon, and its parallel with "Babylon" in the surrounding verses confirms the identification (Jeremiah 25:26; 51:41).

entries.title: Sheshai (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: One of the sons of Anak. Caleb drove him out of Hebron when he finally claimed the land promised to him decades earlier.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Sheshai was one of the descendants of Anak, the giant clan Caleb personally drove out of Hebron once he finally claimed the land God had promised him decades earlier.

entries.title: Sheshan (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: He had daughters and no sons, so Chronicles says he married one of them to his Egyptian servant to keep the family line going.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Sheshan had no sons, only daughters, and Chronicles records that he gave one of them in marriage to his own Egyptian servant to continue his family line.

entries.title: Sheshbazzar (Governor living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: He was handed the temple vessels to carry back, and Ezra 5:14 and 5:16 call him governor. He is probably Zerubbabel under another name.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: O sun-god, defend the lord! (Ezra 1:8, 11), probably another name for Zerubbabel (q.v.), Ezra 2:2; Hag. 1:12, 14; Zech. 4:6, 10.

entries.title: Sheth (Man living at the time before the Flood)
entries.summary: Not a man. Balaam's oracle says a coming ruler of Israel will crush all the sons of Sheth, and most modern translations read it as sons of tumult.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Sheth here is not the name of a person but part of a phrase in Balaam's oracle predicting that a coming ruler of Israel will crush all the sons of Sheth (Numbers 24:17). Most modern translations render this sons of tumult rather than treating Sheth as a proper name, understanding it as poetic language for Israel's warlike neighbors, likely Moab. It is unrelated to the antediluvian patriarch Seth, who is recorded separately.

entries.title: Shethar (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of the seven princes of Media and Persia who could go in to King Ahasuerus and advise him (Esther 1:14).
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shethar was one of the seven princes of Media and Persia who had access to King Ahasuerus and advised him at the start of the book of Esther (Esther 1:14).

entries.title: Shetharboznai (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A Persian official. With Tattenai he asked by what authority the Jews were rebuilding the temple. The inquiry dug up Cyrus's original decree, and the work got official backing instead of being stopped.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shethar-bozenai was a Persian official who, along with Tattenai, questioned the Jews' authority to rebuild the temple, an inquiry that ultimately confirmed Cyrus's original decree and led to official support for the project instead.

entries.title: Sheva (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: There are two. One is a son of Caleb in Judah's genealogy (1 Chronicles 2:49), and the other is one of David's scribes, likely the same official called Seraiah elsewhere.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Two men named Sheva appear in the Old Testament: a son of Caleb in the tribal genealogy of Judah (1 Chronicles 2:49), and one of David's royal scribes or secretaries (2 Samuel 20:25), likely the same official called Seraiah or Shisha elsewhere in the parallel lists of David's officials. Nothing more is recorded of either.

witness.excerpt: He made Sheva the scribe, and appointed Zadok and Abiathar the high priests.

entries.title: Shichemites (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: The clan of Shechem, Manasseh's grandson through Gilead, counted in Numbers 26. They share the name of the city of Shechem.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shichemites were the clan descended from Shechem, a grandson of Manasseh through Gilead, counted among the families of Manasseh in the Numbers 26 census. The clan shares its ancestor's name with the well-known city of Shechem, though the two are only indirectly related.

entries.title: Shicron (Shikkeron)
entries.summary: A landmark on Judah's northern border, between Ekron and Jabneel near the coast. Nothing else is recorded of it, and the site is unknown.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shicron marked one of the landmarks along the northern boundary of Judah's territory, situated between Ekron and Jabneel near the Mediterranean coastal plain (Joshua 15:11). Nothing else is recorded of it, and its exact site is unidentified.

entries.title: Shiggaion (A musical term)
entries.summary: Psalm 7 carries it in the heading, and Habakkuk has the plural. It probably marks something irregular and worked up.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Not a person but a Hebrew musical or poetic term found in the title of Psalm 7, and in its plural form, shigionoth, in Habakkuk 3:1, likely describing an irregular, emotionally intense style of composition, possibly connected to a root meaning "to wander" or "to reel." Its precise musical meaning is uncertain, since no other ancient source explains the term.

entries.title: Shihon (Shion)
entries.summary: A town of Issachar, named only in Joshua 19:19, and still not found.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shihon, a town within the tribal allotment of Issachar, named only in Joshua 19:19. Its location has not been identified.

entries.title: Shihor (Brook of Egypt)
entries.summary: The stream on Egypt's northeastern border. It marks the southwestern edge of the land promised to Israel.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Shihor (Nile)
entries.summary: A stream on Egypt's northeastern edge, used as the marker for the southwest corner of the land promised to Israel.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Shihor was a stream or waterway on Egypt's northeastern border, used in the Old Testament as a marker for the southwestern edge of the land promised to Israel.

entries.title: Shihor-libnath
entries.summary: Not a person but a stream on the southern boundary of Asher. It is generally identified with the Nahr Zarqa, which rises in the Carmel range.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shihor-libnath is not a person but a stream marking part of the southern boundary of the tribe of Asher, mentioned in Joshua 19:26. It is generally identified with the Nahr Zarqa, a river that rises in the Carmel range and empties into the Mediterranean just north of Caesarea. The name, meaning roughly "black-white," may reflect the river's changing color, muddy after rain and clear afterward, and crocodiles were still reported in the Zarqa well into the nineteenth century, a detail later travelers connected to ancient Egyptian associations with the area.

entries.title: Shilhi (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: His daughter Azubah married King Asa and was the mother of King Jehoshaphat, and that is why he is named.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Shilhi was the father of Azubah, who became the wife of King Asa and mother of King Jehoshaphat of Judah (1 Kings 22:42; 2 Chronicles 20:31).

entries.title: Shilhim (Sharuhen)
entries.summary: A town in the south of Judah, near the border with Simeon. It is generally identified with the Sharuhen of Joshua 19:6, which Egyptian sources know as a fortress.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shilhim was a town in the southern territory of Judah near the border with Simeon (Joshua 15:32), generally identified with Sharuhen in the parallel list at Joshua 19:6. Sharuhen appears in Egyptian sources as the fortress where the Hyksos made their last stand after being driven from Egypt, besieged for three years by Pharaoh Ahmose according to the tomb inscription of his officer Ahmose son of Ebana, one of the clearer points of contact between the biblical Negev towns and independently dated Egyptian history.

entries.title: Shillem (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Son of Naphtali. He went down to Egypt with Jacob, and his clan was counted again in the wilderness. Chronicles calls him Shallum.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Shillem was a son of Naphtali and ancestor of the Shillemite clan, counted among the families of Israel who went to Egypt with Jacob and later numbered in the wilderness census; he is also called Shallum in the parallel genealogy of Chronicles (Genesis 46:24; Numbers 26:49; 1 Chronicles 7:13).

entries.title: Shillemites (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: The clan of Shillem, Naphtali's son, in the Numbers 26 census.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shillemites were the clan descended from Shillem, a son of Naphtali, counted in the Numbers 26 census; the same man is called Shallum in 1 Chronicles 7:13.

entries.title: Shiloah (Siloam)
entries.summary: Isaiah set the quiet waters of Shiloah, a gentle channel bringing water from the Gihon spring into Jerusalem, against the flood of the Euphrates. The people had turned down the one, and the other was coming. It was later linked with the pool of Siloam.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The "waters of Shiloah," a gently flowing channel carrying water from the Gihon spring into Jerusalem, later linked with the pool of Siloam (Isaiah 8:6). Isaiah contrasts its quiet flow with the overwhelming flood of the Euphrates as an image of trusting God rather than seeking help from Assyria. The city's ancient water system that this name refers to is documented archaeologically by Hezekiah's Siloam Tunnel and the Hebrew inscription its diggers left inside it, discovered in 1880.

entries.title: Shiloh
entries.summary: The tabernacle stood at Shiloh, north of Bethel in Ephraim, for most of the time of the judges. Young Samuel served there. After the Philistines captured the ark, the place faded.
entries.books: Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, 1 Kings, Psalm, Jeremiah
entries.label: 6 books
entries.dictNote: Shiloh was a town in Ephraim, north of Bethel, where the tabernacle stood through most of the period of the judges until the Philistines captured the ark and the sanctuary's importance faded; it was here that young Samuel served under Eli and heard God's call. Centuries after its destruction, Jeremiah cited Shiloh's ruined fate as a warning to Jerusalem. The same word appears in Jacob's blessing of Judah in Genesis 49:10, where “until Shiloh comes” has traditionally been read as a title for the coming Messiah, though translators have long debated whether the term there is a place name, a title, or a corrupted phrase.

witness.excerpt: So they gathered themselves to Shiloh, out of a prodigious and a just anger; and assembling in a great congregation before the tabernacle, they immediately resolved to take arms, and to treat the inhabitants of Gibeah as enemies.

When the news of this defeat came to Shiloh, with that of the captivity of the ark: for a certain young man, a Benjamite, who was in the action, came as a messenger thither: the whole city was full of lamentations.
Now Elcanah came with his wives to the city Shiloh, to sacrifice, for there it was that the tabernacle of God was fixed, as we have formerly said.
And we fought with them and routed them; and their allies from Shiloh we slew, and we did not leave 3 them power to come in against us.
So she did as her husband bade her, and changed her habit, and came to the city Shiloh, for there did Ahijah live.

entries.title: Shiloh (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Jacob's blessing on Judah says the sceptre stays "until Shiloh comes," and nobody has ever agreed what that means. Some read Shiloh as a title for a coming ruler from Judah.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: In Jacob's deathbed blessing over Judah, the phrase "until Shiloh comes" is one of the most debated lines in Genesis (Gen. 49:10). Some read "Shiloh" as a title for a coming ruler descended from Judah, a reading Jewish and Christian interpreters alike have long taken as messianic; others, following a different vocalization of the Hebrew, render it "until he comes to Shiloh," pointing instead to the town where the tabernacle was later set up. What is gathered here is that prophetic phrase; the town itself is listed separately.

entries.title: Shilonite (Shiloh)
entries.summary: A man from Shiloh. It is what they called the prophet Ahijah, who tore his cloak into twelve pieces to show that God would split Solomon's kingdom.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Shilonite names the prophet Ahijah, who came from Shiloh and famously tore his cloak into twelve pieces to announce that God would split Solomon's kingdom. The plural form elsewhere describes a Judahite clan descended from Shelah, Judah's youngest son, rather than people from the town of Shiloh.

entries.title: Shilshah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A son of Zophah, among Asher's heads of families and fighting men. Nothing else is recorded of him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A son of Zophah, listed among the descendants of Asher noted in Chronicles as heads of families and mighty warriors (1 Chronicles 7:37-40). Nothing else is recorded of him.

entries.title: Shimah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A Benjamite, son of Jehiel the father of Gibeon, whose family settled in Jerusalem. 1 Chronicles 9:38 calls him Shimeam.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Benjamite, son of Jehiel the father of Gibeon, listed among the families that settled in Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 8:32). The parallel genealogy in 1 Chronicles 9:38 calls the same man Shimeam.

entries.title: Shimath
entries.summary: An Ammonite woman. Her son Jehozabad and another man killed King Joash of Judah in his bed, reportedly in revenge for the prophet Zechariah.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Shimath was an Ammonite woman whose son Jehozabad, along with an accomplice, assassinated King Joash of Judah in his bed, reportedly in revenge for Joash's earlier execution of the prophet Zechariah (2 Kings 12:21; 2 Chronicles 24:26). She is identified only through this connection to her son.

entries.title: Shimea (Levite living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Chronicles uses the name often. It belongs to David's brother at 1 Chronicles 2:13 and 20:7, to one of David's sons at 3:5, and to a Levite at 6:30.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shimea was a common name, borne by one of David's brothers and by one of David's own sons.

witness.excerpt: Now the person who was sent against them by David out of his army was Jonathan, the son of Shimea, who fought this man in a single combat, and slew him; and as he was the person who gave the turn to the battle, he gained the greatest reputation for courage therein.

entries.title: Shimea (Levite living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a Levite from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shimeah (David's adversary living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: The man who came out cursing David as he fled Jerusalem, throwing stones and calling him a man of blood. He is from Saul's house, which is the point of it.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Shimeah, also spelled Shammah, was one of David's older brothers, the third son of Jesse, and the father of Jonadab, the nephew who advised Amnon on how to get Tamar alone.

witness.excerpt: When David was at Bahurim, a place so called, there came out a kinsman of Saul's, whose name was Shimei, and threw stones at him, and gave him reproachful words; and as his friends stood about the king and protected him, he persevered still more in his reproaches, and called him a bloody man, and the author of all sorts o

entries.title: Shimeah (David's brother living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: David's brother, a son of Jesse. His son Jonadab was the shrewd nephew who helped Amnon get Tamar alone.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shimeah was one of David's brothers, a son of Jesse, and the father of Jonadab, the shrewd nephew who advised Amnon in his plot against Tamar (2 Samuel 13:3); he is also called Shimea elsewhere. A second, unrelated Shimeah was a Benjamite descended from Gibeon, also known as Shimeam (1 Chronicles 8:32; 9:38).

entries.title: Shimeah (Levite living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A levite from the divided-kingdom years. 1 Chronicles names him once.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shimeah (Levite living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A levite from the divided-kingdom years. 2 Chronicles names him once.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shimeah (Levite living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A levite from the divided-kingdom years. 1 Chronicles names him twice.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shimeah (Levite living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Exodus and 2 other books name him 5 times, and he is a Levite from the wilderness years.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Shimeah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 17 men called Shimeah. This one is a man from the divided-kingdom years, named once in 1 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shimeah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A man from the divided-kingdom years, and 1 Chronicles is the only book that names him. The verse is 1 Chronicles 5:4.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shimeah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shimeah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A man from the divided-kingdom years, and 1 Chronicles is the only book that names him. The verses are 1 Chronicles 4:26 and 1 Chronicles 4:27.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shimeah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 2 Chronicles names him twice, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.

entries.title: Shimeah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A man from the divided-kingdom years, and 1 Chronicles is the only book that names him. The verse is 1 Chronicles 27:27.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shimeah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A man from the exile and the return. Esther names him once.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shimeah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Ezra names him once, and he is a man from the exile and the return.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shimeah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of 17 men called Shimeah. This one is a man from the exile and the return, named once in Ezra.

entries.title: Shimeah (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 17 men called Shimeah. This one is a man from the united kingdom, named twice in 1 Kings.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shimeah (Singer living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 17 men called Shimeah. This one is a man from the united kingdom, named once in 1 Chronicles.

entries.title: Shimeam (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Jehiel founded Gibeon, and Shimeam was one of his descendants among the Benjamite families who resettled Jerusalem. 1 Chronicles 8:32 spells the same man differently.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shimeam was a descendant of Jehiel, the founder of Gibeon, listed among the Benjamite families that resettled Jerusalem after the exile in 1 Chronicles 9:38. The parallel genealogy in 1 Chronicles 8:32 gives the same figure's name as Shimeah, one of several minor spelling variants between the two overlapping lists. Nothing further is recorded of him.

entries.title: Shimeathites (Scribal group in the Old Testament)
entries.summary: Scribes. They were one of the families living at Jabez, Kenites who came from Hammath, the father of the house of Rechab.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shimeathites were one of the families of scribes living at Jabez, named in 1 Chronicles 2:55 and identified there as Kenites descended from Hammath, father of the house of Rechab.

entries.title: Shimon (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A man of Judah whose four sons are listed in 1 Chronicles 4:20, with no story attached.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A man of Judah whose four sons appear in a brief, otherwise unexplained genealogical note in 1 Chronicles 4:20.

entries.title: Shimon-meron (Shimron)
entries.summary: Joshua beat thirty-one kings west of the Jordan, and the king of Shimon-meron was one of them. It is generally taken to be the same place as Shimron.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shimon-meron was one of the thirty-one Canaanite royal cities whose kings Joshua defeated west of the Jordan, named only in the summary list of Joshua 12:20. It is generally taken to be the same place as Shimron, listed among the cities of the northern coalition Joshua defeated at the Waters of Merom (Joshua 11:1) and later assigned to Zebulun (Joshua 19:15).

entries.title: Shimrath (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A Benjamite, one of Shimhi's sons, mentioned once and never again.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shimrath was a Benjamite listed among the sons of Shimhi in the tribal genealogy of Benjamin (1 Chronicles 8:21). Nothing further is known about him beyond this single mention.

entries.title: Shimri (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 4 men called Shimri. This one is a man from the divided-kingdom years, named once in 1 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shimri (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: In 1 Chronicles 4:37 he is one link in a short family line, and nothing more is said of him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shimri (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A common name among David's warriors and the families Chronicles lists. This one gets a single verse.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shimri was a common name among David's warriors and Levitical families listed in Chronicles.

entries.title: Shimri (Warrior living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a warrior from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shimrith (Moabite living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A Moabite woman whose son Jehozabad joined the plot that killed King Joash, in revenge for the prophet Zechariah (2 Chronicles 24:26).
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shimrith was a Moabite woman whose son Jehozabad was one of two officials who conspired to assassinate King Joash of Judah in retaliation for the killing of the prophet Zechariah (2 Chronicles 24:25-26). The parallel account in 2 Kings 12:21 calls her Shomer instead.

entries.title: Shimron
entries.summary: Named twice, in Joshua, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shimron (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: A son of Issachar, and the Shimronites took their name from him.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Shimron is a name shared by a place and a person in the Old Testament. It names a son of Issachar who gave his name to the clan of the Shimronites (Genesis 46:13; Numbers 26:24; 1 Chronicles 7:1), and, unrelated in origin, a royal Canaanite city whose king joined Jabin of Hazor's coalition against Joshua at the Waters of Merom (Joshua 11:1-2) before being allotted to Zebulun (Joshua 19:15); the city is generally identified with a site near the northern edge of the Jezreel Valley a few miles west of Nazareth.

witness.excerpt: Issachar and his sons; and these are the names of his sons: Tola, and Phûa,  and Jâsûb,  and Shimron--five.

entries.title: Shimronites (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: The clan of Shimron, Issachar's son, counted in Numbers 26.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shimronites were the clan descended from Shimron, a son of Issachar, counted in the Numbers 26 census.

entries.title: Shimshai (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A Persian scribe. He and Rehum wrote to King Artaxerxes against the rebuilding of Jerusalem, and the letter stopped the work for a time.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shimshai was a Persian scribe who, along with Rehum, wrote a letter to King Artaxerxes opposing the rebuilding of Jerusalem, an effort that successfully halted the work for a time.

entries.title: Shinab (King living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Admah was one of the five cities of the plain, with Sodom and Gomorrah, and Shinab was its king when Chedorlaomer came. He was one of the kings who rebelled.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shinab was king of Admah, one of the five cities of the plain that included Sodom and Gomorrah, at the time of the invasion by Chedorlaomer and his allied kings described in Genesis 14:2. He and the other city-kings rebelled against Chedorlaomer after twelve years of vassalage and were defeated in the battle that led to Lot's capture and Abraham's rescue. Admah was later destroyed along with Sodom and Gomorrah (Deuteronomy 29:23).

entries.title: Shinar
entries.summary: The old name for the land of Babylon. The tower of Babel went up there, and much later it was the heart of Nebuchadnezzar's empire.
entries.label: 5 books
entries.dictNote: Shinar is the ancient name for the region of Babylon, the setting for the tower of Babel and later for Nebuchadnezzar's empire, tying the Old Testament's first and last major confrontations with Babylonian pride to the same geography.

witness.excerpt: Now the plain, in which they first dwelt, was called Shinar .

And in this year came Chedorlaomer, king of Elam, and Amraphel, king of Shinar, and Arioch, king of Sêllâsar  and Têrgâl,  king of nations, and slew the king of Gomorrah, and the king of Sodom fled, and many fell through wounds in the vale of Siddim, by the Salt Sea.
And for Asshur came forth the second portion, all the land of Asshur and Nineveh and Shinar and to the border of India, and it ascendeth and skirteth the river.

entries.title: Shiphi (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A Simeonite, father of Ziza. In Hezekiah's reign the tribe was pushing out into new pasture near Gedor, and Ziza was one of its leaders.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Shiphi was a Simeonite, father of Ziza, a leader of his tribe during the reign of Hezekiah, a period when the tribe of Simeon expanded into new pastureland near Gedor (1 Chronicles 4:37-41).

entries.title: Shiphmite (People, perhaps from Shiphm)
entries.summary: Zabdi the Shiphmite looked after David's vineyards and the wine stores. He came from Shepham, and nobody now knows where that was.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shiphmite marks Zabdi, the official David put in charge of the royal vineyards and their wine stores, as a native of Shepham, a town whose location is now unknown.

entries.title: Shiphrah (Woman living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Pharaoh told the Hebrew midwives to kill the baby boys as they were born. Shiphrah and Puah would not do it, and God rewarded them.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of the two Hebrew midwives, alongside Puah, who defied Pharaoh's order to kill Israelite baby boys at birth and were rewarded by God for their courage (Exodus 1:15-21). Their names are among the few individual Israelites recorded before Moses' birth.

entries.title: Shiphtan (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Father of Kemuel, Ephraim's man on the commission that divided Canaan among the tribes (Numbers 34:24).
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shiphtan appears only as the father of Kemuel, the man Moses appointed to represent the tribe of Ephraim on the commission that oversaw the division of Canaan among the tribes (Numbers 34:24). Like most of the fathers named alongside the twelve tribal commissioners listed in that chapter, nothing else about him is recorded in the text.

entries.title: Shisha (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Father of Elihoreph and Ahijah, Solomon's two royal secretaries. He is likely the official called Shavsha under David.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Father of Elihoreph and Ahijah, the two royal secretaries who served in Solomon's administration (1 Kings 4:3). He is likely the same official called Shavsha under David and Seraiah or Sheva in the parallel lists of 2 Samuel, the name shifting slightly across transliterations, covered in full under Shavsha.

entries.title: Shishak (Pharaoh living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: The pharaoh who invaded Judah in Rehoboam's reign and stripped Solomon's temple of its treasures. He put the campaign on a relief at Karnak, listing the towns.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Shishak was the Egyptian pharaoh who invaded Judah during Rehoboam's reign and stripped Solomon's temple of its treasures, an episode Shishak also commemorated on a triumphal relief at the temple of Karnak in Egypt, listing the cities he claimed to have conquered.

witness.excerpt: But God sent Shishak, king of Egypt, to punish them for their unjust behavior towards him, concerning whom Herodotus was mistaken, and applied his actions to Sesostris; for this Shishak, (27) in the fifth year of the reign of Rehoboam, made

It had been taken five (34) times before, though this was the second time of its desolation; for Shishak, the king of Egypt, and after him Antiochus, and after him Pompey, and after them Sosius and Herod, took the city, but still preserved it; but before all these, the king of Babylon conquered it, and made it desolate, on

He also dedicated to God at Jerusalem the golden quivers, the entire armor which the guards of Hadad used to wear; which Shishak, the king of Egypt, took away when he fought with David's grandson, Rehoboam, with a great deal of other wealth which he carried out of Jerusalem.

But when Solomon understood his intention and treachery, he sought to catch him and kill him; but Jeroboam was informed of it beforehand, and fled to Shishak, the king of Egypt, and there abode till the death of Solomon; by which means he gained these two advantages to suffer no harm from Solomon, and to be preserved for the kingdom.

entries.title: Shitrai (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Shitrai the Sharonite looked after King David's cattle out on the plain of Sharon.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shitrai was a Sharonite who managed King David's cattle grazing on the plain of Sharon, one of the officials heading David's royal property listed in 1 Chronicles 27:29.

entries.title: Shittim
entries.summary: Israel's last camp before crossing into Canaan, on the plain of Moab across from Jericho. It was there that the men were drawn into idolatry with Moabite women.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Shittim was a plain in Moab east of the Jordan, opposite Jericho, where Israel made its final camp before crossing into Canaan; there the Israelite men were seduced into idolatry and immorality with Moabite women in the incident of Baal-peor (Numbers 25:1-3), and it was from this camp that Joshua sent the two spies into Jericho (Joshua 2:1). The prophets later look back to Shittim either as a byword for that sin (Micah 6:5) or, in Joel's vision of restoration, as the source of a life-giving stream flowing from the temple (Joel 3:18).

entries.title: Shiza (Warrior living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A Reubenite. His son Adina was one of David's thirty mighty warriors, a captain of the Reubenites, and nothing further is recorded about Shiza himself.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shiza was a Reubenite, the father of Adina, one of David's thirty mighty warriors and a captain among the Reubenites (1 Chronicles 11:42). Nothing further is recorded about Shiza himself.

entries.title: Shoa
entries.summary: Not a man but a people or district, named with Pekod and Koa in Ezekiel 23:23 among the lovers who will turn on Oholibah.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Not an individual but a people or district named alongside Pekod and Koa in Ezekiel's oracle against Jerusalem, personified there as one of Oholibah's unfaithful lovers who will turn against her (Ezekiel 23:23). Most scholars identify Shoa with the Sutu, a seminomadic people known from Babylonian and Assyrian records who lived east of the Tigris, making the string of names in this verse a pointed reference to Babylon's own allies and vassals.

entries.title: Shobab (David's son living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of the sons born to David in Jerusalem after he became king.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Shobab was one of David's sons born in Jerusalem after he became king, and also the name of one of David's ancestors through the line of Caleb.

entries.title: Shobab (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the wilderness years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shobach (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: He led Hadadezer's army and brought in troops from beyond the Euphrates to fight for the Ammonites against David. Joab's men killed him at Helam. After that the Arameans backed off.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shobach commanded the army of Hadadezer, king of Zobah, mustering forces from beyond the Euphrates to fight alongside the Ammonites against David. He was defeated and killed by Joab's forces at Helam, a loss that led the Arameans allied with the Ammonites to make peace with Israel (2 Samuel 10:15-19); he is called Shophach in the parallel account (1 Chronicles 19:16).

entries.title: Shobai (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: His descendants were temple gatekeepers who came back from exile with Zerubbabel. The name means captor, or captive, and nothing further is recorded of him.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Shobai's descendants, gatekeepers of the temple, were among those who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:42; Nehemiah 7:45). His name means “captor” or “captive.” Nothing further is recorded of him.

entries.title: Shobal (Edomite living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: An Edomite clan chief, descended from Seir. The name was used again for a man of Judah.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Shobal was a common name, borne by an Edomite clan chief descended from Seir and by a descendant of Judah listed among the founders of Kiriath-jearim.

entries.title: Shobal (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: One of the founders of Kiriath-jearim, from the line of Judah.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shobek (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: He set his seal to the covenant under Nehemiah, with the other leaders of the people. Nothing else is recorded of him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of the leaders of the people who set their seal to the covenant of renewed obedience to the law under Nehemiah after the exiles returned to Jerusalem (Nehemiah 10:24-27). Nothing else is recorded of him.

entries.title: Shobi (Ammonite living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Son of Nahash, the Ammonite king. When David ran from Jerusalem in Absalom's rebellion, Shobi brought food and bedding for him and his men.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Son of Nahash the Ammonite king, Shobi supplied David and his men with food and bedding when they fled Jerusalem during Absalom's rebellion, despite his family's earlier hostility toward Israel (2 Samuel 17:27).

entries.title: Shocho (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 3 men called Shocho. This one is a man from the divided-kingdom years, named once in 1 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shocho (Socoh)
entries.summary: A town of Judah near the Valley of Elah, close to where David fought Goliath.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Socoh was a town in Judah near the Valley of Elah, close to where David's battle with Goliath took place.

entries.title: Shocho (Socoh)
entries.summary: Named once, in Joshua, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shoham (Levite living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A Merarite Levite, son of Jaaziah, in the Levite divisions David set up for the temple.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Merarite Levite, son of Jaaziah, listed among the Levitical divisions organized for temple service under David (1 Chronicles 24:26-27).

entries.title: Shomer (Man living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the years before the monarchy.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shomer (Moabite living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A Moabite woman, the mother of Jehozabad, one of the royal servants who killed King Joash of Judah. She is also called Shimrith.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Two people carry this name in the Old Testament. One was the mother of Jehozabad, a royal servant who joined a conspiracy that killed King Joash of Judah; she is called a Moabite and also named Shimrith elsewhere (2 Kings 12:21; 2 Chronicles 24:26). The other was a man of the tribe of Asher, also called Shamer, listed among the heads of his clan (1 Chronicles 7:32, 34).

entries.title: Shophach (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: General of the Aramean army of Hadadezer, king of Zobah, when Ammon hired Arameans against David. Joab's forces beat them and killed him. 2 Samuel spells him Shobach.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shophach, also spelled Shobach in the parallel account, was the general commanding the army of Hadadezer, the Aramean king of Zobah, when Ammon hired Aramean mercenaries against David; Joab's forces defeated the coalition and killed Shophach in battle (1 Chronicles 19:16-18; compare 2 Samuel 10:16-18). His death broke Aramean support for Ammon and led several vassal kings to make peace with David. The battle marks the high point of David's wars establishing Israelite dominance over the Aramean states to the north.

entries.title: Shua (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: A Canaanite. Judah married his daughter, and she bore Er, Onan and Shelah.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shua was a Canaanite man whose daughter, called Bathshua (“daughter of Shua”), became the wife of Judah and bore him three sons: Er, Onan, and Shelah (Genesis 38:2-5). Her death is noted later in the same chapter (Genesis 38:12).

entries.title: Shua (Woman living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: Heber's daughter, of the tribe of Asher. She is not the Canaanite whose daughter married Judah.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shua was a daughter of Heber, of the tribe of Asher, listed among his children in the tribal genealogy of 1 Chronicles 7:32. She is a different person from the Canaanite woman named Shua whose daughter married Judah in Genesis 38.

entries.title: Shuah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Brother of Chelub, in Judah's genealogy (1 Chronicles 4:11). He is not Abraham's son by Keturah.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: This Shuah, distinct from Abraham's son by Keturah of the same name, was a descendant of Judah named as the brother of Chelub in 1 Chronicles 4:11, in a genealogy that also credits Chelub's line with founding the city of Eshton. Nothing further is recorded about him individually.

entries.title: Shuah (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: One of the sons Abraham had by Keturah. His people settled in Arabia, and Job's friend Bildad the Shuhite probably came from them.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Two men named Shuah appear in genealogies: one was a son Abraham had by his second wife Keturah, whose descendants settled in Arabia and gave their name to the “Shuhites,” the people of Job's friend Bildad (Genesis 25:2; 1 Chronicles 1:32); the other is a much briefer mention in the tribe of Judah's genealogy as father of Chelub (1 Chronicles 4:11). The two are unrelated apart from sharing a name.

witness.excerpt: And she bare him six sons, Zimram, and Jokshan, and Medan, and Midian, and Ishbak, and Shuah, in the two weeks of years.

entries.title: Shual
entries.summary: The land of Shual was a district in Benjamin's hill country. Philistine raiders went through it in Saul's reign.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The name Shual covers two distinct entities that share a headword. The land of Shual was a district in Benjamin's hill country that Philistine raiders passed through during Saul's reign (1 Samuel 13:17). Shual son of Zophah was an unrelated individual, an Asherite clan head listed in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 7:36; his name, which means jackal, was apparently common enough to double as a place name elsewhere in the same territory.

entries.title: Shual (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shuham (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Dan's son, and the only clan Dan had came from him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Son of Dan and ancestor of the Shuhamite clan, one of the tribal divisions counted in the wilderness census (Numbers 26:42-43).

entries.title: Shuhamites (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Dan's one recorded clan in the wilderness census, the family of Shuham, who is also called Hushim.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shuhamites were the family descended from Shuham, also called Hushim, the son of Dan; they formed Dan's only recorded clan in Israel's wilderness census.

entries.title: Shuhite (People, perhaps from Shuh)
entries.summary: Bildad, one of Job's three friends, was a Shuhite. The word probably makes him a descendant of Shuah, Abraham's son by Keturah, whose people lived out in the Arabian desert.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shuhite designates Bildad, one of Job's three friends, likely marking him as a descendant of Shuah, a son Abraham had by his later wife Keturah, whose descendants settled in the Arabian desert.

entries.title: Shulamite (People, perhaps from Shulam)
entries.summary: What the young woman in the Song of Solomon is called. Many take it to mean a woman from Shunem, though the Hebrew could mean something else.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shulamite designates the young woman celebrated throughout the Song of Solomon, an epithet whose meaning is debated; many take it as a feminine form pointing to the town of Shunem, though the underlying Hebrew could also simply mean the peaceful or perfect one.

entries.title: Shumathites (People, perhaps from Shumath)
entries.summary: A family of the clans of Kiriath-jearim, named with the Ithrites, Puhites and Mishraites.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shumathites were one of the families descended from the clans of Kiriath-jearim in Judah's genealogy, named in 1 Chronicles 2:53 alongside the Ithrites, Puhites, and Mishraites.

entries.title: Shunamite (People, perhaps from Shunam)
entries.summary: Someone from Shunem, a village in Issachar. Abishag, brought in to look after David in his old age, was one. So was the woman who took in Elisha and saw her son raised.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Shunamite designates someone from Shunem, a village in the territory of Issachar. Abishag, brought in to care for the aged David, was a Shunammite, and an unnamed Shunammite woman later hosted the prophet Elisha and saw her son restored to life after he raised him from death.

entries.title: Shunem
entries.summary: A village of Issachar near Jezreel. The Philistines camped here before the battle on Mount Gilboa where Saul and his sons died, and a woman here built a room for Elisha.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Village in Issachar's territory near Jezreel where the Philistines camped before the battle in which Saul and his sons died on Mount Gilboa (1 Sam. 28:4). It was also home to the woman who built a room for Elisha to stay in whenever he passed through, and whose son the prophet raised from the dead there (2 Kings 4:8-37). The site is preserved in the name of the modern village of Sulam.

witness.excerpt: 1096.] About the same time, the Philistines resolved to make war against the Israelites; and sent to all their confederates that they would go along with them to the war to Reggan, [near the city Shunem 20 ], whence they might gather themselves together, and suddenly attack the Hebrews.

entries.title: Shuni (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Gad's son, who went down to Egypt with Jacob's family and from whom the Shunites came.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Shuni was a son of Gad who went down to Egypt with Jacob's family and became the ancestor of the clan of the Shunites (Genesis 46:16; Numbers 26:15).

witness.excerpt: And these are the names of their sons who went with him into Egypt: the sons of Gad: Ziphion, and Haggi, and Shuni, and Ezbon, (and Eri) and Areli, and Arodi--eight.

entries.title: Shunites (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: The clan of Shuni, Gad's son, counted in the Numbers 26 census.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shunites were the clan descended from Shuni, a son of Gad, counted in the Numbers 26 census.

entries.title: Shuphamite (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: One of Benjamin's clans in the Numbers 26 census, descended from Shupham, whose name is also spelled Shephupham.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shuphamites were the clan descended from Shupham, also spelled Shephupham, a son of Benjamin, counted in the Numbers 26 census.

entries.title: Shuppim (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shuppim (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: A Benjamite clan name in 1 Chronicles 7:12 and 7:15.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shuppim was a Benjamite clan name, and also the name of a Levitical gatekeeper appointed under David.

entries.title: Shur
entries.summary: The wilderness on Egypt's northeastern frontier, between Egypt and Philistia. The name probably comes from a wall the Egyptians built there against raiders. Hagar ran toward it when Sarah sent her away.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Shur was a wilderness region on Egypt's northeastern frontier, between Egypt and Philistia, likely named for a defensive wall the Egyptians built there against desert raiders. Hagar fled toward it after being sent away by Sarah (Genesis 16:7), and Israel entered this same wilderness immediately after crossing the Red Sea, only to find no water for three days (Exodus 15:22).

witness.excerpt: And in this month Abraham moved from Hebron, and departed and dwelt between Kadesh and Shur in the mountains  of Gerar.
For ye celebrated this festival with haste 3 when ye went forth from Egypt till ye entered into the wilderness of Shur; 4 for on the shore of the sea ye completed it.

entries.title: Shushan (Susa)
entries.summary: The Persian winter capital, east of the Tigris in what is now southwestern Iran, and the Greeks called it Susa. Most of the book of Esther happens here.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Shushan, called Susa by Greek and Roman writers, was the winter capital of the Persian Empire, located east of the Tigris in what is now southwestern Iran. It is the setting for most of the book of Esther, Daniel received a vision there, and Nehemiah was serving as cupbearer in its royal citadel when he learned of Jerusalem's ruined walls. French excavations at the site since the nineteenth century have uncovered the audience hall of Darius and Artaxerxes described in Esther, along with a wealth of Persian and earlier Elamite artifacts, including the stele bearing the Babylonian Code of Hammurabi, carried to Susa centuries earlier as war plunder.

witness.excerpt: After which he made a feast for other nations, and for their ambassadors, at Shushan, for seven days.

entries.title: Shuthalhites (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: One of Ephraim's clans in the wilderness census, the family of Shuthelah.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Shuthalhites were the clan descended from Shuthelah, a son of Ephraim, one of several Ephraimite families listed in Israel's wilderness census.

entries.title: Shuthelah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shuthelah (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Ephraim's son, and his descendants were counted as a clan in the wilderness.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Shuthelah was a son of Ephraim, and his descendants formed one of the clans counted in Israel's wilderness census.

entries.title: Sia (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Head of a family of temple servants, the Nethinim. His descendants came back from exile with Zerubbabel to serve at the rebuilt temple, and Nehemiah spells him Siaha.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Sia headed a family of temple servants, the Nethinim, whose descendants returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel to serve at the rebuilt temple (Ezra 2:44; Nehemiah 7:47, where the name appears as Siaha).

entries.title: Sibbecai (Warrior living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: He killed a Philistine giant from the same line as Goliath, and he is listed with David's mighty warriors.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Sibbecai was one of David's mighty warriors, credited with killing a Philistine giant descended from the same lineage as Goliath.

entries.title: Sibboleth
entries.summary: How the men of Ephraim said shibboleth, because their dialect had no sh sound. Jephthah's men used the word at the fords. It picked them out and got them killed.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Not a person but a word: the way men of Ephraim pronounced "shibboleth" ("ear of grain" or "stream"), since their dialect lacked the "sh" sound. After Jephthah's Gileadites defeated Ephraim, they used the word as a password at the fords of the Jordan, killing any fugitive who could only manage "sibboleth" (Judges 12:5-6). The episode is the origin of "shibboleth" as an English word for a telltale marker of group identity.

entries.title: Sibraim
entries.summary: In Ezekiel's vision of the land restored, the northern border runs past Sibraim, between Damascus and Hamath, at a site nobody has found.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A landmark on the northern boundary of the land as Ezekiel describes it in his vision of Israel's restored territory, situated between the borders of Damascus and Hamath (Ezek. 47:16). The site has not been identified.

entries.title: Siddim
entries.summary: A valley full of tar pits. The kings of Sodom, Gomorrah and three other cities fought Chedorlaomer's invading coalition there, and some of them fell into the pits.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The Vale of Siddim was a valley described as full of tar pits, where the kings of Sodom, Gomorrah, and three other cities clashed with the invading coalition led by Chedorlaomer (Genesis 14:3, 8, 10). Genesis identifies it with the Salt Sea, the Dead Sea, suggesting the battle took place in the region later bordered by, or submerged under, that sea. Its precise location remains debated among geographers of the southern Dead Sea basin.

entries.title: Sidon
entries.summary: The older of the two great Phoenician ports, north of Tyre. It was allotted to Asher, but Asher never took it.
entries.books: Genesis, Joshua, Judges, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Joel, Zechariah, Matthew, Mark, Luke, Acts
entries.label: 14 books
entries.dictNote: Sidon was the older of the two great Phoenician port cities, north of Tyre, and its name is used in some Old Testament passages for Phoenician trade and craftsmanship generally. It was allotted to Asher but never conquered, and it remained an independent trading power through most of the biblical period. Jesus withdrew to its region at least once, and Paul's ship touched there under Julius the centurion's custody on the voyage to Rome. A sarcophagus of Sidon's king Eshmunazar II, inscribed with a long Phoenician royal text, is one of the best preserved records of the city's own royal history.

entries.title: Sidon (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Genesis and 1 Chronicles name him twice, and he is a man from the patriarchs.

entries.title: Sihon (King living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: An Amorite king. Israel asked to pass through his land, and he attacked them instead. It cost him his kingdom east of the Jordan.
entries.books: Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 1 Kings, Nehemiah, Psalm, Jeremiah
entries.label: 8 books
entries.dictNote: Sihon was an Amorite king who refused Israel safe passage through his territory and attacked them instead, a decision that cost him his kingdom when Israel defeated his army and took his land east of the Jordan, territory later assigned to the tribes of Reuben and Gad.

entries.title: Silas (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: A leader in the Jerusalem church who went with Paul on his second missionary journey, after Paul and Barnabas split up. He is probably the Silvanus of Paul's letters.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Silas was a leading member of the Jerusalem church chosen to accompany Paul on his second missionary journey after Paul and Barnabas split up, and he is likely the same person Paul calls Silvanus in his letters. He was imprisoned with Paul at Philippi, where the two of them sang hymns at midnight before an earthquake shook the prison doors open, and the jailer and his household were converted as a result. Silas later worked with Peter as well, helping deliver Peter's first letter to churches in Asia Minor.

entries.title: Silla
entries.summary: King Joash of Judah was killed by his own servants at a place called Silla, somewhere in or near Jerusalem on a road going down. Nobody is sure where.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A location in or near Jerusalem, apparently along a road or ascent, where King Joash of Judah was assassinated by his own servants (2 Kings 12:20). Its precise identification is uncertain.

entries.title: Siloam
entries.summary: The pool of Siloam in Jerusalem was fed by Hezekiah's tunnel. Jesus put mud on the eyes of a man born blind and sent him to wash there, and he came back seeing. Archaeologists have uncovered the pool's stone steps.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: The Pool of Siloam was a reservoir in Jerusalem fed by Hezekiah's tunnel, and it's where Jesus sent a man born blind to wash after applying mud to his eyes, restoring his sight. Archaeologists uncovered the pool's monumental stone steps in 2004, confirming its first-century scale and location.

entries.title: Silvanus (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: The Latin form of Silas. Paul uses it in his letters, and so does 1 Peter.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Silvanus is the Latin form of the name Silas, Paul's companion on his second missionary journey, used in several of Paul's letters and in 1 Peter; see the entry for Silas.

entries.title: Simeon (Jacob's son living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Jacob's second son. With his brother Levi he killed the men of Shechem after their sister Dinah was raped. Jacob held it against them on his deathbed.
entries.books: Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Ezekiel, Acts, 2 Peter, Revelation
entries.label: 13 books
entries.dictNote: Simeon was Jacob's second son, and along with his brother Levi he carried out the massacre of Shechem's men after their sister Dinah's rape, an act of vengeance their father Jacob condemned on his deathbed. His tribe's territory was eventually absorbed within Judah's rather than remaining independent. A very different Simeon, centuries later, was a devout old man in Jerusalem who had been promised he would not die before seeing the Messiah, and he recognized the infant Jesus the moment Mary and Joseph brought him to the temple.

entries.title: Simeon (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 4 men called Simeon. This one is a man from the divided-kingdom years, named once in Luke.

entries.summary: One of the twelve apostles. The title Zealot tells him apart from Simon Peter and probably means he had belonged to a movement opposed to Roman rule. Nothing else about him is recorded.

entries.summary: Simon Peter, called from his fishing in Matthew 4:18 and named first among the twelve apostles. In Matthew 16:16 he is the one who answers the question.
entries.label: 5 books
entries.dictNote: Simon the Zealot was one of the twelve apostles, distinguished from Simon Peter by the title Zealot, likely marking him as a former member of a Jewish nationalist movement opposed to Roman rule. Nothing else about him is recorded in the Gospels beyond his name in the apostolic lists.

entries.title: Simon (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: A tanner whose house was by the sea. Peter lodged with him, and the messengers in Acts 10:17 came to his gate asking for Peter.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.summary: He practised magic and had the people amazed, until he believed and was baptized himself. Then he offered the apostles money for their power, and Peter told him his money could perish with him.

entries.summary: One of 7 men called Simon. This one is a man from the New Testament, named twice in Matthew and Mark.

entries.title: Sin
entries.summary: Israel crossed the Wilderness of Sin after leaving Egypt, and when the people complained of hunger this is where the manna and the quail first came.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: The Wilderness of Sin was a desert region Israel crossed during the exodus, the location where God first provided manna and quail after the people complained of hunger.

entries.title: Sina
entries.summary: Sinai, in its Greek form. Stephen uses it when he tells of God appearing to Moses at the mountain. Paul turns Mount Sinai into an allegory in Galatians.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Sina is the Greek form of Sinai used in the New Testament. Stephen recounts God's appearance to Moses at the mountain in his speech before the Sanhedrin (Acts 7:30, 38), and Paul uses Mount Sinai allegorically in Galatians, contrasting the covenant of law given there, which he associates with slavery, against the freedom of the promise given to Abraham (Galatians 4:24-25).

entries.title: Sinai
entries.summary: Also called Horeb. Israel camped at the foot of the mountain for about a year after the exodus, and the law came down through Moses here.
entries.books: Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Judges, Nehemiah, Psalm
entries.label: 7 books
entries.dictNote: Sinai, also called Horeb, is the mountain where Israel camped for about a year after the exodus and received the law through Moses, its base in the plain of er-Rahah able to hold the whole camp in view of the summit. Tradition since at least the fourth century AD has identified it with Jebel Musa in the southern Sinai peninsula, where the monastery of Saint Catherine now stands, though other locations both within the peninsula and in Arabia have been proposed and the identification cannot be settled with certainty. It was there that Israel entered into covenant as a nation and received instructions for the tabernacle before resuming its journey toward Canaan.

witness.excerpt: He went no more up to mount Sinai: but he went into the tabernacle, and brought back answers from God to what he prayed for.
And going gradually on, he came to Mount Sinai, in three months time after they were removed out of Egypt.

entries.title: Sinim (Syene)
entries.summary: Isaiah 49:12 names it once, as a far land God will gather his scattered people from, with the north and the west. Where it was has never been settled.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Sinim appears once, in Isaiah 49:12, as a distant land from which God promises to gather his scattered people, named there alongside the north and the west. Older interpreters, working only from the traditional Hebrew text, guessed this referred to China, but the great Isaiah scroll found among the Dead Sea Scrolls at Qumran reads "Syene" at this point instead, the ancient name for Aswan in southern Egypt, a reading most modern scholars now consider more likely both textually and geographically.

entries.title: Sinite (People, perhaps from Sin)
entries.summary: A Canaanite clan on the Phoenician coast, in the Table of Nations. The city is generally placed near Arka, though no one is certain.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Sinites were a Canaanite clan named in the Table of Nations alongside other groups settled along the Phoenician coast. Their exact city is no longer certainly identified, though it is generally placed near Arka in that same northern coastal region.

entries.title: Sion (Jerusalem)
entries.summary: Another spelling of Zion. The hill in Jerusalem came to stand for the whole city, and in poetry for the place where God lives among his people.
entries.books: Matthew, John, Romans, Hebrews, 1 Peter, Revelation
entries.label: 6 books
entries.dictNote: Sion is an alternate spelling of Zion, the hill in Jerusalem that became synonymous with the city itself and, poetically, with the dwelling place of God among his people.

entries.title: Sion (Mount Hermon)
entries.summary: Named once, in Deuteronomy, and nowhere else.

entries.title: Siphmoth
entries.summary: After David took back the plunder from an Amalekite raid, he sent a share to the elders of Judah in the Negev towns where he had been sheltered as a fugitive. Siphmoth was one of those towns.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Siphmoth was one of the towns in the Negev of Judah to which David sent a share of the plunder recovered from an Amalekite raid, part of a gesture to the elders of Judah who had sheltered him during his years as a fugitive (1 Sam. 30:28). Its location is unknown.

entries.title: Sippai (Giant living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: A Philistine warrior of great size, of the Rephaim, killed by Sibbechai at Gezer. Samuel calls him Saph.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Philistine warrior of great size, one of the descendants of the Rephaim, killed by David's soldier Sibbechai at Gezer; the parallel account in Samuel calls him Saph (1 Chronicles 20:4; 2 Samuel 21:18).

entries.title: Sirah
entries.summary: Joab's men called Abner back from the well of Sirah, north of Hebron, after David had let him go in peace. Then Joab killed him, in revenge for his brother.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A well north of Hebron from which Joab's men recalled Abner after David had let him leave in peace; Joab then killed Abner in revenge for his brother's death (2 Samuel 3:26). The site is generally identified with a spring still called Ain Sarah.

entries.title: Sirion (Mount Hermon)
entries.summary: What the Sidonians called Mount Hermon. A psalm has Sirion and Lebanon skipping like a young wild ox at the voice of the Lord.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Sirion was not a person but the Sidonian name for Mount Hermon, the snow-capped peak marking Israel's northern boundary (Deuteronomy 3:9). A psalm pictures Sirion, alongside Lebanon, skipping like a young wild ox at the voice of the Lord in a storm theophany (Psalm 29:6).

entries.title: Sisamai (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of Sheshan's descendants through the Jerahmeelite line of Judah. Sheshan had no sons and gave his daughter to an Egyptian servant, and this is the family that came of it.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A descendant of Sheshan through the Jerahmeelite line of Judah, part of the genealogical record tracing Sheshan's family after he had no sons and gave his daughter in marriage to an Egyptian servant (1 Chronicles 2:34-40).

entries.title: Sisera (Deborah's adversary living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: He commanded the Canaanite army that held Israel down for twenty years, until Deborah and Barak beat it. Sisera ran on foot to the tent of a woman called Jael, who took him in and then killed him.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Sisera commanded the Canaanite army that oppressed Israel for twenty years until Deborah and Barak defeated it in battle, and Sisera fled on foot to the tent of a woman named Jael, who offered him hospitality and then killed him with a tent peg while he slept, fulfilling Deborah's prophecy that a woman would get the credit for his death.

witness.excerpt: Sisera was the commander of all this army; and was the principal person in the King’s favour.

entries.title: Sisera (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Ezra and Nehemiah name him twice, and he is a man from the exile and the return.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Sitnah
entries.summary: The second well Isaac's herdsmen dug in the valley of Gerar. The Philistines there fought over it as they had over the first, so it was called hostility.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Not a person but the second of two wells Isaac's herdsmen dug in the valley of Gerar, named "strife" or "hostility" because the Philistines living there disputed Isaac's claim to it, just as they had with the first well (Gen. 26:21). Isaac moved on and dug a third well, Rehoboth, before the dispute finally ended.

entries.title: Sivan (Name of the 3rd month)
entries.summary: Third month, May into June, and Esther dates the king's second decree to it.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The third month of the Hebrew religious calendar, falling roughly in the modern May-June range. Esther 8:9 dates the king's decree allowing the Jews to defend themselves to this month, and it later became associated with the Feast of Weeks.
