entries.title: Smyrna
entries.summary: About forty miles north of Ephesus, on the coast of Asia Minor. The church at Smyrna was one of the seven in Revelation, and it got no rebuke, only a warning that suffering was coming.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Smyrna, an ancient Ionian port city on the western coast of Asia Minor, about forty miles north of Ephesus. Its church was one of the seven addressed in Revelation and received no rebuke, only a warning of coming suffering and a promise of the crown of life (Rev. 2:8-11). Its early bishop Polycarp, a disciple of the apostle John, was martyred there around 155 AD. The city survives today as Izmir, and excavations of its Roman-era agora have confirmed the prosperity the city already had in the first century.

entries.title: So (Pharaoh living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: King Hoshea of Israel stopped paying tribute to Assyria and sent to So, an Egyptian king, for help. That move brought on the invasion that ended with the fall of Samaria.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: An Egyptian king, likely of Nubian origin, whom King Hoshea of Israel appealed to for help against Assyria instead of paying his required tribute, a move that triggered the Assyrian invasion ending in Samaria's fall (2 Kings 17:4). Many historians identify him with Sib'e, a military commander of Egypt defeated by Sargon II at the battle of Raphia in 720 BC according to Assyrian royal inscriptions, though the exact identification remains debated among Egyptologists.

entries.title: Sodi (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Father of Gaddiel, Zebulun's man among the twelve spies.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Father of Gaddiel, the man chosen to represent the tribe of Zebulun among the twelve spies Moses sent to scout Canaan (Numbers 13:10).

entries.title: Sodom
entries.summary: Sodom was destroyed by fire from heaven along with Gomorrah, and the rest of Scripture keeps pointing back to it as the picture of judgment. It was one of the cities of the plain near the Dead Sea.
entries.books: Genesis, Deuteronomy, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Lamentations, Ezekiel, Amos, Zephaniah, Matthew, Luke, Romans, 2 Peter, Jude, Revelation
entries.label: 14 books
entries.dictNote: Sodom was one of the cities of the plain near the Dead Sea, condemned in Genesis for wickedness and destroyed by fire from heaven along with Gomorrah, an event the rest of Scripture repeatedly cites as a byword for divine judgment. No certain trace of the city has survived, though some archaeologists point to Early Bronze Age ruins at sites like Bab edh-Dhra and Numeira near the Dead Sea's southern shore as candidates for the destroyed cities, an identification that remains debated. Jesus himself invoked Sodom's fate as a warning more severe than anything faced by towns that rejected his disciples.

witness.excerpt: Now the King of Sodom met him at a certain place, which they called The King’s dale, where Melchisedeck, King of the city Salem, received him.

Testament of Asher, Chapter 7

7 1 Become not, my children, as Sodom, which sinned against the angels of the Lord, and perished for 2 ever.

entries.title: Solomon (King living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: David and Bathsheba's son, and Israel's third king. He was rushed onto the throne after his half-brother Adonijah tried to take it while David lay dying. Early on he asked God for wisdom.
entries.books: 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Psalm, Proverbs, Song of Solomon, Jeremiah, Matthew, Luke, John, Acts
entries.label: 15 books
entries.dictNote: Solomon was David and Bathsheba's son and Israel's third king, placed on the throne in a rushed ceremony after his half-brother Adonijah tried to seize it while David lay dying. Early in his reign he asked God for wisdom rather than wealth or long life and received all three anyway, and he used the resulting forty-year reign to build the Jerusalem temple his father had wanted to build, organize the kingdom into administrative districts, and turn Israel into a regional power with a reputation that reportedly reached the Queen of Sheba. Gate structures at Megiddo, Hazor, and Gezer, the exact three cities 1 Kings names as his building projects, follow a matching architectural plan and have long been attributed to Solomon's construction program, though archaeologists still argue over whether they actually date to his reign or a century later.
entries.dictSource: Tyndale Bible Dictionary; Baker Encyclopedia of the Bible (Logos)

witness.excerpt: Give me, O Lord, a sound mind, and a good understanding, whereby I may speak and judge the people according to truth and righteousness.

entries.lukeNote: Jesus invokes him twice as a byword for splendor (12:27, dressed lilies outshine him) and for wisdom outdone (11:31, ‘something greater than Solomon is here’). Josephus has Solomon ask God for exactly the thing Luke's Jesus says he had, understanding, not riches, and get it granted beyond any mortal before or since.

entries.title: Sopater (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: A Christian from Berea, son of Pyrrhus, who travelled with Paul through Macedonia carrying the collection for the Jerusalem church.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Christian from Berea, son of Pyrrhus, who was among the group of representatives from various churches who accompanied Paul through Macedonia and Asia carrying the collection for the Jerusalem church (Acts 20:4). He is probably the same man Paul calls Sosipater, his kinsman, in Romans 16:21.

entries.title: Sophereth (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: He headed a family of "Solomon's servants," temple workers whose descendants came back from exile with Zerubbabel. Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Sophereth headed a family descended from "Solomon's servants," temple workers whose descendants returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:55; Nehemiah 7:57). Nothing further is recorded about him.

entries.title: Sorek
entries.summary: Delilah lived in the Valley of Sorek, and the Philistine lords paid her there to find out where Samson's strength came from.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The Valley of Sorek, a wadi running west from the Judean hill country toward the Mediterranean near Joppa, was home to Delilah, the woman Samson loved who was bribed by the Philistine lords to discover the secret of his strength (Judg. 16:4). The same valley, now called Wadi es-Sarar, later carried the cart bearing the captured Ark of the Covenant back from Philistine territory toward Beth-shemesh.

entries.title: Sosipater (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Paul's kinsman, who sent his greetings to the church at Rome along with Paul's. He is probably Sopater of Berea.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Sosipater was a kinsman of Paul who joined him in sending greetings to the church at Rome (Romans 16:21). He is probably the same man as Sopater of Berea, who accompanied Paul from Greece on his return through Macedonia (Acts 20:4).

entries.title: Sosthenes (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: The ruler of the synagogue in Corinth, seized and beaten in front of the judgment seat after Gallio threw out the case against Paul.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Sosthenes was the ruler of the synagogue in Corinth who was seized and beaten in front of the Roman proconsul Gallio's judgment seat after the Jewish community's case against Paul was dismissed (Acts 18:12-17). Paul later names a Sosthenes as a co-sender of 1 Corinthians, calling him “our brother” (1 Corinthians 1:1), and tradition has long identified him with the same man, now a Christian, though the text does not confirm it.

entries.title: Sotai (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: His family were "Solomon's servants," temple workers who came back from exile with Zerubbabel.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Sotai headed a family descended from "Solomon's servants," a class of temple workers grouped alongside the Nethinim, whose descendants returned from exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:55; Nehemiah 7:57). Nothing further is recorded about him.

entries.title: Spain
entries.summary: Paul meant to go on to Spain from Rome, once he had taken the collection to the poor in Jerusalem, and he hoped the Roman church would help him on his way. Whether he ever got there is not known.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Paul mentions his intention to visit Spain on his way from Rome, hoping the Roman church would help him on his journey after he had first delivered the collection for Jerusalem's poor (Rom. 15:24, 28). Whether he ever reached Spain is uncertain; the book of Acts ends with him under house arrest in Rome without recording the trip, though early Christian tradition holds that he was released and completed the journey before his final imprisonment and execution.

entries.title: Stachys (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: "My beloved," Paul calls him, in his long list of greetings to believers at Rome. Nothing more about him is recorded in the New Testament.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Stachys was a Christian at Rome whom Paul greets as 'my beloved' in Romans 16:9, part of the long list of individual believers Paul singles out for personal recognition. Nothing more about him is recorded in the New Testament.

entries.title: Stephanas (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: He and his household were among the first converts in Corinth. Paul praises them for giving themselves to serving the church. Their visit, he says, refreshed him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Stephanas and his household were among the first converts in Corinth, and Paul specifically commends them for devoting themselves to serving the church, describing their visit to him as a source of real refreshment.

entries.title: Stephen (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: He was picked as one of seven to oversee the food for the Greek-speaking widows in the Jerusalem church. He soon became known for miracles and bold debate instead.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Stephen was one of seven men chosen to oversee food distribution for Greek-speaking widows in the early Jerusalem church, but he quickly became known for miracles and bold public debate rather than administrative work. His defense before the Jewish council, a long recap of Israel's history culminating in an accusation that his hearers had betrayed and murdered the Righteous One just as their ancestors killed the prophets, got him dragged out and stoned to death, making him Christianity's first martyr. A young man named Saul, who would later become Paul, held the coats of the men throwing the stones and approved of the killing.

witness.excerpt: Stephen says of the same beauty; that Moses was beautiful in the sight of Acts 7:20.

Now there followed after this another calamity, which arose from a tumult made by robbers; for at the public road at Beth-boron, one Stephen, a servant of Caesar, carried some furniture, which the robbers fell upon and seized.

entries.title: Stoick (Philosophical group in the New Testament)
entries.summary: Not a person. The Stoics followed the Greek school Zeno of Citium founded, which taught self-control and calm acceptance of fate, and some of them argued with Paul in Athens (Acts 17:18).
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Not a person but an adjective describing followers of Stoicism, the Greek philosophical school founded by Zeno of Citium that taught self-control and rational acceptance of fate as the path to virtue. Acts 17:18 pairs "certain philosophers of the Epicureans and of the Stoics" among those who debated with Paul in the Athens marketplace before he addressed the Areopagus.

entries.title: Suah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A descendant of Asher, one of Zophah's sons in 1 Chronicles 7:36.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A descendant of Asher listed among the sons of Zophah in the tribal genealogies of 1 Chronicles 7:36.

entries.title: Succoth
entries.summary: Jacob built shelters for his cattle here, east of the Jordan near the Jabbok, on his way back from Paddan-aram. The name means booths.
entries.books: Genesis, Joshua, Judges, 1 Kings, 2 Chronicles, Psalm
entries.label: 6 books
entries.dictNote: Succoth, “booths,” was Israel's first campsite after leaving Egypt, and separately the name of a town east of the Jordan near the Jabbok where Jacob built shelters for his livestock on returning from Paddan-aram. Its leaders refused to help Gideon's exhausted troops during their pursuit of the Midianites, for which Gideon punished them on his return, and the plain around the town later provided clay for casting the bronze furnishings of Solomon's temple.

witness.excerpt: Hereupon Jacob came to the place, till this day called Tents [ Succoth ], from whence he went to Shechem : which is a city of the Canaanites.

entries.title: Succoth
entries.summary: Israel's first campsite after leaving Egypt.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Succothbenoth (A male deity in the Old Testament)
entries.summary: A god the settlers from Babylon brought with them to Samaria, after the Assyrians conquered the northern kingdom.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Succoth-benoth was a deity brought to Samaria by colonists from Babylon whom the Assyrians resettled there after conquering the northern kingdom of Israel, part of a patchwork of foreign gods the new population continued worshiping alongside a token fear of the Lord (2 Kings 17:24-30). Scholars generally identify the name with a garbled Hebrew rendering of Zarpanitu, the Babylonian goddess who was consort to the chief god Marduk.

entries.title: Suchathite (Scribal group in the Old Testament)
entries.summary: A family of scribes living at Jabez, named with the Tirathites and Shimeathites. They were Kenites, from Hammath, the father of the house of Rechab.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Suchathites were one of the families of scribes living at Jabez, named in 1 Chronicles 2:55 alongside the Tirathites and Shimeathites and identified there as Kenites descended from Hammath, father of the house of Rechab.

entries.title: Sukkiims (People, perhaps from Sukki)
entries.summary: They marched with Shishak's Egyptian army when it invaded Judah in Rehoboam's fifth year, alongside Libyans and Cushites. The name likely means tent-dwellers.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Sukkiims were a people who marched with Pharaoh Shishak's Egyptian army when it invaded Judah in Rehoboam's fifth year, listed alongside Libyans and Cushites among his troops. The name likely means tent-dwellers, and some ancient translators rendered it as troglodytes, cave-dwelling nomads along the Red Sea coast.

entries.title: Sur
entries.summary: One of the gates in Jerusalem where the guard was posted on the day Jehoiada made the young Joash king and removed Athaliah. The account in 2 Chronicles 23:5 calls it the gate of the foundation instead.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Sur is not a person but the name of a gate at the temple or royal palace in Jerusalem, mentioned in 2 Kings 11:6 as one of the posts assigned to the guard during Jehoiada's coup, which placed the young Joash on the throne and removed the usurper Athaliah. The parallel account in 2 Chronicles 23:5 calls the same gate "the gate of the foundation," suggesting either an alternate name for the same entrance or a variation between the two accounts. Its appearance in older name lists likely comes from treating the Hebrew phrase "gate of Sur" as though the second word were a personal name.

witness.excerpt: Even Zimri, the head of the tribe of Simeon, accompanied with Cozbi, a Midianitish women, who was the daughter of Sur; a man of authority in that countrey: and being desired by his wife to disregard the laws of Moses, and to follow those she was used to, he complied with her: and this both by sacrificing after a manner different from h

entries.title: Susanchites
entries.summary: People from Susa, the city in Elam that later became a Persian winter capital, settled in Samaria among the foreign groups who opposed rebuilding the temple in Jerusalem.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Susanchites were people from Shushan, the great city of Susa in Elam that later served as a winter capital of the Persian empire, among the foreign groups settled in Samaria who opposed the rebuilding of Jerusalem's temple. Susa's excavated ruins include the palace of Darius and Xerxes, and the site also yielded the famous law code stele of Hammurabi, carried there centuries earlier as war plunder.

entries.title: Susanna (Woman living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: She traveled with Jesus and the twelve and paid toward their keep out of her own means, named in Luke 8:3 next to Mary Magdalene and Joanna. Nothing more is recorded about her.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of several women who traveled with Jesus and the twelve disciples and helped support their ministry out of their own means, named alongside Mary Magdalene and Joanna in Luke 8:3. Nothing further is recorded about her.

witness.excerpt: They had the like governor or governors allowed them at Babylon under their captivity there, as the history of Susanna implies.

entries.title: Susi (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Father of Gaddi, the man Manasseh sent with the twelve spies into Canaan.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Susi was the father of Gaddi, the representative of the tribe of Manasseh among the twelve spies Moses sent to scout Canaan (Numbers 13:11). Nothing else is recorded about him.

entries.title: Sychar
entries.summary: A Samaritan town near Jacob's well. Jesus sat there and talked with a woman who came to draw water. Tradition from the Crusader period put it at Shechem; most scholars now put it at 'Askar, at the foot of Mount Ebal about a mile from the well.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Samaritan town near Jacob's well, where Jesus rested and spoke with a Samaritan woman in John 4. Early Christian tradition, from the Crusader period on, identified it with nearby Shechem, but most modern scholars instead locate it at 'Askar, a village at the base of Mount Ebal about a mile from the well; the well itself has been preserved and venerated continuously enough that its location, unlike many biblical sites, is not seriously disputed.

entries.title: Sychem (Shechem)
entries.summary: Stephen's Greek spelling of Shechem, in the speech he gave before the Sanhedrin. He says the patriarchs were buried in a tomb Abraham bought there from the sons of Hamor, though Genesis records two separate purchases, Machpelah at Hebron and Jacob's land at Shechem.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Sychem is the Greek form of Shechem, used in Stephen's speech before the Sanhedrin when he recounts that the patriarchs were buried in a tomb Abraham had bought there from the sons of Hamor (Acts 7:16). The Genesis narrative actually records two separate transactions, Abraham's purchase of the cave of Machpelah at Hebron from Ephron the Hittite and Jacob's later purchase of land at Shechem from the sons of Hamor, and Stephen's speech appears to compress the two; Shechem itself, modern Tell Balata, has been extensively excavated and shows a fortified Bronze Age city consistent with the biblical setting.

entries.title: Syene
entries.summary: The southern edge of Egypt, at modern Aswan by the first cataract of the Nile. Ezekiel uses Migdol and Syene the way we would say from one end of the country to the other.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Syene was Egypt's southern frontier town, paired with Migdol in the north as the two ends of the land in Ezekiel's oracles against Egypt (Ezekiel 29:10; 30:6). It sits at modern Aswan, opposite the island of Elephantine at the Nile's first cataract, a strategic gateway between Egypt and Nubia that also gave its name to the region's famous red granite, syenite. Thousands of Aramaic papyri recovered from Elephantine document a Jewish military garrison stationed there in the fifth century BC, evidence of a long-standing Judean presence at this same frontier post.

entries.title: Syntyche (Woman living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: She and Euodia are asked by Paul to agree in the Lord. He never says what the quarrel at Philippi was, and he calls them both women who had labored side by side with him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Syntyche was a woman in the church at Philippi whom Paul urges, alongside Euodia, to "agree in the Lord" after some unrecorded disagreement between them (Philippians 4:2-3). Paul calls both women his fellow workers who had "labored side by side" with him in spreading the gospel, showing the dispute was between valued ministry partners, not marginal figures.

entries.title: Syracuse
entries.summary: A Greek city on the southeast coast of Sicily, founded by Corinth in the eighth century BC and once home to Archimedes. Paul's ship stayed three days there on the way to Rome.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Syracuse was not a person but a major Greek city on the southeastern coast of Sicily, founded as a Corinthian colony in the eighth century BC. Paul's ship stopped there for three days on the voyage to Rome as a prisoner (Acts 28:12), by which time it had long been a Roman provincial city, famous earlier as the home of Archimedes.

entries.title: Syria
entries.summary: The region northeast of Israel, called Aram in the Old Testament. In the New Testament Antioch was its chief city and the base Paul's journeys started from, and Luke dates Jesus's birth by a census under Quirinius.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Syria, called Aram in the Old Testament, was the broad region northeast of Israel stretching toward the Euphrates, home to a number of small Aramean kingdoms before coming under Assyrian, then Persian, then Greek and Roman control. In the New Testament, Syria's chief city Antioch became the base for the earliest Gentile church and the starting point of Paul's missionary journeys; Luke notes that Jesus was born during a census taken while Quirinius governed Syria, and Paul passed through the province repeatedly on his travels.

witness.excerpt: The cities of Syria being oppressed by a long continuance of famine, became destitute of inhabitants, all of them being dispersed in different directions for the purpose of seeking food and providing themselves with necessaries.
So the king of Syria took his army with him, and came to Samaria, and placed his army round about the city, and besieged it.
In Palestine and Syria are the Essenes, more than four thousand in number, namesakes of Holiness (οσιοτητος).
NOW Phoenicia and Syria encompass about the Galilees, which are two, and called the Upper Galilee and the Lower.
And now the King of Assyria invaded all Syria and Phenicia in an hostile manner.

entries.title: Syrian
entries.summary: The Arameans, the people around Damascus, mostly in the wars of the kings in 2 Kings.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Syrian in the Old Testament refers to the Arameans, the people of the region centered on Damascus, covered more fully under the entry for Aram.

entries.title: Syrian (Paddan-aram)
entries.summary: In Genesis the word marks the family in Paddan-aram as Arameans, and Deuteronomy 26:5 uses it once more.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Syrian (Woman living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: One of 3 women called Syrian. This one is a woman from the wilderness years, named once in 1 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Syrophenician (Syria)
entries.summary: A Gentile woman of Phoenician descent from the Roman province of Syria, who begged Jesus to heal her daughter near Tyre. Matthew calls her a woman of Canaan. Her answer to his first refusal is what people remember.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Not a personal name but a term for a Gentile of Phoenician descent from the Roman province of Syria, used in Mark 7:26 to describe the woman whose daughter Jesus healed from a distance near Tyre; Matthew's parallel calls her "a woman of Canaan" (Matt. 15:22). The term distinguished Syrian Phoenicians from the Phoenicians of Libya around Carthage. Her persistent faith, despite Jesus's initial refusal, became a byword for Gentile inclusion in the gospel.

entries.title: Taanach
entries.summary: A Canaanite royal city on the southwest edge of the Jezreel Valley, near Megiddo. Joshua beat its king, the town went to the Levites of Kohath, and its Canaanites were never driven out. Deborah's song puts a battle there by the waters of Megiddo.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Taanach was a royal Canaanite city on the southwest edge of the Jezreel Valley, near Megiddo, whose king Joshua defeated (Joshua 12:21); it was later assigned to the Levites of Kohath, though its Canaanite population was never fully driven out (Judges 1:27). It figures in Deborah's victory song as one of the battle sites near "the waters of Megiddo" (Judges 5:19), and excavations at the site have uncovered Canaanite cult objects and fortifications spanning the period these accounts describe.

entries.title: Taanach
entries.summary: Named once, in 1 Chronicles, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Taanath-shiloh
entries.summary: A point on Ephraim's southern border, named once in Joshua 16:6. The name seems to mean approach to Shiloh, and it is commonly identified with the ruin of Ta'na southeast of Shechem.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Taanath-shiloh marked a point on the southern border of the tribal territory of Ephraim, named only in Joshua 16:6. Its name, roughly "approach to Shiloh," suggests it lay along a route travelers used to reach the sanctuary town of Shiloh, and it is commonly identified with the ruin of Ta'na southeast of Shechem.

entries.title: Tabaoth (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: His family came back from Babylon with Zerubbabel among the temple servants, the Nethinim.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Tabaoth's descendants were among the families of temple servants (Nethinim) who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:43; Nehemiah 7:46). Nothing further is recorded of him.

entries.title: Tabbath
entries.summary: When Gideon's three hundred broke the Midianite camp, the army ran toward Tabbath, near the Jordan south of Beth-shean.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Tabbath, a site near the Jordan south of Beth-shean, marking the route the Midianite army fled after Gideon's three hundred routed their camp (Judg. 7:22).

entries.title: Tabeal (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Two men share the name. Isaiah 7:6 makes one the father of the man Syria and Israel meant to put on Judah's throne instead of Ahaz, and Ezra 4:7 has the other, an official in Samaria who wrote to Artaxerxes against the walls.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Tabeal, also spelled Tabeel, is used of two different men. One was the father of a man whom the kings of Syria and Israel plotted to install on Judah's throne in place of Ahaz, a scheme Isaiah confronted with his sign of Immanuel (Isaiah 7:1-6). The other was a Persian-appointed official in Samaria who joined in writing a letter to King Artaxerxes opposing the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls (Ezra 4:7-8).

entries.title: Taberah
entries.summary: The name means burning. Israel complained in the wilderness, fire from the Lord broke out on the edge of the camp, and it died down when Moses prayed.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Wilderness site where fire from the Lord broke out among the Israelites after they complained about their hardships, burning the outskirts of the camp until Moses interceded and the fire died down (Num. 11:1-3). Its name, meaning "burning," commemorates the event, and Moses recalls it alongside the nearby Kibroth-hattaavah in his closing review of Israel's wilderness rebellions (Deut. 9:22).

entries.title: Tabitha (Woman living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: A disciple at Joppa, known for doing good and giving to the poor. She died, the believers sent for Peter, and he raised her. Luke gives both her Aramaic name and the Greek one, Dorcas, and both mean gazelle.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Tabitha was a disciple at Joppa known for her charity and good works, whom Peter raised from the dead after the local believers sent for him following her sudden death (Acts 9:36-42). Luke gives her Aramaic name, Tabitha, alongside its Greek equivalent, Dorcas, both meaning gazelle, since her circle included both Jewish and Greek-speaking believers.

entries.title: Tabor
entries.summary: A dome-shaped mountain rising out of the Jezreel Valley, on the line between Zebulun and Issachar. Deborah sent Barak there to gather Israel before the battle with Sisera. The psalmist sets it beside Hermon, and Hosea and Jeremiah both name it in oracles of judgment.
entries.books: Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, Psalm, Jeremiah, Hosea
entries.label: 6 books
entries.dictNote: Mount Tabor is a distinctive, dome-shaped peak rising from the Jezreel Valley on the border of Zebulun and Issachar. Deborah summoned Barak and Israel's forces there before their victory over Sisera's army, and Gideon later avenged his brothers' deaths at the hands of Midianite kings near the same mountain. The psalmist pairs Tabor with Hermon as poetic emblems of God's creation, and Hosea and Jeremiah both invoke it in oracles of judgment. A separate Levitical town of the same name belonged to Zebulun.

witness.excerpt: And the Romans received all the fortresses and the cities, excepting Gischala and those that had seized upon mount Tabor; Gamala also, which is a city over-against Taricheæ, but on the other side of the lake, conspired with them.
And after these was Issachar; which had its limits in length, mount Carmel, and the river: but its limit in breadth was mount Tabor.

However, thirty thousand still continued with Alexander, who was himself eager to fight also; accordingly, Gabinius went out to fight, when the Jews met him; and as the battle was fought near Mount Tabor, ten thousand of them were slain, and the rest of the multitude dispersed themselves, and fled away.

entries.title: Tabrimmon (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: King of Aram at Damascus and father of Ben-hadad, the king Asa paid with temple treasure to turn on Baasha of Israel.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Tabrimmon was king of Aram-Damascus and the father of Ben-hadad I, mentioned in 1 Kings 15:18 when Asa of Judah sent temple and palace treasure to Ben-hadad to buy his help against King Baasha of Israel. The reference situates Tabrimmon within the succession of Aramean kings at Damascus who repeatedly clashed with and allied against Israel and Judah in the ninth century BC.

entries.title: Tachmonite (People, perhaps from Hachmon or Tahchemon)
entries.summary: It is Jashobeam's family name, and he was chief of David's three mightiest warriors. 2 Samuel 23:8 credits him with eight hundred men killed at one time. Chronicles spells it Hachmonite.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Tachmonite, also given as Hachmonite in 1 Chronicles 11:11, marks Jashobeam, chief of David's three mightiest warriors, credited in 2 Samuel 23:8 with killing eight hundred men in a single encounter.

entries.title: Tadmor
entries.summary: It was Solomon's city out in the desert northeast of Damascus, on the caravan routes, and the Greeks and Romans knew it as Palmyra.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Tadmor was a city Solomon built in the desert northeast of Damascus, positioned to control the caravan routes crossing the Syrian wilderness (1 Kings 9:18; 2 Chr. 8:4). The Greeks and Romans knew it as Palmyra, and under Roman rule it grew into a wealthy caravan city famous for its colonnaded streets and monumental temples, ruins that stood for centuries as one of the ancient world's best-preserved sites before suffering severe damage during the Syrian civil war.

witness.excerpt:

entries.title: Tahan (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tahan (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: From him came the Tahanites, one of Ephraim's clans in the census of Numbers 26. Chronicles puts him as Telah's son rather than Ephraim's.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Tahan was a descendant of Ephraim and the ancestral head of the Tahanite clan (Numbers 26:35). In the parallel genealogy in 1 Chronicles 7:25, he appears as the son of Telah rather than directly of Ephraim, one of several small discrepancies between the tribal lists.

entries.title: Tahanites (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Ephraim's clan through Tahan, counted in the Numbers 26 census.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Tahanites were the clan descended from Tahan, a son of Ephraim, counted in the Numbers 26 census.

entries.title: Tahapanes (Tahpanhes)
entries.summary: An Egyptian fort town on the eastern edge of the Nile delta. After Gedaliah was murdered the refugees ran there and took Jeremiah with them against his advice, and he said there that Nebuchadnezzar would set his throne over stones buried at the entrance to Pharaoh's palace.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Tahpanhes was a fortified Egyptian city near the eastern edge of the Nile delta where a group of Jewish refugees fled after the assassination of Gedaliah, taking the prophet Jeremiah with them against his counsel. Jeremiah prophesied there that Nebuchadnezzar would set his throne over buried stones at the entrance of Pharaoh's palace, a scene of judgment on Egypt. Archaeologist Flinders Petrie excavated the site, identified as Tell Defenneh, and uncovered a brick platform at a palace entrance that he proposed matched the setting of Jeremiah's prophecy.

entries.title: Tahath
entries.summary: A wilderness camp between Makheloth and Terah in the list of Numbers 33, and nobody knows where it was.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Tahath was an unidentified desert campsite of the Israelites during the wilderness wanderings, listed between Makheloth and Terah in the itinerary of Numbers 33 (Numbers 33:26-27). The same name also belongs to two separate Levites in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles (1 Chronicles 6:9, 22) and to a descendant of Ephraim (1 Chronicles 7:20).

entries.title: Tahath (Levite living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him twice, and he is a Levite from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tahath (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 3 men called Tahath. This one is a man from the divided-kingdom years, named once in 1 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tahpenes (Woman living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: She was Pharaoh's queen in Egypt when Hadad the Edomite fled there from Solomon. Pharaoh gave Hadad her sister as his wife, and Tahpenes raised their son in the palace.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Tahpenes was an Egyptian queen, the wife of the pharaoh who gave asylum to Hadad the Edomite when he fled Solomon's kingdom. She raised Hadad's son in Pharaoh's own household and gave her sister in marriage to Hadad (1 Kings 11:19-20).

witness.excerpt: Egypt, who received him kindly, and assigned him a house to dwell in, and a country to supply him with food; and when he was grown up he loved him exceedingly, insomuch that he gave him his wife's sister, whose name was Tahpenes, to wife, by whom he had a son; who was brought up with the king's children.

entries.title: Tahrea (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Saul's great-grandson through Jonathan and Mephibosheth. The other copy of the list spells him Tarea.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A great-grandson of Saul through Jonathan and Mephibosheth, listed in the genealogy of Benjamin preserved after the exile (1 Chronicles 9:41); the parallel list in 1 Chronicles 8:35 gives his name as Tarea.

entries.title: Tahtim-hodshi (Kadesh)
entries.summary: It turns up once, on Joab's census route east of the Jordan, somewhere north of Gilead. The Hebrew is hard to read here, and many think it is a garbled reference to the Hittites of Kadesh and not a town at all.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Tahtim-hodshi appears only in the account of Joab's census route east of the Jordan, somewhere north of Gilead (2 Sam. 24:6). The Hebrew text is difficult, and many scholars think the phrase is a corruption of a reference to the Hittites of Kadesh, pointing to the Hittite center on the Orontes river rather than naming a distinct town.

entries.title: Talmai (King living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Caleb drove three Anakim giants out of Hebron, and Talmai was one of them.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Talmai was the name of one of the Anakim giants Caleb drove out of Hebron, and also of a king of Geshur whose daughter Maacah married David and became Absalom's mother.

entries.title: Talmai (King living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: A king of Geshur, whose daughter Maacah married David and bore Absalom.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Talmon (Levite living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: He headed a family of temple gatekeepers, and his descendants were still keeping the gates after the exile.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Talmon was the head of a family of temple gatekeepers among the returning exiles, a hereditary role his descendants continued to serve in.

entries.title: Tamah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Head of a family of temple servants, the Nethinim, who came back from Babylon with Zerubbabel. Some lists spell it Thamah.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Tamah, or Thamah, was the head of a family among the temple servants, the Nethinim, who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:53; Nehemiah 7:55).

entries.title: Tamar
entries.summary: Ezekiel names him twice, and nothing else is recorded.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tamar (Absalom's daughter living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: A man from the united kingdom, and 2 Samuel is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tamar (David's daughter living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: David's daughter, raped by her half-brother Amnon. David did nothing, and her full brother Absalom had Amnon murdered for it.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Two women named Tamar stand out in the Old Testament. Judah's daughter-in-law Tamar was widowed twice without bearing an heir and, when Judah failed to give her his third son as custom required, disguised herself as a prostitute and conceived twins by Judah himself, a scheme Judah eventually admitted was more righteous than his own failure to provide for her. A different Tamar was David's daughter, raped by her own half-brother Amnon, an assault that went unpunished by David and led directly to Amnon's murder by Tamar's full brother Absalom.
