For, lo, it made me also to err, so that I was not ashamed of the multitude in the city, in that before the eyes of all I turned aside unto Tamar, and I wrought 6 a great sin, and I uncovered the covering of my sons' shame.

entries.title: Tamar (Woman living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Judah's daughter-in-law, widowed twice with no heir. Judah held back his third son, so she dressed as a prostitute and conceived twins by Judah himself. He ended up saying she was more righteous than he was, and Ruth 4:12 blesses a family in her name.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Tammuz (A male deity in the Old Testament)
entries.summary: In Ezekiel's vision the women sit at the temple's north gate weeping for Tammuz. He was the Mesopotamian god of shepherds and growing things, Dumuzi to the Sumerians, and the weeping mourned his yearly death.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Tammuz was the Mesopotamian god of shepherds and vegetation, known to the Sumerians as Dumuzi and identified by later writers with the Greek Adonis. Ezekiel condemns the women of Jerusalem for sitting at the temple's north gate “weeping for Tammuz” (Ezekiel 8:14), a rite mourning the god's yearly death and descent to the underworld. The name was later applied to the fourth month of the Hebrew civil calendar, corresponding to parts of June and July.

entries.title: Tanhumeth (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A Netophathite whose son Seraiah was one of the army captains who came over to Gedaliah after Jerusalem fell.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Tanhumeth was a Netophathite whose son Seraiah was among the army captains who submitted to Gedaliah, the Babylonian-appointed governor of Judah, after the fall of Jerusalem (2 Kings 25:23; Jeremiah 40:8).

entries.title: Taphath (Woman living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Solomon's daughter, married to Ben-abinadab, one of the twelve officers who fed the court a month each.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A daughter of Solomon who married Ben-abinadab, one of the twelve district officers responsible for supplying provisions to the royal court on a rotating monthly basis (1 Kings 4:11).

entries.title: Tappuah
entries.summary: A town on the line between Ephraim and Manasseh.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Tappuah was a town on the border between Ephraim and Manasseh's territories, and also the name of a son of Hebron in the genealogies of Judah.

witness.excerpt: And the other, the king of Tappuah, as he sat upon his 3 horse, [I slew, and so I scattered all his people.
6 And as we were departing the men of Tappuah set upon our spoil, and delivering it up to our sons we fought with them as far as Tappuah.

entries.title: Tappuah
entries.summary: Named once, in Joshua, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tappuah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 3 men called Tappuah. This one is a man from the divided-kingdom years, named once in 1 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tarah (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Abraham's father, whose family line Genesis 11 traces. Joshua 24:2 names him again.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Tarah was one of the stations where Israel camped during the wilderness wanderings, mentioned only in the itinerary of Numbers 33 between Tahath and Mithcah. Nothing further is known of its location.

witness.excerpt: For Abraham was the son of Terah, as well as Haran and Nahor.

The son of Phaleg, whose father was Heber, was Ragau: whose son was Serug: to whom was born Nahor: his son was Terah: who was the father of Abraham: who accordingly was the tenth from Noah:  and was born in the two hundred and ninety second year after the deluge.

The name of Reuben's wife is ’Adâ  and the name of Simeon's wife is ’Adîbâ’a, a Canaanite;  and the name of Levi's wife is Mêlkâ,  of the daughters of Aram, of the seed of the sons of Terah; and the name of Judah's wife, Bêtasû’êl,  a Canaanite; and the name of Issachar's wife, Hêzaqâ; and the name of Zebulon's wife, †Nî’îmân†;  and the name of Dan's wife, ’Êglâ; and the name of Naphtali's wife, Rasû’û, of

entries.title: Tarah (Terah)
entries.summary: Named twice, in Numbers, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Taralah
entries.summary: A town given to Benjamin, in the hill country near Gibeon. Nobody has found the site.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Taralah was one of the towns allotted to the tribe of Benjamin, listed among the settlements in the hill country near Gibeon (Josh. 18:27). No convincing modern identification for the site has been established.

entries.title: Tarea (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Saul's line again, through Jonathan, Mephibosheth and Micah. Tarea was Micah's son, and 1 Chronicles 9:41 spells him Tahrea.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Tarea, also spelled Tahrea (1 Chronicles 9:41), was a son of Micah descended from King Saul through Jonathan and Mephibosheth, listed in the genealogy of Benjamin (1 Chronicles 8:35).

entries.title: Tarshish
entries.summary: Far to the west, at the edge of what Israel knew of the sea. Solomon's ships went there for gold, and ships of Tarshish came to mean any big ocean-going ship. Jonah boarded one at Joppa to get away from Nineveh.
entries.books: 1 Kings, 2 Chronicles, Psalm, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Jonah
entries.label: 7 books
entries.dictNote: Tarshish appears first as one of the sons of Javan in the table of nations, and later as a distant western port that became proverbial for long ocean voyages and imported wealth; “ships of Tarshish” came to describe any large seagoing vessel regardless of destination. Solomon's navy sailed to a Tarshish for gold and exotic goods, and it was to Tarshish that Jonah tried to flee by ship from Joppa rather than go to Nineveh. Ancient writers and modern scholars have proposed locations ranging from a Phoenician colony in southern Spain, near the mouth of the Guadalquivir, to a port on the Red Sea or Indian coast, and the question remains unsettled.

entries.title: Tarshish (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 4 men called Tarshish. This one is a man from the divided-kingdom years, named once in 1 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tarshish (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Genesis names him once, and he is a man from the patriarchs.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tarshish (Persian living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A man from the exile and the return, and Esther is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tarsus
entries.summary: Paul was born here, in the capital of Cilicia on the Cydnus River, about twelve miles from the sea, and he called it no mean city. It had schools of philosophy and rhetoric that rivalled Athens and Alexandria.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Tarsus was the capital of the Roman province of Cilicia and the birthplace of the apostle Paul, who called it no mean city (Acts 21:39). It sat on the Cydnus River about twelve miles from the Mediterranean and was known for its schools of philosophy and rhetoric, rivaling Athens and Alexandria in the ancient world. Barnabas brought Paul there from Jerusalem, and excavation at the site's mound of Gözlü Kule has confirmed continuous settlement stretching back to the Bronze Age.

witness.excerpt: Now when Antiochus was come to Tarsus in Cilicia, Petus ordered a centurion to go to him, and send him in bonds to Rome.
Josephus understood it, that he went to Tarshish in Cilicia , or to the Mediterranean Sea, upon which Tarsus lay.
But he went not, out of fear: nay he ran away from God to the city of Joppa: and finding a ship there, he went into it, and sailed to Tarsus, in Cilicia. .
Tharsus to the Tharsians, for so was Cilicia of old called: the sign of which is this, that the noblest city they have, and a metropolis also, is Tarsus: the Tau being by change put for the Theta.

entries.title: Tartak (A male deity in the Old Testament)
entries.summary: One of two gods the Avvites worshipped after the Assyrians resettled them in Samaria. The other was Nibhaz, and nothing else is known about this one.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Not a person but one of two gods worshiped by the Avvites, a people the Assyrians resettled in Samaria after deporting Israel's population (2 Kings 17:31). Almost nothing is known about the god's nature or cult beyond this single mention alongside another Avvite god, Nibhaz.

entries.title: Tartan (Leader's title)
entries.summary: An Assyrian title, roughly commander-in-chief, not a man's name. One tartan came with the delegation demanding Jerusalem's surrender from Hezekiah, and an earlier one took Ashdod for Sargon.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Tartan was not a personal name but an Assyrian military title meaning roughly "commander-in-chief." One tartan served as one of Sennacherib's envoys sent to demand Jerusalem's surrender under Hezekiah (2 Kings 18:17). An earlier tartan led Sargon II's campaign against Ashdod, an operation Sargon's own palace inscriptions at Khorsabad independently record (Isaiah 20:1).

witness.excerpt:
The names of the two other commanders were Tartan and Rabsaris.

2.

entries.title: Tatnai (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: He was a Persian governor who challenged the Jews rebuilding the temple and wrote to Darius about it. The search turned up Cyrus's decree, and he was told to help instead.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Tattenai was a Persian provincial governor who questioned the legitimacy of the Jews rebuilding the Jerusalem temple, and his official inquiry to King Darius led to the discovery of Cyrus's original decree, which confirmed the project's authorization and resulted in Tattenai being ordered to support it instead.

entries.title: Tebah (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Nahor's son by his concubine Reumah, and the first one named. Nahor was Abraham's brother.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The eldest son of Abraham's brother Nahor by his concubine Reumah, listed among Nahor's descendants in Genesis 22:24. Nothing further is recorded about him.

entries.title: Tebaliah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Hosah's third son, a Levite of Merari's family who kept the temple gates.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The third son of Hosah, a Levite gatekeeper from the family of Merari, listed among those assigned by lot to guard duty at the temple in 1 Chronicles 26:11.

entries.title: Tebeth (Name of the 10th month)
entries.summary: Tenth month, December into January, and the month Esther was taken in to the king.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Tebeth was not a person but the tenth month of the Hebrew calendar, roughly corresponding to December-January, during which Esther was brought before King Ahasuerus (Esther 2:16). The word is borrowed from Babylonian, where the month Tebetu shares the same name, reflecting the calendar Jews adopted during and after the exile.

entries.title: Tehinnah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: He founded Ir-nahash, the city of Nahash, according to Judah's genealogies.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A descendant of Judah credited as the founder of Ir-nahash, "city of Nahash," named in the tribal genealogies of Judah (1 Chronicles 4:12).

entries.title: Tekoa
entries.summary: It sat about six miles south of Bethlehem, on the edge of the wilderness that carries its name. Rehoboam fortified it, and Amos was a herdsman there when he was called to prophesy against Israel.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Tekoa was a fortified hill town in Judah about six miles south of Bethlehem, overlooking the wilderness that bears its name, strengthened by Rehoboam among his defensive cities (2 Chronicles 11:6). Joab used a "wise woman of Tekoa" to persuade David to bring Absalom back from exile (2 Samuel 14:2), and the shepherd Amos, "among the herdmen of Tekoa," was called from there to prophesy against Israel (Amos 1:1).

witness.excerpt: As soon as it was day, and the King was come into that wilderness which is under the city of Tekoa, he said to the multitude, that “They ought to give credit to what the Prophet had said; and not to set themselves in aray for fighting; but to set the Priests, with their trumpets, and the Levites, with the singers of

Now Rehoboam, the son of Solomon, who, as we said before, was king of the two tribes, built strong and large cities, Bethlehem, and Etare, and Tekoa, and Bethzur, and Shoco, and Adullam, and Ipan, and Maresha, and Ziph, and Adorlam, and Lachlsh, and Azekah, and Zorah, and Aijalon, and Hebron; these he built first of all in the tribe of Judah.

photo.description: panorama of Khirbet Teku’a, which is in the distance at center

entries.title: Tekoite (Tekoa)
entries.summary: Someone from Tekoa, the hometown of Amos. The wise woman Joab sent to David about Absalom was a Tekoite, and so were at least two of David's mighty men.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Tekoite marks someone from Tekoa, a town in Judah's hill country south of Bethlehem. It was the hometown of the prophet Amos, of the wise woman Joab sent to persuade David to reconcile with his exiled son Absalom, and of at least two of David's mighty men.

entries.title: Tel-abib
entries.summary: Ezekiel lived here among the exiles by the river Chebar. The name meant an old ruin-mound in Akkadian, and the founders of Tel Aviv borrowed it in 1910.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A settlement of Judean exiles beside the river Chebar in Babylonia, where the prophet Ezekiel lived among his fellow captives (Ezek. 3:15). The name comes from an Akkadian phrase for an ancient ruin-mound; the founders of modern Tel Aviv borrowed it in 1910 for its Hebrew sense of a mound of spring, joining old ruin and new growth in one name.

entries.title: Tel-haresha (Tel-harsha)
entries.summary: One of the places in Babylonia that exiles returned from. The families from there could not prove they were Israelites, and nobody knows where it was.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Tel-haresha, hill of the wood, was a place in Babylonia from which a group of exiles returned to Jerusalem after the exile, listed alongside Tel-melah among those who could not prove their Israelite genealogy (Ezra 2:59; Nehemiah 7:61). Its Babylonian location has not been identified.

entries.title: Tel-melah
entries.summary: Hill of salt, a place in Babylonia. People who came back from there could not show their Israelite ancestry, and the site is unknown.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Tel-melah, hill of salt, was a place in Babylonia from which a group of Jewish exiles returned after the captivity, named alongside Tel-haresha among those unable to document their Israelite ancestry (Ezra 2:59; Nehemiah 7:61). Its site in Babylonia is unknown.

entries.title: Telah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: An ancestor of Joshua in Ephraim's genealogy, and that line is all that is recorded of him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Telah appears in the genealogy of Ephraim in 1 Chronicles 7 as an ancestor of Joshua, Moses's successor. Nothing beyond his place in that family line is recorded.

entries.title: Telaim
entries.summary: Saul gathered his army here before he went against the Amalekites, in the Negev of Judah. It is probably the Telem of Joshua 15:24.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The place where Saul mustered his army before his campaign against the Amalekites, in the Negev of Judah (1 Sam. 15:4). It is probably the same site as Telem, mentioned in Joshua 15:24.

entries.title: Telassar
entries.summary: The Assyrian king's messenger names it with Gozan and Haran, places already conquered. The children of Eden lived there, somewhere in Mesopotamia.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Telassar is named by the Assyrian king's messenger, alongside Gozan and Haran, as one of the territories already conquered and resettled by the children of Eden before Assyria's assault on Jerusalem (2 Kings 19:12; Isa. 37:12). It lay somewhere in Mesopotamia, and some have proposed identifying it with a site near Sinjar, though the identification remains uncertain.

entries.title: Telem
entries.summary: A town on Judah's southern border, in the list at Joshua 15:24. It may be the Telaim where Saul gathered his army against the Amalekites.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Town on Judah's southern border (Josh. 15:24), possibly the same as Telaim, where Saul mustered his army before attacking the Amalekites (1 Sam. 15:4). The same name also belonged to a temple gatekeeper who, after the exile, agreed to send away the foreign wife he had married (Ezra 10:24).

entries.title: Telem (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Ezra names him once, and he is a man from the exile and the return.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tema
entries.summary: An oasis in the north Arabian desert, on the caravan road between Damascus and the Arabian interior, named for a son of Ishmael. Job's friend Eliphaz compares Job's useless helpers to the caravans of Tema. Much later the Babylonian king Nabonidus made it his residence.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Tema was an oasis town in the north Arabian desert on the caravan route between Damascus and the Arabian interior, named for a son of Ishmael whose descendants settled there (Genesis 25:15; 1 Chronicles 1:30). Job's friend Eliphaz compares the failed hope of Job's rescuers to the caravans of Tema (Job 6:19), and a large inscribed stone found at the site records that the Babylonian king Nabonidus made Tema his residence for a decade in the sixth century BC, confirming its importance into the exilic period.

entries.title: Tema (Arabian living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Genesis and 1 Chronicles name him twice, and he is a man from the patriarchs.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Temani (Edomite living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Teman was Esau's grandson, and his Edomite clan had a name for wisdom. This is the word for that clan, and it is what Eliphaz is called all through Job.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Teman was a grandson of Esau and the ancestor of an Edomite clan renowned for wisdom, and Job's friend Eliphaz is identified as a Temanite.

entries.title: Temeni (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Ashur, the founder of Tekoa, had a son by this name, and the genealogy records nothing else about him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Temeni was one of the sons of Ashur, the founder of Tekoa, listed in the genealogy of Judah in 1 Chronicles 4:6. Nothing else is recorded about him.

entries.title: Terah (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Abraham's father, named once in Luke's genealogy. Josephus tried to give him a date, 292 years after the flood.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Terah was Abraham's father, and Genesis records that he set out from Ur with Abraham, Abraham's wife Sarah, and his grandson Lot, intending to reach Canaan, but the family settled in Haran instead and Terah died there, leaving Abraham to complete the journey after God's call came to him directly.

witness.excerpt: Terah begat Abram in his seventieth year… Terah: who was the father of Abraham: who accordingly was the tenth from Noah: and was born in the two hundred and ninety second year after the deluge.

entries.lukeNote: Abraham's father, named once in the genealogy (3:34). Josephus gives him an actual date: 292 years after the flood, trying to pin Genesis's long lifespans to a real chronology, the same impulse behind Luke's own carefully unbroken chain.

entries.title: Teresh (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: He and Bigthan guarded the door of King Ahasuerus and plotted to kill him. Mordecai found out and reported it, and both men were executed. The record of that service was later read to the king, and it turned the story of Esther.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Teresh was a eunuch who guarded the entrance to the palace of the Persian king Ahasuerus, commonly identified with Xerxes I. Along with a fellow guard, Bigthan, he plotted to assassinate the king, but Mordecai learned of the conspiracy and reported it, and the two men were executed. The record of Mordecai's service was later read to the king and became the turning point that led to Mordecai's promotion (Esther 2:21-23; 6:1-3).

witness.excerpt: Some time after this [two eunuchs] Bigthan and Teresh plotted against the King; and Barnabazus, the servant of one of the eunuchs, being by birth a Jew, was acquainted with their conspiracy, and discovered it to the Queen’s uncle.

entries.title: Tertius (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Paul dictated Romans and Tertius wrote it down. At the end he slips in a greeting of his own, in his own voice.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The scribe who wrote down Paul's letter to the Romans as Paul dictated it, and who added his own greeting to the Roman church in his own voice (Romans 16:22), offering a rare glimpse of the ancient practice of using a secretary, or amanuensis, to produce a letter.

entries.title: Tertullus (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: A hired speaker who put the case against Paul before Felix at Caesarea. He flattered the governor for a long time first, then called Paul a troublemaker, a leader of the sect of the Nazarenes, and a man who tried to profane the temple.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Tertullus was a professional orator hired by the Jewish leadership to present their accusations against Paul before the Roman governor Felix in Caesarea. He flattered Felix at length before charging Paul with stirring up unrest, leading the sect of the Nazarenes, and attempting to profane the temple (Acts 24:1-9).

entries.title: Thahash (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Another of Nahor's sons by Reumah, listed once in Genesis 22:24.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A son of Nahor, Abraham's brother, by his concubine Reumah, listed among Nahor's descendants (Genesis 22:24). Nothing else is recorded about him.

entries.title: Thamar (Woman living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: She is Tamar, in Matthew's spelling: Judah's daughter-in-law, who conceived Perez and Zerah by Judah after he failed to give her his youngest son. She is one of four women in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Thamar is the Greek form of Tamar, the Canaanite woman who disguised herself and conceived twins, Perez and Zerah, by her father-in-law Judah after he had failed to give her his youngest son in marriage (Gen. 38). She is one of only four women named in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus (Matt. 1:3).

entries.title: Thebez
entries.summary: Abimelech, Gideon's son who made himself king, was besieging the tower at Thebez when a woman dropped a millstone on his head. He told his armor-bearer to kill him so nobody could say a woman did it. Joab still remembered it years later.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Thebez was a fortified town northeast of Shechem where Abimelech, Gideon's son who had made himself king, was killed while besieging its central tower; a woman dropped a millstone on his head, and he had his armor-bearer finish him off rather than die at a woman's hand (Judges 9:50-54). Joab later cites the episode as a cautionary example when explaining to David's messenger why the army had kept its distance from a city wall during the siege that got Uriah killed (2 Samuel 11:21).

entries.title: Theophilus (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Luke wrote both his Gospel and Acts to him. He calls him most excellent, the title he also uses for Felix and Festus, and that is all anyone knows.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Theophilus was the person to whom Luke dedicated both his Gospel and the book of Acts (Luke 1:3; Acts 1:1). Luke addresses him with the same title, 'most excellent,' that he elsewhere uses for the Roman governors Felix and Festus, which has led some to think Theophilus held an official rank, though nothing certain is known about him beyond these two dedications.

witness.excerpt: And when Agrippa had entirely finished all the duties of the Divine worship, he removed Theophilus, the son of Ananus, from the high priesthood, and bestowed that honor of his on Simon the son of Boethus, whose name was also Cantheras whose daughter king Herod married, as I have related above.
65.] He also deprived Jesus, the son of Gamaliel, of the High Priesthood; and gave it to Matthias, the son of Theophilus, under whom the Jews war with the Romans took its beginning.

The names of these High-priests, or rather ridiculous and profane persons, were Jesus the son of Damneus; Jesus the son of Gamaliel; Matthias the son of Theophilus; and that prodigious ignoramus Phannias, the son of Samuel.

entries.title: Thessalonian (Thessalonica)
entries.summary: Someone from Thessalonica, the port in Roman Macedonia where Paul planted a church and then had to leave in a hurry. His two letters to them are among the earliest writing in the New Testament.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Thessalonian designates an inhabitant of Thessalonica, a major port city in Roman Macedonia where Paul founded a church during his second missionary journey after a rocky start that forced him to leave the city quickly. His two letters to this church are among the earliest documents in the New Testament.

entries.title: Thessalonica
entries.summary: The capital of Macedonia, a busy port on the Via Egnatia. Paul preached in the synagogue there for a few weeks before opposition drove him on to Berea. Luke calls the city officials politarchs, an unusual title.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Thessalonica was the capital of the Roman province of Macedonia, a busy port city on the Via Egnatia named for Alexander the Great's half sister. Paul preached in its synagogue on his second missionary journey and planted a church there, though opposition from local Jews forced him to flee to Berea after only a few weeks (Acts 17:1-10). Luke's account calls the city's magistrates "politarchs," an unusual Greek title once doubted by critics until archaeologists found the same word inscribed on a Roman arch from the city, confirming Luke's precision. Paul later wrote two letters to the congregation he founded there, and the city, modern Thessaloniki, remains one of Greece's largest.

entries.title: Theudas (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Gamaliel's example of a movement that died with its leader. Theudas raised a following, he was killed, and it came to nothing. Josephus mentions a rebel Theudas around AD 44, later than Gamaliel's speech, and whether that is the same man has never been settled.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Theudas led a failed uprising against Roman rule, cited by the Pharisee Gamaliel as an example of a movement that collapsed once its leader was killed (Acts 5:36). The Jewish historian Josephus describes a rebel named Theudas active around AD 44, a decade or more after Gamaliel's speech, and scholars have long debated whether this is the same man, a different Theudas, or evidence of a common revolutionary name in the period.

entries.title: Thomas (Apostle living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: One of the twelve, called the twin. He would not believe Jesus had risen until he could touch the wounds, and when Jesus showed him his hands and side he said, my Lord and my God.
entries.label: 5 books
entries.dictNote: Thomas was one of the twelve apostles, remembered chiefly for refusing to believe the other disciples' report that Jesus had risen until he could see and touch the wounds himself, earning him the label doubting Thomas ever since. When Jesus did appear and offered his hands and side, Thomas's response was the flattest declaration of Jesus's divinity in any Gospel, my Lord and my God, and Jesus's gentle reply blessed everyone who would believe without that kind of proof. Tradition holds Thomas carried the gospel as far as India, where an ancient Christian community still traces its founding to him.

entries.title: Thummim (A Jewish oracle)
entries.summary: Paired with the Urim in the high priest's breastpiece, and used the same way, to put a question to God.
entries.label: 5 books
entries.dictNote: The Thummim, paired with the Urim, were sacred objects in the high priest's breastpiece used to discern God's will, covered more fully under the entry for Urim.

entries.title: Thyatira
entries.summary: A trading city in the Roman province of Asia, known for its guilds, especially the dyers. Lydia, the seller of purple cloth Paul met at Philippi, came from there, and Revelation sends one of its seven letters to the church there.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Thyatira was a commercial city in the Roman province of Asia known for its trade guilds, especially dyers who worked with a purple dye extracted from the madder root; inscriptions naming the city's dyers' guild have been found among its ruins. Lydia, the seller of purple cloth whom Paul converted at Philippi, came from Thyatira (Acts 16:14). It was also home to one of the seven churches addressed in Revelation, commended for its love and service but rebuked for tolerating a false prophetess who led believers into idolatry and sexual immorality (Revelation 2:18-29).

entries.title: Tiberias
entries.summary: Named once, in John, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tiberias (Sea of Galilee)
entries.summary: In John the Sea of Galilee goes by the Sea of Tiberias, after the city Herod Antipas built on its shore and named for the emperor Tiberius.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Tiberias was a city on the Sea of Galilee built by Herod Antipas and named for the Roman emperor Tiberius, and the lake itself is sometimes called the Sea of Tiberias in John's Gospel.

witness.excerpt: The city itself is situated like Tiberias, at the bottom of a mountain, and on those sides which are not washed by the sea, had been strongly fortified by Josephus, though not so strongly as Tiberias; for the wall of Tiberias had been built at the beginning of

But as soon as he was informed that Tiberias was fond of innovations, and that Tarichere had revolted, both which cities were parts of the kingdom of Agrippa, and was satisfied within himself that the Jews were every where perverted [from their obedience to their
So they sent for him, and allotted him Tiberias for his habitation: and appointed him some income of money, for his maintenance: and made him a magistrate of that city, by way of honour to him.
It hath two lakes in it; that of Asphaltitis, and that of Tiberias: whose natures are opposite to each other.

entries.title: Tiberius (Emperor living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: The second Roman emperor, after Augustus, from AD 14 to 37. Luke dates the start of John's ministry to the fifteenth year of his reign, in the same verse that names Pilate and Herod.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: (in full, Tiberius Claudius Nero), the second Roman emperor, successor of Augustus, who began to reign A.D. 14 and reigned until A.D. 37. He was the son of Tiberius Claudius Nero and Livia, and hence a stepson of Augustus. He was born at Rome on the 18th of November, B.C. 45. He became emperor in his fifty-fifth year, after having distinguished himself as a commander in various wars, and having evinced talents of a high order as an orator and an administrator of civil affairs. He even gained the reputation of possessing the sterner virtues of the Roman character, and was regarded as entirely worthy of the imperial honors to which his birth and supposed personal merits at length opened the way. Yet, on being raised to the supreme power, he suddenly became, or showed himself to be a very different man. His subsequent life was one of inactivity, sloth and self-indulgence. He was despotic in his government, cruel and vindictive in his disposition. He died A.D. 37, at the age of 78, after a reign of twenty-three years. Our Saviour was put to death in the reign of Tiberius.

witness.excerpt: Agrippa lived at Rome: and was generally brought up and conversed with Drusus, the Emperor Tiberius's son: and contracted a friendship with Antonia, the wife of Drusus the Great.

entries.lukeNote: The emperor whose fifteenth regnal year dates the start of John's ministry (3:1), the same verse that names Pilate, Herod, Philip, and Lysanias all at once. Josephus's own account of Tiberius's court, years later, follows the Herodian family Agrippa grew up inside of, the same royal household Luke's chronology is built around.

entries.title: Tibhath
entries.summary: Hadadezer of Zobah held this city, and David carried off a great deal of bronze from it. Solomon later used that bronze for the temple. 2 Samuel 8:8 calls the place Betah.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A city belonging to Hadadezer, the Aramean king of Zobah, from which David took large quantities of bronze after defeating him (1 Chronicles 18:8); the parallel account in 2 Samuel 8:8 calls the same city Betah. Solomon later used bronze from this campaign to make furnishings for the temple.

entries.title: Tibni (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: After Zimri died, half of Israel followed Tibni son of Ginath and half followed Omri. It went on for four years. Then Tibni died and Omri was king.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Tibni son of Ginath was a rival claimant to the throne of Israel after the death of Zimri, backed by roughly half the people for four years while Omri's faction contended against him. Omri eventually prevailed and Tibni died, leaving Omri sole king (1 Kings 16:21-22).

witness.excerpt: Upon which the people of Israel were presently divided, and part of them would have Tibni to be king, and part Omri; but when those that were for Omri's ruling had beaten Tibni, Omri reigned over all the multitude.

entries.title: Tidal (King living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: King of Goyim, one of the four eastern kings under Chedorlaomer who attacked a group of Canaanite cities and carried off Lot. Abraham went after them and beat them. His name matches Tudhaliya, a name several Hittite kings carried.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Tidal, called “king of nations” (Hebrew “Goyim”), was one of four eastern kings, led by Chedorlaomer of Elam, who campaigned against a coalition of Canaanite cities and carried off Lot before Abraham pursued and defeated them (Genesis 14:1-16). His name corresponds to Tudhaliya, a royal name borne by several Hittite kings, and “Goyim” most likely designates a confederation of peoples east of the Tigris rather than a single nation. The episode is the Bible's earliest recorded military campaign and treats Abraham as a regional power capable of defeating an organized royal coalition.

entries.title: Tiglath-pileser (King living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: He was the third Assyrian king of the name, and he took territory from Israel and Syria and collected tribute. His own inscriptions record the same campaigns and payments 2 Kings describes.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Tiglath-pileser the Third was an aggressive Assyrian king whose campaigns against Israel and Syria are recorded both in the Bible and extensively in his own royal inscriptions, which independently confirm the tribute payments and territorial conquests described in 2 Kings.

entries.title: Tikvah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: His son Shallum was married to Huldah, the prophetess who was asked about the law scroll found in Josiah's temple repairs.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tikvah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Father of one of the men who stood against the foreign-marriage decision under Ezra.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Two men in the Old Testament carry this name. One was the father of Shallum, husband of the prophetess Huldah, who confirmed the authenticity of the law scroll found during Josiah's temple repairs (2 Kings 22:14). The other was the father of Jahzeiah, one of the few who opposed Ezra's plan to have Israelite men separate from their foreign wives (Ezra 10:15).

entries.title: Tilon (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of Shimon's four sons in Judah's genealogy, and nothing more.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of four sons of Shimon listed in the genealogy of Judah (1 Chr. 4:20). Nothing beyond his name and parentage is recorded.

entries.title: Timaeus (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Bartimaeus means son of Timaeus, and Mark gives the father's name only to say whose son the blind beggar at Jericho was.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The father of Bartimaeus, the blind beggar Jesus healed outside Jericho (Mark 10:46). Mark names him only to identify his son; the name Bartimaeus itself means "son of Timaeus." Nothing else about Timaeus is recorded.

entries.title: Timna (Woman living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Two Edomites. One was a concubine of Esau's son Eliphaz, and her son Amalek fathered the people who were Israel's enemies for generations. The other was an Edomite clan chief.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Timna was the name of an Edomite clan leader and also of a concubine of Esau's son Eliphaz, whose own son Amalek became the ancestor of Israel's long-standing enemy.

entries.title: Timnah
entries.summary: The Philistine town where Samson saw the woman he wanted to marry. The riddle at that wedding feast started his long fight with the Philistines.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Timnah was a Philistine town, the hometown of the woman Samson wanted to marry, whose wedding feast triggered the riddle contest and violence that began Samson's long conflict with the Philistines.

entries.title: Timnah
entries.summary: Named once, in Joshua, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Timnath-heres
entries.summary: The name means portion of the sun. Joshua was given this town in the hill country of Ephraim and was buried there, north of the hill of Gaash. The book of Joshua spells it Timnath-serah.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Timnath-heres, portion of the sun, was the town Joshua received as his inheritance in the hill country of Ephraim and where he was buried after his death (Joshua 19:50; 24:30; Judges 2:9). It lay north of the hill of Gaash, roughly ten miles southwest of Shechem. The book of Joshua elsewhere calls the same town Timnath-serah, likely a transposed spelling of the same name.

entries.title: Timnite (Timnah)
entries.summary: Samson's Philistine father-in-law, a man of Timnah. When his daughter was given to another man, the trouble that followed ended with his household burned.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Timnite marks Samson's Philistine father-in-law, whose daughter Samson had married, as a man of Timnah. After Samson's wife was given to another man, the Timnite's household was burned in the retaliation that follows in Judges 15.

entries.title: Timon (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: One of the seven chosen to handle the daily food for widows in the Jerusalem church. Nothing more is known of him.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Timon was one of the seven men chosen by the Jerusalem church to administer the daily distribution to widows in Acts 6:5. Nothing further is known of him.

entries.title: Timotheus
entries.summary: Timothy, from Lystra, with a Jewish mother and a Greek father. Paul took him along on his travels and trusted him with hard errands to churches in trouble, and two of Paul's letters are addressed to him.
entries.books: Acts, Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Philippians, Colossians, 1 Thessalonians, 2 Thessalonians, 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, Philemon, Hebrews
entries.label: 12 books
entries.dictNote: Timothy was a young disciple from Lystra, son of a Jewish mother and Greek father, whom Paul recruited as a traveling companion and had circumcised first to avoid unnecessary offense to Jewish audiences. He became one of Paul's most trusted coworkers, sent on sensitive missions to churches in crisis and eventually left in charge of the church at Ephesus, and two of Paul's letters in the New Testament are addressed directly to him with pastoral advice for leading a congregation despite his apparent youth and timidity.

witness.excerpt: After this he went thence in haste against the Ammonites, who had a great and a numerous army, of which Timotheus was the commander.

entries.title: Tipsah (Tiphsah)
entries.summary: Solomon's rule reached as far as Tipsah, a crossing on the Euphrates the Greeks called Thapsacus. Menahem sacked it when he seized Israel's throne because it would not open its gates to him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tipsah (Tiphsah)
entries.summary: Menahem took this town and treated it savagely. The other Tipsah is the Euphrates crossing at the far edge of Solomon's reach.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Tipsah marked the northeastern limit of Solomon's dominion, a crossing point on the Euphrates identified with the Greek Thapsacus, an important ford on the river's trade routes (1 Kings 5:4). Centuries later it was sacked by Menahem, king of Israel, when he seized the throne, because its people had refused to open their gates to him (2 Kings 15:16).

entries.title: Tiras (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Japheth's youngest son in the Table of Nations. Genesis does not say where his people lived. Josephus connected them with the Thracians, and nobody can confirm it.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Tiras was the youngest son of Japheth, listed in the Table of Nations as the ancestor of a people group whose location Genesis does not specify (Genesis 10:2; 1 Chronicles 1:5). Later Jewish tradition, recorded by Josephus, associated his descendants with the Thracians, though the identification cannot be confirmed.

witness.excerpt: And for Tiras  there came forth the seventh portion, four great islands  in the midst of the sea, which reach to the portion of Ham [and the islands of Kamâtûrî came out by lot for the sons of Arpachshad as his inheritance].  14.
The sons of Japheth: Gomer and Magog and Madai and Javan, Tubal and Meshech and Tiras: these are 1324-1372 A.M.

entries.title: Tirathite (Scribal group in the Old Testament)
entries.summary: Scribes at Jabez, named with the Shimeathites and Suchathites. They were Kenites from Hammath, father of the house of Rechab.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Tirathites were one of the families of scribes living at Jabez, listed in 1 Chronicles 2:55 alongside the Shimeathites and Suchathites. The passage identifies them as Kenites descended from Hammath, the father of the house of Rechab, linking these scribal clans to the same Kenite family that produced Moses' father-in-law Jethro.

entries.title: Tirhakah (King living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: The Kushite pharaoh of Egypt in the early seventh century BC, known in his own records as Taharqa. Word that he was marching against Assyria made Sennacherib send Hezekiah a threatening letter during the siege of Jerusalem.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Tirhakah, known in Egyptian and Kushite records as Taharqa, ruled Egypt and Kush as pharaoh of the twenty-fifth (Kushite) dynasty in the early seventh century BC. The Bible names him as the Kushite king whose advance against Assyria prompted Sennacherib to send a threatening message to Hezekiah during the siege of Jerusalem (2 Kings 19:9; Isaiah 37:9). Assyrian records confirm his historicity in detail: the annals and inscribed prisms of both Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal describe their invasions of Egypt and repeated defeats of Taharqa, who was eventually driven back into Nubia.

entries.title: Tirhanah (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Caleb's son by his concubine Maachah, in Judah's genealogy, and that is all.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Tirhanah was a son of Caleb son of Hezron by his concubine Maachah, listed in the tribal genealogy of Judah (1 Chronicles 2:48). Nothing further is recorded about him.

entries.title: Tiria (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Jehaleleel's son, named in 1 Chronicles 4:16. Nothing else is known.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Tiria was one of the sons of Jehaleleel, listed in the genealogy of Judah in 1 Chronicles 4:16. Nothing further is known about him.

entries.title: Tirshatha
entries.summary: A Persian word for the governor of Judah, not a name. It is used of Nehemiah, and on one reading of Zerubbabel.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Tirshatha was a Persian-derived title for the governor of Judah under Persian rule, applied to both Nehemiah and, in some readings, Zerubbabel, rather than being a personal name.

entries.title: Tirzah
entries.summary: An old Canaanite royal city that served as capital of the northern kingdom before Samaria was built. The Song of Solomon sets its beauty beside Jerusalem's. Menahem seized the throne from there.
entries.books: Joshua, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, Song of Solomon
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Tirzah was an ancient Canaanite royal city that became, after Samaria's founding, an earlier capital of the northern kingdom under Jeroboam and his successors, admired enough for its beauty to be paired with Jerusalem as a standard of loveliness in the Song of Solomon. It was also the scene of Menahem's violent seizure of Israel's throne. The same name belongs to the youngest of Zelophehad's five daughters, whose case established Israelite inheritance rights for women without brothers. Tirzah is generally identified with Tell el-Far'ah North, where French excavations uncovered a substantial Iron Age royal quarter consistent with a former capital city.

witness.excerpt: He dwelt in the city Tirzah, having made that his habitation, and reigned twenty-four years.

For Menahem, the General of his army, who was at that time in the city Tirzah, and heard of what had befallen Zachariah, removed thereupon with all his forces to Samaria; and joining battel with Shallum, slew him: and when he had made himself King, he went thence, and came to the city Tiphsah.

entries.title: Tirzah (Woman living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: She was the youngest of Zelophehad's five daughters, named with her sisters each time the family's inheritance comes up.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Tishbite (Tishbe)
entries.summary: Elijah is always the Tishbite, the man from Tishbe. Where Tishbe was, in Gilead or further north in Galilee, depends on how you read the Hebrew of 1 Kings 17:1.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Tishbite identifies the prophet Elijah as coming from Tishbe, though the exact location of that town, whether in Gilead or further north in Galilee, is debated because of an ambiguity in the Hebrew text of 1 Kings 17:1.

entries.title: Titus (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: A Gentile convert who worked with Paul. He carried a hard letter to the church at Corinth and brought back word of how it landed. Paul later left him in Crete to organize the churches, and the letter to Titus is the instructions.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Titus was a Gentile convert and close associate of Paul, entrusted with some of Paul's most sensitive assignments, including carrying a stern letter to the fractious church at Corinth and reporting back on how it was received. Paul later left Titus in Crete to organize the churches there and appoint elders, and the New Testament letter of Titus preserves Paul's instructions for that task. Paul held Titus up as proof that Gentile believers did not need to be circumcised to be fully accepted, refusing to have Titus circumcised even under pressure from other Jewish Christians.

witness.excerpt: For Titus went from Gischala to Cesarea, and Vespasian from Cesarea to Jamnia, and Azotus; and took them both: and when he had put garrisons into them, he came back with a great number of the people, who were come over to him, up

But Titus, intending to pitch his camp nearer to the city than Scopus, placed as many of his choice horsemen and footmen as he thought sufficient opposite to the Jews, to prevent their sallying out upon them, while he gave orders

WHILE Titus was at Cesarea, he solemnized the birthday of his brother Domitian] after a splendid manner, and inflicted a great deal of the punishment intended for the Jews in honor of him; for the number of those that were now slai

NOW, as Titus was upon his march into the enemy's country, the auxiliaries that were sent by the kings marched first, having all the other auxiliaries with them; after whom followed those that were to prepare the roads and measure ou

entries.title: Tizite (Warriors, perhaps from Tiz)
entries.summary: The epithet of Joha, one of David's mighty men. The place it points to is unknown.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Tizite identifies Joha, brother of Jediael, among David's mighty men; the place the epithet refers to is otherwise unknown.

entries.title: Toah (Levite living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: A Kohathite Levite in the line that ran down to Samuel and to Heman the singer. Other lists call him Nahath or Tohu.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Toah was a Kohathite Levite listed in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 6:19-34 as an ancestor of the prophet Samuel and of Heman, the temple musician David appointed. The same family line appears elsewhere in Chronicles and Samuel under the variant spellings Nahath and Tohu, reflecting the normal drift in how genealogical records preserved names across generations of copying. His only role in the text is as a link connecting the priestly and musical branches of the Kohathite family to the house of Elkanah.

entries.title: Tob
entries.summary: Jephthah's half-brothers drove him out for being a prostitute's son, and he went to the land of Tob, east of Gilead. He gathered outlaws there until Gilead's elders came to fetch him back to fight the Ammonites. Men of Tob later hired themselves out to the Ammonites.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: The land of Tob lay somewhere east of Gilead, toward the Syrian desert, and became a refuge for Jephthah after his half brothers drove him from home for being the son of a prostitute (Judges 11:1-3). He gathered a band of outlaws there until the elders of Gilead, desperate for a military leader against the Ammonites, came to recruit him back (Judges 11:4-11). Men of Tob later appear as mercenaries hired by the Ammonites against David (2 Samuel 10:6, 8, where they are called "Ish-tob," meaning "the men of Tob").

entries.title: Tob-adonijah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A Levite Jehoshaphat sent around the cities of Judah with priests and other Levites, teaching from the Book of the Law.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Levite sent out by King Jehoshaphat, along with priests and other Levites, to travel through the cities of Judah teaching the people from the Book of the Law (2 Chronicles 17:7-8).

entries.title: Tobiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Ezra and Nehemiah name him twice, and he is a man from the exile and the return.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Tobiah (Nehemiah's adversary living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: They called him the Ammonite. With Sanballat he mocked Nehemiah's wall and worked against it, and later a priest gave him a room inside the temple courts, so Nehemiah threw him and his things out.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Tobiah was an Ammonite official who, along with Sanballat, mocked and actively opposed Nehemiah's project to rebuild Jerusalem's walls, and Nehemiah later discovered Tobiah had been secretly given a room inside the temple complex itself through a compromised priest, a violation Nehemiah threw him and his belongings out for.

entries.title: Tochen
entries.summary: It belonged to Simeon, and nobody knows where it was.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Tochen was a town assigned to the tribe of Simeon, listed among a handful of Simeonite settlements in a genealogical record (1 Chron. 4:32). Nothing more is known about it, and its location has not been identified.

entries.title: Togarmah (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Gomer's son and Japheth's grandson. Ezekiel's people of Togarmah trade horses and mules, from somewhere in eastern Asia Minor.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Togarmah was a son of Gomer and grandson of Japheth, and his descendants are associated with a people in eastern Asia Minor known in Ezekiel's prophecies for trading horses and mules.

entries.title: Tohu (Levite living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Several generations back in Samuel's family line, before his father Elkanah.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: An ancestor of Samuel in the genealogy of the prophet's Ephraimite Levite family, several generations before Samuel's father Elkanah (1 Samuel 1:1).

entries.title: Toi (King living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: King of Hamath. When David beat Hadadezer, who had been at war with Toi, Toi sent his son with gold, silver and bronze to congratulate him.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Toi was a king of Hamath who sent his son to congratulate David after his victory over their mutual enemy Hadadezer, bringing gifts of gold, silver, and bronze.

witness.excerpt: So when David had made this league of mutual assistance with Toi, (for that was the name of the king of Hamath,) and had received the presents he sent him, he dismissed his son with that respect which was due on both sides; but then David brought those presents that were sent by him,

entries.title: Tola (Judge living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: Judges names him once, and he is a judge from the years before the monarchy.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tola (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Here the verses are the man from the family lists, not the judge. He is in Genesis 46:13 among those who went down to Egypt, and in the Numbers 26 census and 1 Chronicles 7.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Tola was a judge of Israel who led the nation for twenty-three years, though Judges records no specific military deliverance associated with him, only that he rose up to save Israel and judged from his hometown.

witness.excerpt: Issachar and his sons; and these are the names of his sons: Tola, and Phûa,  and Jâsûb,  and Shimron--five.

entries.title: Tolad
entries.summary: Simeon's town in the Negev of Judah. Joshua's lists call it Eltolad.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Tolad, a town of the tribe of Simeon in the Negev of Judah, listed in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 4:29. It is the same place called Eltolad in the earlier town lists of Joshua (15:30, 19:4).

entries.title: Tolaites (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Issachar's clan through Tola, his firstborn, in the Numbers 26 census.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Tolaites were the clan descended from Tola, the firstborn son of Issachar, counted in the Numbers 26 census. A later judge of Israel, also named Tola, belonged to this same tribe and is recorded in Judges 10:1-2.

entries.title: Tophel
entries.summary: Deuteronomy opens with Moses speaking to Israel near Tophel. It is generally identified with Tafileh, on the edge of the Edomite plateau east of the Dead Sea.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Tophel is named in Deuteronomy 1:1 as one of the wilderness locations near which Moses addressed Israel before his death. It is generally identified with modern Tafileh, a town on the edge of the Edomite plateau east of the Dead Sea, whose name is thought to preserve the ancient one.

entries.title: Tophet (Valley of Hinnom)
entries.summary: The place in the Valley of Hinnom where children were burned to Molech, until Josiah defiled it. Jeremiah said the valley would fill with the dead. Later Jewish pictures of Gehenna drew on it.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Tophet was a site in the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem where children were burned as sacrifices to the god Molech, a practice Josiah defiled and abolished during his reforms. Jeremiah repeatedly condemns Tophet and warns that the valley would itself become a place of slaughter and burial in judgment. Its grim associations with fire and destruction contributed to later Jewish imagery of Gehenna as a place of punishment.

entries.title: Trachonitis
entries.summary: The rugged region, a lava field east of the Sea of Galilee. Philip the tetrarch governed it in the year Luke uses to date John the Baptist. Bandits hid in that ground in Herod's day, and it is still called the Lejah.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Trachonitis, meaning "the rugged region," was a volcanic, boulder-strewn district east of the Sea of Galilee, named among the territories governed by Philip the tetrarch in Luke 3:1, part of the political framework Luke uses to date the start of John the Baptist's ministry. Herod the Great had earlier campaigned against bandits who used its lava-field terrain, still known today as the Lejah, as a natural fortress, an account preserved by the first-century historian Josephus. Inscriptions found across the wider Hauran region independently confirm the area's governance first by the Herodian dynasty and then directly by Rome, matching Luke's political framework.

There were robbers that dwelt in Trachonitis; at first their number was no more than forty, but they became more afterwards, and they escaped the punishment Herod would have inflicted on them, by making Arabia their refuge.
Of the four sons of Aram, Uz founded Trachonitis and Damascus: this country lies between Palestine and Celesyria.
But her daughter Salome was married to Philip, the son of Herod, and tetrarch of Trachonitis.

entries.title: Troas
entries.summary: It was a port on the northwest coast of Asia Minor near old Troy. Paul had his vision of the Macedonian man there, come over and help us, and on a later visit he raised Eutychus from the dead during a sermon that went all night.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Troas was a port city on the northwest coast of Asia Minor near the site of ancient Troy, a major stop on Roman sea routes to Macedonia. Here Paul received his vision of a Macedonian man pleading, "Come over and help us," which redirected his second missionary journey into Europe (Acts 16:8-11); he later raised Eutychus from the dead during an all-night sermon there (Acts 20:6-12) and, on his final journey, left a cloak and some books with Carpus in the city (2 Timothy 4:13).

entries.title: Trophimus (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: A Gentile from Ephesus who traveled with Paul. People in Jerusalem thought Paul had taken him into the temple, and that started the riot that ended with Paul under arrest.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Trophimus was a Gentile companion of Paul from Ephesus, and it was the mistaken belief that Paul had brought Trophimus into the Jerusalem temple's restricted area that triggered the riot leading to Paul's arrest in Acts.

entries.title: Tryphena (Woman living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: She and Tryphosa are greeted by Paul at Rome as women who labored in the Lord. The names are so alike that some guess they were sisters, though the text does not say.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Christian woman at Rome, greeted by Paul together with Tryphosa as women who labored in the Lord (Romans 16:12). Their similar names, both suggesting delicacy or refinement, have led some to suggest they were sisters, though this is not stated in the text.

entries.title: Tryphosa (Woman living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Paul greets her at Rome with Tryphena, two women who worked hard in the Lord. The paired names may mean they were sisters. Nothing more is known of her.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Tryphosa was a Christian woman in Rome whom Paul greets alongside Tryphena in Romans 16:12, commending both as women who work hard in the Lord. Their similar names suggest they may have been sisters, since such paired names occur among household members and freedwomen in Roman inscriptions of the period. Nothing further is known of her.

entries.title: Tubal
entries.summary: In the prophets Tubal is a far northern people, usually named with Meshech, trading and making war. The name goes back to a son of Japheth.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Tubal was a son of Japheth and the ancestor of a people the prophets associate with distant northern trade and warfare, frequently paired with Meshech.

witness.excerpt: But Tubal, one of his children by the other wife, exceeded all men in strength, and was very expert and famous in martial performances.

And for Tubal  there came forth the fifth portion in the midst of the tongue which approacheth towards the border of the portion of Lud to the second tongue, to the region beyond the second tongue unto the third tongue.  12.
The sons of Japheth: Gomer and Magog and Madai and Javan, Tubal and Meshech and Tiras: these are 1324-1372 A.M.

entries.title: Tubal (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Genesis and 1 Chronicles name him twice, and he is a man from the patriarchs.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Tubal-cain (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Lamech's son by Zillah, in Cain's line, and the first metalworker the Bible names, forging tools of bronze and iron. His half-brother Jabal fathered the herdsmen and Jubal the musicians.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The son of Lamech and Zillah in the line of Cain, described in Genesis 4:22 as the forger of bronze and iron tools, the first metalworker named in the Bible. He appears in a short list of culture-founders in Genesis 4, alongside his half-brother Jabal, father of nomadic herdsmen, and Jubal, father of musicians, marking early developments in craft and technology outside the covenant line of Seth.

entries.title: Tychicus (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: He carried Paul's letters, Ephesians and Colossians among them, and told the churches in person how Paul was doing.
entries.label: 5 books
entries.dictNote: Tychicus was a trusted companion of Paul who carried several of his letters, including Ephesians and Colossians, to their destinations and delivered news of Paul's situation to the churches in person.

entries.title: Tyrannus (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: After the synagogue in Ephesus put Paul out, he taught every day for two years in the lecture hall of Tyrannus. Whether Tyrannus was a Jewish teacher or a Greek who rented out the room is not said.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The owner or teacher associated with a lecture hall in Ephesus where Paul taught daily for two years after being expelled from the local synagogue (Acts 19:9). Whether Tyrannus was a Jewish teacher whose "school" doubled as a private synagogue, or a Greek rhetorician who simply rented out the space, is not stated.

witness.excerpt: There were two guards of Herod's body, who were in great esteem for their strength and tallness, Jucundus and Tyrannus; these men had been cast off by Herod, who was displeased at them; these now used to ride along with Alexander, and for their skill in their exercises were in great esteem with him, and had some gold and other gifts bes

At which time Antipater took another occasion to send in other persons to his father to accuse his brethren, and to tell him that they had privately discoursed with Jucundus and Tyrannus, who had once been masters of the horse to the king, but for some offenses had been put out of that honorable employment.

entries.title: Tyre
entries.summary: The leading Phoenician port, partly on the mainland and partly on an island offshore, rich from sea trade and purple dye made from murex shells. Its king Hiram sent cedar and craftsmen for David and Solomon. The prophets attacked its pride and said it would fall.
entries.books: Joshua, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Psalm, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Hosea, Joel, Amos, Zechariah, Matthew, Mark, Luke, Acts
entries.label: 17 books
entries.dictNote: Tyre was the leading Phoenician port, built partly on a rocky mainland site and partly on an offshore island, and it grew wealthy on maritime trade and its famous purple dye, extracted from murex shellfish along its coast. Its king Hiram supplied cedar and craftsmen for David's and Solomon's building projects, but the prophets later condemned Tyre's pride and predicted its fall, which came in stages: first to Nebuchadnezzar after a long siege, finally to Alexander the Great, who built a causeway to the island city and took it after seven months. Jesus visited its region, and Paul stopped there on his way back from his third missionary journey. Excavated murex shell middens along the Phoenician coast confirm the large scale dye industry ancient sources describe.

And as he came back to Tyre, he went up into Judea also, and fell upon Tarichee, and presently took it, and carried about thirty thousand Jews captives; and slew Pitholaus, who succeeded Aristobulus in his seditious practices, and that by the pers

For as once they were at a feast at Tyre, and in their cups, and reproaches were cast upon one another, Agrippa thought that was not to be born; while Herod hit him in the teeth with his poverty, and with his owing his necessary food to him.

entries.title: Ucal (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Agur's sayings in Proverbs 30 are addressed to Ithiel and Ucal. Many scholars read the Hebrew there as no names at all but Agur saying how worn out he is, so Ucal may never have been a person.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of two men, along with Ithiel, named as recipients of Agur's sayings that open Proverbs 30 (Proverbs 30:1). Many modern scholars read the underlying Hebrew not as proper names at all but as a statement of Agur's exhaustion, something closer to "I am weary, God, I am weary and worn out," which makes Ucal's status as a real historical person doubtful.

entries.title: Uel (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A man of Bani's family who had married a foreign wife and sent her away under Ezra's reform.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Uel was a member of the family of Bani who had married a foreign wife after the return from Babylonian exile and was required to divorce her under Ezra's reforms (Ezra 10:34). He is one of many men named in this list who complied with the covenant.

entries.title: Ulai
entries.summary: Daniel stood by the Ulai, near Susa, when he saw the ram and the goat. It is identified with the Eulaeus, a channel of the river system there.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: River near Susa, capital of Elam, where Daniel stood when he received his vision of the ram and the goat, symbols of the coming Medo-Persian and Greek empires (Dan. 8:2, 16). It is identified with the Eulaeus, a channel of the river system near ancient Susa in southwestern Iran, a site whose extensive ruins, including the palace of Darius, have been excavated by archaeologists.

entries.title: Ulam (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Two men of Manasseh's line carry the name in 1 Chronicles 7, and the name turns up in Benjamin too, in a family known for its archers.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ulam (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: His name sits in the genealogies of Manasseh and Benjamin. Chronicles notes one family of them for producing a lot of archers.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Ulam was a common name in the genealogies of Manasseh and Benjamin, including a family noted in Chronicles for producing many skilled archers.

entries.title: Ulla (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Head of a family in Asher, in Jether's line.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: An Asherite, head of a family within his tribe, listed among the descendants of Jether in 1 Chronicles 7:39.

entries.title: Ummah
entries.summary: One of Asher's towns in Joshua 19:30. Some Greek manuscripts read Acco here, and many scholars prefer that, since Acco is otherwise missing from Asher's list.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A town on the border of the tribe of Asher, named only in Joshua 19:30. Some manuscripts of the Greek Old Testament read "Acco" here instead, and many scholars favor that reading, since the major Asherite coastal city of Acco, which Judges 1:31 explicitly places within Asher's territory, is otherwise strangely missing from this town list.

entries.title: Unni (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Nehemiah names him once, and he is a man from the exile and the return.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Unni (Singer living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: The name means afflicted. He was a Levite David set to play the harp when the ark came up to Jerusalem.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Unni's name means “afflicted.” One man by this name was a Levite musician David appointed to play the harp when the ark of the covenant was brought up to Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 15:18, 20). A second Unni was a Levite who returned from the Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Nehemiah 12:9).

entries.title: Uphaz
entries.summary: Gold from Uphaz overlays idols in Jeremiah and belts the figure in Daniel's vision. Nobody knows where it was, and it may just be a variant of Ophir.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Uphaz appears in poetic parallel with fine gold, used for idol-overlay and for the girdle of the figure in Daniel's vision (Jer. 10:9; Dan. 10:5). Its exact location is unknown, and many scholars think the name is simply a variant or scribal alteration of Ophir, the better-known source of gold in the biblical world, rather than a separate place.

entries.title: Ur
entries.summary: Abraham's family started out from here, Terah leading them toward Canaan. Ur was a big Sumerian city near the mouth of the Euphrates. Leonard Woolley dug it in the 1920s and 1930s and found a royal cemetery full of gold.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Ur was a major Sumerian city near the mouth of the Euphrates in southern Mesopotamia, the ancestral home from which Abraham's father Terah set out for Canaan (Genesis 11:28, 31; Nehemiah 9:7). British archaeologist Leonard Woolley's excavations there in the 1920s and 1930s uncovered a royal cemetery of some 2,000 burials from the mid-third millennium BC, filled with gold jewelry and the famous inlaid "Standard of Ur," giving a vivid picture of the wealthy Sumerian civilization Abraham's family left behind.

entries.title: Ur (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Urbanus (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: A fellow worker Paul greets in Romans 16:9 along with Stachys. The King James spells him Urbane.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Despite the place tag, Urbanus (called "Urbane" in the King James Version) is a person, a fellow worker of Paul's greeted along with Stachys in Romans 16:9. Nothing further is known about him beyond Paul's brief commendation.

entries.title: Uri (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Bezalel's father. Bezalel was the craftsman God picked to build the tabernacle and its furnishings.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Uri was the father of Bezalel, the master craftsman God appointed to oversee the construction of the tabernacle and its furnishings.

entries.title: Uri (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of 3 men called Uri. This one is a man from the exile and the return, named once in Ezra.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Uri (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Kings names him once, and he is a man from the united kingdom.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Uriah (Bathsheba's husband living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Uriah the Hittite, one of David's best soldiers and Bathsheba's husband. David got her pregnant while he was at war and tried to get him to go home to her, and Uriah would not while his comrades were still in the field. So David had him put where the fighting was worst and left there to die.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Uriah the Hittite was one of David's elite soldiers, married to Bathsheba, and after David got Bathsheba pregnant while Uriah was away at war, David tried repeatedly to get Uriah to sleep with his own wife to cover up the affair. Uriah refused out of loyalty to his fellow soldiers still in the field, so David had him placed at the front of the fiercest fighting and then abandoned there, engineering his death.

witness.excerpt: So the king sent for Joab's armor-bearer from the siege, who was the woman's husband, and his name was Uriah.

entries.title: Uriah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A priest, not the Hittite. 2 Kings 16 has him at work in the temple, and Isaiah 8:2 calls him as a witness.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Uriah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A man of the return, named as a father in Ezra 8:33 and in Nehemiah's list of the men rebuilding the wall.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Uriah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A man from the exile and the return. Nehemiah names him once.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Uriah (Prophet living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: He was a prophet who said the same things Jeremiah did and was killed for it. Jeremiah 26:20–23 is the whole of what is known.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Urias (Bathsheba's husband living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Matthew's genealogy says David fathered Solomon by the wife of Urias. It is Uriah the Hittite, and naming him puts David's sin into the family tree of Jesus.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Urias is the Greek form of Uriah, appearing in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus, where David is said to have fathered Solomon "of her that had been the wife of Urias" (Matthew 1:6), a pointed reference to Bathsheba and to David's sin. The man himself is the same Uriah the Hittite of 2 Samuel 11, one of David's loyal soldiers whom David had killed in battle after committing adultery with his wife. Matthew's choice to name Uriah rather than simply Bathsheba keeps David's wrongdoing visible even within the genealogy leading to the Messiah.

entries.title: Uriel (Levite living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a Levite from the divided-kingdom years.

entries.title: Uriel (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A Kohathite Levite, named twice in 1 Chronicles 15 among the heads of his family.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Uriel was a Kohathite Levite, and also the name of Abijah's maternal grandfather, from Gibeah.

entries.title: Uriel (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 3 men called Uriel. This one is a man from the united kingdom, named once in 2 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Urim (A Jewish oracle)
entries.summary: The Urim and Thummim sat in the high priest's breastpiece. They were used to put yes-or-no questions to God. How they actually worked, nobody knows.
entries.books: Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, 1 Samuel, Ezra, Nehemiah
entries.label: 7 books
entries.dictNote: The Urim and Thummim were sacred objects kept in the high priest's breastpiece, used to seek God's guidance on yes-or-no questions, though exactly how they worked and what they looked like is never described in detail.

witness.excerpt: Otherwise the conduct of providence, as to the sacredness of solemn oaths and vows, in God’s refusing to answer by Urim , till this breach of Saul’s vow or curse was understood and set right, and God propitiated by publick prayer, is here very remarkable; as indeed it is every where else in the Old Testament.

entries.title: Uthai (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: The name means helpful. This one was from Judah through Perez, and he settled in Jerusalem after the exile.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Uthai (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: The name means helpful. This Uthai led a group of returning exiles home.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Uthai's name means “helpful.” One Uthai was a descendant of Judah through Perez who resettled in Jerusalem after the exile (1 Chronicles 9:4). A second man of the same name led a group of exiles back from Babylon with Ezra (Ezra 8:14).

entries.title: Uz
entries.summary: Job lived in the land of Uz. Where it was is uncertain, somewhere east of Israel, perhaps in Edom.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Uz was the land where Job lived, its exact location uncertain but generally placed east of Israel, possibly in Edomite territory.

entries.title: Uz (Edomite living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: One of 4 men called Uz. This one is a man from the patriarchs, named twice in Genesis and 1 Chronicles.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Uz (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
