entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Uz (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: A man from the patriarchs, and Genesis is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Uzai (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Father of Palal, who repaired a stretch of Jerusalem's wall under Nehemiah.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Father of Palal, one of the men who helped repair a section of Jerusalem's wall under Nehemiah's direction (Nehemiah 3:25).

entries.title: Uzal
entries.summary: Named once, in Ezekiel, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Uzal (Man living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Joktan's son, and tradition ties the name to an old city in Yemen.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Uzal was a son of Joktan in the genealogies of Genesis, and his name is traditionally associated with an ancient city in the region of Yemen.

entries.title: Uzza
entries.summary: Uzzah put his hand out to steady the ark when the oxen stumbled, and he died on the spot. David was afraid, and the ark stayed where it was for three months before it went on to Jerusalem.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Uzza, more fully Uzzah, reached out to steady the ark of the covenant when the oxen pulling its cart stumbled, and he died instantly for touching it, a severe judgment that terrified David and delayed the ark's journey to Jerusalem by three months.

witness.excerpt: But as they were come to the threshing-floor of Chidon, a place so called, Uzzah was slain by the anger of God; for as the oxen shook the ark, he stretched out his hand, and would needs take hold of it.

entries.title: Uzza (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Ezra and Nehemiah name him twice, and he is a man from the exile and the return.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Uzza (Man living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 3 men called Uzza. This one is a man from the years before the monarchy, named once in 1 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Uzzen-sherah (Uzzen-sheerah)
entries.summary: The name means ears of Sherah. Sherah, a granddaughter of Ephraim, built this town and both Beth-horons too, which makes her one of the few women in the Old Testament credited with founding towns.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Uzzen-sherah, meaning ears of Sherah, was a town built by Sherah, a granddaughter of Ephraim named in the tribe's genealogy (1 Chron. 7:24). The same verse also credits her with building the upper and lower towns of Beth-horon, making her one of the few women in the Old Testament explicitly credited with founding settlements.

entries.title: Uzzi (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him twice, and he is a man from the wilderness years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Uzzi (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A man from the exile and the return, and 1 Chronicles is the only book that names him.

entries.title: Uzzi (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of 7 men called Uzzi. This one is a man from the exile and the return, named once in Nehemiah.

entries.title: Uzzi (Priest living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: There are several. This one sits in the high priestly line in 1 Chronicles 6, and Ezra 7:4 traces Ezra back through him.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Uzzi was a common Levitical and priestly name, borne by several figures in the high priestly genealogy and among the postexilic returnees.

entries.title: Uzzia (Warrior living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of David's mighty men, from Ashtaroth in Bashan, east of the Jordan.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of David's mighty men, identified as coming from Ashtaroth, a city east of the Jordan in Bashan, and listed among the elite warriors of 1 Chronicles 11:44.

entries.title: Uzziah (King living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: King of Judah at sixteen, he reigned fifty-two years and rebuilt the army and the economy. Then he went into the temple to burn incense himself, which no king was allowed to do. The priests confronted him and leprosy broke out on his forehead while he stood there.
entries.books: 2 Kings, 2 Chronicles, Isaiah, Hosea, Amos, Zechariah
entries.label: 6 books
entries.dictNote: Uzziah, also called Azariah, became king of Judah at sixteen and reigned fifty-two years, a long and mostly prosperous rule that rebuilt Judah's military and economy, until success made him proud enough to enter the temple and burn incense himself, a priestly duty no king was allowed to perform. Priests confronted him in the act, and leprosy broke out on his forehead immediately, forcing him to live in isolation for the rest of his life while his son ruled in his place. The prophet Isaiah dates the beginning of his own famous temple vision to the year King Uzziah died.

entries.title: Uzzielites (Aaron's uncle living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: The Levitical clan from Uzziel, one of the four Kohathite families. Under David some of them kept the temple treasuries.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Uzzielites were the Levitical clan descended from Uzziel, son of Kohath, one of four Kohathite families. Under David, men of this line served among the officials responsible for the temple's treasuries.

entries.title: Vajezatha (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of Haman's ten sons, killed when the Jews of Susa defended themselves on the day Haman had set for their destruction. Purim remembers it.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Vajezatha was one of Haman's ten sons killed by the Jews of Susa when they defended themselves on the day Haman had planned for their destruction, an event the festival of Purim commemorates (Esther 9:6-10).

entries.title: Vaniah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Another of Bani's descendants who had married a foreign wife and agreed to send her away.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of the descendants of Bani who had married a foreign wife during the exile and agreed to separate from her under Ezra's reforms after the return from Babylon (Ezra 10:36).

entries.title: Vashti (Woman living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Queen of Persia until she refused King Ahasuerus's order to come and be shown off to his banquet guests. He deposed her, and that opened the way for Esther.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Vashti was the Persian queen deposed by King Ahasuerus after she refused his order to display herself before his banquet guests, a refusal that opened the way for Esther to eventually become queen in her place.

entries.title: Vedan
entries.summary: Ezekiel lists it among Tyre's trading partners, next to Javan, bringing wrought iron, cassia and calamus. The Hebrew is hard here, and some read Vedan, a place in Arabia, rather than Dan.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A trading partner of Tyre named alongside Javan in Ezekiel's taunt song against the city, supplying wrought iron, cassia, and calamus in exchange for Tyrian goods (Ezek. 27:19). The Hebrew text is difficult at this point, and some scholars read the name as Vedan, an Arabian place, rather than the tribe or territory of Dan.

entries.title: Vophsi (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Father of Nahbi, who went into Canaan for Naphtali with the twelve spies.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Vophsi was the father of Nahbi, the representative of the tribe of Naphtali among the twelve spies Moses sent to scout Canaan (Numbers 13:14). Nothing else is known of him.

entries.title: Zaanan
entries.summary: Micah plays on the name, which sounds like going out, and says its people do not come out. It is generally identified with Zenan in Judah's lowlands.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A town addressed in Micah's oracle against the towns of Judah's lowlands (Micah 1:11), where the prophet puns on its name, related to a Hebrew word for "go out," by saying its people "come not forth." It is generally identified with Zenan, listed among the towns of Judah's lowland district in Joshua 15:37.

entries.title: Zaannannim (Zaanannim)
entries.summary: On Naphtali's border, near Kedesh, by the oak where Heber the Kenite had his tent. Sisera ran there after his army broke at the Kishon, and Heber's wife Jael killed him.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Boundary point of the tribe of Naphtali (Josh. 19:33), near the oak, or plain, where Heber the Kenite had pitched his tent close to Kedesh. It was to this camp that Sisera fled after his army's defeat at the Kishon, only to be killed there by Heber's wife Jael (Judges 4:11, 17-21).

entries.title: Zaavan (Edomite living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: An Edomite chief descended from Seir the Horite, also spelled Zavan.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Zaavan, also called Zavan, was one of the tribal chiefs (“dukes”) of Edom descended from Seir the Horite (Genesis 36:27; 1 Chronicles 1:42). Nothing further is recorded of him.

entries.title: Zabad (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)

entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Zabad was a common name in the Old Testament, borne by several individuals across the genealogies of Chronicles and among those confronted for foreign marriages under Ezra.

He is distinct from the like-named father of Baruch who helped repair Jerusalem's wall, whose record appears in this dataset under the related name Zaccai (Nehemiah 3:20).

entries.title: Zabdiel (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Overseer of the able men doing temple work in Jerusalem after the exile.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Zabdiel was the name of two men. One was the father of Jashobeam, a chief officer in David's army (1 Chronicles 27:2). The other oversaw 128 valiant men engaged in temple-related work in Jerusalem after the exile (Nehemiah 11:14).

entries.dictNote: Son of the prophet Nathan, who served Solomon as "the king's friend," a formal court title for a trusted personal adviser (1 Kings 4:5).

entries.title: Zabulon (Jacob's son living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: The Greek form of Zebulun. Matthew uses it for the country where Jesus started preaching after he left Nazareth for Capernaum, and Revelation counts it among the sealed tribes.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Zabulon is the Greek form of Zebulun, used in Matthew's quotation of Isaiah to describe the territory where Jesus began his Galilean ministry after leaving Nazareth for Capernaum (Matthew 4:13, 15). Revelation also lists Zabulon among the twelve tribes sealed from every tribe of Israel (Revelation 7:8). The underlying territory is the same tribal allotment of Zebulun described in the Old Testament.

entries.title: Zacchaeus (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: A rich chief tax collector at Jericho, too short to see over the crowd, so he climbed a sycamore tree. Jesus called him down and invited himself to his house. Zacchaeus promised half his money to the poor.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Zacchaeus was a wealthy chief tax collector in Jericho, a job that made him wealthy by overcharging his fellow Jews on behalf of Rome and made him widely hated for it, and he was too short to see Jesus over the crowd so he climbed a sycamore tree to get a look. Jesus spotted him and invited himself to Zacchaeus's house, scandalizing the crowd, and Zacchaeus responded by pledging to give half his wealth to the poor and repay four times what he had defrauded from anyone.

entries.title: Zadok (High Priest living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: The priest who stayed with David through Absalom's rebellion. He would have carried the ark out with the king, and David sent it back. Zadok anointed Solomon, and when Abiathar backed Adonijah and was sent away, Zadok was left as the only high priest.
entries.label: 5 books
entries.dictNote: Zadok was a priest who remained loyal to David throughout Absalom's rebellion, even offering to keep the Ark of the Covenant with the fleeing king before David sent it back to Jerusalem, trusting God rather than a sacred object to protect him. Zadok anointed Solomon king and became Israel's sole high priest after Solomon exiled the rival priest Abiathar for backing Adonijah's failed coup, and Zadok's descendants controlled the high priesthood for centuries afterward.

entries.title: Zair (Zoar)
entries.summary: Joram of Judah broke out through an Edomite army that had him surrounded here, when Edom revolted. It was east of the Dead Sea, exact spot unknown.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Zair, a site east of the Dead Sea where King Joram of Judah broke through an Edomite force that had surrounded him during Edom's revolt from Judah (2 Kings 8:21). Its exact location is unknown.

entries.title: Zalaph (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: His son Hanun rebuilt a stretch of the wall under Nehemiah.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Father of Hanun, one of the men who helped rebuild a section of Jerusalem's wall under Nehemiah after the exile (Nehemiah 3:30).

entries.title: Zalmon (Warrior living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Two things. A wooded hill near Shechem, where Abimelech's men cut brushwood to burn the tower of Shechem, and Psalm 68 has snow on it. And Zalmon the Ahohite, one of David's mighty men.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Zalmon names both a person and a place. The wooded hill of Zalmon, near Shechem, supplied the brushwood Abimelech's men used to burn down the tower of Shechem (Judges 9:48), and Psalm 68 pictures snow falling on this same dark, shaded mountain. Separately, Zalmon the Ahohite was one of David's mighty warriors, also called Ilai in the parallel list in Chronicles (2 Samuel 23:28; 1 Chronicles 11:29).

entries.title: Zalmonah
entries.summary: Israel camped here after Mount Hor. The name probably has to do with shade, and it is usually put somewhere in the Arabah south of the Dead Sea, though nobody has pinned it down.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Zalmonah was a stop in Israel's wilderness journey, coming after Mount Hor in the itinerary of Numbers 33 (Num. 33:41-42). Its name likely relates to shade or darkness, and it is generally placed somewhere in the Arabah south of the Dead Sea, on the route toward Edom, though it has not been securely located.

entries.title: Zalmunna (Man living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: He and Zebah were the Midianite kings who had killed Gideon's brothers. Gideon chased them down and caught them, told his young son to kill them, and when the boy was too frightened, did it himself.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Zalmunna was one of two Midianite kings Gideon pursued and captured after they had killed his brothers, and Gideon executed both kings personally once his young son, too frightened to do it himself, couldn't carry out the task.

witness.excerpt: However Gideon did not grudge his pains, but pursued them with all his army: and joining battel with them, cut off the whole enemies army, and took the other leaders, Zebah and Zalmunna, and made them captives.

entries.title: Zamzummim (People, perhaps from Repha)
entries.summary: They were a big people and a numerous one, holding the land east of the Jordan before the Ammonites. Moses says the Lord destroyed them so Ammon could settle there, the way he cleared land for Israel. Some think they are the Zuzim of Genesis 14.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: The Zamzummim were a people of great size and numbers whom the Lord destroyed before the Ammonites so that Ammon could settle their territory east of the Jordan, an episode Moses recalls as evidence that God had cleared land for other nations besides Israel (Deuteronomy 2:20-21). Some identify them with the Zuzim, a similarly obscure people defeated earlier by the coalition of eastern kings in Genesis 14.

entries.title: Zanoah
entries.summary: A town in Judah. Its people repaired one of Jerusalem's gates when Nehemiah rebuilt the walls.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Zanoah was a town in Judah, and its residents helped repair a section of Jerusalem's gates under Nehemiah's rebuilding project.

entries.title: Zaphnath-paaneah (Jacob's son living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: The Egyptian name Pharaoh gave Joseph when he made him governor over Egypt, and what it means is disputed.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Zaphnath-paaneah is not a separate person but the Egyptian title or name Pharaoh gave to Joseph when he made him governor over Egypt (Genesis 41:45). The name is genuinely Egyptian, though scholars disagree on its exact meaning, with proposals ranging from 'God speaks and he lives' to a title connected to Joseph's administrative role.

entries.title: Zaphon
entries.summary: The name means north, and it was a town of Gad in the Jordan Valley. Some scholars find it again in Judges 12:1, where the Ephraimites gather to confront Jephthah. Nobody has located it.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Zaphon, meaning "north," was a town assigned to the tribe of Gad in the Jordan Valley (Joshua 13:27). Some scholars connect the same Hebrew word in Judges 12:1, traditionally translated "northward," to this same town, understood there as the mustering point for the Ephraimites who confronted Jephthah. Its precise site remains unidentified.

entries.title: Zara (Judah's son living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Matthew's spelling of Zerah, Perez's twin, named and passed over because the line runs through Perez.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Zara is the form used in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:3) for Zerah, the twin brother of Perez born to Judah and Tamar (Genesis 38:27-30). Matthew lists him only to mark the line continuing through his brother Perez, since Zerah himself is not an ancestor of Jesus.

entries.title: Zarah (Judah's son living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)

entries.label: 5 books
entries.dictNote: Zerah was Judah's son by Tamar, born as a twin to Perez in a delivery marked by a scarlet thread tied to his hand when he seemed to be arriving first, only for Perez to be born ahead of him after all.

witness.excerpt: Judas had three sons - Sala, Phares, Zerah; and by Phares two grandchildren, Esrom and Amar.

entries.summary: Samson's hometown, better known as Zorah, on the border of Judah and Dan. The angel of the Lord told Manoah's wife there that she would have a son, and Samson was buried between Zorah and Eshtaol.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Zareah, better known as Zorah, was a town on the border of Judah and Dan and the hometown of Samson. It was there that the angel of the Lord announced his birth to Manoah's wife, and the Spirit of the Lord began to stir him between Zorah and Eshtaol. Danite spies set out from Zorah to scout territory for their tribe's migration north, and Samson was buried between Zorah and Eshtaol in his father's tomb.

entries.title: Zared (Zered)
entries.summary: The Zered valley, the brook Israel crossed near the end of the wandering on the way around Edom and Moab.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: The Zered was a valley and brook Israel crossed near the end of their wilderness wandering, marking a stage in their journey around Edom and Moab toward the promised land.

entries.title: Zarephath
entries.summary: Elijah stayed with a widow here during the famine, and her flour and oil did not run out. It sits on the coast road between Tyre and Sidon. Obadiah 1:20 uses it to say how far north the exiles will spread.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Zarephath, a Phoenician town on the coast road between Tyre and Sidon, is best known as the place where the prophet Elijah lodged with a widow during a three-year famine, multiplying her flour and oil and later restoring her son to life (1 Kings 17:8-24). Obadiah later cites it as a name marking how far north Israelite exiles will one day resettle (Obadiah 1:20). Excavations at the site, ancient Sarepta, directed by James Pritchard in the 1970s, uncovered more than twenty pottery kilns, olive-oil and purple-dye workshops, and an inscribed shrine that confirmed the site's identity, along with continuous occupation through the Iron Age. The New Testament refers to it by its Greek name, Sarepta, when Jesus cites the widow's story (Luke 4:26).

entries.title: Zareth-shahar (Zereth-shahar)
entries.summary: Splendor of the dawn. It was a town of Reuben on a hill above the plain by the Dead Sea, usually placed near the mouth of the Wadi Zarqa Ma'in.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Zareth-shahar, "splendor of the dawn," was a town in the territory allotted to Reuben east of the Jordan, situated on a hill overlooking the plain by the Dead Sea (Joshua 13:19). It is usually identified with ruins near the mouth of the Wadi Zarqa Ma'in, close to the ancient hot-spring resort of Callirhoe on the sea's eastern shore. Little survives at the site beyond scattered wall fragments and column pieces.

entries.title: Zarthan (Zarethan)
entries.summary: The Jordan's waters piled up near Zarthan when Israel crossed on dry ground. Centuries later Solomon's bronze for the temple was cast in the clay ground between Succoth and Zarthan. Exactly where in the plain it stood is uncertain.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Zarthan, also spelled Zaretan, was a place in the Jordan Valley near Succoth, in an area of dense clay soil suited for metalworking. The Jordan's waters are said to have piled up near Zarthan when Israel crossed on dry ground (Joshua 3:16), and centuries later Solomon's bronze temple furnishings were cast in molds in the clay ground between Succoth and Zarthan (1 Kings 7:46). Its exact site in the plain is uncertain, though it is sometimes linked to Tell es-Sa'idiyeh.

entries.title: Zattu (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: He was head of a big family that came back from exile, counted by household in both Ezra and Nehemiah.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Zattu was the head of a large family among the returning exiles, listed by household count in both Ezra and Nehemiah.

entries.title: Zattu (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Nehemiah names him once, and he is a man from the exile and the return.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zaza (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of Jonathan's sons in Jerahmeel's line, in Judah's genealogy, and nothing else.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A descendant of Judah in the genealogy of Jerahmeel, listed among the sons of Jonathan (1 Chronicles 2:33). Nothing else is recorded about him.

entries.title: Zebadiah (Levite living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A levite from the divided-kingdom years, and 1 Chronicles is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zebadiah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 9 men called Zebadiah. This one is a man from the divided-kingdom years, named once in 1 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zebadiah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zebadiah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: 2 Chronicles names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zebadiah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 9 men called Zebadiah. This one is a man from the divided-kingdom years, named once in 2 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zebadiah (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: One of several men named Zebadiah, this one in the family lists of 1 Chronicles 8.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zebadiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A man from the exile and the return. Ezra names him once.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zebadiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A common name among Levites, David's soldiers and officials after the exile; this one gets a single verse.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Zebadiah was a common Old Testament name, borne by several Levites, warriors in David's army, and postexilic officials.

entries.title: Zebadiah (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: A man from the united kingdom. 1 Chronicles names him once.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zebah (King living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: Gideon's other Midianite king, caught with Zalmunna. Both had killed his brothers, and he executed them himself.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Zebah was one of two Midianite kings Gideon pursued and captured after their initial defeat, executing them personally in revenge for killing his own brothers.

witness.excerpt: However Gideon did not grudge his pains, but pursued them with all his army: and joining battel with them, cut off the whole enemies army, and took the other leaders, Zebah and Zalmunna, and made them captives.

entries.title: Zebedee (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: He fished, and he was the father of James and John. He had hired men working with him, and when his sons left the boat to follow Jesus, he stayed.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Zebedee was a Galilean fisherman, the father of the apostles James and John, and prosperous enough to employ hired servants alongside his sons, based on the detail Mark includes when the brothers leave the family fishing business to follow Jesus.

entries.title: Zebina (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Of Nebo's descendants, he had married a foreign wife and agreed to send her away. That list is the only place he appears.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of the descendants of Nebo who had married foreign women during the exile and agreed to separate from them under Ezra's reforms (Ezra 10:43). He appears only in this list of names.

entries.title: Zeboiim
entries.summary: One of the five cities of the plain, with Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah and Bela, destroyed with Sodom. In Hosea 11:8 God says he cannot make Israel like Admah and Zeboiim.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Zeboiim was one of the five cities of the plain in the Jordan Valley, listed alongside Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Bela (Genesis 10:19; 14:2, 8). It was destroyed with Sodom and Gomorrah for its wickedness (Deuteronomy 29:23), and Hosea later cites its ruin, alongside Admah's, as a measure of the mercy God chose instead to show Israel (Hosea 11:8).

entries.title: Zeboim
entries.summary: Benjamites resettled this village after the exile, and it is not the Zeboim destroyed with Sodom and Gomorrah.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: This Zeboim was a town resettled by Benjamites after the Babylonian exile, listed among the villages reoccupied in Nehemiah's account (Neh. 11:34). It is a different place from the Zeboim destroyed alongside Sodom and Gomorrah in Genesis, and from the ravine of the same name near Gibeah where a Philistine raiding party once passed in Saul's day (1 Sam. 13:18).

And in this month the Lord executed his judgments on Sodom, and Gomorrah, and Zeboim,  and all the region of the Jordan, and He burned them with fire and brimstone, and destroyed them until this day, even as [lo] I have declared unto thee all their works, that they are wicked and sinners exceedingly, an

entries.title: Zebudah (Woman living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Josiah's wife and the mother of Jehoiakim, who took the throne after his brother Jehoahaz's short reign.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Wife of King Josiah of Judah and mother of his son Jehoiakim, who succeeded to the throne after the brief reign of his brother Jehoahaz (2 Kings 23:36).

witness.excerpt: Now Jehoiakim’s mother was called Zebudah , of the city Rumah.

entries.title: Zebul (Man living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: He ran Shechem for Abimelech. When Gaal stirred the city up, Zebul sent word to Abimelech, and he helped put the revolt down while the city around him turned.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Zebul was Abimelech's deputy governor over Shechem, and he warned Abimelech of Gaal's rebellion and helped defeat it, staying loyal even as the city around him turned against Abimelech's rule.

witness.excerpt: Now there was one Zebul, a magistrate of the Shechemites, that had entertained Abimelech.

entries.title: Zebulonite (Jacob's son living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Someone of the tribe of Zebulun. In Judges it is Elon, who judged Israel ten years and was buried at Aijalon in Zebulun's land.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Zebulonite designates a member of the tribe of Zebulun. In the wilderness census it names the tribe collectively, and in Judges it is applied specifically to Elon, one of the minor judges who led Israel for ten years and was buried in Aijalon within Zebulun's own territory.

entries.title: Zebulun (Jacob's son living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Jacob's tenth son and Leah's last. His tribe's land ran up to the Sea of Galilee, and Isaiah names it with Naphtali as the place where a light would dawn, which Matthew applies to Jesus in Galilee.
entries.books: Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Psalm, Isaiah, Ezekiel
entries.label: 11 books
entries.dictNote: Zebulun was Jacob's tenth son, Leah's sixth and last, and his tribe's territory bordered the Sea of Galilee, making it, alongside neighboring Naphtali, part of the region Isaiah names as the place a coming light would dawn, a prophecy Matthew applies to Jesus's Galilean ministry.

entries.title: Zechariah (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: John the Baptist's father, a priest, and Luke's Gospel opens with him. He is not the Zechariah Jesus mentions later, killed between the altar and the house of God.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Zechariah was an extremely common name in the Old Testament and New, and two of its most significant bearers are gathered here. The prophet Zechariah, active after the exile alongside Haggai, encouraged the rebuilding of the temple through a series of vivid symbolic visions and looked forward to a coming king who would enter Jerusalem humble and riding on a donkey, a prophecy the Gospels connect directly to Jesus's entry into Jerusalem. A different Zechariah, a priest married to Elizabeth, was struck mute after doubting the angel Gabriel's announcement that his elderly wife would bear a son, John the Baptist, and only regained his speech after confirming in writing that the child's name would be John as instructed.

witness.source: Josephus, The Wars of the Jews 4.5
witness.excerpt: So two of the boldest of them fell upon Zacharias in the middle of the temple, and slew him. And as he fell down dead, they bantered him, and said, ‘Thou hast also our verdict: and this will prove a more sure acquittal to thee than the other.’

entries.title: Zechariah (Priest living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Matthew and Luke name him twice, and he is a priest from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.lukeNote: Luke's Zechariah here (11:51, 'killed between the altar and the house of God') is almost certainly the priest murdered in 2 Chronicles 24:20-22, centuries before Jesus spoke, not the same person as John the Baptist's father, who shares the name earlier in this Gospel. Josephus, decades after the Gospel was written, records a startlingly similar killing: a different man, also named Zacharias, cut down 'in the middle of the temple' during the Jewish War of AD 66-70. Two different men, two different centuries, the same name and the same terrible detail, not the same event, but a real and well-known coincidence scholars still discuss.

entries.title: Zedad
entries.summary: They put it on the northern border of the land, near Hamath, both in Moses' description and again in Ezekiel's vision. Some identify it with the Syrian village of Sadad.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Town near Hamath marking Israel's ideal northern border, both in Moses' description of the promised land (Num. 34:8) and in Ezekiel's vision of a restored Israel's boundaries (Ezek. 47:15). Some identify it with the modern Syrian village of Sadad.

entries.title: Zedekiah (King living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: The last king of Judah. Nebuchadnezzar put him on the throne, and he rebelled anyway, against everything Jeremiah told him. Jerusalem was destroyed, he was caught running, his sons were killed in front of him, and then they blinded him.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Zedekiah was the last king of Judah, installed by Nebuchadnezzar after deporting his predecessor, and his reign ended in disaster when he rebelled against Babylon despite Jeremiah's repeated warnings not to. Nebuchadnezzar besieged and destroyed Jerusalem in response, captured Zedekiah trying to flee, executed his sons in front of him, and then blinded him, making the massacre of his sons the last thing he ever saw. A few minor figures elsewhere in the Old Testament, including a false prophet who opposed Jeremiah, also carried the name.

But he took captive the people that were in Mispah, with their wives, and children: among whom were the daughters of King Zedekiah, whom Nebuzar-adan the general of the army of Babylon had left with Gedaliah.

entries.title: Zedekiah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A different Zedekiah from the king. He is the man in 1 Kings 22 and 2 Chronicles 18 who stood with the court prophets, and struck the one prophet who disagreed.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Zedekiah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 6 men called Zedekiah. This one is a man from the divided-kingdom years, named twice in Jeremiah.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zedekiah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A man from the divided-kingdom years, and 1 Chronicles is the only book that names him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zedekiah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Jeremiah names him once, and he is a man from the divided-kingdom years.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zedekiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A man from the exile and the return. Nehemiah names him once.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zeeb (Man living before Israel's Monarchy)
entries.summary: They named a winepress after him, because that is where the men of Ephraim killed him. He was one of two Midianite commanders caught in Gideon's rout.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Zeeb was one of two Midianite commanders killed by the men of Ephraim during Gideon's rout of the Midianite army, and the winepress where he died was afterward named for him.

entries.title: Zeker (Man living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: A Benjamite in Jeiel's family, part of the line Saul came from. 1 Chronicles 9:37 spells him Zecher.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Zeker was a Benjamite listed among the descendants of Jeiel in 1 Chronicles 8:31, part of the genealogy tracing Saul's ancestry. The parallel list in 1 Chronicles 9:37 spells the same name Zecher.

entries.title: Zelah
entries.summary: A town of Benjamin, probably Saul's own. David had the bones of Saul and Jonathan brought back and buried there in the tomb of Kish.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Town in Benjamin (Josh. 18:28), likely Saul's own hometown, where he and his son Jonathan were finally buried in the family tomb of Kish after David had their bones brought back from Jabesh-gilead's earlier rescue at Beth-shan (2 Sam. 21:12-14).

entries.title: Zelek (Warrior Ammonite living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: An Ammonite, and one of David's thirty mighty warriors.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Zelek was an Ammonite who served among David's thirty mighty warriors, an unusual inclusion of a foreigner among David's elite fighting men (2 Samuel 23:37; 1 Chronicles 11:39).

entries.title: Zelophehad (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: He died in the wilderness with five daughters and no sons. They went to Moses and asked for their father's land, and they got it, and the law of inheritance changed because of them.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Zelophehad died in the wilderness leaving no sons, only five daughters, and their successful petition to Moses for the right to inherit their father's land in the absence of a male heir set a new legal precedent that adjusted Israel's inheritance laws.

witness.excerpt: At this time the chief men of the tribe of Manasseh came to Moses, and informed him, that there was an eminent man of their tribe dead, whose name was Zelophehad ; who left no male children, but left daughters: and asked him, whether these daughters might inherit his land or not? he made this answer, That if they shall marry into their own tribe, they shall carry their estate al

entries.title: Zelotes (Apostle living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: The Zealot, Luke's way of telling Simon the apostle from Simon Peter, and Matthew and Mark call him Simon the Canaanite, which means the same thing.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Zelotes, meaning the Zealot, is the epithet attached to the apostle Simon in Luke's lists of the twelve, distinguishing him from Simon Peter (Luke 6:15; Acts 1:13). It likely reflects either former ties to the Jewish Zealot movement, which sought armed resistance to Roman rule, or simply a zealous temperament; Matthew and Mark instead call him Simon the Canaanite, a Semitic term with the same meaning.

entries.title: Zelzah
entries.summary: It was a landmark in the sign Samuel gave Saul, a place near Rachel's tomb on the border of Benjamin.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A place on the border of Benjamin near Rachel's tomb, cited by Samuel as a landmark in the sign he gave Saul confirming his anointing as king (1 Sam. 10:2).

entries.title: Zemaraim
entries.summary: Two places. One is a town of Benjamin, generally put at a ruin north of Jericho. The other is a hill in Ephraim where Abijah of Judah beat Jeroboam's much bigger army.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Zemaraim names two distinct places in the older sources, and the entity's two canonical references reflect both. The first is a town of Benjamin listed in Joshua 18:22, generally located at a ruin north of Jericho. The second is a hill in the Ephraim highlands where King Abijah of Judah routed Jeroboam's much larger army of Israel, a defeat from which the northern king never fully recovered (2 Chronicles 13:4-20).

witness.excerpt: , he was not affrighted at it, but proved of a courageous temper of mind, superior both to his youth and to the hopes of his enemy; so he chose him an army out of the two tribes, and met Jeroboam at a place called Mount Zemaraim, and pitched his camp near the other, and prepared everything necessary for the fight.

entries.title: Zemarite (People, perhaps from Zemar)
entries.summary: A Canaanite people named for Zemar, a Phoenician coastal town under the Lebanon range. The Amarna letters call it Sumur.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Zemarites descended from Canaan and were named for Zemar, a Phoenician coastal town at the western foot of the Lebanon range. The city appears as Sumur in the fourteenth-century BC Amarna letters, where it served as an Egyptian administrative center in Syria, confirming its existence as a real Late Bronze Age settlement.

entries.title: Zemira (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Becher's son, a Benjamite, in a family known for its fighting men.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Benjamite, one of the sons of Becher, listed among the heads of families noted for their military strength in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 7:8. Nothing further is recorded about him.

entries.title: Zenan
entries.summary: A lowland town of Judah. Micah probably means the same place when he says Zaanan's people will not come out, and nobody has found the site.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Zenan was a town in the Shephelah, the lowland district of Judah's territory (Joshua 15:37). It is probably the same town Micah calls Zaanan in his taunting oracle against the towns of the Judean foothills, playing on the sound of the name to say its people will not "come out" (Micah 1:11). Its exact site is unidentified.

entries.title: Zenas (Man living at the time of the New Testament)
entries.summary: Zenas the lawyer. Paul asks Titus to see him and Apollos off well supplied. Whether he knew Jewish or Roman law is uncertain.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Zenas was a Christian identified as 'the lawyer,' whom Paul asks Titus to help outfit for a journey, along with Apollos (Titus 3:13). Whether 'lawyer' refers to expertise in Jewish law or Roman law is uncertain, and nothing more about him is recorded.

entries.title: Zephaniah (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A priest, not the prophet of the book. Jeremiah's verses show him carrying messages between the king and Jeremiah, and 2 Kings 25:18 counts him among those taken when Jerusalem fell.
entries.label: 3 books
entries.dictNote: Zephaniah prophesied during King Josiah's reign, warning of a coming day of the Lord that would bring judgment not just on Judah's idolatry but on the surrounding nations as well, before the book ends with an unexpected turn toward restoration and God rejoicing over his people with singing. His genealogy is traced back four generations in the opening verse, possibly to identify him as a great-great-grandson of King Hezekiah.

entries.title: Zephaniah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Zechariah names him twice, and he is a man from the exile and the return.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zephaniah (Prophet living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of 3 men called Zephaniah. This one is a prophet from the divided-kingdom years, named once in Zephaniah.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zephath
entries.summary: Judah and Simeon took this Canaanite town, destroyed it, and renamed it Hormah. It had beaten back an Israelite attack years earlier in the wilderness. After that the old name drops out.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Zephath was a Canaanite town that the tribes of Judah and Simeon captured and destroyed, renaming it Hormah, "devotion to destruction," after which the name Zephath drops from the biblical record (Judges 1:17). The same city had earlier repelled an unauthorized Israelite attack during the wilderness wandering (Numbers 14:45). Its site is usually placed near Tell es-Seba or Tell el-Meshash in the northern Negev, though the exact identification remains debated among archaeologists.

entries.title: Zephi (Edomite living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: Eliphaz's son and Esau's grandson, one of the clan chiefs of Edom. Nothing more is recorded.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Zephi, also spelled Zepho, was a son of Eliphaz and grandson of Esau, listed among the clan chiefs of Edom (Genesis 36:11; 1 Chronicles 1:36). Nothing beyond his place in this genealogy is recorded of him.

entries.title: Zephon (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Gad's son. His descendants were the Zephonites, and Genesis 46:16 spells him Ziphion.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A son of Gad and head of the clan of the Zephonites counted in the wilderness census (Numbers 26:15); the earlier list in Genesis 46:16 spells the name Ziphion.

entries.title: Zephonites (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Gad's clan through Zephon, counted in the Numbers 26 census.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Zephonites were the clan descended from Zephon, a son of Gad, counted in the Numbers 26 census.

entries.title: Zer
entries.summary: It was a walled town of Naphtali, probably near the southwest shore of the Sea of Galilee, exact site unknown.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A fortified town assigned to the tribe of Naphtali, named only once (Joshua 19:35). It was likely near the southwestern shore of the Sea of Galilee, though its exact site is unknown.

entries.title: Zerah (Man living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)
entries.summary: Genesis and Exodus name him twice, and he is a man from the wilderness years.
entries.label: 2 books

and Jachin, and Zohar, and Shaul, the son of the Zephathite  woman--seven.

entries.title: Zerahiah (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Ezra names him once, and he is a man from the exile and the return.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zerahiah (Priest living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A priest in the high priestly line, one of the links between Ezra and Aaron.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Zerahiah was a priest in the high priestly genealogy, an ancestor of Ezra listed in the line connecting him back to Aaron.

entries.title: Zereda
entries.summary: Jeroboam was born here, on the north side of Mount Ephraim. It may be the Zarethan where the bronze was cast for the temple.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Zereda was a town on the north side of Mount Ephraim, the birthplace of Jeroboam, who later led the ten tribes into revolt against Solomon's son (1 Kings 11:26). It is probably the same place, spelled Zarethan, associated with the clay ground where Solomon's bronze temple furnishings were cast (2 Chronicles 4:17), and has also been connected with the Zererath of Judges 7:22.

entries.title: Zereda (Zarethan)
entries.summary: Named once, in 2 Chronicles, and nowhere else.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zererath (Zarethan)
entries.summary: The Midianites ran toward it when Gideon routed them, down the Jordan valley toward Beth-shittah and Abel-meholah, and the site is unknown.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A place named in the account of Gideon's rout of the Midianites, along the line of their flight down the Jordan valley toward Beth-shittah and Abel-meholah (Judges 7:22). Its exact site is unknown, and some scholars connect it with Zeredah or Zarethan further down the valley.

entries.title: Zeresh (Woman living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: She was Haman's wife. She told him to build the gallows for Mordecai, and later, when things began to go wrong, told him he would fall before a Jew.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Zeresh was Haman's wife, and she encouraged him to build the gallows meant for Mordecai, only to warn him later, once his plans began collapsing, that his downfall before a Jew was now certain.

witness.excerpt: So he went home, and called for his wife Zeresh, and his friends; and when they were come, he shewed them what honour he enjoyed not only from the King, but from the Queen also.

entries.title: Zereth (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Ashhur's son by Helah. Ashhur founded Tekoa, and Zereth has brothers named Zohar and Ethnan, and that is all.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A son of Ashhur, the Calebite clan chief remembered as the founder of Tekoa, by his wife Helah (1 Chronicles 4:5-7). He appears only in this genealogical list, alongside his brothers Zohar and Ethnan; Tekoa later became the hometown of the prophet Amos.

entries.title: Zeri (Levite living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: One of Jeduthun's sons, set by David to prophesy with instruments. He is probably the Izri of 1 Chronicles 25:11.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: One of the sons of Jeduthun appointed by David to prophesy with musical instruments in the temple service, listed in 1 Chronicles 25:3; he is probably the same man called Izri a few verses later in the same chapter's roster of Levitical musicians (1 Chr. 25:11).

entries.title: Zeruah (Woman living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: Jeroboam's mother, named once in 1 Kings 11:26.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Mother of Jeroboam, who became the first king of the northern kingdom of Israel after the nation split following Solomon's death (1 Kings 11:26).

entries.title: Zerubbabel (Governor living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: He came from David's line and led the first exiles back from Babylon to Jerusalem. As governor he laid the temple's foundation and, with Haggai and Zechariah pushing, saw it finished.
entries.books: 1 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Haggai, Zechariah, Matthew
entries.label: 6 books
entries.dictNote: Zerubbabel was a descendant of David who led the first wave of Jewish exiles back from Babylon to Jerusalem and served as governor of the province, overseeing the rebuilding of the temple's foundation and, with the prophets Haggai and Zechariah's encouragement, its eventual completion. His place in David's line, preserved even in exile, keeps the promise of an eventual Davidic king alive in the postexilic books.

witness.excerpt: I have also sent my treasurer Mithridates, and Zorobabel, the governor of the Jews, that they may lay the foundations of the temple… I require also that the expences for these things be given out of my revenues.

entries.lukeNote: The post-exilic governor who rebuilt the temple, buried in the middle of Luke's genealogy (3:27) between the exile and the more familiar names. Josephus (spelling it 'Zorobabel') preserves the actual Persian decree funding the rebuilding out of the royal treasury, the bureaucratic paper trail behind the one line in Luke's list.

entries.title: Zerubbabel (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: Luke's genealogy has him at 3:27, between the exile and the more familiar names. He is the governor who rebuilt the temple.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.lukeNote: The post-exilic governor who rebuilt the temple, buried in the middle of Luke's genealogy (3:27) between the exile and the more familiar names. Josephus (spelling it 'Zorobabel') preserves the actual Persian decree funding the rebuilding out of the royal treasury, the bureaucratic paper trail behind the one line in Luke's list.

entries.title: Zeruiah (Woman living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: David's sister, the mother of Joab, Abishai and Asahel. David said the sons of Zeruiah were too much for him.
entries.label: 4 books
entries.dictNote: Zeruiah was David's sister, and her three sons, Joab, Abishai, and Asahel, became some of David's fiercest military commanders, close enough to the throne that David complained the sons of Zeruiah were too much for him to control.

witness.excerpt:
However, Joab, the son of Zeruiah, prevented the rest; and as soon as he was got up to the citadel, cried out to the king, and claimed the chief command.
2.
But Joab, whose father was Suri, and his mother Zeruiah, David's sister, who was general of David's army, met him, according to David's appointment.
He appointed Amasa to be captain of all his host, instead of Joab his kinsman: his father was Ithra and his mother Abigail: now she and Zeruiah, the mother of Joab, were David's sisters.

And when they told him that he was at Hachilah, he concealed his going away from his own companions, and came to Saul’s camp: having taken with him Abishai, his sister Zeruiah’s son; and Abimelech the Hittite.

entries.title: Zetham (Levite living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A Levite of Ladan's family, one of those David set over the temple treasuries.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Zetham was a Levite of the family of Ladan who served among those David put in charge of the temple treasuries (1 Chronicles 23:8; 26:22).

entries.title: Zethan (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A Benjamite in the tribe's genealogy at 1 Chronicles 7:10, and nothing more.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Zethan was a Benjamite named in the tribal genealogy of 1 Chronicles 7:10.

entries.title: Zethar (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of the seven eunuchs King Ahasuerus sent to bring Queen Vashti before his guests. She refused, and that set off everything that led to Esther.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Zethar was one of the seven eunuchs who attended King Ahasuerus and was sent to bring Queen Vashti before the king's guests, a summons she refused, setting off the events that led to Esther's rise (Esther 1:10-12).

entries.title: Zia (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: He headed a family of Gad, settled in Bashan.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A head of a family in the tribe of Gad, listed among those settled in Bashan (1 Chronicles 5:13).

entries.title: Ziba (David's compatriot living at the time of United Monarchy)
entries.summary: A servant of Saul's house. David put him in charge of Mephibosheth's land, and during Absalom's rebellion Ziba told David that Mephibosheth had turned against him. It was a lie, and it cost Mephibosheth half his property.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: Ziba was a servant of Saul's household whom David put in charge of Mephibosheth's restored land, and Ziba later falsely accused Mephibosheth of disloyalty during Absalom's rebellion, a lie that cost Mephibosheth half his property.

witness.excerpt: When David was gone a little farther, there met him Ziba, the servant of Mephibosheth, (whom he had sent to take care of the possessions which had been given him, as the son of Jonathan, the son of Saul,) with a couple of asses, loaden with provisions, and desired him to take
And when the youth had worshipped him on account of his words and gifts given to him, he called for Ziba, and told him that he had given the youth his father's house, and all Saul's estate.

And Shimei, the son of Gera, came with a thousand men, which he brought with him out of the tribe of Benjamin; and Ziba, the freed-man of Saul, with his sons, fifteen in number, and with his twenty servants.

entries.title: Zibeon (Edomite living at the time of the Patriarchs)
entries.summary: A Horite chief in the Edom lists of Genesis 36, and Esau's wife Oholibamah came from his line.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Zibeon was a Horite chief in Edom's genealogies, ancestor of Esau's wife Oholibamah's family line.

entries.title: Zibia (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: Shaharaim's descendant, a Benjamite, named once.
entries.label: 1 book
entries.dictNote: A Benjamite listed among the descendants of Shaharaim in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 8:9. Nothing further is recorded about him.

entries.title: Zibiah (Woman living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: She was from Beersheba, and she was the mother of King Joash of Judah, the boy hidden from Athaliah and crowned at seven.
entries.label: 2 books
entries.dictNote: Zibiah, from Beersheba, was the mother of King Joash of Judah, the boy king who was hidden from the murderous queen Athaliah and later crowned at age seven (2 Kings 12:1; 2 Chronicles 24:1).

entries.title: Zichri (Levite living at the time of Divided Monarchy)

entries.title: Zichri (Levite living at the time of Egypt and Wilderness)

entries.title: Zichri (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A man from the divided-kingdom years, and 1 Chronicles is the only book that names him.

entries.title: Zichri (Man living at the time of Divided Monarchy)
entries.summary: A man from the divided-kingdom years, and 2 Chronicles is the only book that names him.

entries.title: Zichri (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: One of 12 men called Zichri. This one is a man from the exile and the return, named once in Nehemiah.

entries.title: Zichri (Man living at the time of Exile and Return)
entries.summary: A man from the exile and the return, and Nehemiah is the only book that names him.
